on the anus and penis in the same way? This custom is completely contradictory. / Where washing is prescribed, they do not do it at all!
In ancient times, Soma abducted Tārā, the wife of Bṛhaspati; / Budha was born as a son from her, yet the teacher took her back again!
Indra himself seized Ahalyā, the wife of the sage Gautama; / see what kind of dharma this is!
This and other sinful practices are seen in the world. / Where dharma is of such a kind, what can be considered the highest truth?
Speak, O lord of the Dānavas, speak further, and I shall tell you!" / Hearing the teacher's words, which seemed full of highest truth,
their curiosity was aroused, feeling detached from the ocean of worldly existence. / The Dānavas said: / "Initiate us all, O teacher, who have taken refuge in devotion!
So that we may not fall into delusion again by your command. / We have become utterly detached from worldly existence, which bestows only grief and delusion.
Deliver us all, O teacher, from the well by pulling our hair! / To what deity should we go for refuge, O best of Brahmins?
Reveal to those who have surrendered the true deity, O wise one! / Through remembrance, fasting, meditation, and concentration,
and when worship and offerings are made, emancipation is indeed attained. / We have become detached from family; we will not strive here anymore!"
Thus addressed by those foremost sons of Danu, the disguised teacher / pondered that task: "How shall I do this?
How can these sinful beings be made dwellers of hell, / cast outside the Veda by derision, and made laughingstocks in the three worlds?"

Having spoken thus, O king, Dhiṣaṇa meditated upon Keśava;
knowing his thought, Janārdana [created] Māyāmoha.
and spoke these words to Bṛhaspati: / 'This Māyāmoha will delude all those Daityas
"Out of grace for you and pleased by your devotion, this yogin has come here— / naked (sky-clad), shaven-headed, carrying peacock feathers.

When this was said by the guru, Māyāmoha afterward spoke these words:
"O lords of the Daityas, established in asceticism, speak!"
Do you desire the fruit of your ascetic tapas for this world, or for the other world?" / The Dānavas said: / "Ascetic practice is indeed accepted by us for obtaining the merit of the other world."

This was undertaken by us; what else is meant to be said there?
The naked ascetic said:
‘Carry out my words, if you desire liberation.

All this is of the Arhat, an unobstructed gate to liberation.
This [path] is worthy of liberation through dharma; none other is higher than this.

Remaining right here, you will go to heaven and also to liberation.’
In this way, by many such [assertions] devoid of the true view of liberation,

those Daityas were expelled from the Vedic path by Māyāmoha:
‘This is for dharma; this is for adharma; this is real, and this is unreal;

this is indeed for liberation; this does not grant liberation;
this is exceedingly the supreme reality, and this is not the supreme reality;

this is a duty; this is indeed not a duty; no, it is clear that this is it;
this is the dharma of the sky-clad, and this is the dharma of those with many garments.’

Since those various specious arguments were proclaimed to them by Māyāmoha,
therefore all the Daityas were made to abandon their own duties, O king.

Since they were told by Māyāmoha, ‘Be worthy of my dharma,’
they resorted to that dharma, and on that account became followers of the Arhat (Ārhatas).

Having completely abandoned the path of the three Vedas, those asuras were made to conform to it
by Māyāmoha; and in that manner others were instructed by them.

By them still others, and others by those, and in like manner others by one another,
all standing firm in their assembly, declaring: ‘Salutations to the Arhat!’

In a few days, the three Vedas were largely abandoned by those Daityas.
And again, wearing red garments, Māyāmoha, having subdued his gaze,

went to other asuras and spoke to them in sweet words:
‘If you desire heaven, or even if [you desire] nirvāṇa,

then enough with these wicked dharmas such as the slaughter of animals! Understand:
know that all this without remainder consists of consciousness alone.

Understand my words properly, as it has been spoken here by the wise:
This world is without foundation, completely devoted to erroneous knowledge,

exceedingly tainted by passion and other [vices], and wanders in the distress of cyclic existence.’
He delivered various kinds of discourse directed toward their liberation.

In whatever way he spoke against the dharma, so they abandoned it:
some speaking abuse of the Vedas, others of the gods, O king,

others of the collection of sacrificial rituals, and likewise others of the twice-born:
‘This statement that violence leads to dharma does not stand to reason!

Can oblations burnt in fire yield fruits, O wise ones?
If the attainment of heaven is desired for an animal slain in sacrifice,

why then is the sacrificer’s own father not slain there?
If a man’s satisfaction arises from what is eaten by another,

then one might offer a śrāddha to a traveler, and travelers would carry no provisions.
Having attained godhood through many sacrifices, Indra enjoys himself;

if [the fire-wood] is wood such as Śamī, then a grass-eating beast is better!’
Realizing that this word was unworthy of faith by the people,

ignoring [the Vedas], let the speech uttered by me be pleasing for your welfare:
‘For authoritative statements do not fall down from the sky, O great asuras!

Words endowed with reason should be accepted by me and by others like you.’
The Dānavas said:
‘In the doctrine of truth, we have all taken refuge in you with devotion.

Bestow your favor today, if you are pleased [with us], O Lord;
we shall gather materials in every way, suitable for initiation,

by which, through your grace, liberation may quickly be in our hands.’
Then Māyāmoha said to all those asuras at that time:

‘He who has surrendered to my teaching—my guru of foremost intellect,
the best of beings, will give initiation to you at my command.

Initiate these [disciples], O brāhmaṇa, my children, at my word!’
When Moha had gone, those Dānavas spoke these words to the Bhārgava:

‘Give [us] initiation, O noble one, which releases from all cyclic existence.’
Saying ‘So be it,’ Uśanas said to the Daityas: ‘Let us go to the Narmadā.

Ho, abandon your clothes! I shall administer your initiation.’
Thus, O Bhīṣma, those Dānavas were made sky-clad asuras there
by the wise Āṅgirasa in the form of a Bhṛgu.
Giving them an emblem of peacock feathers and a lovely garland of guñjā beads,

he then performed the pulling out of the hair on their heads.
And the pulling out of hair is the supreme means of achieving dharma:

the god Dhanada, lord of wealth, from the pulling out of hair
and from constantly wearing this attire, attained supreme perfection.

‘Permanence is obtained in this very way,’ as the Arhat himself declared in the past.
‘Through the pulling out of hair, godhood is indeed attained by mortals here;

why should one not do it, therefore, since it grants great merit?
Indeed, it is the desire of the gods: “When, in the mortal world,

in this land of Bhārata, might our birth be in a family of lay disciples (śrāvakas)?
We would bind ourselves to austerity preceded by the pulling out of hair!”’

And the twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras, who were placed in front by them,
shaded by the king of serpents, showing the path of meditation—

praising him with recitation of mantras, heaven will be in the hands of the Arhats,
or liberation will surely come; what doubt is spoken of here?

‘When might we become ṛṣis, equal in splendor to the sun and fire,
free from passion, having recited the fivefold mantra in that way?

Likewise, for those of meritorious deeds who practice austerity and have reached death through the course of time,
the head is broken with a stone.

When indeed will our dwelling be in a desolate wilderness?
And the śrāvakas, focused in mind, will whisper into our ears:

“O ṛṣi, you must not depart, because you follow the path of liberation!
Whatever positions have been obtained, and those that yield a livelihood,

must be abandoned by you, and our word is indeed true!”
By our austerity and various observances,

go to the supreme abode and that path of liberation which the wise,
ascetics endowed with austerity, find through a devotional disposition.

Where there is restraint of the senses and compassion toward living beings at all times,
that is called the dharma of austerity; everything else is mere mockery.

Knowing this, you must attain and reach the supreme state
to which the Tīrthaṅkaras went, the destination to which the yogins have gone.’

Thus indeed formerly the deities, Vidyādharas, and great serpents
contemplated day and night those wishes and desires.

‘If your desire is directed toward detachment from cyclic existence,
then abandon your wives, who are bolts across the path to heaven.

How can you resort to the womb in which your father went?
How can living beings eat meat, which is like their own flesh?’

Then those terrifying Dānavas all spoke these words to their guru:
‘Initiate us, O noble one, who stand before you as your children!’

Having done so, the family priest said to them with the traditional vow:
‘Obeisance is never to be made by you to other gods.

Food is to be eaten at one place in the hollow of the hands;
water resting in that place must be free from hair and insects.

Pleasant and unpleasant must be treated as equal; [food] must never be impaired by the sight of another;
it must be eaten according to this conduct, O lord; act thus!

United together, you will thus share in liberation.’
Having spoken thus and imposed vows on those best of Danu’s sons,

Dhiṣaṇa, O king, went to the heavenly world of the gods;
he reported all that had been done and caused to be done to the Dānavas.

Then those Asuras went and dwelt along both banks of the Narmadā;
having seen those Dānavas there deprived of Prahlāda,
Then the king of the gods, delighted, spoke indeed to Namuci, / to Hiraṇyākṣa, who destroyed sacrifices, destroyed dharma, and reviled the Vedas,
to the rākṣasa of cruel deeds, to Praghasa, and to Vighasa, / to Muci, and likewise to Bāṇa, or even to Virocana,
to Mahiṣākṣa, Bāṣkala, Pracaṇḍa, and Caṇḍaka, / to Rocamāna, the terrifying Suṣeṇa, best of the Dānavas.
Seeing these and other chiefs of the Dānavas, he then spoke: / Indra said: / 'O lords of Dānavas, born in former times, you once ruled in heaven.
How now has this vow destructive of the Vedas / been undertaken by you, naked, with shaven heads and carrying water pots,
bearing peacock-feather banners? Why indeed do you remain here?' / The Dānavas said: / 'We have abandoned all the nature of asuras and stand in the dharma of the ṛṣis.
We perform acts causing an increase in dharma toward all creatures. / Enjoy the entire kingdom of the three worlds, Śakra, and go [your way].'
Saying 'So be it,' Maghavan went back to heaven. / Thus were they all deluded by the priest of the gods, O Bhīṣma.
The best of the Dānavas remained after reaching the Narmadā river. / When he learned [of it], they were all enlightened by Śukra about the incident.

Then they again set their cruel mind on seizing the three worlds.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, named 'The Deeds of the Avatāras,' in the first section, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.

title: caturdaśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Bhīṣma said: / 'How was Arjuna, the slayer of enemy heroes, born from three persons? / And how is Karṇa celebrated as maiden-born and as the son of a charioteer?
How did their boon arise from their very nature? Tell me that. / My curiosity is great; you ought to tell it to me.'
Pulastya said: / 'Formerly, when his head was severed, Brahmā, overcome by great anger, / wiped the sweat produced on his forehead and struck it on the ground.
From the sweat was born an ear-ringed warrior, with bow and great quiver, / equipped with a thousand armors, who said: "What shall I do?"
Viriñci said to him, pointing forcefully to Rudra: / "Let this evil-minded one be slain, so that he is not born again!"
Hearing Brahmā's words and raising his bow behind him, / he set out after the great lord, arrow in hand, with a terrifying gaze.
Seeing that exceedingly fierce man, the three-eyed god, frightened of him, / fled in haste and went to Viṣṇu's hermitage.
"Save me, save me, O Viṣṇu, slayer of enemies, from this man! / A wicked, terrifying [being] in the form of a mleccha has been created by Brahmā.
Act so that the angry one does not kill me, O lord of the world!" / Having bewildered that man with a roaring sound of "huṃ",
the lord invisible to all creatures, whose self is yoga, the all-seeing one, / Keśava comforted Virūpākṣa who had arrived there.
Then, having bowed down upon the ground, he was seen by the god Viṣṇu. / Viṣṇu said: / "You are my grandson, O Rudra. What desire of yours shall I fulfill?"
Seeing the god Nārāyaṇa, he said, "Give alms!" / showing in front of him a skull, blazing with fierce splendor.
Looking at Rudra with a skull in his hand, Viṣṇu thought: / "Who else could be a worthy beggar now for the giving of alms?"
Resolving, "This one is worthy," he offered his right arm. / The moon-crested god pierced it with a very sharp trident.
Then a stream of blood flowed from the arm of the lord, / resembling liquid gold, as if fashioned of a flame of fire.
Begged for by Śambhu, it fell into the skull, / straight, rapid, violent, touching the sky in its rush.
Fifty yojanas in length, ten yojanas in breadth, / it flowed from Hari's arm for a thousand divine years.
For that long time that lord took the alms as a beggar, / given by Nārāyaṇa in that excellent vessel, the skull.
Then Nārāyaṇa spoke these supreme words to Śambhu: / "Is the vessel full or not?" Then indeed the supreme lord,
Hara, whose eyes are the moon, sun, and fire, adorned by the crescent moon, / having heard Hari's words roaring like a rain-cloud,
directing his gaze into the skull with his three eyes at Janārdana, / stirring it with his finger, said: "The skull is filled."
Hearing that speech of Śiva, Viṣṇu withdrew the stream. / Then the lord with his own finger stirred the blood of Hari
for a thousand divine years with the cast of his glances. / Then, as the blood was churned, a dense mass, a bubble gradually formed,
and then arose a crowned figure with a bow, / a pair of quivers bound, with the shoulders of a bull, wearing finger-guards,
a man resembling fire, visible in the skull. / Seeing him, the venerable Viṣṇu spoke these words to Rudra:
"O Bhava, who is this man who has appeared in the skull, O Bhava?" / Hearing Hari's words, the lord said to him: "O Lord, listen!
This man is named Nara, the best among knowers of supreme weapons. / Because he was addressed by you as 'Nara', he shall therefore be Nara.
Nara and Nārāyaṇa, both will be renowned in the age, / in battle, in the duties of the gods, and in the protection of the worlds.
He will be born from all that is Nārāyaṇa, and therefore he will be Nara. / Furthermore, of great splendor, he will assist you in the slaying of asuras.
A sage in the examination of knowledge, he will be a conqueror in the world. / This divine, exceedingly brilliant fifth head of Brahmā,
derived from the glowing splendor of Brahmā, from the blood of your arm, / and from the fall of my gaze—the three splendors which exist,
born from their union, he will conquer the enemy in battle. / Those who will be invulnerable and others difficult to vanquish,
and those who are terrible to Śakra and the immortals, he will terrify them." / Having spoken thus, Śambhu stood, and Hari was amazed at that time.
Standing right there in the skull, placing his hands together in reverence at his head, / that noble-minded hero praised Hara and Keśava.
He said to the two, "What shall I do?" and having spoken, stood bowed down. / The glorious Hara said to him: "A man has been created by Brahmā
with his own splendor, bow in hand; you must slay him!" / Having spoken thus to the man who held his hands joined in reverence and praised him, Śaṅkara,
taking his two hands joined in that very manner, / lifting him out of the skull, spoke words again:
"This is that fierce man who was made known to you by me, / who has been plunged into a stupor-sleep wrought by Viṣṇu's roaring.
Awaken him quickly!" Having spoken thus, Hara vanished / before the eyes of Nārāyaṇa. Then, by this Nara,
struck by his left foot, that mighty one stood up. / Then a great battle took place between the sweat-born and the blood-born.
The whole surface of the earth was made to resound with the twang of bows strung. / One armor of the sweat-born was stripped off by the blood-born.
Thus, as the two joined in battle, two divine years / passed away as they fought, the sweat-born and the blood-born, O king.
Seeing the two-armed blood-born and the sweat-born in conflict, / Vāsudeva pondered and went to the supreme abode of Brahmā.

With agitation Madhusūdana spoke thus to Brahmā:
“O Brahmā, today this sweat-born one was struck down by the blood-born one.”

Hearing this, distressed Brahmā said to Madhusūdana:
“O Hari, in this present birth let this man of mine live, grant him life!”

Pleased by this, Viṣṇu spoke to him: “So it shall be.”
Having gone to the battlefield of the two, he stopped them and said to both of them:

“In another birth, at the junction between the Kali and Dvāpara [ages],
when a great battle arises between you, there I will unite you two.”

Then summoning the lord of planets and the lord of gods, Viṣṇu
said: “These two auspicious men are to be protected by my command.

O thousand-rayed one, this sweat-born one is your own portion on the surface of the earth;
he must be brought down at the end of the Dvāpara for the success of the gods' purpose.

In the lineage of the Yadus there will be a very powerful [king] named Śūra;
his daughter named Pṛthā will be matchless in beauty on earth.

That fortunate woman will be born for the accomplishment of the purpose of the gods;
Durvāsas will give her a boon consisting of a collection of mantras:

‘Whichever god you invoke with devotion through this mantra,
O lady, by his grace a son will be born to you.’

Seeing you at sunrise, desiring you, having menstruated,
and standing seized by anxious thought, she should be approached by you, O sun.

In her womb, this one will be born as an unmarried maiden's son, delighting Kuntī;
he will become a son, O god, to accomplish the work of the gods.”

Saying “So be it,” the sun, that mass of radiance, replied:
“I will father an unmarried maiden's son who will be proud of his might,

Whom everyone in the world will address by the name of Karṇa.
By my grace, O Viṣṇu, for brāhmaṇas whose minds are purified,

There will be no object at all in the world that cannot be given by him, O Keśava.
Such power shall I bestow upon him by your command.”

Having thus spoken to the god, the slayer of Dānavas,
to the great-souled Nārāyaṇa, the thousand-rayed sun vanished right there.

When the god who takes up water, the sun, had gone out of sight,
he also spoke thus with a pleased mind to Vṛddhaśravas [Indra]:

“O thousand-eyed one, this man born of blood, by my favor
having become your own portion, must be dispatched by you to the earth at the end of the Dvāpara.

When the fortunate Pāṇḍu takes Pṛthā as his wife,
and also Mādrī, O illustrious one, he will then go to the forest.

While he is dwelling in the forest, a deer will utter a curse upon him;
and having developed detachment because of that, he will go to Śataśṛṅga.

Desiring sons born of his wife's field, he will speak to his wife;
not wishing for this at that time, Kuntī will say to her husband:

‘O king, I do not at all desire the sons of a mortal;
O ruler of men, by the favor of the gods I desire sons.’

Then, O Śakra, when Kuntī asks you, this man must be given by you;
and by my command, O husband of Śacī, act accordingly.”

Then the lord of gods, distressed, spoke this word to Viṣṇu:
“In this past Manvantara, in the twenty-fourth yuga,

Having descended into the Raghu lineage, in the house of Daśaratha,
for the sake of slaying Rāvaṇa and for the peace of the celestials,

While wandering in the forest in the form of Rāma for the sake of Sītā,
my son was killed by you, O Lord, who wished to benefit the son of Sūrya,

Since the lord of monkeys named Vālin [was slain] by you for the sake of Sugrīva.
Tormented by this grief, I will not take this man as my son.”

To the lord of the gods who would not accept, offering another reason,
Hari spoke to Śunāsīra [Indra] regarding the removal of the earth's burden:

“I myself, O lord, will take an incarnation in the mortal realm
for the destruction of the son of Sūrya and for the victory of your son.

I will act as his charioteer, and I will bring about the destruction of the Kuru clan.”
Then Śakra became delighted by those words of Viṣṇu.

Pleased and accepting the man, [he said,] “May your word come true.”
Having thus granted a boon and dispatched him, the imperishable god himself,

Going forth, the lotus-eyed one said again to Brahmā:
“All this three-world, moving and unmoving, was created by you.

The two of us are your helpers in carrying out the work, O Lord.
Having created it yourself, O god, you do not understand how to cause destruction again.

A loathsome deed was done by you desiring to kill Śambhu,
and by your anger a man was created against the god of gods.

For the purification of this sin, perform the supreme expiation;
taking the three fires, O god, offer the Agnihotra.

At a holy place of pilgrimage, or in a [sacred] region, or in a forest, O Grandfather,
perform a sacrifice together with your wife, out of acceptance of our word.

All the gods, the Ādityas, and the Rudras as well, O lord of the world,
will carry out your order, because you are our master.

One fire is the Gārhapatya, the Dakṣiṇāgni is the second,
and the Āhavanīya is the third: arrange them in three altars.

In the circular one worship yourself; then worship me in the bow-shaped one;
and worship the god Hara in the four-cornered one, with the names of the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman.

Producing the fires through austerity and attaining supreme prosperity,
after offering oblations for a thousand divine years, you shall pacify the fires.

Nothing more purifying than the Agnihotra is proclaimed here;
by the properly performed Agnihotra, twice-born men on earth become fully purified.

These paths to the world of the gods have been shown by brāhmaṇas;
one fire should always be maintained by the twice-born householder.

Without the fire, householdership is not attained here by a twice-born man.”
Bhīṣma said:
“That archer named Nara who was born from the skull,

Was he born from Mādhava, or by his own past actions,
or was he produced by Rudra, or intentionally [by Brahmā]?

O brāhmaṇa, this Hiraṇyagarbha was born from the cosmic egg and has four faces;
how did that wondrous fifth face of his arise?

In sattva, rajas is not seen, nor is sattva ever seen in rajas;
how did the blessed Brahmā, established in sattva, experience such an excess [of passion],

Through which a foolish-minded man was sent by him to kill Hara?”
Pulastya said:
“Maheśvara and Hari, both of these two abide on the righteous path.

Nothing accomplished or unaccomplished is unknown to those two great-souled ones.
The fifth face of the great-souled Brahmā was pointing upward.

Then Brahmā became bewildered, swollen with rajas;
then, having created this by his splendor, he thought, ‘It was made by me.

There is indeed no god other than me by whom creation was set in motion,
together with the gods and Gandharvas, crowded with beasts, birds, and animals.’

Thus bewildered, Viriñci came to have five faces again.
The eastern face of his was the promoter of the Ṛgveda;

His second face was the promoter of the Yajurveda;
the third of the Sāmaveda, and the fourth was for the purpose of the Atharvan.

With the fifth face whose eyes looked upward, he recited the Vedas
along with their auxiliary limbs, secondary limbs, legendary histories, secret doctrines, and compendia.

All the gods and Asuras did not shine in the splendor of that face of wondrous radiance,
just as lamps do not shine at sunrise.

Even in their own cities, they lived agitated and mindless;
he regarded no one else, and cast down others with his brilliance.

All the gods, terrified, could neither approach, nor look upon,
nor come before the lotus-born supreme master.”
Deeming themselves as if overcome, their splendor destroyed, / they all took counsel for the benefit of themselves and the deities.
"Let us take refuge in Śambhu, deprived of energy by his energy." / The gods said: / "Salutations to you, Lord of all beings! O Maheśvara, salutations, salutations!
You are the womb of the universe, the supreme Brahman, the eternal one of all beings. / You are the foundation of all worlds, the cause, along with Viṣṇu."
Thus being praised by the divine seers, ancestors, and Dānavas, / the invisible one said this: "O gods, ask for what is desired."
The gods said: / "Granting direct vision, grant what is desired, O god! / Showing compassion to us, let a boon also be bestowed.
Whatever great virility, splendor, vigor, and prowess we had, / all that has been swallowed by Brahmā through the splendor of his fifth mouth.
All our splendors have perished; by your grace, O Lord, / act in such a way, O Maheśvara, that they arise again as before."
Then, with a serene countenance and bowed down to by the gods, / he went to where Brahmā was, whose intellect was bewildered by the egotism of rajas.
Praising the Lord of the gods and surrounding him, they entered. / Brahmā, veiled by rajas, did not recognize that Rudra who had arrived.
Delighting the universe with the splendor of tens of millions of suns, / the soul of the universe, the creator of the universe, the bringer of the universe into being was then seen.
Approaching the seated Grandfather and the entire assembly of gods, / Rudra then [spoke] to Brahmā, the highest lord:
"Aha! Your face shines exceedingly with splendor, O god!" / Having spoken thus, the moon-crested one unleashed a boisterous laugh.
With the tip of the nail of his left thumb, / he severed the fifth head of Brahmā, like a man cutting the core of a plantain tree with his fingernails.
And the severed head remained thereafter in Bhava's hand, / like a second moon standing in the midst of the planetary circle.
And Maheśvara danced with the skull held up in his hand, / like Mount Kailāsa with the sun resting on its summit.
When the head was severed, the delighted gods then / praised the Kapardin, the god of gods who has a bull on his banner, with various hymns.
The gods said: / "Salutations constantly to the bearer of the skull, the time-keeper of Mahākāla, / who is endowed with lordly knowledge, the bestower of all shares!
Salutations to him whose play is joy, who consists of all gods! / In the Kali age you are the maker of dissolution; indeed, you are remembered as Mahākāla.
You are the destroyer of the distress of devotees, and therefore you are called the end of sorrow. / You bring auspiciousness swiftly to devotees; therefore you are remembered as Śaṅkara.
Because Brahmā's head was severed, and you bear the skull, / therefore, O god, you are the skull-bearer. Praised now, be gracious to us!"
Thus praised, Śaṅkara, serene in mind, dismissed the gods / to their own abodes, and the Blessed One remained right there, filled with joy.
Having understood Brahmā's intent, and then the birth of the hero, / having removed the head at their word to pacify the anger of the worlds,
placing his hands in reverent gesture on his head and having bowed to him, / he then praised Prajāpati in this way, to know the supreme Brahman, the treasure of splendor,
with the secret teachings of etymological hymns spoken in the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman: / Rudra said: / "O immeasurable one, salutations to you, the Supreme Self of the supreme!
You are the source of marvels, the imperishable treasure of splendors, / you are the state of the universe through victory, the maker of creation, O one of great splendor!
Salutations to you whose face is turned upward, whose self is sattva, whose self is the earth! / Salutations to you who lie on the water, who are born from water, whose abode is the water!
O you whose eyes are like the petals of a blooming lotus, victory, O divine Grandfather! / For previously I, the Lord, was brought forth by you for the sake of creation.
Salutations to you whose food is always the sacrificial oblation, the lord of the limbs of the sacrifice! / O golden-wombed, lotus-wombed, god-wombed Prajāpati!
You are the sacrifice, you are the vaṣaṭ-call, you are the svadhā, O lotus-born one! / Yet by the word of the gods, O Lord, the head was severed by me.
I am overcome by the murder of a brahmin; protect me, O Lord of the universe!" / Thus addressed by the god of gods, Brahmā spoke words.
Brahmā said: / "The divine friend Nārāyaṇa will make you pure. / He, fortunate, worthy of praise by you, is to be worshiped by me, the all-pervading one himself.
Surely you have been meditated upon by that divine Viṣṇu, / through whom devotion arose in you and the inclination arose to praise me.
From the severing of the head, you are the skull-bearer, the founder of the Soma doctrine; / and you shall deliver hundreds of millions of brahmins, O one of great splendor!
One should perform the vow for the murder of a brahmin; there is nothing else. / Cruel sinners who kill brahmins, perpetrators of evil, are not to be spoken to.
Engaged in forbidden actions concerning the sacred fires, they are not to be spoken to in any way. / If seen by them, looking at the sun must be done.
If contact with a limb is made, O Rudra, one should enter the water with one's clothes on. / Thus one attains the purification seen of old by the wise.
You are that killer of a brahmin; undertake the vow for purification. / When the vow has been performed, you will once again attain many boons."
Having spoken thus, Brahmā departed; Rudra did not comprehend it. / Then he himself contemplated Viṣṇu through the course of meditation,
the companion of Lakṣmī, the giver of boons, the eternal god of gods. / Prostrating with all eight limbs, the three-eyed god of gods,
having bowed, praised the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace: / Rudra said: / "The immortal, ancient one beyond the high, Viṣṇu beyond the highest, of endless prowess,
I constantly remember the supreme, choice Puruṣa, the peerless, ancient Nārāyaṇa, / beyond the highest, firstborn, of fierce speed, the foremost among those of profound, deep intellect.
I am bowed to the god Hari, the ruler, the supreme abode beyond the highest, and the higher abode, / the ultimate abode, both transcendent and immanent, the vast Puruṣa, lord of the higher and lower.
I praise Nārāyaṇa of pure nature, who emitted this subtle [universe], both higher and lower; / because of his eternal presence, may the tranquil, primary Puruṣa be my refuge.
Nārāyaṇa free of taint, the ancient, Viṣṇu beyond the highest, the boundless shore, / the primeval, the foremost among the prudent, the lord of the earth intent on fortitude, forbearance, and peace;

I constantly praise the auspicious one of great majesty, with a thousand heads, manifold feet, / endless arms, with the moon and sun as eyes, the perishable and imperishable, who sleeps upon the ocean of milk.

I praise Nārāyaṇa, the supreme Lord beyond, higher than the high, who is unapproachable by the thirty [gods], / abiding in the threefold creation, having the three sacrificial fires as eyes, perceived through the three principles, the dissolution of the three, the three-eyed.
I bow to the immeasurable Nārāyaṇa, who is white in the Kṛta age and red in the Dvāpara, / and black in the Kali age; and I bow to him who emitted the brahmins right from his mouth,

and the kṣatriyas from his two arms, the vaiśyas from his pair of thighs, and likewise the śūdras from the tips of his feet. / I bow to him whose body is the universe, the ancient, beyond the highest, who has crossed over, the immeasurable,
whose form is subtle, whose form is great, whose form is knowledge, who is formless, / the armor of all gods; I bow to the lotus-eyed one,
the thousand-headed Lord of gods, thousand-eyed, of mighty arms, / who stands pervading the universe; I bow to the Supreme Lord,
the refuge, the divine refuge, Viṣṇu, victorious, eternal, / resembling a dark blue cloud; I bow to him who holds the Śārṅga bow in his hand.
Pure, all-pervading, eternal, having the form of space, everlasting, / free from being and non-being—I bow to Hari who pervades all.
And I see nothing here distinct from you, O Acyuta, / and I behold all this, moving and unmoving, made of you.
While that Rudra, the supreme lord, was thus speaking, / when he had uttered this, the eternal one himself, higher than the highest, appeared before his sight.
Discus in hand, seated on Garuḍa, illuminating the mountain like the sun, he arose; / 'Choose a boon,' the eternal one said, 'I have come as a giver of boons, the best for you.'
When this was said, Rudra, best among gods, spoke: 'Lord of the gods, may I attain supreme purity! / Indeed, no other remover of this sin is seen as foremost, except you.'
'Overcome by the murder of a brahmin, my body has turned black, / there is a smell of a corpse on my limbs, and my ornaments are of iron.'
'How may this form of mine not remain so, O Janārdana? / What shall I do, O great god, so that my former body may return?'
'By your grace it will come to be; tell me that, O Acyuta.' / Viṣṇu said: / 'The murder of a brahmin is supreme, terrible, and brings all suffering to the utmost.'
'Even in the mind one should not entertain the contemplation of this sin. / By you, through the god's command, this firm practice has been understood.'
'Now, O mighty-armed one, perform what was spoken by Brahmā: / rub ash over all your limbs three times a day upon your body.'
'Bear bones on your crest, on your ears, and in your hand; / as you do so, O Rudra, there will be no hardship at all.'
Having thus instructed him, that lord, accompanied by Lakṣmī, vanished from that place; / Rudra did not perceive him [go].
Skull in hand, the lord of gods wandered over this earth: / to the Himālaya along with Maināka and together with Meru;
to Kailāsa, to the entire Vindhya, and to the great Nīla mountain; / to Kāñcī, Kāśī, Tāmraliptā, Magadhā, and Āvilā;
to Vatsagulma and Gokarṇa, and likewise to the northern Kurus; / to Bhadrāśva, Ketumāla, and the region of Hiraṇyaka;
to Kāmarūpa, Prabhāsa, and Mount Mahendra; / overcome by the murder of a brahmin, wandering about, he found no refuge.
Filled with shame, constantly looking at the skull stuck in his hand, / shaking his hands repeatedly, distracted again and again,
when, as he shook his hands, the skull did not fall, / the thought then arose in him: 'I will undertake this observance.'
'Along my path the twice-born will go in every direction.' / Having reflected thus for a very long time, the god wandered over the earth.
Reaching Puṣkara, he entered an excellent forest, / filled with various trees and creepers, resounding with cries of diverse beasts,
perfumed by a gentle breeze bearing the fragrance of many tree-blossoms, / the ground adorned with flowers dropped as if intentionally,
rich with diverse fragrances and other savors, with ripe and unripe fruits; / delighted by the fragrance of blossoms, he entered among the groves of trees.
'To me who worship here with devotion, Brahmā will grant a boon; / through Brahmā's grace, the desired knowledge associated with Puṣkara will be attained,'
'which destroys sin, calms evil, and increases nourishment, fortune, and strength.' / As Rudra of immeasurable splendor was thus meditating,
Brahmā, the lotus-born, then arrived, pleased by his devotion; / and the teacher, raising up Rudra who had bowed down, spoke:
'Through the practice of divine observances I have been worshipped by you, / by you with exceeding faith, longing for the sight of me.'
'For humans as well as deities behold me when standing in observance; / according to your desire, I grant you a boon—the most excellent boon.'
'Since this observance has been performed for the fulfillment of all desires / with disposition of mind, speech, and body, and with a satisfied inner self,'
'tell me, what desire of yours shall I grant as you wish?' / Rudra said: / 'This very sight, O Blessed One, is today an ample, great boon,'

since you have been seen, O one worthy of worship by the world, O creator of the world, homage to you,
[achieved] through a great sacrifice to be accomplished and acquired over a long time.
'which expends life itself, you, O god, are seen. / This skull, O lord of gods, has not fallen from my hand, O all-pervading one.'
'Shameful among the ṛṣis is this course of conduct, vile, O all-pervading one; / by your grace, this observance of the skull-bearer has been performed.'
'Let this great vow accomplished for one who has surrendered be declared here: / in which holy region should I cast this away? Tell me!'
'So that I may become purified among the sages of cultivated soul.' / Brahmā said: / 'There is an ancient abode of the Lord, [named] Avimukta.'
'Kapālamocana will be your sacred ford there; / I and you reside there, and Viṣṇu too will be present.'
'Upon seeing you there, even those who have committed great sins / will enjoy pleasures and become purified in my abode.'
'The Varaṇā and the Asī are two rivers dear to the gods; / in the sacred precinct between them, the sin of murder never enters anywhere.'
'Foremost of holy fords is this ford, your foremost of sacred fields; / humans who attend this field until the fall of their body,'
'when dead, go to heaven on a swan-borne vehicle, free from all fear. / A sacred precinct measuring five krośas has been given by me to you.'
'When the Gaṅgā flows through the midst of the sacred field toward the ocean, / then that great, holy city will arise, O Rudra.'
'Holy is the northward-facing Gaṅgā, and eastward-flowing is the Sarasvatī; / for two yojanas the river Jāhnavī flows northward.'
'There indeed all the gods together with Indra, along with me, / having arrived, will take up residence; release the skull there!'
'Those who, having gone to that holy ford, will please the ancestors / with offerings of rice-balls and funeral rites, will have an imperishable world in heaven.'
'A man who has bathed in the great ford at Vārāṇasī is freed / from sin committed in seven births; merely by going there he is liberated.'
'That sacred ford is celebrated as the best of all sacred fords; / living beings who, bowed before you, abandon their vital breaths there,'
'having attained the state of Rudra, rejoice together with you. / Even there, whatever gift is given by a self-controlled person, O Rudra,'
'great will be the fruit of that person whose soul is cultivated. / Those men who perform the purification of body and limbs there,'
'having reached the world of Rudra, rejoice, ever happy. / Worship, muttering of mantras, and burnt-offerings performed there by embodied beings,'
'bring endless reward, [granting] heaven to one possessing devotion to Rudra; / and by the gift of a lamp there, a man will obtain the eye of knowledge.'
'Whoever brands and sets free a young, gentle, handsome bull, free from blemish, / goes to the highest state;'
'together with his ancestors he goes to liberation, there is no doubt of this. / What need is there of saying much? Whatever action is performed by men there'
'with an eye to dharma, that shall bear infinite fruit; / that holy ford is regarded on earth as the cause of heaven and final liberation.'
'It brings endless reward through bathing, recitation, and burnt-offerings; / having gone to the ford of Vārāṇasī, devoted to Rudra with faith,'
'those who have met their death there are devotees, of this there is no doubt; / the ancestors should be known as the Vasus, and the grandfathers as the Rudras.'
'Great-grandfathers are thus the Ādityas'—such is the Vedic revelation. / The threefold rule for the offering of the ball of food has been told by me, O sinless one."
The offering of rice-balls must always be made by mortals who come here, / and the offering of rice-balls should be performed in that very place by their sons with devotion.
Those good sons indeed bring happiness to the ancestors. / I have told you of this pilgrimage place, which grants liberation even by its mere sight.
Having bathed in the water there, one is freed from the bond of rebirth. / Freed from the slaying of a brahmin, O Rudra, stay at your ease
in Avimukta, which I have given [you], together with your wife.” / Rudra said: / “In all the pilgrimage places on earth, I together with Viṣṇu
will remain according to your word; this is the boon I have chosen. / I am the god Mahādeva, always to be worshiped by you.
And I will grant you a boon with a contented inner self; / and to Viṣṇu I will grant boons desired in his mind,
as well as to all the gods and sages of purified mind. / I am the giver, I am to be petitioned; no other is to be conceived in any way.”
Brahmā said: / “I will do so, O Rudra, as the auspicious word spoken by you [declares]; / and Nārāyaṇa will fulfill all your words, there is no doubt.”
Having dismissed Rudra in this manner, Brahmā then vanished. / Having gone to Vārāṇasī, Mahādeva established the pilgrimage place.

title: pañcadaśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Bhīṣma said: / “What did Brahmā do, O brahmin, having sent [him] to the city of Vārāṇasī? / What deed was done by Janārdana and by Śaṅkara, O sage?
How was the sacrifice performed by him, and in which pilgrimage place? Tell me! / Who were the members of the assembly and the officiating priests? Tell me all of them!
Which gods were propitiated by him? This is a great wonder to me.” / Pulastya said: / “On the peak of Mount Meru is a city, a receptacle of splendour, adorned with jewels,
the abode of many wonders, crowded with numerous trees, / brilliant with varied minerals, pure as clear crystal,
rich in the beauty of canopies of creepers, resounding with the cries of peacocks, / filled with herds of elephants terrified by the roaring of lions,
cooled by showers of spray rising from cascading waterfalls, / variegated with serene pools beside groves of trees tossed by the wind,
with its entire forest perfumed by the fine fragrance of musk, / where traveling Vidyādharas, weary from amorous sport, slept in bower-dwellings,
resounding with the sweet melody of troops of singing Kinnaras; / therein, having all its grounds beautified with manifold arrangements,
was the dwelling named Vairāja, belonging to Brahmā Parameṣṭhin. / There, [the hall] resounded with the sweet song sung aloud by divine maidens,
garlanded with strings of flower-clusters born of the Pārijāta tree, / multicolored from clusters of rays arising from jewels,
having tens of millions of erected pillars adorned with spotless mirrors, / made radiant by the charming play of the dance movements of Apsarases,
resounding with the combined sound produced by many musical instruments, / beautified by numerous vocal and instrumental melodies accompanied by tempo and rhythm,
the assembly hall named Kāntimatī, bestowing happiness upon the gods, / attended by gatherings of ṛṣis, visited by multitudes of sages,
resounding with the sound of the Sāman chants of twice-born priests and giving joy. / Seated in it, the lord of gods, the Grandfather, intent upon the twilight worship,
meditated on the Supreme God by whom this universe was fashioned. / As he was meditating, the thought arose: ‘How shall I perform a sacrifice?
In what place should the sacrifice be performed by me? Where on the surface of the earth? / Kāśī, Prayāga, Tuṅgā, Naimiṣa, and Śṛṅkhala,
Kāñcī, Bhadrā, Devikā, Kurukṣetra, and Sarasvatī, / Prabhāsa, and other pilgrimage places here on the earth—
whatever sacred fields and holy pilgrimage places exist all around, / as well as the others made on earth by Rudra at my command—
just as I stand as the primordial god among all the gods, / even so I shall make one supreme, primordial pilgrimage place.
The lotus born from the navel of Viṣṇu where I arose / is proclaimed as the Puṣkara pilgrimage place by sages who recite the Vedas.’
While Brahmā Prajāpati was reflecting thus, / this thought occurred to him: ‘I will go to the surface of the earth.’
Reaching that ancient site, he entered that excellent forest, / crowded with various trees and creepers, adorned with diverse flowers,
filled with the calls of various birds, thronged with herds of various animals, / scenting gods and asuras with the fragrance of its heavy load of tree-blossoms,
its ground decorated with flowers that seemed deliberately placed, / with ripe and unripe fruits of diverse smells and tastes born in the six seasons,
fruits rich in golden form, charming to smell and sight. / Where the wind, as if out of kindness, throws out whatever
withered leaves, grass, dry wood, and fallen fruits are produced. / Gathering the perfume of clusters of diverse flowers,
the cool breeze blew, perfuming the sky, the earth, and the directions. / It was adorned with trees of numerous names, bearing crests,
green, glossy, free of holes, grand in a forest untouched by insects, / free of disease, handsome, well-rounded, and radiant—
resembling an assembly of brahmins with their officiating priests on every side. / Covered with sprouts resembling minerals, the trees shone
like men of noble lineage covered with their own flawless virtues. / With their tips shaken by the wind, they seemed to touch one another,
and, with their crest-garlands of flowering branches, they seemed to kiss one another. / In some places, nāgakeśara trees with their flowers, vanīra trees, and filaments
shone like eyes with moving black pupils. / In some places, karṇikāra trees with tops full of blossoms,
growing in pairs, two by two, shone just like husband and wife. / With the mass of their beautiful blossoms, rows of sinduvāra trees
shone like embodied forest deities being worshipped. / Here and there, kunda creepers, bright with their ornaments of flowers,
shone raised up on trees in all directions like crescent moons. / In some forest tracts, sarja and arjuna trees in bloom shone
like men clad in garments of washed silk. / Likewise, trees blossomed over with atimuktaka creepers
stood embraced like beloved men by their own women. / With their leaves intertwined with one another, sāla and aśoka trees
seemed like friends reunited after a long time touching hand to hand. / Bowed down by the weight of fruits and flowers, panasa, sarala, and arjuna trees
seemed to worship one another with flowers and fruits. / With the branches of the sāla trees joined by the force of the wind,
the trees seemed to rise up in greeting toward the people who had arrived near them. / Arranged for great beauty with an enclosure of flowers,
having reached the spring festival, they rivaled men; / with their crests bowed by the heavy beauty of blossoms and shaken by the wind,
they seemed like joyful men dancing, their heads adorned with garlands. / The trees, endowed with rows of flowers and tossed by the wind at the top of their crests,
danced with their creepers like men together with their beloveds. / The trees in some places, covered with creepers bowed by their own flowers,
shone like the autumn sky with variegated hosts of stars. / Or rather, flowering mālatī creepers on the tops of the trees
shone like crests fashioned with deliberate artistry. / The green trees, with golden sheen, were laden with fruit and flowers.
just like men showing friendliness upon meeting virtuous folk. / Bees, tawny from flower filaments, went in all directions,
as if proclaiming the triumph of the kadamba blossoms; / somewhere, drunk on floral nectar, they darted to and fro.
Flocks of male cuckoos stayed with their beloved mates in the thickets of trees; / somewhere parrots, resembling śirīṣa flowers, were seen in pairs,
uttering varied cries like honoured brāhmaṇas [reciting chants]. / Peacocks with variegated plumes, accompanied by their female companions,
danced in the outskirts of the forest, shining like skilled performers. / Flocks of birds chirping and calling out with diverse notes
made the charming forest all the more delightful. / It was teeming with various herds of deer, its birds ever rejoiced.
That forest, equal to the Nandana grove, gladdened both heart and sight. / And the lotus-born Lord, beholding that foremost forest of such beauty,
gazed upon it with a benevolent glance like a mirror, as if purifying it. / Then all those rows of trees, seeing the god arrived in that manner,
offered their abundant blossoms in devotion to Brahmā and shed them before him. / Accepting the flowers from the trees, the Grandfather
said to the trees: "Choose a boon! May good fortune attend you!" / Addressed thus by the Lord, the unrestrained trees,
all joined their hands in reverence, bowed to Viriñci, / and said: "If you grant a boon, O God affectionate toward those who seek refuge,
"then, O Lord, remain ever present in this very forest. / This is our highest wish, O Grandfather; homage to you!
"If you dwell in this forest, O Lord of gods, source of all creation, / then for us who have sought refuge with our whole being, desiring the supreme boon,
"away with ten million other boons—let [only this] boon be granted! / Through your presence, this [place] will become the greatest and foremost of all sacred fords."
Brahmā said: / "This sacred place shall become the most excellent and auspicious of all. / You will always be endowed with flowers and fruits, possessing perpetually stable youth.
"You will go where you wish, assume forms at will, and bestow fruits according to wish; / pleasing to the sight of men, shining through the ascetic accomplishments of human beings,
"and endowed with supreme splendour shall you become by my grace." / Having granted the boon in this way, Brahmā showed favour to the trees.
Remaining there for a thousand years, he cast a lotus (puṣkara) down upon the earth. / Struck by it, the earth fell down and the netherworld trembled.
Helpless, the oceans abandoned their shores, their waves agitated; / and thousands of mountain peaks, struck as if by Indra's thunderbolt,
crumbled away, though they were inhabited by tigers and serpents. / The aerial chariots of gods and siddhas and the cities of gandharvas
shook, wandered astray, fell down, and sank into the surface of the earth. / Pigeon-coloured clouds, appearing like masses of envelopes, dropped from the sky;
covering the celestial bodies, they became fiercely blazing. / By the mighty sound of that [impact], the entire three worlds,
with all that moves and is still, became bewildered, turned mute, blind, and deaf. / The bodies and minds of all the gods and asuras
sank in despair, and they could not fathom: 'What is this? What is this?' / Then, summoning their courage, all of them looked about for Brahmā,
yet they did not see him. 'Where indeed has Brahmā gone? / For what reason has the earth trembled, and why do these portents and omens appear?'
Just then, Viṣṇu went to the place where the gods were gathered. / Bowing down, the denizens of heaven addressed these words [to him]:
"What is this, O Lord? Tell us about the manifestation of these portents and omens! / By which the three worlds have been shaken, overtaken by the law of time,
"and the end of the kalpa has arrived, the oceans having breached their bounds! / What is this that the four elephants of the quarters and the immovable mountains have moved?
"Why has the earth suddenly been covered by the waters of the seven oceans? / O Lord, the occurrence of such a sound cannot be without a cause!
"Such a sound as has been remembered has never been, nor will ever be! / A terrible and fierce upheaval has thrown the three worlds into confusion!
"Is this sound auspicious or inauspicious for the three worlds and the denizens of heaven? / O Lord, if you know what this is, please tell us!"
Addressed thus, Viṣṇu, filled with supreme power, said: / "Do not fear, all you Maruts! Hear the cause of this:
"Having understood it with certainty, I shall tell it to you just as it happened. / Indeed, the Lord Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, holding a lotus in his hand,
"stood ready to perform a sacrifice upon a place on earth that is a heap of merit, / on the slope of the mountains, in a most beautiful forest.
"The lotus fell from his hand onto the surface of the earth; / this great sound is from that [impact], by which all of you have been shaken.
"There he was greeted by the cluster of trees with the fragrance of their blossoms; / and having bestowed his grace upon that forest, along with its deer and birds,
"the Lord chose to take up residence there for the welfare of the world. / That sacred ford is named Puṣkara, and it is indeed a supreme holy field.
"It was brought forth by the Lord who works the welfare of the worlds. / Having gone there indeed, satisfy Brahmā along with me.
"When propitiated, the Lord will grant excellent boons." / Having spoken thus, the Lord Viṣṇu, accompanied by those gods and dānavas,
went to that region of the forest where the lotus-born [Brahmā] was seated. / Joyful, satisfied in mind, accompanied by the songs of cuckoos,
they entered Brahmā's auspicious forest, bright with heaps of flowers. / That forest, reached by all the gods and resembling the Nandana grove,
rich in lotus pools, deer, and blossoms, shone exceedingly bright at that time. / Having entered the forest adorned with all kinds of flowers,
the gods wandered about, longing to see him, thinking: 'The god is here!' / Searching everywhere, all those gods along with Indra,
swift-moving though they were, could not find the end of that wondrous forest. / While searching for the god, the deities then saw Vāyu.
He said to them: "You will not see Brahmā without ascetic austerity." / Then, weary from searching repeatedly on that mountain ridge,
to the south, to the north, and in between, / taking Vāyu's word to heart, Vāyu spoke to them again:
"The means of seeing this Viriñci is always three-fold; / it is declared to be through faith, through knowledge, through ascetic austerity, and through yoga.
"Yogins perceive the god as both with form and formless: / ascetic practitioners see him with form, whereas those possessing knowledge see the supreme formless [aspect].
"Even when knowledge has arisen, one of feeble faith does not see him. / Yogins behold Brahmā quickly through supreme devotion.
"He, the changeless Lord of primal matter and spirit, is to be seen. / Ever joined in action, thought, and word toward the Grandfather,
"practise ascetic austerity—may good fortune attend you!—intent upon the propitiation of Brahmā. / For twice-born devotees who have undertaken the Brāhmī initiation,
"he always knows: 'I must grant my vision.'" / Having heard the words of Vāyu and realising this to be beneficial,
their minds possessed by the desire for Brahmā, they said to Bṛhaspati: / "O wise one among the gods, confer the Brāhmī initiation upon us!"
Desiring to initiate the immortals quickly with the Brahmā-initiation, / that preceptor initiated them according to the procedure declared in the Vedas.
Modest in attire and bowing low, they assumed the state of disciples; / having obtained Brahmā's grace, the knowledge related to Puṣkara was imparted to them.
Bṛhaspati, the best of the Adhvaryu priests, performed the sacrifice according to rule, / having fashioned a lotus endowed with stalks through the ritual application of the lotus initiation.
The sage, prompted by the will of the gods, showed grace to those gods; / being attentive to what is taught in the Veda, he gave to those discerning ones,
having abandoned amazement, the great-minded Bṛhaspati gave initiation; / and the noble-minded one, having consecrated a single fire for the dwellers of heaven,
being pleased, the son of Aṅgiras imparted the recitations prescribed in the Veda: / the Trisuparṇa, the Trimadhu, and the purifying Pāvamānī hymns.
Indeed, the generous-minded one instructed [them] in all the recitations and rites. / The bath [performed with the hymn] 'āpo hi ṣṭhā' is recited as the brāhma bath;
it destroys sin, calms the wicked, increases nourishment, prosperity, and strength, / bestows success and fame, and removes the impurities of the Kali [age].
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the brāhma bath. / Observing silence, self-controlled, initiated, with senses subdued,
all equipped with water-pots, their upper garments loose, wearing rosaries, / bearing staves, dressed in bark garments, and looking magnificent with matted locks,
intent upon bathing, right conduct, and seated posture, practicing meditation with effort, / fixing their minds upon the Brahman and desiring regulated food,
they remained devoid of seeing, conversation, company, or stray thoughts. / Thus observing vows, all bathing at the three periods of the day,
endowed with supreme devotion and supreme ritual order, / in time, through prolonged meditation, their minds attained knowledge of the god.
When their minds had become completely purified, consumed by the fire of meditating on Brahman, / the Lord appeared within the range of everyone's vision.
Overwhelmed by his splendour, their minds became bewildered. / Then courage was summoned, and according to rule, [before] the beloved god,
with glad hearts and intent upon him through the six-limbed Veda, / with folded hands placed upon their heads, and bowing their heads to the earth,
they praised the Creator, the Sustainer, the Supreme Lord. / The gods said: / 'To Brahmā, whose body is the Veda, who is friendly to brāhmaṇas, and who is unconquered,
well-restrained, we bow to the giver of sacrifices and the Veda; / homage indeed to the one compassionate to the worlds, whose form is the creation of the gods!
To the one exceedingly compassionate to devotees, praised with Vedic chants, / whose essential nature is manifold, who bears hundreds of forms;
homage to the lord of Sāvitrī, the divine lord of Gāyatrī! / Homage to you, who sit upon a lotus, who are the lotus, and whose face is like a lotus!
To the granter of boons, worthy of boons, to the tortoise, and to the deer, / to the one adorned with a diadem of matted hair, bearing the sruva and sruc ladles;
homage to you, whose mark is the hare, who possess the nature of a deer, the eye of dharma! / Homage, homage to the All-named, to the All, to the Lord of the All!
O eye of dharma, you ought to grant us protection greater than this; / with thought, word, and bodily posture, we have sought refuge in you, O Grandfather!'
Thus praised by the gods, Brahmā, the best of the knowers of Brahman, said: / 'Indeed, when remembered, I shall grant [it]; my vision to you is never unfruitful.
Speak what you desire, my sons; I shall grant excellent boons.' / Thus addressed by the Blessed Lord, the gods spoke these words:
'O Blessed Lord, this very thing today is an ample and great boon: / this great sound was produced for us when the lotus was cast by you.
For what reason was the earth shaken and the worlds agitated? / This is not without purpose, O Lord; let the cause here be told.'
Brahmā said: / 'This lotus was cast by me indeed for your benefit / and for the protection of the gods; hear the reason for this:
This demon Vajranābha, who steals away the lives of children, / having taken support of the nethermost subterranean world, was stationed there.
Knowing of your coming, that evil-doer wished to kill the gods together with Indra, / who were engaged in austerities and had laid down their weapons.
A blow was dealt to him by me with the dropping of the lotus; / he was arrogant because of royal power, and therefore he was slain by me.
In this world, at this time, may the devoted brāhmaṇas who have crossed to the other shore of the Veda / never go to an evil state; rather, let them attain an auspicious state.
Toward the gods, the Dānavas, humans, serpents, and rākṣasas, / toward the entire host of living beings, I am impartial, O dwellers of heaven.
For your benefit, that wicked one was slain by me with a sacred formula; / he has reached the worlds of the meritorious through the sight of this lotus.
Because the lotus was released by me, on earth this Puṣkara / shall become celebrated as a holy bath, purifying and bestowing great merit.
It is proclaimed to be the giver of merit to all living beings on earth. / Favor has indeed been granted to devotees who desire devotion, O gods.
By abiding constantly in this forest and being requested by the trees, / when I arrived, O sinless ones, Mahākāla did not depart from this forest.
And to you who are practicing austerities, great knowledge has been shown; / hold it in your hearts, O gods, both for your own sake and for the sake of others.
It should be seen by you on earth, assuming various forms. / A man who hates a wise brāhmaṇa is tormented by sin itself;
he will not be freed from sin even after hundreds of millions of births. / One should not kill or revile a brāhmaṇa who has crossed to the other shore of the Vedāṅgas;
for when one is slain, ten million are slain. / If one feeds a single brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedānta with faith,
ten million brāhmaṇas have been fed by him; of this there is no doubt. / Whoever offers alms that fill the bowl of ascetics
is freed from all sins and does not meet an evil fate. / Just as I am the eldest, the best, the Grandfather of all the gods,
so the man of wisdom, free from egoism and possessions, is always worthy of worship. / For the release of the bond of saṃsāra, this vow guarded by Brahman
was established by me for brāhmaṇas, causing the cessation of rebirth. / If one who has not conquered his senses undertakes the Agnihotra and then abandons it,
he goes swiftly to Raurava, led by the servants of Yama. / One who engages in wrangling over mundane life and performs base actions,
whose mind is attached to passion, who is amorous, fond of women and wealth, / who eats alone, enjoys delicious food, and engages in agriculture and trade,
who knows not the Veda, reviles the Veda, and consorts with another's wife— / from merely conversing with one defiled by such faults,
a man goes to hell; and also one who violates virtuous vows. / One who is discontented, fickle-minded, foolish, and performs sinful acts—
one should not touch him with bodily contact; if touched, one becomes pure through bathing.' / Having spoken thus, that Blessed Lord Brahmā, along with those immortals,
established the sacred precinct. I shall tell you in detail: / north of the Candrā river, as far east as the Sarasvatī,
and east of the Nandana, all the way to Kalpa, including Puṣkara. / This altar was indeed prepared at the sacrifice by Brahmā, the maker of the worlds.
The first is known as Jyeṣṭha, a holy bath that purifies the three worlds, / celebrated as having Brahmā for its deity; the middle one belongs to Viṣṇu,
and the lowest belongs to Rudra; Brahmā caused the first to be made. / This first, supreme sacred precinct is recited as a secret in the Vedas.
In the forest named Puṣkara, the Lord Brahmā is present. / Favor was indeed granted on this part of the earth by Brahmā himself,
for the sake of favoring all brāhmaṇas who walk upon the earth. / A raised platform bordered with gold and diamonds was fashioned from the earth,
built with diverse jeweled pavements, splendid in every way. / There sports the Blessed Lord Brahmā, the Grandfather of the world.
Likewise, the two gods Viṣṇu and Rudra, the Vasus, the two Aśvins, / and the Maruts along with Mahendra, as well as the gods of heaven, sport there.
This truth has been declared to you, the cause of favouring the worlds, / according to the sequence of the Saṃhitā, along with mantras according to the rules.
Those brahmins who recite the Vedas, devoted to serving their guru, / dwell in the proximity of Brahmā; they are all brought to majesty by him.
Bhīṣma said: / O lord, by what rule should men, residents of the sacred place, / who desire the world of Brahmā, reside in the forest of Puṣkara?
Should it be by men, or women, or those possessed of caste and stage of life? / What must be performed by those who dwell there? Tell me all of this.
Pulastya said: / It should be resided in by men and women living in the [proper] castes and stages of life, / devoted to the conduct of their own duties, free from hypocrisy and delusion,
devoted to Brahmā in action, mind, and speech, with senses subdued, / free from malice, not petty, and delighting in the welfare of all beings.
Bhīṣma said: / Performing what action is a man said here to be devoted to Brahmā? / And what are the devotees of Brahmā among men considered to be like? Tell me.
Pulastya said: / Devotion is declared to be of three kinds, arising from mind, speech, and body; / and it may be worldly, Vedic, and likewise spiritual.
That which, by the intellect characterized by meditation and retention, is the recollection of the meaning of the Vedas, / pleasing to Brahmā—this is called mental devotion.
Through mantras, Vedic recitations, prostrations, contemplation on the sacred fire, ancestral rites, and so on, / and through prayers and obligatory duties, it is recognized as verbal devotion.
Through observances and fasts with restrained minds and senses curbed, / through ornaments rich in gold and jewels, and likewise through Cāndrāyaṇa penances and the like,
through the Brahmakṛcchra penance, fasts, and likewise through other auspicious observances, / bodily devotion is described. For the twice-born it is threefold.
With cow's ghee, milk, and curd, with jewel-lamps and kuśa-water, / with various perfumes and garlands, and with offerings of minerals;
with incenses of ghee and bdellium, and with the fragrant scents of black aloe, / with ornaments rich in gold and jewels, and with variegated garlands;
with dance, instrumental music, and song, with offerings of all kinds of jewels, / and with foods to be chewed, eaten, and drunk—the worship that is performed by men
dedicated to the Grandfather, that is regarded as worldly devotion. / The devotion that is [performed] through Vedic mantras and sacrificial offerings is regarded as Vedic.
The agnihotra is to be performed on the new-moon day or the full-moon day; / praiseworthy is the giving of priestly fees, the sacrificial cake, and the preparation of the caru oblation;
the sacrifice, steady dedication, the drinking of Soma, every kind of sacrificial rite, / the prayers of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and the study of the Saṃhitā—
[when] these are performed according to the rule, that is called Vedic devotion. / Fire, earth, wind, space, water, the moon, and the sun—
whatever rite is performed dedicated to these, all that has Brahmā as its deity. / But spiritual devotion to Brahmā is situated as two kinds, O king:
one named after Sāṅkhya, and the other born of yoga. Hear from me that division. / Twenty-four are the principles in number, beginning with Pradhāna.
They are insentient, objects of experience; the Puruṣa is the twenty-fifth. / The Puruṣa is sentient, the experiencer, not the agent of that action.
The Self is eternal and imperishable, the presiding overseer and instigator. / The unmanifest Puruṣa is eternal, and the Grandfather is the cause.
The creation of principles, the creation of dispositions, and the creation of elements in their true nature: / enumerating these by counting, as well as the Pradhāna composed of the guṇas;
similarity of nature, measure, sovereignty, and the Pradhāna possessing different properties; / causality, the nature of Brahman, and desirability—this is spoken of.
The capacity to be directed belonging to Pradhāna—this is spoken of as diversity of property. / Brahman is the agent in all things, while the Puruṣa is non-active.
Consciousness in Pradhāna—this is spoken of as similarity of nature. / And the distinction of principles among the principles, and action and cause;
the purpose, and the sovereignty that is not to be directed according to the enumeration of principles— / 'There is an enumeration,' so it is stated by the wise who determine and ponder the reality.

Having thus heard in truth the collection of principles and the enumeration of principles,
and what is higher than the principle of Brahman, the wise know the reality.
This devotion practiced by Sāṅkhya followers has been made spiritual by the virtuous. / Hear also about the devotion born of yoga directed toward the Grandfather by devotees:
constantly intent on breath-control, possessed of meditation, with restrained senses, / eating food obtained by begging, observing vows, or with all senses withdrawn,
he should practice concentration in the heart, meditating upon the lord of creatures, / seated on the pericarp of the heart-lotus, with a red face and beautiful eyes,
with his face shining all around, wearing a sacred thread across his waist, / four-faced, four-armed, with hands granting boons and fearlessness.
The mental perfection born of yoga is remembered as the highest devotion to Brahmā. / One who possesses such devotion toward the god is called a devotee of Brahmā.
And hear, O king of kings, the livelihood that is traditional for residents of the sacred place, / which was spoken in detail of old in the presence of all by the god himself
for the brahmins at the assembly of Viṣṇu and the other [gods]: / devoid of mineness, devoid of egoism, free from attachment, free from possessions,
without affection toward the circle of kinsmen, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal, / constantly granting fearlessness to living beings through diverse rites,
constantly intent on breath-control, devoted to supreme meditation, / sacrificers, ever pure, devoted to the duty of ascetics,
knowing the rules of Sāṅkhya and Yoga, knowing dharma, with doubts severed— / those brahmins residing in the sacred place who sacrifice according to this rule
in the forest of Puṣkara, hear the good fruit for them when they die: / they go to imperishable union with Brahmā, which is very difficult to attain,
having reached which they do not obtain rebirth that brings death; / abandoning return [to saṃsāra], established in the knowledge of Brahman.
There is rebirth for others dwelling in the worldly stages of life. / One who, relying on the rule of the householder, is always devoted to the six duties,
sacrifices properly according to rule with mantras, invited to the sacrifice, / attains a superior fruit, free from all suffering;
and in all the worlds his movement is unhindered. / Endowed with divine sovereignty, mounted on his own vehicle, with his family,
in an aerial chariot possessing great splendor, shining like the newly risen sun, / surrounded by thousands of women, possessing an abode that moves at will,
he wanders unrestrained through all worlds as he pleases; / most coveted among men, best in all virtues, wealthy.
Fallen from heaven, he would be born in an illustrious family, handsome, / knowing dharma, devoted to dharma, and master of the meaning of all sciences.
Likewise, through the celibate student's life, and through serving the guru, / engaged in Vedic study, living on alms, with senses subdued,
always engaged in the vow of truth, diligent in his own duties, / [he is conveyed] by an aerial chariot abundant in all desires, sustaining all desires,
unhindered, like a second sun. / The troops named Brahmā, secret and highly esteemed,
of immeasurable strength and sovereignty, worshipped by gods and Dānavas— / he attains equality with them, endowed with equal sovereignty;
among gods, Dānavas, and mortals, his weapons become unresisted / for thousands of ten million years, and hundreds of ten million years.
Endowed with such sovereignty, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. / Having dwelt [there] with such grandeur, when he falls again,
from the world of Viṣṇu he is born in the realms of heaven by his own action.
Reaching the forest of Puṣkara, established in the stage of studenthood, / by the study of the Vedas he dwells, or dies.
When dead, he departs in a celestial aerial chariot by his own splendor, / shining like the full moon, pleasing to behold like the moon.
Reaching the world of Rudra, he delights together with the Guhyakas; / he attains great sovereignty, lord of the whole universe.
Having enjoyed thousands of cosmic ages, he is glorified in the world of Rudra. / But falling again from that world of Rudra in due course,
ever rejoicing there, having enjoyed untainted pleasure, / he is born in the celestial house of twice-born men, in an exalted lineage.
Among men he becomes righteous, handsome, and an eloquent speaker, / possessing a body desired by women, a powerful lord of great enjoyment.
Observing the conduct of a forest hermit, avoiding cultivated produce, / his progress is unhindered throughout all the worlds.
Feeding on withered leaves and fruits, eating flowers, roots, and water, / [gathering grains] like a pigeon, pounding with a stone, or using his teeth as a mortar,
he should live by [such] means of livelihood, wearing garments of bark and rags, / with matted hair, bathing thrice daily, rid of faults, carrying a staff.
Or devoted to severe vows, even if a Śvapaca or another, / lying in water, practicing the five fires, exposed to clouds in the rains,
sleeping on the ground with insects, thorns, and stones, / devoted to standing postures and the hero-posture, sharing food, steadfast in vows,
eating wild forest plants, granting fearlessness to all beings, / ever devoted to acquiring dharma, having conquered anger and senses,
devoted to Brahmā, dwelling in the sacred site, the sage dwells in Puṣkara, / abandoning all attachment, delighting in himself, free from longing.
And he who dwells here, O Bhīṣma, hear what his destiny is: / with the brilliance of the morning sun, adorned with altars and pillars,
devoted to Brahmā, he travels in an aerial chariot that moves at will, / shining in the sky like a second moon.
Accompanied by troops of Gandharvas and Apsarases skilled in song, instruments, and dance, / united with Apsarases for hundreds of millions of years,
he goes unhindered to the world of whichever god he pleases; / by the grace of Brahmā alone, he shines in this place and that.
Falling from the world of Brahmā, he also goes to the world of Viṣṇu; / fallen from the world of Viṣṇu, he goes to the world of Rudra.
Falling even from that station, he is indeed born in the continents, / and likewise in other heavens, having enjoyed pleasures as desired.
Having enjoyed sovereignty among them, he is then born again among mortals: / he is born as a king or a prince, wealthy and happy,
handsome, fortunate, beloved, renowned, endowed with devotion— / whether Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras dwelling in the sacred site,
devoted to their own duties, O king, of good conduct, long-lived, / entirely devoted to Brahmā, conferring grace upon beings.
Those seekers of liberation who dwell in the great site of Puṣkara, / when dead, they go to the abode of Brahmā in magnificent aerial chariots,
resounding with flocks of Apsarases, moving at will, changing form at will. / Or if someone offers his own body into a blazing fire,
meditating on Brahmā, of great courage, he would go to the abode of Brahmā; / imperishable and eternal is the world of Brahmā for him, along with splendors.
Delightful, supreme above all worlds, it fulfills one's desired goals. / Those who give up their lives in the water at most holy Puṣkara,
for those great-souled ones too, O Bhīṣma, the world of Brahmā is imperishable; / they see directly the god who destroys all sorrow,
the god attended by all the immortals, accompanied by the hosts of Rudra and Viṣṇu. / Men—even Śūdras—who die through fasting in the forest at Puṣkara,
they depart from there in aerial chariots yoked with swans, brilliant as the sun, / rich in various gems and gold, sturdy, fragrant with perfumes,
with peerless qualities and others, echoing with the songs of Apsarases, / fitted with banners and flags, ringing with diverse bells,
endowed with many wonders, displaying sports and arts, / splendid, endowed with good qualities, drawn by excellent peacocks.
Wise men who have died through fasting delight in the world of Brahmā. / Having dwelt there for a long time, enjoying pleasures as desired,
having returned to the mortal realm, he is born rich in a Brāhmaṇa family, an enjoyer. / A person who performs self-immolation in dried cow dung in the forest at Puṣkara,
abandoning all worlds, he goes to the world of Brahmā; / he would dwell in the world of Brahmā as long as an eon's end should come.
He does not behold the mortal realm afflicted by its own actions; / his movement is unhindered across, upwards, and downwards.
Worthy of worship in all worlds, spreading renown, self-controlled, / knowledgeable in the rules of good conduct, charming to all the senses,
skilled in dance, instruments, and song, fortunate, pleasing to behold, / always with unfading flowers, adorned with celestial ornaments,
dark like the petal of a blue lotus, with blue curly hair— / flawless, slender-waisted women filled with all good fortune,
endowed with every sovereign quality, extremely proud of their youth, / women residing there attend to him and delight him in bed.
Awakened from sleep by the sounds of lutes and flutes, / he enjoys the pleasure of a great festival, difficult to obtain for the undisciplined,
by the grace of the god of gods, Brahmā, who brings about auspiciousness. / Bhīṣma said: / Conduct is the supreme virtue; those devoted to the virtues of the sacred site,
devoted to their own duties and proper conduct, having conquered anger and senses, / go to the world of Brahmā—this does not seem surprising to my mind.
And without doubt, twice-born men go to other worlds as well. / But without fasting at Puṣkara and without observance,
women, Mlecchas, Śūdras, birds, domestic animals, and wild beasts, / the dumb, dull, blind, and deaf, destitute of asceticism and observances—
tell their destiny, O Brāhmaṇa, who reside in Puṣkara. / Pulastya said: / Women, Mlecchas, Śūdras, domestic animals, birds, and wild beasts,
having died in Puṣkara, O Bhīṣma, they go to the world of Brahmā / with bodies of celestial form, in aerial chariots brilliant as the sun,
endowed with divine arrays, with excellent golden banners, / adorned with steps of gold and diamond and jeweled pillars,
filled with all enjoyable desires, moving at will, changing form at will; / thronged by thousands of women, they go to [a place] rich in various delights,
to the world of Brahmā, the great-souled ones, and to other worlds as desired. / And falling from the world of Brahmā, they go in due course to the continents;
in an exalted, expansive family, he becomes a wealthy twice-born man. / Those born in an animal womb—snakes, insects, and ants,
land-born, water-born, sweat-born, egg-born, plant-born, and womb-born— / whether dying with desire or without desire in the forest at Puṣkara,
mounted on aerial chariots brilliant as the sun, they go to the world of Brahmā. / In the terrible Kali age, creatures are impelled by sin;
by no other means in this [age] are dharma and heaven attained. / But those men who dwell in Puṣkara, devoted to worshiping Brahmā,
In the Kali age, they achieve their purpose; others suffer in vain. / The sin that a man commits at night with his five senses,
by action, mind, or speech, under the sway of desire and anger— / in the morning, having reached the water at Puṣkara,
and having approached the Grandfather, becoming pure, he is freed from that sin. / Beginning from the rising of the sun until its ascent is seen above,
