meditating in what is called the mental [lake] by the yoga of Brahmā, he removes sin. / Having seen Viriñci at midday, a man is freed from sin.
Whatever sin he commits with his senses from midday until sunset, / he is released merely by the sight of the Grandfather at twilight.
Even if he enjoys all sense-objects like sound and the rest through desire, / one who dwells in Puṣkara devoted to Brahmā, established in austerity,
dwelling in the middle of the Puṣkara forest, eating the taste of sweet food, / even if eating three times a day, is considered equal to one who lives on air.
The men of virtuous deeds who dwell in Puṣkara / attain great enjoyments by the power of this sacred site.
Just as there is no other body of water equal to the great ocean, / so indeed there is no holy place equal to Puṣkara.
There is no holy place superior in virtues to the Puṣkara forest. / Now I will tell you of others who are stationed in this sacred site:
All the celestials headed by Indra, along with Viṣṇu, / the elephant-faced one, Kumāra, Revanta, and the Sun;
Śivadūtī, likewise the goddess Kanyā, and always Kṣemaṅkarī. / Enough with austerities and observances for those who perform auspicious rituals and worship!
Having performed vows and fasts, even great ones, elsewhere, / he who remains inactive in the superior Puṣkara forest,
attains the fulfillment of all desires—a twice-born who always stays right here / goes to the supreme, imperishable place equal to the Grandfather.
In the Kṛta age in twelve years, in the Tretā age in one year, / in the Dvāpara age in a month, O Bhīṣma, and in the Kali age in a day and a night,
that fruit is attained in the world by the dwellers in this holy place. / Thus it was spoken of old to me by the god of gods, Brahmā:
‘There is no sacred site on this earth superior to this; / therefore, with every effort, one should take refuge in this forest.’
A householder, a student, a forest dweller, or a mendicant: / all who act according to what has been taught go to the supreme state.
He who properly performs the duty belonging to a single stage of life, / free from desire and hatred, is honored in the next world.
For a fourfold ladder to Brahmā is established here; / having relied on this ladder, one is honored in the world of Brahmā.
For a fourth part of his lifespan, a student, free from malice / and skilled in dharma and purpose, should reside with his teacher or his teacher's son.
Surpassing the teacher's service in work, one who desires to become [learned] should study; / he should be a giver of fees, and when summoned, he should approach the teacher.
He should be the last to lie down and the first to rise in the teacher's house. / Whatever service and other tasks are to be done by a pupil,
having done all that saying ‘it is done’, he should stand by his side— / a servant who carries out everything and is skilled in all duties.
Pure, diligent, endowed with good qualities, he should speak an agreeable answer; / with steady gaze and controlled senses, he should look at the teacher.
He should not eat when [the teacher] has not eaten, nor drink when he has not drunk; / he should not sit while [the teacher] is standing, nor lie down before he has slept.
With open palms he should gently touch his two feet; / with the right [hand] he should press the right [foot], and with the left the left.
Greeting the teacher respectfully, he should speak, pronouncing his own name thus: / ‘I will do this, O venerable one, and this too has been done by me.’

Having made all this known and having offered the wealth to the guru,
he should perform it; and all that has been done should be reported again to the guru.
Whatever fragrances or tastes a student does not enjoy, / he may enjoy them after returning [home]: such is the determination in matters of dharma.
Whatever observances have been described at length for a student, / a devoted pupil of the teacher should embrace them all.
Having rendered satisfaction to the teacher according to his power, / the pupil should conduct himself by duty only in the non-vulgar stages of life.
The twice-born, eating begged food and sleeping on the ground, / having properly studied from the teacher's mouth one Veda, two Vedas, or the Vedas and their meanings,
having completed the observances for the Vedas diligently during the fourth part [of life], / having given the teacher his fee, should return home according to rule.
Joined with a wife endowed with righteousness, having invoked the fires, he should worship them; / a householder should pass the second part of his lifespan.
Four modes of livelihood for a householder were established of old by the sages: / the first possesses grain in granaries, the second possesses grain in jars,
the third is said to have nothing for tomorrow, and the fourth gleans like a pigeon. / Among these, each subsequent one is superior in righteousness and most victorious over the worlds.
One indeed subsists by six duties, another proceeds by three, / and a fourth twice-born by two: he is established in Brahman.
They do not declare any greater holy place than the observance of a householder: / he should not cook food for himself alone, nor slaughter an animal in vain.
Whether an animal or any living being, it is entitled to sacrifice through consecration; / he should never sleep by day, nor in the first and last parts of the night.
He should not eat between [the fixed] times, nor speak falsehood here; / and no twice-born should live in his house eating without being honored.
So also his guests are to be honored, who are remembered as bearing the oblations to gods and ancestors: / those bathed after vows of Vedic knowledge, learned in the Veda, masters of the Veda,
living by their own duties, self-restrained, performing rituals, ascetic; / for them, oblation to gods and oblation to ancestors are prescribed for worship.
For one who has departed with perishable things, who has strayed from his own duty, / who has abandoned the Agnihotra fire, or who acts falsely toward his teacher,
or who is intent on falsehood, there is no right to these two rites. / Sharing with all living beings is prescribed here;
likewise, [food] should be given by the householder to those who do not cook for themselves. / He should constantly be an eater of leftovers, and constantly eat nectar.
Nectar is the remainder of the sacrifice, a meal equal to the sacrificial offering; / he who eats what remains after everyone has eaten is called an eater of leftovers.

Devoted to his own wife, self-restrained, exceedingly diligent, with subdued senses, / he should not engage in dispute with the group of officiating priest, family priest, teacher, maternal uncle, and guests;
with the old, children, the sick, physicians, kinsmen, relatives by marriage, and relatives; / with mother, father, son-in-law, brother, son, wife,
daughter, and the servants. / Avoiding disputes with these, he is freed from all sins.
By overcoming these [contentions], he conquers all worlds, there is no doubt. / The teacher is master of the world of Brahmā; the father is lord of the world of Prajāpati;
the guest is lord of all worlds; the officiating priest is a lord based in the Vedas; / the son-in-law in the world of the Apsarases; kinsmen in the world of the Viśvedevas;
relatives by marriage and relations in the directions; mother and maternal uncle on the earth; / the aged, children, and the sick are powerful in the atmosphere;

the family priest is lord of the world of the ṛṣis; dependents are guardians of the world of the Sādhyas; / the physician is lord of the world of the Aśvins; the brother is protector of the world of the Vasus;
the wife is mistress of the world of the Moon; the daughter in the abode of the Apsarases; / the eldest brother is equal to the father; the wife and son are one's own body.
Servants, the class of slaves, and a daughter are supremely helpless; / therefore, reviled by these, one should always endure it without feverish anger.
The wise householder devoted to domestic duty, steadfast in righteousness, having overcome fatigue, / should not undertake many tasks; being righteous, he should undertake only a little.
Three are the modes of livelihood for a householder, and among them each is higher in beatitude; / and similarly they proclaim the system of the four stages of life mutually supported.

text_mt:
And whatever observances are prescribed for them, all should be performed by one desiring prosperity: / by those with grain stored in jars, by gleaners of grain-ears and scattered seeds, and by those resorting to the mode of pigeons.

And the kingdom in which these dwellers abide flourishes; / and he purifies ten ancestors going backward and ten going forward.

Even while following this householder's mode of life, one who practices without distress / would attain a destination equal to the realms of the Discus-Bearer [Viṣṇu].

Or rather, this destination is ordained for those with conquered senses: / heaven is the realm, the established foundation for self-restrained householders.

For this order was established by Brahmā; when one is freed from it, / having attained the second in due order, he is glorified in heaven.

I shall speak also of the third; listen to the forest-dweller's stage of life. / When a householder sees wrinkles and gray hair on himself,

and sees offspring born of his offspring, then he should take refuge in the forest alone. / For those exhausted by the vows of a householder and dwelling in the forest-dweller's stage,

let it be heard, O Bhīṣma—may good befall you—for those who are a refuge to all people, / who have turned away [from worldly pursuits] following their consecration and reside in sacred places,

for men endowed with the power of wisdom, possessing truth, purity, and forbearance: / spending the third portion of life dwelling in the forest-dweller's stage,
he should tend those very fires, sacrificing to the celestials, / self-controlled, of regulated diet, devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu.

Then, gathering only what is needed for the fire-offering and all the ancillary elements of sacrifice— / uncultivated rice and barley, wild grains, and remnant forest food—

he should offer sacrificial food in summer, even during the five cold periods. / Even in the forest-dweller's stage, these four modes of livelihood are remembered:
some eat immediately what is gathered; some store for a month; / some keep stores for a year, and some store for twelve years,
making provision for honoring guests and for the ritual system of sacrifice. / In the rains, they remain exposed to the clouds; in winter, they stay in water;
in summer, they perform the penance of the five fires; in autumn, they feed on nectar-food; / they roll on the ground, or they stand on the tips of their toes;
they spend their time standing and sitting, even when their garments are worn out. / Some use their teeth as a mortar; others pound [grain] with stones;
some drink boiled gruel only during the bright fortnight; / some drink it during the dark fortnight, eating in accordance with traditional precepts;
some live on roots, some on fruits, and some, firm in vows, on water; / those holding to the Vaikhānasa vow conduct themselves according to rule.
These and other diverse consecrations belong to those wise men. / And the fourth, based on the Upaniṣads, is regarded as common to all.
The forest-dweller and the householder continually proceed, one after the other; / in that very age, dear one, by the brāhmaṇas who perceived all truths—
Agastya and the Seven Sages, Madhucchandas, Gaveṣaṇa, / Sāṅkṛti, Sadiva, Bhāṇḍir, Yavaprotha, and Atharvaṇa,
Ahovīrya, and likewise Kāmya, Sthāṇu, Medhātithi, Budha, / Manovāka, Śinīvāka, Śūnyapāla, and Kṛtavraṇa—
these, skilled in sacrificial actions, attained heaven from there. / These possessed direct knowledge of dharma, as did the hosts of wandering ascetics.
Among the sages of fierce penance who perceived the subtleties of dharma, / having worshipped the Lord of the Gods, the brāhmaṇas resorted to the forest.
Having cast off fleeting illusion, the brāhmaṇas resorted to the forest; / indifferent to asterisms, unassailable, groups of departed [sages] are seen.
Worn down by old age and afflicted by disease, / they entered the fourth, the remaining stage, from the forest-dweller's stage.
Quickly performing the Sadyaskra rite and giving all his wealth as sacrificial fee, / sacrificing to the Self, gentle-minded, delighting in the Self, relying on the Self,
depositing the sacred fires within the Self and abandoning all possessions, / he should promptly perform sacrifices and the primary offering here at all times.
For those who sacrifice perpetually, the sacrifice proceeds within the Self; / he should properly abandon the three fires within the Self, by means of the Self, in an instant.
Whatever he may obtain and by whatever means, he should eat that without reviling it; / devoted to the forest-dweller's stage, he should cast off his hair, body hair, and nails.
Purified by his rites, he goes at once from stage to stage. / When a twice-born renounces after granting safety to all living beings,
his realms are luminous, and after death he attains infinity. / Possessing virtuous conduct, with impurities removed, he does not desire to wander either here or in the world beyond.

Free from anger and delusion, beyond peace and conflict, he remains indifferent, contemplating the Self; / untroubled even when others depart in the control of death, free from [attachment to] his own treatises, without mental confusion in his heart,

an unobstructed movement belongs to the self-sacrificer, free of doubt, devoted to dharma, and of conquered senses. / Listen now to the supreme fourth stage, superior to this, endowed with excellent qualities, which surpasses the three stages,
proclaimed as the ultimate refuge. / Having received the consecration from those two stages, listen with a focused mind to what is to be done after that,
for the sake of the Supreme Self, in truth: / having donned the ochre robe across the three ordered stages,
he who proceeds to the supreme state of unexcelled renunciation— / hear how he is to conduct himself, having renounced with that meditation.
He should practice dharma alone, without companions, for the sake of spiritual attainment. / He who wanders alone, seeing [truth], does not abandon [virtue] and is not diminished.
Without sacred fires, without a fixed abode, he should visit a village only for alms; / providing nothing for the morrow, the sage should be endowed with contemplative intent.
Eating lightly, of measured diet, he should partake of food only once; / an alms-bowl, the roots of trees, ragged garments, solitude,
and equanimity toward all living beings: this much is the mark of a mendicant. / In whom spoken words enter like dead bodies fallen into a well,
and do not return to the speaker, he may dwell in the stage of absolute isolation. / He should neither see nor hear what should never be spoken by anyone;
especially concerning brāhmaṇas, this should never occur in any way; / he should constantly speak only that which is favorable to a brāhmaṇa.
He should remain silent when censured, administering medicine to himself. / The one by whom space always seems full, though he is alone,
and by whom the empty seems crowded—him the gods know as a brāhmaṇa.
Clothed in anything whatever, fed on anything whatever, / and lying down anywhere whatever—him the gods know as a brāhmaṇa.
Afraid of people as of a serpent, of honors as of hell, / and of women as of a corpse—him the gods know as a brāhmaṇa.
He neither rejoices when honored nor grieves when dishonored; / bestowing freedom from fear upon all creatures—him the gods know as a brāhmaṇa.
He should not welcome death, nor should he welcome life; / he should merely await the appointed time, just as a hired laborer awaits his order.
His mind unassailed, self-subdued, his intellect unbroken, / a man freed from all sins would then go to heaven.
Granting safety to all beings, and having safety from all beings: / for him, released from the body, there is no fear from any quarter.

Just as all footprints of other foot-travelers
are subsumed into the elephant's footprint, so all cognitions are subsumed into the mind.

In this way, all dharma and purpose are elevated in non-violence;
he who resorts to violence is ever as good as dead.

Therefore, the non-violent man, rightly resolute, with senses restrained,
a refuge for all living beings, attains the supreme path.

Thus, for the wise man satisfied with knowledge, devoid of fear,
death has no greater hold, and he goes to immortality.

Freed from all attachments, standing like the sky, a sage
who acts pleasingly to Viṣṇu and is tranquil—the gods know him as a brāhmaṇa.

He whose life is for dharma, whose dharma is only for delight [in truth],
and whose days and nights are for merit—the gods know him as a brāhmaṇa.

Him who has abandoned undertakings, who neither offers nor seeks praise,
undecaying, his actions exhausted—the gods know him as a brāhmaṇa.

All beings delight in pleasure; all suffer manifold sorrows;
he who has become weary of their cycle of birth should perform rites with faith.

The gift of fearlessness given as a sacrificial fee to beings surmounts all gifts in this world;
he who first offers his keen body attains infinite fearlessness from all creatures.

With an open mouth he offers the oblation, and attains infinite stability all around;
from contact with his body, the All-consuming Fire went forth and pervaded all this.

Into the span of a hand, into the heart that has flowed inward, the sacrificer of the self offers with the breath;
what is offered in his Agnihotra, stationed in the Self, is offered in all worlds along with their deities.

Those who know the divine Creator, threefold and golden, as the supreme reality,
honored among all beings, capable gods, they go to immortality.

The Vedas, the object to be known, the entire ritual precept, the Nirukta, and the supreme reality—
all these he who knows in the Self of the body, all rites continually attend upon him.

He who knows that immeasurable, golden [sun] unattached to the earth and residing in heaven, at the end of its orb,
moving clockwise to the south in the atmosphere, its rays shining brightly, as located also in the Self—
He whose mouth protects this universe, that wheel of Time is placed in the secret cave [of the heart].

Because through its grace he attains the cosmic body and all worlds in this life,
by pleasing the gods in that [Self], he becomes truly liberated forever here.

Consisting of light, eternal, ancient, he lives in the world; approaching it with fear of worldly gain,
he from whom creatures feel no fear, and who never shrinks from creatures,

Blameless, reviling no others, that vipra alone sees the supreme in his own Self;
having removed delusion and cleansed impurities, he desires worldly gain neither here nor hereafter.

Free from wrath and delusion, looking equally upon a clod of earth and gold, with grief destroyed, transcending conflict and alliance,
free from censure and praise, indifferent to pleasant and unpleasant, wandering like a detached mendicant.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, named “The Glorification of Residence in the Sacred Field,” in the first book, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.

title: ṣoḍaśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
Bhīṣma said:
This supreme glorification of the pilgrimage site that has been told, O brāhmaṇa,
the pilgrimage site arose on the surface of the earth by the falling of the lotus.

Stationed there, by the Blessed Viṣṇu and by Śaṅkara,
whatever was done, O tiger among sages, declare all of that.

How was the sacrifice indeed performed there by the all-pervading god?
Who were the participants and priests, and which brāhmaṇas assembled?

What were the shares of that sacrifice? What was the offering material? What was the sacrificial fee?
What altar, and of what measure, was constructed there by Virañci?

He who is worthy of sacrifice for all the gods, who is everywhere recited by the Vedas—
meditating on what desire did the Creator perform the sacrifice?

For just as that lord of the gods is undecaying and immortal,
even so the heaven of that god is seen to be imperishable.

And heaven was granted to the other gods by that great-souled one;
the Vedas and medicinal plants were created for the purpose of the Agnihotra.

And whatever other beasts are on earth, all were created by this Blessed Lord
for the sake of the sacrifice—this is the Vedic revelation.

Therefore my curiosity is aroused having heard these words of yours;
taking which single desire as the aim, what fruit, and what conception,

was this sacrifice performed by him? You should explain everything.
And that woman named Śatarūpā is called Sāvitrī here.

She is proclaimed to be the wife of Brahmā, and the mother of the ṛṣis;
she gave birth to the seven sages beginning with Pulastya, and the lords of creatures beginning with Dakṣa,

and Sāvitrī gave birth to the Manus beginning with Svāyambhuva.
How did Brahmā, dear to the brāhmaṇa, having abandoned that lawful wife who bore sons,

chaste, highly fortunate, observing good vows, pleasantly smiling,
and faithful, obtain another wife?

What was her name? What was her conduct? Whose daughter was she, O lord?
Where was she seen by the god, and by whom was she shown to him?

What was her form, that goddess captivating the mind when seen,
beholding whom that lord of gods fell under the power of desire?

Surpassing even Sāvitrī in complexion and in beauty, O sage,
she who captivated the god, the all-pervading lord of all worlds.

How the god took that woman, the beauty of the world,
and how that sacrifice proceeded—tell all of that.

Seeing her at Brahmā's side, what did Sāvitrī do?
And what conduct did Brahmā then adopt toward Sāvitrī?

In their presence, what words were spoken to Brahmā by Sāvitrī
and what did she say again? You should tell all.

What was done there by all of you—anger or forgiveness?
Whatever was done there, whatever was seen, whatever has been asked by me here,

I desire to hear all the deeds of the Supreme Lord in detail and in full,
especially the supreme sacrificial ordinance of the Creator,

the order of rites, the beginning, and the hotṛ duties,
as well as the hotṛ's portion—to whom was the first portion granted?

And how did the Blessed Viṣṇu assist, by what means, and of what kind,
or what was done by the immortals? You ought to tell that, sir.

Having left the world of the gods, how did he arrive in the mortal world?
And how according to rule was the Gārhapatya, the Anvāhāryapacana on the south,

the Āhavanīya fire, the altar, and likewise the dipping ladle,
the sprinkling vessel, the offering ladle, and the concluding ablution bath arranged?

And how did he establish the three fires carrying sacrificial portions,
and make the gods eaters of oblations and the ancestors eaters of funeral cakes,

for the sake of their portions according to sacrificial ordinance, which sacrifices belong to the sacrificial rite,
the sacrificial posts, kindling wood, kuśa grass, soma, the strainer, and the enclosing sticks,

and sacrificial implements, as Brahmā made them?
He shone forth in ancient times through his actions as the Supreme Lord.

Moments, winks, kāṣṭhās, kalās, and the three divisions of time,
muhūrtas, lunar days, months, days, and years,

the seasons and the divisions of time, and the threefold measure of old,
lifespan, fields, decay, characteristic marks, and beauty of form;

the three social classes, the three worlds, the triple knowledge, the three fires,
the three divisions of time, the three rites, the three classes, the three qualities—
The higher worlds were created by the Creator, and whatever other [worlds are created] by one of small intelligence, / as well as the destination of the righteous and the destination of evil-doers;
the origin of the four castes, the protector of the four castes, / the knower of the four Vedas, the refuge of the four stages of life;
he who is heard of as the supreme light, who is heard of as supreme austerity, / who proclaimed the highest beyond the beyond, the supreme one who possesses the Supreme Self;
who is the dam among the dams of the worlds, the pure among pure actions, / the knowable among knowers of the Veda, the lord among masterly souls;
the breath of living beings, the fire of those endowed with the fire's splendor, / the mind of human beings, the ascetic heat of ascetics;
the modesty of those of prudent conduct, and the majesty of the majestic— / having thus created all this entirely, the grandfather of the worlds,
what goal did he seek from sacrifice? Why was his mind set upon sacrifice? / This is my doubt, O brāhmaṇa; this is my great doubt.
The supreme Brahmā is recited as wondrous by the gods and Daityas; / though wondrous by deed, he is truly declared right here.

Pulastya said:
This great burden of a question concerning Brahmā has been asked by you; / according to my capacity I shall speak—let that supreme glory be heard.
[He is] the one of a thousand faces, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet, / a thousand ears, and a thousand hands, imperishable;
possessing a thousand tongues, thousandfold, the supreme thousand-lord, / the giver of thousands, the first of thousands, thousand-armed, imperishable;
the offering, the pressing [of Soma], the oblation, and the hotṛ priest, / the vessels, the purificatory implements, the altar, the consecration, the caru, the sruva-spoon,
the sruc-spoon, the soma, the concluding bath, the sprinkling-water, the sacrificial fee; / the adhvaryu priest, the sāmaveda singer, the priest, the assembly members, the chamber, the assembly;
the sacrificial post, fuel, kuśa grass, the ladle, the cups, and the mortars, / the eastern hall, the sacrificial ground, the hotṛ, and whatever is bound,
short and exceeding measures, measures and immovable objects, / expiations, sacrificial portions, mounds, and kuśa grasses,
the mantra, the sacrifice, the oblation, the fire-portion, the origin, / eating first, eating the oblation, possessed of auspicious luster and raised weapons—
the brāhmaṇas who know the Veda declare him to be the eternal Lord, Sacrifice itself. / Concerning this sacred, divine story which you ask me, O great king,
as to why the blessed Brahmā performed a sacrifice upon the earth, / for the welfare of gods and mortals and for the origin of the worlds:
Brahmā, then Kapila, the supreme Lord, / the gods, the Seven Sages, and the far-famed Tryambaka;
and the exalted Sanatkumāra, Manu of great soul, the blessed Prajāpati; / then the ancient god, radiant like a blazing fire, initiated it.
Formerly, as he who was born from the lotus lay sleeping in its interior / at Puṣkara, where the gods and the hosts of sages arose,
this was the so-called manifestation at Puṣkara of that great-souled one, / where the Purāṇa well-combined with the Veda and Smṛti is related.
And the Boar, whose mouth was the Vedas, manifested from Brahmā; / for the sake of aiding [him], the best of gods assumed a boar's form.
Having made an extensive sacred ford at Puṣkara, Kokāmukha, beneficent, / having the Vedas as feet, the sacrificial post as tusks, the sacrifice as hands, the fire-altar as mouth,
having fire as his tongue, darbha grass as hair, the sacred formulation as head, performing great austerity, / having day and night as his divine eyes, the Vedāṅgas and Vedas as his ornaments,
having clarified butter as nose, the sruva-spoon as snout, the voice of the Sāman-chant as his loud roar, / full of truth and dharma, glorious, honored through ritual strides,

having expiation as claws, resolute, having sacrificial animals as knees, shaped like sacrifice, / with the udgātṛ priest as intestines, the homa as his phallus, having fruit, seeds, and great medicinal herbs,
having the wind as his inner self, mantras as bones, water as buttocks, soma as blood, / the Veda as shoulders, the oblation as fragrance, swift with offerings to gods and ancestors,
having the eastern hall as his body, radiant, worshipped by various consecrations, / with the sacrificial fee as heart, a yogin, composed of the great sacrificial session, magnificent,
delightful with the opening rite and iṣṭi offerings, adorned with the pravargya whirls, / accompanied by his shadow-wife, indeed lofty like a jeweled mountain peak,
he whose nature is the welfare of all worlds lifted up the earth with his tusk. / Then, having brought the earth to her own place, the bearer of the earth,
Hari, attained cessation from holding the earth. / Thus, held by the primeval Boar seeking the welfare of Brahmā,
the earth, which had fallen into the waters of the ocean, was lifted up of old at Puṣkara. / Accompanied by tranquil restraint and self-control, he who stood at the divine Kokāmukha,
together with the Ādityas, Vasus, Sādhyas, and Marut deities, / with the Rudras, with the All-gods, and with Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Kinnaras,
with the cardinal and intermediate directions, the earth, the rivers, and the oceans, / the glorious Brahmā, teacher of the moving and unmoving, the foremost among knowers of Brahman,
spoke this word: 'O Lord, the sacred ford of Kokāmukha / must ever be guarded and protected by you; protection must be made here at the sacrifice.'
'I shall do so, O blessed one,' he then said to Brahmā. / Brahmā spoke once more to that god Viṣṇu standing before him:
'You alone are my supreme god, you alone are my supreme teacher, / you alone are my supreme abode, O best of gods among Indra and the rest!
O one with eyes like blossoming immaculate lotuses, bringer of destruction to the party of enemies! / In such a way that destruction of my sacrifice is not caused by the Dānavas,
and whatever Yātudhānas and Asuras are causers of obstacles at the end, / I will slay them all. Abide in peace, O Grandfather.'
Having spoken thus, he remained there, waiting for the moment to aid. / Auspicious winds blew, and the ten directions grew serene;
and the heavenly bodies shone brightly and circumambulated the moon; / the planets did not conflict, and the oceans became calm;

The earth became free of dust, and the waters granted all delight;
the rivers flowed on their own paths, and the oceans were not agitated.
the senses of men were auspicious in their inner self; / the great sages, free from sorrow, recited the Vedas aloud;
in that sacrifice, when the oblation cooked, the fires were auspicious; / their minds rejoiced, the people followed their rightful duties and good conduct.
Having heard the words of Viṣṇu of true promise concerning the destruction of foes, / then the gods arrived, along with Dānavas and Rākṣasas;
ghosts, departed spirits, and Piśācas—all came there in succession, / as well as Gandharvas, Apsarases, Nāgas, and the Vidyādhara hosts;
trees and medicinal herbs, whatever is here and whatever is not here, / were brought from all directions by the wind at Brahmā's command.
Having reached the sacrificial mountain around the southern direction, / all the gods stayed on the boundary mountain to the north.
Gandharvas and Apsarases, and sages who had mastered the Vedas, / occupied the western direction and remained there at that great sacrifice.
All the groups of gods, the Dānavas, and the hosts of Asuras, / setting aside their enmity, were exceedingly pleased with one another.
All attended upon the sages and served the brāhmaṇas; / sages, royal sages, twice-born, and celestial sages,
the most prominent royal sages, arrived from all sides, [wondering:] / 'Which god will be worshipped in this sacrifice?'
Beasts and birds went there eager to see, / and Brahmins desirous of eating, along with all castes in due order.
Varuṇa personally gave jewels, and Dakṣa personally gave food. / Having arrived from Varuṇa's world, cooked food spontaneously prepared itself.
The Wind cooked varieties of delicacies, and the Sun cooked savory juices; / the Moon made the cooking of rice, and Bṛhaspati bestowed intelligence.
The lord of wealth gave wealth and various garments; / the river goddess Sarasvatī was present, and goddess Gaṅgā along with the Narmadā,
and whatever other sacred rivers, wells, and bodies of water, / marshes, tanks, and various pools,
chief waterfalls, numerous trenches of the gods, / all reservoirs of water, and the seven oceans,
along with their waters of salt, sugarcane juice, liquor, clarified butter, curds, and milk; / the seven worlds with the netherworlds, the seven continents with their cities,
trees, creepers, grasses, vegetables, and fruits; / earth, wind, sky, water, and fire as the fifth,
the elements endowed with bodies, and whatever books of dharma, / commentaries on the Vedas, and sūtras, and whatever was fashioned by Brahmā,
the formless and the fully formed, all that is visible and embodied. / When that was thus arranged at that sacrifice of the Grandfather,
there in the presence of the gods and in the assembly with the sages, / on the right side of Brahmā stood eternal Viṣṇu.
On his left side stood Rudra, the wielder of the Pināka, the boongiver, the Lord. / And the choosing of the officiating priests was performed there by the great-souled one:
Bhṛgu was chosen there as the hotṛ priest, and Pulastya, the best of the adhvaryus; / Marīci was the udgātṛ priest there, and Nārada was appointed as the brahmā priest.
Those such as Sanatkumāra who were members of the sacrificial assembly were present there; / Dakṣa and the other lords of creatures, and the castes beginning with the Brahmins.
The appointment of the officiating priests was performed beside Brahmā. / They were endowed with garments and ornaments by Vaiśravaṇa.
Adorned with finger rings, bracelets, and diadems were the Brahmins— / the four, and the other twelve: the sixteen officiating priests.
They were all honored by Brahmā, preceded by prostration: / “I must be favored by all of you here in this sacrifice.
This Sāvitrī is my wife; O Brahmins, you are my refuge.” / Having summoned Viśvakarman, the shaving of Brahmā's head
was prescribed at that sacrifice, and caused to be done by the best of Brahmins; / garments of fine woven bark were likewise [brought] by the Brahmins for the couple.
With the chanting of the Veda, those Brahmins made heaven resound; / guarding this world, the kṣatriyas stood with weapons.
The vaiśyas prepared various kinds of edible delicacies there; / they prepared food to be chewed and food to be eaten, endowed with abundant flavors.
Having seen what had never before been heard or seen, the Lord of Creatures was pleased; / the all-pervading Creator gave the name “Prāgvāṭa” to those vaiśyas.
“Service to the feet of Brahmins is always to be performed here by the śūdras: / washing the feet, and cleaning up the remains of the meal.”
They too performed that there then. To them the Grandfather spoke further: / “For the sake of service, you have been placed by me in the fourth rank.
Service is to be performed by those such as you to the Brahmins, the kṣatriyas, and their kinsmen—to the three [higher castes].” / Having spoken thus, Brahmā did so.
Likewise, [he appointed] Śakra as superintendent of the door, Varuṇa as the giver of savory juices, / Vaiśravaṇa as the bestower of wealth, the Wind as the giver of perfumes,
the Sun as the provider of light; Mādhava stood in authority; / the Moon was their provider of Soma, taking his place along the left side.
And that well-honored wife, Sāvitrī, an excellent woman, / was called by the adhvaryu priest: “Come, O goddess, with haste!
All the fires have flared up, and the time for initiation has arrived.” / Distracted in performing her chores, by woman's nature she did not come:
“Indeed, nothing has been done by me here; no decoration at the doorway, / no multi-colored designs on the wall, nor any svastika in the courtyard.
The washing of the vessels has not been done at all here. / Moreover, Lakṣmī, the wife of Nārāyaṇa, has not arrived even today,
nor Svāhā, wife of Agni, nor Dhūmrorṇā, wife of Yama, / nor Vāruṇī, nor Gaurī, nor Suprabhā, the wife of Vāyu,
nor Ṛddhi, wife of Vaiśravaṇa, nor Gaurī, wife of Śambhu, beloved of the world, / nor Medhā, Śraddhā, Vibhūti, Anasūyā, Dhṛti, or Kṣamā,
nor Gaṅgā and Sarasvatī, nor have the young maidens arrived today: / Indrāṇī, the wife of the Moon, and Rohiṇī, beloved of the Moon,
Arundhatī, wife of Vasiṣṭha, and the wives of the seven sages, / Anasūyā, wife of Atri, and other ladies here,
daughters-in-law, daughters, female friends, and sisters— / none of them have arrived today, so I have waited a long while.
I will not go alone as long as those women do not come. / Go and tell Virañci: ‘Wait just a moment,
and accompanied by all of them, I will come in haste.’ / Surrounded by all, along with the gods, O wise one,
you will attain supreme splendor, and so will I, without a doubt.” / Leaving her as she spoke thus, the adhvaryu priest went to Brahmā:
“Sāvitrī is busy, O Lord, intent upon household tasks: / ‘As long as my female companions have not arrived, so long will I not come.’
Thus was I addressed, O god; and the proper time is passing away. / Whatever pleases you now, that do, O Grandfather.”
Addressed thus then, Brahmā, somewhat overcome with anger, [said]: / “Quickly bring another wife here for me, O Śakra,
so that the sacrifice proceeds and does not become deficient in its timing; / act swiftly in that way, and bring some woman!
Do not set your mind on her caste until my sacrifice is completed; / I will let her go again once the sacrifice here is finished.”
Addressed thus then, Śakra went through the whole surface of the earth; / and the women who were seen by him were all taken by others.
An Ābhīra maiden, rich in beauty, with a shapely nose and lovely eyes, / neither a goddess nor a Gandharva woman, neither an Asura maiden nor a Nāga maiden,
nor was there any maiden like that excellent woman— / he saw her of fair limbs, like another goddess Śrī,
diminishing the power of the mind's thoughts by the abundance of her beauty. / Whatever object of distinguished beauty may be found anywhere,
that choice quality was seen attached to the body of that slender-limbed girl. / Seeing her, he reflected: “If this girl should be [unmarried],
then no other god exists on earth who has acquired more merit than I! / This jewel of a woman is she; if the Grandfather is fortunate,
or if he should be passionate, then this effort of mine will be fruitful.” / He saw her possessing the luster of a dark cloud, gold, a lotus, and coral,
bearing brilliance with her limbs—hair, cheeks, eyes, and lower lip— / like a blossoming bud of the aśoka tree of the God of Love.
When the god of love was utterly burned by the mass of fiery flames from [Śiva's] eye, / how indeed was she created by the Creator who saw no match for her?
If she was conceived by his own intellect, it was the ultimate reach of his skill! / These two breasts with uplifted tips were fashioned such that joy arises in me as I look upon them;
in whose heart would wonder not arise? / Even though this lower lip has its body touched by passion, clearly...
Even so, it bestows liberation upon the one who serves it; / though bearing crookedness, pleasure is offered by her ringlets of hair.
Even a blemish shines like an excellence when it relies upon abundant beauty. / The two corners of her eyes, adorned, have extended to the vicinity of her ears.
Those who know the truth indeed proclaim that conscious presence arises from a cause: / the two eyes are the ear ornaments, and these two ears are [ornaments] of the eyes.
There is no room at all here for earrings and collyrium. / It is not proper that the side-glances should cause a split in the heart.
How can those related to you here share in sorrow? / Every change of form attains loveliness through natural qualities.
A boundless treasure has been seen by hundreds of matured gazes; / by the Creator, this frontier of skill in the production of beauty was clearly displayed.
With graceful sports, she endows the minds of men with affection." / As he was thus reflecting, his radiance captivated by her beauty,
his body became covered with horripilations that arose continuously. / Beholding her, radiant like fresh gold, with eyes long as lotus petals,
[he thought:] "Among the gods, yakṣas, gandharvas, serpents, or rākṣasas, / no woman possessing such wealth of beauty has ever been seen by me.
Gathering whatever foremost thing exists within the three worlds, / the Creator formed the composition of her beauty."
Indra said: / "Who are you, whose [daughter] are you, and whence have you come, fair-browed one? Tell me. / And why do you stand alone in the midst of the streets?
These ornaments placed upon your limbs which you wear— / they are not for your ornamentation, for you are indeed the ornament to them!
No goddess, no gandharva woman, no asura woman, no serpent maiden, / nor any kinnara woman has been seen before like you, fair-eyed one!
Though spoken to repeatedly by me, why do you give no answer?" / Filled with shame, that maiden, trembling, said to Śakra:
"I am a cowherd maiden, O hero; I sell cow's produce here. / Here is pure fresh butter, and here is curd free from watery scum.
With curd, and with buttermilk, and with essence, O tormentor of foes, / state whatever you desire; take as much as you wish!"
Being spoken to thus, Śakra then grasped her firmly by the hand, / and brought that large-eyed maiden to where Brahmā was present.
Being led away by him, however, she cried out to her father and mother: / "Ah, father! Mother! Ah, brother! This man is carrying me away by force!
If you have any need of me, ask my father; / he will certainly give me to you; the truth is being spoken to you.
What maiden would not desire a husband devoted to loving care? / Yet nothing is to be given to you without my father, O lover of dharma!
Propitiate him with bowed head; he, being pleased, will give me. / If I give myself to you without knowing my father’s mind,
great dharma would surely be destroyed; therefore I do not consent to you. / I will come under your control if my father will give me."
Being addressed in this manner, Śakra, however, led her away, / and placing her before Brahmā, said: "For his sake, O girl,
you have been brought, large-eyed one; do not grieve, fair-complexioned lady!" / Seeing that cowherd maiden of fair complexion and great splendor,
he regarded her as Kamalā herself, with eyes resembling white lotuses, / possessing full breasts resembling an excellent wall of molten gold,
with thighs round like the trunk of an elephant in rut, with the radiance of reddish, prominent nails. / Seeing him, she too thought of herself as walking in the wake of Kama.
Her mind seemed gone with the thought of the means to attain him; / the cowherd girl too deemed herself to have sovereignty in giving herself:
"If he, on account of my beauty, eagerly desires to take me, / there is no woman on earth more fortunate than I.
I was brought by this one and have come within range of his sight; / in being abandoned by him there would be death, in not being abandoned, a happy life.
And from disrespect I would become one whose beauty is ruined, a bringer of sorrow; / but even that woman who is seen by this eye through his favor,
she too is fortunate, without doubt; how much more so the one whom he would embrace! / All the beauty of the world indeed followed separate paths;
that charm has been displayed here assembled in one place by the source of the universe. / Kama is the fitting comparison for him, and the comparison for Kama's splendor is [his] splendor.
This grief is cast aside; father and mother are no consideration. / If he does not accept me, or speaks very little to me,
from remembering him, death born of sorrow will come to pass. / But when an innocent wife has departed quickly, such a one,
with a radiance equal to a pure lotus, for the adornment of a jewel upon her breasts— / as I behold his face, my mind has entered into meditation.
If you do not think highly of the contact of touching his limb, / then wandering about touching [others], you have an utterly useless body.
Or rather, he is not at fault, for you wander about at will. / You have certainly been robbed, O Kama! Protect your own beloved Rati!
For by his beauty he is seen to surpass Kama, even compared to you. / By him, the jewel of my mind, all that is mine, has been firmly stolen.
Whence could that splendor seen in his face exist in the moon, the hare-marked one? / No comparison is praised of that which has a blemish with that which is spotless.
A lotus does not attain equality with his two eyes; / what comparison could be attained by a water conch with the conches of his ears?
Even coral certainly does not find a comparison to his lower lip; / for he, dripping with the nectar abiding within himself, surely stirs.
If any auspicious deed has been performed by me across hundreds of other births, / by its favor, may he become my desired husband!"
While that cowherd maiden was thus consumed with thoughts, / Brahmā then spoke words quickly to Hari for the sake of the sacrifice:
"And this illustrious goddess is Gāyatrī by name, O Lord." / When this was spoken, Viṣṇu then said this to Brahmā:
"Therefore, marry her today, given by me, O Lord of the universe, / by the Gāndharva marriage rite; do not hesitate for long!
Take this hand of hers today, O God, without agitation!" / The Grandsire married her by the Gāndharva marriage rite.
Having obtained her then, Brahmā spoke to the best of adhvaryu priests: / "She has indeed been made my wife by me; usher her into my abode."
Holding a deer horn, veiled in silken cloth, the maiden / was then led to the patnīśālā by the officiating priests who had mastered the Vedas.
With a staff of audumbara wood, wrapped in a deerskin, / Brahmā then shone by his own splendor at the great sacrifice.

And then the hotṛ rites were begun by the brāhmaṇas who had mastered the Vedas; / together with Bhṛgu, the ritual prescribed in the Vedas was performed by them then. / And that sacrifice at Puṣkara continued for a thousand yugas.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, named 'The Acceptance of Gāyatrī', in the first book, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.

title: saptadaśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Bhīṣma said: / "What wonder occurred then at that sacrifice, O best of the twice-born? / How did Rudra remain there, and Viṣṇu too, the foremost of the gods?
What was done there by Gāyatrī, who stood in the role of wife? / And what was done by the Ābhīras, who know righteous conduct, when they found out, O sage?
Relate this account to me as it happened, just as it was done / by the Ābhīras and by Brahmā; this is a great wonder to me."
Pulastya said: / "Whatever wondrous event took place at that sacrifice, O ruler of men, / I shall relate all of that; listen with a single mind, O king!"
Rudra, however, having entered the assembly, performed a great marvel; / assuming a contemptible form, the god came there near the twice-born.
Viṣṇu did not do anything, because he stood in pre-eminence. / But the cowherd boys, having learned of the disappearance of the cowherd girl,
and likewise all those cowherd women, came into the presence of Brahmā, / seeing her bound with a girdle, standing at the boundary of the sacrifice.
“Alas, daughter!” cried the mother then, and the father: “Alas, little daughter!” / “O sister!” cried all the relatives, and her friends with friendliness: “Alas, friend!
By whom were you brought here, beautiful girl marked with red lac? / Having removed your sari, by whom was a woollen garment put on [you]?
And by whom, daughter, was this matted hair bound with red thread?” / Hearing such words, Hari himself spoke:
“She was brought here by us and appointed as a wife; / the maiden has been taken by Brahmā. Do not lament here!
She is meritorious, fortunate, and the delighter of the family of all. / If she were not meritorious, how could she come to the assembly?
Knowing this, O fortunate one, you ought not to grieve; / this highly fortunate maiden of yours has obtained the god Viriñcana.
Yogins endowed with yoga, and Brahmins who have reached the further shore of the Vedas, / do not attain, even praying for it, that state which your daughter has attained.
Knowing you to be righteous, of good conduct, and affectionate toward dharma, / this maiden was then given by me to Viriñci.
Saved by her, go to the divine, magnificent realms! / And in your family, for the sake of accomplishing the work of the gods,
I shall make an incarnation; indeed, that will be my sport. / When Nanda and the others on the surface of the earth
make an incarnation, then I too will dwell in their midst. / All your daughters will dwell together with me.
There will be no fault in that, neither hatred nor envy; / then the cowherds and men will make no fear.
And no fault will ever accrue to her by this act.” / Hearing the words of Viṣṇu, they bowed down and then departed.
[They said:] “Thus this boon, O god, which has been given, will indeed come to pass for me: / that an incarnation, an instrument of dharma, is to be made in our family.
From the very sight of you we become dwellers of heaven; / and this auspicious maiden is a savior of me along with my families.”
[They said:] “So be it, O Lord of gods! May this grant of boons be yours, O all-pervading one!” / The cowherds were then conciliated by the god Viṣṇu himself.
By Brahmā too, indeed, it was spoken thus with his left hand. / But the fair-complexioned girl was filled with shame at the sight of her relatives:
“By whom was I told of, so that they came to this region?” / Then, seeing them, the cowherd maiden Gāyatrī spoke,
with her left hand [raised] toward all of them, preceded by an obeisance: / “I am staying here, mother, having approached Brahmā.
I have obtained as husband the god who is the origin of everything, the lord of the universe; / I am not to be lamented by you, nor by father, nor by relatives.
Let my band of friends depart, and sisters along with children; / my welfare should be reported to all; I remain with the deities.”
When they had all departed, that slender-waisted Gāyatrī / shone together with Brahmā, having entered the sacrificial enclosure as a faithful wife.
Brahmā was begged by the Brahmins: “Grant us our desired boons!” / Then Brahmā also gave them the boon they desired,
and that which was given was approved by that goddess Gāyatrī. / That virtuous woman remained in the sacrifice, standing near the deities.
Then that sacrifice advanced for a full divine hundred years. / But the one with matted hair approached the sacrificial enclosure for the sake of alms,
holding a large skull, adorned with five severed heads; / standing at a distance, he was loathed by the sacrificial priests and the assembly members:
“How have you arrived here, condemned by the expounders of the Veda?” / Even while being thus driven away and reviled by those twice-born,
Maheśvara, having smiled, said to all those twice-born: / “Here in the sacrifice of the grandfather, which gives satisfaction to all,
no one is driven away at all, except me, O best of the twice-born!” / The one with matted hair was then told by them: “Eat food, and then go!”
And by the one with matted hair they were told: “Having eaten, I will go, O twice-born!” / Having spoken thus, he sat down, placing the skull in front.
Observing their deed, the Lord devised a crooked trick: / having left the skull on the ground, looking at those twice-born,
he said: “I am going to Puṣkara for a bath, O best of the twice-born.” / Told by them, “Go quickly!”, the Supreme Lord went away.
Remaining in the sky, having bewildered the dwellers of heaven out of curiosity, / when the one with matted hair had gone to Puṣkara for a bath, the twice-born [said]:
“How can an oblation be performed here while a skull remains in the assembly? / Formerly Prajāpati declared that skull-ends are impure.”
One Brahmin in the assembly said: “I will cast away the skull.” / It was lifted by the assembly member and thrown away with his own hand.
Just as quickly another remained there; it was lifted up yet again; / so a second, a third, twenty, even thirty, alas!
And fifty, and a hundred, a thousand, and ten thousand; / in this way, no end of the skulls could be reached by the best of the twice-born.
Having bowed to the god with matted hair, they approached him for refuge, / reaching the forest of Puṣkara, and intensely with Vedic prayers
they praised him all together; then Hara himself was pleased. / Thereupon Śiva gave a vision to the twice-born on account of their devotion.
Then the god said to those excellent twice-born bowed with devotion: / “The production of the sacrificial cake cannot occur without a potsherd.
Comply with my word, O Brahmins: let there be the Sviṣṭakṛt portion for me. / When this is done, all is accomplished; let this be my command.”
“So be it,” said the twice-born to Śambhu, “we shall indeed carry out your command.” / The Lord, skull in hand, said to the divine Grandfather:
“Choose a boon, O Brahmā, whatever lies dear in your heart! / I will grant you everything; there is nothing not to be given by me, O lord.”
Brahmā said: / “I will not take a boon from you; I am consecrated, seated in the assembly; / and I am the granter of all desires to whoever petitions me here.”
To the Grandfather speaking thus, the giver of boons in that sacrifice, / Rudra said, “So be it,” and asked for a boon from him.
Then, after a manvantara had elapsed, the Lord himself once again / made the place Brahmottara, the god Śambhu himself.
He who had attained complete mastery even in the four Vedas, / at that time, then, the god, for the sight of the city
and conversation with the twice-born, went to the assembly out of curiosity. / In that very guise of a madman, while the sacrificial remnants were being offered, Maheśvara
entered the abode of Brahmā, seen by the gods and best of the twice-born. / Some laughed at him, and some reviled him;
other twice-born sprinkled that madman with dust; / and others, strong and arrogant with power, [struck him] with clods and clubs;
striking him, they made a mocking clapping of hands. / Then other young religious students there, seizing his matted locks, nearby
asked about that observance of his vows: “By whom was this shown to you? / Here there are beautiful women; have you come for their sake?”

"By which teacher, a beholder of sin, was this conduct shown to you,
by which, speaking like a madman, you run around in our midst?

My phallus is the form of Brahmā, and Janārdana is the vulva.
This seed is being sown; yet the world torments [itself] otherwise.

This son was engendered by me, and by him I was engendered.
For the sake of Mahādeva the creation was created, and his wife in the Himālaya.

Umā was given to Rudra; say, whose daughter is she?
You are fools, you know nothing; let the Lord speak to you."

"This conduct was not performed by Brahmā, nor was it ever shown by Viṣṇu,
nor even by the god Giriśa, though he committed the murder of a Brahmin.

Why do you revile the god? You are surely to be killed by us today!"
Being struck thus by the Brahmins there, Śaṅkara,

smiling, said to all the Brahmins, O best of kings:
"Do you not know me, O Brahmins, [taking me to be] a madman whose senses are lost?

You are all compassionate, established in friendship,
[yet you strike] Hara who bears this disguise, who holds the form of Brahman while speaking."

Deluded by the illusory power of that god, those best of Brahmins
struck the wearer of matted hair with their hands, feet, and fists,

and also with sticks and pegs, him who wore the guise of a madman.
Being afflicted by those Brahmins, he then fell into anger.

Then they were cursed by the god: "May you be bereft of the Vedas,
with erect matted hair, fallen from sacrifices, consorting with other men's wives,

delighting in prostitutes and gambling, bereft of fathers and mothers!
No son will inherit ancestral wealth or Vedic learning.

May they all be deluded, deprived of all their senses,
eating the dreadful food of beggars, living on balls of rice given by others,

maintaining themselves, devoid of possessiveness, abandoned by dharma!
However, those Brahmins by whom compassion was bestowed upon me when I was mad now,

theirs shall be wealth and sons, female and male slaves, goats and sheep;
and women born of noble families shall be theirs in this world, since I am pleased!"

Having thus given a curse and a boon, the Lord disappeared.
When the god was gone, the Brahmins, realizing he was the Lord Śaṅkara,

though searching diligently, when they did not see him,
then, observing vows, came to the forest of Puṣkara.

Having bathed in Jyeṣṭhasaras, the Brahmins muttered the Śatarudriya.
At the end of their recitation, the god spoke to them with a bodiless voice:

"An untruth has never been spoken by me even in jest, how much less [now]?
Since punishment has befallen you, I shall grant you well-being once more.

Those Brahmins who are calm, self-controlled, devoted, and steadfast in me,
their Veda is not cut off, nor their wealth, nor their offspring.

Those who are devoted to the fire-offering, devoted to Janārdana,
and who worship Brahmā and the sun, the mass of radiance,

no misfortune exists for them whose minds are established in equanimity."
Having spoken words to this extent, he became silent.

Having obtained the boon and grace from Maheśvara, the god of gods,
they all went together to where the god, the Grandfather, was.

Standing before Viriñci, pleasing him with the recitation of Saṃhitās,
Brahmā, being pleased, said to them: "Let a boon be chosen from me as well."

At that word of Brahmā, all the best of Brahmins were delighted:
"What boon should be asked, O Brahmins, when the Grandfather is well pleased?

May the agnihotras, the Vedas, the various scriptures,
and the realms endowed with offspring be ours by the granting of this boon!"

While they were thus talking among themselves there, anger entered the Brahmins:
"Who are you? Who are the prominent ones here? We are the best!" and so said the others.

"No, no!" [said] the Brahmins to those twice-born assembled there.
Looking at the Brahmins filled with anger, Brahmā said:

"Since you stood outside the assembly in three groups,
therefore let there be one root-dwelling company for you, O twice-born.

Those who stood neutral, let them become indifferent.
Those who stood equipped with weapons, wearing unsheathed swords, desiring to fight,

let a third group be called Kauśika, O twice-born.
This place, arranged in three ways, shall entirely belong to you.

Here, those spoken of from without by the word 'people' are the subjects.
This place cannot be easily known; Viṣṇu will surely protect it.

Given by me, it will be long-lasting and indestructible."
Having spoken thus, Brahmā then looked toward that conclusion.

Those Brahmins gathered together, filled with anger and impatience,
feeding guests and devoted to the study of the Veda,

[remained in] this supreme sacred site named Puṣkara, belonging to Brahmā.
The peaceful Brahmins who reside there dwell as inhabitants of the sacred site.

Nothing will be difficult for them to attain in the world of Brahmā.
At Kokāmukha, Kurukṣetra, Naimiṣa, the gathering of sages,

in Vārāṇasī, Prabhāsa, and likewise at Badarikāśrama,
at Gaṅgādvāra, Prayāga, and the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean,

at Rudrakoṭi, Virūpākṣa, and likewise in the forest of Mitra—
at all these holy places, the accomplishment that requires twelve years

is obtained by men in this world in six months, O best of kings,
at Puṣkara, without doubt, if there is practice of celibacy.

It is the supreme among holy places and the best among sacred sites,
always worshipped by the venerable, endowed with devotion to the Grandfather.

Beyond this, I shall recount the great debate that occurred
between Sāvitrī and Brahmā, which was made in jest.

At the departure of Sāvitrī, all the wives of the gods arrived.
The renowned wife of Viṣṇu, born to Khyāti from Bhṛgu,

the ever-invited Lakṣmī, came there in haste;
and the illustrious Madirā, Yoganidrā who bestows prosperity,

Śrī whose abode is the lotus, Bhūti, Kīrti, wise Śraddhā,
Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi—these goddesses came, having assembled.

Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, the auspicious Pārvatī called Umā,
the goddess who is the beauty of the three worlds, granter of good fortune to women,

Jayā and Vijayā, Madhucchandā, Amarāvatī,
Supriyā, and Janakāntā [came] to the auspicious abode of Sāvitrī.

They arrived together with Gaurī, adorned with beautiful garments and ornaments;
and the daughter of Puloman, Śakrāṇī, along with the Apsarases,

Svāhā and Svadhā arrived, and beautiful-faced Dhūmorṇā;
and Yakṣī, Rākṣasī, and Gaurī of great wealth,

Manojavā, wife of Vāyu, and Ṛddhi, beloved of the giver of wealth;
the divine maidens arrived thus, and the Dānavī women, beloved of the Danus,

the great wives of the seven sages, and the excellent women of the seers;
likewise sisters, daughters, and hosts of Vidyādharīs,

Rākṣasīs, daughters of the ancestors, and other mothers of the world.
With her brides and daughters-in-law, Sāvitrī wished to depart.

All the daughters of Dakṣa, beginning with Aditi, assembled;
surrounded by them, the virtuous Brahmāṇī whose abode is the lotus [departed].

One fair-faced woman took sweetmeats; another, taking a winnowing basket
filled with fruits, set out near Brahmā.

Others took pigeon peas along with niṣpāva beans; and another,
various pomegranates and beautiful citrons.

Others took karīra fruits and lotuses;
another took safflower, cumin, and dates.

Others carried excellent coconuts of all kinds;
one carried a vessel filled with grapes, and likewise water chestnuts.
Various kinds of camphor, auspicious rose-apples, / and walnuts, āmalakas, and lemons were brought by another,
and fully ripened bilva fruits, flattened rice, O lovely-faced one, / while others [brought] cotton rolls and safflower-dyed cloth.
Having placed these and other such things in a winnowing basket, the lovely-faced women, / all together with Sāvitrī, suddenly arrived, radiant.
Seeing Sāvitrī arrive, Indra was terrified there. / Brahmā stood with downcast face, [thinking,] "What will she say to me?"
Viṣṇu and Rudra were filled with shame, and so were all the other twice-born. / The members of the assembly were afraid, as were the other gods in heaven,
the sons, grandsons, nephews, maternal uncles, and brothers, / and the gods named Ṛbhus, deities even of the gods.
All stood in embarrassment, [wondering] what Sāvitrī would say. / But standing at Brahmā's side there was the cowherd girl,
observing silence, listening to the words spoken by everyone. / Though summoned by the adhvaryu priest, the fair-complexioned woman had not come.
Another woman had been brought by Indra from fear, given by Viṣṇu himself, / assented to by Rudra, and likewise given by her father.
"How will she act in the sacrifice, or how will it reach its completion?" / As they were thinking thus, the woman dwelling on a lotus entered.
Brahmā was surrounded by the assembly members, the officiating priests, and the gods, / and offerings were poured into the fires there by Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas.
The cowherd girl stood in the wife's pavilion, wearing an antelope horn and a girdle, / dressed in linen garments, meditating on the supreme abode,
devoted to her husband, holding her husband as her life, placed in the chief position, / endowed with beauty, large-eyed, resembling the sun in splendor,
illuminating that assembly just like the radiance of the sun. / Likewise, the officiating priests resorted to the blazing fire,
joyfully taking their respective share of the animals' sacrificial cake here. / The gods, desiring their share of the sacrifice, then said because of the delay:
"Nothing should be done out of season; what is done [too late] yields no fruit, / because such authority is seen in the Vedas by all the wise."
While the pravargya rite was being performed by the Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas, / combined with both kinds of milk boiled by the adhvaryu priest,
and when the twice-born had been invited and had come upon being summoned, / and the sacrificial food was being prepared, the goddess, seeing this, was filled with wrath.
The goddess said to Brahmā, who was silent in the midst of the assembly: / "Is it fitting, O god, to commit such a deed as this?
That, abandoning me out of desire, you have committed a sin! / She who is not equal even to the dust of my feet has been placed upon your head!
Whatever all these gathered people sitting in the assembly say, / carry out that command of the masters, if you so desire.
Out of greed for beauty, you have committed an act condemned by the world. / You felt no shame before your sons or before your grandsons, O Lord.
I consider this despised deed to have been done out of willful desire. / You are the grandfather of the gods, the great-grandfather of the sages.
How was no shame born in you as you looked upon your own person? / Mockery has been made in the midst of the world, and I have been wronged, O Lord.
If this is your firm intention, remain so, O god, homage to you! / How shall I show my face to my friends?
'A [second] wife was taken by my husband'—how can I say this?" / Brahmā said: / "I was urged by the officiating priests immediately after the time of initiation:
'Without a wife, no oblation can be made here; bring a wife here at once!' / She was brought by Indra, and this one was given to me by Viṣṇu,
and taken by me, O fair-browed one. Forgive this that has been done by me. / I shall never commit another offense against you, O woman of virtuous vows.
I have fallen at your feet; forgive me here, homage to you!" / Pulastya said: / Thus addressed, she became angry then and prepared to curse Brahmā:
"If I have performed penance, if my gurus have been satisfied, / in all assemblies of Brahmā and in various places,

The brāhmaṇas will never perform worship for you at all,
except for your single annual worship in the month of Kārttika.
and all the twice-born shall do it among mortals, nowhere else on earth!" / Having said this to Brahmā, she said to Indra who was present:
"Ho, Indra! You brought the cowherd woman near to Brahmā. / Since yours was a base deed, therefore you shall reap the fruit.
When you shall stand in the midst of battle, O Indra, / then, bound by your enemies, you will be reduced to the most dire state.
Destitute, your courage broken, dwelling in the city of your enemies, / having suffered great defeat, only after a long time will you be freed."
Having cursed Indra then, the goddess then addressed words to Viṣṇu: / "When, by the curse of Bhṛgu, your birth shall occur among mortals,
then you shall experience the sorrow born of separation from your wife there! / Your wife will be carried off by an enemy to the other shore of the great ocean,
and, your mind overwhelmed by grief, you will not know where she was taken. / Together with your brother, you will be miserable, having met with the most terrible calamity.
When you are born in the Yadu lineage and named Kṛṣṇa, / you will wander for a long time, reduced to servitude to cattle!"

Then, O Hara, when you were staying in the Dāruvana forest, angry at Rudra,
the enraged sages will bestow a curse on you, O Hara.
'Ho, base Kāpālika! You wish to take away our wives! / Therefore this arrogant phallus of yours shall fall to the earth today!'
Deprived of your virility and afflicted by the curse of the sages, / your wife, residing at Gaṅgādvāra, will console you.
O Agni, you were made an eater of everything formerly by my son, / by Bhṛgu, who is constant in dharma; how could I burn what is already burned?
O Jātavedas, that Rudra will flood you with his semen, / and in unholy things your tongue will burn even more."
Sāvitrī indeed cursed all the Brahmin officiating priests: / "Maintaining the agnihotra only for the sake of receiving gifts, living in vain in forests,
you shall always resort to sacred bathing-places and sacred sites purely out of greed! / Always satisfied by the food of others, but never satisfied in your own homes,
sacrificing for those for whom one should not sacrifice, accepting gifts from the contemptible, / earning wealth in vain, and expending it just as vainly!
Because of that, the state of hungry ghosts shall befall those ghosts; there is no doubt!" / Having thus in wrath cursed Indra, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Agni,
and Brahmā, and all those Brahmins as well, / having pronounced that curse upon them, she departed from the assembly.
Reaching senior Puṣkara, she then remained there. / She spoke to Lakṣmī, and to that chaste, fair-faced wife of Indra,
and to those young women she said: "I will not remain in this assembly; / and I shall go to that place where I will hear no sound."
Then all those women departed to their own abode. / Sāvitrī, enraged, was prepared to curse them as well:
"Since those wives of the gods have gone away, abandoning me, / I shall, being exceedingly enraged, give a curse to them as well!
Lakṣmī shall never have an abode in one place; / she shall be petty and fickle-minded, and shall dwell among fools,
among barbarians, mountain-dwellers, the vile and despised, / among fools, the arrogant, the accursed, and the wicked!"

"In such a manner, a human shall be your dwelling, caused by my curse."
Having thus cursed her, she then cursed Indrāṇī:
"When your husband Indra is seized by [the sin of] brahmahatyā and you share his grief, / Nahuṣa, having seized the kingdom, shall see you and desire you.
'I am Indra; how shall this foolish woman not attend upon me? / I shall slay all the gods if I do not obtain Śacī!'
Then, ruined, terrified, and grieving, in the house of the Lord of Speech / you shall dwell, you ill-behaved and arrogant woman, because of my curse!"

Then she pronounced a curse on all the wives of the gods:
"And all of you shall never obtain the joy that comes from having offspring!

Tormented day and night, defiled by the epithet 'barren woman'!"
In this manner, fair Gaurī too was then cursed by Sāvitrī.

Weeping, she was seen and propitiated by Viṣṇu:
"Do not weep, large-eyed one; come, arrive, O ever-auspicious lady!
Enter the assembly and grant me the girdle and the two linen garments; / accept the consecration, O consort of Brahmā, and I bow down at your feet!"
Thus addressed, she said to him: "I will not heed your word; / and I shall go to that place where I will hear no sound at all."

Having said this much, she climbed from that place and stood upon the mountain.
Viṣṇu, standing before her with his palms joined together,

bent low, stood full of supreme devotion, and praised her.
Viṣṇu said:
"You go everywhere; you are to be seen among all beings, wondrous on every side.

Whatever is visible, both real and unreal, does not exist without you.
Even so, the places in which you are to be seen by those seeking perfection,

or remembered by those desiring earthly prosperity, I shall declare in your presence:
[You are] named Sāvitrī at Puṣkara, the most excellent and auspicious of sacred bathing places;
Viśālākṣī at Vārāṇasī; Liṅgadhāriṇī at Naimiṣa; / the goddess Lalitā at Prayāga; Kāmukā on the Gandhamādana mountain;
named Kumudā at Mānasa; Viśvakāyā in the atmosphere; / named Gomatī on the Gomanta mountain; Kāmacāriṇī on the Mandara mountain;
Madotkaṭā in Caitraratha; Jayantī at Hastināpura; / likewise Gaurī at Kānyakubja; Rambhā on the Malaya mountain;
Kīrtimatī at Ekāmraka; Viśvā and Viśveśvarī [there]; / Puruhastā at Karṇikā; Mārgadāyikā at Kedāra;
Nandā on the back of the Himavat; Bhadrakālikā at Gokarṇa; / Bhavānī at Sthāṇvīśvara; Bilvapatrikā at Bilvaka;
the goddess Mādhavī at Śrīśaila; Bhadrā and Bhadreśvarī; / Jayā on the Varāha mountain; Kamalā at Kamalālaya;
Rudrāṇī at Rudrakoṭi; Kālī at Kālañjara; / Kapilā at Mahāliṅga; Maṅgaleśvarī at Karkoṭa;
Mahādevī at Śālagrāma; Jalapriyā at Śivaliṅga; / Kumārī at Māyāpurī; Lalitā in the Saṃtāna grove;
Utpalākṣī at Sahasrākṣa; Mahotpalā at Hiraṇyākṣa; / named Maṅgalā at Gayā; Vimalā at Puruṣottama;
Amoghākṣī on the Vipāśā; Pāṭalā at Puṇyavardhana; / Nārāyaṇī at Supārśva; Bhadrasundarī on Trikūṭa;
named Vipulā on Vipula; Kalyāṇī on the Malaya mountain; / Koṭavī at Koṭitīrtha; Sugandhā in the Mādhavī grove;
Trisandhyā at Kubjāmraka; Haripriyā at Gaṅgādvāra; / Śivānandā at Śivakuṇḍa; Nandinī on the bank of the Devikā;
Rukmiṇī at Dvāravatī; Rādhā in Vṛndāvana; / Devakī at Mathurā; Parameśvarī in the netherworld;
Sītā at Citrakūṭa; Vindhyanivāsinī in the Vindhya mountains; / Ekavīrā on the Sahya mountain; Candrikā at Hariścandra;
Ramaṇā at Rāmatīrtha; Mṛgāvatī on the Yamunā; / Mahālakṣmī at Karavīra; the goddess Umā at Vināyaka;
Arogā at Vaidyanātha; Maheśvarī at Mahākāla; / Abhayā at Puṣpatīrtha; Amṛtā in the cave of the Vindhya mountain;
the goddess Māṇḍavī at Māṇḍavya; Svāhā in the city of Māheśvara; / Pracaṇḍā at Vegalā; and Caṇḍikā at Amarakaṇṭaka;
Varārohā at Someśvara; Puṣkarāvatī at Prabhāsa; / Devamātā on the Sarasvatī; residing on the shore of the vast sea;
Mahāpadmā at Mahālaya; Piṅgaleśvarī on the Payoṣṇī; / Siṃhikā at Kṛtaśauca; Śaṅkarī at Kārtikeya;
Lolā at Utpalāvartaka; Subhadrā at the confluence of the Sindhu; / Umā in the Siddha forest; Lakṣmī-Anaṅgā at Bharata's hermitage;
Viśvamukhī at Jālandhara; Tārā on the Kiṣkindha mountain; / Puṣṭi in the Devadāru forest; Medhā in the realm of Kaśmīra;
the goddess Bhīmā on the Himādri; Tuṣṭi at Vastreśvara; / Śraddhā at Kapālamocana; Mātā at Kāyāvarohaṇa;
named Dhvani at Śaṅkhoddhāra; Dhṛti at Piṇḍāraka; / Kālā on the Candrabhāgā; Siddhidayinī at Acchoda;
the goddess Amṛtā on the Veṇā; Urvaśī at Badarī; / Auṣadhī in Uttarakuru; Kuśodakā in Kuśadvīpa;
Manmathā on Hemakūṭa; Satyavādinī on Kumuda; / Vandanīyā in the sacred fig tree; Nidhi in the abode of Vaiśravaṇa;
Gāyatrī in the mouth of the Veda; Pārvatī in the presence of Śiva; / Indrāṇī in the world of the gods; Sarasvatī in the mouth of Brahmā;
named Prabhā in the orb of the sun; Vaiṣṇavī among the mothers; / Arundhatī among chaste wives; Tilottamā among beautiful women;

named Brahmakalā in the mind; the power of all embodied beings.
This excellent [hymn of] one hundred and eight names has been proclaimed by me with devotion,

and this one hundred and eight sacred bathing places has been declared.
Whoever recites it or even hears it is freed from all sins.

Whatever best of men, having bathed in these sacred bathing places, should see [her],
freed from all sins, shall dwell in the city of Brahmā for an eon.
A man who causes these one hundred and eight names to be heard in the presence of Brahmā / on the full moon or on the new moon day shall have many sons.
At the donation of a cow, or at the presentation of a śrāddha, or day after day / during the rite of worshipping the gods, hearing it, he attains the supreme Brahman.

To Viṣṇu who was praising her thus, Sāvitrī of virtuous vows said:
"I have been properly praised by you, son; you shall be invincible.

In your incarnations, you shall have a wife and be dear to your father and mother.
And whoever, having come here, praises me with this hymn,

freed from all sins, shall go to the supreme abode.
Go, bring the sacrifice of Viriñci to completion, my son!

At Kurukṣetra and at Prayāga, I shall become the bestower of food.
Standing near my husband, I will fulfill your word."

Thus addressed, Viṣṇu went to the excellent assembly of Brahmā.
Now, when Sāvitrī had departed, Gāyatrī spoke these words:

"Let the sages hear my word in the presence of my husband,
which I, being pleased, declare, ready to grant a boon:
Those men who worship Brahmā endowed with devotion, / to them will belong clothing, wealth, grain, wives, happiness, and riches.
Likewise, unbroken happiness in the household with sons and grandsons; / having enjoyed this for a very long time, in the end he will attain liberation."

Pulastya said:
Having installed [an image of] Brahmā with every effort according to the ritual rules, / the meritorious fruit that one attains—listen to that with a one-pointed mind.
Whatever fruit is obtained in all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, sacred places, and Vedas, / that fruit multiplied ten million times one would obtain through this installation.
Having observed a fast on the full moon day with devotion, O lord of men, / whatever man worships Viriñci according to this ritual,
on the first day of the lunar fortnight, O mighty-armed one, goes to the abode of Brahmā; / [worshipping] Viriñci and Vāsudeva, especially through the officiating priests.
In the month of Kārttika, the chariot procession of the god is proclaimed, / having performed which with devotion, human beings attain the world of Brahmā.
In the month of Kārttika, on the full moon day, O king of kings, O tormentor of enemies, [one should lead] the four-faced Brahmā, along with Sāvitrī,
accompanied by various musical instruments, through the entire city. / Having led him around, O king, one should bathe the world-protector and the city.
Having first fed the brāhmaṇas and worshipped Śāṇḍileya, / one should mount the god on the chariot amid the sounds of auspicious musical instruments.
Having worshipped the son of Śāṇḍilī in front of the chariot according to rule, / having the brāhmaṇas recite blessings and performing the auspicious ceremony of the auspicious day,
and having mounted the god on the chariot, one should keep vigil / with various kinds of spectacles and abundant recitations of the sacred text.
Having kept vigil for the god, in the morning, O king, / having fed the brāhmaṇas according to one's ability with manifold chewable and solid foods,
and having worshipped the steadfast people with mantra[s] according to rule, O king, / with clarified butter, O mighty-armed one, with milk, and with milk-rice,
having caused the brāhmaṇas to recite blessings according to rule, O king, / and having proclaimed the word 'auspicious day', one should lead that chariot around the city.
One should have Brahmā's chariot drawn by brāhmaṇas learned in the four Vedas— / by Rigvedins, Atharvavedins, O hero, and likewise by Sāmavedins and Yajurvedins.
One should lead that chariot of the god of gods, the best of deities, / clockwise around the entire city along a very smooth path.
The chariot must not be drawn, O hero, by a śūdra desiring welfare; / nor should a wise king climb into the chariot, except for a single priest.
On the right side of Brahmā, O king, one should place Gāyatrī; / on the left side, the priest; and in front, one should place a lotus.
Thus, with sounds of horns and abundant blasts of conches, / having led the chariot, O hero, clockwise around the entire city,
the wise person should reinstall the god in his own place after offering a waving of lamps. / Whoever performs this procession thus, or even gazes upon it with devotion,
or pulls the chariot, goes to the abode of Brahmā. / And whoever performs the lighting of lamps on the new-moon day in the month of Kārttika
in the hall of Brahmā, goes to the supreme abode. / But whoever honors himself with perfumes, flowers, and new garments
on that first lunar day, goes to the abode of Brahmā. / This lunar day is most meritorious, inaugurating the reign of Bali.
It is eternally very dear to Brahmā, proclaimed as Bali's day. / Whoever worships Brahmā on this [day], and especially himself,
goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor. / In the month of Caitra, O mighty-armed one, the first lunar day is the best and meritorious.
On that [day], the best among men who bathes after touching an outcaste / has no misfortune whatsoever, nor mental anguish, nor diseases, O king.
