This is the manifestation named Trivikrama of the teacher of the universe, / accompanied by the origin of the Gaṅgā, destroying all sins.
This origin of the footsteps of Viṣṇu has been related to you, O king, / hearing which a man in this world is freed from all sins.
Nightmares, ill thoughts, hardships, and misdeeds / quickly go to destruction when the three footsteps of Viṣṇu are seen.
Seeing the sinful creatures through the succession of the yugas, / subtlety was shown by Viṣṇu, O Bhīṣma, in the sight of his steps.
A man on earth who climbs that [place] in silence, / having made the pilgrimage to the three Puṣkaras, would obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
He is freed from all sins, and upon death he would go to Viṣṇu's city.

title: ekatriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Bhīṣma said: / O venerable one, a great wonder indeed was the binding of Bāṣkali, / when Bali was restrained, the Trivikrama form having been assumed!
This was heard by me formerly as it was being narrated by the best of the twice-born, / [and that] Bali, the son of Virocana, lives in the netherworld even today.
How did the Nāgatīrtha come to be, and the origin of the Piśācas? / And how is Śivadūtī [here], and by whom was she rendered auspicious?
By whom was Puṣkara carried into the atmosphere, O great sage? / Tell me all of this, as also the binding of Bāṣkali.
The pacing of the earth was performed formerly by the god Viṣṇu; / what was the second cause for which the god did so?
Speak truly of all that in its reality, as it happened; / for this, which brings about the destruction of sins, should be heard by one desiring prosperity.
Pulastya said: / A burden of questions has been stated by you out of sheer curiosity, O king; / I shall tell you all of that as it happened, O best of kings.
In connection with the footsteps of Viṣṇu, the binding of Bāṣkali here / has all been heard by you, as it was proclaimed to you by me.
Again, O Bhīṣma, when the Vaivasvata interval arrived, / the three worlds were strode over by Bali, [and then] by the powerful Viṣṇu.
Going alone to the sacrifice, Bali was likewise restrained; / once again the pacing of the earth was performed by the god of gods.
The manifestation of Vāmana happened in that way, O lord of men: / having become Trivikrama, the dwarf became not a dwarf.
This entire origin has been related to you, O scion of the Kurus; / now listen to how the tīrtha of the serpents came to be, O you of great vows!
Ananta, Vāsuki, and the mighty Takṣaka, / Karkoṭaka the serpent king, Padma, and another reptile,
Mahāpadma, Śaṅkha, and the unconquered Kulika— / these are Kaśyapa's heirs, and by them the world was filled.
By their offspring this world was indeed filled— / crooked, doing terrible deeds, with sharp fangs, and swelling with poison.
Biting heedless men, they would turn them to ashes in an instant; / by their very sight the destruction of men would occur, O ruler of men.
Day after day, an exceedingly terrible destruction took place; / and seeing their own destruction, all creatures from all around
went for refuge to the refuge-giver, Brahmā, the supreme lord, / with this very matter in mind, all the creatures, O king.
Seeing the lotus-born ancient one called Brahman, they said: / The creatures said: / "O God, Lord of gods, source of the worlds, O supreme Lord!
Protect us from the powerful snakes of sharp fangs! / Day after day we see terror, O God, deeply miserable as we are.
Men, beasts, birds, and the rest—all of that turns to ashes! / The creation was made by you, O God, but it is being destroyed by the serpents.
Knowing this, do what is proper, O Grandfather!" / Brahmā said: / "I shall provide protection for you all, there is no doubt.
Go to your dwellings, free from sickness and rid of fear." / Thus all the creatures [were reassured] by Brahmā of manifest form.
Having praised the self-born one, they went away exceedingly pleased. / When the creatures had thus departed, summoning those serpents,
exceedingly enraged, he cursed them, with Vāsuki at their head: / Brahmā said: / "Day after day creatures are devoured by you vile souls;
bitten by snakes, men as well as beasts perish. / Because you constantly bring to destruction men who originate from me,
therefore, by my exceedingly terrible wrath, in another existence / let there be a terrible destruction of you in the future Vaivasvata interval!
Likewise another king, born of the Lunar lineage, Janamejaya, / will burn you in the blazed sacrificial fire with a snake sacrifice.
And Tārkṣya, the son of your mother's sister, will devour you. / Thus will be the destruction of all of you of wicked minds!"
Having cursed a thousand families so that only a single family remained, / when this was spoken by Brahmā, the foremost serpents, trembling,
falling at his feet, then spoke these words: / "O Lord, creator of all beings, crooked is our species;
excessive venomousness, cruelty, and the very nature of serpents / were brought about by you, O god; why do you curse us now?
Brahmā said: / If indeed you were created by me with crooked dispositions, / then why do you constantly devour [creatures] in large numbers, free of remorse?
The serpents said: / Establish an order, O Lord of gods, and separate realms [for each]; / make an agreement, O god, between men and ourselves.
By the curse which was given by you, the mortal Janamejaya / will cause our violent destruction through a snake-sacrifice.
Brahmā said: / There will be [a sage] renowned as Jaratkāru, foremost among knowers of the Veda; / a maiden of old age must be given to him, and a son will be born from her.
That brāhmaṇa, the purifier of your family, will protect you; / and I shall establish an agreement for the serpents along with human beings.
Therefore, all of you listen attentively to my command: / Sutala, Vitala, and thirdly Talātala—
these three kinds of dwellings have been granted to you; you shall go there. / Enjoying manifold pleasures there in accordance with my command,
dwell there repeatedly until the seventh age. / Then, at the beginning of the age of Vaivasvata, there will be a son of Kaśyapa,
an heir to all the gods, Suparṇa, the devourer of serpents. / Then the offspring of serpents will be burnt by the Fire-god.
And [this destiny] will certainly befall all of you; there is no doubt. / Those serpents who are cruel and undisciplined will meet their end; it cannot be otherwise.

Devour a creature when it is overtaken by its time, and a human being when harm has been done to you. / But toward mortals who are protected by mantras, herbs, the rites of Garuḍa, and protective charms,
you must act with fear, and harbor no other thought in your minds, or else destruction will come to you. / When this was spoken by Brahmā, all the serpents went to the realm named Sutala.
They all dwelt enjoying pleasures, staying at ease in Rasātala. / Having thus received both a curse and a favor from the Four-faced One,
they dwelt in their abode in the netherworld with gladdened hearts. / Then, after some time had passed, they again thought in this way:
“There will be a renowned king descended from Bharata, a descendant of Pāṇḍu, / who will cause our destruction through some decree of fate.
"How did the lord of the three worlds, the grandfather of all, / the creator of creation, adored by the world, place a curse upon us?"
Leaving aside the god Virañci, no other refuge is found; / that god resides in the excellent abode of Vairāja.
That god, abiding at Puṣkara, is currently performing a sacrifice; / having gone there, let us propitiate him; pleased, he will grant a boon.”
Thinking thus, all those serpents went to Puṣkara; / having reached the sacrificial mountain, they took shelter by the mountain ridge.
Seeing the serpents thus exhausted, streams of cool water, / flowing northward, emerged, bestowing delight upon all.
Thence arose the sacred site Nāgatīrtha on the earth, O bull among the Bharatas; / some call it Nāgakuṇḍa, and others call it a river.
It is sacred among all tīrthas, destroying the poison of serpents; / mortals who bathe there on the fifth lunar day of the bright half of Śrāvaṇa—
serpents will never cause affliction in their families. / The men on earth who perform an ancestral offering to the ancestors there,
Brahmā will grant them the supreme abode; there is no doubt in this. / Knowing the fear of the serpents, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
then recited to the serpents the words he had previously spoken. / That fifth lunar day is auspicious, destroying all sins and bringing welfare,
since on that very auspicious day the deliverance of the serpents was accomplished. / On this [tīrtha], whoever completely renounces pungent and sour foods,
and bathes the serpents with milk, achieves their friendship. / Bhīṣma said: / How Śivadūtī was born, and by whom she was installed—
all of that according to the truth you ought to tell me. / Pulastya said: / Śivānī reached the Blue Mountain, having resolved her mind on ascetic austerity;
she was the fierce power born from the matted hair [of Śiva]; hear her vow, O king: / “Having performed austerity for a long time, I shall devour the entire world!”
With this intention, that passionate woman practiced the five-fire penance. / Then, after some time had passed as the goddess performed that supreme austerity,
there was an asura of great splendor named Ruru, who had received a boon from Brahmā. / In the midst of the ocean is a very wealthy city named Ratnapura;
there dwelt that lord of the daityas, who struck terror into all the gods, / worshipped by many hundreds of thousands and hundreds of crores of foremost asuras,
the glorious one, like a second Namuci. / Then, after a long time, he went to the city of the world-guardians.
Desirous of victory, surrounded by an army, he chose enmity with the gods. / As that great asura rose up, the water of the ocean surged violently,
inhabited by many serpents, sea-monsters, and fish, flooding the slopes of the mountains; / containing within it numerous hosts of enemies of the gods, brilliant with varied armors and weapons,

a formidable army set in motion, with handsome warriors, emerged expansive from the waters of the ocean. / There elephants, mounted by daitya soldiers, equipped with bells and conveyances, and endowed with magnificence,
marched out, clearly displaying in their forms an equality with huge fish. / Likewise, horses bound with golden cords, like rohita fish at the water’s edge,

arrayed along with them, quickly marched out by hundreds of thousands and crores. / Likewise, chariots equal in speed to the chariot of the sun, fitted with wheels, staffs, axletrees, and bamboo poles,
their bodies secured upon mechanisms, with fluttering banners, made a loud roar. / And warriors standing on boats, desiring to cross, with excellent weapons in hand,
victorious in battle after battle, striking hard, shone brightly, following the asura in great numbers. / When the gods were in enmity and especially when they fled,
the asuras pursued all the gods in every direction. / Then all the hosts of gods, fleeing and overwhelmed with fear,
went to the excellent Blue Mountain where the goddess herself was staying, / the fierce, blessed, supreme power of Śambhu, endowed with austerity,
the goddess who brings about dissolution, whom they know as Kālarātrī. / Seeing the gods terrified and bewildered at that time,
the goddess with eyes like fully blossomed lotuses asked in wonder: / “Behind you I see no danger that has approached;
why have the gods, with Śakra at their head, all fled?” / The gods said: / “Here comes Ruru, the lord of the daityas, of terrifying prowess,
surrounded by a great fourfold army; / miserable because of him, we have sought you, O goddess, as our refuge.”
Hearing this speech of the gods, she laughed aloud; / as she laughed, fair-limbed women emerged from her mouth,
all holding nooses and goads, with plump, prominent breasts, / all bearing tridents, terrible, with fangs and hook-like faces,
all wearing diadems, biting their lips, / terrifying the moving and unmoving world with inauspicious hissing roars;
some wearing white garments, others wearing multicolored garments, / some with dark blue attire, extremely eager to drink blood.
With diverse forms and faces, bearing various disguises and bodies, / surrounded thus by them, the goddess granting fearlessness to the gods,
"Fear not, O gods, may it be well with you!" While she was speaking, / Ruru the Dānava arrived with a fourfold army.
The seeker of the path of the gods, seeing that excellent blue mountain, / and seeing the army in front of the gods distraught by the goddess,
those Daityas arrived shouting, "Stand, stand!" / Then a dreadful battle commenced between them.
Of the Daityas whose bodies were split by iron arrows crawling on the ground, / slithering like serpents broken by sticks in their fury;
their hearts split by spears, their chests crushed by maces, / their heads severed by axes, their skulls crushed by pestles,
their bellies pierced by the tips of tridents, their necks cut off by excellent swords, / the infantry, together with their struck horses, chariots, and elephants, fell in battle.
All the Daityas reached the battlefield, except Ruru. / Then, seeing his force destroyed, Ruru resorted to illusion.
The goddesses and the gods were bewildered by it on the battlefield. / Through the tāmasic illusion of the goddess, everything became blind darkness.
Then the goddess struck that Daitya with a great javelin; / and struck by it in battle, the darkness of the Daitya vanished.
When the tāmasic illusion was destroyed, the Dānava Ruru / quickly entered Pātāla. There too the supreme goddess,
together with the goddesses, stood enraged facing him. / And as Ruru, lord of the Dānavas, went terrified before her,
having severed his head with the tip of her fingernail and seized his hide, she swiftly / flew up from Pātāla and returned to Mount Puṣkara.
With a great host of maidens, multiform and radiant, / she was seen by the astonished gods carrying the hide and head of Ruru.
The supreme goddess seated herself at her own place of asceticism. / Then the glorious goddesses stood surrounding her.
Undistracted but famished, they begged of that goddess: / "We are hungry, O goddess; grant us excellent food."
Having spoken thus, the goddess then contemplated food for them; / but though she reflected, she could find no great food for them.
Then she meditated upon Mahādeva, Rudra, the omnipresent Paśupati; / and he, the three-eyed Supreme Self, rose from meditation.
Rudra said to that goddess: "What is the matter you wish to speak of? / Speak, O goddess Mahāmāyā, what is on your mind!"
Śivadūtī said: / "O God, within the goat you dwell in the form of a goat; / these [goddesses] will respectfully devour you as their desired food.
You ought to give something here for their nourishment, O Lord of gods; / these mighty ones, desiring food, will impale me on a spike.
Otherwise, famished as they are, they may even devour me by force. / Therefore, considering my plight, provide food at once!"
Rudra said: / "O Śivadūtī, I shall relate one incident that occurred in a previous cosmic age: / At Gaṅgādvāra, the sacrifice of Dakṣa was demolished by my retinues.
There, the sacrifice, having become a deer, ran away with great speed. / It was pierced by me with an arrow and drenched in blood.
Then it smelled like a goat, and my name was made by the gods: / 'You indeed smell like a goat.' But I shall grant another food.
Hear from me, O goddess, one food suitable for them as told by me, / O woman of beautiful hips, O Kālarātri of great splendor!
Whatever pregnant woman, O ruler of gods, wears the garment of another woman, / or touches it, especially that of a man,
that shall be the share, O woman of beautiful hips, of some on the surface of the earth. / Seizing by force even a one-year-old child there,
let them remain well-pleased, devouring it even for many hundreds of years. / Others, when unhonored, should seize their opportunity in the birthing chamber.
They shall dwell thus, O ruler of gods, as destroyers of newborn infants / in the house, in the field, by the pool, and in wells and gardens.
And entering the bodies of those women who constantly weep excessively, / some shall obtain satisfaction."
Śivadūtī said: / "Vile is what has been given by you, afflicting creatures! / You do not understand how to give, O Śaṅkara, especially with relish.
That which is shameful and torments creatures / is not fit to be given as food to them, O Śaṅkara."
Rudra said: / "Formerly in Avantī, when Skanda was blessed by me, / when the tonsure rite of Kumāra took place, O auspicious lady,
the mothers, arriving, prepared an unprecedented feast; / from heaven the hosts of gods came to eat with the mothers.
Formerly, in their house, Brahmā and the other best of gods, / Gandharvas, Apsarases, and all the Yakṣas and Guhyakas,
mountains such as Meru, rivers such as the Gaṅgā, / all Nāgas, elephants, Siddhas, birds, and destroyers of asuras,
Ḍākinīs with Vetālas, surrounded by all the planetary spirits then— / what need of saying more, O goddess, whatever was created by Brahmā here—
all that was given as food, but the food desired by themselves did not reach them." / Śivadūtī said: / "Grant them prepared food that is rare even in heaven,
smeared with oil, with jaggery, delightful, well-cooked, / which has never been eaten elsewhere by another, unprecedented, O supreme lord!"
Thus addressed, the god of gods, Maheśvara, / spoke to them for the sake of food in the presence of Pārvatī:
"Food was prepared by me, made in many ways; / all of that has been exhausted, and nothing else is seen here.
Now that you have arrived, tell me what I should give: / something unprecedented for you that I should especially grant,
untasted by anyone else, I shall give as food: / in the lower part of my navel, these two round, fruit-like,
hanging testicles of mine—eat them together! / And by this food there will be supreme satisfaction."
Having obtained the great favor, all those goddesses bowed down to Śiva / and stood there, and Śarva spoke this word:
"Those men who will perform the auspicious rites without mockery— / their wealth, cattle, sons, wives, house, and so forth,
shall be granted by me, as well as whatever else is in their mind. / Through mockery, they will become long-toothed and poor.
Therefore, censure and mockery should not be made by one who understands. / You shall be known as the Mothers in this world.
Those men who will perform the Kaumudī festival with offerings / of chickpeas, pūrikās, and cakes along with testicle-shaped breads,
with relatives and their own folk, their lineage will never be broken. / The childless shall obtain a son, and one desiring wealth shall obtain wealth;
handsome, fortunate, enjoying pleasures, skilled in all sciences, / he is exalted in the world of Brahmā in a chariot yoked with swans.
O Śivadūtī, thus was nourishment granted by me to them. / Why did you call me 'shameful'? Hear that now:
Be victorious, O goddess Cāmuṇḍā! Be victorious, O remover of evil spirits! / Be victorious, O all-pervading goddess! O Kālarātri, salutations to you!
O you who possess universal forms, pure one, deformed-eyed, three-eyed one! / O terrible-formed, auspicious one, wisdom, Mahāmāyā, large-bellied one!"
O conqueror of the mind, O fortress of the mind, O terrible-eyed one, O destroyer of agitation, / O Mahāmārī of varied limbs, O lover of song and dance, O auspicious one!
O Vikarālī, O Mahākālī, O Kālikā, O remover of sin, / O you holding a noose in hand, holding a staff in hand, holding dread in hand, O terrifying one!
O Cāmuṇḍā, O you with a flaming mouth, sharp-fanged and mighty, / O goddess fond of jackal mounts, seated upon a corpse, O Śivā!
O terrible-eyed, O fearsome goddess, O cause of terror to all beings, / O Karālī and Vikarālā, O Mahākālī, O Karālinī!
O Kālikarālavikrāntā, O Kālarātri, praise be to you! / O goddess bearing all weapons, praise be to you who are saluted by gods!
Praised in this way by Rudra, the Supreme Lord, / the supreme goddess, Śivadūtī, was pleased and spoke these words:
“Choose a boon, O Lord of the gods, whatever is in your mind.” / Rudra said: / “O goddess, those who praise you with this hymn, O fair-faced one,
be a grantor of boons to them, O goddess, being all-pervading and true. / Whoever ascends this mountain and worships with devotion,
let him be endowed with sons, grandsons, and cattle, and attain prosperity. / And whoever listens with devotion to this hymn of the goddess's origin,
let him, freed from all sins, attain supreme nirvāṇa. / When a king has fallen from his kingdom, restrained and pure on the ninth,
the eighth, and the fourteenth lunar day, fasting, O best of men, / let him regain his kingdom without obstacle within a year.
This power endowed with wisdom is indeed called Śivadūtī. / Whoever constantly hears this with supreme devotion, O king,
freed from all sins, shall attain supreme nirvāṇa. / And whoever recites this with devotion, having bathed in the waters of Puṣkara,
having obtained all this fruit, is exalted in the realm of Brahmā. / In whatever house this written [text] always stays, O king,
there is no dreadful danger of fire or of all kinds of thieves and the like. / And whoever, O wise ones, worships this existing in a book with devotion,
by him the entire threefold world with moving and unmoving beings is worshipped. / Many sons, wealth, grain, and excellent women are born to them,
and jewels, horses, elephants, and servants swiftly accrue to them. / In whatever house this is copied, there too it will surely be so.”

title: dvātriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Bhīṣma said: / “By the ripening of what deed does one become a ghost again, / or by what may one be freed here? Tell me that, O highly intelligent one.”
Pulastya said: / “I shall tell you all of this in full, / upon hearing which you shall not fall into delusion again, O best of kings;
by what deed one becomes a ghost, and by what one is freed from this, / [and how one] attains a terrible hell that is hard to cross even for the thirty [gods].
In conversation with good people, and in recounting the sacred pilgrimage sites, / human beings who have fallen into ghostly states are indeed freed.
Indeed, it is heard that formerly, O Bhīṣma, there was a brāhmaṇa of strict vows, / named Pṛthu, renowned everywhere and always established in contentment.
Devoted to Vedic study in his home, ever in yoga, a knower of yoga, / he would spend his time engaged in the method of muttered prayer and sacrifice.
Engaged in forgiveness and compassion, and endowed with forbearance, a knower of reality, / with his mind intent on non-violence, he was established likewise in gentleness.
Endowed with celibacy, possessed of the yoga of asceticism, / he was engaged in rites for the ancestors and engaged in Vedic rites.
Possessed of fear of the next world, dedicated to truthful speech, / dedicated to pleasant words, and dedicated to the worship of guests,
Devoted to sacrifices and charitable works, engaged in abandoning pairs of opposites, / devoted to the rites of his own duty, engaged in the duties of Vedic study,
As he was thus performing deeds with the desire to overcome worldly existence, / many years passed for that virtuous brāhmaṇa in his house.
This thought arose in him concerning visiting holy pilgrimage sites: / ‘With the holy waters of pilgrimage sites I shall bathe this body.’
Restrained, having bathed at Puṣkara at the rising of the sun, / having performed his prayers and salutations, he set out upon the path.
Ahead, he saw five extremely terrifying men / in a forest filled with thorny trees, desolate, devoid of birds.
Seeing them of deformed appearance, most terrible, and sinful to behold, / with his heart somewhat alarmed, he stood motionless.
Then, gathering courage and casting fear far away, / speaking sweetly, he asked: ‘Who are you, deformed? Whence [are you]?
Or what deed was done by which you have attained deformity? / Why have all of you, being of such a kind, set out, and on what path?’
The ghosts said: / ‘Constantly filled with hunger and thirst, overwhelmed by great misery, / all of us are bereft of understanding, unconscious, and confused.
We do not know any direction or intermediate direction, / nor the atmosphere, nor the earth, nor do we know heaven.
This misery that has been described might itself be happiness. / Morning shines forth here at the sight of the rising sun.
I am named Paryuṣita, and the other is Sūcīmukha; / Śīghraga, Rohaka, and the fifth is Lekhaka.’
The brāhmaṇa said: / ‘Whence comes the existence of names for ghosts born from deeds? / Referring to what cause are you endowed with names?’
The ghosts said: / ‘I would always eat delicious food and give stale food to a twice-born; / taking this as the cause, my name is Paryuṣita.
Many brāhmaṇas desirous of cooked food and the like were pointed out [spitefully] by this one; / referring to this cause, he is considered named Sūcīmukha.
I went away swiftly when begged by a hungry brāhmaṇa; / referring to this cause, O best of the twice-born, [I am] Śīghraga.
On the roof of the house he always eats delicious food out of fear of the twice-born; / there, with an agitated mind, on that account he is recalled as Rohaka.
And always established in silence, when begged, he would scratch the earth; / most sinful among us, by name he is named Lekhaka.
With difficulty Lekhaka moves, while Rohaka has his head downwards; / Śīghraga has attained lameness, and the needle-like one became Sūcīmukha.
Paryuṣita is called long-necked and large-bellied; / with large testicles and hanging lips he was born from this sin.
All this of our own conduct together with the cause has been related to you. / Ask if you have faith, and being questioned we will speak.’
The brāhmaṇa said: / ‘All living beings that abide on the earth are rooted in food; / I wish to hear truly of your food as well.’
The ghosts said: / ‘Hear about our food, despised by all living beings, / hearing which you will censure it again and again, O brāhmaṇa, constantly.
With phlegm, urine, feces, and the dirt from women's limbs, / in houses where purity is abandoned, the ghosts indeed eat there.
In [houses] ruined by women, scattered, where leftover food is thrown about, / and disgusting with filth, the ghosts indeed eat there.
In those devoid of conscience and shame, and those devoid of burnt offerings, / and those devoid of vows, the ghosts indeed eat there.
Where teachers are not worshipped, in houses dominated by women, / and in those seized by anger and greed, the ghosts indeed eat there.
Shame arises in me, dear one, when our food is being described; / and beyond this, nothing else can even be spoken.’
"We ask you about the cessation of the state of a ghost, O you of firm vows! / Tell me that, O ascetic, so that one does not become a ghost."
The brāhmaṇa said: / "By the one-night, two-night, and other penances, by the Cāndrāyaṇa and so forth, / and by other observances performed regularly, a person is not born a ghost.
Whoever day by day serves the three fires, or five, or even one, / full of compassion for living beings, that person is not born a ghost.
Equal in honor and dishonor, equal towards gold and a clod of earth, / equal towards enemy and friend—such a person is not born a ghost.
Constantly devoted to the worship of gods and guests, and to the worship of elders, / and indeed devoted to the rites for the ancestors, a person is not born a ghost.
When a fourth day of the bright fortnight falls on a Tuesday, / one who performs the ancestral offering on it with faith is not born a ghost.
He who has conquered anger and reflection, who is free from thirst and attachment, / forgiving and of a generous nature—such a person is not born a ghost.
And whoever bows down to cows, brāhmaṇas, sacred bathing-places, mountains, rivers, / and indeed to the deities, that person is not born a ghost."
The ghosts said: / "We have heard of various dharmas; now, afflicted, we ask, O sage: / tell us, O wise one, by what deeds one indeed becomes a ghost."
The brāhmaṇa said: / "Especially by eating the food of a śūdra: / if a brāhmaṇa dies while it is still in his belly, he certainly becomes a ghost.
He who abandons mother, father, brothers, sister, and son / when no fault is seen in them—that person is born a ghost.
By officiating at sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice, and by abandoning those fit to sacrifice, / and devoted to the service of a śūdra, that person is born a ghost.
A stealer of deposits, a betrayer of friends, one always fond of cooking for śūdras, / a destroyer of trust, a deceitful man—such a person is born a ghost.
A killer of a brāhmaṇa, a cow-slayer, a thief, a drinker of liquor, a violator of the guru's bed, / and a stealer of land or a maiden—such a person is born a ghost.
Having obtained a shared sacrificial fee, he hides it away alone; / devoted to atheistic thoughts, he indeed is born a ghost."
While the foremost brāhmaṇa was speaking thus, a sound of kettledrums resounded in the sky, / and a shower of flowers fell upon the earth, released by the thousands by the gods.
Celestial chariots arrived on all sides for the ghosts, / on account of conversation with this brāhmaṇa and the recitation of what is meritorious.
"Therefore, with every effort, converse with the virtuous, / if you are concerned with your highest good, O son of Gaṅgā, without sloth.
The mark of all dharma is this story of the five ghosts; / whoever recites it a hundred thousand times—in his family no man is born a ghost.
Or if one hears it constantly, endowed with supreme faith / or filled with devotion, that person is not born a ghost."
Bhīṣma said: / "For what reason is Puṣkara praised in the sky / by sages endowed with dharma? And how is it attained here?
By whom it is attained, how it was attained, and how, once attained, it bears fruit— / tell me all that, as I ask purely out of curiosity."
Pulastya said: / "Ten million ṛṣis residing in the southern lands arrived / for the purpose of bathing at Puṣkara, O king, but Puṣkara had gone into the sky.
Reflecting on that, all those sages, devoted to breath-control, / meditating on the supreme Brahman, remained for twelve years.
Brahmā, the great ṛṣis, and the gods headed by Indra gathered there; / the ṛṣis, having disappeared from sight, spoke of their very difficult vows:
'Let the invocation of Puṣkara be performed with a mantra, O twice-born! / Through the three Ṛg-verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā", it will become present.
And through the chanting of the Aghamarṣaṇa, it will become fruit-yielding.' / At the end of the speech, all those brāhmaṇas did exactly so.
By what they performed and by the command, those twice-born attained purity; / those brāhmaṇas from the south and the north were censured in the dharmaśāstras,
as well as others from the mountains, not worthy of an invitation to an ancestral rite. / For this reason, O king, it remained thus in the sky.
On the full-moon day of Kārttika, Puṣkara attains purification through bathing, / accompanied by Brahmā, O king, granting merit to all.
Whichever castes come there, they all become vessels of merit, / equal to the twice-born without a doubt, [even] without the mantra, O king.
When the asterism belonging to Agni occurs on that full-moon day of Kārttika, / that lunar day is to be known as great, supreme for bathing and gift-giving.
When the asterism belonging to Yama occurs on that lunar day, / that lunar day is also declared by ascetics to be of great merit.
When the asterism sacred to Prajāpati occurs on that lunar day, O ruler of men, / that is called Mahākārttikī, rare even for the gods.
And when it falls on Sunday, Thursday, or Monday—indeed on these three days of the week— / these three asterisms have been proclaimed by Brahmā himself.
Here, the merit of a horse sacrifice certainly accrues to one who has bathed; / a gift becomes imperishable, and likewise the water libation to the ancestors.
When the sun is in the Viśākhās and the moon is in the Kṛttikās, / that conjunction is named Puṣkara, exceedingly rare at Puṣkara.
When the auspicious sacred place of the Grandfather descends from the sky, / those who bathe there will attain exalted worlds.
They will have no desire for other merit, whether performed or unperformed, / O great king; this is spoken as the truth.
It is recited here as the foremost sacred place among sacred places on earth; / no sacred place more meritorious than this is recited in the worlds, O king.
Especially on the full-moon day of Kārttika, it is auspicious, purifying, and sin-removing; / and the Sarasvatī came forth from that forest of Udumbara trees.
By her that sacred place of Puṣkara, frequented by sages, was filled. / In the south, not far away, shines the peak of the mountain,
resembling a heap of dark collyrium, blue with grassy turf in color; / by her that peak stands as if it were Puṣkara situated in the sky,
resembling a dense mass of clouds rising up, filling the sky in the rainy season, / rich with the fragrance of kadamba flowers, adorned with kuṭaja and arjuna trees,
standing as if to ascend the path of the chariot of the sun, / like the breasts of women, rounded, thrill-swollen, and smooth.
The peak shines with delightful bilva fruits on all sides, / embellished all around with swarms of humming bees,
lovely with the calls of cuckoos, resplendent with the calls of peacocks. / On that enchanting peak arose the most charming,
auspicious river, endowed with holy waters, the daughter of Brahmā; / very broad, she issued from a cluster of bamboos, flowing toward the north.
Having gone not very far from there, she again turns her course away; / from then on, that goddess remained gracious and visible.
Abandoning concealment out of compassion for living beings, / [she became] Kanakā, Suprabhā, Nandā, and the eastward-flowing Sarasvatī.
She was declared by Brahmā as five-streamed at the Puṣkara sacred places. / On her banks are very delightful sacred places and temples,
frequented on all sides by sages and by perfected beings as well; / among all of them, the Sarasvatī will be the cause of dharma.
The giving of gold, land, and cows at those sacred places brings great elevation; / given by men who have bathed, it produces an imperishable fruit.
The foremost sages proclaim the giving of grain to be supreme, and likewise the giving of sesame; / whatever was given by men at those sacred places is designated as supreme, the cause of dharma."
Whichever woman or man, restrained and with effort, observes fasting unto death there, / or fixes their mind on that sacred ford, enjoys at will the fruit in Brahmā's abode.
Those motionless and moving beings who die in its vicinity due to the exhaustion of their karma / all easily obtain the entire fruit of sacrifice, which is otherwise difficult to attain.

Therefore, she is the fire-drill producing the fruit of dharma for those whose minds are tormented by sorrows such as birth; / with all one's being, this great river Sarasvatī, yielding lovely fruits, should be diligently frequented by men.
Those men who continually drink her pure water there / are not mere humans; they are gods abiding here on earth.
The fruit that is attained by twice-born men through sacrifices, gifts, and austerities, / is attained here by Śūdras, by their very nature, through merely bathing.
Even those who are great sinners, merely by seeing Puṣkara, / are freed from their sins and go to heaven upon the dissolution of the body.
The fruit that belongs to the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice is obtained by a man / who fasts there at Puṣkara, quickly and with little exertion.
He who in the month of Māgha gives sesame seeds to a good twice-born man / according to his means and with devotion, shall dwell in the abode of Viṣṇu.
Whatever man undertakes fasting, bathing, and consuming the five products of the cow there, / he too shall attain heaven at the end of his body.
Even those belonging to classes of thieves who dwell in its vicinity / go to heaven by its power, without any doubt.
Furthermore, those men engaged in the occupation of Śūdras who fast for three nights / and bestow wealth upon twice-born men, endowed with the power of Brahman,
when dead, ascend a celestial vehicle, seated on a lotus, four-armed, / and attain companionship with Brahmā, without returning to rebirth.
[Now hear of] the confluence of the Gaṅgā, where the Gaṅgā arrived to see the best of rivers, / the Sarasvatī, which had emerged from the sky for the sake of peace.
Having gone there, the pure water of the Sarasvatī, frequented by gods and Siddhas, / spotless, and venerated by the hosts of Vidyādharas,
was drunk in the measure of a handful by him by whom the highest was attained. / Looking toward the eastern quarter, [Sarasvatī] said: 'O friend Gaṅgā, by you
I am left alone, separated [from you]; where shall I go, bereft of kin?' / Knowing her to be thus weeping, emaciated by grief,
the Gaṅgā came from the eastern country to see her who was dejected in mind; / and seeing that illustrious, afflicted [river], embracing her,
and wiping her eyes, the Gaṅgā then spoke these words: / 'Do not weep, O illustrious one! A difficult deed was performed by you, my friend,
namely the purpose of the gods, which indeed could never have been done by another. / Therefore, O illustrious one, the gods have come to see you;
worship should be offered to them by action of speech, mind, and body.' / Sarasvatī, having performed the ritual sequence of worship to the chiefs of the gods,
gradually, the daughter of Brahmā then met with her group of friends. / Between the eldest and the middle [Puṣkara] is that confluence, renowned in the world.
The daughter of Brahmā faces west, but the Jāhnavī faces north. / Then all those gods who had arrived at Puṣkara,
recognizing her difficult deed, sang a hymn of praise to her: / 'You are discernment, you are intellect, you are Lakṣmī, you are learning, you are the supreme path;
you are faith, you are the highest steadfastness, wisdom, intelligence, delight, forbearance; / you are accomplishment, you are svadhā and svāhā, you are deemed the great purifier;
you are twilight, night, luster, prosperity, wisdom, faith, Sarasvatī; / you are the sacrificial knowledge, the great knowledge, and the auspicious esoteric knowledge;
you are logic, economic livelihood, and what is called the science of governance. / Salutations to you of holy water! Salutations to you who flow to the ocean!
Salutations to you, the deliverer from sins! Salutations, O goddess, dear to the world!' / Having thus been praised by those divine beings intent on their own purpose,
that goddess Sarasvatī stood there, facing east— / the goddess consisting of all sacred fords, accompanied by all the immortals.
She is to be known by the wise as Prācī, and so is the declaration of Brahmā. / There the sacred ford named Śuddhāvaṭa, sacred to Brahmā, is remembered.
Even those who are great sinners, merely by seeing it, / purified, enjoy the pleasures of celestial beings near Brahmā.
Those best of men who observe fasting unto death there, / when dead, go to heaven free from fear in a celestial vehicle of Brahmā.
Even a small gift given there by them to those who know Brahman / is as if given by those purified souls for a hundred future births.
Those men who carry out repairs on broken and cracked [structures] there, / having reached the world of Brahmā, rejoice, ever happy.
Whatever worship, silent recitation, and fire oblation is performed here by embodied beings, / all that fruit is endless for those devoted to the worship of Brahmā.
Through the offering of a lamp there, one acquires the eye of knowledge transcending the senses; / through the offering of incense, one attains the abode frequented by Brahmā.
Or what is the use of speaking much? Whatever is given at the confluence / is declared to bear endless fruit, whether for the living or for the deceased;
from bathing, silent recitation, and fire oblations, it brings about endless fruit. / Rāma indeed came there and offered the funeral ball for Daśaratha,
and performed the ancestral rite there at the place shown by Mārkaṇḍeya. / There is a square stepped-well there; those men who offer funeral balls there,
all go to heaven in a celestial vehicle yoked with swans. / At that stepped-well, Brahmā indeed performed the funeral sacrifice,
a sacrifice with excellent sacrificial fees completed, being the best of sacrifice-knowers. / The Vasus are to be known as the fathers, the Rudras as the grandfathers,
and the Ādityas are designated as their great-grandfathers. / Having summoned all three groups, Viriñci spoke again:
'You should always receive the offering of funeral balls and the rest, abiding here; / and whatever ancestral duty is performed here shall bear endless fruit.'
For their sustenance, their fathers and grandfathers are gratified; / through the libation of water they obtain satisfaction, and through the offering of funeral balls, heaven.
Therefore, setting aside everything, one should offer funeral balls at Prācīna; / having given them with effort, a son should satisfy all the ancestors.
Established in front of Lord Prācīneśvara, / it is called the Primordial Ford, granting liberation merely upon being seen.
Having merely touched the water there, one is freed from the bondage of birth; / by bathing, one becomes an eternal attendant of Brahmā.
Having bathed at the Primordial Ford, whatever man offers food with concentrated mind, / even a little, shall generally attain heaven.
Whatever man, having bathed there, gives wealth to those devoted to Brahmā, / even with dish of rice and lentils or with gold, rejoices happy in heaven.
When the Prācī Sarasvatī is present there, what higher thing can men seek? / From bathing in her comes fruit yielding satisfaction, marked by austerities, sacrifices, and the like.
Those men who drink the holy, eastern goddess Sarasvatī / are not to be known as men, but as gods—so declared sage Mārkaṇḍeya.
Having reached the river Sarasvatī, there is no restriction regarding bathing anywhere— / whether having eaten or not eaten, by day or at night.
That ancient ford is remembered as the most excellent of all fords; / it is celebrated as destroying sin and generating religious merit for living beings.
Moreover, those purified souls who, having bathed there, / worship Janārdana according to their capacity, go to heaven.
Viṣṇu is foremost among the gods; where Sarasvatī was honored by him, / that is the supreme sacred ford on earth: so said the son of Brahmā.
Therefore, regarding that great sacred ford as bringing great fortune, / looking out for the Mandākinī, Sarasvatī remained there.
Svāyambhuva declared that sacred ford to be supreme among all sacred fords, / where a holy junction is obtained together with the Mandākinī.
Remaining in that place, goddess Sarasvatī was praised by the gods; / seeing her alone, with a dejected face and a depressed mind,
Brahmā then created a female companion endowed with beauty, with pure eyes. / Hari also quickly produced Hariṇī, lotus-eyed.
The lord of the gods, wielder of the thunderbolt, also created Vajriṇī. / The god Nīlakaṇṭha, whose emblem is a bull, with the grace of a fine deer,
The three-eyed god produced a companion for Sarasvatī. / Looked upon by her companions, O king, she was a celestial beauty.
delighted, began to flow by the command of the gods, the great river; / then, together with her companions, she set out to flow eastward.
Sarasvatī is remembered as the very best among all of them. / Whichever deer on earth drink the water of the eastern Sarasvatī—
they too will go to heaven, just like the best of the twice-born through sacrifices. / Here this eastern Sarasvatī is to be known as like a wishing-jewel;
likewise, this great river has become the source of desired fruit. / Looking toward the southern quarter, she turned her face westward again.
Thus was she addressed by Gaṅgā: 'Go to the eastern direction; / and do not forget me, O goddess; go as you have arrived.'

title: trayastriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Bhīṣma said: / How indeed was Rāma instructed here by Mārkaṇḍeya? / How did the meeting take place, at what time, and when, O sage?
Whose son was Mārkaṇḍeya of great austerities, and how was he born? / Tell me the origin of his name as it truly happened, O great sage.
Pulastya said: / Now I shall tell you the origin of Mārkaṇḍeya once more. / Formerly, in a past cosmic age, there was a renowned sage named Mṛkaṇḍu.
The son of Bhṛgu, highly fortunate, practiced austerities together with his wife. / A son was then born to him while living in the forest.
When he became five years old, a child endowed with excellent virtues, / he was seen wandering in his courtyard by a wise man.
Having stood for a very long time, he perceived what was to happen. / He was indeed asked by his father: 'How long is the lifespan of my son?'
'Count and declare his years, whether they be few or many.' / Thus addressed by Mṛkaṇḍu, that wise man spoke these words:
'The lifespan of your son ordained by the Creator is six months, O best of sages; / you must not grieve; this which is stated is true.'
Hearing that statement spoken by the wise man, O Bhīṣma, / the father then performed the sacred thread ceremony for the child.
And the father said to the son: 'Pay your respects to the sages.' / Thus addressed by his father, he was delighted in offering salutation.
He knew no distinction of classes, saluting everyone of all classes. / Five months and twenty-five days passed by.
Then seven sages came along that path; / they were seen by that child, and all of them were saluted.
'May you be long-lived,' said they to that child carrying a staff and wearing a girdle. / Having spoken thus, they again saw that the child's life was exhausted.
Knowing that his lifespan was five days, they were frightened, O king; / taking that child, they went into the presence of Brahmā.
Presenting him, O king, they bowed down before the Grandfather. / He was announced by them, and Brahmā was saluted by him.
The boy was told, 'Be long-lived,' by Brahmā in the presence of the sages; / then those sages were delighted, having heard the word from the Grandfather.
Seeing the sages, the Grandfather spoke, filled with wonder: / 'For what purpose have you come? Announce who this boy is.'
Then, O king, those sages reported everything to him: / 'He is the son of Mṛkaṇḍu, whose lifespan is exhausted; endow the boy with life.'
'Knowing he was short-lived, the sage bound this girdle on him, / gave him the sacred thread and a staff, and instructed him:'
"Whomever you see, child, wandering as a person upon the surface of the earth, / to him respect must be offered": thus spoke his father to him.
'Given to saluting, he was seen roaming on the earth / in the course of a pilgrimage to sacred fords, by the decree of fate, O Grandfather.'
"May you have a long life, my son!"—so was that boy addressed there: / "How might our words come true together with you?
Thus addressed by them then, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, [said]: / 'This earth is established on truthful words, free from fear on every side.'
Brahmā said: / 'The child Mārkaṇḍeya will be equal to me in lifespan; / at the beginning and at the end of a cosmic age, he shall be considered the best of sages.'
Thus those sages, having accomplished it from the Grandfather in the world of Brahmā, / sent the boy back again to the surface of the earth.
The Brahmins departed on their pilgrimage; Mārkaṇḍeya went to his own home; / when they had departed, he then spoke to his father:
'I was taken to the world of Brahmā by sages who proclaim the Absolute; / I was granted long life, given boons, and dismissed.'
'This and another boon have been granted to me; the cause of your anxiety is gone: / at the beginning and at the end of a cosmic age, I shall exist continuously thereafter.'
'By the grace of Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, O father, / I shall go to Puṣkara, determined to practice austerities.'
'There I shall worship the Grandfather, the lord of the gods, / who grants all desires and slays all enemies,'
'the god who gives all happiness, the refuge of Indra and the others; / I shall propitiate Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds.'
Hearing the words of Mārkaṇḍeya, Mṛkaṇḍu, the best of sages, / felt the highest joy, sighing with relief for a moment.
Maintaining resolve with a delighted mind, he spoke these words: / 'Today my birth is fruitful, and my life is well-lived,'
'since the Grandfather, the creator of all the worlds, was seen. / Through you, a son who sustains the lineage, I possess an heir.'
'Go, see the Grandfather, the lord of the gods residing at Puṣkara; / when that lord of the universe is seen, old age and death are no more,'
'men obtain joys, sovereignty, and imperishable austerity. / There are three white peaks and three waterfalls,'
'and likewise three Puṣkaras; we do not know the reason for it: / the younger, the middle, and the third, Senior Puṣkara.'
'There are summits bearing names and auspicious streams; / the three—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—are ever present there.'
'At the Puṣkaras, O great king, there is nothing holier on earth; / its dust-free, pure water is renowned across the three worlds.'
'The fortunate behold Puṣkara as the path to the world of Brahmā. / He who tends the sacred fire for fully a hundred years,'
'or dwells at Puṣkara for a single full moon day of Kārttika—these are equal; / that which could not be done by me, nor accomplished by action,'
'that all-destroying death has effortlessly been conquered by you, son; / there you have seen that lord of the gods, Brahmā, grandfather of the worlds.'
No other mortal like you will ever exist upon the surface of the earth, / by whom, with an existence of merely five years, I indeed have been pleased.
By my boon you will become the standard of comparison / for long-lived ones, there is no doubt; such is my blessing.
Speaking thus, they all said, "Go to whatever worlds you desire!" / And by the son of Mṛkaṇḍu, who had thus obtained their grace,
a hermitage was established by him, called the Mārkaṇḍa Hermitage. / Having bathed there and become pure, one obtains the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice.
Cleansed of all sins in soul, a person becomes long-lived. / Pulastya said: / So I shall relate to you another ancient legendary history,
how indeed the sacred ford Puṣkara was constructed by Rāma. / Formerly, Rāma, [departing] from Citrakūṭa with the princess of Mithilā and Lakṣmaṇa,
arrived at the hermitage of Atri and inquired of that best of sages. / Rāma said: / "Which are the holy fords, or what is the sacred place, O great sage,
having gone to which a man never suffers separation from his kinsmen, / O yogin, O blessed one? Tell me that, O you of virtuous vows!
By this dwelling in the forest, and by the death of the king, / and by separation from Bharata, indeed I am tormented by these three."
Hearing that speech spoken by Rāghava, the bull among brāhmaṇas then, / having meditated for a very long time, spoke this word:
Atri said: / "Well asked by you, O hero, increaser of the Raghu lineage! / There is a sacred ford made by my father, renowned by the name of Puṣkara.
Two mountains are famous: the Maryādā and Yajña mountains. / Between the two lies a triad of pools: the eldest, the middle, and the youngest.
Having gone to them, satisfy Daśaratha with an offering of rice-balls! / It is the best ford among fords, and the highest among sacred places.
There is the step-well Aviyogā ('Non-separation') and Surasā, O bearer of the Raghu race, / as well as another, the Saubhāgya well ('Well of Good Fortune'), with sweet water, O joy of the Raghus.
By offering rice-balls in them, the ancestors attain liberation / until the time of the dissolution of the elements: this the grandfather [Brahmā] proclaimed.
Go there, O Rāghava, and let your return [home] be accomplished!" / Saying "So be it," Rāma directed his mind toward departure.
Crossing the Ṛkṣavant mountain and the city of Vidiśā, / and having crossed the Carmaṇvatī, he reached the Yajña mountain.
Having passed beyond it swiftly, he stayed at the middle Puṣkara. / He gratified his ancestors and all the gods with waters.
At the conclusion of the bath, the wise Rāma saw / the bull among sages, Mārkaṇḍa, arriving there accompanied by disciples.
Having gone before him and bowed down with reverence, / he asked: "In which direction is the well that bestows non-separation, O lord?
I am the son of Daśaratha, remembered by people by the name of Rāma. / I have arrived by the command of Atri to behold that step-well of good fortune.
Let the venerable lord tell me that place and the two wells." / Addressed thus by Rāma, Mārkaṇḍa replied:
Mārkaṇḍeya said: / "Well done, Rāghava, good fortune to you! A virtuous deed has been done by you, / since on the occasion of pilgrimage to holy fords you have arrived here now.
Come, come, behold that step-well that grants non-separation! / And non-separation from all indeed arises at this well,
in the next world and in this one, whether one is living or dead." / Hearing this speech of the lord of sages, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa,
Rāma, then remembered King Daśaratha, O king, / and Bharata along with Śatrughna, his other brothers, and the citizens.
While he was contemplating in this manner, the evening twilight arrived. / Having observed the evening twilight along with the sages, Rāghava
slept that night there, accompanied by his brother and wife. / At the end of the night, as the dream drew to a close, the joy of the Raghus [saw]:
He was dwelling in Ayodhyā along with his father, mother, and others; / during the marriage festivities, with many relatives,
he sat with his wife, surrounded by sages. / Lakṣmaṇa too saw in the very same way, and so did Sītā.
In the morning, all of that was reported to the sages. / And by the ṛṣis he was told: "So it is; this is true, O best of the Raghus.
Upon seeing one who has died, a śrāddha is remembered as obligatory to be performed. / The ancestors, desiring prosperity and craving food,
grant a vision in a dream to one endowed with devotion, O Rāghava. / And your non-separation from your brother, father, and Bharata
will surely happen, O Rāghava, after fourteen years. / Therefore perform the śrāddha of King Daśaratha, O hero!
And all these ṛṣis are devoted to you and ready: / I, and Jamadagni, and Bhāradvāja, and Lomaśa,
Devarāta, and Śamīka—these six are indeed the best of twice-borns. / Bring forth the materials for your śrāddha, O mighty-armed one:
chiefly ingudī oil-cake, together with jujube and āmalaka fruits, / ripe bel fruits, and many diverse roots.
And with venison and various grains, / give satisfaction to the brāhmaṇas through the gift of śrāddha, O you of virtuous vows!
Having reached the forest of Puṣkara, self-restrained and on restricted food, / he who satisfies the ancestors would obtain [the fruit of] a horse sacrifice.
We, however, are going to the eldest Puṣkara for bathing, O Rāma." / Having spoken thus to Rāghava, all those sages departed, O king.
And Rāma said to Lakṣmaṇa: "Bring me a sacrificial deer, / and a hare with clear eyes, black vegetables, and honey,
chief lemons, various roots, / and ripe wood-apples, and whatever other fruits there are.
Fetch those quickly for the śrāddha, Lakṣmaṇa!" / And Rāghava did all that according to Rāma's command.
Jujube, ingudī, greens, and various roots: / having gathered them there, a huge heap like a mountain peak was made by Rāma.
And it was cooked thoroughly and prepared by Jānakī, and presented to Rāma. / Having bathed in the Yoga step-well, Rāma waited for those sages.
When the sun had passed midday, at the time of kutapa, / all the ṛṣis who had been invited by Rāma arrived.
Seeing those sages arrived, Vaidehī, the daughter of Janaka, / left Rāma's side and, feeling bashful, stood elsewhere,
her eyes wide with wonder, contemplating, and trembling. / The brāhmaṇas did not know that she had withdrawn at the time of the śrāddha.
The brāhmaṇas were fed by Rāma according to the rules declared in the Smṛti, / and all the Vedic rites of hospitality that are prescribed were performed,
as well as the procedure taught in the Purāṇas, preceded by the Vaiśvadeva rite. / When the brāhmaṇas had eaten, having offered rice-balls in due order
and given them sacrificial fees according to his ability, they were dismissed. / When the foremost brāhmaṇas had departed, Rāma said this to his beloved:
"Why did you run away, O fair-browed one, upon seeing the sages arrived here? / Tell me without delay the whole truth of this reason."
"There must be a reason, so do not conceal it from me. / You are adjured by my life and Lakṣmaṇa's, O lady of pure smiles!"
Addressed thus by her husband, standing with face cast down in embarrassment / and shedding tears, she spoke these words to Rāghava:
"Listen, my lord, to the kind of wonder seen here! / While you were meditating, O Rāma, the king of kings arrived here,
along with two others likewise adorned with all ornaments. / Those three entered into the bodies of the twice-born, O scion of Raghu;
the ancestors were seen by me, O Rāghava, within the limbs of the brāhmaṇas. / Seeing them, I was filled with bashfulness and retreated from your presence.
The brāhmaṇas were indeed fed by you, and the śrāddha was performed according to rule. / Clad in bark and deer-skins, how could I appear before the king?
"How could I, O slayer of enemy warriors? This truth is stated. / And the silk garments were taken away by Kaikeyī,
and ever since then I have been clad in bark, sheltered in the forest. / Knowing this, I said nothing, so that you would not feel sorrow.
I do not think of my mother, nor of my father, O scorcher of foes! / 'When will there be an end to this forest dwelling, O Rāghava?'—
As she continuously reflects upon this very thing again and again, O Rāma, / her days pass away, O lord; I swear by your feet.
How could I give this food with my own hand to the king, / [food] such that even a servant of servants would never consume anywhere?
How could one such as I dare to serve him, / I who was formerly seen by the king adorned with every ornament,
holding a whisk in hand and fanning the ruler of men? / Besmeared with sweat and dirt, how could I look upon the king?
Evidently he has attained heaven, delivered by you, his son. / Seeing me, an innocent young woman, grieving and afflicted in the forest,
there would be sorrow for this monarch; because of that I vanished, O Rāghava. / You are as dear to me as life, Rāma; nothing is to be hidden by me from you here.
And in truth of that, I touch your feet." / Hearing that, Rāghava was delighted with his sweet-spoken beloved.
Drawing her to his lap, embracing her firmly and tenderly, / the two heroes then ate the food, and afterwards Jānakī ate.
Remaining thus that night there, the two descendants of Raghu, / when the thousand-rayed sun arose, set their minds on departing.
Going westward for a krośa as far as Jyeṣṭha Puṣkara, / while Rāghava was staying in the eastern part of Puṣkara,
he heard words spoken by a messenger of the gods: / 'O Rāghava! Hail to you! This sacred place is very hard to attain.
Remaining in this place, O hero, make yourself pure! / You must perform the business of the gods; the enemies of the gods are to be slain.'
Then the hero, with a delighted mind, spoke words to Lakṣmaṇa: / 'O Saumitri, I have been favored by the god of gods, Brahmā.
Having made a hermitage site here for one month, O Lakṣmaṇa, / I wish to perform an observance, the supreme purification of the body.'
When Lakṣmaṇa agreed saying 'So be it,' completing the observance, / with gifts such as offering rice balls and with śrāddhas to his forebears,
Rāma then duly made offerings of water to his ancestors at Puṣkara. / Kanakā, Suprabhā, and Nandā, the eastward Sarasvatī,
the five streams in the Puṣkaras that grant satisfaction to the ancestors; / having performed that daily worship of the ancestors beginning with the fathers,
Rāma then said these words to Lakṣmaṇa: / 'Come, Lakṣmaṇa, quickly fetch water from Puṣkara;
having washed our feet, take rest on the bed of grass. / When the night has passed, we will go to the southern region.'
Lakṣmaṇa, however, spoke these words: 'Let the water be brought by Sītā! / I will not be your servant at all times, Rāma!
She is well-nourished, extremely robust, and dear to me as well. / What will you do with this wife? Tell me now!
Or will this beloved of yours follow behind you when you are dead? / You always protect her, well-nourished at all times.
She is joyful, yet constantly troubles me, O best of the Raghus! / And you trouble me, Rāma; in the next world harm will arise [for you].
For your sake I constantly endure thirst together with hunger, / without doubt; and observe the hereafter!
No one is seen following behind those who are dead— / neither wife, nor son, nor wealth; so say the wise.
Your father died, Rāma, leaving behind an unobstructed kingdom / and casting you into the forest to please Kaikeyī.
Here Kaikeyī remained, and the wealth, and all the kinsmen; / the great king Daśaratha went to his destination all alone.
I think Sītā will certainly not go along with you [in death]. / What will you do with her? Tell me now, O Rāghava!'
Hearing the speech spoken by Lakṣmaṇa, never heard before, / Rāghava stood downcast, and so too Sītā of fair countenance.
Whatever Lakṣmaṇa said, Sītā performed it all. / Then the two heroes, with eyes like lotuses, bathed and ate at Puṣkara;
having spent the night there, they set their minds on departing: / 'Come, arise, Saumitri; we will go to the southern region.'
Saumitri said: 'Rāma, I will not go by any means. / Go along with this wife, O lotus-eyed one!
I will not go to another forest, nor to Ayodhyā, O Rāghava; / I will dwell in this forest for fourteen years.
If you do not return to Ayodhyā without me, / then by this path you must return, O king, O lord!
If I am alive at that time, I will go back to my father's city; / I will practice austerities. What will you do with me?
Go, gentle one; auspicious is the path; may there be no highway robbers for you! / May I see you returned again with your wife, O lotus-eyed one!
The ancestral kingdom is in Ayodhyā, O king of men; / both Śatrughna and Bharata abide in carrying out your commands.
I am contrary to you, especially in this forest-dwelling; / ceaselessly by day and by night, O scorcher of foes,
I am unable to do the work. Go happily, gentle one!' / To Saumitri who was speaking thus, the scion of Raghu said:
'How did you set out formerly from Ayodhyā with me, [saying,] / "I will live in the forest, Rāma, for nine and five years;
separated from you, I would not live anywhere, even in heaven; / whatever destination is yours, O tiger among men, that will be mine as well.
Show favor to me, take me also, O Rāghava!" / How can you stay now halfway along the path, O slayer of foes?'
Lakṣmaṇa, however, said to Rāma: 'I will not go into the forest again.' / Knowing Lakṣmaṇa was resolute, Rāma said these words:
'Do not follow me, Saumitri; I will go alone to the forest, / with this Sītā as my second.' Thus spoken to by Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa,
taking heed of Rāma's words, then arose; / the two scorchers of foes reached the boundary mountain, the border of the sacred field,
and bowing with eight-limbed prostration before the lord of the gods, Ajagandha, / the god of gods, bearer of the Pināka, the three-eyed one, Rāma [worshiped him].
Standing devoutly, his hair bristling with awe, / joining his palms in supplication, he praised Śaṅkara, the beloved of Pārvatī.
Attaining a purely sattvic state, with passion and darkness shaken off, / he recognized the god, the sovereign of the wise, the cause of the worlds.

Rāma said: / He who is the creator of the entire world, moving and unmoving, and gives joy and sorrow for what is done, / and who is also the cause of destruction at the time of the end—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

He who once, upon his head, bore the Gaṅgā falling from the sky like a garland of trembling flowers, / with her pure, lovely, surging waters and rough with great waves—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

When the peak of Mount Kailāsa was violently shaken by the Ten-necked [Rāvaṇa], who resembled a horn of Kailāsa, / it attained stability when held down by his lotus foot—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

By whom the sons of Danu were repeatedly struck down in battle, and hosts of Vidyādharas and Uragas were endowed with all boons, / as were the best of sages living on fruits and roots—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.
Who knocked out Bhaga's eyes at Dakṣa's sacrifice and also the row of Pūṣan's teeth, / and who paralyzed Indra's arm bearing the thunderbolt—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

Relying on whom even people who commit sins, whose minds are attached to sensual pleasures, / and who lack the virtues of wisdom, noble lineage, and learning, become enjoyers of bliss—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

The son of Atri [the Moon] whose brilliance equals ten million suns, a terror to the best of gods and Dānavas; / who violently drank the blazing Kālakūṭa poison—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

The lord Maheśa who would grant many a boon to Brahmā, Indra, the Rudras, the Maruts, and the Six-faced [Kārttikeya], / and who rescued Nandi from the jaws of death—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

Propitiated with intense asceticism in a bower of the Himālaya through the smoke vow, inaccessible even to the minds of others, / the great soul explained the Saṃjīvanī lore to Bhṛgu—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

Who is worshipped by various mighty chiefs of Gaṇas having faces like elephants and cats, the destroyers of Dakṣa's sacrifice, / and by hosts of gods together with the world-protectors—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

Who, mounting a noble bull white as a conch, the moon, and jasmine, followed by the daughter of the king of mountains, / traverses the sky adorned with dissolution-clouds—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

When the tranquil sage was being dragged away by those terrifying, dreadful men intent on executing Yama's command, / he bowed in devotion, absorbed in praise, and was forcibly saved by him—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

The god who with the tip of his left lotus-hand's nail violently severed, in the very presence of the gods, / that fifth head of Brahmā, which resembled a fresh lotus—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

Bowing with devotion at whose feet, the giver of boons, and praising him with pure words, unwearied in spirit, / the radiant Vivasvat dispels darkness with his rays—to that Śaṅkara, the refuge-giver, I go for refuge.

Those foolish men who do not recognize you, the guru of the foremost gods, of this world moving and unmoving, / because of the lingering impression of pride in their mastery of the Vedas, later endure torment, their minds impure.
As he was thus praising him, the bearer of the trident, whose banner is the bull, / delighted, his mind pleased, spoke these words to Rāghava:
Rudra said: / O Rāma, I am pleased, may blessings be upon you! You are born in a spotless race, / and you too are a god deserving the worship of the worlds, having assumed a human form.
With you as their protector, the gods shall indeed be happy for perpetual years; / they will serve [you] for a long time when the fourteenth year has passed.
The mortals on earth who shall see you when you have returned to Ayodhyā / shall enjoy happiness here and an imperishable dwelling in heaven.
Having accomplished a great work for the gods, you may return to the city. / Bowing to the god accordingly, Rāghava departed swiftly.
Reaching the river Indramārgā and fastening his matted locks, / Rāma said to Lakṣmaṇa: 'Hand me this bow.'
Hearing that word of Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa spoke to Sītā: / 'For what reason, O Queen, have I been abandoned by Rāma without any cause?
I know of no offense, yet the mighty-armed one is angry. / Abandoned by Rāma, I shall undoubtedly give up my life.
I have no need for life! Fie, fie upon me, the defiler of the family, / by whom, a doer of evil, wrath has been aroused in the noble one!
To what worlds shall I go, cursed by the great-souled one?' / Placing both hands over his face, his throat choked with tears, he said this:
'I commit no offense against Rāma in deed, mind, or speech. / I have touched your feet, O Queen; I have no other refuge.'
Then Sītā said to Rāma: 'Why have you abandoned your younger brother? / Let harshness be given up toward the youth Lakṣmaṇa, who increases fortune.'
Rāghava said to Sītā: 'I will not abandon Lakṣmaṇa; / never, even in a dream, is Lakṣmaṇa's intention contrary, my beloved.
And I had heard previously, O fair-hipped one, the working of this sacred place: / in this sacred place, truly, all people are devoted solely to their self-interest.
They do not look out for one another or heed words beneficial to themselves. / Sons do not listen to their father, nor do fathers listen to their sons.
Disciples indeed do not listen to the word of the guru, nor the guru to that of the disciple; / affection is bound up with self-interest, and no one is dear to anyone.'
Speaking thus, the descendant of Kakutstha reached the great river Revā, / and took his ritual bath together with his younger brother and Sītā.
and having gratified his ancestors and deities with libations of water, / composed in mind, he repeatedly looked toward the sun and the deities.
Having performed his bath, Rāma, that king of kings accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, / shone like the blessed Lord Īśa, who has bathed with the Daughter of the Mountain and Guha.

title: catustriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Bhīṣma said: / At what time did the blessed Brahmā, the maker of the world, / begin to sacrifice with sacrificial materials? You should tell that, sir.
What were the names of those officiating priests whom Brahmā appointed? / And what fee was given to them by that great soul?
Recount it to me as it happened and as it came to pass. / A very great curiosity has arisen in me regarding the ancestral sacrifice.
Pulastya said: / It was told by me earlier how Svāyambhuva Manu, / having created all the Prajāpatis, was told: 'Perform creation.'
He himself went to Puṣkara, gathered the array of the sacrifice, / assembled the sacrificial implements, and remained in the fire-sanctuary.
Gandharvas sang constantly, and hosts of Apsarases danced; / the Brahmā, the Udgātṛ, the Hotṛ, and the Adhvaryu were the four bearers of the sacrifice.
And three other assistants were assigned to each one of them by himself: / the Brahmā, the Brahmaṇācchaṃsin, the Potṛ, and the Āgnīdhra.
The inquiry into all knowledge—this is indeed the set of four pertaining to the Brahmā. / The Udgātṛ, the Pratyudgātṛ, the Pratihartṛ, and the Subrahmaṇya:
this is proclaimed as the second set of four, belonging to the Udgātṛ. / The Hotṛ, the Maitrāvaruṇa, and likewise the Acchāvāka,
and the Grāvastut as the fourth here—this is the third set of four. / The Adhvaryu, the Pratiṣṭhātṛ, the Neṣṭṛ, and likewise the Unnetṛ:
this is declared to be the fourth set of four, O son of Śaṃtanu. / These sixteen are indeed proclaimed as priests by the knowers of the Vedas.
Three hundred and sixty sacrifices were created by the Self-born; / and they always appoint these brāhmaṇas for all of them.
Some also require an overseer of the assembly, and an Adhvaryu of the three Sāmans. / He made Nārada the Brahmā, and Gautama the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin;
Devagarbha the Potṛ, and Devala the Āgnīdhra; / Aṅgiras the Udgātṛ, and Pulaha the Pratyudgātṛ;
Nārāyaṇa is called the Pratihartṛ, and Atri the Subrahmaṇya. / In that sacrifice, Bhṛgu was the Hotṛ, and Vasiṣṭha the Maitrāvaruṇa;
Kratu was declared the Acchāvāka, and Cyavana the Grāvastut; / Pulastya was the Adhvaryu, and Śibi the Pratiṣṭhātṛ;
Bṛhaspati was the Neṣṭṛ there, and Śāṃśapāyana the Unnetṛ. / Dharma was the overseer of the assembly there, accompanied by his sons and grandsons.
Bharadvāja, Śamīka, Purukutsa, Yugaṃdhara, / Enaka, Tīrṇaka, Keśa, Kutapa,
Garga, and Vedaśiras were made the Adhvaryus of the three Sāmans; / Kaṇva and others as well, and Mārkaṇḍa and Gaṇḍi,
accompanied by sons and grandsons, with their disciples and kin, / performed the rites there day and night, unwearied.
When a Manvantara had elapsed, the concluding bath of the sacrifice took place. / The eastern direction was given as the priestly fee to the Brahmā, and the southern to the Hotṛ;
the western to the Adhvaryu, and the northern to the Udgātṛ. / Brahmā gave them the entire three worlds as the priestly fee.
And a hundred cows should be given by the wise for the success of the sacrifice; / but forty-eight to the main conductors of the sacrifice;
twenty-four are declared for those of the second rank; / and sixteen auspicious cows should be given to those of the third;
and twelve others he should cause to be given to the Āgnīdhra and the rest. / By this same proportion, villages, female slaves, goats, and sheep,
and food for a thousand should be given after bathing at the concluding bath of the sacrifice. / The sacrificer must give away all his possessions: so spoke the Self-born.
Gifts to the Adhvaryus and the members of the assembly are desired according to one’s wish. / And summoning Viṣṇu, Brahmā, filled with joy, spoke these words:
‘Having propitiated Sāvitrī, bring her here, O you of virtuous vows! / Seeing you, that fair-faced lady will not be angry.
With affectionate, concilatory words, especially reasoned ones; / you always speak sweetly; your tongue distils nectar.
No one who disobeys your word is seen in the three worlds. / Having gone together with the Gandharvas, bring my beloved back.
Propitiated by you, that virtuous, content lady will certainly come. / You must not delay; go, Mādhava, without delay!
Let auspicious Lakṣmī go before you to the abode of Sāvitrī; / follow in her footsteps and console my beloved:
“He does not desire to do anything displeasing to you, O goddess, in secret; / looking at your face, O beautiful lady, he always conducts his life.”
Many such sweet words of this kind / should be made known to the goddess, so that she will soon be pleased.’
Thus spoken to by Brahmā, the creator of the world, Viṣṇu / went quickly to where Sāvitrī was staying.
Seeing Keśava coming with his wife from afar, / she stood up quickly and was saluted by Viṣṇu:
‘Homage to you, O goddess of the ruler of gods! Homage to you, wife of Brahmā! / Having bowed to you, every person is freed from sin.
You are devoted to your husband, most fortunate, dwelling in the heart of Brahmā; / thinking of you day and night, he longs for your favor.
Ask this dear friend, Lakṣmī, the virtuous daughter of Bhṛgu, / if you do not believe my word, O fair-eyed lady!’
Having spoken thus, Śauri then touched both feet of Sāvitrī / with both hands, saying, ‘Forgive, O goddess! Homage to you!’
Touching [her feet], he praised [her], saying, "O one adored by the world, O mother of the world!" / Pulling back her feet with her own hand, the goddess [held] the hands of Hari.
took the hands of Hari and said to Viṣṇu, ‘Everything has been forgiven by me, O Acyuta! / This Lakṣmī, my child, shall always dwell in your heart;
without you she will never find pleasure elsewhere. / Born from the wife of Bhṛgu, this wife of yours is steadfast in her vows;
and by the effort of the gods and demons she was born again from the ocean. / Wherever the Lord is, there she incarnates:
in divinity she indeed has a divine body, and in humanity she is human; / your helper without a doubt, practicing the vow of matrimony forever.
Tell me, O Lord, what I should do here!’ / Viṣṇu said: / ‘The sacrifice has ended; I have been sent to you:
“Bring Sāvitrī quickly; she must perform the bath with me.” / Come quickly, O goddess; go there filled with joy;
having gone, behold your husband joined by all the gods!’ / Lakṣmī said: / ‘O noble lady, arise quickly! Go to where the Grandfather is!
Without you I will not go; your feet have been touched by me.’ / Raising her, she, the capable one, took her right hand in her right hand.
Perceiving that Sāvitrī was delaying, the divine Grandfather / then spoke this word to Mahādeva who was standing nearby:
‘Go together with this Pārvatī, O destroyer of asuras! / Let Gaurī go ahead of you; follow behind, O Śaṃkara.
Reason with her and bring her; do that which will make her come quickly!’ / Thus addressed, the two of them, Pārvatī and the Supreme Lord,
went as directed and spoke to the beloved of Brahmā: / ‘A great duty must be performed by you there, O devoted wife!
Ask this Gaurī of lovely hips, daughter of the mountain, / or this wide-eyed Lakṣmī, or Indrāṇī, O fair-faced lady!
Or ask whichever of them you trust, O goddess! Homage to you!’ / A blessing was given by her to the Trident-bearing god of gods:
‘And Gaurī will always reside in half of your body, O Śaṃkara! / You are adorned by her, O god, and she by you, O handsomest in the three worlds!
The entire world will share in happiness with you as protector, O slayer of foes!’ / As she was speaking thus, Sāvitrī, the beloved of Brahmā, was taken
by Gaurī by the left hand, and by Lakṣmī by the right hand. / And having saluted that goddess, Śaṃkara spoke these words:
‘Come, come, O most fortunate lady, to where your husband is! / Go there, O woman of lovely hips! The husband is the supreme refuge of wives.
You ought to go out of love at this great insistence, O goddess! / And this Lakṣmī and Pārvatī are standing before you, O goddess.
By their word, O goddess, and by ours, O fair-faced lady, / it is not fitting for you to maintain wounded pride, O beloved of Brahmā!’

"Besought by us, O goddess, go there filled with joy."

 Gaurī said:
"You always say yourself, O goddess, 'You are dear to me.'

Lakṣmī holds you by one hand, and you are held by me on your right.
Come, O highly fortunate one, to where your husband stands."

She was then led by the two of them, the goddess placed in the middle,
preceded by Viṣṇu and Rudra, and likewise the gods led by Śakra,

and the gandharvas and apsarases, the three worlds with the moving and unmoving.
And the goddess Sāvitrī, the beloved of Brahmā, arrived there.

Seeing fair-faced Sāvitrī, Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds,
together with Gāyatrī, spoke this word:

"This goddess is your servant; I stand under your control.
Command, O fair-hipped one, whatever deed I must do for you here."

Thus addressed by the god Brahmā himself,
the goddess cast down her face in shame and said nothing at all.

Prompted by Brahmā, the goddess Gāyatrī fell at her feet:
"I have committed an offense against you; forgive me, O goddess, homage to you!"

Embracing her respectfully by the neck, holding close the distressed
Gāyatrī, she consoled her: "He is my respected husband.

His word must be obeyed; for women, the husband is the lord of life.
So was it stated long ago by the blessed Viriñci at the time of creation:

'For women there is no separate sacrifice, no vow, nor fasting;
whatever word the husband speaks, she must perform without reproach.'

She who reviles her husband, or likewise reviles his sister,
or slanders or babbles against them, she indeed goes to hell.

While her husband is alive, the woman who performs a vow of fasting
takes away her husband's lifespan, and when dead, she goes to hell.

Knowing this, O virtuous one, you must not do what is displeasing to your husband,
nor must you ever serve his right limb.
