She enjoys heaven for as long as the dissolution of creatures lasts; / fallen from heaven, her husband becomes a sovereign king.
Becoming his chief queen, she subsequently finds happiness; / time and again heaven and royal power are theirs without doubt.
Having thus attained a hundred births, in the end liberation surely occurs." / The twice-born said: "Who is a devoted wife? What are her characteristics?
Tell me, tiger among the twice-born, so that I may know in truth." / Hari said: "A woman who loves her husband a hundredfold more than her son, and serves him as a king out of awe,
and sees her husband as Śauri—she is a devoted wife; / a maidservant in tasks, a courtesan in lovemaking, like a mother in offering food,
a wise counselor to her husband in times of distress—she is a devoted wife; / she who does not transgress her husband's command with mind, speech, or physical action,
who always eats after her husband has eaten—she is a devoted wife; / on whatever bed her husband sleeps with care,
there she continually worships her husband; / she never harbors envy, nor miserliness, nor is she arrogant;
she who looks upon honor and dishonor as equal—she is a devoted wife; / she who, seeing an attractive man, regards him as a brother, father, or son,
and as another [she is] a virtuous woman—she is a devoted wife; / go to her, tiger among the twice-born, and speak according to your desire.
Eight wives of his live there, and among them is a fair-complexioned woman, / endowed with beauty and youth, full of compassion, renowned,
known by the name Śubhā; having gone to her, ask about your welfare." / Having spoken thus, the Blessed One vanished right there.
Seeing his disappearance, the twice-born was then astonished; / and he, having gone to the house of the virtuous woman, questioned the devoted wife.
Hearing the guest's voice, the virtuous woman came out of the house in haste; / seeing the twice-born there, she stood at the doorway.
And seeing her, the best of the twice-born joyfully spoke these words: / "Tell me what is dear and beneficial to me, just as you have seen it."
The devoted wife said: "Right now I am serving my husband, and I have no independence; / afterwards I will attend to your matter; receive hospitality today."
The twice-born said: "In my body there is no hunger, nor thirst, nor exhaustion today; / speak my desired wish, auspicious one, or else I will place a curse upon you."
Then she said to him: "I am not the crane, best of the twice-born; / go to the righteous Tulādhāra and ask him about your welfare, twice-born."
Having spoken thus, that fortunate woman went inside the house; / there the twice-born saw a brāhmaṇa, as in the dwelling of a cāṇḍāla.
Having reflected, filled with astonishment, the twice-born went along with him; / and he saw that twice-born standing there with a glad heart.
Joyfully seeing that twice-born and that virtuous woman, he spoke: / "What happened in another land was indeed told by her!
How does the outcaste know my conduct, and how does the devoted wife? / Therefore I wonder, father; what is this supremely great marvel?"
Hari said: "The reason for everything is known, father, by the well-wishers of all beings, / because of supreme merit and virtuous conduct, which has made you astonished.
And what did she say to you? Speak that now, sage." / The twice-born said: "She directed me to ask the righteous Tulādhāra."
Hari said: "Come, tiger among sages, I will go to him." / And as Hari was walking, he asked: "Where is Tulādhāra situated?"
Hari said: "Where there is a crowd of people in the fair sale of many goods, / selling and buying here and there, is Tulādhāra.
Barley, essence, oil, and a heap of grain—people take everything / and give it right from his presence.
Even when the end of his life was at hand, abandoning truth, / a lie was never spoken by that best of excellent men; therefore he holds the scale of righteousness."
When this was said, he saw him selling many liquids, / a mortal bearing filthy mud, smeared with slime on the buds of his teeth.
speaking various words there concerning goods and wealth, / surrounded on all sides by mortals of many kinds, by women and men.
He addressed him with sweet speech, saying, "How, how? / Explain righteousness to me; I have come near you for my benefit."
Tulādhāra said: "As long as people remain in my very presence, twice-born, / so long I have no leisure, until the night watch.
Taking that instruction, go to Dharmākara; / concerning the fault in the death of the crane and the non-drying of the cloth in the sky,
you will know all of that there; go to Sajjanādrohaka; / there, through his instruction, your desire will bear fruit."
Having said this, Tulādhāra carries out buying and selling. / 'Likewise, dear father, I will go to him who harms good people.'
from Tulādhāra's direction, I do not know his dwelling." / Hari said: "Come, let us go; I will go together with you to his house."
Then, as they went along the path, the brāhmaṇa spoke to Hari; / the twice-born said: "For Tulādhāra there is neither bathing nor libation to gods and ancestors,
his limbs are smeared with dirt, and all his clothing is tainted; / how does he know what happened to me in another country?
Therefore I wonder, father; tell me the whole reason." / Hari said: "By truth and an equanimous mind, the three worlds have been conquered by him.
Through that, the ancestors and the gods together with the hosts of sages are pleased; / and through that, the righteous man knows what happened in the past and the future.
There is no higher duty than truth; there is no greater sin than falsehood, / especially for a man who is sinless and of an equanimous mind.
He whose mind becomes equal towards an enemy, a friend, or an indifferent person, / has all sins destroyed and attains union with Viṣṇu.
One who always conducts himself in this way delivers ten million kinsmen: / truth, self-restraint, tranquility, courage, steadfastness, absence of greed,
absence of astonishment, freedom from sloth—all these are established in him; / by that, the knower of duty knows entirely what happens
in the world of the gods and the world of mortals; Hari resides in his body; / there is no one equal to him in the world, equal in truth and uprightness,
and he is righteousness personified; by him alone the world is sustained." / The twice-born said: "Through your grace I have understood the cause regarding Tulādhāra."
"Tell what the conduct of Adrohaka was, if you please." / Hari said: "Formerly, a prince had a high-born wife in the prime of her youth,
like Kāmadeva's wife [Rati], or Vāsava's [Śacī]; / his wife was as dear to him as life, a beautiful woman named Sundarī.
Suddenly he had to set out on the king's business; / he pondered in his mind about her who was dearer than life itself:
'In what place can I leave her so that she will definitely be protected?' / Having considered this, he went in haste to that man's house.
And he spoke those words to him. Hearing them, he was amazed: / 'I am neither your father, nor your brother, nor your relative;
I am not a friend of her father's or mother's family. / How then, my friend, could you feel at ease with her staying in my house?'
Meanwhile, he replied with appropriate words: / 'In the world there is no one like you, who knows dharma and has subdued his senses.'
He [the host] said to him: 'Even knowing all, you should not speak faultily. / What man is capable of guarding a wife who enchants the three worlds?'
The prince said: 'Having examined [all men] on the earth, I came to you. / Let her remain in your house; I am going to my own residence.'
When this was said, he spoke again: 'In this splendid city / full of many lustful men, how can a woman be protected?'
And he said to him again: 'Protect her, and I shall depart.' / Out of a dilemma of duty, the householder said to the prince:
'I will do an improper act; serving you is proper and beneficial. / But such a wife must always stay in my house, my friend,
under god-like guardianship. Say if you desire this pleasing arrangement: / she must lie on my bed along with me and my wife.
If you regard your own [sense of] deity [as satisfied], let her stay; if not, let her go.' / Reflecting for a moment, the prince then said to him:
'So be it, my friend; do as you please.' / Then he spoke to his wife: 'Whatever is auspicious or inauspicious according to his word,
must be done; you bear no fault, by my command, O beautiful one.' / Having said this, he departed by the command of his father, the king.
Thereafter, at night, it was done just as said: / the righteous man always slept between the two women.
Even so, he did not stray from dharma. Between his own wife and the wife of another, / from touching his own wife, his mind felt desire;
but from contact with that [other woman], he regarded her as a daughter. / When her breasts repeatedly touched his back,
he thought of them as the breasts of a mother to a small boy, her son; / and when her limbs repeatedly touched his limbs,
he considered her day by day as a son [considers] his mother. / From then on, all intimate contact with his own wife ceased.
Thus, after half a year, her husband returned to the city / and inquired among the people about her conduct as reported.
Some informed him of good, though they, as young men, were quite astonished; / others said: 'Given by you, she sleeps with him.
From the joint contact of a man and a woman, how could there be composure? / Even if not asked, a young man would say that he desires her.'
By the power of his merit, he heard this ill report of the people; / to free himself from public slander, an auspicious thought occurred to him.
Gathering wood himself, he kindled a great fire. / At that moment, my friend, the glorious prince
came immediately to his house and saw him and the woman— / the woman with a beaming face, and the man sunk in despair.
Discerning their state of mind, the prince spoke these words: / 'Why do you not converse with me, a friend who has returned after a long time?'
He too, righteous and undamaged in mind, said to the prince: / 'The difficult deed that I performed for your sake,
I consider completely wasted because of the gossip of the people. / Today I will enter the fire; let men and gods watch.'
Having spoken thus, that illustrious one entered the fire; / as he entered the fire, there was not a flower [scorched] in the dwelling of his hair.
nor his limb was burned by the fire, nor his garment, nor a lock of hair. / In the sky all the gods joyfully cried: 'Well done! Well done!'
Showers of flowers fell upon his head from all around. / And on all those who had spoken evil words against those two,
various kinds of leprosy broke out upon their mouths. / Arriving there, the gods joyfully pulled him out of the fire.
Astonished sages worshipped him with lovely flowers. / When that very radiant man was thus honored by all the foremost sages
and by various people, he worshipped them all. / The name Sajjanādrohaka ('he who harms no good man') was bestowed on him by gods, asuras, and humans.
Purified by the dust of his feet, the earth became filled with crops. / And the gods said to the prince there: 'Receive your wife back.
An equal to him has never existed, nor will ever exist in the world; / at present there is no man on earth not conquered by lust and greed.
For gods, asuras, humans, rakṣasas, beasts, and birds, / and all creatures beginning with insects, this lust is very difficult to overcome.
It is born continually in living beings from lust, greed, and anger; / lust binds the cycle of existence; absence of desire is nowhere to be found.
By him alone have all the fourteen worlds been conquered. / In his heart Vāsudeva constantly abides with joy.
Thus by touching and seeing him, human beings are purified of all stain / and, becoming sinless, attain imperishable heaven.'
Having spoken thus, the gods joyfully departed to heaven in their celestial chariots; / the humans went their way contented, and the husband and wife went to their house.
Then divine vision was granted to him: he could see the gods, / and he easily understood the news of the three worlds fully.
Then along his path, he was seen together with him. / He asked him with joy: 'Speak on the instruction of dharma that is beneficial.'
Sajjanādroha said: 'Go, O brāhmaṇa who knows dharma, to the Vaiṣṇava Puruṣottama; / having seen him, what you desire will now bear fruit.
You know whether it is the death of the crane or the drying of the cloth, / and what other desire is situated in your heart.'
Hearing these words, he went towards the Vaiṣṇava; / he went joyfully together with that brāhmaṇa of the form of Viṣṇu.
He saw a pure man standing before him, blazing, / endowed with all auspicious marks, radiant with his own splendor.
That righteous man, recounting whatever had happened, / said to the beloved of Hari seated in meditation: 'I have come to you from afar.'
The Vaiṣṇava said: 'The best of gods, the enemy of the Dānavas, is always pleased with you. / Seeing you, our mind is filled with joy now, O brāhmaṇa.
Unrivalled welfare is yours today; your wish will bear fruit. / Your cloth constantly dries in the sky; it cannot be otherwise,
since you have seen the God, the best of the deities, Hari, abiding in my house.' / When the Vaiṣṇava had said this, he then spoke to him again:
'Where does that Viṣṇu always abide? Show Him today by your grace.' / The Vaiṣṇava said: 'Having entered into this delightful temple, the Supreme Lord—'

"Seeing him, you will be freed from terrible sin and from the bonds of rebirth."
Having heard his words, [the brāhmaṇa] entered the dwelling,

and saw Viṣṇu, that twice-born one, resting upon a lotus-bed.
Bowing with his head, he then joyfully seized his feet:

"Be gracious, O Lord of gods! I did not know you before.
Here and in the next world, O Lord of gods, I am your servant, O master.

Your grace has been seen by me, O Madhusūdana.
I wish to see your form, if there is mercy toward me."

Viṣṇu said:
"O earthly deity, I indeed always have affection for you.
Out of love, I have brought about the vision of virtuous people [for you].

By seeing, touching, meditating upon, praising, and conversing [with them],
even once, only the virtuous attain imperishable heaven.

Indeed, through constant association [with them], there is destruction of all sins;
and having enjoyed endless happiness, one dissolves into my body.

Having bathed at holy pilgrimage sites, and having seen me everywhere,
and having seen the lands of the virtuous, one dissolves into my body.

Having always recounted sacred stories in front of people,
that tiger among men dissolves into my body.

Fasting on my day, hearing my deeds with devotion,
and keeping a vigil through the night, one dissolves into my body.

Ever loudly proclaiming [my praise], with dance, song, instrumental music, and the like,
remembering the name, O best of the twice-born, one dissolves into my body.

You are my devotee and a sacred pilgrimage site. For the release from the sin
that arose from killing the crane, standing, O friend, he said:

'Go to the great-souled Mūka, a sacred pilgrimage site, the best among the virtuous.
By seeing Mūka, my dear, all great people have been seen.'

Only from seeing them, and likewise from conversing [with them], and from connection
with me, you have come to my home.

He whose sins have been destroyed through thousands of millions of births,
he, O knower of dharma, sees me, just as by that [devotion] grace is achieved.

It is only through my grace, O child, that I have been seen by you, O sinless one.
Therefore, choose a boon whatever is in your mind."

Mādhava said:
"Since such an understanding always shines in you, O sinless one,
therefore you shall attain enjoyments like mine in my abode.

However, your parents have not received worship from you, O sinless one.
Only after honoring your parents will you later attain my body.

By the breath of their sighs and by their anger, repeatedly and intensely,
your ascetic heat trickles away constantly; therefore, worship them, O twice-born one!

Upon whichever son the anger of his parents continually falls,
from that hell neither I, nor the Creator, nor Śaṅkara can save him.

Therefore, go to your parents; perform their worship with diligence.
Then, through the grace of those two alone, proceed to my abode."
When this was said, the best of the twice-born spoke again to the teacher of the universe: / 'If you are pleased with me, O Lord, show me your own form, O Acyuta.'

Then, out of love for the twice-born, pleased in heart and self-controlled,
friendly to brāhmaṇas, he showed his own form to the one dedicated to sacred rites:

Puruṣottama, holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus,
the cause of the entire universe, filling the universe with splendor.

Bowing like a stick, the brāhmaṇa spoke again to Acyuta:
"Today my birth has borne fruit; today my two eyes are auspicious.

Today my two hands are praiseworthy; blessed am I, O Lord of the Universe!
Today my ancestors go to the eternal world of Brahmā.

My kinsmen rejoice today through your grace, O Janārdana;
and now all my desires are fulfilled.

Yet I have great astonishment, O Lord: how do those wise ones, Mūka and the others,
know my history, which took place in another land?

In the interior space of his house stood an exceedingly radiant brāhmaṇa;
likewise in the house of the faithful wife, and on the head of Tulādhāra,

and likewise in the home of the harmless one, and you in the abode of the Vaiṣṇava.
Out of grace to me, O brāhmaṇa, you ought to tell me truly."

Adroha has conquered greed and lust, and is remembered as a Vaiṣṇava devoted to me.
Pleased with their virtues, I happily abide in their dwellings,

together with Bhāratī and Kamalā, O best among the twice-born."
The brāhmaṇa said:
"Men become extreme sinners from association with a great sinner:
Thus the knowers of dharma always speak in the treatises of traditional law, / in the Purāṇas, Āgamas, and Vedas; how do you stay in a house?'

The Blessed Lord said:
"Mūka is the doer of all good things in the three worlds.
Even if an outcaste is established in proper conduct, the gods know him to be a brāhmaṇa.

There is no one equal to Mūka in the worlds in terms of virtuous deeds.
Ever devoted to service of his parents, by him the three worlds have been conquered.

Pleased by devotion to the two of them, I, along with all the hosts of gods,
abide in the form of a brāhmaṇa in the space inside his house;

likewise in the house of the faithful wife, in the dwelling of Tulādhāra,
in the house of Adroha, and in the home of the Vaiṣṇava.

I always abide there, O knower of dharma; I do not leave for an instant.
Therefore, even other people who commit sins see me constantly.

And because of virtue, I was seen by you on account of my grace.
Devoted to serving his parents, pure, the outcaste has attained godhood.

Therefore, I dwell in his house with joy together with him;
again and again I converse [with him], O delight of the twice-born.

Unimpeded in thought, I always abide in his mind;
he knows your history, and so do the faithful wife and the others.

I will tell their deeds; listen in regular order,
hearing which a mortal is completely freed from the bonds of rebirth.

There is no holy pilgrimage site superior to a father and a mother among the gods of gods.
He by whom the worship of his parents is performed is himself the supreme man.

The command of parents is equal in fruit to the command of a god and the command of a guru.
From their worship [one attains] the kingdom of heaven; by harming them, one goes to Raurava.

He is in my heart, and I abide in his heart;
there is no difference between us; in the next world and in this one he is equal to me.

In my presence, in my delightful city, together with all his kinsmen,
he will enjoy inexhaustible pleasure, and in the end he will dissolve into me.

Therefore, indeed, that Mūka knows the news occurring throughout the three worlds,
O tiger among men! Whence is this astonishment of yours?"

The twice-born one said:
"Not having performed the worship of parents out of delusion or ignorance,
or having known [it], what good or bad is to be done, O Lord of the Universe?"

The Blessed Lord said:
"He by whom devotion to parents has been performed for a single day, a month, two fortnights,
half a fortnight, or a year, he shall go to my abode.

Having caused pain to their mind, one inevitably goes to hell.
Whether the worship of parents was performed or not performed formerly,

a man, having performed the release of a bull, obtains the fruit of devotion to parents:
food, clothing, cow-products, food with meat or without meat.

All that is given to kinsmen is said to be multiplied a hundred thousand times
by that wise son by whom an ancestral rite has been performed with all his possessions."
He attains recollection of previous births and reaps the fruit of devotion to the ancestors; / in the three worlds, indeed, there is no greater sacrifice than a śrāddha.
Whatever little is given here, one enjoys all of it imperishably; / know that [given] to another it is ten-thousandfold, and to kinsmen it is said to be a hundred-thousandfold.
In the case of a funeral ball of rice, it is said to be ten-millionfold; given to a twice-born, it is said to be endless; / so too in the water of the Gaṅgā, at Gayā, at Prayāga, and at Puṣkara,
in Vārāṇasī, at the Siddhakuṇḍa, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean. / Whoever offers an oblation of food [there]—liberation certainly belongs to him,
and the ancestors attain imperishable heaven, the fruit of his birth. / Especially on the Bhāgīrathī, whoever offers water with sesame seeds
attains the path of liberation; what then to say of the offering of funeral balls? / On riverbanks it is a-thousandfold, but on a great river it is held to be ten-thousandfold.
From combination with an ordinary fruit, the śrāddha becomes a-hundredfold. / On a new-moon day, on a yugādi day, and during an eclipse of the sun or moon,
whoever performs a pārvaṇa rite attains an imperishable realm. / All his ancestors are pleased for ten thousand years,
bestowing dear blessings and endless enjoyment upon the son. / Therefore, on a conjunction day, the pārvaṇa rite must be joyfully performed by sons.
Having performed this sacrifice for the two parents, one is released from the bondage of birth. / The śrāddha [performed] day after day is commemorated as the daily śrāddha (nityaśrāddha).
Whoever causes it to be performed with faith attains an imperishable realm; / and likewise in the dark fortnight, a śrāddha for specific desires according to rule.
Having performed it, he attains the desired object, or whatever is in his heart. / Taking the full moon of Āṣāḍha as the limit, the fortnight that is the fifth—
one should perform the śrāddha there, whether [the sun] has entered Virgo or not. / When the sun has entered Virgo, the sixteen days that follow
are equal to Vedic sacrifices completed with excellent sacrificial gifts. / This highly meritorious śrāddha for specific desires has arrived for him as auspicious.
If unable, one should perform it at the beginning of the dark fortnight when [the sun is] in Libra; / when the new-moon day enters Scorpio, the ancestors depart into despair.
They return to their own abode after uttering a very harsh curse; / by the curse of the ancestors, everything of the son is considered ruined.
Wealth, sons, fame, desired things, and life itself— / all these are obtained by human beings birth after birth
solely through the boon of the ancestors; therefore one should never abandon this. / Having performed the nāndīmukha rite at a marriage, a vow, a sacrifice, or the like, a twice-born
attains imperishable merit, and his lineage flourishes. / A man in whose case the opposite occurs goes to hell;
the destruction of his family occurs, and he lives a life of sorrow. / Then one should first worship Gaṇeśa, the son of Śambhu,
next the sixteen mothers, and after that the multitude of ancestors, / beginning with the paternal great-grandfather, among all the nāndīmukha ancestors.
In a nāndīmukha rite, the wise man should seat all the twice-born facing east; / he should pronounce the word "namaḥ" and elsewhere employ "svadhā".
Offering oblation-water and balls of rice during an eclipse of the moon or sun, / a man attains imperishable heaven and the increase of his ancestors' nourishment.
A man who does not bathe then, nor gives oblation-water and balls of rice / to the ancestors according to his capacity, goes to the state of a caṇḍāla.
Every gift is equal to [a gift of] land, all twice-born are equal to Vyāsa, / and all water is equal to the Gaṅgā when the moon is seized by Rāhu.
It is declared a-hundred-thousandfold during the moon, but a-millionfold during the sun; / when one has reached Gaṅgā water, it is ten million for the moon and a hundred million for the sun.
Whatever fruit comes from a hundred thousand cows properly given— / that same fruit is obtained by bathing in the Jāhnavī when the moon is seized by Rāhu.
And during an eclipse of the moon or sun, whoever plunges into the Jāhnavī / has bathed in all holy places; why should he wander the earth?
A solar eclipse on a Sunday, and likewise a lunar eclipse on a Monday, / is renowned as "Cūḍāmaṇi" (the Crest-Jewel); endless fruit is commemorated on that occasion.
The man who, having fasted on both of those [occasions] before, gives a funeral ball, water, and gifts at a holy sacred site, is established in the world of Satya.

The twice-born said:
Such a great sacrifice and śrāddha for the father has been declared by you; / O dear one, what should indeed be done by a son in the final time and afterwards?
And having done what is the highest good easily attained birth after birth / by an intelligent son? O Lord, you should kindly tell [me].

The blessed Lord said:
When early age is reached, the father is remembered as 'son', / and in the latter [age], the son is 'father', because of protecting, not indeed because of worshiping.
He should worship his father like a god, and show affection like to a son; / he should never transgress his command, even in his mind.
The son who remedies [the illness] of an afflicted father / attains imperishable heaven and is always worshiped by the gods.
Seeing the signs of death even of a father who is about to die, / the son, having performed a sacrifice, would attain equality with the gods.
Listen, I shall speak of the virtue of that wise son / who, by proper fasting alone, gives heaven to his father.
The merit of thousands of horse sacrifices and hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices / would accrue in [such] fasting; in a sacred site, it is multiplied ten million times over those two.
The supreme man who dies in the water of the Bhāgīrathī / will not drink the milk of a mother's breast; he reaches liberation.
He who voluntarily abandons his life-breaths in Vārāṇasī, / having enjoyed his desired fruit, dissolves into my body.
The state that belongs to sages joined with yoga, whose semen is drawn upward, / that state belongs to one who abandons life-breaths in the seven Brahmaputras.
Especially one who resorts to the northern bank of the Lohita / and abandons his life-breaths according to rule, attains equality with me.
And at the Urvaśīkeśa holy sacred site of that very [river], O best of twice-borns, / dead [there, he] is reborn, attains everything, and is not tainted by faults.
For him whose abandonment of life-breaths occurs inside a house, / for as long as a knot remains in the house, so long is there bondage for the body.
Year after year, one [knot] after another diminishes; / while his sons and kinsmen look on, there is no deliverance from bondage.
One who dies on a mountain, in a forest, in an inaccessible place, or in a waterless location, / meets an evil destiny and is born again as an insect and the like.
He whose funeral rite takes place on the following day after death / remains in the Kumbhīpāka [hell] for sixty thousand years.
If one dies impure from touching an untouchable, or as an outcaste, / he stays in hell for a very long time and is born among Mleccha castes.
Likewise, he is born among many insects and animal species; / therefore, after a long time, one should understand merit and demerit.
By merit and by the practice of merit of all who dwell in the mortal world, / whatever state occurs at the time of death for men, such a destiny comes to be.
He who dies at a holy sacred site while meditating on the names of Viṣṇu / is cleansed of sin, goes to heaven, and is not tainted by any faults.
The strong son who carries the body of his dead father / undoubtedly obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice at every step.
First, the son should apply fire to the mouth on the father's body on the pyre / according to rule, purified by mantras; then he should burn the body.
'Endowed with greed and delusion, enveloped in sin and merit— / may I burn all his limbs; may he go to divine worlds!'
Having burned [it], the son should then pass over to the collection of the bones; / when the tenth day arrives, he should abandon his wet garment.
Cutting the red cloth, he should cast it into fire or water; / and then on the eleventh day, the wise man should perform the śrāddha.
He should feed one brāhmaṇa for the nourishment of the dead person's body; / and he should properly give a gift of clothing, a seat, and sandals.
Along with all utensils, equal to land, elephants, horses, and the like, / he should give a black cow for freedom from all sins.
On the fourth day, in the third fortnight, at six months, and at the year's end, / and the twelve monthly ones—these are the sixteen śrāddhas.
For him for whom these are not performed here according to capacity and with faith, / his ghostly state is permanent, even by hundreds of offered śrāddhas.
For a year he should give a water-pot and food combined with meat, / and daily; out of non-existence, one should satisfy [them] by fasting for a month.
When the year has passed, the wise one, best of twice-borns, / should have the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa śrāddha performed according to the rule of the Pārvaṇa.
Impurity for a father is for a year, and for a mother it is six months; / for a wife, three months; and half of that for a brother and son.
Impurity belongs to sapiṇḍas as long as he stays in the house; / listen, O dear one, I shall state what is forbidden for the son:
Chaste and well-conducted, he should never go to a woman; / after seven ghaṭīs and before nine ghaṭīs,
that time is known as kutapa; what is given to the ancestors [then] is imperishable. / Three are purifying in a śrāddha: a daughter's son, kutapa, and sesame seeds.
And three they praise here: truth, freedom from anger, and freedom from haste; / evening twilight worship, food of another, eating again, intercourse,
giving, and receiving a gift—having performed a śrāddha, he should avoid [these]. / Having done a hundred improper deeds, the wise man should perform a śrāddha;
and it attains the status of an obligation, as declared by Viriñci himself. / Listen, O son, I shall tell an ancient tale of many [men]:
Having killed the cow of their guru, they offered a śrāddha and went to heaven; / and by merely recounting them, a śrāddha becomes imperishable.
The seven disciples of the sage Vasiṣṭha, brāhmaṇas of virtuous vows— / when the ancestral śrāddha arrived, the beloved sacrificial cow of their guru
was requested and taken home with joy by the seven brothers; / having deliberated and killed that cow for beef in the ancestral sacrifice,
they gave meat to a priest and fed the remaining vipras. / Having completed the ancestral rites, taking the calf, those twice-born
delivered [it] to their guru, [saying,] 'The cow has been eaten by a tiger.' / Then, knowing their action purely through the power of his asceticism,
he cursed those disciples then: 'You will become Cāṇḍālas!' / Trembling then, those vipras stood with folded hands:
'Givers of cow's flesh in the ancestral rite always, O sinless one, / doing thousands of improper deeds and great sins,
acting in matters of the ancestors, they went to heaven, purified from sin! / Much ancient [lore] of various kinds has been heard from your mouth, O master;
you ought to pardon us, O knower of dharma! Let an end to the curse be ordained!' / Vasiṣṭha said: 'Your curse is according to your sin, not from a deliberation of dharma.
Born as Cāṇḍālas and the like, you will remember what happened previously; / and there will be no loss of knowledge for you, nor destruction of the Smṛti text.
Having crossed over the sinful birth, afterwards you will go to liberation.' / Then, having cast off their life-breaths due to the guru's curse, those twice-born
were born in a Cāṇḍāla womb, all endowed with knowledge; / breast milk was not drunk by them, remembering that previous birth.
Having died, they all were born as deer, and again in the forest as cakravāka birds; / then, O twice-born, they were born as white geese at the sacred site of Mānasa.
About to die, those fortunate ones died out of sorrow; / at that time there was a great king remembered as Dharmaketu.

Then, accompanied by his wife and retinue, he went to the holy place to bathe. / Then, through delusion, the three swans, thinking of kingdom, enjoyment, women,

and foods, departed at that time to another world: / "Having known the Veda and the Vedāṅga, we will attain liberation!"
Thinking thus, the others went from there to another world. / Then three became kings, and four became excellent brahmins.
Then in Kurukṣetra, by the power of their asceticism, they completely knew the Vedas / and Vedāṅgas, and the affairs of the next world and this world.
The three born into royal families were kings deluded by pride; / due to loss of knowledge, they did not know the higher world or their ultimate welfare.
And those brahmins, out of compassion, summoned their own servant: / "Go to the kings out of kindness and deliver this letter in haste:
'[Once] seven hunters in Daśārṇa, deer on Mount Kālañjara, / cakravāka birds in Śaradvīpa, swans in the Mānasa lake—
they have now been born in Kurukṣetra as brahmins who have mastered the Vedas. / They have set forth on the distant path; why do you despond?'"
Taking the letter, the servant showed it to the kings. / Seeing the letter, the kings abandoned their kingdom and went to the twice-born.
Having heard their words, those ascetics departed, / and in no long time they attained liberation together with them.
O twice-born, whoever hears this [story] beginning with the seven hunters at a śrāddha, / imperishable food and drink attend his ancestors.
The twice-born said: / How can the ancestral rite of an indigent brahmin be performed, / or that of an ascetic, a forest-dweller, or a householder, O Keśava?
The Blessed One said: / Having gathered grass and wood, or having begged for a cowrie-shell, / if he performs the rites for the ancestors, the fruit becomes a-hundred-thousandfold.
Whoever, having done a hundred forbidden deeds, performs the ancestral śrāddha— / destruction of all his sins occurs, and that man goes to heaven.
In the absence of everything, whoever gives grass to cows on the ancestor-tithi, / that man obtains a greater fruit than the offering of funeral balls.
Formerly, in the Vairāṭa region, an extremely wretched man wept; / when the ancestor-tithi arrived, he wept due to the lack of everything.
Having wept for a long time, he too asked a wise twice-born: / "O brahmin, on the ancestor-tithi today, what could be done that would be beneficial?
I do not have even a single cowrie-shell or wealth, O best of the knowers of Brahman! / Give me instruction so that I may abide in dharma."
The twice-born said: / "Go quickly to the forest, dear one, right now at the kutapa hour; / swiftly give grass to a cow, intending it for your father."
Then, by his instruction, having gathered a bundle of grass, / he gave it to a cow, delighted, for the nourishment of his father.
By the grace of this merit, he went to the abode of the gods; / and having enjoyed heaven for a very long time, he was born into a wealthy family.
Being wealthy because of his past merit from the sacrifice to the ancestors, / he offered the funeral ball to his father with all his possessions and wealth.
Then, from the spiritual practice of that single birth, he went to the abode of Viṣṇu; / having enjoyed endless happiness there, he became a sovereign universal monarch.
Since there is no duty whatever higher than the ancestral sacrifice, / therefore, with all effort and according to one's capacity, one should perform it without envy.
The man who recites this lineage of dharma in the presence of people / attains the fruit of bathing in the water of the Viṣṇupadī in every realm.
The heap of great sins that has been committed by him through birth after birth— / all that goes to destruction once this is uttered and heard.

title: ekapañcāśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Narottama said: / "He is the lord of the universe, of the thirty [gods] and of all other deities; / he is the master, the creator, the destroyer, the protector, the sustainer, the father, and the mother.
The weariness of our speech is relieved only by discoursing upon Viṣṇu. / Yet curiosity has arisen within me, like thirst or hunger.
When one asks about what has happened, it must indeed be told by a beloved one. / How does a devoted wife (pativratā) know even what is past, O Lord?
Or what power is within her? You ought to explain this in full." / The Blessed One said: / "I told you before, my child; yet curiosity arises again in you, O twice-born!
I will narrate all of that which dwells in your mind. / A devoted wife holds her husband as her life-breath and is always devoted to her husband's welfare.

She is to be worshipped even by the gods, and by sages who proclaim the Absolute (brahmavādin). / A woman who is devoted to a single husband is traditionally regarded as the most venerable in the world.
In honouring her, no burden will remain concealed. / Formerly, my dear child, in the central region (Madhyadeśa), there was a very beautiful city.
In that [city] lived a devoted wife of the brahmin caste named Sevyā. / Her husband had become a leper due to the impediment of his past karma.
Though his sores were suppurating, she was continually dedicated to his service. / Whatever desire he had, she fulfilled it with all her might.
She worshipped him daily like a god and showed him affection without malice. / One day, seeing an exceedingly beautiful courtesan walking along the road,
he was overcome by infatuation and his mind was seized by passion. / He let out a very long sigh and then became dejected.
Hearing him, the virtuous woman came out of the house and asked her husband: / 'Why are you dejected, my lord? Why this deep sigh, O master?
Tell me what is to be done, or even what should not be done, that pleases you. / I will fulfill your desire; you alone are my revered guru and beloved.
Speak your wish, my lord; I will carry it out according to my ability.' / When this was said, he replied to her: 'Why do you speak in vain, my dear?
You are not able, nor am I; it is useless to speak of it. / You are not qualified to ask about it, like a fruit on a very tall tree,
which a dwarf, standing on the ground, desires to reach. / In the same way, out of longing and infatuation for a woman, I desired what is unattainable.
I speak of a retreat that is difficult even for a married couple to achieve.' / The devoted wife said: / 'Once I understand what is in your mind, I am capable of accomplishing the task.
Give the command, my lord; it must be done by any means whatsoever! / If I can accomplish with effort this deed that is difficult for you to attain,
then great auspiciousness will bear fruit for me in the next world and here.' / When she said this, he stood up, exceedingly delighted, and spoke these words:
One who is accustomed to sin surely desires sin. / 'Seeing that exceedingly beautiful courtesan walking on this road,
flawless in every limb, my mind burns [with longing]. / If, by your grace, I could attain that youthful maiden,
then my life would be fruitful; O virtuous woman, bring about my welfare! / If that woman of shapely hips does not yield to me—a wretched leper,
foul-smelling and covered with fresh sores—then death would be better for me.' / Hearing the words he uttered, the virtuous wife said:
'I will do it to the best of my ability; now be at ease, my lord.' / Having considered it in her mind, at the end of the night, swiftly at dawn,
taking cow dung along with a broom, she went with joy. / Having reached the courtesan's house and cleaned the courtyard,
the street gateway, and the lane, she joyfully smeared them with cow dung. / She quickly returned to her house out of fear of being seen by people.
In this manner, that virtuous woman behaved for three days. / Then that chief courtesan asked her female and male servants:
'Whose splendid work is this in the courtyard? / Though I did not order it, who has done this at dawn for the sake of pleasing me?
The road, courtyard, and lanes are shining with charming work.' / Having deliberated among themselves, they said to the chief courtesan:
'This work of sweeping was not done by us, O good lady.' / Then, overcome with wonder, having reflected, at the end of the night
she saw that same woman who had come again just like before. / Seeing that great, virtuous, and devoted brahmin wife,
she held her feet, saying: 'Alas! Forgive me! / Life, body, prosperity, fame, wealth, and renown—
you seem to have appeared for the destruction of all these of mine, O devoted wife! / Whatever you ask, O virtuous woman, I will surely give it to you forever,
be it gold, gems, jewels, fine clothes, or whatever is your heart's desire.' / Then the virtuous wife said to her: 'I have no need of wealth.
There is a certain task for you; I will tell you, and if you do it, / then there will be satisfaction in my heart, and all will be accomplished by you now.'
The courtesan said: / 'Truly, truly I will do it! Speak quickly, O devoted wife! / Protect me, O mother, and tell me quickly what is to be done.'
Shamefully, the [virtuous wife] spoke what had to be said, stating the beloved boon of her husband. / Reflecting for a moment, that courtesan exercised forbearance and said:
'Though deeply grieved by union with a leper who smells foul, / I will do it for one day if he comes to my house.'
The devoted wife said: / 'I will come to your house tonight, O beautiful one; / having enjoyed his pleasure and being made glad, I will bring my husband back to my house.'
The courtesan said: / 'Go quickly to your house, O fortunate one, O devoted wife! / Let your husband come to my house at midnight.
I have many lovers, kings and their equals, / and one of them is always staying in my house without interruption.
Today, out of fear of you, I will make my house empty; / let your husband come, and having attained me, let him depart.'
Hearing this, the virtuous woman went to her own house / and announced to her husband: 'Your task has borne fruit, my lord!
She has agreed for you to go to her house tonight; / but she has many masters, so there is no time to lose.'
The brahmin said: / 'How will I go to her house? I am not able to walk. / Knowing this, where is the relief? How will the task be accomplished?'
The devoted wife said: / 'Placing you upon my own back, I will carry you to her house; / and when the purpose is accomplished, I will bring you back by that very path.'
The twice-born said: / 'O auspicious lady, only by your deed will my entire purpose be attained! / Now a deed has been performed by you that is unbearable even for womanhood.'
In that charming city, much wealth was constantly stolen by citizens from a rich man's house, / and the king then heard of it.
Having heard, the king angrily summoned all the night watchmen [and said]: / 'If you desire to live, you must deliver the thief to me today!'
Having received the king's order, anxious in their eagerness to seize him, / the spies forcefully captured a thief by the king's command.
Near the city, at the root of a tree in a dense forest, / the illustrious, eminent sage Māṇḍavya was absorbed in meditation (samādhi).
The foremost sage among yogins remained standing there like fire; / his breath had entered the inner channels, and nothing appeared [externally] to him.
Seeing that great sage standing equal to Brahman, the wicked men [said]: / 'This thief of strange appearance, a rogue, is standing in the forest!'
Having spoken thus, the wicked ones bound that best of sages; / and those excessively cruel men were neither spoken to nor looked at by him.
Then the king said this: "The thief has been caught by me. / Inflict terrible punishment [upon him] on the path near the gateway."
And the sage Māṇḍavya was impaled there upon a stake on the path; / the stake was driven by them into his anal region up to his head.
And he felt no pain, though his body was pierced on the stake, because of his restraint; / the punishment inflicted by others was made beneficial to his mind by them.
Meanwhile, at night in dense, rising darkness, / that devoted wife, having placed her husband on her back, departed.
From contact with Māṇḍavya's body, the smell of the leper reached him; / thus his meditation was truly broken through association with the leper.
Māṇḍavya said: 'He by whom this distress and bodily torment has just now been caused, / let that very person turn to ashes when the sun rises!'
Having been spoken to thus by Māṇḍavya, he fell onto the ground; / then the devoted wife also said: "Truly, may the sun not rise!"
Having taken [him] home for three days, having gone home from the curse, / the devoted wife remained, holding [him] lying on a lovely bed.
Having cursed him, the best of sages went to his desired region; / and the sun did not rise in the world for three days.
Seeing the entire threefold world with its moving and unmoving beings distressed, / the gods, placing Indra at their head, went to the Grandfather.
The denizens of heaven reported the entire occurrence to the lotus-born [Brahmā]: / "We do not know the cause; do you ordain what is fitting for us."
Brahmā said— / what happened with the devoted wife, and what happened with the sage Māṇḍavya, / and how the sun did not rise—the Creator explained among the gods.
Then the gods, in their aerial chariots, placing Prajāpati at their head, / went near to that place, O brāhmaṇa, and all [came] swiftly to the earth's surface.
By the splendour of those aerial chariots and likewise by the rays of the sages, / it shone as if with a hundred suns within that house and nowhere else.
"Alas, I am undone! How has the sun appeared in my house?" / Then she saw the gods with their aerial chariots resembling swans.
Meanwhile, Brahmā spoke to that devoted wife: / "Of all the gods, and of the twice-born, and of the cows likewise,
how is the destruction of these pleasing to you? / O mother, abandon your anger today regarding the rising of the sun."
The devoted wife said: / "Surpassing all worlds, my husband alone is my guru; / his death will occur from the sage's curse when the sun rises.
For that very reason this maker of day was cursed by me, / not out of wrath, nor delusion, nor greed, passion, or jealousy."
Brahmā said: / "By the death of one alone, the welfare of the three worlds would be achieved; / from that, O mother, even greater merit will accrue to you."
She said to the Ordainer there in front of the gods: / "Abandoning my husband, indeed, no auspiciousness pleases me."
Brahmā said: / "When the sun has risen, gentle lady, and your husband has been reduced to ashes, / and the threefold world has become healthy, I shall accomplish your welfare.
From the ashes a man will arise, equal in splendour to Kāmadeva, / a husband endowed with all virtues, and you [shall be] ever like Rati.
Just as Hari is worshipped by the gods, and just as Lakṣmī is worshipped, / so shall you two spouses be in heaven; therefore do my bidding."
The devoted wife said: / "Upon the death of my husband, O Brahmā, a widow blamed by the world, / into what worlds shall I go, fallen from conduct and defiled?"
Brahmā said: / "Therefore there is no fault in you; indeed, your husband is not dead now. / By our word alone, the leper shall attain the nature of Manmatha."
While the Ordainer was speaking thus, she reflected for a moment, / and she said, "Yes!"; thereupon the rising of the sun took place.
Tormented by the sage's curse, he turned into ashes; / from the midst of the ashes a twice-born was born, tormented by passion.
Seeing [this], all those city-dwellers were struck with wonder; / the hosts of gods were delighted, and the people became very comfortable.
In a sun-coloured aerial chariot that came from the heavenly realm, / along with her husband, that virtuous woman went to heaven together with the gods.
Since an auspicious devoted wife is thus equal even to me, / through that she knows what has occurred, the past, the future, and present activity.
Whoever recites this peerless, holy narrative in the world, / his sin committed across life after life goes to destruction.
He obtains imperishable heaven and is united with the wise; / a brāhmaṇa gains the Veda in birth after birth, O priest.
He who hears it once, purified, is freed from a flood of evil deeds; / he attains the abode of the gods, and fallen from heaven, becomes wealthy.

title: dvipañcāśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: The twice-born said: / "O Viṣṇu, how was there a blow from a stake on the body of the sage Māṇḍavya, / and how was there leprosy on the body of the devoted wife's husband?"
Hari said: / "Out of childishness, not thinking, Māṇḍavya inserted a blade of grass / into the abdomen of a cricket, and out of delusion he let it go.
By the fault of that censure, and by [the decree of] Dharma the knower, / day and night severe distress was endured by that twice-born man.
However, by that absorption, the distress caused by the stake was not felt, / nor all the hardship, by the sage, owing to intense practice of yoga.
From the slaying of a brāhmaṇa, on account of uncontrolled senses, / foul-smelling leprosy arose on the body of the leper, O best of the twice-born.
Formerly four virgin maidens were given by him to a brāhmaṇa, / and three maidens, O brāhmaṇa; therefore he had a devoted wife.
And on account of her, he would attain equality with me. / Whence is there any wonder in this? Know the ancient action!"
The twice-born said: / "Certainly heaven belongs to him who guides a faithful woman; / as this story [shows], O Lord, auspiciousness is wished for all."
Hari said: / "There are some dutiful women who give all their possessions to a man; / yet even toward one who should not be protected, one should not hold [desire] even in mind.
No one is unpleasant to women, nor is anyone truly dear; / like cattle in a forest seeking fresh grass, they crave ever new [men].
Even a man devoid of wealth, deformed, bereft of virtues, / of low birth, and a servant, a passionate woman truly resorts to.
Abandoning a husband endowed with virtues, well-born, very wealthy, / handsome, and skilled in love-making, a woman may resort to a base man.
Know the narrative of the conversation between Umā and Nārada, O earthly god, / by which, O twice-born, the various conduct of women is fully known.
By nature, O brāhmaṇa, the sage Nārada was eager to understand the universe; / having reflected in his own mind, he then went to the excellent Mount Kailāsa.
On the snowy mountain where the abode of the Bull-bannered [Śiva] is established, / that great-souled sage bowed down and asked Pārvatī:
"O goddess, I wish to know the wicked behaviour of women; / through curiosity, the conduct of wives is observed by you.
You know truly the inner heart of all women; / therefore tell me, who am humble and ignorant in all these matters."
The goddess said: / "The mind of young women always rests upon a man, without a doubt, / whether in this suitable union, or whether joined or unjoined."
Upon seeing a well-dressed man, whether a brother or a son, / a woman's womb becomes moist—truly, truly, O Nārada.
There is no place, there is no moment, there is no male suitor; / by that [alone], O Nārada, women's fidelity arises.
Woman is like a pot of ghee, man is like a burning coal; / therefore, one should never place ghee and fire in the same spot.
Just as a driver brings an elephant in rut under his control / by means of the hook and mallet, so too is a woman's protector.
Her father protects her in childhood, her husband protects her in youth, / and her sons [protect her] in old age: a woman does not deserve independence.
Therefore, through the absence of independence and of her own free will, / a steadfast noble woman, when solicited by a man through instigation, becomes unchaste.
Just as cooked food, through lack of protection, falls under the sway of dogs and crows, / so indeed a young woman, through wantonness, goes to wickedness.
Then her family becomes corrupted through association with her; / that one who is born from another's seed is indeed a mixture of castes.
The sinful illegitimate child of mixed caste surely dwells in hell; / [then] all of them, having gone into the species of worms, are born again on the surface of the earth.
Then, O joy of the twice-born, the family is brought to the status of a barbarian; / since the ruin of a lineage results, one should not keep a wicked woman.
That lowest of men who, knowing the fault of women, pardons [it], / remains in the terrible Raurava hell together with his ancestors.
One woman ruins a family, another elevates a family; / therefore, with every effort, a wise man should marry a well-born woman.
An equal woman stands keeping both families united; / a virtuous wife saves the lineages, a wicked woman certainly brings them down.
Heaven and the family, purity and disgrace, fame and ill repute, / son, daughter, and friend in worldly existence are said to depend upon a wife.
Therefore, a wise man should marry one or a second woman; / but she who is taken for offspring or out of desire is fraught with many faults.
And that husband who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after menstruation, / is a slayer of a brahmin, a slayer of an embryo, and goes to a wretched destination.
That evil-doer who, having made a virtuous wife unfortunate out of delusion, abandons her, / goes to hell after experiencing the sin equal to slaying her.
Having abducted a woman, a man goes to the family of a Cāṇḍāla; / likewise, through the abandonment of a woman, a man is born fallen.
Placing a woman on his shoulders, he dwells for a long time in the city of Yama; / feces and urine constantly fall upon his head.
In this way the evil-minded one carries the burden for thousands of years; / then, for as many years as there are body hairs, he goes to Raurava.
Having passed through [births] among worms, he then attains human status; / and then, because of former sin, he incurs strife and sorrow.
Having obtained three such births, a man is freed from the sin; / but that deceitful woman, having experienced hell for that time, becomes a female crow.
Having experienced the hell of leftover food, she becomes a widow among humans. / Furthermore, that man who goes to an outcaste woman, a barbarian woman, or a Pulkasa woman,
having suffered twice, thrice, or four times over as a deceitful sinner there, / [or he who] goes to his mother, his teacher's wife, a brahmin woman, a queen,
or any other wife of his lord, goes to non-rebirth [in a good state]; / [or he who goes to] his sister, his son's wife, and likewise his daughter, his daughter-in-law,
his paternal uncle's wife, his maternal aunt, and likewise his paternal aunt, / or other women such as his mother's sister—having gone to them, there is no expiation.
He becomes a slayer of a brahmin, blind, and falls into dumbness of speech; / born deaf in his ears, he falls; there is no expiation.
Having spoken very excessive obscenity entirely on account of a woman, / the twice-born said: "Having committed such evil deeds, how can there again be liberation?
Explain that, O Blessed One; I wish to hear it in truth." / The Blessed Lord said: / "Having engaged in intercourse with them, [embracing] a red-hot iron doll,
Embracing [it], he should yield his life-breath; purified, he would go to another world. / That man indeed who, having abandoned the household order, becomes fixed in mind on me,
[And] constantly remembers Govinda, achieves the destruction of all sins. / [Even if] ten thousand murders of a Brahmin were committed by him, or the violation of a guru's wife,
A hundred or a hundred thousand [sins] from drinking flour-liquor, / Committing theft of gold and the like, or prolonged association with them—
These and other sins, as well as the great mortal crimes, / Just as cotton or dry grass is destroyed upon reaching fire, perish entirely.
Therefore, having remembered my name, Govinda, a man becomes purified. / Or he who remains in the household order, constantly making the proclamation of Govinda,
And having worshipped, is ferried across sin. / On the delightful bank of the Bhāgīrathī, during an auspicious eclipse of the sun,
Whatever fruit a man obtains by giving ten million cows, / That fruit he fully attains, and a thousand times more,
By chanting Govinda's name, dear one, and he dwells imperishably in my city. / Dwelling at will in my abode, he becomes a sovereign king.
Hearing the stories about me in a Purāṇa, a man attains resemblance to me. / And having narrated a Purāṇa, he attains union with Viṣṇu.
Therefore, a Purāṇa, which is a collection of dharma, should be heard constantly; / It should be recited with effort; he goes to the form of Viṣṇu in that world.
Or whatever other fault is committed with regard to women, it will surely be mitigated as appropriate. / Listen, I will declare it to you in truth, O delight of the twice-born!
By the gift of all kinds of seeds together with a water jar, a great fruit [is won]; / One should give it to a Brahmin on an auspicious day; he immediately becomes purified in an instant.
One should give all seeds such as grains to a twice-born man at the proper time; / Having brought about the destruction of all sins, he enjoys imperishable heaven.
I will speak of the firm virtue of chaste wives, O Brahmin-sage! / Her lineage becomes pure, and fortune constantly attends [her].
There is heaven for both lineages: that of her husband and her own. / The virtue of a devoted wife, O Brahmin, was forgotten as you asked;
I shall speak again for women, an auspicious benefit for all the world. / Having dwelt [thus] in former times, women through merit and demerit,
And thereafter devoted to their husbands, they go to my abode. / For six months or for a year—and more is praised—
She who becomes a devoted wife, as long as she is purified, goes to heaven. / Even a husband who drinks liquor, slays a Brahmin, or is laden with all sins,
She who follows her husband leads him, purified from the mire, to heaven. / A husband like the god of love, and she charming like Ratī,
Enjoys endless pleasure for a long time in the world of Indra. / And she who, by the power of devotion to her husband, when her lord falls afar,
Having obtained a token [of his] and died in the fire, delivers her husband from sin. / And a devoted woman whose husband dies in another land,
She, taking her husband's token and sleeping in the fire, goes to heaven. / But a woman of the Brahmin class who follows her dead husband—
She, by killing herself, does not lead herself nor her husband to heaven. / A Brahmin woman must not die going along [with him], by the ordinance of Brahmā;
She who kills herself attains the fate of an ascetic [who falls from vows] upon dying. / The best of men said: / The Brahmin is declared praiseworthy among all castes,
And [what is done] by the foremost of the twice-born is meritorious; why then is there a reverse here? / The Blessed Lord said: / A rash deed is never proper for a Brahmin woman;
By completely killing her, that man would become a slayer of a Brahmin. / Therefore, a woman of the Brahmin caste, being twice-born, should observe an ascetic vow.
I will declare it as it is; listen truly, O Brahmin! / She should never eat meat from the marketplace.
In one year she obtains the fruit of a thousand horse sacrifices. / Worship of one's chosen deity, Hari, is an unequalled observance;
She should offer water and rice balls for her master without envy. / For thousands of crores of cosmic ages, and hundreds of crores of cosmic ages,
That virtuous woman remains joined with her husband in the world of Viṣṇu. / Then, having undertaken that great vow, a Brahmin wife in hell
Would deliver both lineages by the hundreds and by the thousands. / Therefore, the relatives themselves—sons, brothers, and the like, who are wise—
Restraining her, should never cause the breach of her vow. / If, on reaching the day of Hari, a widow does not observe the vow,
That unfortunate woman attains widowhood again in birth after birth. / From the eating of fish and meat, and from the abandonment of vows,
Having gone to hell for a long time, she surely becomes a female dog. / The wicked widow, a destroyer of her family, who engages in sexual intercourse,
Having experienced hells, then becomes a female vulture for ten births, / Becomes a female jackal for two births, and then attains human status.
Likewise, from child-widowhood she falls into servitude. / The twice-born said: / Speak of the fruit of giving a daughter in marriage; tell also what the fruit of giving a female slave is,
And the ritual procedure as prescribed, if you have favor toward me, O Lord! / The Blessed Lord said: / To one endowed with beauty, full of good qualities, of noble birth, youthful,
Prosperous, and filled with wealth—hear the fruit of giving a daughter [to such a groom]: / He who gives a virgin endowed with all ornaments,
By him the entire earth with its mountains, forests, and groves is given. / By the gift of [a maiden with] half the ornaments, the fruit surely accrues to the giver;
For a maiden without ornaments, there is a fourth of the fruit. / But the man who takes a bride-price goes to hell;
Having sold his own daughter, the fool does not turn back from hell. / He who out of greed gives his daughter to an unsuitable man,
Attaining the Raurava hell, goes to the state of a Cāṇḍāla. / For this very reason, a wise man never takes a bride-price from a son-in-law
Even in his mind; what is given to him becomes imperishable. / Land, a cow, gold, wealth, clothing, and grain—
Having given [these] as a dowry to the son-in-law, all becomes imperishable. / At the time of marriage, my child, by people of the same gotra or of another gotra,
Whatever dowry is given, all that becomes imperishable. / If the giver does not remember the gift, and the recipient does not ask for it,
The two of them go to hell, like a jar whose rope is severed. / A dowry gift must certainly be given by a virtuous person;
Not having given it, he reaches hell and incurs servitude. / To one who is too close, too far away, exceedingly rich, exceedingly destitute,
Lacking noble birth, and foolish—to these six a daughter is not given. / To one who is exceedingly old, exceedingly pitiable, sickly, [merely] residing in the country,
Exceedingly angry, or discontented—to these six a daughter is not given. / Having given a virgin to these, one goes to hell,
Out of greed, desire for honor, or an exchange of maidens. / A woman dear to sages, youthful and endowed with beauty,
Having given [her] with ornaments and a bed, he obtains endless fruit. / And the fruit of these two, a young woman and a maiden, for you:
One should be given to a bridegroom, but the other to a Brahmin. / A purchased woman should be given to a deity by a steadfast man of untroubled action;
His stay in heaven will last for an eon, or he will be a king possessing great wealth on earth. / In each birth he obtains an excellent wife of radiant complexion.
He who constantly listens to this unequalled sacred narrative, / His sins are all destroyed, and he masters the meaning of all scriptures;
He attains imperishable heaven, becomes beloved to women, / Or, as a kṣatriya, he will surely become victorious and a lord of the world.
the heard [account] takes away the sins committed in birth after birth; / and likewise a noble woman obtains good fortune in the world."

title: tripañcāśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: The twice-born said: / "You ought to speak in full, O lord, of the deeds and peerless majesty of Tulādhāra, / if you have favor toward me."
The Blessed Lord said: / "Whoever gives out of a truthful nature, from lack of greed, and from absence of malice, / for him a hundred sacrifices are perpetually completed with good sacrificial gifts.
By truth the sun rises, and likewise the wind blows; / the ocean does not transgress its shore, nor the tortoise [transgress] the earth.
By truth all the worlds endure, and all the mountains; / and that being who has fallen from truth certainly becomes a dweller of the lower regions.
He who is devoted to truthful speech and always devoted to truthful action, / having reached heaven with his physical body, attains imperishability.
By truth all the sages have reached me and attained stability; / by truth King Yudhiṣṭhira went to heaven with his physical body.
Having conquered the entire host of enemies, the world was protected by him through dharma; / and he performed the pure, very rare Rājasūya sacrifice.
And eighty-four thousand brahmins / he would feed daily from golden vessels and with royal utensils.
Having fed them, he would dismiss them after giving them the utensils; / and whatever wealth was desired by the twice-born, he would have given to them beyond that.

Then, knowing the assembly of the twice-born to be free from poverty, he would let them depart; / likewise, sixteen thousand snātakas / the king, free from malice, would feed daily solely through truth.
Formerly they stayed long in his house out of a desire for victory; / by him the whole world was conquered on account of bestowing grace on living beings.
And through truth the asura King Bali will become Indra; / for him who dwells in Pātāla, I constantly abide in his dwelling.
And I dwell perpetually in the heart of him whose deeds are solely meritorious; / or, as formerly he was bound by me, because of his release from the demon womb,
I grant the nether world, immortality, and the status of Indra. / King Hariścandra, through truth, along with his vehicles and retinue,
is established in Satyaloka with his own pure body. / Many other kings and those who are perfected great sages,
wise men, and ascetics, all became imperishable through truth; / therefore, one devoted to truth in the world is capable of deliverance from cyclic existence.
The great-souled Tulādhāra is indeed firmly established in truthful speech; / there is none equal to him in the world on account of his truthful speech.
Truth was weighed on a balance against a thousand horse sacrifices; / indeed, truth alone outweighs a thousand horse sacrifices.
Everything can be achieved through truth; truth is indeed insurmountable; / through truthful speech, that cow Bahulā went to heaven.
Having pacified the whole kingdom, return [to worldly existence] is rare; / likewise, this witness is always [truthful]; he is never untruthful.
A wise man, in buying and selling, whether high-priced or low-priced, / should have truthful speech that is praised, especially in the case of a witness.
Witnesses, having spoken the truth, have gone to imperishable heaven; / an eloquent master of speech, having entered an assembly, speaks the truth;
he goes to Brahmā's abode, which is difficult to attain even through other sacrifices. / Whoever speaks the truth in an assembly obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Speaking falsely out of greed or hatred, one goes to the Raurava hell. / Tulādhāra is the witness of all, and indeed a hero among men.
Particularly by renouncing greed, one attains immortality in heaven. / There was a certain noble Śūdra who was never given to greed.
His livelihood was made with difficulty by vegetables and by gleaning ears of grain; / his pair of garments was worn out, and his hands were always his eating vessel.
Though always lacking gain, he never took another's property. / To test him, I took a pair of garments,
and, remaining on the riverbank under a cover, placed it respectfully. / Seeing that pair of garments, he did not set his mind on greed.
Knowing it belonged to someone else, he went to his own house with patience. / Then, O twice-born, reflecting in my heart: 'This is too little,'
I dropped an udumbara fruit containing gold right there, / on the riverbank, in an isolated, deserted bend.
When he went to that place, that wonder was seen by him: / 'Enough! This seems to be an artificial arrangement.
If I take it now, my freedom from greed is utterly lost. / Guarding it is misery, and it is a cause of egotism.
Where there is greed, there is [desire for] gain; from gain, greed proceeds. / And for a man seized by greed, there is eternal hell.
If flawed wealth stays in the house, / then madness indeed arises in my wife and sons.
From madness comes delusion of mind through distortions born of lust; / from delusion comes confusion, then egotism, and after that anger and greed.
And through their abundance, asceticism will go to destruction. / When asceticism is destroyed, the mind-deluding impurities persist,
and bound by those chain-like attachments, one can never attain deliverance.' / Considering this, that Śūdra left it and went home.
Standing in heaven, the gods joyfully said there: 'Well done! Well done!' / Then, assuming the form of a Jain ascetic, near his house
I went and spoke of divine counsel, narrating what had occurred. / Then, through repeated contact and the gathering of people,
his wife came and asked about the divine matter. / Then I told her what was in her heart at once;
secretly the cause of the sound of fortune was told by me: / 'What was intended for you, given by destiny, was abandoned by your husband like a fool.
It was cast away, O fortunate lady! There is no more wealth for you here. / As long as he lives, he will undoubtedly experience misfortune.
Go home, mother, to the empty house; ask him about what was not obtained.' / Hearing that speech, she went to her husband's presence,
and spoke of his bad conduct. Hearing that, he was astonished. / Reflecting, he came with her into my presence.
Secretly he said to me: 'Tell me of your ascetic state.' / The ascetic said: 'How could something visible, long purified, be cast aside by you like grass, in sport?
Because, dear friend, there is no unhindered fortune [greater than that] which you abandoned! / Incomparable sovereignty, heroism, and prosperity crumble away.
You will continually see with your own eyes the great suffering of your kin, / from birth until death, which is the certain fate of those who die.
Therefore, let it be taken quickly! Enjoy unhindered pleasure, / incomparable sovereignty, heroism, and the supreme wonder of the worlds.'
The Śūdra said: 'I have no desire for wealth. Wealth is the snare of saṃsāra; / a mortal fallen into its grasp does not attain liberation again.
Hear the fault of wealth in this world and in the next: / fear of thieves, of kinsmen, and of kings and their taxes.
All mortals are murderous, like animals, fish, and birds of prey. / Likewise, for the wealthy, how can worldly goods bring happiness?
Wealth is the destroyer of life and the accomplisher of wicked deeds; / it is the dear home of death and others, the supreme cause of misfortune.'
The ascetic said: 'He who has wealth has friends; he who has wealth has kinsmen; / [wealth brings] lineage, good character, learning, beauty, enjoyment, fame, and happiness.
For one devoid of wealth, however, and abandoned by sons and wife, / how can there be a friend? How dharma? What kind of birth is it for the wretched?
The performance of sacrifices such as sattva and others, the beneficial digging of ponds, / and giving gifts, which is the stairway to heaven—none of these is accomplished for a man of no means.
Observing the performance of vows, the constant hearing of dharma and such, / rites for the ancestors and pilgrimages—none is accomplished for one without wealth.
Likewise, the remedy for disease, proper diet, the accumulation of medicine, / protection, war, and certainly the conquest of enemies [require wealth].
And the livelihood of women from birth is obtained through the union with wealth. / Whatever good deeds and bad deeds are performed by the past and the future—
therefore, he who has abundant wealth can enjoy at will. / You will attain heaven very soon from charity alone.'

The Śūdra said: 'Through desirelessness is all observance; through freedom from anger is resort to holy places; / through compassion and recitation of prayers is one equal and pure; contentment alone is wealth.
Non-violence is the supreme perfection; the life of gleaning ears of grain is best; / an intake of vegetables is equal to nectar; fasting is supreme austerity.
Contentment is my great enjoyment; a cowrie shell is my great gift; / another's wife is like a mother, and another's goods are like a clod of earth.
Another's wife is like a serpent. This is my entire sacrifice. / Therefore I will not take it; truly, truly, O mine of virtues!
Better than washing off mud is not touching it from afar.' / When this was said, O best of men, a shower of flowers fell,
O twice-born, upon the crown of his head and his body, released by all the gods. / The drums of the gods resounded, and the hosts of apsarases danced.
The lords of the gandharvas sang, and an aerial chariot descended from the sky. / The hosts of gods said there: 'Mount this aerial chariot!
Reaching Satyaloka, enjoy pleasures like great Indra! / Even if calculated, your period of enjoyment will endure, O righteous one!'
And when the gods had spoken thus, the śūdra said these words: / 'How can there be knowledge, gesture, and speech in this Nirgrantha?'
Is he Hari and Hara, or Brahmā? Or is he Indra or Bṛhaspati? / Or has Dharma himself come here in person to test me?'
When this was said, that mendicant smiled and spoke these words: / 'In order to know your dharma, I, Viṣṇu, have come here.'
Go to heaven in the aerial chariot with your family, O great sage! / By my favor, you all shall possess eternal youth;
it shall be so, O very wise one! You will obtain boundless fortune.' / Endowed with divine ornaments and adorned with divine garments,
they immediately went to heaven, accompanied by all their kinsmen. / Thus, O best of twice-born, through the renunciation of greed they went to heaven.
Likewise, the wise Tulādhāra is established in truthful dharma, / by which he knows that event which occurred in another land.
There is no one equal to Tulādhāra established in the realm of the gods. / Therefore, you too, O earthly god, become equal to him and go to heaven.
The mortal who hears this, being established in all dharma, / has the sin accumulated over many births destroyed in that very instant.
By merely reading it once, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices. / He shall become venerable among gods and before men, O vipra.

title: catuḥpañcāśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: The Blessed Lord said: / The greatness of Adrohaka, unbearable to the world, has been told; / having forgiven a beautiful woman who shared his bed, he became all-conquering.
Hard to master even for the wise, for sages, and for celibate students, / an uneven path for gods, asuras, and humans—he traversed it smoothly.
What man is capable of conquering passion, which is perverse by nature? / Except for Adrohaka, O twice-born, that man alone conquered worldly existence.
From the abduction of Ahalyā alone did the lord of the gods become marked with vulvas; / and by the grace of the goddess he became renowned as the Thousand-Eyed.
It is known in the entire world, in the three worlds with the moving and unmoving. / The twice-born said: And how did the abduction of Ahalyā by the god of gods happen, O Lord?
And how did the lord of the gods, the Thousand-Eyed, become marked with vulvas? / How did the king of the gods, though not marked with signs, become marked with vulvas?
Ill is the hearing of the disfigurement of a god; I wish to hear it accurately. / The Blessed Lord said: Formerly, the lord of the world, the high-minded Creator,
gladly gave to Gautama a maiden born of his own mind, in the presence of the guardians of the world. / Then, of the guardians of the world whose minds were possessed by love,
and of the husband of Śacī, a delusion remained in their hearts like an arrow: / 'Bypassing the guardians of the world, this fair-complexioned woman, beautifully adorned,
who is like a gem, was given to a twice-born! What am I to do?' / Thus deliberating, while her youth was unfolding,
her exceedingly radiant form was again seen by him through illusion. / Still thinking of her, he went to the dwelling of Gautama.
Hear from me what happened after he went there: / Once, Gautama went to Puṣkara to bathe.
And the virtuous woman was occupied with cleansing the house and household belongings, / engaged in offering oblations for the dwelling of the deities,
gathering firewood, performing fire-rites, and attending to daily duties. / In the meantime, Śakra assumed the form and body
of that great sage and gladly entered the hut. / Seeing her husband, the faithful and devoted wife,
with supreme faith, prepared to arrange the articles in the place of the gods. / Then Hari, wearing the garb of the sage, afflicted [with passion], said to her:
'Subdued by Pradyumna, O lovely one, give me a kiss and the rest.' / In the meantime, she, filled with bashfulness, spoke these words:
'You ought not to speak to me, O lord, setting aside rites for the gods and the like. / You know everything, O knower of dharma, the certainty of merits, O sage.
Indeed, this matter is not suitable at this very hour.' / Then, seeing her who was lovely in every limb, afflicted by passion,
[he said:] 'Enough, beloved, do not speak so; love is born within my heart! / What ought to be done and what ought not to be done is determined by the husband's word.
She who always does so is a devoted wife. / But she who transgresses his command, especially in sexual intercourse,
her merit is destroyed and she meets a wretched fate.' / She said: 'The divine articles are meant for the gods, O sage;
and the other daily rites—how can there be any disruption of them?' / He said to the chaste woman: 'Give me your embrace and the rest;
abandoning fear in your mind, they have been granted by me.' / Having spoken thus and embraced her, his desire was accomplished by him.
In the meantime, O twice-born, a blemish appeared in the sage's heart; / then, entering into meditation, he discovered the deed of the husband of Śacī.
He quickly went and stood at the entrance of the doorway. / Śakra, however, noticing the sage, entered the body of a cat.
He ran along the path of the fleeing cat; / the sage spoke to him there: 'Who are you, assuming the form of a cat?'
Out of fear, Śakra stood before that sage with folded hands. / Seeing Maghavan before him, the preeminent sage was enraged:
'Since such a deed of reckless deceit was done by you for the sake of the vulva, / therefore let a thousand splendid vulvas be upon your limbs!
May it be so here, O most wicked one; and your penis shall fall off! / Depart from my presence, fool! The denizens of heaven in the realm of the gods,
