And you reside in all stationary and moving beings alike, / through the sinful gateway of the womb, full of māyā and delusion.
Through two breasts and two hips, and through youth she shines forth; / and here an excess growth of chest-flesh is seen, no doubt.
A form of delusion has been displayed for the downfall of living beings. / She who has been spoken of by you is not truly a woman at all.
The Creator makes [her] in play, always for his own amusement. / Just as in a woman, so in a man the living soul resides everywhere.
Those who are devoid of breasts and womb are always the living-liberated. / Man is declared to be the spirit (puruṣa); woman is called material nature (prakṛti).
He indeed sports with her; she is never liberated. / Joined with material nature, you are seen among men.
Who feels shame before whom? Knowing this, walk in happiness! / I shall explain the old woman, the eternally old one, O fair-faced lady:
whose skin on her limbs has become withered, O fair-faced lady, / and who is covered with white and grey hair,
destitute of strength, wretched, and covered with wrinkles then— / this is not the old woman; another is called old.
The characteristic of that one has been described; I now speak of the young woman. / Constantly growing through knowledge, taking refuge at the side of the individual soul,
she is named 'good discernment' (sumati); she is both the old woman and the young woman, / established always among men and women in the worlds.
Shame should be felt before her; and I shall declare another thing. / I shall indeed explain the mother who was mentioned by you:
Consciousness resides constantly in the bodies of living beings, / and that which bestows supreme knowledge is called wisdom (prajñā).
Discernment is proclaimed as the mother; she is established / for the protection of living beings in all the worlds, for their nourishment and welfare.
The one called right-mindedness is proclaimed as the mother; / all the forms that constantly lead along the path to the gates of saṃsāra,
these indeed become mothers who reveal manifold sorrow. / Thus the form of the mother has been explained. What else shall I tell you?
The Self said: / Who are you that have arrived, destroyer of my anguish? / Explain to me in detail your own essential nature.
Freedom-from-Attachment said: / [I am he] from whom desires turn away, all of them becoming hopeless, / whom people, out of malice, do not see—these actions are not otherwise;
near whom longing never approaches at all, / and through fear of whom anger, greed, and delusion have perished.
I am Freedom-from-Attachment, may you be blessed; Discernment is my kinsman. / The Self said: What is he like, this brother of yours named Discernment?
Describe to me the characteristics of that brother and of yourself. / Freedom-from-Attachment said: I will not merely describe his characteristics and form before you;
O fortunate one, I will call that brother myself. / O Discernment, my brother, listen to our words!
Come, come, O most fortunate one, out of love for me, O highly intelligent one! / Kaśyapa said: Accompanied by his two wives, Tranquility and Forbearance, he arrived—
all-seeing, all-pervading, omnipresent, devoted to all truths, / the enemy of all doubts, affectionate toward knowledge.
Retention and Intellect were the two daughters of that great soul, / and Yoga was his eldest son, whose supreme master is liberation.
Stainless, free from ego, free from desire, devoid of possessions, / serene in mind at all times, beyond the pairs of opposites, of great intellect,
that Discernment arrived, adorned with the jewels of virtues, / whose two noble and wise ministers were Dharma and Truth.
Accompanied by Forbearance and Tranquility, that Discernment arrived / and spoke thus to Freedom-from-Attachment: 'Summoned by you, I have come;
therefore, brother, let the whole reason be told to me, / relying upon which you have just now summoned me.'
Freedom-from-Attachment said: / This person standing before us is bound fast by great snares, / bewildered by the arrows of delusion and by the fetters of saṃsāra.
He is the all-pervading master, this Self of mine, / pervaded by the five elements, destitute of knowledge and meditation.
Question this Self, since you are learned in the true principles. / Hearing the words of Freedom-from-Attachment, Discernment spoke:
Discernment said: / Do you abide in happiness, O Lord, ruler of the universe? / Having arrived in saṃsāra, what happiness have you yourself enjoyed?
The Self said: / Dwelling in the womb was a great, unbearable, terrible suffering / that I have experienced, O exceedingly wise one, being ever devoid of knowledge.
In the body too, fallen from knowledge, I became many things; / then, having reached the state of childhood, I committed what should and should not be done.
In youth, play was indulged in, and a wife was enjoyed many times; / reaching old age, I was tormented by grief for sons and the like.
By separations from wife and kin I am scorched day and night; / by sorrows of manifold kinds I am tormented day after day.
Day and night, O wise one, I find no happiness anywhere; / thus exceedingly tormented by sorrows, what shall I do, O high-minded one?
Tell me that expedient by which I may indeed find happiness; / free me today from this flood of worldly traps, from this strong bondage.
Discernment said: / You are pure, beyond dualities, and sinless, O lord of the world; / go to this great soul, Freedom-from-Attachment, who gives happiness.
Undoubtedly you have seen him—naked, devoid of outward ritual; / for he reveals happiness and destroys all anguish.
Hearing this, the pure Self went back to Freedom-from-Attachment; / sighing and miserable, he said to him: 'Listen to my words:
show me that path by which I may find happiness.' / [Freedom-from-Attachment said:] 'So be it, O very wise one, I shall do as you say;
go again to Discernment, for you had conversation about happiness with him; / he will indeed be the teacher of the path of happiness for you.'
Sent by meritorious Freedom-from-Attachment, the Lord went, / and spoke to that great-souled Discernment, the best of the pure:
'Show me happiness; indeed, I was sent by Freedom-from-Attachment; / having taken refuge in you, save me from terrible saṃsāra.'
Discernment said: / 'Go to Knowledge, O very wise one; he will tell you everything.' / Thus addressed, the Self reached the place where Knowledge was established.
[The Self said:] / 'O Knowledge of great splendor, revealer of all truths, / I have taken refuge in you; reveal to me the path of happiness.'
Knowledge said: / 'I am your servant, O Lord of the world; do you not recognize me, O keeper of noble vows? / Previously, by means of meditation, you were restrained by me again and again.
Through association with the five elements you have fallen into calamity; / go to Meditation, O wise one, and he will grant you happiness.'
Sent by Knowledge, the Self stood taking refuge in Meditation: / 'Meditation, show me that happiness which is absolute and perfected;
protect me, who have thus come to your refuge!' / Hearing those words spoken by him,
Meditation, highly gladdened, spoke in turn to that Self: / 'I am not to be abandoned, my dear, firmly resolved in all actions;
accompanied by Freedom-from-Attachment and Discernment, always / become endowed with meditation and behold your Self!
Possessed of the Self, becoming steady, free from distress, beyond conceptualization, / just as a lamp set in a windless place burns steadily without flickering,
so having burned away faults, one indeed attains nirvana. / Remaining in solitude, abstaining from food, or eating moderately at all times,
free from dualities, devoid of sounds, seated motionless on your seat, / meditating on the Self by means of the Self, with intellect fixed on me alone,
you shall attain the supreme abode, that highest place of Viṣṇu.'

title: navamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Kaśyapa said: / Thus instructed there by Meditation and the others at that time, / that wise Self, desiring to abandon that fivefold body-effect,
seeing only the instrumental causes, having attained them, departs; / having cast aside the body as unworthy of regard, when it has fallen, he does not look back at it.
There is no lasting connection between the vital breath and the body, though nurtured together; / by what cause then could there be any connection with wealth, sons, and wives?
Knowing this, attain tranquility; do not give in to weakness, O beloved! / He alone is the Supreme Brahman; he alone is the eternal one;
he resides within the demons and the gods in the form of the Self; / he is Brahmā, he is Rudra, and he is eternal Viṣṇu;
he creates the universes, he protects the creatures, / and he destroys them—this righteous one, Janārdana whose form is dharma.
By him the gods were produced, and the demons as well, O beloved; / the gods are freed by dharma, while your sons are devoid of dharma.
This dharma is a limb of Mādhava, protected by all the gods; / therefore, O goddess, one should contemplate dharma and truly uphold dharma.
To him Viṣṇu, the righteous soul, is always gracious. / Indeed, the gods conduct themselves in dharma, in truth, and in asceticism.
With those with whom Viṣṇu is pleased, dharma is protected by them here in this world. / This dharma is the body of Viṣṇu, and truth is his very heart.
Viṣṇu is pleased with him who constantly maintains those two. / He who corrupts truth and dharma fosters only sin.
Viṣṇu becomes enraged with him; exceedingly powerful, he destroys him. / Dharma is protected by the Vaiṣṇavas who abide in asceticism and truth.
The righteous soul is pleased with them, and thus grants protection. / Your sons, the sons of Danu, and likewise the Saiṃhikeyas,
behaving with unrighteousness and sin, their minds evil, / were slain in battle by Vāsudeva holding the discus in hand.
That self which was spoken of by me earlier in your presence, / that is this Viṣṇu, without doubt, the righteous soul, protector of all.
Dwelling within the bodies of the Daityas, established in sin itself, / he, very wise, became enraged, O queen, and struck down the Dānavas.
Becoming both external and internal, your sons were struck down. / And by whom they were generated, O queen, by him indeed they were cast down.
No delusion should be entertained regarding them by you; listen to my word: / whoever behaves with sin, that very one goes to destruction.
Therefore, abandoning delusion, always resort to dharma.' / Diti said: 'Let it be so, highly fortunate one; I shall do your bidding.'
Having thus addressed Kaśyapa, best of sages, the sorrowful woman, / enlightened by the sage, abandoned her sorrow and remained [calm].

title: daśamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: The sages said: / 'Then what course of action did all those Dānavas, led by Hiraṇyakaśipu, / broken in battle, undertake, O highly wise one?
Tell us at length of their supreme conduct; / we all wish to hear it now from you, O twice-born one.'
Sūta said: / 'Broken from the battle, all of them devoid of strength at that time, / their pride gone, deeply afflicted with sorrow, those Daityas went to their father.
Bowing down with devotion, all of them then said to Kaśyapa: / The Dānavas said: 'From your semen is our origin, O best of the twice-born,
and of the deities as well, O highly fortunate one, and of the Dānavas. / And we Dānavas are all endowed with strength, vigour, and valour,
knowing means, very steadfast, and endowed with effort. / But we are many, father, while the gods are few.
How is it that they all conquer and we are broken from the great battle? / What indeed is the cause of that, father, [when we are] endowed with strength and brilliance?
Each single Daitya, O highly wise one, possesses the strength / of thousands of elephants in rut; there is no such [strength] among the gods.
Yet victory is seen only among the gods in the great battle, father. / Tell us all that; you should dispel our doubt.'
Kaśyapa said: / 'Listen, all my sons, to the cause of victory, / on account of which all the deities became victorious in battle.
The father is the caster of the seed, while the mother is ever this field; / so it is indeed in holding, in protecting, and in nourishing.
What could a father do in a diverse matter, even regarding a son? / Here action alone is primary; thus has my intellect concluded.
The connection of action is twofold, arising from sin and merit. / Relying on truth alone, supreme dharma is performed.
Combined with asceticism and meditation, it is conducive to deliverance, O sons; / sin is declared to cause downfall always, there is no doubt.
By strength, by retinue, and by noble birth, O sons, / for a man devoid of merit, that strength becomes impaired.
There are tall trees in mountain fortresses, O good sons; / they fall down with roots together by the force of the wind, dense as they are.
Those devoid of truth and dharma go likewise to Yama's abode. / And this dharma is common to all living beings, O good sons,
by which a creature crosses over both here and in the hereafter. / That truth endowed with dharma was abandoned by you.
Unrighteousness was resorted to, O sons, by you who are devoid of truth. / Fallen from truth, dharma, and asceticism, you have fallen into an ocean of sorrow.
And the gods are endowed with truth and endowed with welfare, / possessed of asceticism, tranquility, and self-restraint, exceedingly virtuous, and free from sin.
Where there is truth and dharma, and likewise asceticism and merit, / and where Viṣṇu Hṛṣīkeśa is, there victory is seen.
Eternal Vāsudeva has become their ally; / therefore those gods, endowed with truth and dharma, conquer.
With an ally, with strength, and likewise with human effort— / indeed, O sons, you are devoid of asceticism and truth.
He who has Viṣṇu as ally, and likewise asceticism and strength, / his victory alone is seen; thus know the knowers of dharma.
You, however, are devoid of dharma and devoid of asceticism and truth; / previously you attained Indra's station by force alone.
Without asceticism, O very wise ones, without dharma, without fame, / Indra's station is not to be attained by the qualities of strength and pride, O sons.
Even having attained Indra's station, O sons, they fall from it indeed. / Therefore, perform asceticism, O sons, united together,
endowed with freedom from hostility, endowed with knowledge and meditation; / and enmity should never be made with Keśava.
When, O sons, you become blessed like this, / then you all will attain supreme perfection; there is no doubt.'
Thus addressed by the great-souled Kaśyapa, / those Dānavas of great majesty, hearing their father's speech,
bowed down to Kaśyapa with devotion, stood up, and filled with haste, / those Daityas held good counsel, assembled among themselves.
King Hiraṇyakaśipu then spoke to those Dānavas: / 'We shall perform severe asceticism that grants all things.'
Hiraṇyākṣa then said: 'I shall perform fierce asceticism; / then by force I shall seize the three worlds, there is no doubt here.
Having conquered Govinda in battle, that evil-minded one, / and having destroyed all the deities, I shall attain Indra's station.'
Bali said: 'It is not fitting for you to act thus, O lords of the sons of Diti; / that enmity which is with Viṣṇu, that enmity is the cause of destruction.
By acts of giving, dharma, merit, austerities, and the performance of sacrifices, / men go to happiness after worshipping that Hṛṣīkeśa.'
Hiraṇyakaśipu said: / 'I myself will never perform the worship of Hari. / Abandoning one's innate nature, should the service of an enemy be practiced?
The wise consider that indeed worse than death. / The service of Viṣṇu should not be done by me or by the other Dānavas.'
Bali again spoke to that great-souled grandfather: / 'Whatever has been seen in the Dharmaśāstras by sages who know the truth,
the counsel endowed with statecraft, especially concerning an enemy: / knowing oneself to be inferior, and that enemy to be strong,
one should go to his side and await the time of victory; / darkness always dwells resorting to the shadow of a lamp.'
Seeing that the oil of the lamp has reached the wick, its light departs swiftly, / and once again the great power of darkness increases.
In the same way, one should conciliate in secret, pointing out affection truly, / having formed an affectionate bond with the gods through righteous intentions, O enemies of the gods!
Indeed, such excellent counsel was formerly spoken by the sage Kaśyapa. / Self-possessed, O king of kings, accomplish your task by that counsel!"
Hearing his word, the majestic Daitya said: / "O grandson, I will not do this, causing my own dishonour!
And all the other kinsmen spoke to that scholar of conduct: / "What Bali has said is meritorious and pleases the gods;
it confers honor on Indra, but brings fear to the Dānavas. / We all shall perform supreme asceticism alone.
Having vanquished the gods by asceticism, we will seize our own realm." / Thus deliberating together, having rejected Bali at that time,
the great Asuras, harboring great enmity toward Viṣṇu in their hearts, / then all practiced asceticism in the mountain fastnesses and on the peaks.
Thus all those Dānavas, shedding desire, firmly resolved, / free from lust and anger, abstaining from food, conquered fatigue.

title: ekādaśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: The sages said: / "You, omniscient one, have recounted the battle between the Daityas and Dānavas. / Now we wish to hear about the high-souled Suvrata.
Whose son was that wise one, and in whose lineage was he born? / What was the asceticism of that Brahmin, and how was Hari propitiated [by him]?"
Sūta said: / "Just as the narrative was heard by me of old through the power of wisdom, / even so, O Brahmins, I will declare the story of the high-souled Suvrata,
his holy, divine, and auspicious Vaiṣṇava conduct / before you all, entirely through the grace of Viṣṇu.
In a previous kalpa, O fortunate ones, in a holy land that destroys sin, / on the sacred bank of the Revā, at the sacred site named Vāmana,
a best of Brahmins named Somaśarman was born in the family of Kuśika. / But he was childless and overwhelmed by much grief.
Constantly tormented by poverty and sorrow, / he would ponder day and night the means to obtain a son and wealth.
Once, however, his beloved, a virtuous woman named Sumanā, / observed her husband dejected with his face downcast due to worry.
Seeing her beloved then, the ascetic woman said to him: / "Your mind is overwhelmed by countless nets of sorrow.
You are bewildered by delusion; cast off your worry, O highly intelligent one! / Disclose your sorrow to me; become composed and attain happiness!
There is no misery like anxiety, for it emaciates the body. / He who lives having abandoned anxiety rejoices in happiness.
Declare before me, O Brahmin, the cause of your anxiety." / Having heard the words of his beloved, Somaśarman said to his wife:
Somaśarman said: / "Worry brought on by longing, O blessed lady, is the cause of sorrow. / I will explain all that; listen and understand!
I do not know by what sin I am destitute of wealth, O virtuous one, / and likewise bereft of a son; this is the cause of my sorrow."
Sumanā said: / "Listen, I shall proclaim the destruction of all doubt, / the essential nature of instruction, the vision of all knowledge.
Greed is indeed the seed of sin, and delusion is its root; / falsehood is its trunk, and deception its widespread branches;
hypocrisy and crookedness are its leaves; it is ever in bloom with evil intellect; / unfaithfulness is its fragrance, and ignorance alone is its fruit;
fraud, heresy, hostility, envy, cruelty, and crookedness—these sinners / are birds residing in the illusory branches of the tree of delusion;
ignorance is its delicious fruit, and adharma is the sap of that fruit; / nurtured with the water of craving, disbelief is its delightful sap;
adharma is its sweet juice, which appears violently delicious. / Such are the fruits borne by the tree of greed.
The man who, resorting to its shade, is fully satisfied, / eats its well-ripened fruits day after day;
and nurtured by the juice of its fruits, by adharma, / that mortal, becoming content, proceeds toward his fall.
Therefore, setting aside worry, a man should not indulge in greed; / he should not give way to anxiety over wealth, sons, or wives.
When one who is wise walks in the path of fools, O beloved, / like a fool he constantly worries: 'How can wealth become mine?
How can I obtain a good wife, and how can I gain sons?' / Thus, being bewildered, he worries continually day and night.

For a moment in the midst of worry he may perceive great happiness, / but then returning to consciousness, he is tormented by great sorrow.

Abandoning anxiety and delusion, conduct yourself rightly, O Brahmin! / In saṃsāra there is no lasting relation with anyone, O wise one!
Friends, kinsmen, sons, fathers, mothers, servants, / and wives alike are merely transient relations.
Somaśarman said: / "What kind of relation is it, O blessed one? Tell me in detail, / by which all—wealth, sons, and kinsmen—become connected to us."
Sumanā said: / "Some are related through debt; some are stealers of deposits; / some bestow profits, while others are neutral.
In these four divisions are sons, friends, women, / wives, fathers, mothers, servants, relatives, and kinsfolk born.
They are born upon the earth according to their respective connections. / When one has misappropriated a deposit belonging to another in this world,
the owner of that deposit becomes a virtuous and handsome son on earth, / born without doubt in the house of the very one who stole the deposit.
The owner of the deposit, having departed after suffering terrible grief from the theft of his deposit, / became a good son to the embezzler of the deposit.
Virtuous, handsome, and endowed with all auspicious marks, / showing devotion to him, he lives as his son day after day,
speaking pleasant words, gentle, sickly, showing immense affection, / seizing his own wealth [by expenses] and generating excellent affection [in his father].
Just as intense, life-destroying sorrow was formerly caused / by the embezzler through the theft of the deposit, O fortunate one,
even so, having become a son possessing great virtues through that friendship, / he becomes short-lived and goes to his death.
Having inflicted grief, he departs thus, being born again and again. / When that [father] wails, 'Alas, my son! My son!',
[the departed spirit] laughs, thinking: 'Whose son is anyone, and who is the father? / The deposit that was mine, a means of sustenance, was stolen by this man.
Through the misappropriation of my wealth, did not my life depart formerly / in great and truly unbearable grief?
In that same way, having inflicted grief and reclaimed my excellent wealth, / I shall depart swiftly today. Whose son am I in such a manner?
He is not my father, nor was anyone ever anyone's son before. / The state of a ghost has been inflicted by me upon this wicked-souled man.'
Having spoken thus, mocking him repeatedly, he departs. / By this path he departs, having inflicted the most terrible grief.
Such sons indeed belong to one who embezzles a deposit, beloved; / in this worldly existence, they are seen here and there to be full of misery.
I shall explain to you the sons bound by debt.

title: dvādaśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Sumanā said: / I shall describe before you a son connected through debt; / having taken whose debt one indeed meets death,
that creditor is born as a son, a brother, a father, or a beloved wife, / or behaves under the guise of a friend, but is ever exceedingly wicked.
Cruel, of harsh appearance, he would never see any virtue; / he always speaks harsh words among his own relatives.
He eats only the sweetest foods and constantly enjoys pleasures; / always devoted to gambling, he has a craving for theft.
he consumes the property of the household by force; when restrained, he becomes angry; / and he reviles his father and mother day by day.
He is a driver-away, a terrifier, one who utters much harsh speech. / Having consumed that wealth in this way, he lives in comfort.
From childhood, through birth rites and the like, the cruel one seizes wealth, / and again through marriage alliances in various ways and repeatedly.
Thus wealth is acquired; indeed, [the parent] gives it to him thus: / 'House, fields, and everything are his alone, no doubt.'
Day after day he injures his father and mother / with sharp pieces [of wood], with pestles, and with all manner of exceedingly severe blows.
When that father dies, he is extremely harsh to the mother; / he becomes devoid of affection and cruel, without any doubt.
He never performs ancestral rites or gives gifts. / Such sons indeed arise on the face of the earth.
I shall describe to you the enemy-son, O best of the twice-born. / When he reaches childhood, he always acts with enmity.
Even while playing, he strikes his father and mother; / having struck them, he runs off, laughing again and again.
Frightened, he comes back to his father and mother; / he is constantly angry and reproaches them again and again.
Thus he constantly engages in acts of hostility at all times. / Having caused the death of his father and then of his mother,
the wicked-minded one departs, by the power of former enmity. / Now I shall explain the one from whom love is received.
As soon as he is born, he brings joy; in childhood, by fondling and games; / having grown older, he then brings joy to his mother and father.
He constantly satisfies them with devotion; he gladdens them both / with affection, with words, and with affectionate conversation.
Knowing his elder has died, he weeps again out of affection. / All the ancestral rites, the offering of rice-balls, and the rituals,
Afflicted with immense grief, he indeed performs [the duties] and provides sustenance for them; / bound by the three debts, out of affection he feeds [them] constantly.
From whom a reward is due, O dear one, he gives it, without doubt, / having become a son in this manner, O very wise one.
I will now speak before you of an indifferent one, O dear one: / he always behaves with a disposition of indifference.
He does not give, nor does he take; he neither gets angry nor is pleased; / nor does he give up anything and depart, being neutral, O best of the twice-born.
All this has been told to you: such is the nature of sons. / As is a son, so is a wife, a father, a mother, and relatives;
servants and others are also described thus, as well as cattle, horses, / elephants, female buffaloes, and slaves: these are bound by debt.
No debt was taken by him, nor by the two of us from anyone; / nor was any deposit embezzled by anyone in a previous life.
Listen, beloved, we owe a debt to no one; / nor was enmity made with anyone in a previous birth.
By the two of us, O chief of the twice-born, no one was abandoned, O husband. / Knowing this, attain peace; cast away useless anxiety.
Whose are sons? Whose is a dear wife? Whose are kinsmen and relatives? / Nothing was stolen from anyone, nor was anything given back by you.
How, then, did wealth come? Do not be bewildered! / Wherever wealth is destined to be attained, O best of the twice-born,
it comes into his very hand without effort. / And a man guards his wealth with great effort;
when he departs, he departs alone, and the wealth remains right there. / Knowing this, attain peace; cast away useless anxiety.
Whose are sons? Whose is a dear wife? Whose are kinsmen and relatives? / In this worldly existence, who belongs to whom, when there is no connection, O best of the twice-born?
Deluded by great ignorance, evil-minded men think: / 'This is my house, this is my son, these women are mine.'
This is seen to be false, beloved, a mere bond of worldly existence. / Instructed thus at that time by his devoted wife and lady,
he spoke again to his beloved wife, Sumanā, who spoke words of wisdom. / Somaśarman said: / You have spoken the truth, auspicious lady, destroying all doubts.
Nevertheless, virtuous and truly wise men desire a lineage. / Just as I have anxiety for a son, so I do for wealth, dear wife.
By whatever means possible, I shall produce a son. / Sumanā said: / Through a son one conquers worlds; a son saves the family;
through a good son, O fortunate one, the father, mother, and creatures [are saved]. / A single wise son is preferable; what is the use of many devoid of virtue?
One saves the lineage, while others cause torment. / I have already said that the others merely go after debts.
Through merit a son is obtained; through merit a noble family is obtained; / a good birth is obtained through merits; therefore, practice merit.
Death is certain for one who is born, and birth is certain for one who has died. / A good birth is obtained through merits, and so too a good death.
Happiness and heap of wealth, beloved, are enjoyed through meritorious deeds. / Somaśarman said: / Tell me the practice of merit, dear wife, and also about [good] births.
What is true merit like, auspicious one? Tell me the characteristic of merit. / Sumanā said: / First I shall describe merit, as merit was heard by me,
how a man or a woman should conduct themselves daily, / and how through merits one obtains fame, sons, loved ones, and wealth.
I shall explain all the characteristics of merit, beloved: / by chastity, truthfulness, observing the five great sacrifices,
by generosity, observances, forgiveness, and purity, dear one, / by non-violence, great capacity, and practice of non-stealing.
Through these ten limbs one should fully accomplish dharma. / Dharma becomes complete just as bodily nourishment is filled by morsels.
The righteous person generates dharma through threefold action. / With its heart pleased, dharma brings about merit for him.
Whatever the wise one reflects upon, that hard-to-attain thing he attains. / Somaśarman said: / What is the form of dharma, and what are its limbs, fair lady?
Tell me with affection, in private; faith has arisen in me to hear it. / Sumanā said: / In this world, by whom has the form of dharma ever been seen, O best of the twice-born?
Its path invisible, its essence truth, it has not been seen by gods or demons. / Born in the lineage of Atri, a twice-born, the son of Anasūyā—
By him, Dattātreya indeed, great Dharma was always seen. / But these two great-souled ones performed supreme asceticism,
Living in dharma, and by asceticism and strength, / They were to become superior in form to Indra, distinguished.
While they remained in the forest for ten thousand years, / Feeding on air, without food, they became fair to behold.
For ten thousand years, during so much time, mighty asceticism / Was being thoroughly accomplished by the two, and there Dharma became visible.
The five fires were mastered by the two for so long, O best of the twice-born; / It was accomplished at the three junctures of the day, and they abstained from food.
For that long they stood in the water—the ascetic Dattātreya, / And Durvāsas, best of sages, emaciated by asceticism.
Against Dharma that righteous one, the best among sages, grew angry. / When he, that best of sages, became enraged, O fortunate one, then—
Then Dharma arrived in his own form indeed at that time, / Endowed with celibacy and other virtues and with austerities, intelligent.
Truth in the form of a brāhmaṇa, and celibacy likewise; / Asceticism was the best of the twice-born, and Self-control was a wise, foremost twice-born.
Observance was of great wisdom, and Charitable Giving likewise; / In the form of agnihotrins they indeed approached the son of Atri.
Patience, Peace, Modesty, Non-violence, and Simplicity— / All these arrived in female forms, O best of the twice-born.
Intellect, Wisdom, Compassion, Faith, Retentive Memory, Hospitality, and Equanimity, / As well as the sacred five sacrifices, and the Vedas with their auxiliary limbs at that time,
Assuming each their own form, they all attained manifestation; / The holy rites beginning with the establishment of sacred fires, and the horse sacrifices and others,
Endowed with beauty and grace, adorned with all ornaments, / Wearing heavenly garlands and garments, anointed with divine fragrant perfumes,
Provided with diadems and earrings, adorned with divine ornaments, / Radiant, handsome, surrounded by flames of splendor—
Thus Dharma arrived, accompanied by his retinue, / Where Durvāsas was standing, wrathful like Death.
Dharma said: / Why has anger been aroused, O learned twice-born, you who are endowed with asceticism? / For anger destroys welfare and asceticism itself, without doubt.
It brings about universal ruin; therefore, one should abandon anger in this matter. / Be at ease, O best of the twice-born; highest is the fruit of asceticism.
Durvāsas said: / Who are you, who have arrived together with these foremost twice-born? / Seven women stand here, shapely and adorned.
Tell me this at length before me, O highly intelligent one. / Dharma said: / This one in the form of a brāhmaṇa, endowed with all splendor,
With a staff in his hand, very gracious, and carrying a water pot— / Behold, this is Celibacy who has come before you.
Look upon the other radiant one, O foremost twice-born, / Tawny and with reddish-brown eyes; this is Truth, O best of the twice-born.
Behold such a one, O virtuous one, with radiance equal to the Vaiśvadeva, / Who is the Asceticism that you practiced, supported by all the gods.
Behold him who has come to your side, O highly fortunate one, / Of gracious speech, full of radiance, devoted to compassion for all living beings.
This is Self-control, who always nourishes you; / Matted-haired, fierce, reddish-brown, extremely intense, a great lord,
A destroyer of sins, sword in hand, O best of the twice-born, / Deeply peaceful, of great merit, devoted to daily rituals—
Observance has arrived at your side, O best of the twice-born; / Unbound, intensely bright, resembling pure crystal,
With a water pot in his hand, a twice-born holding a tooth-stick; / This is Purity who has arrived here in your presence.
Most virtuous, highly fortunate, adorned with the ornament of truth, / Her limbs graceful with every decoration, this Service has arrived.
Exceedingly steadfast, serene of limb, fair-complexioned, with a smiling face, / Lotus in hand, this supporter, lotus-eyed, lotus-like—
Endowed with divine ornaments, Forbearance has arrived, O best of the twice-born; / Deeply tranquil, well-established, endowed with abundant auspiciousness,
Her beauty made of divine jewels, adorned with divine decorations, / Your Peace has arrived, O highly intelligent one, in the form of wisdom.
Engaged in benefiting others, filled with abundant truth, / Ever speaking measured words, this Simplicity has arrived before you.
Gracious, endowed with forbearance, adorned with all ornaments, / Seated on a lotus, shapely, dark-complexioned, renowned—
This Non-violence, highly fortunate, has approached you; / With limbs the color of molten gold, sporting red garments,
Very serene, of sacred counsel, who does not gaze aimlessly here and there, / Pervaded by a spirit of knowledge, with pure hands, practicing austerities,
Rich with the beauty of pearl ornaments, spotless, charmingly smiling— / Behold, behold, this Faith has arrived, O highly fortunate one!
Pervaded by great intellect, filled with profound wisdom, / Form inclined toward noble enjoyments, serene, beautifully auspicious,
Absorbed in meditation on all desires, mother of the world, renowned, / Rich with the beauty of all ornaments, with full hips and breasts,
Fair of complexion, she has arrived adorned with garlands and garments; / This is Retentive Memory, O highly intelligent one, standing near you.
Resembling a swan and the moon, with dangling pearl necklaces, / Adorned with every ornament, very gracious, noble-minded,
Clothed in white garments, holding a lotus in her hand, / With a book in her lotus hand, ever radiant—
This is Wisdom, O highly fortunate one, who has approached you, the blessed one; / Bearing the color of lac-dye, ever very serene,
Wearing a garland of yellow flowers, adorned with necklaces and armlets, / Provided with finger-rings and bracelets, decorated with ear-pendants,
The goddess ever shines forth in yellow garments, / Unrivaled for the benefit and nourishment of the three worlds;
Whose virtuous character, O best of the twice-born, is ever celebrated— / That very Compassion has arrived safely at your side, O best of the twice-born.
This elderly woman, O highly intelligent one, is the ascetic wife of Bhāva; / She is my mother, O best of the twice-born, and I am Dharma, O you of noble vows.
"Knowing this, attain tranquility; protect me in this way." / Durvāsas said: "If Dharma has now approached near me,"
Tell me the reason for this: what shall I do for you, O Dharma? / Dharma said: / Why are you angry, O chief of twice-born? What unpleasant thing have they done?
Tell me the reason for that, O Durvāsas, if you deem fit. / Durvāsas said: / The reason on account of which I am angered, O god—hear that:
By self-restraint, purity, and severe penances, my body has been purified; / Indeed, ascetic practice for the span of a hundred thousand years was performed by me.
You see me thus, yet compassion does not arise from you in this way! / Therefore I am enraged this very day; I pronounce a curse thus!
Having heard this then from him, the wise one spoke to him. / Dharma said: / If I am destroyed, O highly intelligent one, the world will go to ruin.
Rooted in suffering, I, O dear one, severely emaciate [a person], O twice-born; / Afterwards I grant happiness, provided one does not abandon truth.
Sin is rooted in pleasure, but merit is obtained through hardship; / Performing merit in this way, a living being yields up life.

"In this way, I grant great happiness in the hereafter, no doubt."
Durvāsas said: "Happiness is obtained by one, but through that another experiences extreme misery.

For a mortal abandons it, and it is enjoyed by another.
Who understands that happiness? One does not see certainty at all.

I do not see that as good; what you do is indeed unjust.
By whichever body [an act] is performed, that happiness is not enjoyed [by it].

Affliction is performed by one, and it is also experienced by another.
Who understands that happiness, or whether it is injustice or righteousness?

Trouble is caused by one, and again happiness is enjoyed
by another person; if that is righteousness, all of it is combined with the highest good.

Merit also is performed by this one, and through this one experiences the fruit;
again, the merit that is being performed is enjoyed by another.

All that is indeed declared as happiness, which is such and possesses such characteristics.
And what is declared in the treatise on dharma is performed everywhere, not otherwise.

By whichever body they act, by that they endure suffering;
by that they enjoy in the hereafter, and likewise through this [body] too.
"Knowing this, may you, virtuous in soul, behold: / just as great-sinning thieves are struck together with their own bodies,"

harsh and severe through suffering, why is it not likewise with happiness?"
Dharma said: "By whichever body sinners perform their crime,

by that very [body] they indeed endure torment; for that is the fruit of crime.
A single punishment has been perceived as supreme in the treatises on dharma by the learned.

Know that [punishment] to be preceded by dharma, through these very principles, O king of dharma!"
Durvāsas said: "I do not accept such reasoning; listen likewise, O Dharmarāja!

Being enraged, I shall give you three curses; it will not be otherwise."
Dharma said: "When you are enraged, O greatly wise one, please forgive me!

If you do not forgive me, O king of brahmins, make me the son of a maidservant,
and you may make me a king, and a cāṇḍāla, O great sage!

A brahmin's face is always cheerful with grace toward one who bows."
And then Durvāsas, enraged, cursed Dharma:

Durvāsas said: "Become a king from dharma, and the son of a maidservant, not otherwise;
and go to the womb of a cāṇḍāla, O Dharma; go as you wish!"

Having thus given three curses, that best of brahmins departed.
Indeed, in this very connection, Dharma was seen in the past.

Somaśarman said: "What was Dharma like, having been cursed by that great soul?
Describe to me that form of his, if you know, O radiant woman!"

Sumanā said: "Dharma was born in the family of the Bharatas, having become Yudhiṣṭhira;
and he was Vidura, the son of a maidservant; and I shall mention the other one.

When King Hariścandra was tormented by Viśvāmitra,
then that highly intelligent Dharma attained the status of a cāṇḍāla.

Thus the fruit of action was experienced even by the great soul Dharma
from the curse of Durvāsas indeed; the truth has been spoken before you.

title: trayodaśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
Somaśarman said: "Tell me in detail the characteristic of celibacy;
and what kind of celibacy is it, if you know, O radiant woman?"

[Sumanā said:] "He whose delight is constantly in truth, a virtuous soul, would attain contentment;
when the fertile period has arrived, he may go to his own wife, free from fault.

He never abandons the virtuous conduct of his own family.
This alone is declared for the householder, O best of brahmins.

Celibacy for householders has indeed been described by me as supreme.
I shall explain that of ascetics; listen to it as I speak:

Endowed with self-restraint and truth, always afraid of sin,
having avoided intercourse with a woman, established in meditation and knowledge:

The celibacy of ascetics has thus been described before you.
I shall explain austerity itself; listen to it as I speak:

One should act with good conduct, free from desire and anger,
engaged in sustained effort for the benefit of living beings.

Austerity has thus been declared; I declare truth thus:
absence of greed toward others' possessions, and likewise toward others' wives;

he whose mind does not waver upon seeing them is called truthful.
I shall explain generosity, by which human beings live:

One who desires one's own happiness, whether here or in the hereafter,
[should know that] the great gift of food is indeed the giver of steady happiness.

Even a mere morsel should be given to one afflicted by hunger, without a doubt;
when it is given, great merit is gained, and he always enjoys nectar.

Day by day it should be given according to the capacity of one's wealth:
grass, a bed, words, and very cool shade of the house,

land, water, and likewise food, exceedingly pleasing speech,
a seat, conversation, devoid of deceit;

he who constantly does this for the sustenance of himself,
and who gives such a gift after worshipping the gods and ancestors,

rejoices here itself, and likewise in the hereafter.
He who, having become human, makes his day fruitful

through acts of giving and study, is a god, no doubt in this.
I shall also declare observance, the supreme means to dharma:

He who is devoted to the worship of the gods and the brahmins,
always endowed with observances, faithful in the vows of generosity, O one of good vows,

in benefactions and meritorious deeds—this is celebrated as observance.
I shall explain the nature of patience; let it be heard, O best of brahmins:

Having heard abuse by another, and when struck by someone,
one should not give way to anger, and struck, one should not strike back.

He should be forbearing; he is a virtuous soul, and he does not fall into passion;
he experiences supreme happiness both here and in the next world.

Thus patience has been declared; I declare purity thus:
He who is clean outside and inside, free from passion,

and behaves according to custom by bathing and sipping water—
thus purity has been declared; I shall explain non-violence:

Even a blade of grass should not be cut without purpose by a discerning person;
one should be devoted to non-violence toward others just as toward oneself.

I shall explain tranquility; through tranquility one enjoys happiness.
Tranquility alone should be cultivated; one should not abandon [virtue] out of distress.

Having cast off hostility toward creatures, one should train the mind in this manner.
Thus tranquility has been declared; I shall explain non-stealing:

Another's property must never be stolen, nor likewise another's wife;
with thought, words, and body one should so direct the mind.

I shall explain self-restraint before you, O best of brahmins:
by subduing the senses, and even the wavering mind,

one should destroy their insolence; then that conscious being is master [of himself].
I shall explain service, as it is in the treatises on dharma,

as it was declared by earlier teachers; I shall declare it thus:
With speech, body, and mind, one should accomplish the business of the guru.

That by which grace arises is spoken of as service.
Dharma with all its parts has been declared before you, O best of brahmins.

And I will tell you something else that you wish to hear, O husband:
Whatever man constantly abides in such dharma,

his rebirth does not occur again in the cycle of transmigration;
he goes to heaven through dharma: I speak the truth, the absolute truth."
Knowing this, O very wise one, follow dharma alone; / for everything that is [otherwise] unattainable on earth is obtained [through it], my beloved!
Through the grace of dharma, therefore, do heed my word! / Hearing his wife's word, the very wise Somaśarmā
spoke once again to that wife, Sumanā, who declared what is dharma.

title: caturdaśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Somaśarmā said: / How do you know such an auspicious, supreme exposition of dharma, O auspicious one? / And from whom was it heard by you?
Sumanā said: / Born in the lineage of the Bhārgavas, O high-minded one, was my father, / renowned by the name Cyavana, skilled in all knowledge.
I was his beloved daughter, dearer to him even than life. / Wherever he went, among sacred bathing sites and groves, O one of good vows,
and in assemblies of sages, and in shrines of deities, / I went with him alone, constantly playing.
Born in the lineage of Kuśika, the wise Vedaśarmā, / a friend of my father, arrived by chance while wandering about.
Overcome with great grief, thinking constantly [in sorrow], / my father said to that arrived great-souled one:
"I see that you are tormented with sorrow, O one of good vows; / why have you become sorrowful? Tell me the reason for that!"
Then, hearing these words of the great-souled Cyavana, / that one of good vows spoke to that great-souled father of mine:
"Vedaśarmā [am I], O very wise one; the cause of all my sorrow / is that my wife, highly virtuous and devoted to her husband,
has become childless, and my lineage does not continue. / This cause is declared to you, since I have been asked by you."
In the meantime, a certain Siddha arrived. / Standing up, by my father as well as by that Vedaśarmā,
that Siddha was worshipped by both of them with devotional offerings, / with gifts along with edible foods, and with words of sweet syllables.
The inner desire was asked by both, as was spoken earlier by you. / That righteous one addressed both of them—my father along with his friend:
"The entire cause of dharma has been declared to you by me indeed: / through dharma one obtains a son, wealth, grain, and wives."
Then, full dharma was performed by that Vedaśarmā; / from that dharma, great happiness arose, along with a son.
From the association with him, this firm conviction of mine arose, / which, my beloved, has been declared by me to you as supremely auspicious.
It was heard from that great Siddha, dispelling all doubt: / resorting to the dharma of a brāhmaṇa, follow it always!
Somaśarmā said: / Tell me what kind of death and what kind of birth occurs through dharma; / tell me all the characteristics of both, O beloved!
Sumanā said: / Through truth, purity, patience, tranquillity, and sacred bathing sites, merits, and so on, / by whoever dharma is protected, I shall describe his death:
Disease does not arise for him, nor pain in his body, / neither weariness nor languor, nor sweat, nor confusion.
Gandharvas and brāhmaṇas, having assumed divine forms, / endowed with the recitation of the Vedas, skilled in musical knowledge,
come to his side and sing peerless praise. / He is indeed at ease, seated on a seat, intent on worshipping the deity;
and the wise man, intent on dharma, attains a sacred place for bathing, / in the fire sanctuary, in a cowshed, and in shrines of deities,
in a pleasure grove, and at a pond where there is a sacred fig or banyan tree, / having taken recourse to a palāśa tree, and likewise to a bilva tree,
or having taken recourse to a stable for horses, or gone to a stable for elephants, / or when staying having taken recourse to an aśoka tree or a mango tree,
or in the presence of brāhmaṇas, or gone to a royal palace, / or having taken recourse to a battlefield where he might previously die.
Holy are the places of death, dharma alone being the cause; / having attained the rescue of cows, and likewise [the sacred place] Amarakaṇṭaka,
doing pure dharma continually, adhering to dharma, loving dharma, / he attains such a place when he meets death.
The best among men sees his virtuous mother and father, / his brother endowed with auspiciousness, and other relatives and kin,
being praised again and again by virtuous bards. / He does not at all see a sinful mother, father, or others.
Gandharvas sing songs, panegyrists praise with hymns, / and brāhmaṇas with the recitation of mantras; his mother honors him with affection,
and his father and circle of relatives [honor] the righteous, wise one. / Such are the messengers described, and such are your holy places, O lord.
He sees the messengers before his eyes, free of agitation, full of smiles and affection; / he [sees them] neither in sleep nor in delusion nor joined with distress.
The very wise Dharmarāja summons him: / "Come, come, O highly fortunate one, to where dharma abides!"
For him, no delusion, no wandering, no languor, no loss of memory / arises—there is no doubt of this; he remains with a serene soul.
Endowed with knowledge and discernment, remembering the god Janārdana, / he departs with them in this way, contented and joyful in mind.
A state of oneness arises there as he abandons his body; / taking recourse to the tenth door, his self departs.
A palanquin arrives for him, [or] a charming swan-vehicle, / or an aerial chariot arrives, or a horse, or an excellent elephant.
Being fanned all around with a held umbrella, / with chowries, and with fans by virtuous beings,
the righteous one is sung of and praised by learned men, / by bards, divine cāraṇas, and brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas.
Praised by virtuous men and endowed with all happiness, / there he attains the fruit in accordance with the power of his gifts.
He travels happily through gardens and groves, / surrounded by divine apsarases, accompanied by auspicious things.
Praised by the gods, he beholds Dharmarāja, / and the gods endowed with dharma go out to meet him face to face:
"Come, come indeed, O highly fortunate one, enjoy pleasures pleasing to your mind!" / In this way he beholds Dharma of gentle form and great wisdom.
By the power of his own merit, he enjoys heaven itself; / when his pleasures are exhausted, that righteous one enters rebirth indeed.
Through the favor of his own dharma, he enters an auspicious family / of a highly virtuous brāhmaṇa, or likewise of a kṣatriya,
or of a highly virtuous, wealthy vaiśya, O wise one; / through dharma he rejoices there, and again performs merit.

title: pañcadaśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Somaśarmā said: / With what kinds of characteristics is the death of sinners accompanied, O auspicious one? / Tell me that in detail, O fair lady, if you know it!
Sumanā said: / Listen, I shall explain what was heard by me from that Siddha, / as to what sign [appears] at the death of sinners, O beloved.
I shall tell of the place and the agony of great sinners: / a ground filled with feces, urine, and filth, accompanied by sins;
reaching that, that very wicked-souled one gives up his life-breaths with agony. / Having reached the ground of an outcaste, he goes to death in misery;
having resorted to ground frequented by donkeys or a courtesan's house, / or having gone to the house of a liquor-distiller, he approaches death.
Filled with bones, skin, and nails, enveloped by sins and crimes— / having reached such a place, that wicked-souled one certainly goes to death.
Having reached another ground of sinful conduct, he goes to death. / Now I will describe the movement of the messengers who desire [to seize] him:
formidable, harsh, frightful, extremely black, with huge bellies, / with tawny eyes, yellow and blue, extremely white, with huge bellies,
very tall, terrifying, looking like dried flesh and fat, / with fierce fangs, formidable, with lion-faces and serpents in their hands.
Seeing them, he trembles and grieves again and again. / Terrible loud roars like the howling of jackals, O highly intelligent one,
all the messengers release at the base of his ears. / Binding him at the throat with nooses, and binding his waist and belly,
overpowering him, they cast him down; he cries out repeatedly, 'Alas, alas!' / I shall declare the agony of the one dying, just as it is.
The theft of another's wealth, the violation of another's wife, / a debt, the entire property of another seized by sinners,
which was never returned due to delusion caused by greed for pleasure, / and likewise other great sins, and even improper acceptance of gifts—
all these rise up into the throat of that dying man. / And whatever sins were previously committed,
they come to the base of his throat, of that great sinner, not otherwise; / they generate severe agony through the obstruction of phlegm.
With severe pains his throat rattles; / he weeps, trembles excessively, and repeatedly [recalls] his mother and father,
he remembers his brother there, and his wife and sons again and again; / again he enters forgetfulness, bewildered by great sin.
His life-breaths depart, agitated by abundant pain; / he falls, and he trembles, and he faints again and again.
Thus afflicted with agony, he experiences misery, utterly bewildered. / His life-breaths, stirred with great difficulty by severe distress,
depart through the downward passage, hear, O beloved! / Thus the living being, deeply deluded, endowed with greed and confusion,
is led away by Yama's messengers; I will tell of his misery.

title: ṣoḍaśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Sumanā said: / He is led along a path strewn with burning coals, dragged along; / burning, that wicked-souled one struggles again and again,
where the heat is very fierce, heated as if by twelve suns; / he is led by that path, scorched by the rays of the sun,
over impassable mountains that are devoid of shade, the evil-minded one; / he is led by that path, afflicted with hunger and thirst.
Struck by the messengers with clubs, swords, and axes, / and beaten with whips, reviled by the messengers,
then on an icy path he is blown upon by the wind again; / through that cold, becoming miserable, he proceeds, without a doubt.
Being dragged by the messengers, he is led through diverse impassable places; / thus the sinner, that wicked-souled reviler of gods and Brahmins,
who engaged in all manner of sins, is led by Yama's servants. / The wicked-souled one beholds Yama, resembling a mass of black collyrium,
fierce, terrible, dreadful, surrounded by dreadful messengers, / encompassed by all diseases, accompanied by Citragupta,
mounted upon a buffalo, the god Dharmarāja, O best of Brahmins, / with terrifying fangs, very fierce, his mouth resembling death itself,
wearing yellow garments, club in hand, anointed with red fragrant paste, / adorned with red garlands, mace in hand, terrifying.
The evil-minded one beholds Yama of such form, huge in body; / seeing him arrived, excluded from all dharma,
Yama beholds that wicked, most sinful thorn of dharma; / he punishes him with great miseries, with torments, and with wooden mallets.
He is cooked for as long a time as the end of a thousand yugas; / and in various kinds of hell he is cooked again and again.
The evildoer goes to a hellish womb among crores of worms; / he is constantly cooked in filth, crying 'Alas, alas!', devoid of consciousness.
And thus that sinful-souled one certainly goes to death; / thus the evil-minded one experiences the consequence of his sin.
I will tell of his rebirth, and in which wombs he goes: / having obtained a hundred wombs of dogs, he experiences the sin again;
the wicked-souled one becomes a tiger, and again goes to the womb of a female ass, / to the womb of a cat, a sow, and likewise to the womb of a snake,
among all the different varieties of beasts again and again; / he enters into sinful birds, and into other large creatures;
the evildoer goes to the womb of an outcaste, of a Bhilla, and of a Pulinda woman. / All this has been declared to you, both the birth of sinners
and, hear, O beloved, their very terrible agony at death. / The conduct of sin and merit has been narrated before you by me;
I shall speak of another matter thus, if you ask, O honor-giver.

title: saptadaśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Somaśarmā said: / O goddess, all the excellent establishment of dharma has been fully related. / How might I obtain a son who is all-knowing and endowed with virtues?
Tell me, O highly fortunate one, if you know, O lady of good vows; / charity, dharma, and the like [bear fruit] in the hereafter and here, without doubt.
Sumanā said: / Go to Vasiṣṭha, who knows dharma, and pray to that great sage; / from him you will surely obtain a son who knows dharma and is fond of dharma.
Sūta said: / When this speech was spoken by her, Somaśarmā, the best of Brahmins, [said]: / 'I will do thus, O auspicious lady, according to your word, without doubt.'
Having spoken thus, Somaśarmā, the best of Brahmins, went swiftly / to Vasiṣṭha, the knower of all, divine, the best among ascetics,
standing on the bank of the Gaṅgā, holy, residing in his hermitage, the best of Brahmins, / surrounded by blazing splendor, like a second sun,
shining, great-souled, devoted to the sacred, the best of Brahmins. / Bowing with devotion to the lord of Brahmins like a staff, again and again,
the sinless son of Brahmā, of great splendor, spoke to him: / 'Sit down on a sacred seat with ease, O very intelligent one.'
Having spoken thus, that lord of yogins spoke again to the ascetic: / 'In your house, among your sons, my child, your wife, and your servants, is there always
welfare, O highly fortunate one, and in your meritorious rites and sacred fires? / Are you free from disease in your limbs, and do you always preserve dharma?'
Having spoken thus, the very wise one spoke again to Suśarmā: / 'What pleasing deed may I do, very agreeable to you, O best of Brahmins?'
Having thus addressed the Brahmin, that jar-born sage paused, / when that was spoken by the highly fortunate Vasiṣṭha, the eminent sage.
He spoke to the great-souled Vasiṣṭha, best among ascetics: / 'O lord, please listen to my words with a deeply gracious mind.
If you are to do me a great favour, O foremost among sages, / then dispel the doubt of my inquiry, O best of the twice-born.
By what sin has this poverty come, and why is there no joy from sons? / Resolve this doubt of mine, dear sir; tell me from what sin it arises.
Bewildered by great delusion, I was awakened by my beloved wife, O twice-born one. / Sent by her, distressed, I have come to your presence, dear sir.
Explain all that, which destroys all doubt; / become the giver of liberation for me from the bond of worldly existence.'
Vasiṣṭha said: / 'Sons, friends, brothers, and other kinsmen and relatives— / these come to be for a man through five distinct divisions.
Those were indeed told to you earlier in your presence by Sumanā; / they are all bound by debt, they are bad sons, O best of the twice-born.
I shall explain before you the meritorious characteristic of a son: / one whose self is attached to merit, who is always devoted to truth and dharma,
endowed with purity and higher knowledge, an ascetic, foremost among the eloquent, / steadfast in all deeds, dedicated to the study of the Vedas,
a knower of all scriptures, a worshipper of gods and brāhmaṇas, / a performer of all sacrifices, generous, renounced, pleasant of speech,
always devoted to meditating on Viṣṇu, calm, self-controlled, always a good friend, / constantly devoted to his father and mother, affectionate to all his kinsmen,
a saviour of his lineage, learned, a sustainer of his family— / endowed with such virtues, he is a son who brings happiness.
Others are merely bound by connection, givers of grief and torment. / What purpose is served by such a one who is devoid of fruit?
They come and go, all of them, having inflicted terrible torment; / in the form of sons they all appear in worldly existence, O best of the twice-born.
The merit done in a previous life that was maintained by you— / I shall tell you all of that; listen once more to this wonder.'
Vasiṣṭha said: / 'In your previous birth, O very wise one, you were indeed a śūdra, not otherwise; / a farmer, devoid of knowledge, filled with great greed.
Having one wife, always hostile, having many sons, never giving; / you did not know dharma, nor did you listen to truth.
No gift was given by you, no scripture listened to; / nor did you ever make a pilgrimage to a sacred ford, O noble-minded one.
Thus the way of agriculture was pursued by you again and again, O twice-born one; / the rearing of animals and cattle, O best of the twice-born,
and the repeated keeping of buffaloes and horses; / such was the work previously done by you, O best of the twice-born.
And abundant wealth was likewise amassed through greed; / yet its expenditure was never made by you on anything truly virtuous.
A gift was not given to a worthy recipient; even seeing a weak man, / no wealth was given by you out of compassion.
Cattle, buffaloes, and the rest—all livestock was accumulated by you; / and selling them, O twice-born one, vast wealth was hoarded by you.
Having sold buttermilk, clarified butter, and milk, and then curd, / you contemplated famine, O twice-born one, deluded by the māyā of Viṣṇu.
Grain was made truly expensive here by you, O best of brāhmaṇas; / being merciless, a gift was never given by you at any time.
Worship of the gods was never performed by you, O twice-born one; / even when holy festival days arrived, wealth was not given to the brāhmaṇas.
When the time for ancestral rites arrived, it was not performed by you with faith; / your virtuous wife would say, "This day has arrived,
the time for the ancestral rites of your father-in-law and mother-in-law, O noble-minded one." / Hearing that word of hers, you would flee, abandoning your home.
The path of dharma was never seen by you, nor ever heard by you; / greed was your mother, father, brother; greed was your kinsmen and relatives.
Greed alone was cherished, having always abandoned dharma; / therefore you have become sorrowful, severely afflicted by poverty.
Day after day great thirst increased in your heart; / whenever wealth in your house grew,
being burned by that thirst which had the form of fire, / even while sleeping well at night, you pondered anxiously:
"When day comes, I am always seized by great delusions: / when will a thousand, a hundred thousand, a crore, or ten million be mine?
When will a hundred billion, or a trillion, be in my house?" / Thus, though a thousand, a hundred thousand, a crore, and ten million,
a hundred billion, and a trillion came to be, the thirst never departs; / rather than leaving your body, it continually increases.
Nothing was ever given, offered into fire, or enjoyed by you, O twice-born one; / dug into the ground, it was hidden away, and your sons did not know of it.
You constantly adopted other means for the sake of the arrival of wealth, O twice-born; / wise as you were, you questioned people.
Asking about magical spades, salves, transmutation, and alchemy beyond that, / you wandered alone, utterly deluded by craving.
You constantly pondered the philosopher's stone and recipes granting magical success; / contemplating entry into subterranean cavities, you questioned eagerly.
Consumed by the fire of thirst, you found no happiness; / blazed by the fire of thirst, you cried "Alas, alas!", deprived of sense.
Thus deluded, O chief of twice-borns, you came under the sway of death; / even when your wife and sons inquired about that wealth,
the truth was never told by you; having abandoned your life-breaths, you went to Yama. / Thus your whole past account has been related by me.
By this action, O twice-born, you have become destitute and poor. / In this world, the one whose sons are good, always possessing devotion,
virtuous, endowed with knowledge, and always devoted to truth and dharma, / are born in his house when Viṣṇu is pleased with him.
Wealth, grain, a wife, and endless sons and grandsons / he enjoys in the mortal world, when Viṣṇu is gracious to him.
Without the grace of Viṣṇu, one cannot obtain wife and sons, / nor a good birth and noble family, O twice-born one, [which lead to] that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.'

title: aṣṭādaśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Somaśarman said: / 'The sin committed in my previous birth has been recounted to me by you, O sage; / but that state of being a śūdra was abandoned by me, O chief of the twice-born.
How then was the status of a Brahmin attained by me, O best of the twice-born? / Tell me the entire cause of that, O scholar learned in theoretical and experiential wisdom!
Vasiṣṭha said: / 'Whatever deed based on dharma was undertaken by you previously, O twice-born one, / that I shall declare; listen, if you please.
A certain sinless brāhmaṇa, of virtuous conduct, very learned, / a devotee of Viṣṇu, righteous in soul, was ever intent upon Viṣṇu.
Under the guise of a pilgrimage to sacred fords, he wandered alone over the earth; / wandering about, that high-minded one came to your house.
He requested a single place to dwell, O best of the twice-born; / and it was granted by your wife, and by you together with your sons.
"Come, come, O holy brāhmaṇa, comfortably into my good house!" / Thus you said repeatedly to that pure Vaiṣṇava brāhmaṇa.'

"Stay here comfortably, O one of good vows; this house is yours.
Today I am blessed; today I have gone to a sacred pilgrimage place.

Today the fruit of a pilgrimage has been attained from seeing your pair of feet."
A holy and excellent cow-shed was offered [to him] for lodging.

Having massaged his limbs and rubbed his feet,
and washed them with water, he bathed in the water from his feet.

You offered fresh ghee, curd, milk, food, and buttermilk
to that very brāhmaṇa, the great-souled one.

In this way the twice-born sage was satisfied by you, together with your wife
and your sons, O highly fortunate one—a Vaiṣṇava learned in knowledge.

Then, when morning arrived on an auspicious, fortune-giving day,
the sin-destroying Ekādaśī of the bright half of Āṣāḍha,

arrived on that day, destroying all sins,
on which the god Hṛṣīkeśa enters the sleep of yoga.

Reaching that [day], the people, wise with understanding, abandoned
all household tasks, intent on meditation on Viṣṇu, O twice-born.

They made a great festival with songs and auspicious instrumental music;
all the brāhmaṇas praised [him] with the Vedas and auspicious hymns.

Having reached such a great festival, that best of brāhmaṇas
remained there on that day; fasting took place.

The glorification of Ekādaśī was recited by the brāhmaṇa;
together with his wife and sons, he heard the unsurpassed dharma.

When that great holiness was heard, [you were] urged by your wife and sons:
"Through association with this twice-born, observe this vow."

Having heard that great speech giving all religious merit,
with a resolved mind: "I will observe this vow,"

going with your wife and sons, a bath in the river was performed by you;
with a joyful heart, O twice-born, Madhusūdana was worshipped

with all sacred offerings, and with perfumes, incenses, and the like,
keeping a vigil at night with dances, songs, and so forth.

In the company of the brāhmaṇa, bathing in the river was done again;
the lord of the gods was worshipped with auspicious flowers, incenses, and the like.

Bowing with devotion to Govinda and bathing him again and again,
such an offering was given to the great-souled brāhmaṇa.

Bowing to that twice-born with devotion, a good sacrificial gift was given to him;
he broke the fast, O twice-born, together with his sons, wife, and others.

He was sent off by you alone with devotion and good intent;
thus this vow was observed by you, O best of the twice-born.

Through association with that brāhmaṇa and by the grace of Viṣṇu,
you attained the status of a brāhmaṇa, endowed with true dharma.

By the power of that vow, a noble family was attained by you,
of brāhmaṇas, highly wise, endowed with true dharma.

To that very brāhmaṇa, the great-souled Vaiṣṇava,
well-prepared food was given with faith and true disposition.

By the power of that gift, sweet food is available [to you];
yet you were bewildered by great delusions, and your mind was filled with thirst.

In your previous birth, O twice-born, wealth alone was amassed;
it was not given by you to brāhmaṇas, or to the poor and others,

as you were dying out of greed for your wife and sons.
By the effect of that sin, poverty entered you.

Having completely cast off greed for a son and rejected affection far away,
you became sonless as the fruit of that very sin.

A good son and family, O twice-born, wealth, grain, excellent women,
a good birth and a good death, good enjoyments and happiness,

kingship, heaven, and liberation, whatever is difficult to obtain,
[come] through the grace of that god, the great-souled Viṣṇu.

Therefore, having worshipped Govinda, the healthy Nārāyaṇa,
you will reach that highest abode, the supreme step of Viṣṇu.

Good sons, wealth, grain, good enjoyments, and happiness—
all your past actions performed in the previous birth,

that has been fully recounted by me before you, O twice-born.
Knowing this, O fortunate one, be devoted to Nārāyaṇa."

Enlightened indeed by the son of Brahmā, that eminent twice-born of great majesty,
filled with joy, having bowed down with devotion to Vasiṣṭha there,

taking leave of the twice-born, went home, joyful on reaching his well-disposed wife:
"All the past deeds of mine were revealed by that very twice-born, through your favor,

O noble lady, brought to light by Vasiṣṭha; today my delusion has been destroyed.
I shall worship Madhusūdana; I shall go to liberation, that supreme step."

Having heard this supreme, great speech, highly auspicious and truly granting auspiciousness, / filled with joy, she said to her beloved: 'You are meritorious; you have been enlightened by the brahmin.'

title: ekonaviṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Sūta said: / The most wise Somaśarman, the best among men, together with Sumanā, / went to the auspicious confluence of the Kapilā on the bank of the Revā, which grants great merit.
Having bathed there, the wise man, offering libations to the gods and ancestors, / performed austerity with an entirely tranquil mind, murmuring [the name of] auspicious Nārāyaṇa.
Joined in meditation through the twelve-syllable mantra, the high-minded man of firm vows / [meditated] on that very god of gods, Vāsudeva.
While sitting, lying down, moving, and in dreams, he beheld Keśava, / always remaining steady, freed from desire and anger.
And that virtuous, fortunate woman, devoted to her husband, / Sumanā, served her beloved who was endowed with austerity.
While he was meditating, fear was displayed to him by obstacles; / black serpents fierce with poison approached that great-souled man.
Beside that Somaśarman as he practiced austerities, / seen lions, tigers, and elephants brought about terrible fear.
Vetālas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, and fierce Pretas / displayed terrifying, life-destroying fear.
Various immensely terrifying lions assembled there; / their mouths formidable with fangs, they roared most dreadfully.
From the meditation on Viṣṇu, that righteous-minded, wise man did not swerve, / nor was that best of sages shaken by the deep-rooted, great obstacles.
Thus the best of brahmins, Somaśarman, did not waver from his meditation, / though severely afflicted by howling windstorms, cold, and heavy rain.
A lion arrived there, most terrifying with a roaring sound; / seeing it, terrified with fear, the brahmin remembered Nṛhari:
Resembling sapphire, clad in yellow garments, endowed with great splendor, / the god bearing the conch and discus, holding the mace and lotus,
with a great pearl necklace imitating the luster of the moon, / radiant also with the Kaustubha gem—Janārdana,
whose chest shines with the divine mark of Śrīvatsa, / his limbs adorned with every ornament, his eyes resembling a hundred-petaled lotus,
with a gently smiling face, fully gracious, adorned with garlands of gems, / gleaming Hṛṣīkeśa—unwavering meditation was performed by him [saying]:
'You alone are my refuge, Kṛṣṇa, compassionate to those seeking refuge; / homage be to the god of gods! What can cause me fear?
Within the belly of which great soul are the three worlds and the seven others— / I have entered his refuge; where indeed can fear be for me?
From fear of whom the immensely powerful Kṛtyās and other [spirits] depart— / in him, the destroyer of all fear, have I taken refuge.
The great terror of all sins and of the Dānavas, / the protector of the devotees of Viṣṇu—in him have I taken refuge.
Of all the gods and the high-souled Dānavas, / he who is the refuge of the devotees of Kṛṣṇa—in him have I taken refuge.
The fearless one, for the destruction of fear, possessed of knowledge for the destruction of sin, / and the sole one in the form of Indra—in him have I taken refuge.
The destroyer of diseases, who has the nature of medicine, / free from illness and free from transient joy—in him have I taken refuge.
Immovable, he moves the worlds, free from sin, and knowledge itself; / having taken refuge in him, what will fear do to me?
The protector of all the virtuous, who is free from sickness, / who protects the universe, the Self of the universe—in him have I taken refuge.
He who in the form of the king of beasts shows fear before me— / having taken refuge in him, I bow down to Narasiṃha.
A wild elephant, intoxicated with rut and huge in body, has arrived; / the god whose gait is sportive as an elephant, affectionate to those seeking refuge,
who has an elephant face, endowed with knowledge, holding a noose and a goad, / whose mouth is Death, elephant-trunked—I have thoroughly taken refuge in him.
The striker of Hiraṇyākṣa, the Boar—in him have I taken refuge; / to Vāmana I surrender, affectionate to those seeking refuge.
Short ones, dwarfs, hunchbacks, Pretas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, and others, / all wearing the form of death, show fear to me.
I have surrendered to the immortal one; what will fear do to me? / The friend of brahmins, the giver of Brahman, Brahmā, Hari consisting of knowledge of Brahman—
to him have I surrendered for refuge; what will fear do to me? / He who is fearlessness to the world, destroyer of fear, and creator of fear—
to him who takes the form of fear have I surrendered; what will fear do to me? / The savior of all worlds, the destroyer of all sinners,
in him, Janārdana who is the form of dharma, have I taken refuge. / He who assumes a wonderful form in battle to protect the gods—
I will go to his refuge; he is my perpetual resort. / The storm wind is exceedingly violent; my body suffers greatly.
To him have I surrendered for refuge; he is my perpetual resort. / Extreme cold, torrential rain, and heat causing torment—
in that god who is in the form of these have I taken refuge. / These fearful agitators of mine have arrived in the form of Time;
in them, who are always the manifestations of Hari, have I taken refuge.
Whom as the god of all, the Supreme Lord, pure and isolated, a lamp consisting of knowledge, / they call Nārāyaṇa, the eternally realized, Lord of the Siddhas—to him I surrender for refuge.'
Thus meditating and constantly praising Keśava, the destroyer of distress, / Hari was brought by him with devotion into his own heart at that moment.
Beholding that effort and courage of Somaśarman, / Hṛṣīkeśa, having manifested himself, said to him joyfully:
'O Somaśarman of great wisdom, listen together with your wife! / I am Vāsudeva, best of brahmins; ask for a boon, O you of noble vows!'
Addressed by him, that best of brahmins, opening both his eyes / and seeing the Lord of the universe, dark as a storm cloud, of great majesty,
his limbs adorned with all ornaments, equipped with all weapons, / endowed with divine marks, his eyes resembling the white lotus,
clad in yellow garments, radiant, the Lord of gods, / mounted upon the son of Vinatā, bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
the true benefactor of Brahmā and others, of glorious fame in this universe, / always beyond this universe, beyond form, the teacher of the world—
filled with great joy, falling down prostrate like a staff before him / who was accompanied by Śrī, radiant, with the splendor of ten million suns,
joining his hands in supplication together with Sumanā, / said to him, 'Victory, victory! Victory, O Mādhava, giver of honor!
Victory, O Lord of Yogins, Indra among yogins! Victory, O you who recline upon the body of the serpent! / O limb of the sacrifice, victory, O Lord of sacrifice! Victory, O eternal, all-pervading one!
Victory, O Lord of all, infinite one, embodiment of sacrifice, homage be to you! / Victory, O foremost of the wise! Victory to you, leader of knowledge!
Victory, O giver of all, omniscient one! Victory to you, creator of all! / Victory, O Lord whose form is the soul! O great life, homage be to you!
Victory, O giver of wisdom, whose limbs are wisdom! Victory, O giver of life-breath! / Victory, O destroyer of sin, Lord of merit! Victory, O Master of merit, Hari!
Victory, O Lord whose essence is knowledge! Homage to you who are reachable by knowledge! / Victory, O lotus-petal-eyed one! Homage to you who have a lotus at the navel!
Victory, O Govinda, Gopāla! Victory, O conch-bearing, stainless one! / Victory, O discus-bearer, unmanifest one! Homage to you whose form is manifest!'

[He prayed:] "Victory to the one whose limbs shine with valor, victory to the lord of valor!
Victory to the one whose body delights in Lakṣmī; homage to you who are composed of the Vedas!

Victory to the one whose limbs shine with valor, victory to the giver of exertion!
Victory to exertion and to time; homage, homage to exertion!

Victory to the one capable of effort, the sustainer of the three exertions;
homage to you, that dharma who sets exertion in battle into motion!

Homage to the golden-seeded one; homage to you, that radiance,
to the one whose nature is supreme radiance, and who consists of all radiance!

To the destroyer of the radiance of Daityas, and the remover of the radiance of sins,
for the benefit of cows and brāhmaṇas, homage to the Supreme Self!

Homage to the enjoyer of oblations, and homage to you who carry the havis!
Homage indeed to the bearer of the kavya, homage to you whose form is svadhā!

To the sacrifice whose form is svāhā, to the purifier, homage, homage!
Homage to you who hold the bow Śārṅga, to Hari, the remover of sin!

To the impeller of the existent and the nonexistent, homage to the possessor of discernment!
Homage to the embodiment of the Vedas, to the purifier, homage, homage!

Homage to Harikeśa, to you the remover of all afflictions,
