Abandoning this wicked, deeply sinful woman, be resolute! / Terrible suffering and great sin are destined to be experienced.
"O beloved, enjoy that which brings well-being in the world together with me." / The female pig said this sentence; having heard that good advice, that best of twice-born
set his mind on abandoning [me]. I was then summoned; / all my clothes and adornments were given to me; hear, O auspicious one:
“Only through your misconduct, O wicked woman who ruins the family, / has the wise Brahmin Śivaśarman, best of the twice-born, departed.
Go without a doubt to where your husband stays! / Whatever place pleases you, do according as it is destined.”
Having been spoken to thus, O noble lady, abandoned by father, mother, and family, / shameless, I quickly went away, O fair-faced one.
I did not find even a dwelling place or happiness, O fair one. / People reviled me: “This unchaste woman has arrived!”
Wandering, devoid of family honor, I departed from the country / to the holy Gurjara country, to Saurāṣṭra, the abode of Śiva.
In the city known as Vanasthala, crowded with prosperity, / hear, O lady: I was then exceedingly afflicted with hunger.
Taking an earthen begging-bowl in hand, I went about for alms. / Deeply miserable, I approached the doorways of householders.
Seeing my appearance, O lovely lady, people reviled me: / “This sinful woman has come!” and they gave me no alms.
Thus, afflicted by poverty, a collector of sorrow, / while wandering, I saw an unequaled house,
surrounded by a high wall, endowed with a hall for Vedic study, / filled with the sound of the Vedas, crowded with many Brahmins,
abounding in wealth and grain, adorned with female and male servants. / That delightful house, radiant as Lakṣmī, was entered [by me].
That house, auspicious on all sides, belonged to that very Śivaśarman. / Then, afflicted by distress, Sudevā said: “Give alms!”
Śivaśarman, best of the twice-born, then heard the cry for alms. / To his wife named Maṅgalā, fair-faced, the very form of Lakṣmī,
the righteous and wise Śivaśarman, smiling, said to her: / “This frail woman has arrived, come to the doorway for alms.
Calling her, my dear, give her food, O fair one.” / Filled with supreme compassion on knowing that I had come,
Maṅgalā said to her husband: “My beloved, I will give food.” / Having said this to her husband, Maṅgalā, full of auspiciousness,
fed me, very weak as I was, with sweet food again. / That righteous, great sage Śivaśarman said to me:
“Who are you who have come here? Or to whom do you belong, wandering the world? / For what purpose do you wander everywhere? Tell me before me.”
Hearing those words of the great-souled husband, / my husband was then recognized by his voice by me, a sinful woman.'
When I saw my husband, I bowed my head in shame. / Mangalā, whose limbs were entirely lovely, said this to her husband:
"Tell [me], who is this woman who is embarrassed upon seeing you? / Please tell [me], who will this [woman] be?"

title: dvipaṃcāśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Śivaśarman said: / "O Maṅgalā, listen to my words if you ask now. / Learn the reason for which you have asked, O fair-faced woman.
Indeed, this wretched woman has now arrived disguised as an ascetic. / She is the daughter of the brahmin Vasudatta, O lovely-eyed woman.
Named Sudevā, she was always my beloved wife, O auspicious one. / For some reason, she abandoned the country and has come here.
She was burned by sorrow and by separation from me, O fair-faced woman. / Recognizing me, she has come to your house disguised as an ascetic.
Knowing this, O auspicious woman, a splendid hospitality should be offered / by you without doubt, if you desire what is very dear to me."
Having heard the word of her husband, the exceedingly auspicious Maṅgalā, to whom her husband was a deity, / was seized with great joy of her own accord.
That devoted wife provided for me a bath, clothing, and food, / along with ornaments studded with gems and gold, O fair-faced woman.
"Indeed, I was adorned, O auspicious woman, by that very one desiring [to please] her husband. / By her I was honored, O lady, with baths, respect, and meals.
I was honored by my husband, O lady, [yet] an endless sorrow arose / exceedingly sharp within my heart, destroying all my life-breaths.
I saw honor shown to her, and likewise the sorrow that resided within myself. / A dreadful anxiety arose in me, by which my life-breaths departed:
'An auspicious word was never spoken by me, a sinner, / to this best of brahmins, while committing evil deeds.
Washing of the feet was never done, nor massaging of the limbs; / privacy was never granted by me to that great-souled man.
How shall I, determined in sin, converse with him?' / That very night I fell there into an ocean of sorrow.
While thinking thus, my heart burst. / Then my life-breaths departed, abandoning my body, O fair-faced woman.
Then the messengers of Dharmarāja arrived there: / valiant, dreadful, cruel, wielding maces, discs, and swords.
Bound by them with chains of firm fetters, O highly fortunate woman, / I was taken to Yama's city by them, weeping and deeply distressed.
Struck with mallets, tormented along an impassable path, / and rebuked, I was ushered by them there before Yama.
I was looked upon with anger by the great-souled King Yama; / I was cast into a heap of live coals, cast into an accumulation of hells.
Having fashioned a man of iron heated by fire, / it was hurled onto my chest because of cheating my own husband.
Deeply tormented by various pains, scorched by the fires of hell, / I was cast into a vat of oil, and onto hot gruel-like sand.
Cut to pieces by sword-leaves, swept along by the Vaitaraṇī river, / and thrown onto thorny Śālmali trees by that great-souled one,
I fell into pus, blood, and feces teeming with worms. / Thus I was cast into all the hells, O princess,
intensely painful hells, by that very great-souled one. / I was ripped apart with saws and beaten heavily with spears.
Cast down into still other hells, O princess, / I was thrown into womb-pits and plunged into a crisis of suffering.
Cast down into hells by that Dharmarāja, / I entered the womb of a bat and experienced dreadful suffering.
I entered the womb of a jackal, and then entered the womb of a bitch; / I went to that of a hen, of a female cat, and indeed to the womb of a female mouse.
Thus was I cast by Dharmarāja into particular wombs, / into sinful wombs, and afflicted in all kinds of births.
By him I was made a sow upon the earth, O princess. / In your hand, O highly fortunate woman, are numerous holy waters.
Sprinkled with that water by you, O woman of excellent complexion, / my sin has departed, O lady, by your favor, O beautiful one.
Through your very power and merit, knowledge has arisen in me, O fair-faced woman. / Now deliver me, who have fallen into the distress of hell.
If you do not deliver me, O lady, I shall again go to dreadful / hell, O highly fortunate woman; protect me who am an heir to sorrow.
I have gone [astray] through sinful disposition; I am wretched and without refuge." / Sudevā said: "What virtuous deed arising from merit have I done, O auspicious one,
by which I might deliver you? Tell me that now." / The sow said: "This king is highly fortunate, an Ikṣvāku and descendant of Manu.
He is Viṣṇu, full of great wisdom; and you are Śrī, not otherwise. / You are a devoted wife, highly fortunate, intent on fidelity to your husband.
You are a faithful wife always, O auspicious one, dear and embodying all holy waters; / you, O lady, continually embody everything and are made of all the gods.
You alone in the world are a great devoted wife, beloved of the king, / by whom, by your ladyship, her husband is served day and night."
“Give me the merit of even a single day, O fair-faced one, / of the service done to your husband, if you wish to do me a favor.
You are indeed my mother and my father; you are my eternal teacher. / I am a sinful woman of evil conduct, false, and devoid of knowledge.
Deliver me, O noble lady; I am terrified of the beatings of Yama.” / Sukalā said: Having heard what was said by her thus, looking at the king at that time,
“What shall I do, O great king? What is this beast saying?” / Ikṣvāku said: “This wretched, miserable woman who has entered a sinful womb, O auspicious one,
deliver her with your own merits! Great welfare will come to pass.” / Addressed in this way, the excellent woman Sudevā, of charming auspiciousness,
said: “The merit of one year is given to you by me, O fair-faced one!” / At that very instant, by the words spoken by that lady,
she became endowed with beauty and youth, adorned with divine garlands; / and possessing a divine body, she arose enveloped in flames of splendor.
Rich in the splendor of all ornaments, and adorned with various gems, / she took on a divine form, anointed with celestial fragrant perfumes.
Mounted on a celestial chariot, that virtuous woman went into the sky. / Then she, bowing low with bent neck, said to the queen:
“May there be well-being for you, O noble lady; by your grace, O beautiful one, / freed from sin, I go to heaven, most meritorious and auspicious!”
Bowing in this way, Sudevā went to heaven, listen, O best of men! / All this that was told to you has been narrated by Sukalā.

title: tripaṃcāśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Sukalā said: “Thus was dharma formerly heard by me in the Purāṇas. / Bereft of my husband, how shall I, resolved on sin, enjoy pleasures?
Without that beloved one, how may I maintain life in my body?” / Viṣṇu said: Having thus spoken of the supreme dharma, the unexcelled devotion to a husband,
those female friends, excellent women, were filled with great joy / upon hearing the supreme, meritorious dharma that grants the ultimate goal to women.
They praised that noble Sukalā, who was devoted to dharma. / The brahmins, all the gods, and virtuous women, O best of men,
meditate upon her because of the power of her love for her husband. / Considering her extreme steadfastness, Indra, the lord of the gods,
reflecting well upon the supreme state of Sukalā, the ruler of the immortals / [thought]: “I shall shake her resolve and love for her husband, without a doubt.”
Hastening, the ruler of the gods remembered the god Manmatha. / Grasping his bow of flowers, the fish-bannered [god] arrived.
Accompanied by his beloved Ratī, of seen and mighty strength, / making a hollow-handed gesture of reverence, he spoke to the thousand-eyed one:
“Why, O lord, have I now been remembered by you, O all-pervading one? / Let a command be given to me today with your whole heart, O bestower of honor!”
Indra said: “This Sukalā is a noble woman, devoted to the duty of fidelity to her husband. / Listen, O god of love, render excellent assistance!
Lure away this noble Sukalā, who is meritorious and auspicious!” / Having heard those words of Śakra, he then said to him:
“So be it, O thousand-eyed one! I will do it, without a doubt, / to assist you, O lord of the gods, for the sake of your amusement.
Having spoken thus, the immensely splendid Kandarpa, difficult even for sages to conquer, [said]: / “I am capable of conquering the gods, the munis, and the best of sages;
what then of a passionate woman, O god, who has no strength in her body? / For, O god, I dwell in the limbs of passionate women:
on the forehead, the breasts, the eyes, and always on the tips of the hair, / in the navel, the waist, the region of the back, the hips, the circle of the vulva,
on the lower lip, the parts of the teeth, and indeed in the armpit, without a doubt. / Thus I dwell everywhere in the limbs and minor parts of the body.
A woman is my home, O god; I dwell there always. / Remaining there, I destroy all men, without a doubt.
By nature, a woman is weak, O god; tormented by my arrows, / seeing her father, her mother, or any other kinsman or relative,
handsome and virtuous, O god, struck by my arrows, a woman / strays, there is no doubt here; she does not consider the consequences.
The vulva of women throbs, as do the tips of their breasts, O lord of gods. / There is no steadfastness, O ruler of the gods; I shall destroy Sukalā.”
Indra said: “I will become a man, handsome, virtuous, and wealthy. / For amusement, I shall agitate this woman, O mind-born one,
not out of desire, nor out of fear, nor out of greed, nor out of any [selfish] cause, / nor out of delusion, nor out of anger, truly, truly, O beloved of Rati!
How may her great truth and devotion to her husband be seen by me? / Going there, I shall test her; you will be the cause of infatuation here.”
Having thus instructed Kāma, the king of the gods went himself, / having transformed himself, handsome and virtuous on his own,
his body adorned with all ornaments, accompanied by all pleasures, / abounding in amorous play, and endowed with generosity at all times.
Where that lady, the beloved of Kṛkala, was staying, O king, / he displayed his amorous play, his form, virtue, and affection.
She did not even look at that man, the embodiment of beauty; / wherever she went, O king, there he looked at her.
With a longing mind, he gazed upon her in this manner. / The thousand-eyed one displayed amorous gestures through all emotional expressions.
At the crossroads, on the path, at the holy ford, wherever the lady went, / there, precisely there, the thousand-eyed one watched her alone.
A female messenger sent by Indra went to Sukalā. / Laughing gently, she spoke to the very noble Sukalā:
“Oh, your truth! Oh, your steadfastness! Oh, your radiance! Oh, your patience! / There is no woman with a fair face like hers in the whole world!
Who are you, O auspicious one? Whose wife will you be? / The man whose virtuous wife you are is blessed and fortunate on earth.”
Hearing her words, that high-minded woman said to her: / “Born in the Vaiśya caste, righteous-souled, loving the truth,
I am indeed the beloved wife of that wise man true to his pledge, / of the Vaiśya Kṛkala; I tell you the absolute truth.
My husband is righteous and wise, and has gone on a pilgrimage. / Since he, my husband, departed, O noble lady, at present,
listen, three full years have already passed. / Therefore I have become sorrowful without that great-souled one.
All this has been related to you, my own story. / You ask about me: ‘Who will you be?’ Tell me.”
Hearing Sukalā’s words, the female messenger addressed her again: / “You ask me thus, O good woman; I shall tell you all of that.
I have arrived near you for an important matter, O fair-complexioned one. / Let it be heard; I will declare it, and having heard it, keep it in mind.
Your pitiless husband has gone away, having abandoned you, O fair-faced one! / What will you do with him, the destroyer of his beloved?
That sinner who abandoned you, endowed with virtuous conduct, and went away— / where has he gone, O girl? Does he live there, or is he dead?
What will you do with him? In this way you grieve in vain. / Why do you waste your body, celestial and brilliant like gold?
When the age of childhood is reached, a human being does not find / any pleasure, O noble and auspicious lady, except children’s play.”
"In old age, suffering arrives; decrepitude harms the body. / In youth, enjoyment is experienced fully from pleasure, O fair-faced woman.
As long as youth remains, so long do mortals enjoy / all kinds of pleasures and the like; at his own will a man takes delight.
As long as youth remains, so long do they enjoy pleasures. / When age has passed, O auspicious woman, what will one do in youth?
When old age arrives, O lady, nothing at all succeeds. / An old person may constantly ponder, but pleasurable pursuits do not occur.
When age has passed, O girl, a dam is built [too late]. / Such would this body become when auspicious youth has departed.
"Therefore enjoy happily, and drink sweet intoxicating wine; / the arrows of the god of love burn these limbs of yours, O lovely-eyed one."
Here has arrived a man, handsome and virtuous. / He is indeed a tiger among men, omniscient, virtuous, and wealthy.
He is constantly devoted to your purpose out of affection, O woman of excellent complexion." / Sukalā said: "Childhood does not belong to the soul, nor does youth belong to life;
nor indeed does old age belong to it. It is self-perfected and grants true perfection, / immortal, undecaying, all-pervading, thoroughly perfected, and the best of all knowers.
Free of desire, it grants desires in the world and abides as the Self. / Just as the structure of a house is, so the structure of the body is perceived.
Just as the body is [formed] by the carpenter, so a mansion is [laid out] with measuring cord, / with assemblages of numerous pieces of wood and various collections of timber.
With clay and water too, one transforms it on all sides; / the wood is smeared by plasters and made variegated by painters.
First the house, measured out by the cord, attains form; / and day by day they maintain it through plastering.
Constantly shaken by the wind, the house becomes soiled. / The middle period of the house is declared to be the period of wear.
Loss of form occurs to it; the owner of the house replasters it, / and according to his wish, the owner brings the house back to good form.
That is declared to be the youth of that house, O female messenger. / But through collections of timbers over long periods of time, it goes to decrepitude.
They become displaced from their positions, and they shake at their bases and tips; / it cannot endure the weight of plaster, and it rests [only] on its support.
"Listen, O female messenger! This is described as the old age of the house: / seeing the house falling down, the master of the house abandons it.
He quickly departs to enter another house. / In the same way, mortals experience childhood, youth, and old age.
In childhood, having the form of a child, one behaves devoid of knowledge. / One adorns the body with garments and ornaments,
and with ointments, sandalwood, and other things derived from betel. / The body attains youth and becomes exceedingly beautiful.
One nourishes it externally and internally with all kinds of essences; / by means of that nourishment, it becomes well nourished.
An increase of flesh takes place through fresh and excellent essences. / The limbs, being refreshed, expand, O king!
Indeed, through these essences the various limbs assume their respective forms: / the teeth, the lips, the breasts, the arms, the waist, the back, both thighs,
the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet likewise attain growth; / indeed, through both of these they grow.
The limbs become shapely through essences and flesh. / By means of those forms, O female messenger, a mortal becomes bound by essences.
A mortal is called handsome, but by whom would he be beloved in the world? / This body, O messenger, is merely a receptacle of feces and urine.
This impure body constantly oozes, disgusting. / Why is its form praised, O fair one, which is like a water bubble?
It remains firm only as long as fifty years; / thereafter, day by day, decay surely befalls it.
The teeth become loose, and the mouth drools saliva; / one cannot see with both eyes, nor hear with both ears;
and with hands and feet one is unable to walk, O female messenger! / Afflicted by old age, the body becomes incapacitated.
Its essence dries up, withered by the heat of the fire of old age. / It becomes incapacitated, O female messenger; no beauty is perceived.
Just as a worn-out house goes to ruin, of this there is no doubt, / so the body falls into ruin in old age.
My form, which has come to be, you describe day by day in this manner. / With what form am I endowed? By whom is beauty acknowledged?
Just as a house falls into ruin, by what is that man strong? / For whose sake, O messenger, have you come? By whom does your ladyship praise him?
What did you see on my limb? Tell me now! / In this world, there is nothing lacking or superior in his limbs compared to mine, O messenger.
As you are, so is he, and so am I; of this there is no doubt. / Who does not have a form? There is no one on earth who possesses [true] form.
High trees and mountains have their end in falling, O fair one; / afflicted by time, they perish, and so do living beings—it is not otherwise.
The Self, formless yet possessing forms, is divine, all-pervading, and pure / in all immovable and movable beings, O female messenger.
The one pure [Self] resides [in them], like the single water in jars; / upon the destruction of the jars, it attains unity—you do not understand this oneness.
Upon the destruction of the body, this Self becomes of a single form. / One form has been perceived by me, residing constantly in worldly existence.
Speak thus having understood him for whose sake you have come here. / Show me something extraordinary, if you wish to enjoy [anything] here.
When one is tormented by disease and covered with phlegm, / the blood wanders from the limb, displaced from its proper site.
In all the joints of the limbs, it turns into flesh and goes within; / on one side it meets destruction, and it surely abandons its own form.
Quickly it turns into feces, and worms appear in it; / likewise, it abandons its own form, causing pain.
Listen! Afterward, it becomes swarming with foul-smelling worms; / lice or worms surely arise there, of this there is no doubt.
That worm causes an eruption and dreadful itching; / a louse produces torment and disturbs the whole body.
Scratched with the tips of the nails, that itch is relieved; / listen, sexual intercourse is just like that, of this there is no doubt.
A mortal consumes food essences and drinks aplenty; / by that vital breath, it is carried to the seat of digestion.
Whatever food is eaten by living beings, O messenger, having gone to the seat of digestion, / all that is covered there, and the bodily wind expels the waste.
The essence that constitutes the core becomes blood there; / and pure, unblemished semen goes to the seat of Brahman.
Drawn by the samāna breath and carried along by that wind, / the semen finds no resting place and moves restlessly.
Indeed, in the skulls of living beings there are five worms: / these two at the roots of the ears, and then in the place of the eyes;
they have the size of a little finger, with red tails, O messenger, / and with the color of butter, but black tails, of this there is no doubt.
Hear from me their names also spoken, O gentle one: / Piṅgalī and Śṛṅkhalī are the names of the two worms at the roots of the ears;
Capala and Pippala are the two at the tips of the nostrils; / and Śṛṅgalī and Jaṅgalī, two others, reside inside the eyes.
There are one hundred and fifty such worms, of this there is no doubt; / all of them reside in the forehead, having the size of a mustard seed.
All these cranial diseases produce deformities, of this there is no doubt. / Two hairs exist in his mouth; listen, O female messenger!
Know that the destruction of living beings occurs at that very moment, of this there is no doubt. / Even when residing in its own place, in the mouth of the progenitor,
that semen falls in the form of essence, of this there is no doubt. / He drinks the semen through the mouth, and because of that he becomes intoxicated.
And in the region of the middle of the palate, it moves restlessly. / The channels called Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumṇā are located there.
Even with great strength, inside that cage of the network of channels, / the itch of lust arises, O messenger, for all living beings.
The penis of the male twitches, and so does the vulva of the female, O messenger. / Then the woman and man, deeply intoxicated, enter into union.
The rubbing together of body with body is produced by sexual intercourse; / for just a moment there is pleasure in the body, and then the itch returns just as before.
Everywhere, O messenger, such an occurrence is seen. / Go to your own place; there is nothing extraordinary here.
There is nothing extraordinary that I would ever do, of this there is no doubt."

title: catuḥpaṃcāśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Viṣṇu said: / Addressed thus by that Sukalā, the female messenger then departed. / Having deliberated upon what had been concisely spoken, Purandara,
considering the meaning of her words endowed with truth and righteousness, / her boldness, firmness, and her true knowledge, Purandara [reflected]:
"Who indeed among women on the surface of the earth would speak like this— / words united with the nature of yoga and washed by the waters of propriety?
This illustrious woman is pure, the very embodiment of truth, of this there is no doubt; / she would be capable of bearing the burden of the entire three worlds!"
Having reflected on this matter, Jiṣṇu said to Kandarpa: / "I shall go with you to see that beloved of Kṛkala."
Manmatha, proud of his strength, answered the thousand-eyed one: / "Let us go there, O lord of gods, where that devoted wife stays."
"Her pride, her prowess, her strength, her courage, and her true devotion as a faithful wife— / having gone there, I will destroy them; how insignificant is she, O lord of the gods?"
Having heard the words of Manmatha, the thousand-eyed Indra said: / "O Ananga, listen to you who speak so boastfully in vain!
She is steadfast through the power of truth, firmly established by righteous deeds. / Sukalā is truly invincible; your virility will not prevail there."
Having heard this, then Manmatha, enraged, said to Indra: / "The power of the sages and of the gods was destroyed by me."
How trifling is her strength that you speak of to me? / While you watch, O lord of the gods, I shall ruin that woman.
Just as fresh butter turns liquid upon seeing the heat of fire, / so I will melt her by my own form and radiant power.
Go there, a great deed is now certainly at hand. / Why do you disparage my splendor, which destroys the three worlds?"

Viṣṇu said: / Having heard the word of the mind-born Kāma, [Indra said,] "I know she is unattainable to you, O Kāma— / she whose body is virtuous, rousing her courage, pure through merit, following a path of great virtue.
Let me see your fierce prowess when you go hence with your bow." / Then with him, along with Rati and the female messenger, he went again to that devoted wife.

[She was] alone, exceedingly virtuous, dwelling in her home, absorbed in meditation on her husband's feet, / just as a noble yogi, directing his mind, would make it free from conceptual wavering and not imagine anything.
Then, to bewilder the virtuous woman, the high-souled fish-bannered Kāma and Purandara / assumed a wondrous form endowed with endless splendor, adorned in blue and full of delights.
Seeing that noble man moving about gracefully in such a state of desire, / the wife of the noble vaiśya thought him endowed with beauty and appreciative of virtues.
Just as water resting on a lotus petal acquires the fame of a pearl, / even so the naturally truthful disposition of that devoted wife arose [unaffected].
"Previously, a female messenger was sent by him to me, a young woman, praising his virtues; / and this playful form of his in many aspects reveals all of his inner desire to me.

Considering that my own time has come powerfully, this truly vile man has approached with solitary virtues; / yet, accompanied by Rati, how could he live once crushed by the weight of the stone of truth?
Even if this beloved embraced my feelings, how could he survive, however intelligent he might be? / For my body is instantly empty, devoid of motion, almost like a corpse.

The citizens of the village that is the body have vanished, having taken up the activity known as great agitation; / yet Kāma has brought my dear husband's radiant appearance, equal to the supreme, to its peak.
When, though dead, the powerful one full of joy dances before his own eyes, / he who desires to enjoy me must thus speak wondrous things to him."
Having reflected thus, that great chaste woman, her consciousness firmly bound with the rope called truth, / entered her own house in order to understand his intention with restraint.

title: paṃcapaṃcāśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Viṣṇu said: / Knowing her intention, the king of gods said to Kāma standing before him: / "She cannot be conquered by you, O Smara; the chaste woman is fully armored with meditation that is the truth.
Taking the bow called righteousness in her hand, and the excellent arrow named knowledge, / this chaste woman stands in the battle to fight, like a hero proud of his prowess.
Through desire to win, she pursues the aim of human life, whereas you display your pride; / she is capable of conquering you in battle today; whatever must happen should be considered right here.
Formerly you were burned right here by the high-souled Śambhu; having made enmity with him, / as the fruit of that wrong deed you became bodiless, O Smara, in truth.
Just as the deed was done by you of old, O Smara, so too was the sharp fruit obtained; / you will surely attain a despicable womb, being described right here along with this virtuous woman.
Those knowledgeable men who cultivate enmity with high-souled beings in the three worlds / reap only the fruit of that evil deed, accompanied by sorrow and the destruction of their form.
Let us proclaim and depart, O Kāma, leaving this chaste woman alone; / formerly, in connection with a truthful woman, an unbearable sinful result was obtained by me.
You yourself know this history, how I was cursed by Gautama / and had the testicles of a ram, while you, leaving me behind, departed.
Incomparable is the power of the splendor of chaste women; neither the creator nor the sun can endure it. / May this contemptible form protect [us]; of old, Anasūyā was cursed by the sage.
By stopping the swift sun from rising, blazing as it was with radiance, / she averted her husband's death resulting from the curse of Māṇḍavya and Kauṇḍinya.
By that truthful, devoted wife, beloved of Atri, the triad of gods was reduced to her sons; / have you not heard of it of old, O Manmatha? Faithful women endowed with refinement always prevail.
She named Sāvitrī, daughter of Dyumatsena [or father of her spouse], brought back her taken beloved / from Yama right here, the noble son of Aśvapati; thus has the power of chastity been heard.
Who would touch the flame of fire? Who, having tied a heavy stone around his neck with his arms, / would foolishly swim across the ocean? Or who can subdue a chaste woman free from passion?"
When these words full of prudent counsel were spoken by Indra to instruct Kāma, / having heard those words, the dolphin-bannered [god of love] then spoke to the lord of gods:
Kāma said: / "I have come at your command; yet abandoning courage, friendship, and masculine purpose, / you speak to me to that end, making me appear devoid of strength and full of fear.
If I turn back with confused mind, O lord of gods, my fame in the world will be ruined; / without honor I would become an object of ridicule, and everyone will say that I was defeated by a woman.
The hosts of gods and demons, and the foremost sages engaged in austerities who were defeated by me before, / will now laugh at me: 'This terrible Manmatha has been conquered by a woman!'
Therefore, I will go along with you; her strength and pride, O lord of gods, / and her radiance and courage I will destroy; why are you afraid in this matter, O Śakra?"
Having thus addressed the lord of the gods, taking his bow together with an arrow of flowers, / he spoke to Krīḍā standing before him: "Assuming an illusion, you must go!
To Sukalā, the very pure wife of the vaiśya, steadfast in truth, knowing righteousness, appreciative of virtues, / go hence and carry out the assigned task as an ally; listen, dear friend!"
Having addressed Krīḍā, the mind-born god then called Prīti, who was standing beside: / "A duty of yours is my supreme duty; permeate her with tender affections!
So that this fair-eyed woman, seeing Indra, will follow him with affection, / bring her under control by various powers and words of praise; listen, dear friend!"

"O friend, go quickly, prepare an illusion-filled place possessing the appearance of the Nandana garden, / furnished with flowers, prominent with fruits, resounding with the cries of cuckoos and bees."
Summoning the hero Makaranda, an elixir endowed with sweet qualities, / along with the wind and the others engaged in their own tasks, and having dispatched Kama again,
Having thus instructed his great army, which bewilders the three worlds, Kama / set out together with the king of gods to bewilder that noble, chaste woman in this manner.

title: ṣaṭpaṃcāśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Viṣṇu said: / When Manmatha, along with the lord of gods, had set out to destroy her truth, / Satya then spoke to Dharma regarding Sukala:
"Behold, O Dharma, O greatly wise one, the scheming of Manmatha / against your purpose, my own, and that of the noble Merit.
I am sending forth the great site, dwelling-shaped, an arising of happiness, / named Satya, Supriya, and Sudeva—an excellent house.
Going there, this Kama of heedless mind might destroy it; / he has taken the form of an enemy and is utterly wicked toward us, no doubt.
The husband rich in austerities, the brahmin, the noble and devoted wife, / and the truly upright king, O Dharma, are without doubt my dwellings.
Where I am nourished with growth, there indeed is your dwelling; / merit arrives there and plays together with faith.
Forgiveness endowed with tranquility comes to my abode, / as do truth, self-restraint, compassion, and benevolence.
One endowed with wisdom, free from greed, is where I dwell; / a pure nature is there too, and these are my kin.
Non-stealing, non-violence, and forbearance, as well as prosperity, / have come into my house; hear of its blessedness, O Dharmarāja!
Service to elders, Viṣṇu accompanied by Lakṣmī, / and the gods headed by Agni surely enter my house.
He who reveals the path to liberation, endowed with the radiance of knowledge— / with all these I reside among chaste women and among the righteous.
In all these virtuous ones who are my dwelling-places, / even with the family I have described, I constantly dwell together with you.
Those beings of virtuous form were made into my houses by Brahmā; / O fortunate one, I roam about at will in sport.
And Īśvara, the master of the world, three-eyed and bull-mounted, / abides in my house in his true form together with Śivā.
That very essence of worldly existence, the lordly abode in the form of a house, / the dwelling named Śaṅkara, has indeed been destroyed by Manmatha.
Relying on Menakā, this Kama previously conquered / the noble Viśvāmitra who was practicing excellent tapas.
The chaste and devoted Ahalyā, Gautama's auspicious beloved, / was displaced from noble truth by that wicked Manmatha.
The sages who know the true dharma, and various devoted wives— / all these who are my houses have been burned by the fire of desire.
Difficult to restrain, unbearable, pervasive, cruel toward the truthful, / he constantly watches me: 'Where does Satya abide?'
Knowing me, he arrives with arrows in hand, holding a bow; / that wicked one, with fires of various names, would destroy my house.
Cruel traces of sin and other things that rely on hypocrisy— / all of those, harmful to wisdom, enter the house of truth.
Accomplished by that deceit with false commanders of the army, / the wicked one, with malignant weapons, would cause the house to fall and crush it.
That wicked, mighty-powered Manmatha strikes me thus; / burned by his splendor, I surely go into emptiness.
I desire a new house called woman, with husband and king; / this auspicious, blessed beloved of the meritorious Kṛkala—
The wicked one has undertaken to burn that house of mine named Sukalā; / here comes this mighty thousand-eyed [Indra] accompanied by Kama.
Because of lust, why does he not remember what happened before? / Through his liaison with Ahalyā, he was made to bear a ram's testicles.
Having seen the sage's power and because of violating a true woman, / the king of gods was ruined there through the fault of desire.
He suffered a dreadful curse, filled with great sorrow; / yet toward this beloved of Kṛkala, Sukalā, who walks in righteousness,
This thousand-eyed [Indra], joined with Kama, has risen to destroy her; / act in such a way that Kama does not come with Indra.
O Dharmarāja, greatly wise one, you are the best among the intelligent." / Dharmarāja said: "I shall diminish Kama's splendor, and also cause his death.
I have seen one expedient; let him see it right here. / And this Wisdom, highly intelligent, roaming in the form of a bird,
Let her proclaim her husband's auspicious arrival from the sky by her call; / for through the power of an omen and through the husband's arrival,
She will not be ruined by the wicked, and will be steady-minded, no doubt." / Sent by him, Wisdom went to Sukalā's house.
Making a loud cry, she appeared as if seen by the gods; / Wisdom was then worshipped and honored with incense, lamps, and other offerings.
Sukalā asked a brahmin: "What does she say to me?" / The brahmin said: "She speaks of the arrival of your husband, O fortunate one, be steady;
Within seven days he will arrive, not otherwise."
Having thus heard the very auspicious word, she was suddenly filled with joy: / that one virtuous husband who knew dharma, indicated indeed by an omen, had arrived.

title: saptapaṃcāśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Viṣṇu said: / Krīḍā, having assumed the form of a chaste woman, took command and went to the house of the beautiful, devoted wife; / having arrived there, that blessed one who possessed the nature of truth addressed her with respectful words.
Worshipped with most virtuous words, that Krīḍā laughed and spoke to Sukalā; / an answer following illusion, bewildering everyone, yet endowed with the measure of truth:
"My husband too was powerful, appreciative of virtues, steadfast, learned, and dignified; / abandoning me, a most sinful one, my most righteous lord, of glorious fame, departed; hear,
Having heard all that Sukalā spoke with virtuous words out of a woman's nature, / Krīḍā, considering her to be of completely pure disposition, said: 'Why has your lord departed today, O fair one,
Abandoning your truly lovely form? Tell me everything about your noble husband; / intent on meditation, she does everything; having assumed the form of a friend, she has come to my house.'
Krīḍā said: / "Hear this true account of the nature of my husband's life: / I am his beloved, ever attached to him, and whoever he desires, I conciliate toward him.
Following the very auspicious word of the noble husband, intent on meditation, I do everything; / with solitary virtue, suitable to his qualities, alone in serving him here, O lady.
This ripening of my past actions is now taking effect, / since my husband has left me, unfortunate as I am, and gone.
O friend, I cannot bear my life or my own body; / how can pitiless women live a good life when separated from their husband?
Beauty, adornment, good fortune, happiness, and prosperity—nothing else— / for the husband is sung in the scriptures as the great fortune of women."
Having heard everything that was spoken by Krīḍā at that time, / perceiving her intention to be true, she believed what was spoken then.
Trusting [her], the fortunate Sukalā, who regarded her husband as her deity, / again spoke to her all the words following her own actions.
She briefly related her own previous story: / how her husband had departed on a pilgrimage, devoted to acquiring merit,
and her own grief, which was very genuine, and her ascetic practice, O wise woman. / That chaste wife, having been enlightened and consoled by Krīḍā,
Sūta said: / Once, Krīḍā said to Sukalā: / “Friend, behold this delightful forest, adorned with heavenly trees!
There is a supreme holy place there, destroying sins, / and adorned with canopies of various creepers and lovely flowers.
We two must also go for the sake of merit, O fair-faced woman!” / Having heard [this], Sukalā then went with her by [her] deceitful power.
She entered the celestial forest resembling the Nandana garden, / endowed with blossoms of all seasons, echoing with hundreds of cuckoos,
resounding with the very sweet humming of bees, / and crowded with the holy calls of chirping sacred birds,
shining with sandalwood and other trees, and with fragrances, / fully endowed with all pleasures, [created] by Mādhava in the spring.
Indeed, it was created for the delusion of Sukalā alone. / Accompanied by her, she entered that forest which was the source of all things.
She saw that bliss-giving, sacred [forest], not perceiving its illusory nature. / Beholding the heavenly forest together with her, O ruler of people,
Śakra too arrived there, shining in divine form. / Arriving together with that female messenger, Kāma came there.
Having become the master of all pleasures, agitated by amorous sport, / addressing Kāma, he spoke: “Here is that Sukalā arrived!
Strike her who stands before Krīḍā, O noble one! / Having devised an illusion, she has been brought by Krīḍā into your presence.
Show your prowess this very day, if you have any; act with resolve!” / Kāma said: / “Display your own clever form endowed with charm,
so that I may strike her with my five arrows, O thousand-eyed one!” / Indra said: / “Where is your prowess, fool, with which you mock the world,
that, relying upon my support, you now wish to fight?” / Kāma said: / “My form was taken away previously by that god of gods,
the trident-bearing Mahādeva; I have no body. / When I wish to strike a woman, listen now [how I act]:
relying upon the body of a man, I show my form. / Or, O thousand-eyed one, to [strike] a man, I resort to the form of a woman.
When a previously seen woman constantly contemplates that very [man], / or when a man constantly meditates upon the form of a woman,
then, relying on the unseen [affection], I madden the man. / In like manner do I certainly madden a woman through [his] form, without a doubt.
From remembrance (saṃsmaraṇa), my name has become Smara, O lord of gods! / Having seen her, I take recourse to the material form of such a body.
By the radiance of its own splendor, the relationship of victim and tormentor arises. / Relying upon a woman's form, one may utterly delude a steadfast man;
relying upon a man's form, I arouse a noble woman. / I am formless, O Indra; [hence] I must take recourse to our [chosen] form.
Relying upon your form, I shall win her as desired.” / Having thus spoken to the king of gods, the flower-armed one,
the friend of Mādhava, entered the body of that great-souled one.
Eager to strike that virtuous and holy wife of Kṛkala, / the flower-armed one stood ready, eyeing her body as a target for his arrows.

title: aṣṭapaṃcāśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Viṣṇu said: / Directed by Krīḍā, Sukalā, the slender-bodied wife of the merchant, having entered the forest, / saw the entire captivating thicket and asked that very friend, being a chaste woman:
“This foremost, most sacred, and celestial forest, delightful to the mind, O friend, / perfected by all excellent desires—whose is it?” Sukalā asked that friend with joy.

Krīḍā said: / “This forest is endowed with heavenly virtues, reflecting the nature of perfected beings; / filled with flowers and yielding desired fruits, behold all that belongs to the crocodile-bannered [god]!”
Then, having heard these words, filled with great joy, / and having observed the grand conduct of that wicked Kāma,
she smelled that fragrance being carried by the wind. / By its very nature, the wind blows endowed with fragrance;
his arrow enters the nostrils easily and sportively. / Yet that fair-faced woman did not take in the scent of the flowers,
nor did that great chaste woman relish the delicious savors. / That playful companion of the love-god was defeated.
Ashamed, turning his face away, he fell to the ground with drops of juice; / produced from fully ripened fruits and adorned with flower-clusters,
the sap fell to the earth in the form of drops, conquered by her. / The nectar, very dejected, having fallen from the fruit to the earth,
was devoured by flies, just as a dead body [is devoured] on a battlefield. / Being devoured by flies, it flowed away in a stream.
It flowed away very slowly, and the birds laughed at him; / they flitted about with various calls filled with joyous delight.
The birds perched on the trees in the middle of the forest rejoiced. / Indeed, he was defeated by Sukalā and took to a downward path.
Approaching joyfully, Rati, the wife of Kāma, went and smilingly said to Sukalā: / “Hail to you! Welcome indeed, auspicious lady! Delight yourself affectionately in this pleasing sight!
Your spotless beauty is desired even by the great-souled Indra. / Tell me whatever you desire, and I will bring it, without a doubt.”
Sūta said: / Seeing those two women speaking and hearing their eloquence, she said: / “My wise husband has gone, taking my love (rati) with him.
Where my husband stays, there I am united with my husband; / there lies my desire and my joy; this body here is without support.”
Having heard what was said, both Rati and Prīti felt ashamed. / Feeling embarrassed, those two went to where the mighty Kāma was.
They spoke to that great hero who had entered Indra's body, / that mighty one drawing his bow, aiming his glance [at her]:
“She is invincible, O very wise one! Abandon your prowess! / She longs only for her husband; the fortunate one is ever devoted to her husband.”
Kāma said: / “If the form of this great-souled Indra is seen by her, / O goddess, then I shall strike her, without a doubt.”
Then the king of gods, assuming a disguise, of magnificent beauty, / was quickly followed by her with supreme playfulness.
Surrounded with every luxury, adorned with all ornaments, / wearing celestial garlands and garments, and anointed with celestial fragrances,
he arrived together with that Rati to where that woman devoted to her husband was, / and addressed the fortunate, truthful Sukalā:
“Previously, a female messenger was sent by me affectionately to your presence; / why do you not respect me, auspicious lady, who have come here loving you?”
Sukalā said: / “May you be blessed! I am protected by the noble sons of my husband; / even though alone, with their help I have no fear of anyone.”
And protected everywhere by heroic sons possessing human form, / I am not at liberty to speak, being engaged in his service.
In the twinkling of an eye, O intelligent one, / why do you not feel ashamed, seeking to sport with me?
Who are you that have come here, fearless even of death? / Indra said: / Indeed, I see you thus arrived in the middle of the forest;
moreover, heroic sons of your husband were mentioned by you. / How may I see them? Show them before me!

Sukalā said: / Having installed truthful speech as ruler over his own entire group, along with those named steadfastness, mind, course, and intellect, / the great-souled one, whose entire dharma is unshakable, ever vigilant, whose nature is dharma strong against Kama, has constantly protected me.

Thus Dharma always protects me with virtues of self-restraint and purifications; / see Truth arrived before me, accompanied by peace and forbearance,

title: bhyāṃyutam
text_mt: And Intellect is exceedingly mighty, of far-reaching fame, who never releases me; / I am bound by firm bonds born of his virtues, and thus he has approached my presence.
All these, beginning with Truth, have now been made to guard me; / all of them—gain of dharma and others, self-restraint, intellect, and valour—
truly protect me in this manner. Why do you solicit me by force? / Who are you that, having become fearless, have come along with a messenger?
Truth, dharma, merit, and also powerful knowledge and others— / these companions of my husband protect me in the house.
Ever endowed with protection, devoted to self-restraint and peace, / not even the lord of Śacī himself is able to conquer me.
Even if the mighty Manmatha himself comes, / I am always armoured by Truth, by Sātyaki alone, not otherwise.
His arrows will become useless, there is no doubt. / Thus the great warriors, Dharma and the others, will slay you.
Go far away! Flee! Do not stay here now! / If you stay when forbidden, you will be turned to ash.
If you look upon my form without my husband, / just as fire burns wood, so shall I burn [you], not otherwise.
Having heard this, the thousand-eyed one [spoke] to Manmatha's face: / 'Look at her virile valour! Fight with your own virile powers!'
Just as they had come, so all of them, afflicted by the fear of a great curse, / then departed, O great king, Indra and the others, each to his own place.
When all of them had gone, that faithful wife, Sukalā, / endowed with merit, returned to her home by meditating upon her husband.
O king, that woman whose deity was her husband reached her home, / which was endowed with merit, composed of all sacred places, and composed of all sacrifices.

title: ekonaṣaṣṭitamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Viṣṇu said: / Having accomplished [visits to] all the sacred places, Kṛkala set out towards home / accompanied by a caravan, filled with great joy.
Thus he constantly reflected: 'My worldly existence has borne fruit; / my ancestors, fully satisfied, will attain heaven, not otherwise.'
Meanwhile, [someone] in visible form, having bound his ancestors, / said directly before him: 'There is no supreme merit for you.'
One of divine form and huge body spoke these words to Kṛkala: / 'You have no fruit of the sacred places; you have made this exertion entirely in vain.
You obtain satisfaction only for yourself; there is no supreme merit for you.' / Having heard this, the vaiśya Kṛkala was afflicted with sorrow:
'Who are you that speak thus? Why are my grandfathers bound? / Tell me the cause of that: through the power of which fault?'
'Why is there no fruit of the sacred places? How is my pilgrimage in vain? / Tell me everything clearly, if you know.'
Dharma said: / He who sets out having abandoned his pure, most meritorious wife— / all the fruit of his merit becomes useless, not otherwise.
He who sets out on a righteous deed, abandoning even that wife / devoted to virtuous conduct, holy, intent on pious vows, devoted to her husband, virtuous, and fond of merit—
all the dharma performed by him becomes useless, not otherwise.
Devoted to all proper conduct, noble, intent on the means of dharma, / constantly devoted to her husband, always fond of wisdom—
in whose house there is a wife possessing such qualities, holy and a great faithful wife, / the gods of great splendour reside permanently in his home.
Dwelling within the house, the ancestors desire his welfare; / the sacred rivers such as the Gaṅgā and the oceans are there, not otherwise.
In whose house there is a holy faithful wife devoted to truth, / sacrifices, cows, and sages are there, not otherwise.
All the sacred places and various meritorious [sites] / abide there through union with a wife, all these, not otherwise.
Householder life comes to be through union with a virtuous wife; / there is no second dharma superior to householder life on the surface of the earth.
The house of a householder is sacred, endowed with truth and merit; / O vaiśya, it consists of all sacred places and is accompanied by all the gods.
Depending upon the householder stage of life, all living beings live; / I do not see any other stage of life as excellent as that.
Mantras, the agnihotra fire, the gods, all eternal dharmas, / and practices of charity proceed in the home of the man
who [has a wife]; but the house of one destitute of a wife becomes like a forest; / sacrifices do not succeed, nor do charities of various kinds.
For a man destitute of a wife, not even a great vow succeeds, / nor any righteous deeds, nor various meritorious acts.
There is no sacred place equal to a wife for accomplishing dharma; / listen, for a householder there is no other dharma in the three worlds.
Where a wife is, there is home, even for a man, not otherwise; / whether in a village or in a forest, she is the means of accomplishing all dharma.
There is no sacred place equal to a wife, there is no happiness equal to a wife, / there is no merit equal to a wife for deliverance and benefit.
O lowest of men, you who went forth abandoning a faithful wife endowed with dharma, / having forsaken your home and your dharma, where is the fruit of your dharma?
Since the offering of śrāddha was made by you at the sacred places without her, / through that fault, indeed, your earlier grandfathers have been bound.
You are a thief, and these are thieves, who being intensely greedy ate / the food of the śrāddha offered by you without her in this manner.
When a good son endowed with faith gives the gift of śrāddha / with the rice-ball offered alongside his wife, I shall tell his merit:
Just as the satisfaction of men arises from drinking nectar, / so it does for the ancestors through śrāddha; I speak the truth, the truth.
The wife is the mistress of the householder's life and of dharma; / she was deceived by you, O fool, and your act of theft was in vain.
These grandfathers are thieves, by whom [food] was eaten without her; / if a wife cooks food with her own hand, resembling nectar,
the ancestors partake of that food alone with joyful minds; / by that alone they attain satisfaction, and they become well-pleased.
Therefore, without a wife, dharma does not succeed for a man; / there is no sacred place equal to a wife that bestows a good destination upon men.
And whatever religious duty is performed without a wife becomes completely fruitless."

title: ṣaṣṭitamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Kṛkala said: / "How will my spiritual success come about? How will the deliverance of my ancestors occur? / Tell me this at length, O Dharmarāja, right now."
Dharma said: / "Go home, O fortunate one; without you, she suffers grief. / Console your wife Sukalā, who walks the path of dharma.
Having gone home, perform the offering of ancestral rites with her own hand; / remembering the sacred places of pilgrimage, worship the foremost among the gods.
The spiritual success accomplished by pilgrimage will surely become yours. / But in this world, whoever wishes to practice dharma without a wife,
he should abandon householder life and wander through the forest alone; / he becomes fruitless in this world, and the gods do not esteem him.
Sacrifices attain success only when a housewife is in the home; / alone, he is not capable of accomplishing religious duty and prosperity."
Viṣṇu said: / Having spoken thus to that merchant, Dharma went as he had come; / and Kṛkala, righteous in soul, set out toward his own home.
Having reached his home, the intelligent one saw that devoted wife; / with that caravan leader, the wise man reached his own place.
Seeing her husband, skilled in dharma, arrived, / she then performed an auspicious and sacred rite at her husband's homecoming.
That righteous-souled man related the deeds of Dharma. / Hearing her husband's joy-bringing words, the noble woman,
having praised the words of Dharma, consented to it accordingly. / Viṣṇu said: / Then that merchant Kṛkala, together with her,
faithfully performed a most sacred śrāddha, remaining in the temple of the deity. / The ancestors, gods, and Gandharvas arrived in aerial cars.
They, the great-souled sages, praised the couple, / as did I, Brahmā, and Maheśvara along with the Goddess.
All the gods along with the Gandharvas arrived in aerial cars; / indeed, I, then Brahmā, and Maheśvara along with the Goddess,
and all the gods accompanied by Gandharvas were pleased by her truthfulness. / And they spoke to the two great-souled ones, who knew dharma and were learned in truth:
"Together with your wife, may good befall you: choose a boon, O you of noble vows!" / Kṛkala said: / "By the influence of whose merit and austerity, O foremost among the gods,
have you come to grant a boon to me together with my wife?" / Indra said: / "This virtuous, fortunate Sukalā possesses lovely auspiciousness.
We are pleased with her truthfulness and wish to grant you a boon." / And in brief, that previous account was related [to him].
Hearing the greatness of her conduct, her husband rejoiced. / Together with her, that righteous-souled man, his eyes agitated with joy,
bowed down to all the deities and spoke again and again: / "If the three eternal gods, who are of great fortune,
and other holy ṛṣis are pleased, having shown compassion upon me: / birth after birth, let me have such devotion to the gods;
may I have delight in dharma and truth, through your favor. / Furthermore, together with my wife and with my forefathers,
I wish to go to the world of Viṣṇu, O gods, if you of great might are pleased." / The gods said: / "So be it, O fortunate one; all this shall indeed come to pass."
Then they rained down flowers upon the two of them, O king. / Then they sang a most holy, charming song in lovely tunes.
Gandharvas who knew the truth of song and hosts of Apsarases danced. / Then the gods along with the Gandharvas, O best of kings,
having granted the boon and praising the devoted wife, went to their respective abodes. / The sacred pilgrimage of the wife has been fully recounted; I shall tell you of something else.
This entire unexcelled sacred narrative has been recounted to you. / A man who hears it, O king, is freed from all sins.
If a woman hears this excellent narrative of Sukalā with faith, / she is never parted from good fortune, truth, sons, or grandsons.
She rejoices with wealth and grain, and becomes happy together with her husband. / She will be a devoted wife birth after birth; it cannot be otherwise.
A brāhmaṇa becomes learned in the Vedas, and a kṣatriya becomes victorious; / wealth and grain will surely be in the house of a vaiśya, without a doubt.
He becomes a knower of dharma, O king, endowed with good conduct, and happy; / a śūdra attains happiness and prospers with sons and grandsons.
Abundant fortune arises, adorned with wealth and grain.

title: ekaṣaṣṭitamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Vena said: / "The sacred pilgrimage of the wife has been declared the supreme among all holy places; / relate now the sacred pilgrimage of the parents, the ultimate means of deliverance for sons."
Viṣṇu said: / "In the great sacred place Kurukṣetra, there was a brāhmaṇa named Kuṇḍala; / Sukarmā was the virtuous son of the noble Kuṇḍala.
His parents were very elderly, knowers of dharma, learned in the scriptures; / both of these great-souled ones were sorely afflicted by old age.
He then rendered service to both of them with supreme devotion, / knowing dharma, endowed with love, day and night without ceasing.
From him, his father, he studied the Vedas and numerous scriptures; / devoted to all proper conduct, capable, knowing dharma, loving knowledge.
He himself massaged the limbs of his two elders, / and washed their feet, and attended to their bathing and feeding.
Out of devotion and by his very nature, he became absorbed in meditating upon them; / O lord of kings, he carried out attendance upon his mother and father."
Sūta said: / At that current time, O best of kings, / there was a brāhmaṇa named Pippala, belonging to the noble Kaśyapa line.
He performed austerities, abstaining from food, self-conquered, free from malice, / endowed with compassion, charity, and self-restraint, having conquered desire and anger.
Having gone to the Daśāraṇya forest, wise and devoted to knowledge and peace, / restraining all his sense faculties, the noble-minded one performed austerities.
By the power of his austerity, creatures there, free from hostility, / lived as if in the golden age, as though born from one womb.
Seeing that austerity of his, the sages fell into wonder: / 'Such austerity has not been practiced by anyone, as this sage practices.'
And the gods, headed by Indra, fell into supreme wonder: / 'Oh, how intense is his austerity, his tranquility, and his restraint of the senses!
Free from change, free from agitation, devoid of desire and anger, / enduring cold, wind, and heat, he stands like a mountain.
Averse to sense-objects, steadfast, having transcended the mind's grasping, / the best of the twice-born hears no sound from anyone whatsoever.'
Having reached such a steady posture, standing with one-pointed mind, / absorbed in meditation on Brahman, his lotus-face filled with bliss,
having become like stone or wood, motionless, he stood like a mountain; / and he appeared like a pillar, firmly fixed, devoted to dharma.
His body was emaciated by austerity, exceedingly full of faith, free from envy; / in this way, one thousand years passed for that wise sage.
A heap consisting of a mass of earth was made by numerous ants; / upon him, as their own abode, [rose] an anthill of huge size.
Standing within the interior of the anthill, he stood as though turned to stone; / in this way that brāhmaṇa Pippala practiced immense austerity.
The best of twice-borns was surrounded on all sides by black serpents; / fraught with fierce venom, they bit that sage of dread energy.
Reaching the vital parts of his body, their venom could not penetrate him; / by the fiery energy of that twice-born, the snakes then became calm.
From his body of blazing energy arose flames of light, / manifold in form, seen repeatedly and distinctly,
fiercer than fire itself, of such a kind, O best among men! / Just as the sun, having entered the belly of a cloud, shines with its rays,
so the brahmin Pippala, seated in the anthill, shone with fiery power. / Angrily the snakes bit that sage with their fangs;
yet from the tips of their fangs they could not pierce his skin, O best of kings. / Thus, while he was practicing austerity for a thousand years,
there passed away, O king of kings, for that great-souled sage / who persevered during the three divisions of the day through cold, rain, and heat,
the time, O great king, of the high-souled Pippala; / likewise, that great soul subsisted on air alone.
Three thousand years passed while he practiced austerities. / Then upon his head a shower of flowers was poured by the gods of old.
"You are a knower of Brahman, O fortunate one; you are a knower of dharma, without a doubt; / you are full of all knowledge, born [to it] by your own action.
Whatever desire you wish for, that very thing you will attain, not otherwise; / you will become one whose every wish is fulfilled of his own accord."
Hearing that momentous speech, the high-minded Pippala, / having bowed to all the deities with his neck bent in devotion,
overcome with great joy, replied with these words: / "So that this entire universe might become subject to my control,
make it so, O lords of the gods, and let me become a Vidyādhara!" / Having spoken thus, that wise man paused, O best of kings.
"So be it!" the gods then said to the best of twice-borns. / Having granted the boon to that great-souled one, the blessed ones departed.
When those gods had gone, the excellent brahmin Pippala / constantly cultivated brahminhood and thought of bringing the universe under his control.
From then on, O king of kings, the excellent brahmin Pippala, / having attained the rank of a Vidyādhara, moving wherever he wished, was glorified.
Thus that twice-born Pippala, having attained the rank of a Vidyādhara, / became a lord in the world of the gods, proficient in all sacred treatises.
Once, however, the mighty Pippala reflected: / "The whole universe must be in my power, [for] an excellent boon was granted to me."
To put it to the test, that foremost among twice-borns set about: / whomever he thought of subduing, that very one he brought under control.
When this proof had thus occurred, he thought in his mind: / "There is no second person in the world equal to me, the best of men!"
Sūta said: / While the high-souled Pippala was thinking thus, / having perceived his mental state, a crane said to him;
standing on the bank of the lake, O king, with a melodious sound, endowed with distinct syllables, / with an utterance full of elegance, he said to Pippala:
"Why do you harbor such pride, [imagining yourself] supreme? / I do not consider that power of universal subjugation to belong to you alone.
This matter of what is submissive or unsubmissive is praised as recent; / you do not know the ancient [truth], Pippala, for you are dull of intellect.
Just because three thousand years of austerity / have been performed by you, why do you vainly show pride, O twice-born?
The son of Kuṇḍala, the steadfast and wise Sukarman, free of affliction— / the whole world was subject to him, both compliant and uncompliant; hear [of him] now.
That wise one knows both the recent and the ancient; / there is no great sage in the world equal to him; hear, O Pippala!
You are not equal to Sukarman, the son of Kuṇḍala. / No gift was given by him, nor was [esoteric] knowledge meditated upon;
sacrifices with offerings and the like were never performed by him; / he went on no pilgrimage, nor [did he engage in] worship of fire.
When did he ever perform, O twice-born, the highest service to dharma? / Moving at will, possessing knowledge, he is ever a friend to his father and mother,
rich in Vedic study, skilled in the meaning of all treatises. / Such as the knowledge of that boy Sukarman is,
such knowledge you do not have; you bear pride in vain!" / Pippala said: / "Who are you, reproaching me in the form of a bird?
Why do you disparage my knowledge, and of what kind is the ancient [truth]? / Tell me that in detail; how could there be knowledge in you?
The whole state of the recent and of the ancient now, / declare it, O best of birds, along with knowledge in full detail.
Are you Brahmā, or Viṣṇu, or Rudra?" / The crane said: / "There is no disposition toward austerity in you, nor is there any fruit of it.
Hear now about the austerity not fully mastered by you: / such virtue as belongs to the son of Kuṇḍala, even though he is a boy,
just so, knowledge has not been attained by you, nor that state grasped. / Going from here, ask him about my form, O best of twice-borns.
That virtuous one will speak all knowledge to you." / Viṣṇu said: / Having heard all that which was spoken by the crane,
he departed swiftly for the Daśāraṇya, the great hermitage.

title: dviṣaṣṭitamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Viṣṇu said: / Having gone to the hermitage of Kuṇḍala, crowded with truth and dharma, / he then saw Sukarman devoted to his father and mother,
that high-souled one serving his parents, of true valor, / possessing great beauty, great splendor, endowed with great knowledge.
He saw him seated at the feet of his mother and father, / endowed with great devotion, tranquil, a great treasure of all knowledge.
And by the son of Kuṇḍala, the great-souled Sukarman, / seeing Pippala of great intellect arrived at the doorway,
rising quickly from his seat, welcoming respect was made: / "Come, O fortunate one, high-minded Vidyādhara!"
The wise one offered him a seat, foot-water, and respectful offering: / "Are you free from obstacles, O deeply wise one? Do you fare well?"
And he inquired after the health of Pippala who had arrived: / "For what reason you have come today, all that I shall tell [you].
For as long as three thousand years, austerity / was practiced by you, O fortunate one, and from the gods you obtained a boon;
power of subjugation was obtained by you, and likewise freedom of movement; / puffed up by that, you do not understand, and you bear pride in vain.
Seeing all your behavior, the great-souled crane / spoke my name and my unsurpassed knowledge."
Pippala said: / "Who was that crane who addressed me on the riverbank, O twice-born, / saying, 'He will speak all knowledge to you'? Who was that lord, that ruler?"
Sukarman said: / "The crane who spoke to you on the riverbank, / know him to be Brahmā, of great knowledge, the supreme lord.
What else do you ask? Tell me, and I will declare it to you." / Viṣṇu said: / Thus addressed, that righteous Sukarman, O son of the king—
Pippala said: / "'The entire world is subject to you'—so we have heard on earth. / Therefore show that wonder to me, O twice-born, with effort!"
“Behold now a miracle—the reason behind what is submissive and not submissive.” / That righteous Sukarmā said to Pippala:
Then Sukarmā remembered the gods to produce conviction: / Indra and the other world guardians, and the gods headed by Agni.
Summoned, they gathered, along with various Vidyādharas. / Then the gods headed by Agni said to Sukarmā:
“Why have you remembered us, O Brahmin? Speak the reason for this matter.” / Sukarmā said: “This Pippala, a Vidyādhara, has arrived here.
He speaks to me, O Brahmin, about the reason for things being submissive and not submissive. / You have been summoned for the conviction of this great-souled one.
Go each to your own abode,” he said to the gods. / Then those gods said to Sukarmā of great intellect:
“The sight of us, O Brahmin, does not become fruitless; it is a boon. / Choose a boon, good fortune to you, whatever pleases your mind.
We will grant it to you, there is no doubt.” Thus said the best of the gods. / Having bowed to those gods with devotion, that best of the twice-born requested:
“Grant unwavering, excellent devotion endowed with love, O lords of the gods, / and for my mother and father, always. That indeed is the unsurpassed boon.
May my father go to the world of Viṣṇu—this is the highest boon; / likewise my mother, O lords of the gods. I ask for no other boon.”
The gods said: “You are devoted to your parents, O best of Brahmins; because of your devotion, O twice-born, / O Sukarmā, hear our word: we are always pleased with you.”
Having spoken thus, the gods departed to heaven, O son of the king. / All this sovereign power was demonstrated before him by him.
Pippala also saw the wonderful and exceedingly marvelous sight. / That righteous one said to Pippala, the son of Kuṇḍala:
“This is the lower form; what is the higher form like? / Tell of the power of both, O best of speakers.”
Sukarmā said: “I will tell you the mark of the higher form, / by which the worlds, Indra and the rest, with mobile and immobile beings, rejoice.
He alone is the Lord of the universe, all-pervading, the pervasive Master; / his form has never been seen by any yogin at all.
The scripture speaks thus, as if hesitant to describe him: / ‘Without hands, feet, or nose, earless, devoid of a mouth,
he sees every deed done by the inhabitants of the three worlds. / Devoid of ears, he hears what they have said, providing true witness.
Deprived of locomotion, he travels; he is indeed seen everywhere. / Devoid of hands he grasps; devoid of feet he runs.
Everywhere he is seen, O Brahmin, all-pervading, devoid of feet. / Him the lords of the gods and the sages who perceive reality do not see,
yet he sees all of them situated in the realm of truth and falsehood— / pervasive, spotless, perfected, bestower of perfections, leader of all,
whom the great yogin Vyāsa, skilled in dharma and artha, knows. / He is an embodiment of splendor, like space, of a single color, infinite.’
The scripture definitely declares this pure form. / Vyāsa knows, and Mārkaṇḍeya knows that state.
I shall describe the lower form; listen with a single-pointed mind: / when the Soul of beings, having withdrawn [all], goes forth alone,
taking his bed upon the waters, resting on the seat of the coils of Śeṣa, / relying upon him, Janārdana sleeps alone for a long time.
The great sage Mārkaṇḍeya, tormented by the darkness in the water, / seeking a place, yogic in soul, grew weary from wandering.
While wandering, he saw the one who lies upon the couch of Śeṣa, / resembling ten million suns, adorned with divine ornaments,
wearing a divine garland and garment, the all-pervading Lord, / who had entered into the sleep of yoga, lovely, holding the conch, discus, and mace.
There was a fortunate woman, resembling a heap of black collyrium, / her face dreadful with fangs, of terrifying form, O best of the twice-born.
That foremost of sages, the great sage, was told by her: ‘Do not fear!’ / A vast lotus leaf, five leagues long,
upon that leaf Mārkaṇḍeya was placed by the great goddess: / ‘Even though Keśava is asleep, you have no fear here.’
That lord of yogins said to her: ‘Who are you, O beautiful lady? / In this desolate [realm], you alone are thriving.’
Thus questioned by the sage, the goddess respectfully said, O Brahmin: / ‘He who sleeps on the couch of the serpent’s coils is Keśava.
I am his Vaiṣṇava power, called here the Night of Time. / Know me thus, O best of Brahmins, endowed with all magical illusion.
In the Purāṇas I am called Mahāmāyā for the delusion of the universe.’ / Having spoken thus, that goddess disappeared, O Pippala.
When the goddess had departed, as Mārkaṇḍeya watched, / a lotus with the luster of gold arose from his navel.
From that was born the grand ancestor of the world, Brahmā of great splendor; / from him were born all the worlds, mobile and immobile.
the guardians of the worlds beginning with Indra, and the gods headed by Agni. / This immanent form was indeed shown by me, O king.
This immanent form is [visible], while the transcendent one is without support. / Whenever he shows a body, they take the forms of bodies.
All worlds beginning with Brahmā are indeed immanent, O Pippala; / immanent are these worlds that exist in the three worlds.
He, the transcendent Self of beings, is what yogins behold clearly: / the supreme abode having the nature of liberation, identical with the supreme Brahman,
unmanifest, imperishable, the Swan, pure, endowed with supernatural powers. / What the form of the transcendent is, O Vidyādhara, [has been set] before you.
All this has thus been declared by me; what else shall I tell you? / Pippala said: Whence has this great knowledge arisen in you, O man of good vows?
Knowing the immanent state and likewise the transcendent state, / the supreme knowledge of the threefold world thus abides in you alone.
I do not see the supreme culmination of asceticism [in you], O man of good vows. / Have you performed sacrifices, officiating for others, pilgrimages to sacred fords, or asceticism?
Tell that power in this way: by what means do you possess all knowledge? / Sukarma said: I do not know asceticism, nor have I emaciated my body.
Sacrifices, officiating for others, or undertaking pilgrimages to sacred fords—I know not; / meditation and the meritorious time arising from good deeds have not been practiced by me.
One thing clearly I know: the worship of father and mother. / With my hands I continually [attend] both parents.
I myself perform the meritorious washing of the feet; / and likewise massaging of the limbs, bathing, and meals.
Absorbed in meditation at the three junctions of the day, I accomplish [it] day after day; / and the water from the feet of both mother and father, day after day,
I receive with devotional disposition, and I worship them with genuine love. / For as long as my two teachers are living, O Pippala,
for so long indeed does incomparable benefit arise for me. / At the three junctions of the day I worship these two with a pure heart.
I roam freely in playful movement, O Pippala! / What need have I of other asceticism? What need of emaciating the body?
What need have I now of pilgrimages to holy fords or other meritorious acts? / The fruit that is attained from all sacrifices, O twice-born,
that fruit has been seen by me through service to the father, / and service to the mother likewise brings the supreme destination to sons.
It is the all-in-all among all deeds, the essence in the threefold world. / A son attains a world even through service to the mother.
Likewise, in service to the father, great merit arises. / The Gaṅgā is there, the sacred ford Gayā is there, and Puṣkara is right there,
wherever mother and father dwell for a son—there is no doubt. / The other diverse, meritorious sacred fords—
all these accrue to a son from service to the father. / From service to his father comes the fruit of giving and asceticism
for a good son, O brahmin; other religious duty turns to mere toil. / From service to the father, a son obtains unexcelled merit.
It is the entirety of one's own duty, both here and in the hereafter. / When his own mother and father, the two venerable teachers, are alive,
and one serves them as a son, hear the meritorious fruit of that! / The gods are pleased with him, and the sages affectionate toward merit.
The three worlds are indeed pleased by service to the father in this world. / Whoever daily washes the feet of his mother and father,
for him a bath in the Bhāgīrathī occurs day after day. / Whoever feeds his father and mother with meritorious, sweet food and drink,
daily and with devotion, I shall declare his merit: / the fruit of the horse sacrifice arises for that son.
By betel, clothing, drinks, and meals, / and with devotion and pure food, by whoever the two venerable elders are worshipped,
he becomes all-knowing, and he attains fame and renown. / Beholding father and mother, a son should converse with joy;
treasures, well-pleased with him, dwell in his house; / cows are affectionate toward the son, bestowing happiness at all times.

title: triṣaṣṭitamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Sukarma said: And, O best of the twice-born, when drops of water fall / upon all the limbs of a son from both parents as they are bathed,
a bath equal to all sacred fords is fully attained by that son. / Fallen, impaired, aged, incapable in all activities,
diseased, leprous—the son who attends upon such a father, / and upon a mother in like condition—I shall declare his merit.
Viṣṇu becomes pleased in heart with him; of this there is no doubt. / He goes to the Vaiṣṇava realm, which is unattainable even by yogins.
When the two parents are crippled, wretched, aged—these two teachers— / and struck by a great disease, if an evil-minded son abandons them,
that son goes to a frightful hell crowded with worms. / When called by the two aged teachers here at that moment,
if he being a son does not go, I shall declare his sin: / that fool becomes a village swine feeding on feces, without a doubt,
for a thousand births, and then he is born as a dog. / When the aged mother and father are staying in the son's house,
the son who eats food himself without first feeding them / feeds on urine and feces for a thousand births.
That sinner becomes a black serpent for two hundred births. / Disregarding an aged mother and father, if he acts [arrogantly],
that wicked one becomes a crocodile for even a hundred crores of births. / If a son reviles those two with harsh words,
that sinner becomes a tiger, and afterward is born as a bear. / The wicked-minded son who does not show respect to his mother and father
shall dwell in Kuṃbhīpāka for as long as a thousand yugas. / There is no sacred ford equal to a mother, nor any equal to a father for sons,
for salvation and for welfare, both here and in the hereafter. / Therefore, O greatly wise one, I worship the father as a god,
and the mother as a god, all the gods; thus I have become an accomplished yogin. / By the grace of mother and father, supreme knowledge has arisen.
This entire threefold world has come under my control. / I know the immanent state of this great-souled god,
and likewise the transcendent state of that same Vāsudeva, O highly intelligent one. / All knowledge has arisen through the grace of father and mother.
What wise man does not worship his father and mother? / Of what use are the Vedas, studied with their limbs and secondary limbs,
endowed with the scriptures of revelation, O brahmins, if the father is not worshipped by him? / If the mother is not worshipped by him, his Vedas are useless.
What is the use of sacrifices and asceticism, O brahmin, of gifts and worship? / It all comes to vanity for him by whom the mother is not worshipped,
