Thus all this has been told to you in truth by me, O king:
how a bad destination and a good destination are obtained through actions.

A man who acts adversely toward others goes to a dreadful, exceedingly terrible hell;
for a man who lives always favourably [to others], joy-bringing liberation is stationed not far away.

title: saptanavatitamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
Kuñjala said:
Having heard this destination of dharma and adharma spoken by the sage,
the king then addressed that sage.

Let one worship Madhusūdana with oblations and with japa."
Having performed sacrifices and undertaken austerities, that king [went to] the world of Viṣṇu.

Adored with all desired objects, he arrived quickly with joy.
When he had gone to that great world, he did not see the god of gods.
A very acute hunger arose, and an intense thirst began to burn; / and both of these, O greatly wise one, caused immense torment to the soul.
The king too, along with his beloved wife, tormented by hunger and thirst / and beset with immense distress, did not behold Hṛṣīkeśa.
Sūta said: / Thus the king, full of sorrow together with his beloved wife, O best of men, / became utterly bewildered and distraught, exceedingly afflicted by hunger.
The ruler of the earth ran swiftly here and there, / his limbs adorned with every ornament, decked with fine garments and sandalwood paste.
His limbs made radiant by flower garlands, necklaces, earrings, and bracelets, / his body shining with the brilliance of jewels, the king wandered about.
Thus experiencing sorrow even while being praised by panegyrists, / overwhelmed by sorrow and grief, he spoke these words to his beloved:
'I have reached the world of Viṣṇu together with you, O lovely woman, / praised even by sages, mounted upon an aerial chariot, O splendid lady!
By what past action of mine does this fierce hunger increase? / And though I have arrived in Viṣṇu's realm, Madhusūdana is not seen.
What indeed is the cause of this, O fortunate one, that I do not enjoy great fruit? / Or does this sorrow arise from some action of my own?'
Having heard those words of his, she spoke thus to the king.
The wife said: / 'You have spoken the truth, O king; there is no futility in dharma. / The brāhmaṇas who recite the Vedas, the treatises, and the Purāṇas—
shaking off distress and sorrow here, one is freed from all sins / simply by uttering the name of the Lord, Viṣṇu who bears the discus.
Virtuous and exceedingly fortunate people meditate upon Janārdana. / You indeed worshipped the god who holds the conch, discus, and mace;
yet no gift of food or the like was given to the brāhmaṇas as prescribed by the twice-born. / I recognize this as its fruit, that Madhusūdana has not been seen.
Hunger torments me, O king, and thirst parches me dry.' / Kuñjala said: / Being thus addressed by his beloved, the king, his senses troubled with anxiety,
then beheld a highly sacred hermitage that dispels fatigue, / crowded with heavenly trees and beautified by reservoirs,
[It was] filled with stepped wells, reservoirs, and ponds overflowing with holy water, / teeming with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks, and adorned with white water-lilies.
The hermitage looked splendid, O son, with sages who know the reality, / dense with heavenly trees and graced by herds of deer,
thick with various flowers, filled with delightful fragrances, / crowded with twice-born and perfected beings, and bustling with disciples of sages,
resounding with yogins and lords of yoga, adorned by hosts of gods, / dense with groves of banana trees and decorated with fine fruits,
thronged with diverse trees, endowed with all objects of desire, / always adorned with fine-smelling sandalwood trees and abundant fruits.
It was thus holy, filled with the marks of the absolute. / King Subāhu, then, along with his dearly beloved wife,
entered that most sacred forest that fulfills every wish, / illuminating all quarters, where resided one resembling the sun.
Shining with great, supreme brilliance, resembling the sun, / seated in a yogic posture, wrapped in a yogic band,
Vāmadeva, the best of sages and foremost among Vaiṣṇavas, / was meditating upon Hṛṣīkeśa, who bestows both enjoyment and liberation.
Having seen that great-souled Vāmadeva, the best of sages, / the king went quickly with his beloved wife and bowed down.
Then, seeing the excellent king bowed low, / Vāmadeva greeted the king, accompanied by his beloved, with blessings.
Having seated Subāhu, the best of kings, upon a sacred seat, / he honored him with a seat and other courtesies, with water for washing the feet and the guest-offering.
Honored by the sage, the king, who had arrived with his beloved, / was then questioned [by him], the best of great devotees of the Lord.
Vāmadeva said: / 'I know through divine knowledge, O best of kings, that you are the Cola king, / knower of Viṣṇu's dharma, devoted to Viṣṇu, the best of men.
Have you arrived free from illness, along with your wife of eagle-like eyes?' / The king said: 'I have arrived free from illness, having attained the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
For with supreme devotion, the God of gods, Janārdana, / the Lord of the world, was worshipped by me; pleased with devotion, the Lord of gods—
Why, O revered father, do I not see the god, the lord of Kamalā? / Hunger torments me, O revered father, and an intensely terrible thirst;
from these two we find no peace, nor do we obtain any comfort. / This is the cause of sorrow that has befallen me, O best of sages;
so tell me the cause of it, and out of grace be pleased toward me.' / Vāmadeva said: 'You are indeed always devoted to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, O best of kings.
Madhusūdana was worshipped by you with supreme devotion, / with offerings of devotion such as ablutions, and likewise with incense, flowers, and the rest;
yet the Lord of the worlds was not worshipped with food offerings and fruits. / Arriving at the tenth lunar day, O best of kings, you always observed
eating only one single meal, but good food was not given to a brāhmaṇa; / and having arrived at the eleventh lunar day, no food was consumed by you,
yet no food was given to a brāhmaṇa dedicated to Viṣṇu. / Food always exists upon the earth in the form of nectar.
The gift of food in particular was never given by you at any time. / Listen to the herbs and plants, O great king, in their various divisions:
pungent, bitter, astringent, sweet, sour, and saline, / and all the condiments like asafetida in their various forms, O ruler of the earth.
All the plants, the sources of nourishment, were born from nectar. / Having well-prepared that food, combining it with herbs and cooked dishes,

"To the gods who have the form of Viṣṇu"—intending thus, [a gift] is given,
and "to the ancestors who have the form of Viṣṇu", into the hand of a brāhmaṇa.
then, having given to guests, one should feed one's dependents; / and afterward they themselves eat that food resembling nectar.
After death, there is no suffering at all for him, but only happiness, O ruler of the earth. / Brāhmaṇas, ancestors, and gods are in the nature of fields, O king.
Just as a farmer always carries out good cultivation, / so a mortal should carry out cultivation in the field of a brāhmaṇa's mouth, O king.
With the plow of one's natural disposition, one should break the soil using the blade of faith; / the two bullocks are held to be constant intellect and austerity;

The lord who experiences true knowledge, whose self is pure, with water in hand
should dismiss [the brāhmaṇa] in the great field called 'brāhmaṇa' with bows.
Just as a farmer always breaks up the clods of dirt, O king, / engaged in working the field, desiring Viṣṇu, one should propitiate [it];
in the same manner, one should propitiate brāhmaṇas with auspicious, holy words. / The occasion of festivals and holy pilgrimage places is like a cloud for raining:
the field-owner wishing to sow then sows in the field. / In the same way, O king, gifts are given to a pleased brāhmaṇa.
Just as the owner of the field enjoys the fruit / of the field wherein seed has been sown, O great king, so also does the donor enjoy;
both in the hereafter and right here, he becomes constantly satisfied—not otherwise. / Brāhmaṇas, ancestors, and gods are the forms of fields, without a doubt.
Sown for the sake of mortals, O great king, they yield [their fruit]; / the fruit is just like that, of this there is no doubt: as one sows, so one surely reaps.
For sweet fruit does not arise from bitter, O king, / nor, likewise, does bitter arise from that which is called sweet.'

Just as the seed one sows, so is the fruit one enjoys;
he who does not sow a field does not enjoy its fruit.

Likewise, the brāhmaṇas, the gods, and the ancestors have the nature of a field;
they show the fruit even of what has been given, O king, of this there is no doubt.

Whatever action was performed by you, auspicious or inauspicious,
enjoy such [fruit], O king; it cannot happen otherwise.

Never in the past was sweet food or drink
given with a pure mind to gods, brāhmaṇas, or ancestors.

Plentiful, delicious, sweet food to be chewed, sucked, drunk,
and eaten was enjoyed by you yourself; to whom did you ever give [anything]?

Your own body was nourished by you with foods like nectar;
because that was done, O great king, therefore hunger arises [now].

Action alone, O king, is the cause of men's pleasure and pain,
and of birth and death, O fortunate one; enjoy the fruit of that action.

Even ancient great-souled ones reached heaven through their own action,
and went back to the earthly realm when the time came for the exhaustion of their action.

Nala, Bhagīratha, Viśvāmitra, and Yudhiṣṭhira
reached heaven only through action, O king, at their proper time.

Destiny is indeed previous action; through it one obtains pain and pleasure;
who, O king, even an almighty lord, is capable of transgressing that?

Now therefore, O best of kings, even though you have gone to heaven, there arose for you
the violent onset of hunger and thirst; for your action was corrupt.

If a remedy for your hunger is desired by you, O best of kings,
then go and eat your own body remaining in the forest of Ānandāraṇya.

And this great queen of yours appears exceedingly emaciated by hunger."
Subāhu said: "For how long must this deed be done together with my beloved?

Tell me that, O fortunate one: when will favour be seen?
By the giving of what substance is there what merit, O best of sages?

Tell that, O very wise one, if you are pleased now."
Vāmadeva said: "From the gift of food comes great happiness, and from water, O highly intelligent one.

Mortals enjoy heaven indeed, and are not afflicted by sins,
only when a gift has been given by human beings.

Even when the time of death has arrived, all give gifts;
first of all food should be given, accompanied by water.

He should give a good parasol and shoes, and an attractive water pot,
land, fine gold, and a cow—whoever gives these eight gifts,

in heaven the arising of hunger, thirst, and the like does not happen to him;
he is not tormented by hunger, O king, satisfied from the gift of food.

Severe thirst does not arise for him; he is always satisfied.
By the gift of sandals and by the gift of a parasol, O lord of the earth,

the giver obtains shade and a vehicle, O best of kings;
by the gift of shoes... another [result] I declare thus:

from the gift of land, O fortunate one, one obtains all desires;
by the gift of a cow, O great king, one is always nourished with tastes.

Enjoying all pleasures, a man dwells in the world of heaven;
the giver becomes satisfied indeed by the gift of a cow, there is no doubt.

Free from disease, endowed with happiness, contented, and possessed of wealth,
by gold one becomes of fair complexion; of this there is no doubt.

A man becomes glorious, handsome, generous, and an enjoyer of jewels.
When the time of death has arrived, if one gives a gift of sesame,

becoming master of all enjoyments, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus, through exceptional gifts, supreme happiness is attained.

The gift of a cow, the gift of land, and food and water
were never given to a brāhmaṇa by you while living, O king of kings,

nor given even at the time of death; therefore hunger arises.
This cause, arisen subject to the power of action, has been told to you.

For just as an action has been done, so it is experienced.
Subāhu said:
How will my hunger go to cessation, O best of sages?

Dried up by it, my body is exceedingly tormented.
Declare to the two of us an expiation for hunger, O best of the twice-born,

so that there may be peace for me from this terrible deed.
Vāmadeva said:
There is no expiation apart from experiencing [the fruits], O best of kings.

You yourself, being sound, will experience all the fruit of this deed.
Where your body has fallen, and that of your beloved, O lord of the earth,

you two must indeed go from here, without a doubt;
and both of you must consume that very imperishable body,

each your own, O king, without doubt, you together with your beloved.
The king said:
For how long must it be consumed in this way by me together with my beloved?

when you hear it, holy, then you will attain liberation.
All this has been told to you; go, O king, and consume it."

Having heard thus, the king, together with his wife once again,
eats the flesh of his own body along with his beloved.

Daily in this way, O greatly wise one, the body becomes whole just as before;
daily the king eats it, and his queen, O son.

And just as the king eats his body,
the two women constantly laugh; I shall tell their disposition.

Prajñā, the greatly virtuous, together with [Śraddhā, looks at] that king’s conduct;
his unfailing faith indeed constantly laughs.

Prompted by understanding, food dedicated to a Vaiṣṇava,
well resolved upon, was not given to brāhmaṇas with faith.

Thus he eats the flesh of his own body every day,
and the woman also [eats] her own body, which has tastes resembling nectar.

Then, at the end of a hundred years, remembering the great sage Vāmadeva,
he reviled himself, O one of good vows:

"Food was never given by me to the ancestors, to the gods, to the brāhmaṇas;
it was not given to guests, and especially to the aged;

nor was it given out of compassion to the poor and the afflicted."
Thus he eats his own flesh, reviling his own action.

Seeing Subāhu eating his own flesh together with his beloved in this way,
the two women, Prajñā and Śraddhā, laughed then.

At that ripening of his action, the pure-souled one laughs, O king:
"In the context of association with me, it was not given, O evil-minded one."

And Prajñā, with those words, mocks the king again:
"Where has that great delusion gone, by which you were deluded, O king?

By greed joined with delusion one is thrown into the pit of darkness;
falling there, [he says,] 'Cast into a snare of grief, alas!'

Abandoning the path of giving, you went along the path of greed, O king;
consume along with your wife, overcome intensely by hunger!"

Thus Prajñā laughs at him, Subāhu, accompanied by his beloved.
This was indeed the entire reason for the laughter of the two, O son.

While the body of the grieving king was being eaten then,
they two said, "Give, give!"—he was constantly begged.

Hunger and Thirst, O greatly wise one, fearsome in form, terrifying,
begged the lord of kings for food mixed with milk.

All this has been recounted to you, which was asked by you.
What else shall I declare to you? Speak that, O greatly wise one!

Vijvala said:
Recite to me that hymn named Vāsudeva, O father,
by which the king may go to liberation, that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.

title: aṣṭanavatitamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
Sūta said:
When these auspicious words were spoken by the great-souled Vijvala,
Kuñjala, the best of speakers, uttered the sacred hymn.

Having meditated on and bowed to Hṛṣīkeśa, the destroyer of all afflictions,
the giver of all blessings, the hymn to Hari was uttered.

That hymn named after Vāsudeva gives all blessings;
it is the gateway to liberation, joined with joy, giving peace, and increasing nourishment;

it gives all desires, grants knowledge, and increases knowledge—
that hymn of Vāsudeva which was revealed to Vijvala,

named after Vāsudeva, immeasurable, increasing merit.
Having understood all that from his father, Vijvala, the best of birds,

began to go there, having questioned his father then, O king.
To Vijvala, who had resolved to go thus and was a master of knowledge,
the righteous-minded one spoke to his son who was prepared to render aid.

Kuñjala said:
O son, I know that great sin of the king, listen:
go and recite there while Subāhu listens.

The more he hears the supreme hymn, the more he will become full of knowledge;
by the grace of glorious Vāsudeva, indeed, there is no doubt that what I have said will be very auspicious."

Having taken leave of the teacher, flying up with swift strides,
Vijvala then reached the sacred Ānandakānana.

Resorting to the shade of a tree, he sat filled with joy,
having looked out for that king who had come again by aerial chariot.

"When will this king Subāhu come along with his beloved?
At some point I shall release him from his sin by means of this hymn."

Meanwhile, the aerial chariot arrived, adorned with a network of tiny bells,
filled with the ringing of bells, accompanied by lutes and flutes.
resounding with the songs of Gandharvas, accompanied by Apsarases, / abundant in all desires, yet entirely devoid of food and water.
Seated in that chariot, King Subāhu, along with his beloved— / along with his beloved Tārkṣyā—stepped down from the aerial vehicle.
Just as he took up a sharp weapon and began to cut that corpse, / right then a call was made by Vijvala:
"O tiger among men! You who resemble a god! / You commit this merciless act, which even cruel men cannot bring themselves
to do, O tiger among men! What reversal of destiny is this? / A sinful, rash deed, ever censured in the worlds—
why have you undertaken it here, devoid of Vedic conduct? / Tell me truthfully all the reason for this."
Having heard the speech thus uttered by that noble Vijvala, / the great king spoke these words to his beloved:
"O beloved, for a hundred years this has been eaten by me, an evildoer, / yet never has anyone spoken as this one speaks.
While I was thus afflicted by hunger, O beloved, / [that torment] has left my heart, and peace now arises in my mind, O lovely one!
“As long as his speech, which pacifies all sorrow, is heard, / so long does delight abide in my heart, O sweet-smiling one!”
Who is this? A god, a Gandharva, or could he be the thousand-eyed [Indra]? / May the word of the sages come true, which was spoken by the sage long ago!"
Having heard the words thus spoken by her beloved, his beloved, / the wife wholly devoted to her husband, then answered the king:
"What you have spoken is true, my lord; this is a supreme wonder! / Just as it is in your heart, beloved, so it is in my mind as well.
Who is this, bearing the form of a bird, who inquires like a well-wisher?" / Hearing this spoken by his beloved, the lord of the earth,
folding his hands in reverence, said to the bird: / Subāhu said: "Welcome to you, O bird-formed lord of great wisdom!
With my head, together with my wife, / I bow to your two lotus feet; may merit be ours by your grace!
Who are you, speaking such pious words in the form of a bird? / Whatever deed was done in a previous body, O best of beings,
good or evil, its fruit is reaped right here." / Then he recounted his own story before him,
just as had been heard previously when told by his father, Kuñjala: / "Tell me your own tale: who are you that speak to me?"
The excellent bird then spoke these words in reply to Subāhu: / Vijvala said: "Born among the parrots, my father is named Kuñjala;
I am named Vijvala, the third among his sons. / I am no god, nor a Gandharva, nor a Siddha, O mighty-armed one!
I constantly behold such terrible deeds [done by you]. / For how long will you perform such great, violent deeds,
O great king? Tell me that now." / Subāhu said: "The hymn named Vāsudeva, which was spoken of formerly by brāhmaṇas—
when I hear it, O noble one, then I shall attain my proper state. / Indeed, so it was spoken by the pure-souled, self-controlled sage:
'Then I shall be freed from sin, without doubt.'" / Vijvala said: "For your sake I questioned my father, and what he told me,

that eternal truth I shall tell you today; listen, O best of men!"

—Of this hymn named Vāsudeva, Nārada is the ṛṣi, the metre is anuṣṭubh,

[the praṇava] is the deity, and the application in repetition is for the destruction of all sins and the attainment of the four aims of life.

title: —namobhagavatevāsudevāyaitimaṃtraḥ
text_mt: Purifying, supreme, meritorious, knowing the Veda, the abode of the Veda, / the support of knowledge, the support of existence—to the Praṇava, indeed, I bow.
Dwelling nowhere, formless, brilliantly luminous, of great elevation, / devoid of qualities yet bound to qualities—I bow to the supreme Praṇava.
Supremely beloved, of great energy, destroyer of great delusion, / pervading the entire universe, transcendent of qualities—to it I bow.
Who shines everywhere, having become the augmenter of the prosperity of beings, / fearless, connected with mendicants—to the auspicious Praṇava I bow.
Singing the Gāyatrī and the Sāman, the chant itself, lover of song, auspicious, / enjoyer of the songs of Gandharvas—to the Praṇava I bow low.
Reflection itself, the form of the Veda, present in the sacrifice, loving toward devotees, / the source of all the world—to the syllable Oṃ I bow low.
The deliverer of all beings, shining in the form of a boat / for those submerged in the ocean of worldly existence—to the Praṇava, Hari, I bow.
Dwelling in all worlds in a single form and manifold forms, / the abode having the nature of sole liberation—to the auspicious Praṇava I bow.
Subtle, subtler than the subtle, pure, devoid of qualities, the ruler of qualities, / free from material states, the seat of the Veda—to it I bow.
Ever free from unions and separations of gods and Daityas, through contentment, / to be meditated upon by deities and yogins—to that syllable Oṃ I bow.
All-pervading, knower of the universe, supreme wisdom, auspicious, / benevolent, possessing auspicious qualities, tranquil—to the Praṇava, the Lord, I pay homage.
Into whose māyā entered the gods and asuras headed by Brahmā, / yet do not find the supreme, pure gate of liberation—to it I bow.
To the root of bliss, whose intellect is pure, to the pure Haṃsa, higher than the high and lower than the low, / homage be to that leader of hosts, to glorious Vāsudeva of vast radiance!
Shining with the glorious Pāñcajanya and with the Sudarśana bright as the sun, / resplendent with club and lotus—to that Lord I take refuge forever.
Whom the Vedas keep secret, qualified, the support of all qualities / and of the moving and unmoving, possessing splendour equal to sun and fire—in that Vāsudeva I take refuge.
The treasure that ends hunger, stainless, beautiful in form, resplendent with measured bliss, / reaching whom the worlds of the gods and others live—in that Vāsudeva I take refuge.
Who ever destroys masses of darkness with his rays, the cause of creation, / radiant with splendour bright as the sun—in that Vāsudeva I take refuge.
Who shines everywhere with the splendours of the sun, who dries up and gives sap, / who, as wind, moves inside living beings—in that Vāsudeva I take refuge.
The god who, according to his own will, ever sustains all worlds and rulers of earth, / and who acts like a boat for crossing over—in that Vāsudeva I take refuge.
Gone within, identical with the world, he ever digests [food] for the stationary and the moving; / having the Svāhā-offering as mouth, the cause of the host of gods—in that Vāsudeva I take refuge.
Who, gentle and granting virtues, nourishes food in the world / with all meritorious saps and spotless splendour—in that Vāsudeva I take refuge.
He who is everywhere, the cause of destruction, the refuge of all, composed of all, being everything, / who enjoys sense objects without sense organs—in that Vāsudeva I take refuge.
Who in the form of the soul sustains the worlds, and from it all moving and unmoving embodied beings, / absolute, composed of knowledge, entirely pure—in that Vāsudeva I take refuge.

I seek refuge in that Vāsudeva, the destroyer of the Daityas, the root cause of the destruction of suffering, / who is peaceful, supreme, full of power, vast, and reaching whom the gods attain humility.

I seek refuge in that Vāsudeva, who is happiness, the culmination of happiness, bestower of happiness, lord of the gods, / an ocean of knowledge, lord of the sages, ruler of the immortals, who abides in truth and is endowed with the quality of truth.

I seek refuge in that Vāsudeva, whose form is the sacrifice's limbs, whose form is the supreme reality, who is joined with Māyā, lord of Lakṣmī, intensely auspicious, / the sole consciousness, the abode of the worlds.
His bed lies in the midst of the ocean, his bed rests on the vast coils of the serpent's body; / I bow down constantly to the pair of auspicious lotus feet of that very Vāsudeva.
Those lotus feet of his, endowed with merit, conferring peace constantly, / attended upon by numerous sacred places, of glorious Vāsudeva, destroy all sin.
I bow down constantly to the lotus foot of glorious Vāsudeva, / shining like a great red water lily, adorned with ankle-bells and rings, which conquers the marks of the lotus.
Ever praised with deep devotion by the gods, accomplished beings, sages, and lords of serpents, / I bow down constantly to that holy lotus foot of glorious Vāsudeva.
I seek refuge in that Vāsudeva, dipping in whose foot-water they go to heaven, purified and free from taint, / and the deeply contented sages attain liberation.
Wherever the water of Viṣṇu's feet is present, there all the sacred fords, such as the Gaṅgā, ever reside; / whoever drink it, even if having sinful bodies, go pure to Murāri's lovely home.
Sprinkled with the water from his feet, even those whose bodies are smeared with grave sins / go to the liberation of the Supreme Lord; I bow down constantly to his feet alone.
By the mere eating of the food-offering of that great-souled one who bears the discus, / men obtain the fruit of the glorious Vājapeya sacrifice and become endowed with all their aims.
I seek refuge in that Vāsudeva, Nārāyaṇa, the destroyer of hell and misery, / devoid of illusion, complete, knower of virtues, meditating upon whom people attain a good destiny.

He who is worthy of praise by sages, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas, and ever worshipped by the gods, / who is the cause of the creation of the universe, the lord of Brahmā and other gods, / who is affectionate, the rescuer of one fallen into the great ocean of worldly existence—to his two pure, supreme, purifying feet I bow with devotion.

Glorious Vāmana who was seen in the sacrificial pavilion by the hosts of gods, a chanter of the Sāma hymns, / who delighted the hosts of gods with the chanting of the Sāma, the sole ruler of the three worlds, / who cleansed Bali of sin through the auspicious glances of his eyes—I praise his supreme, purifying pair of lotus feet.

I praise the lord Vāmana, shining in the assembly of the twice-born at the start of the sacrifice, adorned with the glory of sacred knowledge, / radiant with divine luster, full of grace, resembling a sapphire, / who, wishing the good of the gods, begged the fair son of Virocana: “Let three steps be given to me!”

To behold him, the sages ascended to the solar disc in heaven; / he who then indeed covered the space between moon and sun with his stride— / the hosts of gods instantly merged into the body of him, the holder of the discus, the revealer of the universe; I praise the incomparable stride of that Lord.

title: navanavatitamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Viṣṇu said: / Having heard the purifying hymn, supreme, ancient, destroying sins, full of merit, auspicious, / blessed, a noble sacred song, most worthy of recitation, the king became happy.
His thirst departed, along with hunger; the ruler of the earth became like a god, / and his wife also shone with beauties; both attained the severance of the bonds of sin.

Surrounded by the gods, by the twice-born, and by accomplished beings endowed with devotion to Hari, / that deity, holding the glorious conch, discus, lotus, mace, and sword, approached the taintless king.
Glorious Nārada, Bhārgava, and the virtuous Vyāsa, along with the son of Mṛkaṇḍu, arrived there; / the sage named Vālmīki, devoted to Viṣṇu, arrived, and Vasiṣṭha the son of Brahmā;
the great-souled Garga, endowed with devotion to Hari, Jābāli, Raibhya, and Kaśyapa— / these, dear to Viṣṇu, the foremost of the devotees of the Lord, arrived together with Hari.
Those holy, most fortunate ones, free from stain, devoted to the auspicious lotus feet of Hari, / stood surrounding glorious Vāsudeva, praising the king in various ways.
All the gods, with Agni at their head, Brahmā, Hari, and also the heavenly goddesses, / as well as the kings of the Gandharvas and other fine singers, sang divine, sweet, enchanting songs.

With most sacred hymns filled with Vedic knowledge and conforming to the supreme reality, the sages offered praise. / Seeing the sovereign, the ruler of the earth, the god Hari spoke an enchanting word:
“Choose a boon as you wish, O king; I grant it to you, for I am well-pleased.” / Hearing Hari's word and seeing Murāri speaking before him,
the Lord, dark as a blue lotus, the slayer of Mura, bearing the conch, discus, sword, and mace, / accompanied by Śrī, the supreme Lord, radiant with jewels, adorned with bracelets and garlands,

bright as the sun, well served by the multitudes of gods, well adorned with costly necklaces and ornaments, / with divine fragrances and excellent ointments—with devotional disposition the king bowed to the ground before Hari.
Then, bowing like a stick repeatedly with the word “Victory!”, the great king [said]: / “I am your servant, your attendant standing before you; I know neither devotion nor supreme contemplation.

I have come here with my wife, O Hari; protect me who have taken refuge in you! / Fortunate indeed are those twice-born and mortal men, O Mādhava, whose minds are constantly absorbed in meditation on you,
who, chanting 'O Śiva, O Mādhava,' depart completely pure from here to Vaikuṇṭha. / And those who carry upon their heads the holy water that issued from your lotus feet,
bathed in the water that springs from all the sacred places, those mortals go to the splendid abode of Hari.
I have no yoga, I have no devotion, I have no knowledge, I have no rituals; / through association with whose merit do you grant me a boon?”
Hari said: / “The recitation of the name of Vāsudeva, which destroys great sins, / was heard by you from the virtuous Vijvala, O king, making you free from taint.
Because of that, you have become a partaker of liberation; of this there is no doubt. / Enjoy divine pleasures according with your heart's desire in my realm!”
The king said: / “If indeed a boon is to be given by you to me, a wretched man, O god, / give the foremost excellent boon to Vijvala first.”
Hari said: / “Vijvala's father is the virtuous Kuñjala, adorned with knowledge; / he recites the great hymn to Vāsudeva every day, O ruler of the earth.
Together with his beloved wife and his sons, he shall go to my abode; / and to the one who recites this hymn, I shall always grant the fruit.”
When these auspicious words were spoken, the king said to Keśava: / “Make this most holy hymn fruitful, O Keśava!”

Hari said:
In the Kṛta age, O great king, when human beings praise [me with this hymn],
they attain liberation that very moment; of this there is no doubt.

In the Tretā age in merely a month, but in the Dvāpara age in six months;
and in the Kali age, the mortals who recite it for a single year,

go to the realm of Viṣṇu, O king of kings, which grants liberation.
If a brāhmaṇa, having bathed, recites it at the three junctures of the day or at a single time,

whatever desire he wishes for, that very thing shall become his.
A kṣatriya attains victory, adorned with wealth and grain;

a vaiśya becomes prosperous, and a śūdra becomes happy.
He who recites it to an outcaste will be freed from sin;

the listener never sees dreadful hell at all.
And by the grace of my hymn he will attain all accomplishments.

And he who recites it at the time of a śrāddha while brāhmaṇas are being fed—
his ancestors, satisfied, will go to the world of Viṣṇu, O lord of the earth.

Whether a brāhmaṇa or a kṣatriya recites it at the end of a libation,
his ancestors drink nectar, their minds gladdened.

When a man recites it with devotion during oblations and in the midst of a sacrifice,
no obstacles arise there, and every accomplishment will be attained.

In a dangerous, inaccessible place, in peril from ferocious tigers,
or when facing danger from thieves, he should utter that hymn there.

Peace will surely arise there, O great king, there is no doubt.
When a man approaches the king's gate or in other grand enterprises,

a man should recite ten thousand [repetitions] of the [hymn] named after Vāsudeva,
observing celibacy, properly bathed, and free from anger and greed.

Having worshipped Vāsudeva with a restrained mind, he should offer a tenth part [in] homa
with sesame and grains of rice mixed with clarified butter.

Mortals should then offer an oblation with meditation for each verse.
I never leave the side of such people, always serving them like a good servant.

When the Kali age has arrived, he will attain servitude through this hymn.
It should not be given to just anyone because of the risk of violating the Veda;

he will surely have all his desires abundantly fulfilled.
Listen, O king, to how this hymn was made fruitful by me.

It was created by Brahmā; it was formerly recited by Rudra.
Indra was freed from the murder of a brāhmaṇa and released from sin.

The gods and the ṛṣis, Guhyakas, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and immortals,
and the Nāgas who worshipped this hymn obtained their desired attainment.

He will be meritorious, fortunate, generous, and endowed with sons,
who recites my hymn; there is no deliberation needed here.

Come with your wife to my abode, O best of kings!"
A supporting hand was offered by Hari to that lord of the earth.

Kettledrums sounded there, the Gandharvas sang delightfully,
the best of Apsarases danced, and they showered flowers.

The gods and all the ṛṣis praised them with Vedic hymns.
Then, accompanied by his beloved, the king went to Hari.

Rejoicing in his heart, Vijvala sees him being praised by the hosts of gods and Siddhas,
and having arrived in haste, the glorious [bird] stays where his father and mother are.

title: śatatamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
Viṣṇu said:
On the charming bank of the Narmadā, under a banyan tree, the father truly dwells.
Vijvala, having arrived, bowed down to his father.

The highly intelligent and virtuous [bird] related the majesty
of the hymn named after Vāsudeva before his father,

and how Viṣṇu had arrived and granted him an auspicious boon;
he related all that with a very joyful heart.

Kuñjala too, having heard the king’s account,
filled with great joy, embraced his son Vijvala,

and said, "A meritorious deed was done by you, my child, for the great-souled king—
a very auspicious benefit, through the glorification of Vāsudeva!"

Having spoken thus to his son, greeting him with blessings,
and repeatedly praising his son who was accompanied by the god,

he remained on the charming bank of the river, while Cyavana looked on.
All this has been told to you: the conduct of those great-souled

Vaiṣṇavas, O great king. What else shall I tell you?
Vena said:
Nectar was presented to me in a conch vessel for drinking.

Hence, what mortal on earth would not have faith to drink it?
Knowledge of Viṣṇu is supreme among drinks in this world at all times.

As this is told by you, there is no satiety in drinking it;
indeed, O lord of the gods, my faith in hearing grows.

By your favor, tell me also of Kuñjala's deeds,
and what that great soul said to his fourth son;

kindly tell me the truth in great detail.
The holy Lord said:
Listen, I shall relate the life of Kuñjala,

and the life of Cyavana, which is endowed with much welfare.
This sacred narrative, O best of men, destroys sin.
A man who hears it with devotion obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.

title: ekādhikaśatatamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
Sūta said:
The lord of gods, Hṛṣīkeśa, recounted to the son of Aṅga, the best of kings,
the great, auspicious narrative that destroys sin:

"Listen, I will tell the story that bestows welfare,
and the account of the twice-born, the great-souled Kuñjala."

Viṣṇu said:
Kuñjala, the righteous, called his fourth son,
and filled with joy, spoke thus to Kapiñjala:

"What unprecedented thing have you seen, my son? Tell me.
Whither did you go from here to eat, O best of sons?

Declare that, O fortunate one, if you saw anything that bestows great merit.
Kapiñjala said:
What was asked by you, father, that unprecedented thing I shall relate.

What was not seen or heard by anyone, and whence it was never heard by me—
that I will tell right here; listen now, father.

Let all my brothers listen; mother, listen now!
Mount Kailāsa is the best of mountains, white like the moon,

abounding in various minerals, adorned with diverse trees,
and washed on every side with the auspicious and sacred waters of the Gaṅgā, father.

Thousands of diverse, divine rivers,
from which, father, diverse streams have arisen,

and thousands of ponds filled with water are on that great mountain;
there are wide rivers frequented by swans and sārāsa cranes.

On that best of peaks, giving merit and destroying sin,
there are diverse blooming and fruiting forests,

furnished with diverse trees, green and auspicious,
endowed with hordes of Kinnaras and crowded with Apsarases,

splendidly adorned by Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, Siddhas, and hosts of gods,
provided with groves of celestial trees and filled with divine states,

rich in beauty with divine fragrances, endowed with diverse gems,
and very beautiful with rocks of white crystal,

made of the brilliance of the sun, O king, filled with radiant lights,
with lovely-scented sandalwoods and with bakula trees having dark flowers.
Adorned everywhere with trees laden with various blossoms, / it is made sweet with the melodious sounds of celestial birds.
Made sweet by the humming of bees and the multitude of trees, / that forested mountain shines with the calls of cuckoos.
Crowded with ten million gaṇas, the temple of Śiva is there, / white with radiant beams, holy, a rocky height that is a heap of merit.
With roaring lions, buffaloes, and then elephants, / and resounding everywhere with the trumpetings of the world-elephants,
thronged with diverse beasts, teeming with troops of monkeys, / and filled with reverberating sounds in its caves by the cries of peacocks,
resplendent with caves, plastered cliffs, peaks, and ridges, / endowed with diverse cascades, and glistening with medicinal herbs,
celestial, of divine virtue, holy, crowded with sacred abodes, / frequented by holy folk—a great mountain that is a heap of merit.
The best of mountains, frequented by Pulindas, Bhillas, and Kolas; / with jagged crests and peaks, the king of mountains shines.
With diverse other sacred, auspicious wonders and blessings, / and by the currents of the Gaṅgā's water, it poured forth a mighty sound.
I went there to Kailāsa, the home of Śaṅkara; / there I saw a marvel such as was never before seen or heard.
Listen, father, and I shall tell all that was spoken by me. / From the peak of the mountain king Meru, holy and of immense majesty,
a stream resembling snow, milk, and gold falls to the earth, / of the Gaṅgā, O noble one, adorned with roar and rushing speed.
Reaching the crest of Kailāsa, it expanded there; / ten yojanas in extent, there lies the great lake of the Gaṅgā.
It shines with abundant, holy, and spotless water; / possessing all-around beauty, it is graced by great geese.
With the sacred, divine, and sweet chanting of the Sāman, / the geese warble there; the lake shines with them.
On its bank, upon a rock indeed, O highly intelligent one, / sat a maiden of the snows, her hair loosened, endowed with the wealth of beauty,
possessed of divine form, endowed with virtues, having divine marks, / and adorned with heavenly ornaments, she shines on its bank.
I do not know whether she is the daughter of the king of mountains, or of the great ocean; / or is she the wife of Brahmā, or could she be Svāhā?
Or might she be the fortunate Indrāṇī, or could she be Rohiṇī? / Such abundance of beauty is not seen among young maidens,
nor among any other truly celestial women whatsoever, O father, / such as the manifestation of form, virtue, and character that is seen here.
The apsarases never possess such beauty and signs / as that limb of hers, bewitching the universe, which was seen by me.
Seated on a slab of rock, overcome by sorrow, / without her many kinfolk, the young girl weeps in sweet tones.
Shedding tears, numerous and resembling pearls, / spotless, they fall right into this lake, O highly intelligent one.
Those drops, resembling pearls, fall into the vast water; / from them arise charming, fragrant lotuses.
Lotuses were born from those tears of her eyes, O highly intelligent one; / in the water of the Gaṅgā they float, countless in number.
Fallen, very delightful, carried along by the current / in the midst of the Gaṅgā's stream, frequented by flocks of geese.
Now, the stream of the Bhāgīrathī has issued from that place; / reaching the peak of Kailāsa, a lovely glen called Ratna,
full of water, it extends for two yojanas, / crowded with flocks of geese and filled with water-birds.
There are lotuses of distinct, various colors there, / in the clear stream, O father, resorted to by hosts of sages.
The lotuses that were born from her tears in the morning / float in the Gaṅgā's water, fragrant and large.
They float upon the clear stream filled with water, / among fine geese, resounding with water-birds.
Sūta said: / On that mountain named Ratna, the Great Lord Ratneśvara, / worshiped by gods and daityas, always abides, O father.
There I saw, O father, a certain holy sage, / covered with a burden of matted locks, wearing no clothes, holding a staff,
supportless, taking no food, exceedingly feeble from austerities, / emaciated in body, a mass of bones bound only with skin.
All the limbs of that great-souled one were smeared only with ashes; / he eats dry leaves that have decayed and fallen.
Absorbed in devotion to Śiva, difficult to approach, performing great penance; / taking the fragrant lotuses born from those tears,
bringing them from the water of the Gaṅgā, the highly fortunate one, / skilled in song and dance, worships the god of gods, Ratneśvara.
Standing at the doorway of that enemy of Tripura, he sings and dances; / then coming to the hermitage, the righteous one weeps in sweet tones.
This unprecedented sight was seen by me, O father, best of speakers! / Tell me by your favor, if you know the cause:
Who is that noble woman? Why does she weep, O father? / Why does that divine man worship the god Maheśvara?
Tell me that in detail, the cause of all my doubt. / Thus addressed by his son, the very wise Kuñjala
spoke in detail to Kapiñjala, while the sage was listening.

title: dvyadhikaśatatamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Kuñjala said: / I shall tell you everything, my child, which you have now spoken to me, / regarding the sorrow of both of them, and from what it arose, O best of the twice-born.
Once the great goddess Pārvatī, foremost among women, / sporting, spoke this word to the great-souled Īśvara:
‘O Mahādeva, a great pregnancy-craving has arisen in my heart; / show me the forest, the best of forests, before my eyes.’
The glorious Mahādeva said: / ‘So be it, O Mahādevī! I shall show you the holy Nandana, / filled with gods and frequented by the twice-born and the Siddhas.’
Having thus addressed that goddess, eager to go to that Nandana grove itself / together with her and his gaṇas, the god [mounted]
the bull that goes everywhere, handsome, its divine back adorned with ornaments, / equipped with garlands of bells, wearing nets of tinkling bells,
adorned with chowries, silken cords, and strings of pearls, / resembling a swan and the moon, possessing charming auspicious marks.
Mounted upon it, Mahādeva was surrounded by ten million gaṇas: / Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, Mahākāla, Skanda, Caṇḍa, and the delightful ones,
Vīrabhadra, Gaṇeśa, Puṣpadanta, Maṇīśvara, / Atibala, Subala by name, Meghanāda, Ghaṭāvaha,
Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Kālida, Pulinda, Vīrabāhuka, / Keśarin, Kiṅkara by name, Caṇḍahāsa, Prajāpati.
These and many others, Sanaka and the rest, mighty in penance— / accompanied by tens of millions of gaṇas, Śiva was surrounded.
Reaching the Nandana grove, frequented by gods and kinnaras, / Mahādeva entered along with his gaṇas and the goddess.
The lord of gods showed the mountain's daughter the very beautiful [grove], / endowed with various trees and filled with many flowers,
abounding with divine plantain groves, and flowering campaka trees, / with lovely blooming mallikās, and dense with clusters of mālatī.
shining with excellent groves of pāṭala trees with ever-blossoming branches, / and with great sandal trees of charming fragrance;
frequented by groves of devadāru trees, filled with lofty trees, / with sarala pines and coconuts, and likewise with areca-nut palms;
filled with large trees accompanied by the wafting of fragrances, / with divine date and jackfruit trees bent low by the weight of their fruit;
adorned with saptaparṇa trees glowing like the radiance of fire, / and ever endowed with the beauty of blossoms through rājavṛkṣa and kadaṃba trees;
filled with large rose-apple and neem trees, with citron trees, / with oranges and sindhuvāras, with priyālas, śālas, and tindukas;
adorned with rose-apple trees, with uduṃbaras and kapitthas, / filled with lakucas having fragrant flowers and blossoming nāgas;
and with mango trees, foremost of fruits, dark like rain-clouds; / with divine groves of dark śāla trees, and thickets of creepers stretching around;
and frequented by large tamāla trees resembling the sun: / the auspicious Nandana grove, thus adorned, was shown by Śiva;
and adorned with all other trees resembling a dark forest, / endowed with all desired fruits and yielding auspicious rewards;
the Nandana forest was adorned with most sacred wish-granting trees, / and filled with the diverse cries of birds in sweet voices;
echoing with the sweet, auspicious songs of cuckoos, / and resounding with the calls of birds greedy for floral nectar;
crowded with various trees, filled with herds of diverse beasts; / and because of the various fragrant blossoms fallen from the trees onto the ground,
that earth shines, O son, as though worshipped with fragrant flowers. / There are most sacred ponds there, clear with the fragrance of lotuses,
filled with waters, O son, frequented by geese and kāraṇḍava ducks, / with lakes resembling oceans, revered for their fragrant waters.
The great Nandana shines everywhere with hosts of apsarases, / with aerial chariots, white finials, and splendid golden poles.
The Nandana, the king of forests, with palaces coated with stucco, / shines brightly here and there with great hosts of kinnaras,
with gandharvas and beautiful apsarases, O best of the twice-born, / with the pastimes of the gods, and with multitudes of sages who are excellent yogins.
Everywhere the sacred abode of Nandana shone.
Having thus beheld the auspicious Nandana—the abode of the meritorious, a mine of bliss endowed with the quality of tranquility—the noble and magnanimous Bhava together with the goddess,

where the wish-granting tree, endowed with the capacity to grant desires through blossoms and fruits, / its golden form shining with rays equaling the brilliance of hosts of suns, stood in the Nandana forest,
beholding such a king of trees, the goddess spoke to Śiva: / “Tell me the name of this, O Lord, the sacred [tree] among all sacred trees.”
Like the foremost sun among luminous bodies all around, Śiva spoke to the goddess: / Śiva said: “Great and auspicious is its renown; just as Madhusūdana is chief among the gods,
and the river of the gods is chief among rivers, and the Creator Dhātṛ is the maker of creation, / and just as the gentle moon is foremost among bringers of delight, and the earth among the elements,
and just as the king of mountains is chief among mountains, and the ocean among reservoirs of water, / and as grain is chief among healing herbs, O goddess, and the Himālaya among mountains,
and just as the science of the self is supreme among sciences, and a monarch among all people in the worlds, / even so is this king of trees foremost: a host to all, dear to the lord of the gods.”

Śrī Pārvatī said: “O Śambhu, recount to me the auspicious, most sacred virtues of this sovereign of trees.” / Hearing her speech, the god spoke all concerning the beneficial nature of that tree to the goddess:
“Whatever the most holy gods, godlike beings, and foremost deities imagine, O beloved, / that very thing this tree gives to them for their welfare; its name is the Kalpadruma, the highest [of trees].
And from it arise all meritorious things, difficult to attain here even by those rich in austerities; / the supreme gods enjoy its divine gems, dearer than life itself.”
The goddess heard the words of Śiva and wondered in her mind; / with his consent, she conceived in thought a jewel of a woman, virtuous and fair.

From that excellent tree the mountain-born goddess obtained [a maiden] beautiful in every limb, endowed with virtues, lovely, / who sat as if to enchant the universe, an embodiment of aid to the god whose banner is the sea-monster.

She was a receptacle of play, an embodiment of the accomplishment of joy, endowed with everything, having eyes long as lotus petals, / lotus-faced, with lotus hands, auspicious as a lotus, like a fair image made of gold.
Her radiance was likewise spotless and brilliant; her charms were radiant, and her long locks, / fine and braided, were gracefully curled, smeared with perfumes and decked with flowers.
With hair securely gathered up in firm braids, that young maiden shone with supreme beauty; / and along the parting of her hair a garland of pearls shone like [dewdrops] upon trees.

The auspicious mark at the root of the fair goddess's parting shone like the radiant guru of the Daityas when risen; / on her forehead, O Lotus-born one, it shone with masses of brilliance arising from a lotus of musk.
The radiance of the mark at the root of her parting illuminated the beauty of her form in the world; / in her hair and on her forehead, the pearls continually enhanced her great loveliness.
Just as the gentle moon shines with luster, she too shone with charming movements; / and just as the full moon, cool-rayed, shines with an awning of moonlight,
so her face shone, producing beauty and enchanting the universe; / while the moon indeed has spots and constantly wanes, deprived of its digits,
her face was entirely full, ever joyful, and completely spotless; / beholding her, the lotus found no joy in its own fragrance and blooming.
“This lotus-faced maiden, endowed with all virtues, was fashioned from my own sentiments; / seeing that the wind of the universe blows fragrance from her face, the lotus [shrank].”
Overcome with shame, it at once took refuge in the water and remains there forever. / Wise men of resolute intellect say with thought that she is the treasury of King Love with the arts of the ocean.
She was engaged in playful smiling with teeth like excellent gems, and her face was adorned with lower lips red as bimba fruits.
Fair were her eyebrows, fair her nose; her lovely ears were adorned with gems; / endowed with the luster of gold, her cheeks were full of brilliance.
Three lines shone situated upon her neck, / indeed the three lines of good fortune, virtue, and love right here.
Her breasts were shapely, firm, plump, and round in form, / like two pitchers of Kāma fashioned for his consecration.
Her shoulders shone exceedingly, well-proportioned and endowed with grace; / her arms were lovely, round, smooth, golden, and marked with auspicious signs.
Her lotus hands were well-matched, lotus-hued, very cool, / endowed with divine signs, and marked with lotuses and svastikas.
Her fingers were straight, lotus-like, and furnished with nails; / and her nails were very sharp and gleamed like drops of water.
The complexion arising from her limbs resembled the interior of a lotus; / having the fragrance of a lotus over her entire body, the passionate woman shone like [the goddess] Padmā.
Endowed with all auspicious marks, the daughter of the mountain was exceptionally lovely. / Her two feet resembled red water-lilies, being very smooth and extremely beautiful.
The nails arising on the tips of her feet had the appearance of the lustre of jewels; / and just as is indicated in the scriptures, so too was it seen upon her limbs.
Her limbs adorned with the splendour of all ornaments—necklaces, bracelets, and anklets— / she shone with a girdle upon the hip-string, resounding with tinkling bells.
Clothed in a blue silk garment, the auspicious lady attained supreme splendour, / and endowed with virtues, [she shone] even with an exquisite bodice of brilliant red.
Having obtained supreme prosperity of virtue from the intention formed by Pārvatī, / she derived joy from the wish-granting tree. Then she spoke these words to Śaṅkara:
“Just as was spoken by you, O god, even so has this tree been seen by me. / Whatever kind of intention is formed, just such is seen.”
Sūta said: / Then that fair lady, lovely in all her limbs, approached the side of the two, / and then with devotion she bowed down to the lotus-feet of the two parents of the world.
Then she spoke affectionate, pleasing, and charming words: / “For what reason was I created by you, O lord, O mother? Speak your purpose.”
The blessed goddess said: / “Out of wonder at the tree, a test was indeed made by me in my mind; / and immediately the fruit was obtained, O gentle lady, in the form of your abundant beauty.
By the name Aśokasundarī you will attain renown in the world. / Endowed with all good fortune, you are without doubt my daughter.
Famous in the lunar dynasties as is god Puraṃdara [among gods], / an emperor named Nahuṣa shall become your husband.”
Having thus granted a boon to her, the mountain-born goddess went to the mountain, / to Kailāsa, together with Śaṅkara, filled with supreme joy.

title: tryadhikaśatatamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Kuñjala said: / Then Aśokasundarī was born, the foremost of all women; / she took delight in the auspicious Nandana grove, endowed with the qualities of all desires.
With the lovely daughters of the gods, the sweetly smiling woman, / enjoying all pleasures, was skilled in singing and dancing.
The son of Vipracitti, Huṇḍa, fierce and perpetually violent, / roaming at his own will, exceedingly lustful, entered the Nandana grove.
Seeing Aśokasundarī adorned with all ornaments, / at the mere sight of her, the Daitya was pierced by the arrows of Kāma.
He of immense body said to her: “Who are you, and to whom do you belong, O auspicious one? / For what purpose have you come here to this excellent forest?”
Aśokasundarī said: / “Listen now: I am the daughter of Śiva, who is very holy. / I am the sister of Kārttikeya, and my mother is born of the mountain [family].
In childhood innocence, in sport, I have reached the Nandana forest. / But who are you, and why do you question me thus?”
Huṇḍa said: / “I am the son of Vipracitti, endowed with qualities and auspicious marks, / renowned by the name Huṇḍa, arrogant with the pride of strength and valour.
I am the best among Daityas; there is no Rākṣasa equal to me / among gods, in the worlds of mortals, in austerity, fame, or lineage,
or in the other Nāga worlds, in wealth and pleasures, O fair-faced one! / From seeing you, O wide-eyed one, I have been smitten by the arrows of the god of love.
I have indeed come to you for refuge; be gracious, O fair-faced one! / Become my beloved wife, dear to me as my very life.”
Aśokasundarī said: / “Listen, I shall explain the principle of every union. / In this world, there must be a proper match of woman and man of good birth;
similarly, a husband must be one who is equal in virtues to the woman. / This is the way of the world in saṃsāra; listen, O Huṇḍa, according to rule.
Indeed, there is a reason here why I cannot become / your good wife, O king of the Daityas; listen with an attentive mind.
At the time when I was born from the king of trees, O highly intelligent one, / having fully grasped Śambhu’s inclination, I was fashioned by Pārvatī.
With the approval of the god, my husband was indeed designated by the goddess: / in the lunar dynasty there shall be an exceptionally wise, righteous-minded one,
victorious, equal to Indra in valour, like fire in splendour, / all-knowing, true to his word, and equal to Vaiśravaṇa in generosity,
a sacrificer, a master of giving, and like the god of love in beauty; / righteous-minded, named Nahuṣa, a great treasure of virtues and character.
He who was granted to me by the goddess and the god shall be my famous husband. / From him I shall obtain a handsome son endowed with all good qualities,
Yayāti, equal to Indra and Viṣṇu in the world, beloved by the people, / steadfast in battle—him I shall obtain from the grace of Śambhu.
I am devoted to my husband, O hero, and particularly another’s wife. / Therefore, O Huṇḍa, abandon your delusion completely and go away from here.”
Laughing aloud, he spoke these words to Aśokasundarī. / Huṇḍa said: / “What was said by the goddess and the god is not fitting at all.
The righteous-minded one named Nahuṣa will be born in the lunar dynasty; / you are senior in age; a younger man is not suitable.
A younger woman is praised, but a [younger] man is not praised. / When, O gentle lady, will that man become your husband?
Your adolescence and youth will thus go to destruction. / Through the strength of youth, women are always beautiful;
they attain the state of being cherished by men, O fair-complexioned one. / For adolescence is the great treasure of young women, O fair-faced one.
Depending on it, they enjoy pleasures and desires agreeable to the heart. / When will that son of Āyu come, O gentle lady? Listen to me.
Your youth is here this very day, and it will merely go in vain. / Consider: the embryonic state, infancy, and childhood—
when, endowed with youth, will he become suitable for you? / By the power of your youth, drink the wine of springtime!
Enjoy yourself in happiness with me, O wide-eyed one!” / Having heard the words of Huṇḍa, the daughter of Śiva again,
filled with apprehension, spoke to that lord of the Dānavas: / “When the twenty-eighth [age], named the Dvāpara age, arrives, then
the righteous incarnation of Śeṣa, the mighty son of Vasudeva, Bala, / will take the divine daughter of Revata as his wife.
She was born, O illustrious one, in the supreme age called Kṛta; / by the measure of three ages, she is indeed older than Bala.
Revatī became dear to Bala, equal to his very life. / When the future Dvāpara arrives, she will indeed be there.
Long ago, Māyāvatī was born, the excellent daughter of a Gandharva; / having abducted and restrained her, the best of Dānavas, Śambara,
declared that her husband would be the mighty son of Mādhava, / named Pradyumna, the lord of heroes, the son of the lord of the Yādavas.
What is to happen in that future age has been seen by the ancients, / the highly fortunate, wise great souls beginning with Vyāsa.
Even so, O Daitya, are the words seen that were spoken then by the goddess / to me—by the supporter of the universe, the daughter of Himavat.
You, however, greedy with longing and lust, speak of an evil deed / attended by sin, excluded from the Veda and the scriptures.
Whatever is fated for one, firmly, whether auspicious or inauspicious, / according to one's past deeds, that happens to that person.
Whatever well-spoken word comes forth from the mouth of the gods and the brāhmaṇas, / if it comes forth, it is true; it never turns out otherwise.”
By my destiny, indeed, it has been ordained, and also Nahuṣa's: / having considered our union in this way, it was spoken by the Goddess and by Śiva.
Knowing this, find peace; cast away the delusion residing in your mind! / You are certainly not able, O daitya, to shake my resolve.
Devoted to my husband, firm in my mind—who is capable of shaking me? / I will burn you with a great curse! Depart from here, O great asura!”
Having heard those words, the mighty dānava Huṇḍa / pondered in his mind: “How might she become my wife?”
Pondering, the illusory Huṇḍa vanished, / and departing in haste from that place into the sky, / when another day arrived, he created an illusion made of darkness.
Assuming a celestial, illusory form of a woman, that dānava / by illusion took the form of a young maiden, O delighter of my heart.
That maiden, shapely-hipped and assumed through illusion, went then, / endowed with laughing playfulness, to where the daughter of Śiva was staying.
She spoke gently, as it were, to Aśokasundarī: / “Who are you, whose daughter are you, O fortunate one, who stand in the penance grove?
Why, O girl, are you performing this desire-withering penance? / Tell me that, O fortunate one: what is the purpose of this difficult [austerity]?”
Hearing that auspicious speech uttered by the dānava / who was disguised in an illusory form and full of desire, she quickly,
exceedingly distressed, related the full account of her own origin, just as it occurred of old, / and the entire purpose of her penance.
She told also of the assault by that evil-minded dānava; / not knowing the illusory form, she spoke out of friendship.
Huṇḍa said: / “You are devoted to your husband, O goddess, dedicated to righteous vows, / well-behaved, upright in conduct, a great chaste wife!
I too, gentle one, am devoted to my husband, dedicated to devotion to my husband; / for my husband's sake, O fortunate one, do I perform penance, being a great chaste wife.
My husband was slain by that evil-minded Huṇḍa; / for his destruction indeed I perform formidable, great penance.
Come to my sacred hermitage; I dwell on the bank of the Gaṅgā.” / Thus addressed with other charming words that inspired trust,
the daughter of Śiva was bewitched by Huṇḍa in the guise of a female friend; / bewildered by a great delusion, she was drawn along in great haste.
She was brought to his divine, peerless, and very beautiful home, / upon the peak of Meru, O son, the foremost city called Vaiḍūrya,
endowed with every excellence, called Kāñcana, very auspicious, / crowded with lofty palaces, with urns, staves, and flywhisks,
with groves endowed with various trees, dark like rainclouds, / with oblong ponds, wells, lakes, and with rivers and reservoirs,
resplendent with great gems and ramparts adorned with gold, / filled with all desired riches for the dānava.
Aśokasundarī then saw that delightful city / [and said]: “Whose divine abode is this? Tell me, my friend!”
He said: “It belongs to the lord of dānavas whom you saw before; / this is his abode, O highly fortunate one, and I am that foremost of dānavas.
By me you have been brought here by illusion, O fair-complexioned one!” / Having spoken to her, she was led into the exceedingly beautiful golden palace,
furnished with various chambers, resembling the peak of Kailāsa. / Having seated the beautiful woman there upon a swing, afflicted by desire,
the lord of daityas, restored to his own form and tormented by the arrows of desire, / then folded his hands and spoke these words:
“Whatever you desire, gentle one, that very thing I shall grant, without doubt! / Love me, O wide-eyed one, who love you and am tormented by desire!”
The goddess said: / “You, the lord of dānavas, are not able to shake me at all; / even in my mind, no delusion has overtaken me to be entertained!
By great sinners like you, whether gods or lowest of dānavas, / I am unobtainable, without doubt; do not speak again and again!”
She, the younger sister of Skanda, endowed with penance and blazing with great wrath, / desired to destroy that dānava, darting like the tongue of Death.
Again that goddess spoke thus to that lowest of dānavas: / “A terrible deed has been done by you, O wicked one, for the sake of your own destruction!
For the destruction of your own lineage and indeed of your kin, / a blazing flame of fire has been brought by you into your own house.
Just as an ominous bird of prey, arisen with all sorrows, / brings destruction to the house into which it enters,
to all one's kin, together with wealth and family— / when that bird enters a house, it surely desires [its] ruin—
so have I entered your house, seeking your destruction, / and now that of your sons, your wealth and grain, and your lineage.
Your life, lineage, wealth, grain, sons, grandsons, and the rest— / having caused it all to be destroyed by him, I shall depart, there is no doubt.
Just as I was brought away by you while performing supreme penance, / desiring a husband and longing for Nahuṣa, the son of Āyu,
so also shall my husband destroy you, O dānava! / This means having me as its cause was indeed foreseen of old by the God.
True is this worldly saying that wise people sing; / it is visibly seen in the world, yet the foolish do not understand it:
‘By whom, where, and from what cause pleasure, pain, and the like are to be experienced, / that very person experiences it there, from that very cause, without doubt.’
Reap the fruit of your own deed on the earth's surface! / You shall go to the realm of hell from violating another's wife!
Who strikes a very sharp, keen-edged, excellent sword / with the tip of his finger out of anger? Know me to be such now!
Approaching face to face a lion that is enraged and roaring, / who, filled with rash daring, pulls the hairs from its mouth?
I am one of truthful conduct, endowed with self-control, restrained, abiding in penance; / he who desires my ruin, he indeed desires to enjoy me!
He who desires to seize the gem of a living black serpent / is surely one who has been sent by Death!
You, fool, have been sent by Death, deluded by Death; / hence such foolishness has arisen in you; do you not see?
Who indeed, except the son of Āyu, may look upon me? / Any other person surely goes to destruction from gazing upon my form.”
Having thus addressed him, the chaste woman went to the bank of the Gaṅgā, / sorrowful, agitated with grief, restrained and observing vows.
“Previously a terrible penance was performed by me with the desire for a husband; / now, wishing for your destruction, I shall perform dreadful [penance] once again!
When, O wicked one, you are slain by the great-souled Nahuṣa / with sharp arrows resembling thunderbolts and like venomous serpents,
and I see you fallen in battle, sinful, with disheveled hair, covered with blood, / and lifeless, then I shall go to my husband!”
Having made such a firm resolve, the daughter of Śiva / remained steadfast on the unsurpassed bank of the Gaṅgā for the destruction of Huṇḍa.

Like a brilliant, blazing tongue of fire endowed with splendor that would burn the worlds, / glowing with anger, the daughter of the lord of the gods performed difficult penance on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
Kuñjala said: / “Having spoken thus, O highly fortunate one, the daughter of Śiva went, / and after bathing in the water of the Gaṅgā, in her city called Kāñcana,
that slender-limbed girl, Aśokasundarī, endowed with truth, / performed penance for the sake of the slaying of Huṇḍa.”
Huṇḍa too became distressed, his mind burned by the curse; / tormented intensely by the fires of her words, he pondered.
Then, summoning his minister named Kampana, he spoke; / he related the whole great occurrence arising from her curse:
“I have been cursed by Aśokasundarī, the virtuous daughter of Śiva: / ‘You shall surely die at the hands of Nahuṣa, my husband!’
Yet that embryo is not even born, and Āyu’s wife is pregnant. / Act in such a way that her curse turns out false rather than true.”
Kampana said: / “Abduct Āyu’s beloved and bring her here; / in this way too, your enemy will not be born.
Or else cause her embryo to miscarry by terrifying means; / in this way too, your enemy will not be born.
Or wait for the time of birth of that wicked Nahuṣa, / and having abducted and brought him here, slay the evil-minded one.”
Thus taking counsel with that Kampana, the Dānava / became prepared for the destruction of Nahuṣa.
Viṣṇu said: / “O noble one, there was a lord of the earth named Āyu, son of Ilā, / a universal monarch, righteous, devoted to the vow of truth,
a king equal to Indra and Upendra in austerity, renown, and strength, / in gifts, highly meritorious sacrifices, truth, and self-restraint.
The best of kings ruled over the earth under a single umbrella, / knowing all righteousness, the ornament of the lunar dynasty.
The king had no son, and because of that he grew grieved; / the righteous-minded one pondered: ‘How can a son be born to me?’
Thus king Āyu fell into anxious thought, / and, concentrating his mind, he made the utmost effort for the sake of a son:
The great ascetic Dattātreya, the great-souled son of Atri, / was sporting with a woman, his eyes red from wine.
Intoxicated with liquor, the righteous one was surrounded by groups of women, / holding on his lap an auspicious young woman, the best of all women.
The brāhmaṇa sang, danced, and drank wine copiously, / devoid of a sacred thread, the supreme lord of great yogins.
With divine flower-garlands, adorned with pearl necklaces, / his body smeared with sandalwood and agallochum, the lord of sages shone resplendent.
Going to his hermitage and seeing that best of twice-borns, the king / made obeisance with his head, bowing down like a rod with deep concentration.
Seeing that best of kings arrived before him with devotion, / the righteous son of Atri then sat in meditation.
In this manner a hundred years passed for that king, O best of men, / his mind unwavering, attaining peace, wholly devoted to worship.
Calling him, [Dattātreya] said this: ‘Why do you trouble yourself, O king? / I am devoid of brāhmaṇa conduct; I possess no brāhmaṇa status whatever.
I crave wine and meat, and I am always attached to a woman. / I have no power to grant boons; attend upon another brāhmaṇa.’
Āyu said: / ‘O noble one, there is no brāhmaṇa superior to you, / the granter of all desires, indeed the supreme lord in the three worlds.
In the lineage of Atri, O noble one, you are the supreme lord Govinda; / in the form of a brāhmaṇa, you indeed are the bird-bannered [Viṣṇu].
Salutations to the God of gods! Salutations to the Supreme Lord! / I have come to you for refuge, O you who are affectionate to those who seek refuge!
Deliver me, O Hṛṣīkeśa! Having assumed an illusion, you remain / as the wise leader of the universe for the creatures residing in the cosmos.
I know you to be the Lord of the Universe, the slayer of Madhu. / Protect me, O Govinda! O you of universal form, salutations to you!’
Kuñjala said: / When much time had passed, Dattātreya said to the best of kings / in the guise of a drunken man: ‘Carry out my word:
Give me wine in a skull-cup, and a cooked meal of meat.’ / Hearing those words, that lord of the earth, Āyu,
eagerly and swiftly brought wine in a skull-cup, / and slicing well-cooked meat with his hand, with haste
the king gave it to Dattātreya, O best of men. / Then the mind of that eminent sage became pleased.
Seeing his devotion, his excellence, and his supreme service to his teacher, / he spoke to that king Āyu, whose mind was bowed in reverence:
‘Choose a boon, may it be well with you, rare on earth, O king! / I will grant you everything, whatever you now desire.’
The king said: / ‘You are a grantor of boons in truth out of compassion, O best of sages. / Give me a son endowed with virtues, all-knowing, gifted with good qualities,
having divine prowess and great splendor, unconquerable by gods and Dānavas, / by kṣatriyas, terrible rākṣasas, Dānavas, and Kinnaras,
devoted to gods and brāhmaṇas, especially a protector of his subjects, / a performer of sacrifices, a lord of charity, valiant, affectionate to those seeking refuge,
generous, an enjoyer, noble-minded, learned in the Vedas and Śāstras, / skilled in the science of archery, and devoted to the scriptures,
[He wished for a son] of unimpaired intellect, steadfast, undefeated in battles, / endowed with such virtues, and handsome, from whom the lineage might continue.
Give me a son, O noble one, the upholder of my lineage, / if indeed a boon is to be granted to me out of your grace, O omnipresent one.’
Dattātreya said: / ‘So be it, O noble one! A son shall be born to you / in your house, the founder of your lineage, holy, bringing compassion to all beings,
endowed with these qualities, possessing a portion of Viṣṇu, / a universal monarch, a lord of men equal to Indra.’
Having thus granted the boon, the great yogin indeed gave an incomparable fruit, / and said to the king: ‘Let it be given to your virtuous wife.’
Having spoken thus and dismissed that Āyu bowing before him, / greeting him with blessings, he vanished right there.

title: caturadhikaśatatamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Kuñjala said: / When that noble and great sage Dattātreya had departed, / the great king Āyu returned to his own city.
Delighted, he entered the home of Indumatī, endowed with splendor, / abundant in the fulfillment of every wish, resembling the abode of Indra.
That wise king ruled the kingdom just as Purandara does in heaven, / together with Indumatī, the daughter of Svarbhānu, O best of twice-borns.
And Queen Indumatī, by eating the fruit according to Dattātreya’s word, / conceived an embryo endowed with divine splendor.
An incomparable dream was seen by Indumatī, O noble one, / at night, attended by day[like radiance], O father, bestowing great auspiciousness:
Entering inside the house was a man resembling the sun, / a twice-born endowed with a string of pearls, adorned with white garments.
A garland made of white flowers shone upon his neck; / his limbs were beautified with all ornaments, anointed with divine perfume.
He was four-armed, holding a conch in his hand, bearing a mace, discus, and sword, / with a parasol being held over him resembling the disc of the moon,
shining with great majesty, adorned with divine ornaments, / resplendent with a necklace, bracelets, armlets, and anklets,
resplendent with earrings resembling the disc of the moon— / such a highly wise person arrived.
Calling Indumatī, that lovely lady was then bathed with milk / from a conch filled with milk, of the color of the moon.
Filled again and again [with milk], set with gold and jewels; / and a white serpent, handsome, excellent, with a thousand heads,
endowed with a great gem, radiant, an abode full of flames— / it was placed by him near her mouth, and a pearl was given again.
That lord of the gods placed [the pearl] upon the neck of famous Indumatī, / then gave a lotus into her hand and went away to his own abode.
Having seen such a great dream foretelling an excellent son, / the fortunate woman recounted it to Āyu, the lordly ruler of the earth.
Having listened, the great king reflected once more; / then, having summoned his guru, he related the excellent dream
to the most fortunate Śaunaka, omniscient, best among the wise. / The king said: “Tonight, O fortunate one, O best of the twice-born, by my wife
a brahmin was seen entering the house. What is the cause of this dream?” / Śaunaka said: “A boon was granted to you formerly by the wise Dattātreya,
and an auspicious fruit for [obtaining] a son was instructed for kings. / What became of that fruit, O king? To whom was it given by you?”
“It was given by me to my good wife,” thus spoke the king. / Hearing this, the very wise Śaunaka, best among the twice-born, said:
“By the grace of Dattātreya, in your house an excellent son / endowed with a portion of Viṣṇu will be born; there is no doubt.
This which I have told you, O king, is the cause of the dream. / A son equal to Indra and Upendra will be born, of divine valor.
Your son will be entirely devoted to dharma, an increaser of the Lunar dynasty; / he will be accomplished in the science of archery and in the Veda.”
Having spoken thus to the king, Śaunaka went to his home. / Filled with great joy, the king rejoiced with his beloved.

title: paṃcottaraśatatamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Kuñjala said: / She had gone to the Nandana grove to play with her friends. / There she heard a momentous statement, but one disagreeable to her father,
as celestial bards and noble siddhas spoke with delight: / “In the house of Āyu a son of great valor, whose prowess equals Viṣṇu’s,
an excellent son shall be born, who will make an end of Huṇḍa.” / Hearing such a momentous statement, disagreeable and bringing sorrow,
she returned and reported it before her father. / In brief she related that grief-causing matter
before her father. Having heard it, the father was astonished, / and he remembered the curse formerly made by Aśokasundarī.
For his sake that Aśokasundarī performed austerities. / Solely for the destruction of Indumatī's embryo, that Dānava,
evil and drawn by death, the wicked-minded one made an effort. / Thereupon constantly seeking a flaw in Indumatī,
whenever he saw that queen endowed with beauty, generosity, and virtues, / accompanied by divine splendor and protected by the radiance of Viṣṇu,
endowed with divine splendor, resembling the disc of the sun, / O fortunate one, he constantly stood at her side for [malicious] observation.
From afar that wicked Dānava displayed to her / many sorts of fierce magic, terrifying sights, and dread apparitions.
Endowed with the splendor of the embryo and protected by the radiance of Viṣṇu, / fear never arose in her mind at any time.
The Dānava was frustrated, and his endeavor was fruitless; / the desire of his heart was not realized for the wicked-souled Huṇḍa.
Thus as a full hundred years passed for him watching, / she, the daughter of Svarbhānu, then gave birth to a son.
At night itself her son was born, O best of sons; / with his brilliance he shone exceedingly, like the sun in the sky.
Sūta said: / Then a certain very wicked maidservant came to the lying-in chamber, / practicing impure conduct yet speaking of great auspiciousness.
Knowing everything about her, Huṇḍa, the lowest of Dānavas, / entered the body of that maidservant and thus entered Āyu's palace.
While the multitude of people slept, exceedingly stupefied by slumber, / he abducted that son who resembled an offspring of the gods, and went outside.
Arriving at his own city named Kāñcana, the lowest of Dānavas / summoned his dear wife Vipulā and spoke these words:
“Slay this great sin, my enemy who has assumed an infant's form! / Afterward let him be given into the hand of the cook for food.
Have him cooked without pity in various ways and modes. / Afterward, O fortunate woman, from the cook's hand I shall eat him, no doubt.”
Hearing that speech of her husband, Vipulā was astonished: / “Why has my husband become so pitiless and excessively cruel?
Why and for what reason should he, devoid of forbearance and extremely ruthless, / devour this son endowed with all auspicious marks, resembling the offspring of a god?”
Reflecting thus, filled with compassion, / she again asked her husband: “Why do you devour the child?”
