Hari does not delight so much in Lakṣmī, nor does he delight so much in his own abode, / as he always delights in the circle of the Śālagrāma stone.
The agnihotra has been performed by him, and the earth with the oceans has been given away by him, / by whom Hari has been worshipped in the circle born of the Śālagrāma stone.
O vaiśya, if twelve stones born of the Śālagrāma stone / are worshipped according to the rules by anyone, I shall declare his merit to you:
Whatever [merit] there would be through one hundred and twenty million liṅgas worshipped with golden lotuses / across twelve seasons, that is obtained in a single day.
Moreover, he who devotedly worships a hundred Śālagrāma stones / dwells in Hari's realm and is born here as a universal emperor.
Even the lowest of men, when pervaded by lust, anger, and greed, / also goes to Hari's realm through the worship of the Śālagrāma stone.
And the man who joyfully worships Govinda in the Śālagrāma [stone] / does not fall from heaven until the cosmic dissolution.
Without sacred bathing-places, without gifts, without sacrifices, without deep understanding, / men attain liberation, O vaiśya, from worshipping the Śālagrāma stone.
A worshipper of the Śālagrāma stone, even if sinful, O vaiśya, does not go / to hell, or to dwelling in a womb, or to an animal state, or to birth as a worm.
He who knows the rites of initiation and mantras, and offers an oblation upon the circle— / the Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, and Revā, and whichever rivers bestow liberation,
all of them reside indeed in the water of the Śālagrāma stone. / With various food offerings, flowers, incense, lamps, and ointments,
with songs, musical instruments, hymns, and the like, whichever human, / devoted to worship in the Kali age, performs the worship of the Śālagrāma stone,
delights in the presence of Hari for thousands of millions of kalpas. / Whatever fruit is obtained by seeing ten million liṅgas or by worshipping them,
indeed that fruit comes from the Śālagrāma stone in a single day. / When worship is performed even once to the liṅga born of the Śālagrāma stone,
men surely attain liberation, even if devoid of Sāṃkhya knowledge. / Wherever Keśava stands in the form of a Śālagrāma stone,
there are the gods, the suras, the yakṣas, and the fourteen worlds. / But the man who performs a śrāddha on a Śālagrāma stone—
his ancestors remain satisfied in heaven for a hundred kalpas. / Those men who continually drink water from the Śālagrāma stone,
what need have they of partaking of thousands of pañcagavyas? / What need have they of visiting thousands of ten million sacred bathing-places,
if one drinks the holy water that has touched the body of the Śālagrāma stone? / Wherever a Śālagrāma stone is, for three yojanas around is a sacred bathing-place.
There, gifts and fire oblations all become multiplied ten-millionfold. / A man who drinks water from the Śālagrāma stone, even an amount equal to a drop,
never drinks mother's milk again; he partakes of Viṣṇu. / Near a Śālagrāma [stone], indeed for the distance of a krośa all around,
even an insect who dies goes to the supreme abode of Vaikuṇṭha. / He who gives the circle of a Śālagrāma stone as an excellent gift,
by him the entire orb of the earth, along with its mountains and forests, has been given. / The man who sets a price upon a Śālagrāma stone,
and the seller, and he who consents, and he who takes pleasure in its evaluation— / all of them go to hell until the cosmic dissolution.
Therefore, O vaiśya, one should completely avoid the buying and selling of the circle. / What need is there of saying much, O vaiśya? By one who fears sin,
the remembrance of Hari Vāsudeva, which removes all sin, should be performed. / The fruit that a man attains by practicing severe austerity / in the forest with controlled senses,
with senses well restrained, that [very fruit] one obtains by bowing to the Garuḍa-bannered Lord. / Even having committed sin repeatedly, a man overwhelmed by delusion
does not go to hell once he has gone to Hari, who removes all sin. / Whatever sacred bathing-places and holy sanctuaries are upon the earth,
he attains them all from chanting the name of Viṣṇu. / Those dedicated ones who have taken refuge in the god Viṣṇu, holder of the Śārṅga bow,
for them there is no residence in Yama's realm; they would not be dwellers of hell. / A Vaiṣṇava man, O vaiśya, who speaks ill of Śiva
does not find the realm of Viṣṇu; he goes to a great hell. / Having fasted on even a single Ekādaśī, even casually, a man
does not go to Yama's torment; so it has been heard from Lomaśa. / There is nothing so purifying in the three worlds
as either day of the lotus-navelled [Viṣṇu], which destroys wickedness. / Sins reside in this body here, O best of the people,
only so long as a creature does not fast on the auspicious day of the lotus-navelled [Viṣṇu]. / Thousands of horse sacrifices and hundreds of royal consecration sacrifices
are not worth a sixteenth part of fasting on Ekādaśī. / Whatever sin has been committed through the eleven senses by men, O vaiśya,
By fasting on Ekādaśī, all of that goes to dissolution; / no merit equal to Ekādaśī is found in the world.
Those by whom it is observed even as a pretext do not come under the power of the sun-god's son; / for it bestows heaven and liberation, and grants bodily health.
Indeed, it grants a good wife, and it grants living sons. / Neither the Gaṅgā nor Gayā, O vaiśya, nor Kāśī nor Puṣkara,
nor indeed any Vaiṣṇava sacred field equals the day of Hari; / the Yamunā and the Candrabhāgā do not equal the day of Hari,
by which the Vaiṣṇava abode is attained here without exertion. / Keeping vigil at night and fasting on the day of Hari,
ten ancestors on the paternal side and ten on the maternal side, / and those ten of one's beloved wife, O vaiśya—he undoubtedly delivers them.
Free from the attachment to dualities, having made their dwellings no longer domestic, / wearing garlands and clad in yellow garments, they go to the abode of Hari.
In childhood, or in youth, or in old age, O best of the vaiśyas, / having fasted on Ekādaśī, certainly even a sinner does not go to extreme misfortune.
Fasting for three nights here, or bathing at sacred places, / and giving gold, sesame seeds, and cows, men go to heaven in this world.
Those who do not bathe at sacred places, O vaiśya, and by whom no gold has been given, / and by whom no austerity has been performed at all—they will be sorrowful everywhere.
Briefly spoken is dharma and the description of hell: / harmlessness toward all beings through speech, mind, and bodily actions;
restraint of the senses, generosity, worship of Hari, / and always observing the duties of caste and life-stage according to the rules.
One who desires heaven should never proclaim his austerity or gift, O vaiśya; / he should give according to his capacity, desiring the welfare of himself.
Footwear, cloth, foods, leaves, roots, fruits, and water: / a day should not be made fruitless, even by a poor man, O vaiśya.
What is not given does not serve one in this world or in the next; / givers do not see those various torments of Yama.
They become long-lived and rich in wealth here again and again. / What is the use of speaking much on this? By adharma they go to an evil state;
by dharma men ascend to heaven everywhere and at all times.
Therefore, starting from childhood, the accumulation of dharma should be made. / Thus everything has been told to you; what else do you wish to hear?
Vikuṇḍala said: / Having heard your words, gentle one, my mind has indeed become serene. / Gaṅgā water destroys sin at once; the word of the good removes sin.
To do good and to speak kindly is the innate quality of the virtuous; / by whom is the cool-rayed moon made into a cool orb of nectar?
O divine messenger, therefore tell me who am asking out of compassion: / How may immediate deliverance from hell arise for my brother?
Hearing his words, the divine messenger spoke, / observing his meditation, contemplating for a moment, bound by the cord of his friendship.
'Whatever merit was accumulated by you in your eighth birth, O vaiśya, / let all of that be given to your brother, if you desire heaven for him.'
Vikuṇḍala said: / 'What is that merit, how did it arise, and what was that former birth? / Let all that be told, messenger; then I will give it immediately.'
The divine messenger said: / 'Listen, O vaiśya, I will tell you of that merit together with its cause. / Formerly, in the holy Madhuvana, there was a sage named Śākuni,
endowed with austerity and sacred study, equal to Brahmā in splendors. / To him through Revatī were born nine sons, like planets:
Dhruva, Śīla, Budha, Tāra, and Jyotiṣmat the fifth; / these were devoted to the agnihotra fire and delighted in the duties of a householder.
Nirmoha, Jitakāma, Dhyānakośa, and Guṇādhika: / these four sons of the twice-born were detached from householder life.
Having entered the fourth stage of life, free from all desires, / staying for one night in a village, without attachments, without possessions,
without cravings, effortless, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal, / covered with whatever was at hand, fed on whatever was at hand,
gathering food only in the evening, and constantly devoted to meditation on Viṣṇu, / conquerors of sleep, conquerors of food, enduring wind and cold,
seeing the entire world, moving and unmoving, in the form of Viṣṇu, / they wandered about freely on the earth, established in mutual silence.
Those yogins performed no ritual acts, being dedicated solely to the highest reality, / having perceived knowledge, without doubts, skilled in the transformations of consciousness.
Thus, when you were a brāhmaṇa in your eighth prior birth, / living in the Middle Country, endowed with sons, wife, and household,
they came to your house at midday, hungry and thirsty, / at the time following the vaiśvadeva rite; and they were seen by you in the courtyard of your home.
With a faltering voice, with tearful eyes, with joy, and with agitation, / prostrating like a staff, preceded by great respect,
bowing with your head to their feet and making an añjali with both hands, / they were all welcomed by you then with sincere and pleasant words:
“Today my birth has become fruitful, and my life is fruitful as well; / today Viṣṇu is pleased with me, today I have a protector and am purified;
today I am blessed, my house is blessed, and my family members are blessed today; / today my ancestors are blessed, and blessed are the cows, sacred learning, and wealth;
since your feet, which remove the three kinds of suffering, were seen by me. / Because the sight of you is like the sight of Hari himself for a blessed person.”
Having thus worshiped them and washed their feet, / it was placed on your head, O best of the vaiśyas, with supreme faith then.
Where the foot-water was placed on your head with faith, O vaiśya, / and having worshiped them with fragrances, flowers, unbroken grains, incenses, and lamps with devotion,
the ascetics were thus fed with delicious food; / satisfied, those paramahaṃsas rested in your house during the night,
meditating upon the supreme Brahman, which is considered the light of lights. / The merit born of hospitality toward them that arose for you, O best of vaiśyas—
indeed, I cannot declare that even with a thousand mouths. / Living creatures are the highest among beings; among living creatures, those living by intellect;
among the intelligent, gods are best; among men, the brāhmaṇa classes; / among brāhmaṇas, the learned; and among the learned, those of resolved intellect;

among those of resolved intellect, the performers of duty; and among performers of duty, the knowers of Brahman. / Therefore they are truly worthy of worship, and thus the highest in the three worlds.
Association with them, O best of vaiśyas, destroys great sins. / Satisfied, the knowers of Brahman resting in a householder's home
destroy in an instant sin accumulated since birth. / Whatever sin of a householder has been accumulated until the end of life,
an ascetic who has stayed for one night completely burns it all. / Give that merit to your brother, by which he will be freed from hell.'
Hearing the messenger's words, the brother quickly gave his religious merit / with a joyful heart, and he too departed from hell.
Honored by the gods with a shower of flowers, they both went to heaven. / Thoroughly worshiped by the two, the messenger departed as he had come.

Having heard the words of the divine messenger, which bring awakening to the entire world and are equal to Vedic statements, / and having saved his brother by the gift of his own accumulated merit, the son of the vaiśya went with him to the supreme realm of Indra.
Whoever, O king, recites or even listens to this legendary history, / freed from sorrow, attains the fruit of the gift of a thousand cows.

title: dvātriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Nārada said: / Then one should go, O king of kings, to the world-renowned Sugandha; / purified of all sins, one is honoured in the realm of Brahmā.
Then, O ruler of men, the pilgrim visiting sacred bathing-places should go to Rudrāvarta; / having bathed there, O king, a man is honoured in the heavenly realm.
And at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Sarasvatī, O best of men, / having bathed, one obtains [the merit of] a horse sacrifice and goes to the heavenly realm.
Having bathed there in Karṇahrada and worshipped god Śaṅkara, / one does not meet an unfortunate state and goes to the heavenly realm.
Then the pilgrim visiting sacred bathing-places should go in order to Kubjāmraka; / he obtains [the merit of giving] a thousand cows and goes to the heavenly realm.
The pilgrim visiting sacred bathing-places should go to Arundhatīvaṭa, O ruler of men; / having touched the water at Sāmudraka and fasted for three nights, a man
would obtain the fruit of a thousand cows and goes to the heavenly realm. / Then one should go to Brahmāvarta, celibate and concentrated;
he obtains [the merit of] a horse sacrifice and goes to the heavenly realm. / One should go to the source of the Yamunā; having touched the water of the Yamunā,
and having obtained the fruit of a horse sacrifice, he is honoured in the realm of Brahmā. / Having reached Darvīsaṃkramaṇa, the sacred bathing-place famed across the three worlds,
he obtains [the merit of] a horse sacrifice and goes to the heavenly realm. / And having gone to the source of the Sindhu, frequented by siddhas and gandharvas,
having dwelt there for five nights, he should give away much gold. / Then, reaching the Goddess who is exceedingly difficult to access,
a man obtains [the merit of] a horse sacrifice and would go to the realm of Uśanas. / Having reached Ṛṣikulyā and Vasiṣṭha, O Bhārata—
having passed beyond Vasiṣṭha, all the castes and the twice-born— / a man, having bathed in Ṛṣikulyā, proceeds to the realm of the ṛṣis.
If he should reside there for a month subsisting on vegetables, O ruler of men, / and reaching Bhṛgutuṅga, he would obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
And having gone to Vīrapramokṣa, he is freed from all sins. / And having reached the rare sacred bathing-place of Kārtika and Māgha,
the meritorious doer obtains the fruit of both the Agniṣṭoma and Atirātra sacrifices. / Then, having reached Saṃdhyā, the unsurpassed Vidyātīrtha,
if he touches its water, he will reach the further shore of all knowledges. / He should reside for a night in Mahāśrama, which frees one from all sins;
taking no food for one mealtime, he dwells in auspicious worlds. / Residing for a month at Mahālaya with fasting at the sixth mealtime,
having crossed over, he causes ten ancestors and ten descendants to cross over. / Having seen the holy, supreme Māheśvara honoured by the gods,
having accomplished his purpose in all duties, he never grieves over death; / purified of all sins, he would acquire much gold.

Then one should go to Vetasikā, frequented by the Grandfather;
he attains [the fruit of] a horse sacrifice and reaches the supreme state.

Then reaching the sacred ford Sundarikā, frequented by Siddhas,
he becomes an enjoyer of beauty; this was seen by the ancients.

Then going to Brāhmaṇikā, celibate and composed,
he reaches the world of Brahmā in a chariot of lotus hue.

And then one should go to Naimiṣa, holy and frequented by Brahmins;
there Brahmā dwells perpetually along with the hosts of gods.

Half of the sin of one longing for Naimiṣa is destroyed;
and the man who has merely entered is freed from all sin.

A wise man, devoted to sacred fords, should dwell there in Naimiṣa for a month;
whatever sacred fords there are on earth are there in Naimiṣa, O descendant of Bharata.

Having performed ablution there, restrained and eating measured food,
a human being attains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.

He purifies his family up to the seventh generation, O best of Bharatas,
who, devoted to fasting, abandons his life breaths at Naimiṣa.

He rejoices dwelling in the heavenly world—thus the wise have said;
Naimiṣa is perpetually pure and holy, O best of kings.

Having reached Gaṅgodbheda, a man having fasted for three nights
attains [the fruit of] a Vājapeya and becomes perpetually absorbed in Brahman.

Having reached the Sarasvatī, one should offer libations to the ancestors and gods;
he rejoices in the worlds of Sarasvatī, there is no doubt about this.

And then one who frequents sacred fords should go to Bāhudā, O ruler of men;
having stayed there for one night, he is glorified in the heavenly world.

A human being attains the fruit of the divine sacrificial session;
and then one should go to Rajanī, holy and attended by holy folk.

Devoted to worshiping ancestors and gods, he would attain [the fruit of] a Vājapeya;
having reached Vimalāśoka, he shines like the moon.

Having stayed there for one night, he is glorified in the heavenly world;
then one should go to Gopratāra, an excellent sacred ford on the Sarayū,

where Rāma went to heaven together with servants, army, and mounts,
having abandoned his home in the past, O king, through the power of that sacred ford,

and by Rāma's grace and his own resolve, O descendant of Bharata;
having bathed in that sacred ford Gopratāra, O ruler of men,

his soul purified of all sin, he is glorified in the heavenly world;
having bathed at Rāmatīrtha on the Gomatī, O delight of the Kurus,

a man attains [the fruit of] a horse sacrifice and purifies his family;
there is the sacred ford Śatasāhasraka there, O best of Bharatas.

Having touched the water there, restrained and eating measured food,
he attains the holy fruit of a thousand cows, O bull of Bharatas.

Then one should go, O knower of dharma, to the unsurpassable Ūrdhvasthāna;
having bathed at Koṭitīrtha, O king, and having worshiped Guha,

he obtains the fruit of a thousand cows and also becomes radiant;
then going to Vārāṇasī and worshiping the bull-bannered [Śiva],

and having bathed in the pool of the Kapilās, he obtains the fruit of a Rājasūya;
having reached the rare sacred ford of Mārkaṇḍeya, O lord of kings,

at the world-famous confluence of the Gomatī and the Gaṅgā,
he attains [the fruit of] an Agniṣṭoma and thoroughly elevates his family.

title: trayastriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ

text_mt:
Nārada said:
In this regard I shall relate the legendary history concerning the virtues of Vārāṇasī,
by the mere hearing of which one is freed from the murder of a Brahmin.

Formerly on the peak of Meru, the Goddess seated on a divine seat
asked the god, the Sovereign, the enemy of Tripura, Mahādeva:

The Goddess said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, destroyer of the distress of devotees,
how does a person behold you, the god, in no time at all?

Sāṃkhya-yoga, likewise meditation, karma-yoga, or Vedic practice,
and whatever other practices there are in the world, O Śaṅkara, involve great exertion;

by what [means] is the Lord, subtle, to be seen indeed
by yogins, by workers whose minds are resting, and by all embodied beings?

Tell this most secret knowledge, hidden, attended to by Indra and the gods,
for the benefit of all beings, which destroys the fire of desire.

My supreme and most secret sacred field is the city of Vārāṇasī,
which carries all beings indeed across the ocean of worldly existence.

There, through devotion, O great goddess, undertaking my vow,
great souls dwell, adhering to the supreme discipline.

The best of all sacred fords, and the best of all abodes,
the best knowledge among types of knowledge is my supreme Avimukta.

Holy sacred fords and temples are in other locations,
fixed on cremation grounds, and located in celestial lands;

my abode is in the atmosphere, not touching the earthly realm at all;
the unliberated see it there, while the liberated see it with the mind.

This cremation ground is famous, renowned as Avimukta;
becoming Time, I dissolve this world here, O beautiful one.

O goddess, this place is the dearest to me among all secrets;
my devotees go there and enter into me alone.

Whatever is given, muttered, offered into fire, sacrificed, whatever austerity is performed,
meditation, study, and knowledge—everything becomes imperishable there.

Whatever sin has been accumulated previously in thousands of other births,
all of that goes to destruction for one who has entered Avimukta.

Brahmins, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, śūdras, and mixtures of castes,
women, mlecchas, and whatever other mixed beings of sinful wombs,

insects and ants, and whatever other beasts and birds,
reaching their demise in due course in Avimukta, O fair-faced one,

with crests of crescent moons, three-eyed, riding great bulls,
men are born there in my auspicious city, O goddess.

No sinner having died in Avimukta goes to hell;
for, graced by the Lord, all go to the supreme state.

Considering liberation very difficult to attain and worldly existence exceedingly terrible,
a man should break both feet with a stone and dwell in Vārāṇasī.

Rare even through austerity is that state which frees one from worldly existence,
for one who has died, O supreme sovereign, having perished anywhere [there].

It arises properly by my grace, O daughter of the king of mountains;
the unevolved do not see it, deluded by my māyā.

They dwell again and again in the midst of feces, urine, and semen;
yet that wise man who would dwell there, even though stricken by hundreds of obstacles,

he goes to the supreme abode, having gone where he does not grieve;
they go to the supreme abode of Śiva, freed from birth, death, and old age.

That indeed is the state of those who do not die again, of those who desire liberation,
having reached which one would be one who has accomplished his purpose—thus the learned consider.

Not by gifts, nor by austerities, nor by sacrifices, nor even by learning
is that eminent state attained which is obtained in Avimukta.

People of various castes and outcasts, cāṇḍālas and other contemptible ones,
and those whose bodies are filled with offenses and severe sins,

the wise know Avimukta to be the supreme medicine for them;
Avimukta is supreme knowledge, Avimukta is the supreme abode;

Avimukta is the supreme truth, Avimukta is supreme Śiva;
having undergone a lifelong initiation, those who dwell in Avimukta—
I give them that supreme knowledge, and in the end the highest state. / Prayāga, Naimiṣa Forest, Śrīśaila, and Mahābala,
Kedāra, Bhadrakarṇa, Gayā, and Puṣkara, / Kurukṣetra, Bhadrakoṭi, the Narmadā, and Āmrātakeśvarī,
Śālagrāma, Kubjāmra, unsurpassable Kokāmukha, / Prabhāsa, Vijayeśāna, Gokarṇa, and Bhadrakarṇaka—
these sacred places are renowned in the three worlds, / yet they do not reach the supreme reality as do those who have died in Vārāṇasī.
Especially in Vārāṇasī, the Ganges flowing along three paths, / when entered, destroys sin committed over hundreds of other lifetimes.
Elsewhere the Ganges, ancestral rites, giving, asceticism, recitation of mantras, / and vows are easy to find; all of this is very difficult to find in Vārāṇasī.
A man living in Vārāṇasī who constantly recites, offers oblations, / gives, worships the immortals, and continually feeds on air—
whether he is a sinner, whether he is a scoundrel, or whether he is a righteous man, / by reaching Vārāṇasī, he purifies his entire family.
Those who worship and praise Mahādeva in Vārāṇasī, / freed from all sins, are to be understood as lords of the Gaṇas.
Elsewhere, through yoga and knowledge, or through renunciation elsewhere, / that supreme abode is reached only after a thousand lifetimes.
Those devotees, O ruler of the gods, who dwell in Vārāṇasī, / attain supreme liberation in just a single lifetime.
Where yoga, knowledge, and liberation [come] in a single birth, / having reached that Avimukta, one should desire no other penance grove.
Because it was never abandoned by me, it is remembered as Avimukta. / It is the secret of secrets; this is called discernment.
For those devoted to knowledge and non-knowledge who desire supreme bliss, / whatever state is known, O fair-browed one, that belongs to one who dies in Avimukta.
Whatever [spots] of Avimukta are seen completely in the body, / the city of Vārāṇasī is even superior and more auspicious than those places.
Where, directly at the end of the body, the Lord Mahādeva himself / explains the saving Brahman right there for the sake of liberation;
That which is heard as the higher reality called Avimukta, / one may attain that in a single lifetime in Vārāṇasī, O goddess.
Between the brows, in the navel, in the heart, and likewise at the crown of the head, / just as Avimukta is situated in the sun, so it is in Vārāṇasī.
And within this, between the Varaṇā [and the Asī], is the city of Vārāṇasī; / right there the reality is established, always thus detached.
There was never a higher place than Vārāṇasī, nor will there ever be, / where the god Nārāyaṇa, Mahādeva, and the Lord in heaven dwell;
Where the gods together with the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, serpents, and Rākṣasas / constantly revere him, as does the god of gods, the Grandfather [Brahmā].
O goddess, great sinners, even those who have committed the worst sins, / by reaching Vārāṇasī, attain the supreme state.
Therefore, a seeker of liberation, restrained, should dwell [there] until death. / Obtaining knowledge from Mahādeva in Vārāṇasī, he is liberated.
However, obstacles will arise for one whose mind is afflicted by sin; / therefore one should not commit sin with body, mind, or speech.
This is the secret of the gods and the Purāṇas, O lady of good vows; / no one truly understands the knowledge that rests on Avimukta."
Nārada said: / "While the gods and the supreme ṛṣis were listening, / this destroyer of all sins was spoken by the god of gods:
Just as Nārāyaṇa is the best of the gods, the Supreme Spirit, / and as Giriśa is the best of lords, so is this the best of places.
Those by whom Rudra was propitiated in a previous lifetime / know this supreme field, Avimukta, the abode of Śiva.
Those whose minds are impaired, having arisen from the impurities of Kali, / are not able to know that abode of the Supreme Lord.
Those who always remember and speak of this city, / their sin is quickly destroyed here and in the hereafter.
And whatever sins those who have made their dwelling here commit, / the god Śiva, whose body is Time, destroys all of them.
One should come to this place resorted to by those who desire liberation, / and for those who die [here], there is no rebirth in the ocean of worldly existence.
Therefore, with every effort, a man should dwell in Vārāṇasī, / whether a yogi or a non-yogi, a sinner or a performer of most virtuous deeds.
Not by the words of people, nor of parents, nor by the speech of a guru, / should the mind be diverted from proceeding toward Avimukta."

title: catustriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Nārada said: / "There is this pure, auspicious liṅga named Oṃkāra, / merely by the remembrance of which one is freed from all sins.
This higher knowledge, the excellent group of five shrines, / is constantly resorted to by sages in Vārāṇasī, bestowing liberation.
There Mahādeva himself, in the form of the five shrines, / the blessed Lord Rudra who grants release to living beings, takes delight.
This Pāśupata knowledge is called the five shrines; / it is this pure liṅga, Oṃkāra, that is present.
Beyond Peace, Peace, Higher and Lower Knowledge, / Support, and Withdrawal—such is the fivefold divine liṅga.
The support even of the five liṅgas, Brahmā and the others, / the liṅga that makes known [Oṃ]kāra is called the five shrines.
A wise man who remembers the imperishable divine liṅga of the five shrines, / enters the supreme light and bliss at the end of the body.
There in former times, divine sages, perfected ones, and brahmin sages, / having worshipped the Lord Īśāna, attained the supreme state in the end.
On the holy bank of the Matsyodarī is the most secret, auspicious place, / measuring merely a bull's hide, O king of kings: the excellent [Oṃ]kāreśvara,
the Kṛttivāseśvara liṅga, the excellent Madhyameśvara, / Viśveśvara, likewise Oṃkāra, and Kandarpeśvara.
These are the secret liṅgas in Vārāṇasī, O Yudhiṣṭhira; / no one knows them here without the grace of Śambhu.
Listen, O king, to the glorification of Kṛttivāseśvara: / at that place in ancient times a daitya became an elephant and [came] into Śiva's presence,
arriving to kill the brahmins where they constantly worshipped; / from their liṅga Mahādeva, the three-eyed one, appeared.
For the sake of protecting his devotees, Mahādeva, who is affectionate to his devotees, / Hara, having disdainfully slain with his trident the daitya in the form of an elephant,
made its hide his clothing, and hence he is Kṛttivāseśvara. / There, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the sages attained supreme perfection,
and in that very body they attained that supreme state. / The Rudras who are the Vidyāvidyeśvaras and those proclaimed to belong to Śiva,
continually dwell relying upon the Kṛttivāseśvara liṅga. / Knowing the Kali yuga to be terrible and full of unrighteousness, people
do not leave Kṛttivāsa; by that they have accomplished their aim, without a doubt. / Liberation, which may or may not be attained elsewhere after a thousand lifetimes,
liberation is attained in a single lifetime here at Kṛttivāsa. / Indeed, they call this place the dwelling of all perfected beings,
concealed by the god of gods, Mahādeva Śambhu. / Here, in age after age, self-controlled brahmins who have mastered the Vedas [dwell].

They worship the Great Soul and chant the Śatarudrīya hymn; / they constantly praise the god, the three-eyed one clad in hides; / they meditate in their hearts upon the god, the immovable, inward Śiva of all.
Indeed, the Siddhas sing songs: "For the brāhmaṇas who dwell in Vārāṇasī, / who have taken refuge with the one clad in hides, liberation comes in a single birth."

Having obtained in the world a birth in brāhmaṇa lineages—desired by all worlds and exceedingly hard to attain— / having concentrated in meditation, ascetics chant Rudra and meditate in their hearts upon the Great Lord.
Residing in the midst of Vārāṇasī, the great sages worship the Lord, the Ruler; / free from selfish motives, they sacrifice with offerings, praise Rudra, and bow to Śambhu:

"Salutation to Bhava, the abode of stainless yoga! I take refuge in the immovable one, the ancient Lord of the Mountain! / I remember Rudra seated in the heart; I know the Great God who has manifold forms."

title: paṃcatriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Nārada said: / Now, there is another excellent liṅga there named Kapardīśvara. / Having bathed there according to rule and satiated the ancestors, O king,
one is freed from all sins and attains enjoyment and liberation. / Beyond that is located another sacred bath named Piśācamocana.
There the wondrous god grants liberation and removes all faults. / Once a certain Daitya, a tiger bearing a terrifying form, went there
to the excellent Kapardīśvara in order to devour a doe. / There, her heart terrified, she circumambulated again and again,
and as she ran completely bewildered, she fell into the power of the tiger. / Tearing her apart with his sharp claws, that exceedingly powerful tiger
went away to another deserted region upon seeing the great sages. / As soon as she died in front of Kapardīśa, that young doe
was seen as a great flame in the sky, radiant as the sun, / three-eyed, blue-throated, with hair marked by the crescent moon,
mounted upon a bull and surrounded by attendants resembling herself. / From all around, sky-dwellers showered rains of flowers upon her.
Having become a female leader of the Gaṇas herself, she was seen no more from that moment. / Seeing that supreme wonder, the gods and others offered praise.
That excellent liṅga of the Great Lord is Kapardīśvara; / merely by remembering it, one is quickly freed from an entire flood of sins.
The faults such as desire and anger belonging to the inhabitants of Vārāṇasī, / and all obstacles, are destroyed through the worship of Kapardīśvara.
Therefore, the excellent Kapardīśvara should always be seen, / carefully worshipped, and praised with Vedic hymns.
And for yogins of peaceful mind who meditate constantly here, / the perfection of yoga arises in six months; there is no doubt.
Sins such as killing a brāhmaṇa are destroyed through its worship, / since one who has bathed in the Piśācamocana pool attains peace.
In that sacred place long ago, an ascetic brāhmaṇa of strict vows / renowned as Śaṅkukarṇa worshipped Śaṅkara.
He constantly chanted Rudra and the Praṇava, which is identical to Brahman, / with flowers, incense, and the like, with hymns, salutations, and circumambulations.
Engrossed in yoga, having undertaken a life-long vow, he worshipped there. / Once, he saw a ghost arrive, stricken with hunger,
its limbs bound only by bone and skin, sighing again and again. / Seeing him, that best of sages, filled with supreme compassion,
said: "Who are you? From what country have you resorted to this country?" / Afflicted by hunger, the Piśāca spoke these words to him:
"In my previous birth, I was a brāhmaṇa endowed with wealth and grain, / accompanied by sons, grandsons, and others, eager to maintain my family.
The Great God was not worshipped by me, nor cows, nor guests, / nor was merit ever performed, whether small or great.
Once, the divine Lord whose mount is the lord of bulls, / Viśveśvara, was seen, touched, and saluted by me in Vārāṇasī.
Then, after a long time, I attained death. / That exceedingly terrible abode of Yama was not seen by me, O sage.
Now overpowered by thirst, I do not know what is beneficial or harmful. / If, O lord, you see any means to deliver me,
please employ it! Salutations to you; I have come to you for refuge!" / Addressed thus, Śaṅkukarṇa then spoke this to the Piśāca:
"Indeed, no doer of merit greater than you exists in this world, / since the divine Viśveśvara, Śiva, was formerly seen by you,
touched, and praised again! Who else is equal to you on earth? / Due to the ripening of that karma, you have arrived in this region.
Quickly take a bath with concentrated mind in this pool, / by which you will immediately abandon this vile state of birth."
Addressed thus by the compassionate sage, the Piśāca, remembering the three-eyed foremost of gods, / Kapardīśvara, the Ruler, focused his mind and plunged into the water.

Having bathed there in the presence of the sage, he died and became endowed with divine ornaments; / he was seen in an aerial chariot, resembling the sun, his lovely crown marked by the crescent moon.
He shone accompanied by Rudras dwelling in heaven, surrounded by immeasurable, foremost yogins / and the Vālakhilyas and others—this god, like the sun, the lord of all gods, at its rising.
In heaven, the hosts of Siddhas and gods praise him, and delightful celestial Apsarases dance; / Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Kinnaras, and others shower rains of flowers mixed with water.
Being praised then by hosts of great sages, having attained knowledge by the grace of the Lord, / he entered that supreme sphere consisting of the three Vedas, where Rudra shines.
Seeing that the Piśāca had become liberated, the sage, delighted in mind, / contemplating the Great Lord, Rudra, the wise one, the unique fire, bowed and praised that Kapardin:
Śaṅkukarṇa said: / "I go to you, Kapardin, who are beyond the beyond, the sole protector, the ancient Puruṣa, / the Lord of Yoga, the object of desire, the sun, the fire, who ride the tawny cow.

To you, the essence of Brahman seated in the heart, the golden yogin who are the beginning and the end, / I go for refuge—to Rudra who dwells in heaven, the great sage, consisting of Brahman, the pure one.
Possessing a thousand feet, eyes, and heads, of a thousand forms, beyond darkness— / to that Śambhu, the supreme boundary of Brahman, the lord of Hiraṇyagarbha, the three-eyed one, I bow.
In whom is the origin and the destruction of the universe, by whom as Śiva all this is pervaded— / to that Lord, the Ruler, the supreme boundary of Brahman, having bowed, I constantly take refuge.

Devoid of mark, of form beyond perception, the self-luminous master, the lord of consciousness, uniform— / to you, the supreme Lord, the supreme boundary of Brahman, I shall pay homage, than whom there is nothing else.

Whom yogins who have abandoned seeded yoga, having attained absorption and become the Supreme Self, / behold—to that god, whose essential nature is supreme, the supreme boundary of Brahman, I am perpetually bowed.

In whom there is no conceptualisation of distinct features such as name, whose essential form does not stand within sight— / to you, the self-existent one, the supreme boundary of Brahman, I am perpetually bowed and take refuge.

Whom those devoted to the teachings of the Veda behold as bodiless, identical with the knowledge of Brahman, one without difference, / yet manifold as your own form—to that supreme boundary of Brahman, I am perpetually bowed."
From whom the primordial matter [originates], the ancient spirit bears his splendor, and the gods bow down— / I bow to him who is situated in the light, the great Time, your true nature.
I constantly take refuge in the Lord of the cave; I take refuge in Sthāṇu, the ancient Giriśa; / I take refuge in Śiva, Hari, the moon-crested one, bearer of the Pināka; I go to you for refuge.
Having thus praised the Lord Kapardin, / Śaṅkukarṇa fell like a staff upon the ground, loudly uttering the supreme praṇava.
At that moment a supreme linga appeared, consisting of Śiva, / infinite knowledge and bliss, resembling the fiery flame of ten million fires.
Then the liberated-souled Śaṅkukarṇa, having become identical with it, all-pervading and stainless, / dissolved into that pure linga; it was as though a wondrous marvel occurred.
This secret has been told to you, the glorification of Kapardin; / no one knows it because of darkness; even a learned person is bewildered in this matter.
Whoever hears this sin-destroying story constantly, / cleansed of all sins, purified in soul, attains closeness to Rudra.
And whoever, purified, constantly recites the great praise, the Brahmapāra, / at dawn and at midday, will attain the supreme yoga.

title: ṣaṭtriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Nārada said: / In Vārāṇasī, O great king, is Madhyameśa, higher than the highest. / In that place, Mahādeva, the great lord, along with the goddess,
the Lord delights constantly, surrounded by the Rudras. / Formerly, Hṛṣīkeśa, the Soul of all, the son of Devakī,
Kṛṣṇa dwelt there for a year, always accompanied by Pāśupatas, / his entire body smeared with ashes, devoted to the study of the Rudra hymns,
worshipping Śambhu, Hari having undertaken the Pāśupata vow. / His many disciples, devoted to celibacy,
having obtained knowledge from his mouth, beheld the great lord. / The god Mahādeva, Nīlalohita, visibly appeared to him;
the boon-giving Lord granted an excellent boon to Kṛṣṇa: / 'Whoever worships Govinda, being devoted to me according to the prescribed rules,
to them that divine knowledge comprising the world shall arise. / He is to be paid homage, worshipped, and meditated upon by people devoted to me.
Twice-born ones will arise by my grace, without doubt. / Those who see the Lord of gods here, the god wielding the Pināka, having bathed,
their sins, such as slaying a brahmin, are immediately destroyed. / Mortals who relinquish their vital breaths here, even if attached to sinful deeds,
they go to that supreme abode; no doubt should be entertained here. / Truly fortunate are those wise ones who have offered water in the Mandākinī,
having worshipped Mahādeva, the Lord Madhyameśvara. / Knowledge, charity, austerity, śrāddha, and the offering of rice balls here,
each deed performed purifies up to seven generations of the family. / By bathing at Sannihatī when the sun is seized by Rāhu,

whatever fruit a mortal obtains, ten times that is obtained here. / Thus, O great king, the glorification of Madhyameśvara has been told; / whoever hears it with supreme devotion goes to the supreme abode.

title: saptatriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Nārada said: / And hear now, O great king Yudhiṣṭhira, / of other purifying holy places situated here in Vārāṇasī.
There is a holy place greater than Prayāga, the supremely auspicious Prayāga, / and likewise the holy place Viśvarūpa, and the unsurpassed Tālatīrtha;
the great holy place called Ākāśa, and the supreme Ārṣabha holy place; / the great holy place Sunīla, and the unsurpassed Gaurītīrtha;
likewise the Prājāpatya holy place, and also Svargadvāra; / that which is called Jambukeśvara, and the excellent holy place named Dharma;
the supreme Gayā holy place, and likewise the holy place Mahānadī; / the supreme Nārāyaṇa holy place, and the unsurpassed Vāyutīrtha;
the supreme secret Jñānatīrtha, and the excellent Vārāhatīrtha; / the meritorious Yamatīrtha, and the auspicious Sammūrtika holy place;
Agnitīrtha, O great king, and the excellent Kalaśeśvara; / Nāgatīrtha, Somatīrtha, and likewise Sūryatīrtha;
the great secret called Parvata, and the unsurpassed Maṇikarṇya; / the excellent holy place Ghaṭotkaca, Śrītīrtha, and Pitāmaha;
and the Gaṅgātīrtha of the Lord of the gods, the excellent holy place of Yayāti; / Kāpila, Someśa, and the unsurpassed Brahmatīrtha.
When Brahmā arrived there to install the ancient linga, / at that time Viṣṇu installed that linga of the Lord.
Having bathed there and approached, Brahmā said to Hari: / 'This linga was brought by me; why have you installed it?'
Viṣṇu said to him: 'Even more than yours, my devotion to Rudra is firm. / Therefore, the linga installed will be named after you.'
And likewise the holy place Bhūteśvara, and the holy place originated from Dharma; / the very auspicious Gandharvatīrtha, and the excellent Vāhneyatīrtha;
Daurvāsika, Vyomatīrtha, and Candratīrtha, O Yudhiṣṭhira; / the holy place Cintāṅgadeśvara, and the sacred Vidyādhareśvara;
the Kedāratīrtha named Ugra, and the unsurpassed Kālañjara; / Sārasvata, Prabhāsa, and the auspicious pool of Rudrakarṇa;
the great holy place called Kokila, and likewise the holy place Mahālaya; / Hiraṇyagarbha, Goprekṣa, and the unsurpassed holy place;
Upaśānta, Śiva, and the unsurpassed Vyāghreśvara; / the great holy place Trilocana, and Lokārka called Uttarāhva;
the holy place Kapālamocana, destroying the sin of slaying a brahmin; / the greatly sacred Śukreśvara, and the excellent Ānandapura.
Such are the holy places situated in Vārāṇasī; / it is not possible to describe them in detail even in hundreds of millions of cosmic ages.

title: aṣṭatriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Nārada said: / The glorification of Vārāṇasī and the holy places within it, O lord, / have been declared in brief; hear now of other holy places.
Then, having reached Gayā, celibate and composed in mind, / one obtains [the fruit of] a horse sacrifice merely by going, O descendant of Bharata.
Where there is the banyan tree named Akṣayyavaṭa, renowned in the three worlds; / whatever is given there to the ancestors becomes imperishable, O lord.
Having bathed in the Mahānadī and satisfied the ancestral spirits and deities, / one attains imperishable worlds and uplifts one's family.
Then one should go to Brahmasaras, frequented by the forest of Brahmā; / one attains the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice, [just as] dawn attains the night.
In that lake, an excellent sacrificial post was erected by Brahmā; / having circumambulated that sacrificial post, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to Dhenuka, renowned in the world; / having stayed for one night, O king, one should donate a sesame cow.
Purified of all sins, one surely goes to the world of the Moon; / there is a sign there, O great king, even today, without doubt:
a tawny cow wanders on the mountain together with her calf; / the footprints of her and her calf are seen even today, O descendant of Bharata.
Having touched water in those footprints, O king of kings, O best of kings, / whatever inauspicious sin exists is destroyed, O descendant of Bharata.
Then one should go to Gṛdhravaṭa, the abode of the trident-bearing god; / bathing there in ashes, having approached the bull-bannered god,
a Brahmin would fulfill a twelve-year vow; / and for the other castes, all sin is destroyed.
Then one should go to the Udyanta mountain, echoing with songs; / for the footprint of Savitṛ is seen there, O bull of the Bharatas.
There a Brahmin of strict vows should perform the twilight devotion; / indeed, by him the twilight devotion will have been observed for twelve years.
And right there is the famous Yonidvāra, O bull of the Bharatas; / having gone there, a person is freed from the constriction of rebirth.
A man who resides in Gayā during both fortnights, the bright and the dark, / purifies his family up to the seventh generation, O king; there is no doubt about this.
Many sons should be desired, so that even one might go to Gayā, / or perform a horse sacrifice, or release a blue bull.
From there, O king, ruler of men, the pilgrim should go to Phalgu; / he obtains the horse sacrifice and attains supreme perfection.
Then, collected in mind, O king of kings, one should go to Dharmapṛṣṭha, / where Dharma always stays, O great king Yudhiṣṭhira.
Having approached Dharma there, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice. / Then one should go, O king of kings, to the excellent pilgrimage place of Brahmā.
Having gone there, restrained in vows, one should worship Brahmā; / one obtains the fruit of both the royal consecration and the horse sacrifice, O Bhārata.
From there, the pilgrim should go to Rājagṛha, O ruler of men; / having touched water there, one rejoices like Kakṣīvat.
There, a pure man should first eat the regular offering to the Yakṣiṇī; / by the grace of the Yakṣiṇī, he is freed from the murder of a Brahmin.
Then one should go to Maṇināga and obtain the fruit of a thousand cows; / a person who eats the regular offering of Maṇināga,
if bitten by a venomous serpent, the venom does not affect him, O king; / staying there for one night, he is freed from all sins.
Then one should go to the forest of the divine sage Gautama, O king; / having bathed in the pool of Ahalyā, one attains the supreme state.
Having approached Śrī, O king, one finds supreme fortune. / There is a water reservoir, O knower of dharma, renowned in the three worlds;
one should perform a bath there and obtain a horse sacrifice. / And the well of the royal sage Janaka is worshipped by the gods;
having bathed there, one attains the world of Viṣṇu. / Then one should go to Avināśana, which releases one from all sins;
one obtains a horse sacrifice and goes to the world of Soma. / And having reached the Gaṇḍakī, which contains the waters of all holy places,
one obtains the Vājapeya sacrifice and goes to the world of Sūrya. / Then, O knower of dharma, entering the hermitage of Dhruva,
one rejoices among the Guhyakas, O fortunate one; there is no doubt about this. / Having reached the Karmadā river, frequented by the Siddhas,
one obtains the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice and goes to the world of Soma. / Then, having reached the Viśālā river, famous in the three worlds,
one obtains the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and goes to the heavenly world. / Then, having reached Māheśvarīdhārā, O ruler of men,
one obtains a horse sacrifice and delivers his family. / Reaching the lotus pond of the celestials, a pure man
does not suffer a bad rebirth and obtains the Vājapeya sacrifice. / Then a celibate student, collected in mind, should go to Māheśapada.
Having bathed at Māheśvarapada, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice. / There, ten million holy places are celebrated, O bull of the Bharatas,
which were taken away by the evil-minded asura in the form of a tortoise, O king of kings, / and recovered by the mighty Viṣṇu, O king.
One should perform a bath there at Tīrthakoṭi, O ruler of men; / one obtains the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Then, O best of men, one should go to the abode of Nārāyaṇa, / where Hari always dwells, ever-present, O Bhārata.
Where Brahmā and the other gods, and the sages rich in austerity, / the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Rudras worship Janārdana,
known as Śālagrāma, belonging to Viṣṇu of wondrous deeds. / Having approached Viṣṇu, the imperishable lord of the three worlds, giver of boons,
one obtains a horse sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. / There is a water reservoir, O knower of dharma, which releases one from all sins;
the four oceans are always present there in that well; / having touched water there, O king of kings, one does not suffer a bad rebirth.
Having approached Mahādeva and the immutable Viṣṇu who grants boons, / one shines like the moon, freed from debts, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Pure and with restrained mind, having touched the water at Jātismara, / having bathed there, one gains memory of previous births; there is no doubt.
Having gone to Vaṭeśvarapura and worshipped Keśava, / through fasting one obtains the desired worlds; there is no doubt.
Then having gone to Vāmana, which destroys all sins, / and bowed to the god Hari, one does not suffer a bad rebirth.
Having gone to the hermitage of Bharata, which releases one from all sins, / one should visit the Kauśikī river there, which destroys great sins.
A person obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice. / Then, O knower of dharma, one should go to the excellent Campakāraṇya.
Staying there for one night, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows. / Then, reaching Govinda, the highly esteemed pilgrimage place,
fasting for one night, one obtains the fruit of an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. / Having seen Viśveśvara there, together with the goddess, of great splendor,
one attains the worlds of Mitra and Varuṇa, O bull of the Bharatas; / having fasted there for three nights, one obtains the fruit of an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Reaching Kanyāvasatha, restrained and regulated in diet, / one attains the worlds of Manu Prajāpati, O bull of the Bharatas.
Those who give even a minute gift at Kanyā, O Bhārata— / that, say the sages of strict vows, is imperishable.
Reaching Niṣṭhāvāsa, renowned in the three worlds, / one obtains a horse sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
The men who give gifts at the confluence of the Niṣṭhā, / they go, O tiger among men, to the sorrowless world of Brahmā.
There is the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha, famous in the three worlds; / performing a bath there, one obtains the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Reaching Devakūṭa, frequented by hosts of divine sages, / one obtains a horse sacrifice and delivers his family.
Then, O king of kings, one should go to the pool of the sage Kauśika; / there Kauśika Viśvāmitra attained supreme perfection.
Where a wise man dwells for a month on the Kauśikī, O bull of the Bharatas, / whatever merit belongs to a horse sacrifice, he attains it in a month.
Whoever resides at the great pool, the best of all holy places, / does not suffer a bad rebirth, and acquires abundant gold.
Having approached Kumāra, who dwells at Vīrāśrama, / one obtains a horse sacrifice and goes to the world of Śakra.
And reaching the well frequented by the thirty [gods] at Nandinī, / one obtains whatever merit belongs to a human sacrifice, O upholder of the Kurus.
Having bathed at Kālikāsaṃgama, where the Kauśikī and Aruṇā [meet], / a wise person who has fasted for three nights is freed from all sins.
Reaching the Urvaśī pilgrimage place, and likewise Somāśrama, / a wise man, having bathed at Kumbhakarṇāśrama, is honored on earth.

Likewise, bathing at Kokāmukha, chaste and composed,
one attains memory of past lives; this was seen by the ancients.

Reaching the river once, a twice-born achieves his aim;
his soul purified of all sins, he goes to the heavenly realm.

Reaching Ṛṣabhadvīpa, having served the slayer of Krauñca,
and sipping water in the Sarasvatī, he shines seated in an aerial chariot.

There is the Audyānaka holy bath, O great king, frequented by sages;
if one bathes there, one is freed from all sins.

Reaching Brahmatīrtha, the holy place frequented by divine sages,
a man obtains [the fruit of] a Vājapeya sacrifice; of this there is no doubt.

Then, having reached Campā and offered libations in the Bhāgīrathī,
and having approached Daṇḍārpaṇa, he obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.

Then one should go to Lāviḍhikā, holy and visited by the meritorious;
he obtains [the fruit of] a Vājapeya sacrifice and is honored, seated in an aerial chariot.

title: navatriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
Nārada said: / Then, having reached Sandhyā and Savidyā, an excellent holy bath,
and sipping water, a man becomes learned; of this there is no doubt.

By the grace of Rāma, the king of holy baths was created anciently;
reaching that Lauhitya, he would obtain much gold.

Reaching the Karatoyā and fasting for three nights, a man
obtains [the fruit of] a horse sacrifice and goes to Indra's realm.

Moreover, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, O king of kings,
the wise declare [the fruit is] ten times that of a horse sacrifice.

Whoever reaches the further island of the Gaṅgā and bathes, O Bhārata,
fasting for three nights, O king, will obtain every desire.

Then, going to the Vaitaraṇī, the river that liberates from sin,
and reaching the Viraja holy bath, he shines like the moon.

Purifying his family by its power, he removes every sin;
having obtained the fruit of a thousand cows, the man purifies his own family.

Dwelling pure at the confluence of the Śoṇa and the Jyotirathā,
having gratified the ancestors and the gods, he obtains the fruit of an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.

At the source of the Śoṇa and the Narmadā, O best of Kurus,
having sipped water at Vaṃśagulma, he obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.

Reaching the Ṛṣabha holy bath in Kośalā, O ruler of men,
a man who fasts for three nights obtains [the fruit of] a horse sacrifice.

Reaching Kośalā, one should sip water at the Kāla holy bath;
he receives eleven times [the fruit of the gift of] a bull; there is no doubt about this.

Sipping water at the Puṣpavatī, a man who fasts for three nights
would find the fruit of a thousand cows and elevate his lineage.

Then, having bathed at the Badārikā holy bath with a restrained mind,
he attains a long life and goes to the heavenly realm.

Then, reaching Mahendra, frequented by the son of Jamadagni,
a man who bathes in Rāmatīrtha obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.

Mataṅga's Kedāra is also right there, O bull of the Bharatas;
having bathed there, O king, a man obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.

Approaching Śrīparvata, one should touch the water of the riverbank;
he obtains [the fruit of] a horse sacrifice and attains supreme perfection.

On Śrīparvata, the great god Mahādeva of great splendor,
exceedingly pleased, dwelt together with the Goddess, and Brahmā surrounded by the gods.

Bathing there in Devahrada, pure and with a restrained mind,
he obtains [the fruit of] a horse sacrifice and attains supreme perfection.

Going to Mount Ṛṣabha, revered by the gods among the Bhāṇḍas,
he obtains [the fruit of] a Vājapeya sacrifice and rejoices upon the surface of heaven.

Then one should go to the Kāverī, surrounded by troops of apsarases;
having bathed there, O king, a man obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.

At that holy bath of the ocean, one should sip water at Kanyātīrtha;
having sipped water there, O king of kings, one is freed from all sins.

Then, having reached Gokarṇa, renowned in the three worlds,
in the midst of the ocean, O king of kings, bowed to by all worlds,

where gods headed by Brahmā, sages rich in asceticism,
spirits, yakṣas, piśācas, and kinnaras along with great serpents,

siddhas, cāraṇas, gandharvas, human beings, and snakes,
rivers, oceans, and mountains worship the husband of Umā,

worshiping Īśāna there, a man who fasts for three nights
obtains [the fruit of] ten horse sacrifices and acquires leadership of the Gaṇas.

Fasting for twelve nights, a man achieves his aim.
Right there is the abode of Gāyatrī, renowned in the three worlds.

Staying there for three nights, he obtains the fruit of a thousand cows;
and there is an ocular proof for brāhmaṇas, O ruler of men:

If a twice-born born of miscegenation recites the Gāyatrī,
his speech turns into a secular verse or a song, O king.

When a non-brāhmaṇa recites it, the Sāvitrī is destroyed.
Having reached the hard-to-attain pool of the brāhmaṇa sage Saṃvarta,

one becomes endowed with beauty and is born fortunate.
Then, having reached the Veṇā, one should gratify the ancestors and gods;

a man obtains an aerial chariot joined with peacocks and swans.
Then, reaching the Godāvarī, ever frequented by the perfected ones,

he obtains [the fruit of] a Gavāmayana sacrifice and goes to the realm of Vāyu.
Bathing at the confluence of the Veṇā, he obtains the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice.

Bathing at the confluence of the Varadā, he obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.
Reaching Brahmasthūṇā, a man who fasts for three nights

would find the fruit of a thousand cows and go to the heavenly realm.
Reaching Kubjāvana, chaste and composed,

fasting for three nights and bathing, he obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.
Then, bathing in Devahrada, at the source of the Kṛṣṇaveṇā's waters,

and at the Jyotirmātra pool, and likewise at Kanyāśrama, O king,
where, having sacrificed with a hundred rites, the king of the gods went to heaven,

he would find [the fruit of] a hundred Agniṣṭomas merely by going there.
Bathing in the pool of all gods, he obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.

Bathing in the Jātimātra pool, a man will remember his past lives.
Going to the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga and of the great-souled Śuka,

devoted to worshiping the ancestors and the gods, he obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.
Reaching the Daṇḍaka forest, O great king, one should sip water.

Going to the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga and of the great-souled Śuka,
a man does not meet an evil destiny and purifies his family.

Then one should go to Sūryāraka, frequented by Jamadagni;
bathing in Rāmatīrtha, a man would obtain much gold.

Bathing in Saptagodāvarī, self-controlled and eating restricted food,
he attains great merit and goes to the realm of the gods.

Then one should go to Devapatha, self-controlled and eating restricted food;
whatever merit belongs to a divine sacrifice, that a human being obtains.

Reaching the Tuṅgaka forest, chaste and with senses restrained,
[where] in ancient times Sārasvata taught the Vedas to the sages.

There, the son of the sage Āṅgirasa, seated upon the upper garments
of the great sages, when the Vedas were lost, O Bhārata,

with the [oṃ]kāra properly uttered according to rule—
whatever had been studied by someone before presented itself to him.

The sages were there, and the gods, Varuṇa, Agni, Prajāpati,
Hari, the god Nārāyaṇa, and Mahādeva likewise,

and the divine Grandfather of great splendor, along with the gods,
appointed the intensely radiant Bhṛgu for the purpose of performing the sacrifice.
Then that lord, following the rule, performed for all the sages / the re-establishment [of their sacred fires] through the rite seen by the gods.
Gratified there properly with their share of clarified butter, / the gods went to the three worlds, and the sages as they pleased.
Of one who enters that forest, Tuṅgaka, O best of kings, / the sin of a woman or a man is immediately destroyed.
A wise man should dwell there for a month, restrained and eating measured food; / he goes to the world of Brahmā, O king, and purifies his family again.
Reaching Medhāvana, one should satisfy the ancestors and gods; / he attains the Agniṣṭoma and acquires memory and intelligence.
Going there to Kālañjara, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows; / O king, one should cultivate the self there on Mount Kālañjara.
A man is honored in the heavenly world; of this there is no doubt. / Then, O lord of the people, at Citrakūṭa, the foremost of excellent mountains,
having reached the Mandākinī, the river that frees one from sin, / performing ablutions there and devoted to worshipping the ancestors and gods,
one obtains [the fruit of] a horse sacrifice and goes to the supreme destination. / Then, O king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed place of Guha,
where the god Mahāsena is eternally present, O king; / by merely going there, a man attains perfection, O best of men.
Bathing at Koṭitīrtha, a man obtains the fruit of a thousand cows; / having circumambulated, a man goes to the abode of fame.
Having approached Mahādeva, he shines like the moon. / There is a well there, O great king, renowned, O bull of the Bharatas,
in which the four oceans reside, O Yudhiṣṭhira. / Having sipped water there, O king of kings, and having circumambulated,
a self-restrained man, purified, goes to the supreme destination. / Then, O best of the Kurus, one should go to great Śṛṅgaverapura,
where previously the very wise Rāma, son of Daśaratha, crossed [the Gaṅgā]. / Bathing in the Gaṅgā, a celibate student with senses conquered,
having shaken off his sins, becomes pure and obtains [the fruit of] the Vājapeya. / Then one should go to Muñjavaṭa, the abode of the wise god [Śiva].
Having approached and worshipped Mahādeva, O ruler of men, / and having circumambulated, one attains the state of a leader of [Śiva’s] hosts.
Then, O king of kings, one should go to Prayāga, praised by the sages, / where the gods headed by Brahmā, the quarters, and the lords of the quarters,
the guardians of the worlds, the Siddhas, the devoted ancestors, / and the great sages headed by Sanatkumāra [reside],
as well as the Nāgas, the Suparṇas, the Siddhas holding brilliance, / the rivers and the oceans, and the Gandharvas and Apsarases;
and the divine Hari is present there, honored by Prajāpati. / There are three pools there, and between them flows the Jāhnavī;
passing through Prayāga, she is honored above all holy places. / There the daughter of the sun, renowned in the three worlds,
the Yamunā, joins with the Gaṅgā, blessing the world. / Between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā is remembered as the hips of the earth;
the sages know Prayāga as the end of the hips, the generative organ. / Prayāga, Supratiṣṭhāna, both Kambala and Aśvatara,
and the holy place Bhogavatī are declared as the altar of Prajāpati. / There the Vedas and the sacrifices, embodied, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
and the great, sinless sages attend upon Prajāpati; / they worship the gods with sacrifices, and likewise the wielder of the discus, O king.
Therefore, there is nothing more holy in the three worlds, O descendant of Bharata; / Prayāga surpasses all holy places in its power, O lord.
From hearing of that holy place, from even chanting its name, / or from bowing one's head [to it], one is freed from all sins.
One who takes a bath at that confluence, firm in vows, / attains the very great merit of the Rājasūya and the horse sacrifice.
For this is the sacrificial ground even of the gods; so it is told. / Even a very small gift given there becomes great, O descendant of Bharata.
Neither by the word of a god, dear one, nor by the word of the people / should your mind be turned away concerning dying at Prayāga.
Ten thousand holy places and another sixty crores [of them], / whose presence is proclaimed right here, O joy of the Kurus.
Whatever merit lies in the four Vedas, and whatever in those who speak the truth, / one who merely bathes at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā obtains that.
Then there is the excellent holy place named Bhogavatī, belonging to Vāsuki; / one who takes a bath there would obtain [the fruit of] a horse sacrifice.
There is the holy place Haṃsaprapatana, renowned in the three worlds, / and Daśāśvamedhika upon the Gaṅgā, O joy of the Kurus.
The Gaṅgā is equal to Kurukṣetra wherever it is plunged into, / especially at Kanakhala, while Prayāga is supreme and great.
Even if one who has committed a hundred misdeeds serves the Gaṅgā, / the water of the Gaṅgā burns all of it away, as fire burns fuel.
The water of the Gaṅgā burns all, like fire burns a heap of cotton. / Puṣkara is remembered as holy in all the Kṛta age, and in Tretā;
in Dvāpara it is Kurukṣetra, and the Gaṅgā is remembered in the Kali yuga. / At Puṣkara one should practice austerity; at Mahālaya one should give gifts;
at Malaya one should enter fire; at Bhṛgutuṅga [one should undertake] fasting. / At Puṣkara, at Kurukṣetra, and among those who enter the waters of the Gaṅgā,
a creature instantly redeems seven ancestors and seven descendants. / Praised, she purifies sin; seen, she grants merit.
Plunged into and drunk, she purifies the family up to the seventh generation. / As long as a man's bone touches the water of the Gaṅgā,
for that long, O king, that person is honored in the heavenly world. / Just as holy places and holy shrines,
once attended upon and merit gained, make one share in the other world, / [so] there is no holy place like the Gaṅgā, no deity higher than Keśava,
and nothing higher than the Brahmins; thus spoke the grandfather [Brahmā]. / Wherever the Gaṅgā is, O great king, that region extends for a yojana,
and it should be known as a Siddha field, resting upon the bank of the Gaṅgā. / This is the truth in the minds of twice-born men and good people,
and one should whisper liberation into the ear of a disciplined and faithful disciple. / This is lawful, this is pure, this leads to heaven, this brings happiness;
this is most holy, charming, purifying, the highest dharma, / this secret crown of the earth, delivering from all sins.
Reciting it in the midst of the twice-born, one attains purity; / it is auspicious, heaven-bestowing, greatly meritorious, quelling rivals, benevolent.
The recitation of the succession of holy places is the foremost source of wisdom: / the childless obtains a son, the poor attains wealth,
a king conquers the earth, a Vaiśya obtains wealth, / a Śūdra attains his desired wishes, and a Brahmin, reading it, crosses over to the far shore.
And he who constantly hears this, ever pure with the merit of the holy places, / attains recollection of past births and rejoices on the summit of heaven.
The holy places described are accessible, and some are inaccessible; / one may also approach them mentally with devotion to all holy places.
These were made by the Vasus, Sādhyas, Ādityas, Maruts, and Aśvins, / and by sages like gods, who sought meritorious deeds.
Thus you too, O descendant of Kuru, steadfast in vows, according to this rule, / go to the holy places with self-restraint; merit increases through merit.
By means of senses previously purified, out of faith and insight into the scriptures, / these holy places are reached by the virtuous who follow the righteous.
Not one who has failed to act, nor one whose self is uncultivated, nor an impure person, nor a thief / bathes in the sacred fords, O descendant of Kuru, nor does a deceitful man.

By you, however, of upright conduct, who ever discern duty and purpose, / all the fathers, dear one, and great-grandfathers have been gratified with libations, / as have the gods headed by the grandfathers, along with the hosts of seers.
Vasiṣṭha said: And you, O knower of dharma, have by your righteousness ever delighted them; / O Dilīpa, you will attain great and eternal fame on earth.
Nārada said: Having spoken thus and taken his leave, the blessed seer Vasiṣṭha, / pleased in his heart, vanished right there.
Dilīpa, O tiger among the Kurus, through seeing the true purpose of the scriptures / and on Vasiṣṭha's word, traversed the earth.
Thus, O fortunate one, this highly sacred pilgrimage to fords, / freeing from all sins, has been established at Pratiṣṭhāna.
Whoever wanders the earth according to this rule / shall, having departed, enjoy the full fruit of a hundred horse sacrifices.
And after that, O son of Pṛthā, you will attain supreme righteousness eightfold, / just as King Dilīpa, O son of Pṛthā, previously attained it.
Because you guide the seers, your reward will be eightfold; / for these sacred fords, O descendant of Bharata, are overrun by hosts of demons.
There is no recourse for anyone else apart from you, O joy of the Kurus. / This deed of the divine seer pertains to all the sacred fords.
Whoever rising early recites it is freed from all sins, / where the foremost seers are ever present: Vālmīki, then Kaśyapa,
and Ātreya, then Kauṇḍinya, Viśvāmitra, then Gautama, / Asita, and Devala, and Mārkaṇḍeya, then Gālava,
and the disciple of Bharadvāja, the sage Uddālaka, / Śaunaka together with his son, and Vyāsa, the foremost of ascetics,
and Durvāsas, best of sages, and Jābāli of great austerities. / All these excellent seers, rich in austerities, await you.
Together with them, O fortunate one, visit these sacred fords; / you will attain great fame just like King Mahābhiṣa.
As righteous Yayāti, and as King Purūravas, / so you, O tiger among the Kurus, shine through your own righteousness.
As King Bhagīratha, and as celebrated Rāma, / and as indeed the slayer of Vṛtra consumed all his rivals in ancient times,
and the king of gods protected the three worlds free from anxiety, / so, having destroyed your enemies, you will protect the subjects.
Having obtained the earth won through your own righteousness, O lotus-eyed one, / you will attain renown through prowess, like Kārttavīrya Arjuna.
Sūta said: Having spoken thus to the king, the blessed seer Nārada, / taking leave of the great king, vanished right there.
Righteous Yudhiṣṭhira also, true to his vows, the lord of the earth, / with deep reverence went to all the sacred fords together with the seers.
O all you seers, this narrative regarding the pilgrimage to fords has been told by me; / whoever recites or hears it is freed from all sins.
All the essential truth has been told by me; what more do you wish to hear? / Indeed, of the seers of holy renown, there is nothing that I should not say.

title: catvāriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Sūta said: Thus the sacred fords have been spoken of, bodies of Viṣṇu, O you of noble vows; / from contact with any one of these, a man becomes liberated.
Blessed is the hearing of sacred fords, blessed is the resort to sacred fords; / there is no other means for the destruction of the mass of sins in the Kali age.
"May I dwell at a sacred ford; likewise may I touch a sacred ford"— / whoever speaks thus daily goes to the highest, supreme [state].
His sins are destroyed merely by conversing about sacred fords; / sacred fords are indeed blessed, to be attended by the blessed, O you of noble vows.
By the very attendance on sacred fords the Lord is attended, / Nārāyaṇa, the creator of the world; there is no abode higher than a sacred ford.
A Brāhmaṇa, the tulasī, the aśvattha tree, an assemblage of sacred fords, / and Viṣṇu, the supreme Lord—these should ever be served by men.
Especially the service of Brāhmaṇas, O bull-like sages, / the first-born know to be greater than bathing in all sacred fords and the like.
Therefore, a wise person should daily worship the foot of a twice-born, which is auspicious and embodies all sacred fords; / that would be greater than a sacred ford.
One should circumambulate the aśvattha tree, the tulasī, and cows; / having obtained the fruit of all sacred fords, one is exalted in the world of Viṣṇu.
Therefore one should destroy evil actions through the resort to sacred fords; / otherwise one goes to hell, for [sin] is pacified through the experiencing of karma.
The residence of sinners is in hell; the virtuous one enjoys heaven; / therefore, a discerning person should certainly resort to a sacred ford, which is merit.
The seers said: Indeed, the sacred fords have been heard together with their glorifications, O you of noble vows; / now we wish to hear the particulars of Prayāga.
Prayāga was spoken of in brief by you formerly, O Sūta; / we wish to hear of it in detail; let it be told to us, O Sūta!
Sūta said: Well asked, O fortunate ones, of noble vows, concerning Prayāga; / well then, I will declare the detailed description of Prayāga,
which was recounted formerly by Mārkaṇḍeya to the son of Pāṇḍu, / when the Bhārata [war] had taken place and the son of Pṛthā had obtained the kingdom.
In the meantime, King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, / tormented by grief for his kinsmen, kept thinking again and again:
"King Duryodhana was the lord of eleven armies; / having tormented us exceedingly, all of them have gone to destruction.
Relying on Vāsudeva, only five Pāṇḍavas remain. / How [did we slay] Droṇa, and Bhīṣma, and Karṇa of mighty strength,
and King Duryodhana together with his brothers and sons? / All the kings have been slain, and whoever else considered themselves heroes.
Bereft of kingdom, what should be done? What with pleasures or with life? / Woe! Alas!"—thinking thus, the king was overwhelmed with despair.
Motionless, without enthusiasm, he stood for a while with downcast face. / When the king regained his senses, he kept pondering again and again:
"What practice, observance, or sacred ford should I follow by rule, / by which I might quickly be liberated from the defilement of great sins,
where a man, having bathed, goes to the unexcelled world of Viṣṇu? / Indeed, how can I ask Kṛṣṇa, by whom this great deed was caused to be done?
How can I ask Dhṛtarāṣṭra, whose hundred sons have been slain? / How can I ask Vyāsa, whose family has been destroyed?"
Thus Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, was reduced to despondency; / all the Pāṇḍavas wept, overwhelmed with grief for their kinsmen,
as did the great-souled ones gathered there who depended on the Pāṇḍavas, / and Kuntī and Draupadī, and whoever had arrived there.
All fell to the earth, weeping all around. / In Vārāṇasī, however, Yudhiṣṭhira was perceived by Mārkaṇḍa,
how he was reduced to despondency, weeping and deeply sorrowful. / In a very short time, Mārkaṇḍa of great austerities
arrived at Hastināpura and stood at the royal gate. / The doorkeeper, seeing him, spoke quickly to the king:
"The sage Mārkaṇḍa, wishing to see you, stands at the gate." / Then the son of Dharma, eager, approached the gate quickly.

Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Welcome to you, O greatly wise one! Welcome to you, O great sage!
Today my birth has borne fruit; today my family is purified.

Today my ancestors are satisfied, now that you have been seen, O great sage!
Having placed him upon a throne, with washing of the feet, worship, and the like,

the great-souled Yudhiṣṭhira indeed worshipped that sage.
Then Mārkaṇḍa said to him: "I have been honored by you, O lord.

Speak swiftly, O king, why was [this done] in haste by you?
Or by what have you become distressed? Tell it before me."

Yudhiṣṭhira said:
And what happened to us for the sake of the kingdom, O great sage—
knowing all this indeed, the venerable one has come here.

how much less so through the duty of kings, especially for a kṣatriya!
Therefore, keeping this in your heart, one should not worry about sin.

Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, having bowed his head to the sage, [said:]
"I ask you, O best of sages, who always see the three times:
tell me concisely, whereby I may be freed from sin."

Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, O fortunate king, to what you ask me, O descendant of Bharata:
thus Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and also the holy ford, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

How much more [merit] was indeed praised of old by meritorious brāhmaṇas, O lord!
Going to Prayāga is the best for men of virtuous deeds.

title: ekacatvāriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O venerable one, I wish to hear how it stood in an earlier cosmic age,
and how is the journey to Prayāga, of what nature for men there?

What is the destination of those who die there, and what is the fruit for those who have bathed?
And what is the fruit for those who reside at Prayāga? Tell [me].
Tell me all of this, for my curiosity is great indeed.

Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall tell you, my child, whatever fruit is desired by the lord,
which was heard by me of old being spoken by the ṛṣis and vipras.

From Prayāga up to Pratiṣṭhāna, from the Dharmakī pool to Vāsuki's pool,
the two Nāgas Kambala and Aśvatara, and the Bahumūlika Nāgas—

this field of Prajāpati is celebrated in the three worlds.
Having bathed here, they go to heaven; those who have died are free from rebirth.

There the gods, headed by Brahmā, assemble and keep guard.
And there are many other holy fords that destroy all sins,

which cannot be spoken of, O king, even in many hundreds of years.
I shall proclaim concisely the celebration of Prayāga.

Sixty thousand bows protect the Jāhnavī.
Savitar, drawn by seven steeds, always protects the Yamunā.

Vāsava himself especially protects Prayāga.
Hari, along with the gods, protects the circle agreed upon.

The trident-bearing Maheśvara constantly protects that banyan tree.
The god indeed protects the auspicious place that removes all sins.

A person enveloped in adharma never goes to that abode.
When his sin has become slight or very small, O ruler of men,

for one remembering Prayāga, everything comes to destruction.
Even by the sight of that holy ford, or by reciting its name,

or by obtaining its clay, a man is freed from sin.
There are five pools, O king of kings, in the midst of which is the Jāhnavī.

For one who has entered Prayāga, sin dissolves that very moment.
The man who remembers the Gaṅgā across thousands of yojanas,

even if he has committed evil deeds, attains the supreme destination.
By praising [her] he is freed from sins; having seen [her] he sees good fortune;

having bathed and having drunk, he purifies his family up to the seventh [generation].
Speaking the truth, having conquered anger, fully dedicated to non-violence,

following dharma, knowing reality, devoted to the welfare of cows and brāhmaṇas,
bathed between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, one is freed from sin.

He fully obtains his desired wishes in abundance, conceived in mind.
Then, having gone to Prayāga, which is protected by all the gods,

living as a celibate student for a month, he should offer libations to ancestors and gods;
he obtains desired wishes wherever he is born.

Where the goddess, the daughter of Tapana, renowned in the three worlds,
the fortunate river Yamunā, joins [the Gaṅgā],

there the god Maheśvara is always directly present.
Virtue at Prayāga is hard to attain for human beings, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

Gods, dānavas, gandharvas, ṛṣis, siddhas, and cāraṇas,
having touched water there, O king of kings, are glorified in the heavenly world.

title: dvicatvāriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen again, O king, to the glorification of Prayāga,
having gone to which one is freed from all sins, there is no doubt in this.

For the afflicted, the poor, and those of firm resolve,
setting aside the place Prayāga, there is never anything imperishable.

The one who, having reached the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, abandons his life,
in an aerial chariot shining with the color of gold, with the radiance of the sun,

in the midst of gandharvas and apsarases, that human being rejoices in heaven;
