Water from Viṣṇu's feet is auspicious, destroying all sins. / Whoever bears even a single drop gains the fruit of all sacred fords.
Water from Viṣṇu's feet, O Brahmin, destroys sin upon mere touch; / there is no untimely death [for him], and he gains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
If a sinner drinks water from Viṣṇu's feet, / the sin lodged in his body is destroyed, O Brahmin; there is no doubt.
The water from Viṣṇu's feet combined with a tulasī leaf, O twice-born, / whoever carries [it] on his head with devotion goes to Hari's abode at the end.
Whatever fruit is obtained by giving gold equal [in weight] to Mount Meru, / that fruit is obtained by men by touching the water from Hari's feet.
Whatever fruit men obtain by giving tens of millions and thousands of cows, / that fruit is certainly obtained by touching the water from [his] feet.
Whatever fruit is obtained by performing tens of millions and thousands of sacrifices, / men [obtain] ten million times that by touching the water from Hari's feet.
Whatever fruit is obtained by people by giving away ten million maidens [in marriage], / by touching water from Viṣṇu's feet, O twice-born, the fruit is greater than that.
By giving ten million elephants, by giving ten million horses, / whatever fruit a mortal obtains [from that, he obtains] by touching the water from Hari's feet.
Whatever fruit a mortal obtains by giving the seven continents together with their crops, / by touching the water from Viṣṇu's feet, O Brahmin, he obtains more than that.
Listen, O Brahmin, I shall tell [you] briefly; what more [need be said]? / Touching the water from Viṣṇu's feet, even a sinner goes to Hari's abode.

Śaunaka said:
By touching and drinking [it] in ancient times, what living being reached the abode of Hari? / Tell me [this], O Sūta, out of your compassion.

Sūta said:
In ancient times, in the Tretā age, there was a sinful Brahmin named Sudarśana. / He would constantly eat on the day of Janārdana, O best of the twice-born.
He constantly reviled the scriptures; he always reviled vows. / He knew nothing else apart from his own belly.
Once, when his time had come, he met his death, O twice-born. / The messengers of Yama arrived, bound him, and led him to Yama's abode.
Seeing him, the brother of Yamunā angrily asked his minister: / 'O minister, declare thoroughly his merit and his sin.
This Brahmin is a great sinner; he appears to be one of cruel deeds.'

Citragupta said:
'Listen to his sin; he does not have even an atom of merit. / Even on the day of Hari, he constantly ate food, O lord.
Whatever vile man eats on the day of Kamalā's husband, / he shall eat feces, O king, and go to a dreadful hell.
Assign this one a place in hell for a hundred Manvantaras; / then indeed his birth shall be in the womb of a village pig.'

Sūta said:
Then, by Yama's command, O Brahmin, by his terrifying messengers / he was cast into feces for more than a hundred Manvantaras.
Then he was released and became a village pig on earth. / One must suffer hell for a long time on account of eating on Hari's day.
Then, O Brahmin, his time having come, he passed away; / he obtained rebirth in the womb of a crow, constantly eating feces.
One day, O Brahmin, having drunk water from the feet of glorious Hari / that was standing at a doorway, he was freed from all sins.
On that very day, the crow fell [victim] to a Śabara; / the crow reached the state of death at the proper time by the hunter.
When a divine, auspicious chariot joined with royal swans arrived, / the bird mounted it and went to Hari's temple, O Brahmin.
The glorification of the water from [his] feet, which destroys sins, has been told. / Whatever sinful man hears it, his sin is destroyed.

title: aṣṭādaśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
Śaunaka said:
If someone, deluded, should approach a forbidden woman, O Sūta, / by what means does his purification come about? Tell [me this] thoroughly.

Sūta said:
If a Brahmin approaches an outcaste woman such as a Caṇḍālī or a Śvapākī, / he should fast for three [days] and then perform the Prājāpatya vow.
He should shave [his head] including the topknot and give two cows; / having given an appropriate priestly fee, that twice-born attains purification.
If a kṣatriya or a vaiśya goes to a Caṇḍāla woman or the like, / he should perform the Prājāpatya penance and give two pairs of cattle.
If a Śūdra pursues a Śvapākī woman, O rich in asceticism, / he should give four pairs of cattle and perform the Prājāpatya vow.
If, deluded, he approaches his mother, sister, own daughter, / or daughter-in-law, he should then perform three Kṛcchra penances.
Having performed three Cāndrāyaṇa penances, he should give three pairs of cattle; / having shaved [his head] including the topknot, he should then drink pañcagavya.
And when an offering is made into the fire here, in this way he is purified, O rich in asceticism. / [If he approaches] the father's wife, O best of the twice-born, or his mother's sister,
the guru's wife, a maternal uncle's wife, a brother's wife, or a woman of his own gotra, / if he approaches [any of them] out of delusion, he should perform two Prājāpatyas,
three Cāndrāyaṇas, O Brahmin, and give five pairs of cattle / as a priestly fee to Brahmins; he is purified, there is no doubt here.
The fool who approaches a cow should fast for three [days]; / having given a cow and also food, he is purified here, there is no doubt.
[If he approaches] a prostitute, a female donkey, a sow, a female monkey, or a female buffalo, O twice-born, / having immersed himself up to the neck in mud of cow dung and water,
he should remain there without food; he is purified in just three nights. / Having shaved [his head] including the topknot, he should fast for three nights;
staying in water for one night, he is certainly purified, there is no doubt. / But when a man, deluded by passion, approaches a Brahmin woman,
he should perform three Prājāpatyas and three Cāndrāyaṇas; / he should also give three cows; he is certainly purified, O rich in asceticism.
The Brahmin woman should drink pañcagavya for five nights, O twice-born, / and give two cows as a priestly fee; she is purified here, there is no doubt.
When one goes to another's woman, he should perform the Sāṃtapana penance. / As is a crossbar, so is a woman; therefore, one should avoid her.
If a man should go even once to an outcaste, low-born woman, / he should perform the Prājāpatya penance; he is surely purified, there is no doubt.
A woman is like a burning coal; a man is like a pot of clarified butter. / One should never stay in her vicinity, O Brahmin.
A woman who conceives a child by a paramour, bringing ruin to her family, / must be abandoned in every way, O Brahmin; there is no fault in that.
A woman who leaves home, abandoning even her own kin, / is ruined and cast out of the family; there is to be no association with her again.
When a woman goes, bewildered, to another man, / she should perform the Prājāpatya penance and then drink pañcagavya.
She should then give two cows; she is certainly purified, there is no doubt. / If a foolish Brahmin woman, O Brahmin, deluded, goes to another man,

she should then be abandoned by people; there is no fault [in that]. / If an earthly god Brahmin, deluded by lust, approaches a Brahmin woman, / he should then give a cow and sesame seeds; he is purified here, there is no doubt.

title: ekonaviṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Śaunaka said: / Having consumed feces and urine out of ignorance, or having touched liquor, / I shall explain how their purification takes place; listen, O twice-born.
One should perform two Prājāpatya vows, visit sacred bathing places, O sage, / give a gift of a bull and eleven cows, and then shave [one's head] along with the topknot.
Having gone to a crossroads, [performing] the entire Prājāpatya vow likewise, / one should then give two cows, and then drink the five products of the cow.
Having fed the brāhmaṇas, he is indeed purified; there is no doubt about this. / If, even knowingly in times of distress, any man eats the food
If a man eats [such forbidden food], he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; / having shaved his head including the lock of hair, he should then drink pañcagavya.
One, two, three, or four cows should be given to brāhmaṇas respectively. / If one consumes the food of a śūdra, food during birth-pollution, uneatable food, or water,
or the leftovers of a śūdra, knowingly or in times of distress, / he should perform two Prājāpatyas and likewise three Cāndrāyaṇas.
He should then give two cows, and drink the five products of the cow, O twice-born. / Having offered oblations into the fire and fed many brāhmaṇas, he certainly becomes pure.
If food has been eaten by mice, mongooses, or cats, O twice-born, / sprinkling it with water mixed with sesame seeds and darbha grass purifies it; there is no doubt.
If any man eats onion, garlic, horseradish, bottle-gourd, carrots, or meat, / O brāhmaṇa, he should observe the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
A śūdra fond of liquor and meat, through following vile deeds— / a brāhmaṇa should avoid such a śūdra from afar, as if he were an outcaste.
Those who are devoted to serving twice-borns, free from liquor and meat, / and dedicated to giving gifts and their own duties, are to be known as the best of śūdras.
If brāhmaṇas eat out of ignorance during [the impurity of] birth or death, / a brāhmaṇa becomes pure through ten thousand [recitations of the] Gāyatrī.
A kṣatriya [becomes pure] with [the same number of] thousands, a vaiśya with five thousand, / and even a śūdra becomes purified through the five products of the cow, O you rich in asceticism.
If one drinks ghee, water, or yogurt placed in a vessel belonging to a low-caste person, / whatever caste he belongs to, even if done out of ignorance, he should perform the Prājāpatya vow.
He should give a generous gift, and is purified by fire according to the rule. / Even for śūdras there is no fasting; one is purified through gifts alone.
One should shave [one's head] along with the topknot after fasting for a day and a night. / A man who is struck with sticks and the like by low-caste men, O twice-born,
should perform the Prājāpatya vow, or else the Cāndrāyaṇa vow; / and having shaved [his head] along with the topknot, he should then drink the five products of the cow.
He should then give two cows, and offer food and other offerings into the fire. / If any man knowingly or unintentionally eats where liquor is drunk in the house, O brāhmaṇa,
that man is also to be cast out from the family. / A brāhmaṇa who destroys the seed of a cow, or cuts off its tail,
One who steals gold should perform three Prājāpatya penances; / having shaved his head including the lock of hair, he should likewise drink pañcagavya.
Having offered oblations into the fire according to the rule, he should likewise give three cows. / Only then may his water and food be accepted, O you rich in asceticism.
One should eat [unsolicited food] in the morning for three days, and unsolicited food in the evening for three days, / and then not eat at all for three days; this is the Prājāpatya vow.

Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, ghee, and water with kuśa grass— / a brāhmaṇa should drink these for two days, fasting for one night; / this Sāṃtapana penance, O sage, is declared to remove all sins.
Eating a single morsel in the morning for three days, and one unsolicited in the evening for three days, / and then fasting for three days; this vow is the Atikṛcchra.
For three days each, O twice-born one, he should drink hot water, milk, and ghee, / bathing once; this Taptakṛcchra, O sage, is declared to remove sins.
Abstaining from food for twelve days is the penance that destroys sin; / it is known by the name Parāka, and is renowned, O you rich in asceticism.

One should increase one mouthful each day during the bright fortnight, and decrease it in the dark fortnight, / not eating on the day the moon disappears; this is traditionally known as the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
Collected in mind, a brāhmaṇa should eat four mouthfuls in the morning, / and four when the sun has set; this is known as the Śiśucāndrāyaṇa.

A woman who cuts a pumpkin gourd should drink the five products of the cow for three days; / she should donate five pumpkin gourds along with gold and garments. / Only then may her water and cooked food be accepted, O you rich in asceticism.

title: viṃśatitamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Śaunaka said: / What good deed has been declared by doing which people will cross the ocean of worldly existence / in the Kali age, O Sūta, like frogs in a dark well?
Sūta said: / In the month of Kārttika, which is dear to Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, one should take a morning bath, / and, concentrated in mind, worship Rādhā and Dāmodara with devotion.
Giving up deceit and the like, O brāhmaṇa, and devoted to the service of her husband, / she goes to glorious Hari's abode, known as Goloka, which is very difficult to attain.
She who offers incense and a lamp to Rādhā and Dāmodara in Kārttika / goes to Viṣṇu's abode, freed from her sins.

The woman who gives garments at the abode of Rādhā and Dāmodara in Kārttika, O brāhmaṇa, / dwells with glorious Hari for a long time.

She who offers fragrant flowers and a garland to Rādhā and Dāmodara / in the month of Kārttika goes to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
She who also gives perfume, food offerings, sugar, and other things / to Rādhā and Dāmodara goes to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Whatever she gives to a twice-born in Kārttika, O brāhmaṇa, / for the pleasure of Rādhā and Dāmodara, her merit becomes imperishable.
The woman who worships Rādhā and Dāmodara with devotion in the morning / during Kārttika, O twice-born, does not go to hell for a long time.
Never on this earth will she become a widow in birth after birth, / nor will she ever become unpleasant to her husband, as occurred before.
Formerly, in the Tretā age, O brāhmaṇa, there was a śūdra named Śaṅkara, / who lived in the Saurāṣṭra region; his wife was named Kalipriyā.
She constantly longed for a paramour, and regarded her husband as mere straw, thinking: / 'This husband is not fit for me; another man is my master.'
Thinking thus, she constantly gives him the leftovers [of food]; / through association with the vile, the greatly deluded woman ate meat and drank liquor.
Cruel as she was, she continually insulted her husband at will, [thinking:] / 'He is a shackle on my feet; why hasn't he died yet?
When he is dead, I will enjoy pleasures as I please.' / Reasoning thus in her heart, that foolish woman then, with a paramour,
made a pact: 'We two shall go to another country,' O twice-born. / At night, while her husband was asleep, [she cut] his throat with a sword, O twice-born.
Having cut [his throat] for the sake of the paramour, she went to the rendezvous spot. / The paramour who had arrived had been devoured by a leopard, O twice-born.
Seeing this, she wept and fell down in a faint. / Having recovered after a long time, the foolish woman lamented piteously:

title: svakīyaṃsvāminaṃhatvācāgatāparapūruṣam
text_mt: By fate, a tiger has devoured that lover who was my master. / What shall I do? Where shall I go? I have been deceived by the creator!'
Sūta said: / Then, O brāhmaṇa, Kalipriyā returned to her own house; / placing her face on her husband's mouth, she wept aloud:
Kalipriyā said: / 'Alas, my lord, what an exceedingly dreadful deed have I done! / To what realm shall I go? Speak a few words, O husband!'
"Reproach me as much as you wish, for I am thoroughly blamed. / You say nothing, my lord; there is no other refuge for me."
Sūta said: / She bowed at his feet and went to another city. / Entering there, the woman saw many virtuous people,
Devoted to the morning bath in the month of Ūrja and Vaiṣṇavas in the Narmadā, / And women also at the river, O twice-born, [worshiping] Rādhā and Dāmodara,
And worship being performed with sounds of conches and great festivities, / With fragrances, flowers, incenses, lamps, garments, and various fruits,
And with mouth-perfumes. Endowed with devotion and filled with humility upon seeing [it], / She asked: "Tell me, women, what is this being done?"
The women said: / "In Ūrja, the best of all months, [we worship] the auspicious Rādhā and Dāmodara. / Having performed this worship, O mother, which removes all sins and brings auspiciousness,
Sin accumulated over ten million births is destroyed, and an abode is attained." / Renouncing meat, she performed worship on the day of Hari;
She met her death on the full moon day, purified, O twice-born. / The servants of Yama quickly arrived at his abode
To take her, filled with wrath, and bound her with leather ropes. / Then the messengers of Viṣṇu arrived in a chariot made of gold,
Bearing conch, discus, mace, and lotus, wearing forest garlands. / They struck with the edges of their discuses, and the messengers of Yama fled.
Mounted on the golden aerial chariot yoked with royal swans, O twice-born, / Surrounded by them, she went to the abode of Viṣṇu.
There she dwelt for a long time, enjoying pleasures as she desired. / The woman who worships Rādhā and Dāmodara in Kārttika, O twice-born,

Goes, with sins abandoned through worship, to the charming place named Goloka. / Whatever man or woman hears this with devotion and concentrated mind, / The sin accumulated over ten million births of his or hers is destroyed.

title: ekaviṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Śaunaka said: / "Speak, O sage Sūta, of the rule for Kārtika, the best of all months; / You ought to explain the observances fully."
Sūta said: / "On the full moon day of Āśvina, O best of the twice-born, one should maintain focus / And perform the vow of Kārtika until the Awakening [Eleventh]."
By day, O twice-born, a man should discharge urine and feces facing north; / Let him be silent and fully mindful, and at night facing south.
On the path, in water, in cowpens, in cremation grounds, or on an anthill, O twice-born, / One observing the vow should never discharge urine or feces.
One should not discharge feces or urine in very excellent places. / Having taken clean clay, one should then wash the left hand.
For purification with water and clay, the count was formerly twenty: / one on the penis, five on the anus, and ten on the left hand.
Ten times on both hands, and three times each on the feet. / Then he should cleanse his mouth and make the resolve for the bath.
Meditating on Dāmodara in the heart, he should then recite this mantra: / 'In Kārtika, I shall perform the morning bath, O Janārdana,
For the pleasure of Dāmodara along with Rādhā, destroying sins. / Salutation to the lotus-navelled one, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who reclines on the waters;
Salutations to You along with Rādhā! Accept the argha-offering; be gracious to me!' / Then he should bathe, O twice-born, and apply the forehead mark according to rule.
If one performs any rite devoid of the upright mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), / All that work is fruitless; this truth is spoken by me.
The body of men made without an upright mark / Should not be looked upon; having seen it, one should gaze upon the sun.
On whose forehead a white upright mark made with clay is seen, / Even an outcaste is a purified soul and worthy of worship, without doubt. / But those vile men who make an upright mark without a gap,
On their foreheads is always the footprint of a dog, without doubt. / Having completed the duty prescribed for the morning, [the plant] beloved of Hari,
Namely tulasī, which destroys sins, he should worship with devotion, O twice-born. / Then, hearing the Purāṇic narrative of glorious Hari with a steady mind,
The observer of the vow should worship a twice-born man with devotion according to rule. / Another's seat, another's food, another's bed, another's wife:
One should always avoid these, O twice-born, and especially in Kārttika. / Sour gruel, black gram, meat, and honey,
Kidney beans and the like, the observer of the vow should continually avoid in Kārtika; / Lime, meat, lime-powder, and stale food, O twice-born.
Lentil is proclaimed among grains, [yet] milk of cows is not meat. / Salt produced from the earth, O twice-born, and parts of living beings are indeed meat;
All liquids purchased from a twice-born, and water situated in a small pond. / Celibacy, dining in the fourth part of the day from a leaf-plate,
A tiger among the twice-born should observe, and avoid anointing with oil; / Mushrooms, radish stalks, asafoetida, onion, pūtikā leaves,
Garlic, radish, horseradish, and likewise bottle gourd fruit, / Wood-apple, eggplant, ash gourd, and eating from bell-metal,
Twice-cooked food, food from a woman in childbirth, fish, a bed, a menstruating woman, / Eating twice or thrice, and contact with women, the observer of the Kārtika vow should avoid.
The householder should always abandon myrobalan on a Sunday, O twice-born. / Through ash gourd, there is loss of wealth; through bṛhatī, one forgets Hari;
Through pointed gourd, there is no prosperity; through radish, loss of strength; / One becomes stained through bilva fruit, and is born in animal wombs through lime;
Through palm fruit, there is destruction of the body; through coconut, foolishness; / Bottle gourd is equal to beef; there is cow-slaughter through watermelon;
Flat bean is said to cause sin; pūtikā is like killing a brahmin; / Through eggplant, loss of sons occurs; through black gram, one becomes chronically ill;
Through meat, great sin arises; he should avoid these on the first day and subsequent days [of the fortnight]. / Whatever food one avoids for the pleasure of glorious Hari, O twice-born,
That, again, after giving it to a brahmin at the end of the vow, becomes his food. / Regarding the man observing the Kārtika vow and acting according to instruction, O twice-born,
The messengers of Yama flee, just as elephants seeing a lion. / The vow of Viṣṇu is supreme, O twice-born; a hundred sacrifices are not equal to it.
Having performed a sacrifice, one goes to heaven; the observer of the Kārtika vow goes to Vaikuṇṭha. / Whatever evil deed has arisen from the actions of mind, speech, and body, O twice-born,
Dissolves in an instant upon seeing the observer of the Kārtika vow. / Even the four-faced Brahmā is not capable of describing
The merit of the observer of the Kārttika vow who performs it as prescribed. / Upon doing this, all sins flee in the ten directions, O twice-born, [saying]:
'Where shall I go? Where shall I dwell out of fear of the observer of the Kārttika vow?' / On the full moon day, according to one's capacity, food, clothing, and the like, O twice-born,

He should give for the pleasure of glorious Hari, and feed the brahmins as well. / At night, the observer of the vow should keep vigil with dances, songs, and the like. / Whoever hears this with devotion, his sin is destroyed.

title: dvāviṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Śaunaka said: / "Speak, O omniscient one, of the glorification that destroys sins for those who listen, / For the benefit of all living beings, out of compassion, concerning tulasī."
Sūta said: / O twice-born, in whose surroundings stands a grove of Tulasī, / because his house has the nature of a sacred site, Yama's servants do not come.
O brāhmaṇa, the grove of Tulasī is auspicious and removes all sins; / the best of men plant it, and thereby they do not see the son of the Sun.
Whoever should plant, protect, attend, see, or touch it, / all his sin would be destroyed, O best of the twice-born.
Those who worship Hari with tender leaves of Tulasī, / those high-minded men, O brāhmaṇa, do not go to the abode of Death.
The best rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Maheśvara, / along with the gods and sacred sites beginning with Puṣkara, abide in a Tulasī leaf.
A sinner who, in contact with leaves of Tulasī, gives up his vital breaths, / goes to the abode of Viṣṇu: this has been spoken by me in truth.
A man smeared with the clay of Tulasī, even if bound by hundreds of sins, / when he yields up his vital breaths, goes to the temple of Hari.
The man who bears Tulasī-wood and sandalwood, O brāhmaṇa, / sin does not touch his body; he goes to the supreme state.
He who wears a garland of Tulasī-wood around his neck, / even if impure or ill-behaved, goes through devotion to the home of Hari.
On whose body is seen a garland made of dhātrī fruits / or arising from Tulasī-wood, he indeed is a Bhāgavata man.
He who wears around his neck a garland made of Tulasī leaves / that is the remainder from Viṣṇu's offering, is especially worthy of reverence by the gods.
Furthermore, he who, having placed a Tulasī garland on his neck, / worships Janārdana, obtains with each flower the merit of ten thousand cows.
Those rationalists of sinful minds who do not wear the garland, / burned by the fire of Hari's anger, do not return from hell.
One should not abandon the garland of Tulasī, especially the garland of dhātrī, / which destroys mortal sins and grants duty, desire, and wealth.
As many body hairs of men as the garland of dhātrī touches in the Kali [age], / for that many thousands of years does he reside in Keśava's abode.
Offering the garland made of Tulasī-wood to Keśava, / the man who wears it with devotion has no sin at all.
Seeing a garland of Tulasī-wood, the messengers of the King of Ghosts / flee far away, like a leaf tossed by the wind.
In a forest of Tulasī, in the shade of a dhātrī, the best of men / who offers an ancestral ball of rice—his ancestors attain liberation, O best of the twice-born.
He who holds a dhātrī fruit in his hand, on his head, on his neck, / at his ears, and in his mouth, O twice-born, is to be known as Hari himself.
If a twice-born brāhmaṇa worships Śrī Hari with dhātrī leaves and fruits, / sin accumulated through ten million births is destroyed by that single worship.
Sacrifices, gods, sages, and sacred sites in Kārttika, O twice-born, / taking refuge in the dhātrī tree, always abide [there] in Kārttika.
The man who plucks a dhātrī leaf in Kārttika, or a Tulasī leaf on the twelfth lunar day, / would go to hell, full of torment.
O brāhmaṇa, he who eats food in the shade of a dhātrī in Kārttika, / his sin arising from the contact of food is destroyed for a year.
In the midst of a Tulasī grove and at the foot of a dhātrī in Kārttika, / whoever performs worship of Hari, O brāhmaṇa, surely goes to Vaikuṇṭha.
The water staying at the base of a Tulasī, O best of the twice-born, / which a sinner receives upon his head with devotion, goes to the house of Hari.
He who carries on his head water dripping from a Tulasī leaf, / has bathed in all sacred sites, and in the end goes to the house of Hari.
Long ago in the Dvāpara age, O great sage, there was a certain best of the twice-born; / having bathed one day, and given an oblation of water to Tulasī, he went home.
He was Āditya by name, radiant like the sun by his merit. / A certain eater afflicted by thirst, possessing many sins, arrived.
Drinking water from the base of the Tulasī, his sin was destroyed. / Quickly a hunter also arrived, Asimardana by name.
He said: 'Has the food been eaten, and after eating, have you broken [it] and gone away? / Why, having made [a mess] of what was in my cooking pot, have you come, you injurer?'
He struck him dead. To take him away by the command of Yama, / angry servants arrived, noose and club in hand.
They resolved to bind and lead him away, when the servants of Viṣṇu arrived. / Then, cutting the leather noose, upon a charming chariot,
they quickly made him mount. Filled with modesty, they asked: / 'By what merit, O good sirs, is he indeed being carried away?'
They said: 'Long ago this man was a king; he performed very great merit. / [Yet] he abducted a certain beautiful woman.'
'Because of this sin, the king went to the abode of Yama. / There distress was indeed inflicted by you all at Yama's command.'
'He lay down and engaged in sport with a woman made of copper / on a burning iron bed, [experiencing] despair due to his action, O king.'
'A fearful, hot iron pillar was heated by Yama's order; / then, standing embracing it, the king experienced sorrow for a long time.'
'He was sprinkled with streams of caustic water by others in the abode of Yama; / then, at the conclusion of hell, again and again in a womb of sin,'
'having obtained birth, he experienced sorrow for a long time by his own karma. / By drinking water from the base of the Tulasī, he goes to the home of Hari.'
Now, having heard that speech, the messengers went just as they had come. / Along with him, the messengers of Viṣṇu went to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
The sin-destroying glorification of Tulasī has been related, O brāhmaṇa. / What might become of those who render service with devotion, I do not know, O sage!

title: trayoviṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Śaunaka said: / Speak, O sage Sūta, out of compassion, the glorification / that destroys impurities, of the remaining five days of Kārttika.
Sūta said: / Hear, O Śaunaka, what has been asked, the sin-destroying glorification; / I will tell of the remaining five days of the month of Ūrja.
O tiger among sages, the Viṣṇupañcaka is the foremost of observances; / during it, whoever worships Śrī Hari with Rādhā with devotion,
with fragrant pastes, flowers, incenses, lamps, garments, and various fruits, / freed from all sins, goes to the abode of Viṣṇu.
A student of the Veda, a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic / does not attain the supreme place without performing the Viṣṇupañcaka.
The renowned Viṣṇupañcaka is meritorious and removes all sins; / whoever performs a bath during it obtains the fruit of all sacred sites.
Before Śrī Hari, O brāhmaṇa, and near a Tulasī, / whoever should offer with devotional disposition a lamp filled with clarified butter,
in the sky for the pleasure of Śrī Hari, he goes to the abode of Viṣṇu; / even a sinner goes to the abode of Hari: this has been spoken by me in truth.
And if one bathes Acyuta with devotion, with honey, milk, ghee, and so on, / pleased, what will Hari not give to that good person?
One should offer sweet milk-rice as an offering to the Lord of the lords of gods; / the four-faced [Brahmā] is unable to enumerate his merit.
Having worshipped Hṛṣīkeśa on the eleventh lunar day with concentrated mind, / having properly obtained cow dung, one attends [it] with mantras.
The observer of the vow should again consume cow urine with mantras on the twelfth day, / milk on the thirteenth, and curd on the fourteenth.
Having obtained [these] for the purification of sins, fasting for four days, / on the fifth day he should bathe and worship Keśava according to the rule,
feed brāhmaṇas with devotion, and give them a fee; / then at night he should consume properly consecrated five products of the cow.
He who is unable to do so should eat fruits and roots, / or he may consume oblation food, O brāhmaṇa, according to the prescribed rule.
He who observes the five-day vow of Śrī Hari, O brāhmaṇa, and worships him with tulasī leaves, / is to be recognized as the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself.
Long ago in the Tretā age there was a śūdra dedicated to the occupation of a bandit, / by name Daṇḍakara, who constantly reviled dharma.
He was a speaker of untruth, a killer of friends, lusting after the charms of courtesans, / a robber of brāhmaṇas' property, cruel, and delighting in intercourse with other men's wives.
He killed those who sought refuge, kept company with heretics, / ate beef, drank liquor, and constantly reviled others.
He betrayed trust and destroyed the livelihood of his kinsmen, O best of the twice-born. / Seeing such a wicked man in his house, the twice-born,

title: jñātayaūcuḥ
text_mt: "Hey, you fool, evil-doer! Ruin is being brought upon / the reputation that was earned by our ancestors in our spotless lineage!"
Enraged thus, O best of the twice-born, and out of fear of ill repute, / they all abandoned family respect for that foremost among sinners.
Then, having lost all his wealth, he went to the great forest; / he would constantly carry out banditry together with bandits.
Out of fear for those traveling on the road, O brāhmaṇa, they obtained nothing to eat; / tormented by hunger, they went to another place.
Entering there, they all saw many virtuous people, / Vaiṣṇavas, the best among the twice-born, seated at the root of a dhātrī tree, O brāhmaṇa.
All those bandits went away, O brāhmaṇa, but that Daṇḍakara / approached their presence and bowed down.
Daṇḍakara said: / "I am afflicted by hunger, O best of the twice-born; my vital breaths will surely depart. / Give me something to eat! I have come to you for refuge."
Hearing his word, those devoted to dharma said to him: / "During the renowned Viṣṇupañcaka, which removes all sins,
how is it that you desire to eat food today, on the day of Hari? / Tell in detail: what is your name now?"
He said joyfully to the brāhmaṇas: "I am known by name as Daṇḍakara. / I am laden with every sin; how can my deliverance come about?"
They said to him: "Perform the best vow, the Viṣṇupañcaka!" / By the command of the brāhmaṇas, O twice-born, he performed the Viṣṇupañcaka.
Having died, he ascended a splendid chariot and went to Hari's abode; / attaining the form of Śrī Hari, he remained free from rebirth.
Whoever hears this sin-destroying narrative with devotion, / their sin accumulated over ten million births is destroyed in that very instant.

title: caturviṃśatitamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Śaunaka said: / "O best among the wise, knower of truth, tell me now, O great-minded sage, / in order, the glorification of gifts."
Sūta said: / "The gift of land, O best of sages, is considered the foremost among gifts. / By him who has made that gift, the fruit of all gifts is deemed to be obtained.
He who gives land bearing crops to a brāhmaṇa, O best of the twice-born, / enjoys happiness in the world of Viṣṇu for as long as fourteen Indras reign.
Then, attaining birth on earth as a sovereign king, / having enjoyed the entire earth for a long time, he goes to the abode of Śrī Hari.
He who gives to a twice-born a plot of land measuring a cowhide / goes to Hari's abode, freed from all sins.
Where a hundred cows and one bull can stand without restraint, / the great sages declare that land to be measured as a cowhide.
Both the leader of land and the giver of land go to heaven; / land should be accepted by wise twice-born persons, even setting aside hundreds of other gifts.
An ignorant brāhmaṇa who, deluded, rejects land, / that twice-born would become an experiencer of extreme misery in birth after birth.
Having obtained land from another, whoever gives it to a twice-born— / to him the Lord of the World grants the supreme state, O brāhmaṇa.
He who seizes land, whether given by himself or given by another, O twice-born, / goes along with ten million families to a most terrible hell.
Whoever steals land belonging to gods or brāhmaṇas, O brāhmaṇa, / no expiation is seen for him even in hundreds of millions of cosmic ages, O sage.
The king who protects land given by another, O twice-born, / his merit becomes ten million times greater than that of the giver.
The merit that is obtained by giving the earth with its seven continents, O twice-born, / that merit a mortal obtains by giving a milk cow to a twice-born.
He who gives a bull to a poor family man, / being completely freed from all sins, goes to the world of Śiva.
He who gives to a brāhmaṇa gold even of the measure of a sesame seed / goes to Hari's abode along with ten million families.
Whoever gives silver to a virtuous brāhmaṇa, O twice-born, / reaches the world of the Moon and drinks nectar there forever.
He who gives coral, pearls, diamond, and gems, / O best of the twice-born, goes to the heavenly realm.
The merit a person attains by the gift of a man's weight in gold— / by giving a śālagrāma stone he obtains ten million times more than that.
The merit one obtains by giving the earth of seven continents along with its mountains and forests, / indeed, that belongs to the giver of a śālagrāma stone.
He who gives a śālagrāma stone to a brāhmaṇa, / by him, O twice-born, the fourteen worlds are given.
He who makes the gift of a man's weight in gold, O bull among the twice-born, / has no rebirth in a mother's womb.
The man who gives an adorned maiden, O best of the twice-born, / goes to Brahmā's abode; there is no rebirth for him.
For a seller of a maiden there is no release from hell; / for a giver of a maiden there is no return from heaven.
He who gives shoes or a parasol to a twice-born, / having died, goes to the city of Indra and dwells there for four cosmic ages.
He who gives divine garment to a virtuous twice-born, / wearing divine clothing in heaven, dwells there for a long time, O best of the twice-born.
Whoever gives an old cow, worn-out cloth, O twice-born, / or a maiden who has already menstruated, goes likewise to hell.
A wise man should not look at the face of a seller of a maiden, O brāhmaṇa; / and if he has seen it through ignorance, he should gaze upon the sun.
A man who gives fruit goes to heaven, O best of the twice-born, / and enjoys fruit resembling nectar there for thousands of cosmic ages.
The mortal who gives vegetables goes to Śiva's abode, O twice-born, / and enjoys for two cosmic ages rice milk that is hard even for the gods to obtain.
The giver of clarified butter, the giver of curds, the giver of buttermilk, and the giver of milk, / having gone to Viṣṇu's abode, drinks nectar.
A mortal who gives perfume and gives flowers goes to the abode of the gods; / adorned with perfumes and flowers, he remains there for thousands of yugas.
He who gives the gift of a bed—the essence of gifts—to a brāhmaṇa, / goes to the abode of Brahmā and rests on a couch for a long time.
The giver of a seat and the giver of a lamp, freed from all evil deeds, / sits on a throne in heaven surrounded by rows of blazing lamps.
The man who gives betel enjoys the entire earth happily; / asleep in heaven on the lap of a divine woman, he surely chews betel.
The best of men who makes the gift of knowledge, the foremost of gifts, / dwells after death in the presence of Viṣṇu for three hundred cosmic ages.
Attaining knowledge there, rare indeed [to obtain], O best of the twice-born, / he attains rare liberation through the grace of glorious Hari, O twice-born one.
The best of men who teaches a helpless, suffering vipra / goes to the dwelling of glorious Hari, freed from rebirth.
The man who gives a manuscript, endowed with devotion and faith, / obtains for each syllable the merit produced by the gift of ten million brown cows.
A mortal who gives honey and gives jaggery goes to the ocean of sugarcane juice; / and the man who bestows salt goes to the world of Varuṇa.
Among all gifts, food and water, O best of the twice-born, / are proclaimed the best by all the sages who know reality.
By him who has given food and water on the surface of the earth, O best of the twice-born, / all gifts have been given, O bull among the twice-born.
The man who is a giver of food, O vipra, is proclaimed a giver of life; / therefore, the giver of food obtains the fruit of all gifts.
As is food, so is water: both are proclaimed to be equal; / and without water, food cannot be prepared, O best of the twice-born.
Hunger and thirst, O tiger among the twice-born, both are proclaimed to be equal; / therefore both food and water are declared to be foremost by the wise.
The best of men who give food on the earth, O brāhmaṇa, / freed from all sins, go to the abode of Hari.
As many morsels of food, O vipra, as one gives on the circle of the earth, / just so many killings of a brāhmaṇa are destroyed, O ascetic.
The sins of those who give gifts of food suddenly leave their bodies / and go to the limbs of those who receive them, O Śaunaka.
Therefore, the wise do not accept food from the most sinful; / the fools who receive it out of delusion become partakers of sin.
Should one place even a single [vessel of] water on the ground, O best of the twice-born, / he would be freed from all sins and go to the abode of Hari.
With effort, O best of the twice-born, the accumulation of wealth should be made; / and accumulated wealth, O brāhmaṇa, one should apply to the act of giving.
Those who hoard wealth out of miserliness are exceedingly miserable; / in the end, abandoning all wealth, they depart destitute, O sage.
Those men who always give gifts again and again and become poor— / they should not be considered poor; they are great lords in the human world.
In the next world, O tiger among the twice-born, lacking the restraint of the virtuous, / merciless, and destitute of kin, what was not given does not wait upon one.
Though wealth exists, the man who neither eats nor gives / should be recognized as truly poor; having died, he heaves sighs [of despair].
Giving is declared to be better even than austerity by the seers of reality; / therefore, with effort, O best of the twice-born, one should perform the act of giving.
If a giver, having set aside [a gift], does not give it to a twice-born, / he goes to a terrible hell that causes fear to all creatures.
If the giver does not remember the gift, and the recipient does not ask for it, / there is residence in hell for both of them as long as the moon and the sun endure.
Whatever sins there are, such as the killing of a brāhmaṇa, O best of the twice-born, / they are destroyed by giving; therefore, one should practice giving.

title: paṃcaviṃśatitamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Śaunaka said: / The glorious deeds of Viṣṇu destroy all calamities, / effect the destruction of all sins, and ward off malignant planets.
They bestow nearness to Viṣṇu and grant the fruits of the four aims of life; / the man who hears them with devotion goes in the end to the house of Hari.
The glorification of the utterance of the name is heard to be greatly wonderful, / by the mere utterance of which a man would go to the supreme state.
Speak now of that rule regarding the chanting of the name, O Sūta. / Sūta said: / Listen, O Śaunaka; I shall tell of the dialogue that is the means to liberation.
Nārada formerly questioned the Kumāra; I shall tell you that. / Once, seated on the bank of the Yamunā with a tranquil mind,
Nārada, with folded hands, asked Sanatkumāra, / having heard of the various kinds of dharmas and the transgressions of dharma.
Glorious Nārada said: / That transgression of dharma among men which has been spoken of by the Lord— / how can its destruction take place? Let it be told, O beloved of the Lord.
Glorious Sanatkumāra said: / Listen, O Nārada, dear to Govinda, knower of the dharma of Govinda, / to that cause of the liberation of the world beyond darkness which you have asked.
Those devoid of all proper conduct, deceitful in mind, outcasts, deceivers of the world, / devoted to hypocrisy, egotism, drinking, and slander, and those who are cruel and sinful,
and whatever others are devoted [only] to wealth, wife, and son, all of them base— / taking refuge at the lotus feet of glorious Govinda, they surely become pure, O twice-born one.
Yet people who are bent on offenses transgress even that divine, / compassionate, supreme [name] that grants liberation to the immovable and the moving; truly, the Name casts them down here.
Even one who commits all offenses is freed when taking refuge in Hari; / but whoever commits offenses against Hari is a defiler among two-legged beings.
If he should ever take refuge in the Name, he surely crosses over through the Name; / for through offense against the Name, which is the friend of all, one falls down.
Glorious Nārada said: / What are those offenses committed against the Name of the Lord, O chief of vipras, / which destroy men's merit and bring them into ordinary worldly existence?

title: yataḥkhyātiṃyāṃtaṃkathamusahatetadvigarahām
text_mt: Whoever here sees all the qualities, names, and the like of auspicious, glorious Viṣṇu / as different in his intellect—he indeed works against the Name of Hari.

Disregard of the guru, censure of the Vedic scriptures, and interpreting the Name of Hari as mere praise or inventing it— / for him whose mind turns to sin through offense against the Name, there is no purification even by the Yamas.

Equating [the Name] with all auspicious rites such as dharma, vows, renunciation, and oblations is negligence; / and instructing one who lacks faith, is averse, or will not listen is an offense against the auspicious Name.

Even after hearing the glorification of the Name, that base person who is devoid of love, / clinging to 'I' and 'mine' and the like, is also an offender against the Name.

Thus, out of compassion, the highest, happiness-bearing name of the Lord / was spoken to me by Śaṃkara, O Nārada, which is always to be recited diligently by sages.
Those who, even though knowing, do not quickly avoid the ten offenses against the Name / grieve like a child refusing to eat, [crying] even to an angry mother.
Being free from offenses, always practice the recitation of the Name; / through the Name alone, O divine sage, will everything of yours be accomplished, not otherwise.
Glorious Nārada said: / O Sanatkumāra, for those prone to reckless deeds, devoid of discernment and dispassion, / and devoted to the body, wealth, and ego, how can freedom from offenses arise for us?

Śrī Sanatkumāra said:
When an offence against the Name has occurred through heedlessness in any way,
one should constantly chant the Name, taking sole refuge in it.

For those beset by offences against the Name, the Names alone destroy the sin,
applied unceasingly, for they alone accomplish the objective.

A single name of his, being remembered or reaching the base of the ear, / whether pure or impure in syllables, uninterrupted, truly delivers [the soul].

If, however, it is thrown into greed and hypocrisy born of the body and wealth,
it does not produce its fruit quickly here, O brahmin.

This supreme secret, destroying all evil and averting offences,
was heard of old, O Nārada, from Śaṅkara.

The men engaged in offences who know the Name of Viṣṇu,
even for them there is liberation simply through reciting it, O Nārada.

The entire glorification of the Name is sung in the Purāṇa;
therefore, O giver of honor, you ought to hear the entire Purāṇa.

O brother, he who has faith every day in listening to the Purāṇa,
with him Śiva and Viṣṇu along with their followers become directly pleased.

The fruit one obtains having bathed at the holy site of Puṣkara, at Prayāga, or at the confluence with the sea—
double that fruit belongs to him who listens with faith.

Those who read the Purāṇas and attentively listen to them,
with every syllable they obtain the fruit born of the gift of a brown cow.

One without a son obtains a son; one seeking wealth obtains wealth;
one seeking knowledge obtains knowledge; one seeking liberation attains liberation.

Those who listen to the Purāṇas, having destroyed the web of sins
acquired across ten million births, indeed go to Hari's abode.

With a devotional disposition one should honor the brahmin Purāṇa-reciter
with cattle, land, gold, and garments, and with fragrant unguents and flowers, O sage,

and, full of joy, with a vessel made of bell-metal, a water pot,
earrings as well, and a signet ring made of gold.

So too one should give a seat and a flower garland, O ascetic;
one should not practice deceit regarding wealth, for [then] the gift bears inferior fruit.

A brahmin should cause the Purāṇa to be recited for the accomplishment of all desires and purposes,
[offering] gold, silver, cloth, a flower garland, and sandalwood.

Whoever gives the book with devotion goes to Hari's abode.
And those who complete the book according to this rule—
Citragupta does not write down their names, O twice-born.

title: ṣaḍviṃśatitamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
Śaunaka said:
I wish to hear from you, O wise one; explain from the very root
the merit in keeping an oath and what sin there is in breaking it.

Or what happens in a false oath and in a true one, O sage,
having given the right hand? Show mercy, O ocean of mercy!

Sūta said:
Listen, O tiger among sages; I shall explain from the very root.
You are foremost among Vaiṣṇavas, devoted to the welfare of all people.

The fruit a man obtains by giving a hundred cows—
ten million times greater than that is the merit in keeping an oath, O twice-born.

From breaking an oath, a fool goes to a terrible hell;
he is roasted for a hundred Manvantaras, there is no doubt of this.

Then, having obtained a birth here in the house of a pauper,
he is destitute of food and clothing, and suffers through his own actions.

If one takes an oath falsely in the presence of the gods, fire, and the guru,
so long does his body burn, [yet] Viṣṇu's lineage is not destroyed.

Regarding a false oath, O brahmin, what can I say now?
For a hundred Manvantaras, O brahmin, [he goes to] hell; what more of falsehood?

Having touched the floral offerings of Śrī Hari falsely, O best of sages,
he takes seven ancestors and is roasted in hell for a long time.

Sometime obtaining a birth, he becomes a leper in birth after birth.
If it is so even with truth, O brahmin, what is to be said of falsehood?

The mortal who, having given his right hand, keeps it—
his attainment becomes Kṛṣṇa; I speak the truth, truly.

Having given his hand, the mortal who does not keep his word,
so long do his ancestors experience torments.

He himself, O tiger among sages, goes to an exceedingly dreadful hell,
and dead, he goes with ten million ancestors [to suffer]; there is no doubt.

Śaunaka said:
Who of old attained Kṛṣṇa from keeping [the pledge of] his hand,
of the right hand, O sage? Tell me, I wish to hear with respect.

Sūta said:
Of old, in a certain city, there was a Śūdra named Vīravikrama,
who ate much, had a stout body, was talkative, and very handsome.
He was wealthy, endowed with sons, cultured, learned, dear to all people, / and ever a worshiper of brahmins and guests.
Devoted to his father, O best of the twice-born, he always kept his promises, / obeyed the words of his elders, and served Hari.
Once, an outcaste, handsome, young, and clever, / having assumed the form of a brahmin, came in disguise to his house.
The brahmin said: / Listen to my words, O wise one: my auspicious wife has died. / What shall I do? Where shall I go? Tell me today out of compassion.
If a person arranges a marriage, especially for a brahmin, / what need is there for gifts, what need for sacred bathing places, or for sacrifices and millions of vows?
Having heard this, that Vīravikrama said to the brāhmaṇa: / "Hear my word, O brāhmaṇa: my maiden daughter is [yet] a child."
If it is your desire, O brahmin, I will give her [to you] according to the rites; / I give my right hand, and it will not be otherwise.
Hearing this word of his, the outcaste seized his right hand. / Filled with joy, he indeed spoke these words:
The brahmin said: / Having fixed an auspicious moment, give me your auspicious daughter; / in delay there are many obstacles—so it is settled in the scriptures.
Vīravikrama said: / Tomorrow, O brahmin, I will give you my daughter; it cannot be otherwise. / Even a base man, having given his right hand, would not do [the opposite].
Sūta said: / Calling the brahmin Kṛṣṇaśarman, the family priest, / he told him all this, O sage, and related the agreement, O twice-born.
'Why do you wish to give your daughter, being a śūdra, to a brahmin? / Especially do not give her to one who is unknown and of noble lineage.'
All his kinsmen, his father and the rest, said, O one rich in asceticism: / 'Hear our words, dear Vīravikrama:
To one whose family, country, lineage, wealth, / character, and age are not known, a daughter is never given by relatives.'
He said, O best of the twice-born: 'My right hand has been given; / I can by no means ever act otherwise.'
Having spoken thus to them, he proceeded to give the maiden to the brāhmaṇa; / seeing this, all the relatives were filled with wonderful astonishment.
Hearing that truthful word, the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace / suddenly appeared, having mounted Garuḍa, O sage.
The blessed Lord said: / Blessed is your family and your virtue, blessed are your mother and father, / blessed is your truthful word, and blessed is your right hand!
Blessed is your deed and your birth; none such exists in the three worlds. / By such a deed, O virtuous one, you deliver your lineage!
Sūta said: / While Śrī Kṛṣṇa was speaking thus, a celestial chariot made of gold arrived, / accompanied by Hari's attendants, bearing Garuḍa's emblem everywhere.
All his family, O brahmin, along with the outcaste and the family priest, / the holder of the conch and lotus placed upon the chariot Himself.
Taking them all, Hari went to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha; / there they remained for a long time, enjoying pleasures very hard to attain.
Whoever transgresses his word, or whoever violates his right hand, / goes to hell along with his family; truly, truly do I say this.
His food and water, O brahmin, cannot be accepted by the ancestors or the gods; / virtue, abandoning his house, flees in terror, O best of the twice-born.
Whatever foolish-minded person, having given hope, causes despair, / goes to hell, dragging along ten million generations of his own people.
Whoever transgresses his word, his virtue is transgressed / by kings, fire, and thieves, O brahmin; truly, truly this is certain.
Having properly heard this Svargottara, one goes beyond heaven; / liberated while living here, he goes hereafter to the supreme abode named after Kṛṣṇa.

sanskrit_iast:
atha śrīpādme mahāpurāṇe pañcamaṃ pātālakhaṇḍaṃ prārabhyate
śrīgaṇeśāya namaḥśrīkuladevatāyai namaḥ
śrīgurucaraṇāraviṃdābhyāṃ namaḥ
meaning:
अथ श्रीपाद्मे महापुराणे पञ्चमं पातालखण्डं प्रारभ्यते
श्रीगणेशाय नमःश्रीकुलदेवतायै नमः
श्रीगुरुचरणारविंदाभ्यां नमः
title: Pātāla Khaṇḍam
text_mt:
Now begins the fifth [section], the Pātālakhaṇḍa, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.

Obeisance to glorious Gaṇeśa! Obeisance to the glorious family deity! / Obeisance to the lotus feet of the glorious guru!

title: prathamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
Having bowed down to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men,
and to the goddess Sarasvatī and to Vyāsa, one should then recite 'Victory!'

The sages said:
Everything has been heard from you, O fortunate one—the charming Svargakhaṇḍa.
Now, O long-lived one, tell us indeed the deeds of Śrī Rāma.

Sūta said:
Then, on one occasion, the excellent sage Vātsyāyana asked the Lord of Serpents,
the supporter of the earth, this purest account.

the distinct determination of principles such as the creation of the Mahat-principle;
and the diverse deeds of kings have been related by you, O sinless one,

and the wondrous deeds of kings born in the solar dynasty.
Among them is the narrative enacted by Rāma, which removes many great sins.

The story of the horse sacrifice of that heroic Rāma was heard
in brief by me from you; I desire it in full detail—

that which, heard, remembered, and recited, takes away great sins,
grants desired aims, and bestows satisfaction to the minds of devotees.
Śeṣa said: / "Fortunate are you, O best of the twice-born, whose intellect is such, / longing for the nectar of the pair of feet of the hero of Raghu's race.

All sages say that the company of virtuous people is excellent,
from which arises the tale of the lord of the Raghu lineage, destroying sins.

A favor was bestowed upon me by you, in that Rāma was brought to mind again—
he whose feet are illuminated by the jewels from the hosts of diadems of gods and asuras.

In the ocean of the tale of Rāvaṇa's enemy, what is a gnat such as I,
wherein gods such as Brahmā are deluded and do not comprehend?

Nevertheless, O sage, it must be spoken by me to you according to my own capacity;
birds go in the vast sky, relying on their own movement.

The life of the lord of the Raghus extends to a hundred crore [verses];
people speak of it according to the nature of their intellect.

The virtuous renown of the lord of the Raghus will purify my soiled mind
through its own contact, just as fire does to gold.

Sūta said:
Having spoken thus to that excellent sage, with eyes motionless in meditation,
he beheld through knowledge the sublime, auspicious tale.
With a voice choked with emotion and his limbs marked by great joy, / he again narrated the lucid story of Daśaratha's son.
Śeṣa said: / When the lord of Laṅkā, the tormentor of gods and demons, / who stole the beauty of the moon of the lotus faces of the Apsaras troop, was slain,
all the gods, headed by Indra, then attained happiness; / having attained happiness, they offered praise, bowing down like servants.
And having installed the righteous Bibhīṣaṇa in Laṅkā, / Rāma, together with Sītā, mounted the Puṣpaka [aerial chariot].
Accompanied then by Sugrīva, Hanumat, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa, / Bibhīṣaṇa too, along with his ministers, followed, eager at the separation.
Beholding Laṅkā in many ways with broken ramparts and city gates, / and seeing the Aśoka grove there, the dwelling place of Sītā, he fainted.
And [seeing] the śiṃśapā trees there, blossoming and full of buds, / strewn with female rākṣasas who had died out of fear of Hanumat,
having quickly seen all this, Rāma set out toward his city, / accompanied by Brahmā and the other gods, each in their own aerial chariots,
hearing the sounds of celestial kettledrums that brought pleasure to the ears, / and being worshipped likewise by the dances of the Apsarases, the best of the Raghus,
showing Sītā on the way the sacred bathing places and hermitage sites, / the sages, the sons of the sages, and the devoted wives of the sages.
Wherever dwellings were previously made by the wise Rāma, / he, together with Lakṣmaṇa, showed them all to her.
Showing it thus to her, Rāma saw his own city; / then, near it, he beheld Nandigrāma.
where King Bharata truly dwelt, protecting dharma, / bearing many signs of grief born of separation from his brother,
sleeping in a ditch, living as a celibate student, wearing matted hair and bark garments, / his slender staff-like body distressed by grief, constantly narrating Rāma's story,
not even eating barley grain, not drinking water frequently, / and who, having bowed to the rising sun, said:
“O eye of the universe, O lord of the gods, remove my great sin! / For my sake, even Rāmacandra, worshipped by the world, went to the forest.
Attended by Sītā of delicate limbs, he went to the wilderness— / that Sītā who felt distress upon a bed of flowers just by encountering a stalk!
That faithful Sītā who never felt the burning heat of the sun, / that Jānakī wanders from forest to forest for my sake! Alas!
That Sītā who was never seen by the eyes of hosts of kings, / that Sītā is now surely seen by Kirātas of death-like form!
That Sītā who, fed with sweet food, did not wish to eat, / that Sītā today desires forest fruits! Alas!”
Approaching the sun thus every day, / the great king Bharata, beloved of Rāma, says this every morning."
And when spoken to by the wise ministers who shared his joy and sorrow, / who knew statecraft and were skilled in the treatises, the king spoke to them:
“O ministers, why do you address me, unfortunate and the lowest of men? / For my sake my elder brother Rāma languishes having reached the forest.
I respectfully perform the cleansing of the sin of my unfortunate mother / by constantly remembering the feet of Rāmacandra, O good ministers!
Blessed exceedingly is Sumitrā, the mother of a hero, dear to her husband, / whose son serves Rāma's feet every day.”
In whichever village Bharata, affectionate toward his brother, indeed stayed / and uttered loud lamentations, that village he saw.

title: dvitīyo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Śeṣa said: / Then, with his mind overwhelmed by longing to see him, / the brother Bharata, foremost of the righteous, was remembered again and again.
And he spoke to the mighty Hanumat, the son of the wind, / his inner darkness destroyed by the splendor of the moon in the guise of his flashing teeth:
“O hero Hanumat, hear my words prompted by [love for] my brother, / faltering and overwhelmed by long separation!
Go, O heroic son of the wind, to that brother / who stubbornly bears a body with a staff-like frame emaciated by separation from me,
who wears bark garments, wears matted hair on his head, / and would not even eat fruits, tormented by separation;
to whom another’s wife is like a mother, and gold is like a clod of earth, / who looks upon the subjects as sons—my kinsman who knows dharma.
Quickly sprinkle him, whose body is burned by the flames of the fire of sorrow born of separation from me, / with a rain of water in the form of news of my arrival!
Announce from joy that Rāma, accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, / by monkey lords headed by Sugrīva, and by rākṣasas with Bibhīṣaṇa,
has arrived, seated in the Puṣpaka [chariot], / so that this younger brother of mine may quickly attain joy from my arrival.”
Having heard these words of the wise hero of Raghu's line, / the messenger went to Bharata's dwelling named Nandi.
Having gone to Nandigrāma, the wise one saw Bharata, / surrounded well by aged ministers and melting with grief from separation from his brother,
narrating the tale of Rāmacandra to the aged ministers, / brimming over with the nectar of his lotus feet.
He bowed to Bharata, who was dharma incarnate, / fashioned as it were by the Creator with a full portion of goodness alone.
Seeing him, Bharata quickly stood up with folded hands / and said, “Welcome! Tell me of Rāma’s welfare!”
Even as he was speaking thus, his right arm throbbed; / grief departed from his heart, and his face was filled with tears of joy.
Beholding the king like that, the lord of monkeys replied: / “Know that Rāma with Lakṣmaṇa has arrived near the city!”
His body sprinkled with the nectar of the message of Rāma's arrival, / he attained a flood of joy; I, the thousand-faced one, do not know [its extent]!
He said: “There is nothing of mine that could be given to you by me; / I am your servant for the rest of my life, O bringer of Rāma's message!”
Vasiṣṭha also took the water offering; and the aged ministers, overjoyed, / went toward Rāmacandra along the path shown by Hanumat.
Seeing from afar the delightful Rāmacandra approaching, / seated in the Puṣpaka [chariot], with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa,
and Rāma also seeing Bharata coming on foot, / wearing matted hair, bark garments, and a loincloth,
he saw the ministers dressed like his brother, identically clad, wearing matted hair, / their forms emaciated by constant weariness from austerities.
Rāma also thought, upon seeing the king like that: / “Ah! This son of Daśaratha, the wise king of kings,
comes on foot, wearing the dress of matted hair and bark garments! / Truly, no other sorrow of mine while dwelling in the forest
was like that which turns about in his mind through separation from me! / Ah, look at my brother, my friend dearer than life!
Hearing that I have arrived nearby, with overjoyed aged ministers / and accompanied by Vasiṣṭha, Bharata comes to see me.”
Speaking thus, the lord of men [descended] from the Puṣpaka [chariot] into the courtyard of the sky, / shown honor by Bibhīṣaṇa, Hanūmat, and Lakṣmaṇa.
He descended swiftly from the vehicle, his heart melted with longing, / crying out again and again, "O brother, brother, and again brother, brother, brother!"
Seeing that Rāmacandra had disembarked accompanied by the gods, / the wise Bharata, melted with longing for his brother, beheld him; / and shedding tears of joy, he bowed down prostrate like a staff.
Raghunātha too, seeing him fallen prostrate like a staff upon the earth, / raised him up and embraced him with both arms, his gaze filled with joy.
Though raised up, he did not stand up at all, weeping repeatedly, / his arms clinging firmly in grasp around Rāmacandra's lotus feet.
Bharata said: / "Have mercy on me, wicked, vicious, and sinful as I am, / O Rāmacandra, mighty-armed one, out of compassion, O treasure of mercy!
That very foot which deemed the touch of the Videha princess's hand too harsh, / wandered in the forest, O Rāma, on my account!"
Having spoken thus, distressed, his face covered in tears, embracing [him] again and again, / he stood before [him] with joined palms, his face overcome with joy.
Raghunātha, the ocean of compassion, having embraced his younger brother, / bowing and respectfully inquiring after the chief counselor,
sat upon the seat of the Puṣpaka together with his brother Bharata. / Bharata beheld Sītā, his blameless sister-in-law.
Was she Anasūyā to Atri, or Lopāmudrā to the pot-born [Agastya]? / He regarded the devoted wife, the daughter of Janaka, and bowed down to her.
"Mother, forgive whatever sin was committed by me, devoid of sense. / Women devoted to their husbands like you bring welfare to all."
The illustrious daughter of Janaka too, looking upon her brother-in-law with affection, / bestowed blessings upon him and inquired about his well-being.
All those who had mounted that excellent aerial chariot in the courtyard of the sky / beheld within a moment their father's city close at hand.

title: tṛtīyo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Śeṣa said: / Having seen the capital city, the dwelling place of his own people, / the wise and heroic Rāma, eager to see it after a long time, rejoiced.
Bharata too sent his friend, the minister named Sumukha, / toward the city to arrange for the city festival.
Bharata said: / "Let the people quickly prepare the festival of Raghunātha's arrival, / delightful in every mansion, with various festive arrangements.
Let the royal highways be cleared of dust, sprinkled with sandalwood water, / decorated with masses of flowers, and crowded with glad and flourishing people.
Let all their courtyards be decorated with the luster of colorful banners; / let the monkeys look upon it just like a rainbow at the arrival of clouds.
Let people cause incense of aloe to be burnt in every home, / seeing whose smoke the peacocks may dance at play.
Let them decorate my mountain-like elephants, well-governed by drivers, / in many ways with red chalk and other secondary minerals.
Let swift horses, painted beautifully, shine repeatedly, / at the mere sight of whose speed the steed of heaven abandons its pride.
Let thousands of lovely maidens adorned with all ornaments, / mounted upon elephants, scatter pearls.
Let the wives of brāhmaṇas, holding vessels with dūrvā grass and turmeric, / auspicious married women, perform the lustration of the great king Rāma.
May Kausalyā, distressed at the message of reunion with her son, / though very emaciated, attain joy, greatly eager to behold him."
"Let the joyful populace make such arrangements / that bring beauty to the city for the arrival of Rāma."
Śeṣa said: / Hearing this speech, Sumukha, best of counselors, / went to the city to erect festive archways.
Having reached that city, the minister named Sumukha / announced to the people the great festival of Rāma's arrival.
Hearing that Raghunātha had reached the city, the people were exceedingly delighted, / having previously abandoned pleasures and comforts due to separation from him.
Brāhmaṇas accomplished in the Vedas, pure, with darbha grass in their hands / and wrapped in washed upper garments, went to the venerable Raghunāyaka.
Kṣatriyas who were the most heroic, best bearers of bows and arrows, / heroes victorious in battle many times, also went to him.
Vaiśyas abundant in wealth, their hands adorned with coins, / wearing clean white garments, approached the lord of men.
Śūdras who were devoted to twice-borns, steadfast in their own proper conduct, / devoted to Vedic customs, also went to the lord of the city.
Whatever people practiced a trade, established in their own respective work, / taking their own wares, went to the glorious king Rāma.
Thus, at the prince's command, filled with an inundation of joy / and accompanied by various celebrations, they came to the lord of men.
Śeṣa said: / Raghunātha too, surrounded by all the deities in their respective vehicles, / entered high into the city, which had been made enchanting.
The monkeys, leaping about, traversing the pathways of the sky, / their limbs arrayed in their own splendor, followed toward the excellent city.
Having quickly descended from the Puṣpaka, Rāma, together with Sītā / and surrounded by his retinue, then mounted a palanquin.
He then entered Ayodhyā, where festive archways had been erected, / which was crowded with joyful and well-nourished people, and adorned with celebrations.
Shining amid loudly sounded lutes, paṇava drums, bherī drums, and other instruments, / praised by sūtas, māgadhas, and bards:
"Victory to Rāghava Rāma! Victory to the ornament of the solar race! / Victory to the son of Daśaratha, the Lord! May the protector of the worlds be victorious!"
Hearing such auspicious speech of the citizens, whose limbs were thrilled with joy, / who shone with the bristling of their hair born from the sight of Rāma,
he entered the excellent highway, adorned with crossways and squares, / sprinkled with sandalwood water, and furnished with flowers and fresh shoots.
Then certain women of the city, resorting to the openings of the latticed windows, / filled with longing to behold the form of Raghunātha, said:
The women of the city said: / "Blessed indeed were the Bhilla maidens in the forests who drank in Rāma's lotus face / with their blue-lotus eyes—these women whose great fortune came to fruition!
Behold the blessed, lotus-eyed face of Lord Śrī Rāma, the abode of heroism, / the sight of which even the gods headed by Brahmā attained; ah, we too are endowed with great fortune!
Behold this face of sweet smile, its noble head shining with a diadem, / bearing high nostrils and lips whose radiant hue puts the bandhūka flower to shame!"

Looking with glances like lotus petals upon those women who had spoken thus with an abundance of affection, / the teacher of all, joyful, his limbs worn from traveling, desired to go to his mother's house, observing the people who bore an undiminished weight of love.

title: caturtho'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Vātsyāyana said: / "O sovereign lord of serpents, master capable of bearing the burden of the earth, / listen to a single doubt of mine, and kindly explain it to me.
From the very moment when Raghunātha's departure to the forest took place, / she remained with a void mind within her body,
distressed by separation from him, emaciated in body, and extremely sorrowful; / having heard from the minister Sumukha that Raghunātha had returned,"
How did she rejoice? What happened? What kind of sign was marked there? / What did she say to the one who brought the message of Rāmacandra?
Dispel this doubt of mine concerning the rising of the virtues of Raghunātha; / tell it to me, who am listening attentively, out of your favor.
Śeṣa said: / Well asked, O highly fortunate one, foremost among the twice-born! / Therefore, hear it directly from me as I speak, with single-minded attention.
Having drunk again and again that nectar of Rāma's arrival flowing from his lotus mouth, / she became bewildered, her limbs rendered motionless—ah!
"Is this a dream of mine, bewildered as I am? Or is it a speech that causes delusion? / For me, ill-fated as I am, how could there be the sight of Rāma again?
By much austerity this infant son was obtained; / and through some sin of mine he fell into separation once again.
O Sumantra, is Rāma well, together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa? / How does the hero, dwelling in the forest, remember me, who am so grief-stricken?"

Thus she lamented loudly, having remembered the lord of Raghu's line; / utterly bewildered, she did not perceive anything of her own or of another. / Sumukha too, seeing his mother so exceedingly grieved,
fanned her with the hem of his garment; and she regained consciousness. / He spoke gentle, repeatedly joy-bringing words to the mother;
bringing to mind the arrival of Raghunātha, he made her joyful once more: / "Mother, know that Raghunātha has arrived home, together with Lakṣmaṇa,
and accompanied by Sītā. See them and shower them with blessings!" / Having heard those truthful words spoken by Sumukha,
she attained such joy as I cannot even comprehend. / Rising, she went into the courtyard, the hair on her body bristling with joy;
her limbs trembling with joy, shedding tears, she looked upon Rāma. / Meanwhile, King Rāma, mounted on a palanquin,
prudent as he was, reached the dwelling of his own mother, Kaikeyī, before all others. / Kaikeyī too, bent low under the weight of shame before Rāma standing in front of her,
did not say anything, but fell into great and repeated anxiety. / Rāma, the banner of the Solar dynasty, seeing his mother ashamed,
spoke, consoling her with words filled with modesty. / Śrī Rāma said: / "Mother, having gone to the forest, everything was done by me accordingly.
What else shall I do now by your command, O mother? / Nothing deficient has been done by me; why do you not look at me again?
Welcome him, Bharata, and look at me with blessings!" / Even hearing that speech of his, O sinless one, she, her face cast down,
slowly and softly replied: "Rāma, go to your own abode." / Rāma too, that best among men, having heard the words of his mother,
bowed down and, being a treasure-house of compassion, went to the house of Sumitrā. / Sumitrā, the high-minded, seeing Rāma along with her son,
spoke with blessings, saying: "Live long! Live long!" / And Rāmabhadra, having bowed at his mother's feet
and embraced her with delight, spoke these words again: / "O mother, bearing jewels in your womb, no one has ever done what was done by my brother,
just as this wise one dispelled my grief.
That Sītā, abducted by Rāvaṇa, has been regained by me— / know, mother, that all that is the deed of Lakṣmaṇa!"
Accepting with his head the blessing given by Sumitrā, / he set out for the abode of his own mother, surrounded by the wise.
Seeing his mother thrilled with joy, eager for the sight of him, / Hari quickly descended from his carriage and grasped her feet.
His mother, her mind overwhelmed with longing to see him, / embracing Rāma again and again, attained sheer delight.
Horripilation occurred on her body, and her voice became choked with emotion; / tears of joy, indeed warm, flowed forth as if from a flood of calamity.
Seeing his mother, humble, devoid of her two earrings, / wearing a body destitute of hand ornaments and foot ornaments,
emaciated in limbs, yet slightly delighted by the sight of him, he felt grief; / but thinking, "This is not a time for sorrow," he spoke to her.
Śrī Rāma said: / "Mother, for a long time your feet were not served by me; / therefore, forgive the offense of ill-fated me!
Those sons who are not zealous in the service of their mother and father, / they, O mother, must be considered merely worms born of semen.
What could I do? By our father's command I went to the Daṇḍaka forest; / even there, by the gracious glance of your mercy, I crossed the ocean of sorrow.
Sītā was abducted by Rāvaṇa and taken to Laṅkā; / by your grace, having slain that lord of the rākṣasas, she was regained by me.
Here is Sītā, devoted to her husband, fallen at your feet; / favor her quickly, bewildered as she is, with her mind placed at your feet!"
Having heard those words, she bestowed blessings / upon that devoted wife, her daughter-in-law who had fallen at her feet, and spoke to her:
"O Sītā, delight for a long time together with your husband, O radiant woman! / Bearing sons, purify your own family, O purifying one!
Women devoted to their husbands like you, who follow the joys and sorrows of their husbands, / do not suffer grief in the three worlds—this is the truth.
O daughter of Videha, by your own self your lineage has been purified by you, / as you followed the pair of Rāma's lotus feet to the great forest.
What wonder is it that men crush millions of enemies, / when in their house there is a virtuous wife desiring what is dear to her husband?"
Having spoken thus to the wife of the lord of Raghu's line, whose eyes were lovely, / she fell silent, delighted, the hair on her body standing on end with joy.
Then his brother Bharata offered up to the wise Rāmacandra / the great kingdom bestowed upon him by his father.
Those ministers, their bodies thrilled with joy, summoned astrologers / skilled in counsel and inquired with supreme reverence for an auspicious moment.
At an auspicious moment, on a favorable day endowed with an auspicious asterism, / they, being ready, performed the consecration to the great kingdom.
Having drawn the earth possessing seven continents upon a beautiful tiger skin, / the king of kings, the great monarch, sat upon it.
From that very day, the minds of the virtuous went to great delight, / while the minds of the wicked, who torment others, became dejected.
Women were devoted to fidelity to their husbands through devotion to their husbands; / never did people commit sin even in their minds, O sage.
Daityas, gods, snakes, yakṣas, asuras, and great serpents— / all, staying on the path of righteousness, bore Rāma's command upon their heads.
They were engaged in helping others, delighted in the happiness of their own duty; / the auspicious moments of day and night were passed in the joys of learning.
Even a strong wind did not forcibly snatch away fine garments / from travelers along the road; no mention was there of thieves.
Rāma was a giver of wealth to supplicants, full of pity, a treasure of compassion; / accompanied by his brothers, he daily offered praise to the guru and gods.

title: paṃcamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Śeṣa said: / Then the gods, bowing low, their minds gladdened by the slaying of the lord of the daityas named Rāvaṇa, / praised Rāma who had been consecrated.

The gods said: / "Victory, O son of Daśaratha, remover of the distress of the gods! Victory, victory, burner of the race of dānavas! / Victory, destroyer of the enemy whose hands were eager to seize the celestial nymphs!"
Poets are eager to describe that destruction of the lord of demons wrought by you; / but at the cosmic dissolution, Lord of the Universe, you playfully swallow the masses of the worlds again.

Victory, O you freed from the sorrows of birth, old age, and the rest! Powerful one, uplift, uplift! / Victory, O you who took birth in the ocean of the solar dynasty, unaging, immortal, infallible one!
Through the names of you, the supreme deity, even great sinners have been purified; / what then of good people led by excellent twice-borns, who have obtained a fine human body?

We desire in our hearts with devotion the pair of your feet, praised by Hara and Viriñci, / which bestows the fulfillment of desired wishes, adorned with purified marks like the barley-grain and others.

If you, who possess a radiance surpassing the form of the god of love, did not bestow freedom from fear upon the earth, / then how, O compassionate and pure one, could the hosts of gods ever experience happiness again?

Whenever the sons of Danu cause us suffering, then and there may you take birth on earth, / though unborn, imperishable, and supreme Lord, O all-pervading one, assuming your own nature, worshipped by your own.

After covering the surface of the earth with your virtuous deeds resembling the nectar of the dead, destroying sin, / and praised by immortals proclaiming your qualities, return quickly indeed to your own realm.

Beginningless, the foremost, wearing an unaging form, enchanting, crowned, radiant like the god of love— / may he who forcefully struck down his enemies, whose lotus feet are served by the enemy of Smara, bring victory!
Having spoken thus, all those gods, headed by Brahmā and Indra, / gratified by the destruction of their enemy, bowed down repeatedly to the leader of Raghu's line.
Exceedingly delighted by this praise, the glorious lord of Raghu's line, / seeing those gods bowed down with their necks bent, spoke:

Śrī Rāma said:
