text_mt: Śeṣa said: / In chariots yoked with noble steeds, full of splendor, laden with all weapons and missiles, / accompanied by various gems, they advanced against that vile Rākṣasa.
Seeing them, the Rākṣasa, standing in his flying chariot, spoke / in a voice deep as a thundercloud, as if repeatedly terrifying them:
“Let the warriors not fight; let them go back to their own dwelling! / Let them not abandon their lives; I will not release this excellent horse.
I am known as Vidyunmālin, a dear friend of Rāvaṇa; / I have come to make retribution on behalf of my departed friend.
Where is that Rāma who departed after striking down my friend Rāvaṇa? / And where is his brother, the crest-jewel of all warriors?
Having slain him, the younger brother of Rāma, I will obtain retribution for him, / drinking the blood rising with bubbles from the passage of his throat!”
Having heard these words, Puṣkala, the foremost and best among warriors, / addressed him who was endowed with valor and prowess.
Puṣkala said: / “Warriors do not utter boasts in battle; / they demonstrate their prowess through showers of their own weapons and missiles.
Having seized the horse of him by whom Rāvaṇa was slain / along with his friends and kin, where will you go, O arrogant fool?
You will fall by the arrows released from the bow of Śatrughna; / jackals will eat you as you lie fallen on the ground, bereft of life.
Do not roar, O wicked one, while I, the servant of Rāma, am present! / Warriors roar in battle after conquering the enemy, because of their great triumph!”
Śeṣa said: / As that heroic Puṣkala, wild in battle, was speaking thus, / the foremost Rākṣasa struck him forcefully in the heart with a javelin.
As that great iron javelin mounted with gold came flying, / that Puṣkala cut it down with three very fierce, sharp arrows.
Deprived of its brilliance by the arrows, it fell to the earth in three pieces; / as it fell, it shone like the threefold power of Viṣṇu.
Seeing that spear broken, the tormentor of foes, the Rākṣasa, / swiftly seized a three-pronged trident made of iron.
The lord of Rākṣasas hurled it, sharp-pointed and blazing like fire; / as it came, he named Puṣkala reduced it to sesame-sized pieces with arrows.
Having swiftly shattered the trident, that servant of Rāghava, / Puṣkala, took up his bow and sharp arrows swift as thought.
Those arrows struck swiftly into his heart, making it red with blood, / just as the captivating virtues of Viṣṇu produce devotion in the heart of a Vaiṣṇava.
Tormented by the pain of the piercing of those arrows, the haughty Vidyunmālin / seized a terrible club, intent on killing Puṣkala.
The club hurled by him named Vidyunmālin / struck [Puṣkala] in the heart, quickly bringing about fainting.
Struck by the club, shaking and trembling, that hero / Puṣkala, the tormentor of foes, fell onto the seat of his chariot.
Then his brother Ugradaṃṣṭra fought Lakṣmīnidhi / with various weapons and missiles discharged, which take away the lives of heroes.
Instantly regaining consciousness, Puṣkala said to the Rākṣasa: / “Blessed are you, foremost of Rākṣasas; your prowess is supreme!
Now look at my own great vow, honored by heroes: / today I will cast you down to the ground from your chariot with sharp arrows!”
Having spoken thus, he seized a sharp and irresistible arrow, / blazing with the fiery energy of fire and endowed with great nobility.
As soon as [the Rākṣasa] showed his prowess to counter it, / that very fierce arrow with a sharp point penetrated his heart.
Perplexed by that arrow, his mind reeling, that Rākṣasa / fell from the seat of his flying chariot to the ground, bereft of consciousness.
His elder brother was seen falling by Ugradaṃṣṭra; / grasping him, fearing the enemy, he brought him inside the chariot.
In great rage, he spoke to the enemy, Puṣkala, the foremost among the strong: / “Having struck down my brother, where will you go, O wicked-minded one?
Only by utterly conquering me in battle will you attain supreme victory; / while I remain, let the hope of victory be turned away from your heart!”
While he was speaking thus, [Puṣkala], his eyes filled with wrath, / swiftly struck that wicked one in the heart with ten arrows.
Struck with ten arrows by the high-souled Puṣkala, / the evil-minded one grew enraged in his heart and set out to slay him.

Grinding his teeth in anger, he raised his fist and struck,
roaring loudly, creating in [every] heart the fear of a thunderbolt strike.

Struck by the fist, the hero Puṣkala, skilled in supreme missiles,
did not tremble, desiring the crushing of that wicked-souled one.

He unleashed sharp calf-tooth-tipped arrows into [the demon's] chest;
pained by those arrows, the daitya seized a trident.

Blazing, three-pronged, exceedingly terrifying with garlands of flames,
that dreadful [trident] struck the chest of the great hero Puṣkala.

Struck by that trident, the best of archers swooned;
having fallen into a deep faint, he collapsed onto his chariot.

Knowing that he had fallen into a swoon, Hanūmān, the son of the wind god,
his heart agitated with fury, spoke to that rākṣasa:

"Where are you going, evil-minded one, while I remain as a fighter?
I will kill you with kicks of my feet—you who have come as the thief of the horse!"

Having spoken thus, standing in the sky, he tore with the tips of his claws
and killed the great daityas, the enemy soldiers standing in the aerial chariot.

Some were struck with his tail, some struck with the soles of his feet,
and some were torn apart with both arms by the son of the wind.

Some were destroyed and killed, some were struck down in a faint,
and others fled, afflicted by the terror of the blows of his feet.

Many exceedingly dreadful rākṣasas were killed there;
they were cut down, torn asunder, and split into two by the son of the wind.

That aerial chariot which moved at will, its walls and archways broken,
was surrounded on all sides by asuras crying out in despair.

As Hanūmān fought heroically, now on the ground, now in the sky,
that vehicle moving at will, difficult to approach, could be seen here and there.

Wherever that aerial chariot went, right there the monkey born of the wind,
assuming forms at will, was seen striking.

When the great multitude standing in the aerial chariot was thus thrown into confusion,
the daitya lord Ugradaṃṣṭra approached Hanūmān.

"O monkey, you have performed a great feat in striking down the warriors!
If you stand for a moment, I shall sever your life!"

Having spoken thus, that evil-minded one struck Hanūmān
with a very sharp trident shining with the brilliance of blazing fire.

The mighty one caught in his mouth that incoming trident
and crushed it entirely, though forged completely of iron.

Having crushed that iron trident discharged by the daitya,
the powerful Hanumān struck him with many slaps of his hand.

Struck by the lord of monkeys with slaps here and there,
he, in agony, unleashed an illusion that caused terror to all the worlds.

Then an intense darkness arose in which no one at all could be seen,
wherein many people did not recognize their own kin from strangers.

Rocks resembling mountain peaks fell upon the good warriors;
struck by them, they all became bewildered.
Lightnings flashed there, dense rain clouds roared, / they rained pus and blood, and released filthy water.
And many headless trunks were seen falling from the sky, / with severed heads adorned with earrings.
Naked, exceedingly deformed, with disheveled hair, and terrible faces, / dreadful Daityas causing terror were seen on every side.
Then the people, agitated and terrified of one another, / took to flight, considering it a great portent of disaster.
Then the highly renowned Śatrughna arrived standing in his chariot; / remembering Śrī Rāma, he placed arrows upon his bow.
Having dispersed that illusion with the Mohanāstra weapon, the valiant one, / scattering showers of arrows in the sky, rained them down upon the demon in battle.
Then the directions became clear, and the sun shone bright; / the clouds dispersed the way they came, and the lightnings subsided.
Then a flying chariot filled with Rākṣasas was seen ahead, / exceedingly large and turbulent with shouts of "Cut! Pierce!"
Hundreds of thousands of arrows adorned with golden fletchings / repeatedly fell upon the flying chariot moving at will in the sky.
Then the flying chariot was broken and was no longer seen on high; / it lay on the ground in one place like a shattered piece of its own city.
Then the enraged Daitya fitted arrows to his bow; / scattering Rāma's brother with those arrows, he roared.
Hundreds of those sharp-pointed arrows struck his body in abundance; / they looked splendid, carrying streams of blood.
Endowed with supreme power, Śatrughna placed upon his bow / the Vāyavya weapon whose deity is Vāyu, which caused the Rākṣasas to tremble.
Struck by that weapon, demons falling from the sky with disheveled hair / were seen like swarms of sky-faring bhūtas and vetālas.
Seeing that weapon discharged by Raghunātha's brother, / the son of Danu fitted the Pāśupata weapon onto his bow.
Thereupon vetālas, bhūtas, pretas, and night-roving demons surged forward, / bearing skulls and shears, drinking abundant blood.
Indeed, they joyfully drank the blood of Śatrughna's heroes, / even of the living, irresistible and resplendent with shears in hand.
Seeing that weapon pervading all, crushing the warriors, / he discharged the weapon named Nārāyaṇāstra to repel it.
The Nārāyaṇāstra immediately warded off all of them; / urged on by the night-roamer, they all met their destruction.
Then the enraged night-roamer Vidyunmālin seized / a fierce, sharp, and dreadful trident to kill Śatrughna.
As Vidyunmālin approached in battle with the trident in his hand, / [Śatrughna] struck his arm with crescent-tipped arrows.
His arm severed by those arrows, he rushed forward to strike with his head: / "You are slain! Begone, Śatrughna! Who will be your protector?"
As he was speaking thus, with sharp arrows he swiftly severed / the head, adorned with earrings, of that strong and heroic [warrior].
Seeing him decapitated, the powerful Ugradaṃṣṭra / began to strike with his fist Śatrughna, who was attended by heroes.
Śatrughna, however, with a razor-sharp arrow cut off the head / of the warriors skilled in all weapons who were rushing onto the battlefield.
The surviving Rākṣasas, now left leaderless, all fled; / then, bowing before Śatrughna, they surrendered the captured horse.
Then the sounds of vīṇās and the blasts of conches on every side, / and the charming victory shouts of the valiant warriors, were heard.

title: paṃcatriṃśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Śeṣa said: / Having recovered that horse captured by the Rākṣasas, King Śatrughna, / accompanied by Puṣkala, experienced immense joy.
Those warriors, their limbs sprinkled with blood, along with Lakṣmīnidhi, / praised the great king who was filled with enthusiasm for battle.
When that great, unconquerable Daitya Vidyunmālin was slain, / all the gods cast away their fear and attained great happiness, O sage.
The rivers became clear, and the sun became bright; / breezes blew, sprinkled with fragrant water and possessing pure vigor.
Those great heroes, clad in armor, standing in chariots, with clean bodies, / and endowed with the glory of victory, all said to the king:
The heroes said: / By good fortune, O highly wise one, the Daitya Vidyunmālin has been slain by you, / out of fear of whom the gods were terrified and driven from heaven.
By good fortune the splendid, great horse of Raghunātha has been regained; / by good fortune you shall march everywhere and conquer the circle of the earth.
O lord, release this steed, charming and swift as thought; / let there be no delay in time here, O highly wise one.
Śeṣa said: / Having heard those timely words of the heroes, / praising them with "Well done! Well done!", he released the excellent horse.
Released, it roamed toward the northern region, well-protected / by the best charioteers, infantrymen, and horses, skilled in all weapons and missiles.
Listen, O Vātsyāyana, to this captivating account of what happened there to Śatrughna, / which burns away heaps of sins.
He then reached the bank of the Revā, served by hosts of sages, / which was like the essence of a heap of blue sapphires under the guise of water.
Bowing to all those best sages, surrounded by warriors, / he followed behind the gem of a horse that roamed wherever it pleased.
While proceeding, [he saw] there an aged hermitage built of palāśa leaves, / sprinkled by the billowing waves of the Revā, an abode that removes sin.
Seeing it, Śatrughna, skilled in all duties regarding dharma and practical affairs, / spoke to Sumati, who was omniscient and versed in policy:
The king said: / O minister, tell me, whose sacred-looking hermitage is this? / O best among those skilled in inquiry, tell this to me who am asking.
Śeṣa said: / Having heard these words, Sumati spoke to the king / in clear, smiling speech, showing his own affection:
Sumati said: / By seeing him, O great king, we shall indeed become cleansed of sin, / [seeing] that best of sages devoted to all sacred scriptures.
Therefore, having bowed, inquire of him; he will tell you everything; / he is exceedingly eager for the nectar of Raghunātha's lotus feet.
Known by the name Āraṇyaka, a worshipper of Raghunātha's feet, / he is filled with exceedingly severe asceticism and skilled in the meaning of all sacred treatises.
Having heard those words of his, reinforced with dharma and worldly welfare, / he then set out, accompanied by a few attendants, to see him.
Hanumān, the heroic Puṣkala, Sumati the best of ministers, / Lakṣmīnidhi of foremost majesty, Subāhu, and Sumada—
Surrounded by these, the noble-minded King Śatrughna arrived at the hermitage / to pay homage to Āraṇyaka, the best of the twice-born.
Having approached, he then offered obeisance to that best of ascetics, / together with all those heroes whose necks were bent in modesty.
Seeing all those kings, headed by Śatrughna, bowed low, / he then offered water for hospitality and foot-washing, along with fruits and roots.
He said to all those kings: "Where have you met together? / How have you come here? Tell all of that, O sinless ones."
Hearing these words of that best of sages, O brāhmaṇa, / Sumati, skilled in disputation, spoke:
Sumati said: / "This horse of the king of Raghu's lineage is guarded by all; / the hero will perform a sacrifice supplied with every requisite."
Hearing that statement of theirs, the best of sages spoke, / as if dispelling all terrible darkness with the radiance of his teeth:
The forest-dweller said: / "What use are diverse other sacrifices supplied with every requisite, / which certainly yield meager merit and grant a perishable status?
A deluded person, abandoning Hari, worships another— / [Hari,] the hero of the Raghus, the lord of Ramā, who bestows a state of enduring sovereignty.
He who, merely remembered by men, carries away a mountain of sins— / abandoning him, a fool torments himself with sacrifices, yogas, vows, and the like.
Ah, behold the delusion of people, how exceedingly deceived they are! / Leaving aside the worship of Rāma, which is easy to attain, one practices what is hard to attain.
He is contemplated by those with desires or even by yogins free from desires; / he grants liberation to men, destroying all sins merely when remembered.
Formerly, in my search for reality, seeking out a wise man, / I went to many holy sites, but no one pointed out the truth to me.
Then, through great fortune indeed, the sage Lomaśa was encountered— / arrived from heaven with the desire of making a pilgrimage.
Then, bowing down to that great sage, I questioned him— / that long-lived one, whose two feet are served by great yogins:
"O master, today a wondrous and hard-to-attain human birth has been obtained by me; / wishing to cross over the terrible ocean of cyclic existence, what should be done?
Deliberate and tell: Is that a vow, a gift, a muttered prayer, a sacrifice, / or a god who indeed conveys one across the ocean of cyclic existence?
Knowing which, from the ocean of your mercy, I may cross this terrible cyclic existence— / tell me that, O lord of yoga, you who have crossed to the other side of all scriptures' meaning."
Having heard these words of mine, the best of sages said: / "Listen with a single-pointed mind, O brāhmaṇa, endowed with supreme faith!"
There are gifts, holy sites, vows, restraints, observances, / and yogas, and likewise many sacrifices; they are bestowers of heaven.
I shall proclaim the supreme secret, the destroyer of all sins; / hear that, O highly fortunate one, which conveys one across the ocean of cyclic existence.
It must not be told to an atheist, nor again to one without faith; / it must not be given to a slanderer, a rogue, nor an enemy of devotion.
It should be told to a devotee of Rāma, peaceful, free from desire and wrath— / this supreme [secret] that causes the destruction of all suffering.
There is no god higher than Rāma; there is no vow higher than Rāma; / there is no yoga higher than Rāma; there is no sacrifice higher than Rāma.
Remembering him, murmuring his name, and worshipping him supreme, a man / attains the highest prosperity, both in this world and the next.
Recalled and meditated upon with the mind, he grants the fruits of all desires; / he gives supreme devotion, which conveys one across the ocean of cyclic existence.
Even an outcaste, having remembered Rāma, attains the supreme destination; / what then of those like you, devoted to the Vedas and scriptures?
The secret of all the Vedas and scriptures has been revealed to you; / act accordingly, so that your desire may be fulfilled.
There is one god: Rāmacandra; there is one vow: his worship; / there is one mantra: his name; and scripture is indeed his praise.
Therefore, worship delightful Rāmacandra with all your being, / so that the ocean of cyclic existence becomes trifling like a cow's hoofprint."
[The forest-dweller said:] "Having heard those words of his, I made another inquiry: / 'How is the god meditated upon, or how is he worshipped by men?
Tell me in full, O all-knowing one of great intellect, / knowing which I may achieve my goal in the three worlds, O best of sages.'"
[The forest-dweller said:] "Having heard this speech of mine and having reflected, that Lomaśa / told me everything, beginning with meditation on Rāma:
[Lomaśa said:] "Listen, O best of brāhmaṇas; I shall tell what was asked by you, O sinless one, / how the lord of Ramā, the burner of the fever of cyclic existence, is pleased.
In the delightful city of Ayodhyā, adorned with splendid pavilions, / at the base of the wish-fulfilling tree that grants the fulfillment of all desires, one should meditate
upon a throne adorned with great emeralds, gold, sapphires, and other gems, / captivating to the mind, dispelling darkness by its radiance.
Seated upon it, the delightful king of the Raghus, / his body dark as a blade of dūrvā grass, worshipped by the lord of the gods,
possessing a face that scorns the beauty of the full moon of the full-moon night, / bearing a forehead resembling the crescent of the eighth-day moon,
abounding in the beauty of black locks, adorned with a jewel-crested crown, / radiant with beautiful earrings shaped like makaras,
shining with lips having the fine luster of coral, / beautifully adorned with rows of teeth shaped like the rays of the moon,
his face adorned with a sweet tongue like a china-rose, / upon which dwell the Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, along with the scriptures,
adorned with the beauty of a neck possessing the luster of a conch shell, / bearing broad, fleshy, noble shoulders like a lion,
bearing arms with long limbs, marked with armlets and bracelets, / adorned with the splendors of rings and diamonds, reaching down to the knees,
bearing a broad chest adorned by the dwelling of Lakṣmī, / marked with the wondrous signs of Śrīvatsa and others, exceedingly captivating,
with a large belly, a deep navel, radiant with fine hips, / endowed especially with beauty by means of a jeweled girdle,
with two spotless thighs, splendid knees adorned with glory, / and two feet adorned with the auspicious lines of the thunderbolt, the barley-corn, and the goad,
which are to be meditated on by yogins, tender and radiant. / Having meditated on and remembered [him], you will cross the ocean of cyclic existence.
Always worshipping him with sandalwood paste and the like as one wishes, / one attains supreme prosperity, both in this world and the next.
The supreme meditation on Rāma was asked by you, O great king; / that has been told to you. Cross now the ocean of cyclic existence."

title: ṣaṭtriṃśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Śeṣa said: / Having heard this supreme, great [teaching] from Lomaśa, the chief of brāhmaṇas / again questioned that sage, all-knowing and best among yogins.
The forest-dweller said: / "O best of sages, tell me this; I ask you, O highly intelligent one! / Endowed with compassion, teachers speak everything to a servant.
Who is this Rāma, O highly fortunate one, who is constantly meditated on by you? / What are his deeds? Tell me, O bull among the twice-born!
For what purpose did he descend? Why did he take on human state? / Tell me all that swiftly, for the dispelling of my doubt."
Śeṣa said: / Having heard this exceedingly beautiful speech of the sage, / Lomaśa related the wondrous deeds of Rāma:
[Lomaśa said:] "Seeing the worlds plunged into hell, the lord of lords of yoga [descended] / in order to spread fame in the world, by which one will cross what is terrible.
Knowing this, the ocean of mercy, the captivating supreme Lord, / accompanied by Śrī, took an incarnation here in four forms.
Formerly, when the Tretā age arrived, the delight of the Raghus, with his complete portion, / the lotus-eyed Rāma was born in the solar dynasty."
That Rāma, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, wearing side-locks of hair, was a youth; / and by their father's command, the two were devoted to following Viśvāmitra.
The two boys were given by the king to protect the sacrifice; / self-controlled, bow-bearing heroes, devoted to following Viśvāmitra.
As the two were journeying along the path, an ogre named Tāṭakā / met them in the dreadful forest, indeed to cause an obstacle to them.
By the ṛṣi's command, Rāma, the Rāghava, dispatched Tāṭakā / to the torment of Yama by his mastery of the science of archery.
Ahalyā, Gautama's wife, who had been turned into a rock through the act of Indra, / by the touch of the sole of his foot was reborn in her true form.
When Viśvāmitra's sacrifice was well underway, the best of Raghus / struck down Mārīca and Subāhu with supreme arrows.
The bow of the Lord that stood in Janaka's palace was broken; / in his fifteenth year, Rāma [won] the princess of Mithilā, then six years old.
He wed in marriage the charming Sītā, who was not born of a womb; / having won Sītā, the Rāghava was then fulfilled in his aim.
Then for twelve years Rāma took delight with her; / in his twenty-seventh year, [the king] arranged his heir-apparency.
Then Kaikeyī begged two boons of the king; / by one of them: "Let Rāma, together with Sītā and accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa,
wearing matted hair, wander forth for fourteen years here; / and by the second, let Bharata be my master of heir-apparency!"
The king sent Rāma into exile together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa; / for three nights he had only water as food, and on the fourth day ate fruit.
On the fifth day, Rāma made his dwelling on Citrakūṭa; / then in the thirteenth year, O great sage, at Pañcavaṭī,
Rāma disfigured Śūrpaṇakhā, the night-roaming ogre-woman; / and as he roamed the forest together with Jānakī,
the ogre came to abduct her as a consequence of sins; / then on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, in the hour named Vṛnda,
the ten-necked one abducted Sītā in the absence of the two descendants of Raghu. / As she was thus being carried off by him, she wailed like an osprey:
"Rāma, Rāma! Save me, save me who am carried off by an ogre!" / Just as a hawk overcome by hunger might carry off a crying quail,
so Rāvaṇa, overcome by lust, carried off Janaka's daughter. / As he was thus carrying off Janaka's daughter, Jaṭāyu, the king of birds, then
fought with the lord of ogres; and struck down by Rāvaṇa, he fell. / But on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, as she was living in Rāvaṇa's abode,
Sampāti told of her among the monkeys in the tenth month. / On the eleventh day, from Mount Mahendra, [Hanumān] leapt across a hundred leagues.
Hanumān searched through Laṅkā during that night; / at the end of that night, Hanumān indeed had the sight of Sītā.
On the twelfth day Hanumān took his station in a śiṃśapā tree; / in that night there was conversation to gain the confidence of Jānakī.
Then on the thirteenth day a battle took place with Akṣa and others; / and on the fourteenth day the monkey was bound with the weapon of Brahmā by the conqueror of Indra.
The burning of Laṅkā was accomplished by fire joined to his tail; / on the full-moon day the monkey returned to Mount Mahendra.
Five days were spent on the path from the first day of the dark fortnight of Mārga; / having returned, on the sixth day, the Honey Grove was indeed destroyed.
On the seventh day occurred the delivery of the token of recognition and the reporting of everything; / on the eighth, under the asterism Uttarā Phālgunī, at the hour named Vijaya,
when the thousand-rayed sun had reached the meridian, occurred the setting out of the Rāghava; / having made a vow, Rāma departed for the southern direction:
"Crossing even the ocean, I will slay the lord of ogres." / When he departed for the southern direction, Sugrīva also became his friend.
In seven days occurred the pitching of the camp by the ocean; / from the first day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa up to the third,
the arrival of the Rāghava with his army took place at the ocean; / and on the fourth day, Bibhīṣaṇa united with Rāma.
For crossing the ocean, he undertook deliberation on the fifth day; / Rāma undertook waiting for death without food for four days.
There was the obtaining of the boon from the ocean together with the indication of a means; / then on the tenth day was the commencement, and on the thirteenth the completion.
On the fourteenth day Rāma stationed his army on Mount Suvela; / from the full-moon day to the end of the second, the ferrying across of the army took three days.
Having crossed the ocean, Rāma, accompanied by the army of the lord of monkeys / and accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, besieged the city of Laṅkā for the sake of Sītā.
From the third to the end of the tenth day was the encampment, for eight days; / the arrival of Śuka and Sāraṇa took place there on the eleventh day.
On the twelfth day named the dark fortnight of Pauṣa occurred the counting of the army, / and the description by Śārdūla of the sudden assault of the monkey lords.
From the thirteenth to the new-moon day, in three days, in Laṅkā / Rāvaṇa then carried out the muster of the army and the rousing for battle.
Aṅgada went on the embassy on the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha; / and then occurred Sītā's seeing of her husband's illusory head and other limbs.
From the second day of Māgha for seven days up to the eighth, / there was tumultuous battle between the ogres and the monkeys.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, at night, in battle by Indrajit, / the binding of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa with the serpent-noose was indeed done.
When the monkey leaders were distraught and despondent on all sides, / to release the serpent-noose the Wind whispered on the tenth day
into the ear the true nature of Rāma; then came Garuḍa. / On the eleventh and twelfth days, the slaying of Dhūmrākṣa was accomplished.
On the thirteenth day, Kampana was slain in battle by that very [hero]; / from the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha to the first day of the dark fortnight,
in three days, the slaying of Prahasta was executed by Nīla; / from the second day of the dark fortnight of Māgha to the fourth, in three days,
Rāvaṇa was routed from the battle by Rāma in a tumultuous fight; / from the fifth day up to the eighth, [Kumbhakarṇa] was awakened by Rāvaṇa.
Kumbhakarṇa then feasted for four days; / Kumbhakarṇa, in six days from the ninth to the fourteenth,
the devourer of many monkeys, was slain in battle by Rāma; / on the new-moon day there was a cessation of hostilities out of grief.
From the first day of the beginning of Phālguna to the fourth, in four days, / five ogres, Bisatantu and others, were slain.
From the fifth to the seventh occurred the slaying of Atikāya; / from the eighth to the twelfth, over five days, were slain
Nikumbha and Kumbha, and after that Makarākṣa in three days; / on the day of the second of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, victory was won by the conqueror of Indra.
From the third to the end of the seventh, for five days, / there was a cessation of hostilities because of preoccupation with bringing the herbs.
Then, up to the thirteenth, in five days, Indrajit, / renowned for strength and manly valour, was slain in battle by Lakṣmaṇa.
On the fourteenth day the ten-necked one received consecration after the cessation; / on the new-moon day the ten-necked one went forth to battle.
From the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra to the fifth, in five days, / while Rāvaṇa was fighting, there was an abundant slaughter of ogres.
From the sixth of Caitra to the eighth occurred the slaying of Mahāpārśva and others; / on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the piercing of the son of Sumitrā by the spear [occurred].
The ten-necked one was put to flight by Rāma filled with wrath; / Mount Droṇa was brought by the son of Añjanā for the sake of Lakṣmaṇa.
On the tenth [day] there was a withdrawal in the night battle of the demons; / but on the eleventh, Mātali the charioteer,
sent by Indra, offered a chariot to Rāma with devotion in the battle. / Then, enraged, from the twelfth up to the dark fourteenth,
in eighteen days, Rāma slew Rāvaṇa in single combat. / When the fierce battle took place, Rāma attained victory.
From the bright second of Māgha to the dark fourteenth of Caitra, / thus among the eighty-seven days, an interval of fifteen days
was the battle's cessation, [and] the combat lasted seventy-two days. / The funeral rites of Rāvaṇa and the others took place on the new moon day.
On the first lunar day of Vaiśākha, Rāma dwelt upon the battlefields. / On the second, Vibhīṣaṇa was consecrated to the kingdom of Laṅkā.
On the third was Sītā's purification and the receiving of boons from the gods. / Having finally slain the lord of Laṅkā, he, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa,
took the holy Jānakī, who had been grieved by the demon; / taking Jānakī with supreme love, he returned.
On the fourth of Vaiśākha, Rāma mounted the Puṣpaka [chariot]; / he returned through the sky once again toward the city of Ayodhyā.
When the fourteenth year was complete, on the fifth of Mādhava, / Rāma, along with his retinue, arrived at the hermitage of Bharadvāja.
On the sixth he met with Bharata at Nandigrāma; / on the seventh he, the scion of Raghu, was consecrated in Ayodhyā.
For eleven months and fourteen days, / the princess of Mithilā lived separated from Rāma in Rāvaṇa's abode.
In his forty-second year, Rāma ruled the kingdom; / and Sītā was thirty-three years [old] then.
At the end of the fourteen years, entering the city, / the lord Rāma, joyful, having slain Rāvaṇa in battle,
then ruled the kingdom there together with his brothers. / As he was ruling the kingdom, his family priest, the best of speakers,
Agastya, the jar-born, will come to that lord of Raghu. / At his word, this lord of Raghu will perform a horse sacrifice.
His horse will indeed come to your hermitage, O you of noble vows; / his warriors, full of joy, will come to your hermitage.
Before them you will recite the delightful tales of Rāma; / together with them you will go to Ayodhyā, O best of the twice-born.
Beholding Rāma in Ayodhyā, whose eyes resemble lotus petals, / instantly cross beyond the ocean of worldly existence.’
Having spoken thus to me, the best of sages, Lomaśa, who was wise in all matters, / said: "What is to be asked by you?" Then I spoke what was beneficial.
‘By your grace, all the wondrous deeds of Rāma are known; / by your favor, I shall reach the lotus feet of Rāma.’
Bowed to by me, that lord of sages then departed; / by his favor, the worship of Rāma's feet was attained by me.
That very I remember the feet of Rāma daily and repeatedly; / I sing of his life constantly, untiring.
I purify other people with song that captivates the mind; / I rejoice, remembering again and again the sage’s word with the longing to see him.
Blessed am I! Accomplished in my purpose am I! Fortunate am I on the earth’s surface! / The desire to see the lotus feet of Rāmacandra will be mine.
Therefore, with all one's heart, the enchanting Rāma is to be worshipped; / indeed, he is to be revered by all who wish to cross the ocean of worldly existence.
Therefore, for what purpose have you all arrived? Or which king of men, / virtuous in nature, is performing the great sacrificial rite, the horse sacrifice?
Let all of that be told here by you who go to guard the horse; / may they remember the foot of the lord of Raghu, recalling it again and again!”
Having heard these words of the sage, struck with wonder, / remembering the lord of the Raghus, they addressed the sage Āraṇyaka:

title: saptatriṃśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Śeṣa said: / Questioned by the best of sages concerning the wondrous deeds of Rāma, / considering themselves blessed and fortunate, they spoke with respect.
The people said: / “We all are now purified by your sight, / since you purify us people now with the story of Rāma.
Listen to our true word; you are the best of brahmin seers. / Whatever you have asked of us, we shall tell it all.
At Agastya's word, for the removal of the sin of slaying a brahmin, the glorious, / great Rāma is performing a sacrifice, equipped with all provisions.
Protecting that [horse], all of us have indeed arrived at your hermitage / together with the horse, O brahmin; know this, O noble-minded one!”
Having heard these words, which were an enchanting elixir, / the brāhmaṇa, devoted to Rāma, attained supreme joy.
“Today the tree of my desire, endowed with beauty, has borne fruit; / today my mother is blessed, who gave birth to me who am born.
Today a kingdom free from thorns has been attained by me; / today the treasuries are fully prosperous; today the gods are well satisfied.
The fruit of the agnihotra, offered with clarified butter, has been attained by me today, / since I shall behold the two lotus feet of Rāmacandra.
The lord, ruler of Ayodhyā, who is constantly meditated upon in the heart, / that charming one will surely come within the range of my sight.
Embracing me, Hanūmat will ask of my welfare; / seeing my great devotion, that best of beings will attain satisfaction!”
Having heard these words, Hanūmān, the best of monkeys, / seized indeed the pair of feet of the sage Āraṇyaka.
“O master, O brahmin seer! I, Hanūmat, your servant, stand before you; / know me, O lord of sages, as akin to a grain of dust to the servant of Rāma!”
When he had spoken thus, the sage, exceedingly delighted, / embraced Hanūmān, who shone brilliantly with devotion to Rāma.
Both overcome with love, both drenched with nectar, / they stood motionless there as if painted in a picture.
Seated there, their minds filled with love for the lotus feet of the lord of Raghu, / they exchanged most delightful stories.
Hanūmat addressed these words of manifold beauty / to the forest hermit, the best of sages, engrossed in meditating on Rāma's feet:
“O master, this great diamond-sprout of Daśaratha's lineage, / Rāma's brother, the mighty hero Śatrughna, bows to you.
By him was slain Lavaṇa, the terrifier of all the worlds, / and all the sages, rich in asceticism, were made happy.
This one named Puṣkala bows to you, served by eminent warriors, / by whom great champions have now been conquered on the battleground.
Know this highly virtuous, mighty minister of Rāma, / dear as life to the lord of Raghu, omniscient, skilled in dharma.
This Subāhu is extremely fierce, a forest fire to the lineage of his enemies; / a bee at the lotus of Rāma's feet, of great fame, he bows to you.
And this Sumada, granted by Pārvatī through service to Rāma's feet, / has now attained a great crossing of the ocean of worldly existence.
This Satyavān, who, hearing from a servant that the horse had arrived, / offered up his kingdom, bows down to you on the earth.”
Having heard these words, having embraced him with deep respect, / the sage Āraṇyaka extended a welcome with fruits and other offerings.
Delighted, they spent the night there in the hermitage of the best of sages. / In the morning, having performed their daily rites in the Revā, those greatly energetic men,
Placing the sage together with his attendants upon a litter, / Śatrughna brought [him] to Ayodhyā, where Rāma had made his abode.
Seeing from afar the city inhabited by the kings of the solar dynasty, / he swiftly proceeded on foot out of a desire to see Raghunātha.
Having reached the delightful city of Ayodhyā, adorned with people, / he mounted upon thousands of longings to behold Rāma.
There, on the bank of the Sarayū in an adorned pavilion, / he saw Rāma, dark as a blade of dūrvā grass, with eyes possessing the splendor of a lotus,
Bearing an attractive deer horn at his waist, endowed with royal majesty, / surrounded by hosts of sages headed by Vyāsa, well-served by heroic warriors,
Surrounded by Bharata and Sumitrā's son [Lakṣmaṇa], / distributing gifts requested by the poor and the blind.
Beholding him, this one named Āraṇyaka considered himself fulfilled: / “My eyes, resembling lotus petals, behold Rāma!
Today my knowledge of all the treatises has become immensely fruitful, / since having learned of Śrī Rāma, I have reached this city of Ayodhyā!”

Having spoken many such words, rejoicing, / his body radiant with great delight at the sight of Rāma's feet, / he departed for the presence of the Lord of Ramā, inaccessible to others, / far beyond even the masters of yoga devoted to reflection.
Saying, “Blessed am I today! I shall bring Rāma’s feet into the range of my vision,” / speaking charming words, he looked upon Rāma.
Rāma also, seeing the best of Brahmins blazing with his own splendor, / an embodiment of asceticism, then rose up to greet him.
The great Rāmacandra bowed down for a long time at his feet: / “O deity devoted to Brahmins, today my body has been sanctified!”
As he was uttering these words, the lord fell at his feet, / his feet illuminated by the crest-jewels of gods and asuras bowing down.
Lifting that best of kings who bowed down, the great ascetic, chief among Brahmins, / embraced the beloved Lord in his arms.
The son of Kausalyā placed him on a lofty jewel-studded seat, / and the Lord washed both his feet with water.
Hari himself placed that foot-washing water upon his head, / saying, “Today I, along with my retinue and family, am purified.”
Having anointed him with sandalwood paste, he gave [him] a milch cow, / and he who is served by the lord of gods spoke charming words:
“Master, the sacrifice named the horse sacrifice is being performed by me; / through the arrival of your feet, today it will become complete.
Today, purified by your feet, / the horse sacrifice will effect the destruction of my sin born of killing a Brahmin.”
To him who was uttering these words, served by kings and emperors, / the sage Āraṇyaka, smiling, said this in a voice as sweet as mead:
“O master, ruler of the earth who honors Brahmins, your words are indeed fitting; / Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas are your forms, O great king.
When you perform auspicious deeds such as the worship of Brahmins, / then all kings will worship the Brahmin, O king.
As for what you said, O great king, ‘I perform a spotless sacrifice to dispel the killing of a Brahmin’— / that indeed is laughable speech!
From remembering your name, a fool destitute of all learning in the treatises, / crossing over the ocean of all sins, would go to the supreme abode.
This is clearly the essential meaning of all the Vedas and legendary histories: / that the remembrance of Rāma’s name is practiced as the deliverer from sin.
Sins, even those equal to killing a Brahmin, roar only so long / as your name, O Rāmacandra, is not clearly uttered.
Hearing the roar of your name, the elephants of great sins / flee anywhere, O great king, seeking a place of refuge.
Therefore, how could there be the sin of killing for you, the sight of whom yields great merit? / O Rāma, hearing your auspicious story, one becomes instantly purified.
Formerly in the Kṛta age, I heard this statement / from the mouth of sages dwelling on the bank of the Gaṅgā who knew antiquity:
‘Fears of sin exist for timorous, deeply sinful men only so long / as one does not speak with one's voice the charming name of Rāma.’”
"Therefore, fortunate am I today; the destruction of my cycle of rebirth / has now become easy to attain, O Rāmacandra, from the sight of you."
When he had spoken thus, all the sages there worshipped that sage, / saying, "Excellent, excellent are these words!"
Śeṣa said: / There a great wonder occurred; hear that from me as I tell it, / O Vātsyāyana, best of sages, devoted to devotion to Rāma.
Seeing the great king Rāma, such as he appears within the scope of meditation, / he experienced extreme joy and addressed the lords of sages:
“O lords of sages, hear my very charming statement! / Who in the world of mortals could ever be as fortunate as I?
There is no one equal to me, none has been born, nor will there ever be, / since Rāmabhadra, having bowed to me, inquired after my well-being!
He the dust of whose lotus feet is ever sought by the Vedas, / today drinking the water from my feet, considered himself purified!”
As he was speaking thus, a bursting forth from the Brahma-aperture took place; / the splendor arising from it came forth and entered into the leader of the Raghus.
As all the people looked on in the pavilion on the bank of the Sarayū, / he attained the liberation of union [with the Lord], difficult to obtain even by yogins.
In heaven there was the sound of horns, and then the sound of vīṇās; / a shower of flowers fell before them, a wonderful and marvelous sight for those looking on.
The sages too, seeing this, praised the lord of sages: / “Fulfilled is this best of sages, since Rāma’s body was beheld by him!”

title: aṣṭatriṃśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Sūta said: / Having heard this narrative, the noble-minded Vātsyāyana / experienced supreme joy and said to the lord of serpents:
Vātsyāyana said: / “There is no satiation for me as I listen to the story, O lord of serpents, / of Raghunātha, who dispels the distress of his devotees and creates renown.
Blessed is the supreme sage named Āraṇyaka, a knower of the Vedas, / who, having gazed upon Raghunātha, abandoned his perishable body!
Where did the king’s horse go after that? By whom was it restrained? / How did the glory of the Lord of Ramā arise there, O lord of serpents?
Tell me all in truth, since you are omniscient, / bearing the form of the supporter of the earth, possessing his direct form.”
Vyāsa said: / Having heard this speech, with a joyful inner self, / he spoke the story of Rāma’s deeds, an arising of tales of his various virtues.
Śeṣa said: / “Well do you ask, O Brahmin sage, again and again about the virtues of Raghunātha, / treating what was heard as if unheard, bearing an eager craving for them.
Then the horse set forth, surrounded by many soldiers, / along the charming bank of the Revā, frequented by hosts of sages.
Then all the soldiers, skilled in battle, advanced wherever the horse went, / watching its path in every direction.
Then the steed, bearing a golden plate on its forehead and with its limbs worshipped, / entered a pool in the Revā that contained fathomless water.
Then that excellent horse of Rāmacandra sank into the water; / at that time all the great heroes there were struck with astonishment.
They said among themselves: “How shall we recover the horse? / Who here will enter into the water to bring back that magnificent steed?”
While they were anxiously taking counsel with one another, / just then the lord of Raghu's line arrived along with hundreds of heroes.
Seeing all of them dejected, the crest-jewel of heroes, known as Śatrughna, / asked in a voice deep as a thundercloud:
"Why are all of you standing gathered today at the water? / Where is the horse of the lord of the Raghus, adorned with the golden plate?
Has it sunk in the water, or has it been seized by some proud man? / Tell me that quickly! Why are you bewildered?"
Śeṣa said: / Having heard these words of the king, the best of the Raghus, / those heroes reported everything to the crest-jewel of heroes.
The men said: / "O master, we do not know. It was in the water for a moment, / and then it sank down; your handsome horse did not emerge from there.
You yourself, having gone there, bring back that horse with speed! / O wise one, we should go there along with you."
Having heard those words of the soldiers, the scion of Raghu / felt sorrow upon seeing the people preparing to cross the water.
He said to the chief minister: "What must be done after this? / Speak of that: how will the retrieval of the horse take place?
Which heroes should be dispatched there to search for the horse in the water? / Or who will bring back the horse, and by what means? Tell that!"
Having heard the words of the king, Sumati, the best of ministers, / addressed Śatrughna at the proper time, as if bringing him joy:
"O illustrious master of wondrous deeds, you possess the power / to travel clearly to Pātāla from the midst of the water here.
Moreover, the great-souled Puṣkala also has the power, / and so does Hanūmat, who is devoted to the service of Rāma's feet.
Therefore, the three of you go and surely bring back the horse, / so that the horse sacrifice of the wise lord of the Raghus may proceed."
Śeṣa said: / Having heard these words, Śatrughna, the slayer of enemy heroes, / entered beneath the waters himself, accompanied by Hanumat and Puṣkala.
As soon as he entered the water, a city appeared, / an immeasurable fortified city, rich with the beauty of many gardens.
There he saw the horse of Rāma, adorned with the golden plate, / tied to a golden pillar inlaid with rubies.
Excellent women bearing captivating beauty / were attending upon a single lovely woman who sat comfortably upon a couch.
Seeing them, all those women said to their mistress: / "These men are youthful in age, their bodies plump with flesh.
They will become the great and excellent reward for your meal; / sweet is the blood of these men whose life-spans have run out!"
Hearing these words of her servants, the faultless, excellent woman / laughed slightly, making her face dance with her eyebrows.
Meanwhile, the three arrived, resplendent with the splendor of their armor, / wearing helmets, endowed with valor and prowess.
Seeing those women there endowed with the splendor of beauty, / they said in wonder, O twice-born: "What great sight is seen here?"
All those great-souled men then paid homage to the celestial women, / their pairs of feet illuminated by the radiance of the crest-jewels.
She, the proud lady, the best of all, asked those men: / "Who are you that have arrived here, bearing bows, as mortals?
My place is inaccessible even to all the gods, great and bewitching; / for anyone who reaches here, there is indeed no return anywhere.
To which king does this horse belong, fanned with chowries / and rich in beauty with its golden plate? Let them speak before me!"
Śeṣa said: / Having heard her words, coupled with enchanting conduct, / Hanūmān, devoid of fear, answered her as if laughing:
"We are indeed the servants of the king who is the crest-gem of the three worlds, / to whom, the crest-jewel of all the gods, the three worlds bow.
Know him to be Rāmabhadra, the initiator of the horse sacrifice! / Release our horse! Why has it been tied up, O excellent lady?
We are skilled in all mystical weapons and knowledgeable in all arms and missiles; / we will take the horse by force after slaying those who obstruct it!"
Having heard these words of the monkey, the noble woman / standing in the cave, skilled in speech, smilingly replied:
"No one is able to release this horse brought by me, / even in ten thousand years with crores of sharp arrows of blazing crests.
However, being a female servant performing service at Rāma's lotus feet, / I will not seize that horse of the wise king of kings.
A great disrespect was committed by me in leading away the fine horse; / may Rāmabhadra forgive that, he who is the refuge, affectionate to his devotees!
You men are distressed on account of the horse of that protector; / ask for a boon unobtainable even by the gods, O excellent ones,
so that the supreme person may forgive this very terrible offense of mine! / Casting away all hesitation, choose an excellent boon!"

Hearing her supreme words, Hanūmān said to her: / "By the grace of the lord of the Raghus, everything of ours is prosperous.

"Even so, I ask for one supreme boon: / grant that which is desired by my mind."
In birth after birth, let the leader of the Raghus be our lord, / and may we be the performers of his deeds and his attendants!"
Hearing these words of the monkey, the lady then / spoke sweet words, laughing, honoured for their virtue:
"That which you have requested, difficult to obtain even by all the gods, / will come to pass, without a doubt, O servants of that lord of the Raghus!
Moreover, I, who committed an insult, shall give you one boon / for the satisfaction of the lord of the Raghus, so that my word may prove true:
Ahead, King Vīramaṇi, accompanied by great heroes, / guarded by Śiva, will seize your horse.
For conquering him, receive my great missile, O ones of very great might! / In single combat on chariots, that great man must be fought by you, Śatrughna.
When, however, you discharge this missile in battle, / purified by it, he will directly realize the true nature of Rāma.
Knowing that, he will give up the horse and fall at [his] feet; / therefore, accept that missile of mine which tears through enemies!"
Hearing that, the brother of the lord of the Raghus took the missile; / facing north, with a purified body, [he received] the wondrous gift given by the yoginī.
Obtaining that missile, he of great splendor became an afflicter of enemies, / difficult to overcome, hard to resist, a veritable goad to the elephant of his foes.
Bowing to her, Śatrughna, the best of the Rāghavas, taking the excellent horse, / went out from that water to the pleasant bank of the Revā.
Seeing him, all the soldiers, their limbs thrilled with delight, filled with joy, / praising him with 'Well done, well done!', asked about the emergence of the horse.
Hanūmān related the great return of the horse / and the attainment of the boon from her; hearing it, they too were filled with joy.

title: ekonacatvāriṃśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Śeṣa said: / As the mṛdaṅgas resounded and the sounds of the vīṇās [arose] on all sides, / the horse was released from there toward Devapura, built by the gods.
Where, with their crystal wall constructions, the mansions of mortals / laugh at the spotless Vindhya mountain inhabited by serpents;
Where houses of silver are seen, surpassing even nature, / fitted with marvelous gems and possessing gates adorned with various rubies;
Where charming, lotus-like women in house after house / captivate the minds of men with their lotus faces and gentle glances;
Where ruby gems set into the fine floors of every house / seem, O brāhmaṇa, as if competing with their lower lips;
Where pleasure hills made of sapphires at every dwelling / cause the crested peacocks to mistake them for rainclouds;
Where swans kept in the crystal houses of mortals / feel no fear of clouds, nor do they remember Lake Mānasa;
Where, in that abode of Śiva, darkness is perpetually dispelled by moonlight, / so that among men there is no distinction between the light and dark fortnights.
There King Vīramaṇi, foremost among the righteous, / rules over a vast kingdom endowed with all pleasures.
His mighty son, a great hero named Rukmāṅgada, / went into the forest to play accompanied by lovely-bodied women.
The tinkling of their anklets and the sound of their bracelets / bewitched the mind of the god of love himself; what need to speak of any other, sir?
He went to a very great forest filled with flowering trees, / made into a dwelling place by Sadāśiva, splendid in all six seasons;
Where campaka trees, abundantly adorned with blooming buds / and seen on every side, torment lovers with the pain of desire;
Where mango trees are bent low with fruits and myriad blossoms, / along with nāga and punnāga trees, sāl trees, palms, and tamālas;
Where the cooing of cuckoos reaches the ear, / and fine jasmine flowers are ever awakened from sleep by the humming of bees;
Which is radiant with clusters of pomegranate trees mixed with karṇikāras, / ketakīs, and lines of various other forest trees.

Into that forest, his mind full of delight, singing softly with a sweet voice out of a desire for pleasure, / surrounded on all sides by women with rising breasts, his body a storehouse of beauty, he entered without fear.
Some pleased that handsome prince with their knowledge of dance, / some with their arts of singing, and some with clever, well-timed speech.
Other impassioned women delighted him with signals of their eyebrows, / and the women made him glad with skillful embraces.
Gathering flowers with them, he adorned those women; / praising them with tender words, he sported like Kāma incarnate.

While the wise king of kings was occupied in this way, / that exceedingly handsome horse arrived at that forest region.

...that [horse] whose single forehead region was adorned with a golden plaque, / whose body was yellowed with saffron paste resembling the Ganges...

with a gait that surpassed the speed of the wind— / seeing that steed whose body was an abode of supreme wonder,

...reddish-brown in color like the center of a lotus, / the striking lustre of whose coppery lower lips defeated coral, spoke to their husband:
with faces radiant with smiles that revealed rows of teeth, / and whose eyes resembled the bewitching arrows of Kāma, said to their lord:

The women said:
“Beloved, what great horse is this, adorned with a single gold plate? / Whose magnificent steed is it? Seize it by your own might!”

Śeṣa said:
Hearing the words spoken by them, his eyes playful and charming, / he playfully seized the horse with one lotus hand.
Having read the gold plate inscribed with clear letters, / he laughed in the midst of the women and spoke once more.

Rukmāṅgada said:
“On earth there is none equal to my father in valor and majesty; / how then can King Rāma display such arrogance toward him?
He whom Rudra, wielder of the Pināka, protects at all times, / and before whom gods, Dānavas, and Yakṣas bow with jeweled crests—
let my father of great power perform a horse sacrifice instead! / Let this horse go to the stable, and let my warriors tie it fast.”
Having heard these words, those charming women / became joyous-faced and embraced their beloved.
Taking the horse, the great son of King Vīramaṇi, / accompanied by his wives, entered the city with tremendous enthusiasm.
Amid the loud striking of mṛdaṅga drums all around, / eulogized by bards, he proceeded to his father's grand palace.
He told him that the horse of the lord of the Raghus had been seized— / that wondrous horse released for the horse sacrifice, wandering at will,
and protected by the slayer of enemies who was joined by a mighty army. / Hearing his words, the great king Vīramaṇi,
though very wise, did not overly praise that deed; / taking it and returning seemed to him like the conduct of a thief.
He reported it to his son-in-law, Śiva of wondrous deeds, / who bears a woman on half his body, whose body is adorned with serpents, and who wears the moon.
The great king Vīramaṇi consulted with him / about this rash deed committed by his son, which is blameworthy in the opinion of the wise.

Śiva said:
“O King, a most astonishing deed has been performed by your son, / who seized the great steed of the wise Rāmacandra!
Today a great battle will take place, bewitching gods and asuras, / against the great king Śatrughna, who alone protects tens of millions of warriors.
He whom I hold in my heart and constantly utter with my tongue— / your young son has stolen the sacrificial horse of that very Rāma.
Yet a great gain will indeed come from this in battle: / we shall behold Rāma’s lotus feet, which are served by me.
A great effort must be made here in protecting the horse; / for they will take the horse by force even though it is protected by me.
Therefore, O great king, bow humbly and offer this horse / along with your kingdom; feed it well, and then gaze upon his pair of feet.”
Having heard these words of Śiva, that best of kings / spoke to him, whose pair of lotus feet is worshipped by the lord of the gods and others:

Vīramaṇi said:
“This is the duty of kṣatriyas: the protection of their own prowess. / Yet he is preparing to overcome that through this sacrifice called the horse sacrifice.
Therefore one’s own prowess must be protected by any proud man by whatever means, / even by sacrificing his body, after doing all that lies within his power.
All this was done by my son because the horse has been captured; / O Lord, act as is suitable to the occasion toward the angered King Rāma.
This cannot be an action worthy of being done by kṣatriyas— / that one should suddenly bow down at the feet of an enemy, overwhelmed with fear.
Enemies laugh at such a one, thinking: ‘This vile king is a coward, / a petty, low person like a vulgar man, who has bowed down agitated by fear!’
Therefore, when battle is at hand, after considering what is proper / and what ought to be done, you must indeed protect your devotee.”

Śeṣa said:
Hearing this speech, the moon-crested god replied, / laughing, with a voice deep as a thundercloud that captivated the mind:
“Even if the thirty-three crores of gods should come forth, / still, who could take the horse from you while I protect it?
If Rāma himself comes and shows himself, / then I shall bow down to his exceedingly tender feet.
One should never fight with one's master; that is called a great impropriety. / The other warriors are like blades of grass, completely unable to accomplish anything.”
"Therefore fight, O king of kings, while I stand well as your protector. / Who can seize the horse by force, even if the three worlds unite?"
Śeṣa said: / Having heard these supreme words of the Moon-crested God, the king / rejoiced greatly in his mind, eager for the act of battle.

title: catvāriṃśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Śeṣa said: / The scouts of the great king, endowed with great strength, / arrived searching for that horse of King Rāma.
"Where is that horse? By whom has it been taken? Or why is it not to be seen? / Who is this very foolish person who would go to the city of Yama after stealing the horse?"
While the scouts of Raghu's descendant were searching along his trail, / just then the great king arrived, surrounded by a mighty army.
He questioned all the servants: "Where is my horse now? / Why is the horse adorned with the gold plate not seen?"
Having heard those words of his, the attendants following the horse / said: "O master, the steed, swift as thought, [has been captured] in the forest by someone!"
carried off; therefore it is not seen by us, skilled though we are in tracking. / Therefore, an effort must be made here, O Lord, toward recovering the horse."
Hearing their words, King Śatrughna questioned Sumati— / he who caused the destruction of enemies, endowed with an enchanting form.
Śatrughna said: / "Who is the king that lives here? How was the encounter with the horse? / How great is the strength of that king by whom my horse has been carried off today?"
Sumati said: / "O King, this is indeed Devapura, built by God himself, / impassable as Kailāsa to closely united hosts of enemies.
In it King Vīramaṇi, a mighty hero endowed with prowess, / rules the kingdom according to dharma, protected by Śiva.
He who is the author of dissolution abides here, subjugated by devotion— / the Moon-crested God, always showing partiality toward his own devotee.
Therefore, if it has been seized, a great battle will take place here. / Alert, let them indeed protect the camp."
Hearing this, that Śatrughna, crest-jewel of all kings, / having formed a battle array of his army, stood there, illustrious in fame.
Then, as he sat at ease taking counsel with his good minister, / that divine sage arrived, eager for battle.
Seeing that sage, a treasure-house of austerities, arrived, / Śatrughna stood up, seated him on a seat, and offered the honey-mixture.
And pleasing with his speech Nārada, the best of sages, who was gratified by the welcome, / he, skilled in eloquence, spoke:
Śatrughna said: / "Where is my horse, O brahmin? Tell me, O noble-minded one! / Its path is not perceived by my skilled servants.
Declare by which proud kṣatriya it was carried off! / How will the recovery of the horse come about here, O rich in austerity?"
Having heard these words of Śatrughna, Nārada, / sounding his vīṇā and singing repeatedly the story of Rāma, spoke:
Nārada said: / "This is Devapura, O King; the great Vīramaṇi is its king. / By his son staying in the forest your royal steed has been seized.
There a great and exceedingly terrible battle will happen for you today; / in it heroes endowed with might and valor will fall.
Therefore, you must remain here with great effort, O mighty one; / construct an array formation impenetrable to enemy warriors!
Victory will be yours, O King, with difficulty, over this best of kings; / who indeed could defeat Rāma in the entire world?"
Having spoken thus, the brāhmaṇa vanished and then took his stand in the sky, / wishing to behold the exceedingly fierce battle, like that between gods and dānavas.
Śeṣa said: / Then King Vīramaṇi, crest-jewel of all heroes, / in order to sound a loud drum in the middle of his own city,
summoned his commander-in-chief, a champion against enemies, lofty in stature, / and spoke quickly in a voice deep as a thundercloud:
Vīramaṇi said: / "O commander, issue the proclamation of the drum in my splendid city: / 'Hearing it, well-equipped, let them march against Śatrughna!'"
Having heard these words, he then caused King Vīramaṇi's / kettle-drum to resound with a mighty roar.
"In every house and on every road the sound of the drum is heard: / 'Let all heroes residing in the royal city march against Śatrughna!
Those proud warriors who transgress the command of the king, / whether sons or brothers, shall be put to death by royal order!
Let the heroes hear again the sound when the drum is struck; / having heard it, let what is to be done be performed quickly, with no delay!'"

title: naravaravīravarāyayurnṛpottamam
text_mt: their bodies adorned with golden armor, / the store of their hearts delighted by the great festival of war.
Some went wearing splendid helmets on their heads, / richly adorned with armor, splendid as hundreds of millions [of suns].
By chariot with a pair of horses, gleaming with jewels and gold, / they went at the king's command toward the monarch's palace, intoxicated with zeal.
Some on rutting elephants, others on splendid horses, / all fulfilling the king's command, went to the ruler's residence.
Adorned with pure gold armor and a helmet, / Rukmāṅgada too stood in his own chariot that was swift as thought.
His younger brother, Śubhāṅgada, wearing on his body an excellent armor / made of great jewels, set out for the festival of battle.
The king's brother, Vīrasiṃha, skilled in all weapons and missiles, / went there by the king's order, obeying the command of the monarch.
The son-in-law of that king, known as Balamitra, / fully equipped, armored, and sword-bearing, went to the king's palace.
The commander Ripuvāra also, having made ready / that fourfold army, then announced it, great as he was, to the king.
Then King Vīramaṇi mounted an excellent chariot / filled with all weapons and missiles, its high wheels fashioned of gems.
Then, in that ocean of warriors, the blast of conches was heard on every side, / as if urging timid heroes on in the combat.
Drums were struck on all sides, beaten by skilled drummers, / where his army divisions stood ready, having set out for battle.
All, having received blessings, adorned with all ornaments, / fully supplied with all weapons and missiles, went to the field of battle.
And the mountain caves were filled with the roar of drums and conches; / did that sound go, as it were, to summon those who dwell in heaven?
While that tumult was taking place, the great king Vīramaṇi, / filled with the enthusiasm of battle, went to the battle ground.
Having arrived, he stood there, densely filled with chariots and foot soldiers, / as if an ocean had come to flood men from that place.
Seeing that army arrived, raised to a tumult / by car-warriors skilled in weapons, the king said to Sumati:
Śatrughna said: / "The mighty Vīramaṇi, captor of my horse, has arrived / with a great fourfold army to fight me again.
How should the battle be fought? Who are those formidable in strength who will fight? / Point out all those warriors to me, so that the desired victory may be attained."

Sumati said:
"O Lord, this great king, surrounded by a mighty army,
has arrived for battle, endowed with devotion to Śiva.

Now let the heroic Puṣkala, who knows supreme missiles, fight,
as well as other warriors skilled in battle, headed by Nīla and Ratna.
"You must fight with Śiva, O sinless one, or with the king; / he of great strength and prowess must be conquered in single combat."

By this method, O king, your victory will come to pass here;
afterwards, do whatever pleases you, O lord of great intellect!"

Śeṣa said:
Having heard this speech, Śatrughna, slayer of enemy warriors,
resolved upon battle and then commanded his fine warriors:

"Along with all the armies, for battle with the kings skilled in weapons,
effort must be made again so that my victory will come swiftly!"

Having heard this, those skilled in war, for the sake of Rāghava's victory,
filled with great zeal, went forth to fight with their soldiers.

title: ekacatvāriṃśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
Śeṣa said:
Well-equipped for battle, Śatrughna's mighty men,
endowed with valor, advanced into the midst of Vīramaṇi's army.

Releasing arrows, piercing many soldiers,
those men bearing bows were seen standing within the battle.

Many were slain there: elephants and chariots adorned with gems,
and shattered ones along with their horses were seen in the field of battle.

Hearing that slaughter had been wrought upon them, the mighty Rukmāṅgada,
standing in his gem-studded chariot, advanced with his soldiers to fight.

Placing arrows on his bow, holding inexhaustible quivers,
with the corners of his eyes blood-red, terrifying, filled with great fury,

making heroes tremble by thousands with his numerous arrows,
causing lamentation, the mighty Rukmāṅgada advanced.

The mighty prince challenged Śatrughna's [son] Puṣkala,
[son of] Bhāratī, who was his equal in strength, fame, and splendor.

Rukmāṅgada said:
"Come forth, you whose deeds are heroic, of great strength and valor,
to fight with me, a radiant prince possessing mighty power!

What is the use of other men being terrified and slain by the millions, O hero?
Engage in a great fight with me and achieve victory!"
To him who had spoken thus, the mighty Puṣkala, laughing heartily, swiftly / struck right in the middle of his broad chest with sharp-jointed [arrows].

Not enduring that, the prince placed arrows on his great bow
and struck the hero Puṣkala with ten shafts in his chest.

Both eager for battle, both desiring victory,
they shone in battle like Kumāra and Tāraka.

Fixing ten exceedingly sharp arrows upon his bow,
the heroic Puṣkala deprived the prince of his chariot.

With four he felled the four horses, with two the charioteer,
with one his flag, and with two the two chariot-guards.

With one, the swift warrior pierced the prince in the heart;
seeing that wondrous feat, all the heroes were delighted.

With his bow severed, chariotless, his horses and charioteer slain,
he became exceedingly enraged and mounted another chariot.

Standing in that excellent chariot adorned with the best of horses,
taking up a mighty, very firm bow, strung with a cord,

Rukmāṅgada addressed this speech to the heroic Puṣkala:
"Having displayed great valor, where will you go, O scorcher of foes?

Behold today my prowess, wrought by my strength!
Stand firm with effort, O hero; I shall cast your chariot into the sky!"
Having spoken thus, he placed an exceedingly terrible arrow upon his bow; / then, having consecrated a whirling missile, [he hurled it] at the chariot of Puṣkala's son.

he released the sharp arrow adorned with golden feathers;
by that arrow, his chariot was carried a full yojana.

Held back with difficulty by his charioteer, the chariot whirled upon the earth;
having regained his place with difficulty, Puṣkala, knower of supreme missiles,

bearing an arrow on his bow, spoke these words to him:
"Attain heaven, O best of heroes, served by all the gods!

Those like you are not fit for the earth, O best of kings,
but fit for the assembly of Śatakratu; therefore, go to the abode of the gods!"
Having spoken thus, he released a mighty weapon that sent [its target] into the sky; / by that arrow, he along with his chariot flew upwards into the air.

Passing beyond all the worlds, he reached the orb of the sun;
by its flame his chariot was burned, along with his horses and charioteer.

With his body mostly scorched by its rays, deeply distressed,
he fell down, holding in his heart the Crescent-Crested God who relieves affliction.

Fallen there upon the ground, his body scorched by the rays,
plunged into extreme agony, he swooned on the battlefield.

When that prince had fallen to the ground in a swoon,
there was a great cry of lamentation at the forefront of the battle.

Those enemies headed by Puṣkala obtained the fortune of victory;
the enemy horse-guards became intent on flight.

Then, seeing the swoon of his son, King Vīramaṇi,
filled with anger, advanced toward Puṣkala, who stood in the midst of battle.

Then this earth shook, along with its excellent mountains and forests;
the heroes were filled with joy, while the cowards were afflicted with fear.

Holding a great bow and two inexhaustible quivers,
breathing heavily in wrath, he challenged his enemy.

title: dvicatvāriṃśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
Śeṣa said:
Seeing that king challenging Puṣkala in the ocean of the great army,
Hanūmān, lord of monkeys, also rushed toward him.

Raising his tail, his body enormous, / spreading a roar like the rumbling of a raincloud...

[passing by] the foremost heroes standing in the fight, the monkey-lord
went toward that best of kings, Vīramaṇi.

Seeing that Hanūmān approaching, the formidable Puṣkala
gazed at him with eyes very red with anger toward the foe.

Puṣkala, knower of supreme missiles, addressed Hanūmān
with a voice deep as a thundercloud, making the battleground resound:

Puṣkala said:
"Why have you come to fight in battle, O great monkey?
How much is this little strength of King Vīramaṇi?

Where all the three worlds have assembled in front,
there do you wish to go to fight in sport or not?

Who is this King Vīramaṇi? How trifling is his strength!
Your coming here in such fierce fury is not fitting, O hero.

By the glance of Raghunātha's grace, crossing over what is impassable,
I shall finish him in an instant, O lord of monkeys; do not set your mind on the battle!

By you the ocean of rakṣasas was crossed by the power of Rāma's grace;
likewise, meditating well on Rāma, I shall cross over what is impassable.

Whoever, facing what is impassable, remember Raghunātha,
their ocean of grief will dry up, of this there is no doubt.

Therefore go to the side of Śatrughna, O mighty hero!
Having conquered King Vīramaṇi in an instant, I am coming!"
Śeṣa said: / Having heard these steadfast words spoken by Puṣkala, / the slayer of enemy heroes spoke once again to Puṣkala.
Hanumān said: / “My son, do not act rashly against King Vīramaṇi. / He is generous and a granter of refuge, endowed with might and valor.
You are a boy, while the king is an elder, the foremost knower of all weapons and missiles. / Many heroes shining with great valor have been conquered by him in battle.
Know that Sadāśiva is at his side as his protector, / Sthāṇu, united with Umā, brought under his power through devotion and dwelling in this city.
Therefore, Puṣkala, I myself will fight with this king. / You, conquer other heroes and win abundant renown.”
Puṣkala said: / “Śiva was brought under control through devotion and established by him in his city; / but Maheśvara does not reside directly within that [king's] heart.
That very Sadāśiva, having worshiped whom he reached the supreme station, / is Rāma, who never departs anywhere, abandoning my heart.
Where Rāma is, there is the entire universe, both motionless and moving. / Therefore, I will conquer King Vīramaṇi in battle.
Go, O monkey, to fight in battle with the other proud, foremost kings / headed by Vīrasiṃha; do not worry about me, O lord.”
Having heard this speech cherished by the wise, / Hanūmān went into battle to fight Vīrasiṃha, the king's younger brother.
Lakṣmīnidhi engaged in a chariot duel with his son, / the celebrated Śubhāṅgada, an expert in great weapons and missiles.
With Balamitra, Sumada, exalted by the power of his own majesty / and armed with weapons, advanced into the battle to fight, that prince.
Seeing that king issuing a challenge to single chariot combat, Puṣkala, skilled in warfare, / mounted upon his gold-inlaid chariot, went straight toward him.
Seeing that Puṣkala, skilled in battle, had approached, / the king, addressed with pleasant words, spoke in the midst of the fight with a fearless voice.
Vīramaṇi said: / “Boy, do not approach me, enraged and fiercely wrathful in battle! / Go, to save your life; do not fight with me!
Kings like me take pity on boys such as you, / and they never strike them. Therefore, depart from the battle!
As long as I have not beheld you with my eyes, I was agitated; / now, my mind has no desire to strike you.
As for your having pierced my son with arrows and rendered him unconscious, / all of that has been forgiven by me today, because of your childish understanding, great as it was.”
Having heard these words, Puṣkala said to him: / Puṣkala said: / "I am a boy; you are very old, skilled in all weapons and missiles."
Yet this is the conviction of kṣatriyas: those endowed with superior strength / are the truly aged, O foremost of kings, not those who have merely advanced in years.
Your son, proud of his valor and might, was struck down unconscious by me. / Now I will fell you with weapons in the contest of war.
Therefore, O king, take your stand with effort at the head of the battle! / No one, even standing in Indra's rank, can conquer me, a devotee of Rāma.”
Hearing this spoken by Puṣkala, the leader of kings / laughed on looking at the boy, and then became angry once again.
Seeing him enraged, Bharata's furious son / struck the king in the chest with twenty sharp arrows.
Seeing those arrows released by him approaching, the king, / exceedingly enraged, cut them into many pieces with sharp arrows.
Seeing the cutting of his arrows, the son of Bharata, slayer of enemy heroes, / grew intensely angry in his heart, and with three arrows,
that king's son named Puṣkala pierced [him] in the forehead. / Lodged there, they shone—were they the three peaks of Trikūṭa?

Afflicted by those arrows, the king, filled with great fury, / struck heroic Puṣkala in the chest with nine arrows. / By those calf-toothed shafts, much blood of the son of Rāma's younger brother was drunk;
they remained fixed in his body like enraged venomous serpents. / Falling into supreme anger, Puṣkala once again
swiftly pierced the ruler of the earth with a hundred sharp-jointed arrows. / By those arrows, his armor was shattered, and his diadem along with his helmet,
his chariot, and his great strung bow were severed by the overflow of wrath. / Drenched in blood, his body pierced by arrows,
he mounted another chariot and advanced toward Bharata's son: / “Blessed are you, O hero, bee at the lotus feet of Rāma!
A great deed was done by you today, in that I was deprived of my chariot. / Protect your life, O hero, while I fight now!
Your life will not be easily kept, with me standing before you in the form of Death!” / Having spoken thus, the master of weapons struck him with countless arrows.
On the earth and in every direction, nothing was seen there except his arrows. / Many thousands of elephants were pierced, and horses on all sides;
chariots along with their charioteers were cut, shattered, and cleaved in two by him. / A river with torrents of blood flowed forth there on the battlefield,
where furious elephants appeared like mountain peaks, / and hair from the heads of creatures looked like moss again and again.
Severed hands of many heroes, splendid with rings / and smeared with sandal paste and other unguents, appeared there like serpents.
The heads of the foremost warriors bore the likeness of tortoises, / and the flesh of great heroes formed the mud there.
While such a tumult was taking place, hundreds of yoginīs in the battle / drank the blood of creatures fallen in the fight from vessels.
Filled with joy and curiosity, they devoured flesh; / having drunk the blood there and eaten the flesh, maddened with frenzy,
they danced, laughed aloud, and sang loudly on the field of slaughter. / Piśācas on that battlefield, taking in both hands
the heads of creatures, their limbs intoxicated, set about beating them like cymbals. / Jackals there, having devoured the great flesh
of those fallen on the battleground, howled in frenzy, inspiring terror in cowards. / Stricken with fear, the cowards entered the hollows of elephants,
and were devoured by the yoginīs—for the wicked have no refuge anywhere! / Observing this destruction of his own army, that foremost of chariot-warriors,
Puṣkala, also wrought slaughter in the circle of battle: / the heads of elephants were split open, and pearls spilled forth;
that river filled with hair appeared like the Tāmraparṇī. / The arrows shot by Puṣkala, striking the limbs of men, / severed the lives of even the heroes on all sides.
All their limbs drenched in blood, all with their own bodies mutilated, / the fine warriors on the field of slaughter appeared like kiṃśuka trees.
At that moment, enraged, having challenged the king, / [Puṣkala], overwhelmed by a flood of fury, struck him with many arrows.
With his limbs pierced by the penetration of those arrows and his armor shattered, the king, / considering him to possess great might, struck back with ten million arrows.
Discharged through his armor by those arrows, abundant blood flowed forth; / his handsome body became the object of a cage of arrows.
Standing within that cage of arrows, his mind overwhelmed, / that son of Bharata was unable either to draw or to fit his shafts.
