There [he saw] a wish-fulfilling tree, bowed down with various flowers and fruits,
with tender leaves of all seasons dripping with drops of sweet nectar,

made radiant by shoots waving in the wind as if raining down,
resounding with parrots, flocks of cuckoos, mynas, pigeons,

playful cakora birds, and charming birds,
filled with the humming commotion of royal bees.

Beneath it stood a most wonderful, divine temple of glorious gems,
charming with glittering jewels like a rising forest fire.

There stood a jewel-throne, exceedingly captivating with great golden radiance;
upon it [he saw] her, resembling the morning sun, adorned with various ornaments,

endowed with fresh youth, her creeper-like four arms shining
with goad, noose, bow, and arrows, very gracious, and enchanting,

her lotus feet illuminated by the jewel-rays from the crowns of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others,
surrounded by the supernatural powers of Aṇimā and the rest;

the goddess of smiling countenance, who grants boons and is fond of her devotees.
Having made himself known, saying, 'I am Arjuna,' and bowing down again and again,

standing alone with folded hands, filled with an abundance of devotion,
she, a treasury of mercy, knowing his worship, granted her favor.

Overwhelmed by the remembrance of him, the goddess spoke out of compassion.
The blessed Goddess said:
'What rare gift was given by you, dear child, to a worthy recipient?

What sacrifice was offered here, or what austerity was performed?
Or what spotless devotion to the Lord was acquired by you previously?

Or what rare [virtue], what great auspicious deed [was done] in this world,
by which such grace has been granted with joy by the Lord to you who took refuge?

A grace most deeply hidden and unattainable by anyone else has been bestowed by the Lord.
There is nothing like this for mortals, nor for dwellers on the earth,

nor for dwellers in heaven, gods and others, nor for ascetics, lords, and yogins,
nor indeed for all devotees—never, never, and never at all!

Yet grace was bestowed upon you, child, as by the Soul of the universe.
Therefore, come, and having understood, worship at the Kulakuṇḍa, my lake.

This goddess grants all desires; go together with her.
Bathe there according to the rules and quickly return here.'

Having gone there at that very moment and bathed, Pārtha returned as directed.
When he had returned, having performed his bath, the nyāsa, mudrās, offerings, and the rest,

having been caused to be performed, the supreme vidyā of Bālā,
which yields immediate siddhi, was then spoken by the goddess into his right ear:

the second [vidyā], adorned by the universe, beyond the half of the syllable *ha*.
And the practice, the worship, and recitation numbering one hundred thousand,

and the application properly performed with oleander buds—
having had all this carried out, the supreme Mistress said this to him out of compassion:

'By this very method let my worship be performed.
Then, when I am pleased, for the sake of bestowing grace upon you,

you shall then have the entitlement to enter those [innermost] precincts.
This was the rule established previously by the Lord himself.'

Having heard this, Arjuna worshipped her with that armour;
then, having performed the worship and recitation, the goddess was pleased.

Then, having performed the auspicious homa and bath according to the rule,
considering himself as one who had achieved his purpose, having almost fulfilled his desire,

Pārtha thought all spiritual perfection to be in the palm of his hand.
At that moment, the goddess approached him with a smiling face

and said: 'Go now, dear child, into the inner chamber of that mansion.'
Then, thrilled with excitement, Pārtha stood up full of joy,

his heart filled with boundless joy, and bowed down to her like a stick.
Commanded by her, Arjuna, accompanied by the goddess's female companion,

went to the abode of Rādhā's Lord, which is beyond the reach even of the Siddhas.
And then, having been directed, [to that realm] situated above Goloka,

unmoving, supported by the wind, eternal, true, the abode of all happiness,
named the eternal Vṛndāvana, where the great festival of the eternal Rāsa dance takes place,

he beheld the supreme secret, the essence of the nectar of complete love.
Indeed, at her mere word, beholding that secret with his eyes,

overcome and bewildered by burgeoning love, he fell down there.
Then, regaining consciousness with difficulty, raised up by her with her arms,

and having somehow attained composure through her soothing words,
[he asked:] 'Tell me, what other austerity remains to be performed by me?'
Thus he became restless under the weight of longing to see him; / then, taking her by his hand at that right foot,

reached an auspicious spot, and having arrived, spoke these words:
'For bathing, enter this expanse of auspicious water, O Pārtha,

the central bud of a formation situated in a thousand-petalled lotus,
with four lakes, four streams, filled with an abundance of marvels.

Entering inside it, you will see a wonder here.
To the southern part of this, here is a lake

which is the drinking of honey and mead, named the Malaya Stream;
and this is the blossoming garden where in the spring the festival of love

Govinda celebrates, suitable for spring blossoms,
where they praise Kṛṣṇa's incarnation day and night,

and by whose mere remembrance a sprout of love arises in the sage's heart.
Therefore, having bathed in this lake and gone to the bank of the eastern lake,

sip its water and attain your desired purpose.'
Then, having heard her words, into the water of that lake,

which was tinged with pollen fallen from white water-lilies, night-blooming lotuses, red lotuses, and blue lotuses,
and charmingly scented with drops of honey,

swaying with the sounds of royal swans and other birds on its broad banks,
with its four shores paved with jewels, rippled by gentle breezes—

when Pārtha had plunged into the water, she vanished right there.
Rising up and looking around, bewildered, sweetly smiling,

with a slender creeper-like body fair and radiant as the rays of freshly purified gold,
in the prime of her blooming youth, her face resembling the autumn moon,

with glossy, deep-blue, curling locks of hair adorned with glistening gems,
her forehead band resplendent with the radiance of a sindūra mark,

the playful movement of whose unfolding creeper-like brows surpassed the bow of love,
with wagtail-like eyes playfully darting and flashing, deep and dark,

the orbs of whose cheeks were gleaming with the radiant light of jeweled earrings,
with splendid, wondrous creeper-like arms tender as lotus stalks,

her sprout-like hands stealing all the beauty of autumn lotuses,
with an inner garment held by a girdle of gold crafted by a skilled artisan,

her hips radiant with the ends of a jingling zone of bells,
her rounded hips and thighs, an abode of beauty, enveloped in shining silken cloth,

her lovely lotus feet adorned with tinkling jeweled anklets,
possessing skill in the various arts of glowing passion,

endowed with all auspicious marks, adorned with every ornament,
she looked upon herself as a wondrous, foremost maiden.

And through the illusory power of the Lord of the cowherd maidens' lives,
she completely forgot whatever belonged to her previous body immediately after that.
Bewildered as to what to do, she stood there in great wonder; / in the meantime, a deep, sudden sound arose in the sky.

'O fair-browed one, go by this very path to the eastern lake;
sip its water and fulfill your cherished desire.

For your female companions are there, do not despair, O fair-complexioned one!
They will indeed bestow your desired boon right there.'
Hearing this divine voice, she went to the eastern lake, / which had diverse ancient streams and was filled with various birds,
shining with blooming white water-lilies, red lotuses, blue water-lilies, and others, / with rubies, and its fine banks with lotus steps.

its four shores adorned with charming bowers, creepers, and trees abounding in various blossoms;
she sipped the water and stood for a moment.

Just then, into the hollow of her attentive ears, she heard the tinkling of small bells,
accompanied by the jingling of a resonant girdle and charming anklets.

And then [she saw] a band of beautiful women, endowed with wondrous youth,
with wondrous ornaments in place, and wondrous appearance and speech.
Having wonderful limbs, unprecedented, she [possessed] distinct wondrous charms, / wonderful speech, wonderful laughter, glances, and the like,
charming, wonderful beauty, endowed with all sweetness, / reaching an endless realm of pure beauty, captivatingly and delightfully fair,
endowed with wondrous tender loveliness, wondrous grace and favors, / a gathering of all wonders, wondrous in glances and the rest.
Having seen that supreme wonder, pondering somewhat in her heart, / drawing on the earth with her big toe, she stood with a bowed face.
Then there was agitation among them, and mutual glances: / “Who is this of our own kind, long an object of boundless curiosity?”
Seeing all of them, [saying,] 'She should be known,' for a moment / those skilled in counsel invited [them] and, out of curiosity, came to see.
Having come, one among them, renowned by the name Priyamudā, / a wise woman, with sweet speech lovingly spoke to her:
Priyamudā said: / “Who are you? Whose daughter are you? Whose beloved are you? / Where were you born? By whom were you brought here, or did you come yourself?
Tell all this to us; what use is anxiety? / In this place of supreme bliss, can anyone have sorrow?”
Questioned thus by her, she bowed down in humility / and spoke in a sweet voice, charming their minds:
Arjuna said: / “Who I am, whose daughter I am, or where born, whose beloved, / or by whom brought here, or whether I came myself—
I know none of this; may the noble lady know it yet. / Listen to that which I tell, if you have faith in my word:
On the very southern side of this place there is a lake; / I came there to bathe, and there I remained.
Filled with deep longing, then looking around in all directions, / I heard a wonderful sound arisen from the sky:

'O fair-browed one, go by this very path to the eastern lake;
sip its water and fulfill your cherished desire.
For there are your friends, O woman of excellent complexion, do not despond! / For they will bring about your desired boon right there!’
Hearing his words, she came here from there, / her heart filled with dejection and joy, overwhelmed with anxiety.
Having come and touched its water, I heard various auspicious sounds, / and after that I saw your supreme ladyships.
This much alone I know in body, mind, and speech; / this very thing has been told by me, O goddesses, if it pleases you.
Who are you? Whose daughters? Where born? Whose beloveds?” / Having heard that speech of hers, that Priyamudā indeed spoke:
“Let it be so: we are the life-friends of that very [Lord], O auspicious one, / maiden-companions in sport with the moon of Vṛndāvana, happily [dwelling here].
Delighting in the Self with him, those maidens of Vraja have come here; / these are known as the multitudes of Vedic texts, and these likewise as the sages.
We are indeed cowherd maidens, told to you in our true nature. / Here, born from the body of Rādhā's lord, are the foremost dearest ones,
eternal, eternal sporting maidens, roaming the grounds of eternal play. / This goddess is Pūrṇarasā, and this is Rasamantharā;
this is named Rasālayā, and this is Rasavallarī; / this is Rasapīyūṣadhārā, this is Rasataraṅgiṇī;
and this is Rasakallolinī, and this is Rasavāpikā; / this very one is Anaṅgasenā, and this is Anaṅgamālinī;
this maiden is Madayantī, and this is Rasavihvalā; / and this is named Lalitā, and this is Lalitayauvanā;
and this is Anaṅgakusumā, this is Madanamañjarī; / this is named Kalāvatī, this is remembered as Ratikalā;
this is named Kāmakalā, this is indeed Kāmadāyinī; / this maiden is Ratilolā, this maiden is Ratotsukā;
and this is Ratisarvasvā, but that one is Raticintāmaṇi. / Certain ones among these are Nityānandās, grantors of the flavor of eternal love.
Next are the groups of Vedic texts; listen to some of them here: / This is Udgītā, this is Sugītā, and this beloved is Kalagītā;
this is known as Kalasvarā; this maiden is Kalakaṇṭhikā; / this is Vipañcī, this is Kramapadā, this is considered Bahuhutā;
this is Bahuprayogā; this young woman is known as Bahukalā; / this is known as Kalāvatī, and this is considered Kriyāvatī.
Next are the groups of sages; here are some of them: / This is named Ugratapā, this is remembered as Bahuguṇā;
this is named Priyavratā, and this is considered Suvratā; / this maiden is considered Surekhā; this is Suparvā, bestowing much;
this is known as Ratnarekhā, and that one is considered Maṇigrīvā; / and this is Suparṇā, this is Ākalpā, Sukalpā, Ratnamālikā;
this is Saudāminī, a fair-browed woman, and this is Kāmadāyinī; / and this is known as Bhogadā; this chaste one is considered Viśvā;
and this is Dhāriṇī, Dhātrī, Sumedhā, and that one Kānti; / this is Aparṇā, this is Suparṇā, and this is considered Sulakṣaṇā;
this is Sudatī, and this is Guṇavatī, that one is considered Sukalinī; / this is known as Sulocanā, and this is remembered as Sumanas;
and Aśrutā, and Suśīlā, who bestows the happiness of love. / Hereafter are the cowherd maidens, we who have come here;
may some of them be recognized, O lotus-faced one: / That one is Candrāvalī, and this is Candrikā, considered auspicious;
this is Candrāvalī, this is Candrarekhā, and that one is Candrikā; / this is known as Candramālā, and this is considered Candrālikā;
this is Candraprabhā; this young woman is remembered as Candrakalā; / this is Varṇāvalī, this is Varṇamālā, this is Maṇimālikā;
this is celebrated as Varṇaprabhā, this is Suprabhā, this Maṇiprabhā; / this is Hārāvalī, this is Tārāmālinī, considered auspicious;
this is Mālatī, this is Yūthī, Vāsantī, Navamallikā; / this is Mallī, this is Navamallī, that one is considered Śephālikā;
this is Sauganthikā, Kastūrī, this is Padminī, Kumudvatī; / this very one is Rasollāsā, and this is Citravṛndasamā;
this is Rambhā, and this is Urvaśī, Surekhā, Svarṇarekhikā; / this is Kāñcanamālā, and this other is Satyasantatikā.
All these have been introduced; others are also to be recognized. / Accompanied by these, along with us, you will sport, O passionate lady!
Come to the shore of the eastern lake; having bathed you there / in accordance with the rules, O friend, I will then impart the mantra that brings realization.”
Having quickly brought her thus and bathed her according to the rules, / with the supreme mantra of the beloved of the lord of arts of Vṛndāvana,
she made her receive in brief, preceded by the initiation rites: / higher than the seed-syllable of Varuṇa, placed after the seed-syllable of Agni,
joined with the fourth vowel, adorned with nāda and bindu, / enclosed by two praṇavas, and exceedingly rare in the three worlds.
By the mere reception of the mantra, all realization comes to pass. / The rule for preparatory rites, meditation, the count of fire-offerings and muttering [were taught]:
[Meditation upon] the one whose limbs are fair as molten gold, adorned with various ornaments, / of wondrous form and beauty, gracious, granting boons,
with kalhāra flowers, karavīra and other flowers, campakas, lotuses, / and other fragrant flowers along with saugandhika lilies,
and with water for washing the feet, respectful offerings, sipping-water, enchanting incenses and lamps, / and various divine food-offerings joyfully brought by the host of female companions.
Having duly worshipped the goddess, recited one hundred thousand mantras, / sacrificed in accordance with the rules, praised her, and bowed like a stick upon the earth,
then that praised goddess, unblinking within, / having fashioned her own shadow by her power of illusion, according to her own desire,
and then stationing that beloved at her side as if by force, / surrounded by her female companions, delighted by the pure acts of worship, recitation, and so on,
and by the hymns of praise, devotion, and prostrations, she then appeared out of compassion, / shining with the hue of golden campaka flowers, resplendent with diverse ornaments,
her form charming with grace and beauty in every major and minor limb, / her auspicious face like the spotless full autumn moon,
enchanting the three worlds with her gentle, charming smile and gaze, / completely illuminating the ten directions with her own radiance.
Then that goddess, granting boons and affectionate toward her devotees, spoke. / The goddess said: 'The word of my companions is true; therefore, you are my dear friend.
Arise! Come! I shall fulfill your desire.' / And having heard that word of the goddess, which was her own cherished desire,
Arjunī, her limbs charming with horripilation, her eyes filled with tears, / and overcome with love, fell once again at the goddess's feet.
Then she said to Priyaṃvadā, the goddess [spoke] to this companion: / 'Taking [her] by the hand, comforting her, bring her along with me.'
Then Priyaṃvadā, eager by the command of the goddess, / taking her along in that very manner, went in the company of the goddess.
Having gone to the northern shore of the lake and bathed her according to rule, / having performed the preliminary rites beginning with the declaration of intention and worshipped properly,
the goddess, beloved of Hari, graciously made her receive / that mantra of the glorious Lord of the arts of Gokula, which grants complete success.
The observance named Gokulanātha, adorned of old by Mohana, / a mantra bestowing all accomplishments, kept secret in all the Tantras,
she, understanding its significance, gave her unwavering devotion to Govinda; / and the meditation upon Him was told, and this king of mantras, the enchanting one,
taught in the Mohana Tantra, the mere memory of which grants success: / 'Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, adorned with various ornaments,
having the beauty of ten million Kāmadevas, immersed in the aesthetic rapture of the rāsa-dance, one should meditate upon Him.' / Desiring to purify her, she spoke this secret to Priyaṃvadā:
The glorious Rādhikā said: / 'Until her excellent preliminary observance is complete, / you, being attentive together with the female companions, must protect her.'
Having spoken thus, she went into the presence of Kṛṣṇa's lotus feet, / leaving behind a shadow born of herself for her beloveds.
Rādhikā, beloved of Kṛṣṇa, stood there just as before. / There, by the instruction of Priyaṃvadā, an auspicious eight-petaled lotus
was fashioned with gorocanā, saffron, and sandalwoods, / [drawn] with these various substances mixed together, bestowing success.
Having inscribed the king of yantras and that pure, wondrous mantra, / having performed the preliminary placement of mantras and the rest, and water for the feet and guest-water according to rule,
with flowers born of various seasons, with saffron and sandalwoods, / with incenses, lamps, food offerings, betel leaves, and mouth perfumes,
and with garments, ornaments, and garlands, having worshipped the delight of Nanda / along with all his retinue, equipped with weapons and with mounts,
having praised and bowed according to rule, she engaged her mind in recollection. / Then the lord, the son of Yaśodā, subservient to devotion,
his gestures rippling with side-glances accompanied by smiles, / said to the goddess Rādhikā: 'Quickly bring her here.'
Thus commanded, that very goddess, having dispatched the companion Śāradā, / swiftly brought her before the soul of the rāsa-dance.
Approaching the presence of the glorious Kṛṣṇa, overcome with love, / she fell onto the golden ground, beholding everything wonderful.
Having risen with difficulty, slowly opening her eyes, / being overwhelmed by the burden of emotions, with perspiration, horripilation, and trembling,
she first saw a wonderful, enchanting place there; / and then the wish-fulfilling tree there, with glistening emerald leaves,
endowed with sprouts of coral, tender, with a golden trunk, / with roots of crystal and coral, granting the fulfillment of desires and riches,
granting the desired fruit to supplicants; beneath it, a jewel-palace, / a jewel-throne there, and upon it an eight-petaled lotus;
the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma, situated to the right and left, / and in the four directions, in their proper places, the wish-fulfilling cows.
All around was the Nandana garden, served by the Malaya breeze, / and by the enchanting fragrances of flowers
of all seasons, everything was perfumed, surpassing dark agallochum; / cooled by a shower of pollen particles, exceedingly charming,
with its interior constantly resounding with the swarms of humming / female bees intoxicated by savoring the nectar,
resounding with the sweet calls of pigeons, male and female cuckoos, / female starlings and parrots, and other beloved birds;
thronged with the dances of intoxicated peacocks, heightening desire; / [she saw Kṛṣṇa,] the luster of whose body was like dark collyrium sprinkled with nectar-water,
whose glossy, black, curling locks were scented with reddish perfume, / the crest of his hair bound with the plumage of an intoxicated peacock and other birds,
with an ear-ornament of flowers on his left ear attended by bees, / illuminated by his mirror-like cheeks shining with moving locks of hair,
resplendent with the beauty of his forehead adorned with an extraordinary tilaka, / whose charming nose was like a sesame flower or the beak of the king of birds,
with charming bimba-fruit lips, awakening Kāmadeva with his gentle smile, / enchanting with a necklace resembling wild flowers,
whose two lovely, plump shoulders shone with a garland of celestial trees / served by thousands of intoxicated, hovering female bees,
his chest gleaming with a pearl necklace and adorned with the Kaustubha jewel, / marked with the Śrīvatsa sign, charming with arms extending to his knees,
with a deep navel, exceptionally handsome with a waist like that of a lion, / charming with thighs like well-grown, shapely trees and shapely knees,
adorned with bracelets, armlets, anklets, and other supreme ornaments, / the master of the shapely hips encircled by yellow silk garments,
surpassing ten million Kāmadevas through his charm and beauty, / with charming musical modes and songs played on the flute,
enchanting and immersing the three worlds in an ocean of joy, / displaying the onset of love in every limb, languid with the rapture of the rāsa-dance;
[she saw him attended by maidens] respectfully holding fly-whisks, fans, garlands, perfumes, sandalwood, / betel, mirrors, drinking vessels, vessels for chewed spices,
and whatever other items belonged to amusement, each individually, / and various charming instruments of music,
stationed in their appropriate places, watching his gestures, / their trembling eyes fixed one by one upon his lotus-face;
and [attended] on the left side by the glorious goddess Rādhikā with reverence, / worshipping him, offering him betel, smiling purely.
Beholding this, Arjunī was overwhelmed by the onset of passion. / Then, knowing her to be in that state, Hṛṣīkeśa, the omniscient,
taking her by the hand in the interior of the grove of all sports, / the all-pervading lord of great yogins, sported in secret as he pleased.
Then, having placed his sprout-like arm upon her shoulder, / he approached and said to Śāradā: 'In this western lake,'
"Quickly bathe this slender-limbed woman, who is tired from sport and softly smiling." / Then goddess Śāradā, in that lake of pastimes,
said to her, "Take a bath!" And weary as she was, she did so. / Entering into the water, she became Arjuna once again.
He emerged where the Lord of the gods, the glorious master of Vaikuṇṭha, was. / Seeing that Arjuna dejected, his mind shattered,
Kṛṣṇa touched him with his hand by his illusory power and restored him to his natural state. / The blessed Kṛṣṇa said: "O Dhanañjaya, I cherish you; you are my dear friend.
There is no one equal to you in the three worlds who knows the secret. / The secret about which you asked has now been experienced by you.
If you speak of it to anyone, Arjuna, then you are bound by an oath to me!" / Sanatkumāra said: Having thus received his favor, his resolve sealed by oaths,
he departed with a joyful heart from that place to his own abode, recollecting the wonder. / Thus everything that was within the range of my knowledge has been told to you,
and likewise there is Govinda's oath to you regarding the telling of it to another." / Īśvara said: Having heard his words, the son of Upagu attained perfection and departed.
He went to Vṛndāvana, the dwelling of Nara and Nārāyaṇa. / Even today he resides there, knowing the eternal sports and pastimes of Kṛṣṇa.
Even when questioned by Nārada, I did not reveal that secret; / yet he attained it after assuming female form.
The secret which I revealed to you out of affection, / that, O auspicious lady, must not be disclosed to anyone, just as your own womb.
Whoever reads or even listens to this wondrous chapter on the greatness of the Lord's devotee / finds delight in Hari.

title: paṃcasaptatitamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Pārvatī said: / The secret of Vṛndāvana has been told by you in many ways, O lord. / By what special merit did Nārada attain female form?
Īśvara said: / Long ago, this wondrous account was inquired into by me. / It was the secret spoken by Brahmā, which he had heard from the lotus-mouth of Kṛṣṇa.
Nārada questioned me; then I received this [knowledge]. / "I am not able to speak of that glorification in any way.
What shall I do? Remembering his oath, my mind is depressed." / When, hearing these words of mine, he became dejected,
then, having summoned Brahmā, I commanded him, my dear: / "Tell Nārada that which was spoken by you to me."
Then Brahmā, having heard my words, went together with Nārada / into the presence of Kṛṣṇa, bowed, and asked that very thing.
Brahmā said: / "What is this forest of thirty-two woods, Vṛndāraṇya, O lord of the people? / I wish to hear, O Blessed One; tell me if I am worthy."
The Blessed One said: / "This charming Vṛndāvana is purely my own abode, / where the beasts, trees, insects, humans, and immortals are directly mine.
Those who live close to me, when dead, come into my presence. / And the wives of the cowherds who dwell here in my abode,
they are indeed yoginīs devoted to me, my deities. / This forest of five yojanas is indeed of divine form.
This Kālindī river is named Suṣumnā, carrying the supreme nectar, / where gods and spirits abide in subtle form.
I am all-pervading and I shall never abandon the forest anywhere. / Appearance and disappearance occur here age after age.
This place is full of light, invisible to the eyes of the flesh. / Behold my secret and my majesty, Vṛndāvana in this age.
It cannot be seen in any way by the deities beginning with Brahmā." / Īśvara said: Having heard that, Nārada bowed to Kṛṣṇa and to Brahmā,
and came to the earthly world, to the sacred forest of Naimiṣa. / There he was honored by Śaunaka and the other chief sages,
and questioned: "O holy one, where have you come from now? Tell us!" / Hearing that, Nārada said: "I have come from Goloka,
having heard the secret of Vṛndāvana from the lotus-mouth of Kṛṣṇa." / Nārada said: "Various kinds of questions were asked there again and again.
All the mantras and the yogas were heard by me there; / I shall recount those very things according to the question, in truth."
Śaunaka and the others said: / "Explain to us the secret of Vṛndāraṇya which was spoken to you by Brahmā, / if you have compassion for us."
Nārada said: / Once on the bank of the Sarayū Gautama was seen by us, / wise, yet deeply sorrowful, his mind agitated by worry.
Seeing me, divine Gautama fell to the surface of the earth. / I myself said to him: "Rise, child, my child!
Why are you so pensive? Speak, if it pleases you." / Gautama said: "From your mouth alone was the reality of Kṛṣṇa heard as it is,
and the secret known as Dvārakā and that known as Mathurā repeatedly by me; / but the secret of Vṛndāvana has not been heard from your lotus-mouth,
by which steadfastness of my mind will come to be, O true guru!" / Nārada said: "This is indeed the supreme mystery, the secret beyond secrets,
pertaining to Vṛndāvana, as was told to me long ago by Brahmā. / [I had said,] 'O lord of the gods, O father, tell me the secret of Vṛndāraṇya!'
Hearing what was inquired, he became silent for a moment; / then [he said]: 'Do not [worry], O child; go to Mahāviṣṇu, my master.'
I too must go there along with you, without a doubt.' / Having spoken thus and taken me along, he went to the abode of Viṣṇu.
And that very thing which had been stated by me was told to Mahāviṣṇu. / Hearing that, Mahāviṣṇu then commanded the Self-born Brahmā:
'By my command, take the sage Nārada / and direct him to bathe in the lake called Amṛtasaras.'
Commanded by Mahāviṣṇu, the Self-born did so with me. / There I entered the lake of nectar and performed my bath.
Instantly, on the other bank of that lake, I was in the presence of women, / endowed with all auspicious marks, transformed into a woman, thoroughly astonished.
Seeing me approach, they questioned me repeatedly. / The women said: / 'Who are you? From where have you come? Tell of your doings!'
Hearing their affectionate speech, listen to what was said by me: / 'From where? Who am I that have arrived? Or how do I have the form of a woman?
Everything appears like a dream, or am I deluded on the earth?' / Hearing these words of mine, a goddess spoke in sweet tones:
'This city is named Vṛndā, ever dear to moon-like Kṛṣṇa; / and I am goddess Lalitā, beyond the fourth state and devoid of parts.'
Having said this, the great goddess, her mind dense with compassion, / said to me again: 'O goddess, come along with me.'
And all the other women, devoted to Kṛṣṇa's feet, / also said to me in this way: 'Come along with her!'
Then, out of grace, the fourteen-syllabled mantra of moon-like Kṛṣṇa / was spoken by that great-souled goddess.
From that very moment I attained resemblance to them, having various likenesses. / Together with them, I went to where eternal Kṛṣṇa was,
who is pure existence, consciousness, and bliss, the Lord Himself filled with female nature. / His heart filled with the bliss of women, seeing me, he spoke repeatedly:
"Come, beloved lover! Embrace me with devotion!" / And there, O best of the twice-born, he took delight with me for the span of a year.
Then it was said by the Lord of lovers to the goddess Rādhikā: / "This was my prakṛti there, bearing the form of Nārada.
Having led [her] to the delightful nectar lake, direct [her] to bathe." / After that, sweet words were spoken to me by my lover:
"I am the goddess Lalitā, and I am celebrated as Rādhikā; / and I am named Vāsudeva, constantly composed of the arts of love.
Truly, I am female in my essential nature, and I am the eternal female; / and I am the goddess Lalitā who has taken male form as the body of Kṛṣṇa.
There is no difference between us two; truly, truly indeed, O Nārada! / The one who thus knows my reality, the ritual observance, and the mantra,
the proper conduct, and the secret sign, is dear to me like Lalitā. / This [place] named Vṛndāvana is my secret home.
It must never be revealed anywhere, nor ever spoken to a beast." / Thereupon the goddess Rādhikā, having led me to that lake,
stood [there], and then went back to the feet of the moon-like Kṛṣṇa. / Then, solely from plunging into [the water], I returned as Nārada.
With vīṇā in hand, devoted to singing that secret over and over with joy, / having bowed to the Self-born [Brahmā], I went there as an attendant of Viṣṇu.
It was seen as such by the Self-born, and nothing further was spoken then. / Thus, my child, this most secret matter has been told to you by me.
You also must conceal with great effort this realm of the moon-like Kṛṣṇa, which is pure consciousness and art, / just as a mother's paramour [is kept secret], O dear one.
Just as it was spoken by me to my disciple Gautama with its secrets, / so it has been told to you all in its entirety, and it is most concealed.
If it is ever revealed anywhere, O foremost among sages, / then the curse of the moon-like Kṛṣṇa will surely fall, O brāhmaṇas!
Whoever reads or even hears this excellent chapter, / endowed with the pastimes of Kṛṣṇa, attains the supreme abode.

title: ṣaṭsaptatitamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: The Lord said: Hearing that Śiśupāla had been slain here, Dantavaktra came to Mathurā to fight with Kṛṣṇa.

Hearing that, Kṛṣṇa mounted his chariot and came with him to Mathurā.

Then, having slain him, crossed the Yamunā, and gone to the cowherd station of Nanda, he greeted his parents, comforted them, and was embraced by them.

title: sakala
text_mt: the elder cowherds, embraced them, comforted them, he gratified all those who lived there with many garments, ornaments, and the like.
On the delightful bank of the Yamunā, crowded with sacred trees, he lived there for three nights in the joy of sport with the cowherd women day and night.

All the people living there, beginning with the cowherd Nanda, together with their sons and wives, and even the beasts, birds, and wild animals, assumed divine forms by the grace of Vāsudeva, mounted celestial chariots, and attained the supreme realm, Vaikuṇṭha.
Lord Kṛṣṇa, having bestowed his own disease-free realm upon all the inhabitants of the cowherd station of Nanda, entered the glorious Dvāravatī while being praised by the hosts of gods.

Worshipped there daily by Vasudeva, Ugrasena, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Akrūra, and others, and bearing a universal form, he dallied with his sixteen thousand and eight queens inside bower-dwellings made of divine jewels, upon very soft couches covered with the flowers of celestial trees.

Thus, for the welfare of all the gods and for the destruction of the entire burden of the earth, descending into the Yadu lineage, having destroyed all the demonesses and removed the great burden of the earth, he [delivered] the moving and unmoving beings dwelling in Nanda's Vraja and Dvārikā...
and having established them in the supreme, eternal, and delightful abode meditated upon by yogins, Vāsudeva, constantly served by his divine queens and others, spoke to all:
"The unmanifest Brahman was like water and ghee; / abiding in Prakṛti, released from the guṇas, having liquefied, he went to heaven."

title: saptasaptatitamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Pārvatī said: / Explain in detail the majesty of the words and meanings of the names, / the essential nature of the Lord, and the glorious manifestations of his abodes;
that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, the various emanations of Hari, / and indeed that which is called nirvāṇa in its essential truth, tell me all, O Lord of gods!

The Lord said: / [Meditation should be done on] Kṛṣṇa in the quintessential Vṛndāvana, surrounded by ten million gopīs; / the Gaṅgā is the supreme power there, and situated therein is the forest of bliss,
fragrant with breezes laden with the perfume of various beautiful flowers, / cooled by the beauty of the divine waves of the daughter of the sun [Yamunā],
touched by the devotees of the Lord, foremost among sages, headed by Sanaka, / adorned by herds of cows with delightful and sweet lowing.
surrounded by dancing boys adorned with lovely garlands and ornaments. / There stands the glorious wish-fulfilling tree, adorned with gold,
abounding in sprouts of various jewels, shining with fruits of various gems. / At its base is an altar of jewels, illuminated by the radiance of gems.
Upon it is an unsurpassed jewel-throne embodying the three Vedas. / Seated there is the Lord of the universe, beyond the three guṇas, imperishable,
resembling ten million moons, brilliant as ten million suns, / having the loveliness of ten million gods of love, illuminating the ten directions,
three-eyed, two-armed, fair, with the radiance of molten gold, / being embraced by women, and ever revered on every side,
meditated upon by Brahmā and others, and by Sanaka and others, subjugated by his devotees; / [surrounded] by women whose eyes are ever rolling, dancing in great festivals,
kissing, laughing, embracing him again and again— / the tens of millions of Vedic verses that have attained the bodies of gopīs,
their minds fixed on the nectar of his lotus feet, surrounded on all sides. / But in their midst is the goddess who has the lustre of molten gold,
shining and making all the directions blaze like lightning, / the sovereign Lady, Pradhāna, by whom all this is pervaded,

who is of the form of creation, preservation, and dissolution, who is knowledge, ignorance, the three Vedas, the supreme, / whose form is intrinsic nature, whose form is power, whose form is Māyā, and who consists of pure consciousness,
the ultimate cause of the bodies of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others, / by whose Māyā the entire universe of moving and unmoving beings is embraced;
she is called the Queen of Vṛndāvana, Rādhā, because of imitating the Creator. / Having embraced her, dwelling there joyfully is that Lord of Vṛndāvana.
Reeling from intoxication and passion in mutual kissing and embracing— / one should thus meditate on Lord Kṛṣṇa, and he will attain perfection.
The knower of mantras who recites or hears this king of mantras, this secret, / and her mantra as well—that great-souled person is exceedingly rare.
Rādhikā, Citrarekhā, Candrā, Madanasundarī, / Śrīpriyā, Śrīmadhumatī, Śaśirekhā, Haripriyā,
having golden splendour, casting enchantments, adorned with horripilation from love, / accompanied by pallor and perspiration, attached to love, sweet-speaking,
wearing golden garlands, tranquil, delightful, a connoisseur of rasa, / the life of all women, affectionate to the humble, of pure intention,
who has drunk the nectar of the name—she is celebrated as Rādhā, / possessed of a very long smile, with the brilliance of molten gold.
[She is] a fainting river of love, collyrium for the eyes of the choice of Rādhā; / joined with jealousy and delusion, she lives in the empire of the gift [of love].
She is proclaimed Citrarekhā, a battlefield in the festival of amorous dalliance; / fair-limbed, not too tall, and always intent on playing music.
Bewildered by faintness and horripilation from the acting of humility and longing, / she stands at Hari's right side, loving all mantras.
Endowed with the sweet charm of the god of love's desire, she is proclaimed Candrā; / she walks with a graceful, slow gait, her eyes charmingly half-closed.
Overflowing with an effulgent stream of love, radiant as crushed collyrium, / a connoisseur of love for Kṛṣṇa, eager for the sound of the rāsa-dance,
joined with pride, her face reproaching the moon, / skilled in charming speech, the crest-jewel of those who have mastered their senses,
endowed with a beautiful smile—she is indeed Madanasundarī, / delighting in the solitary rāsa-dance, a youthful maiden charming to the dark-hued Lord.
Bewitching Hari's heart with love and an affectionate sidelong glance, / with conquered senses and anger subdued, she is proclaimed his beloved.
Fair-limbed like well-refined gold, beautiful in her playful movement, / her form is sweet with the varied thrill of horripilation born of love's passion.
Endowed with a beautiful smile, her face reproaches the moon; / skilled in charming speech, she is the crest-jewel of those who have conquered their senses.
She is proclaimed Madhumatī, devoted to the practice of love, / accompanied by the fever of bewilderment, horripilation, and a stream of love.
Sporting in the dust of the toll [of love], a great dancer to the music of the rāsa-dance, / she should be known as Śaśirekhā, always beloved of the cowherd boy.
Possessing Kṛṣṇa's very soul, supreme, a youthful maiden with reddish-brown eyes like honey, / occasionally kissed by horripilation through the bewilderment of love for his feet.
In Śivakuṇḍa she is Śivānandā, on the bank of the Dehikā she is Nandinī; / in Dvāravatī she is Rukmiṇī, and in the Vṛndāvana forest she is Rādhā.
In Mathurā she became Devakī, my Supreme Sovereign; / likewise Sītā at Candrakūṭa, and the dweller of the Vindhya mountains in the Vindhyas;
Viśālākṣī in Vārāṇasī, and Vimalā in Puruṣottama. / And the sovereignty of Vṛndāvana was granted to her by Kṛṣṇa when he was pleased with her,
whereas elsewhere the goddess is distinct. But Rādhā is in the forest of Vṛndāvana. / Śauri, whose form is eternal bliss, is said to be bodiless [by the ignorant];
he is described as the presiding deity residing in the limbs of wind, fire, ether, and earth, / and indeed the very form of Govinda is described as [identical to] Brahman.
Just as the sun, though endowed with sense faculties, is not perceived because of its intense splendor, / so Kṛṣṇa, full of brilliance, surely bewilders time.
His form is not material, born of fat, flesh, and bones; / he is the yogin and the Lord, distinct [from nature], the Soul of all, of eternal form.
His solidity is by divine agency, like that of hailstones and clarified butter. / Even the back of the foot of Kṛṣṇa, whose true nature is boundless, is not a [mere created] deity.
In the multitudes of dust particles of Vṛndāvana, there are millions of Viṣṇus; / in the ray of bliss is the moon, having pervaded the universe with its digits.
Just as the nature of the qualities is in the Self, so living beings are the limb-like rays of that [Lord]. / Kṛṣṇa is endowed with two arms; he is never four-armed.
Accompanied by a single cowherd maiden, he sports there always; / Govinda alone is the male, while Brahmā and the other gods are merely women.
Therefore, this is the inherent nature: the Lord is the being beyond nature; / the primordial Male and Nature are Rādhā and the Lord of Vṛndāvana.
All is a transformation of material nature, except the Lord of Vṛndāvana.

This [universe] would arise from origin itself; it has undergone division, for from its destruction / there is no destruction of gold. Just so, even upon the disappearance of the Fish and other incarnations, there is no departure of Kṛṣṇa.
This manifestation of the three qualities and the rest belongs to the one who sports in Vṛndāvana; / it is like the wave of the ocean, whereas the ocean does not become [the wave].
There is no woman equal to Rādhikā, no man equal to Kṛṣṇa; / there is no age beyond youth; his essential nature is beyond material nature.

Youth is to be meditated upon, to be meditated upon; the forest of Vṛndāvana is the forest [above all]; / the dark form alone is the supreme form; the primordial God is the supreme aesthetic experience.
Childhood lasts until the fifth year; boyhood extends up to the tenth; / adolescence is from eight to five [more], its limit extending up to the fifteenth year.
Adolescence burgeoning into youth is called early youth; / that age is his very life; any other age is a worldly manifestation.
I praise that charming age comprising childhood, boyhood, and adolescence, / him who embodies child Gopāla, the cowherd boy, and the love-enchanted Gopāla.
I praise Madanagopāla, wondrous in his adolescent form, / whom they call the glorious Madanamohana, budding with youth.
A great ocean of the joy of undivided, matchless nectar, / triumphant is the hidden body of the Lord of Śrī, having the form of an adolescent boy.

Though he is one, imperishable, primordial, moving in the midst of the cowherd women, / and accessible through meditation, persons of differing minds behold him differently according to the differences in their tastes.
Whose toenail-moon's radiance is Brahman, to be meditated upon by Brahmā and the other gods— / I praise him, the Lord of Vṛndāvana, who has surpassed the three qualities.
There is no departure from Vṛndāvana for Govinda; / whatever form is elsewhere is indeed an artificial manifestation—of this there is no doubt.
Easily attained by the women of Vraja, but difficult to attain by seekers of liberation, / I worship that son of Nanda, the radiance of whose toenails is the supreme mantra.
Pārvatī said: / As long as the demoness of longing for enjoyment and liberation remains in the heart, / how can there arise here the bliss of divine love?
The Lord said: / Well asked by you, O auspicious lady! Whatever is in my mind, / all that I shall tell you; listen attentively.
Remembering his qualities, chanting his name, or singing what delights the mind, / one awakens the self by the self and is constantly absorbed in divine love.

title: aṣṭasaptatitamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Pārvatī said: / Tell me truly the entire duty of Vaiṣṇavas, / by performing which all men indeed cross over the ocean of worldly existence.
The Lord said: / Now the twelvefold purification of Vaiṣṇavas is declared here: / smearing the floor of [the Lord's] house, and likewise following behind Hari;
circumambulation with devotion, and the cleansing of the feet; / and plucking leaves and flowers with devotion for the worship of Hari;
[this is] for the hands. Among all purifications, this purification is exalted: / chanting his names and also chanting his virtues
with devotion to the glorious Lord Kṛṣṇa is considered the purification of speech. / Listening to stories about him and beholding his festivals
are properly declared here as the purification of the ears and the eyes. / Wearing the water washed from his feet, the remnants of his offerings, and his garlands,
is declared the purification of the head bowed before Hari. / Inhaling the fragrance of his flowers and remnants of offerings, O beloved,
would be the purification of the nose within, so it is prescribed. / Whatever flowers and the like are offered to the two feet of Kṛṣṇa,
that alone is the purifier in the world; that indeed purifies everything. / And worship is declared to be fivefold; listen to the distinctions among them from me:
approaching, gathering, devotion, personal recitation of sacred texts, / and sacrifice—the fivefold worship I shall declare to you in order.
There, approaching is the sweeping of the deity's abode, / smearing [with cow dung], and removing the remnants of offerings.
Gathering is the plucking of perfumes, flowers, and the like; / yoga is the contemplation of one's own deity as one's own self with one's own soul.
Svādhyāya is japa preceded by contemplation of the mantra's meaning, / chanting of hymns and praises, and the glorification of Hari;
and study of scriptures on truth and other topics is declared as svādhyāya. / Ijyā is the worship of one's deity according to proper procedure.
Thus the fivefold worship has been told to you, O lady of virtuous vows, / which successively grants equal power, proximity, dwelling in the same world, union, and having the same form.
In this context I shall speak of the worship of the śālagrāma stone / in the sequence of Keśava and the rest, each four-armed, beginning from the upper right hand.
Holding conch, discus, mace, and lotus, he is called Keśava, bearer of the mace; / Nārāyaṇa has the weapons of lotus, mace, discus, and conch respectively.
Mādhava has discus, conch, lotus, and mace; / with mace, lotus, conch, and discus, he is called Govinda, bearer of the mace.
Homage to you in the form of Viṣṇu, holding lotus, conch, discus, and mace; / to the form of Madhusūdana with conch, lotus, mace, and discus.
Homage to Trivikrama endowed with mace, discus, conch, and lotus; / to the Vāmana form with discus, Kaumodakī, lotus, and conch.
Homage to the Śrīdhara form holding discus, lotus, conch, and mace; / O Hṛṣīkeśa, holding discus, mace, conch, and lotus, homage be to you.
To Padmanābha's own form with lotus, conch, mace, and discus; / O Dāmodara, holding conch, mace, discus, and lotus, homage be to you.
Homage to Saṃkarṣaṇa holding conch, lotus, discus, and mace; / O Vāsudeva with discus, conch, mace, and lotus, homage be to you.
To the manifested form of Pradyumna with conch, discus, mace, and lotus; / homage to Aniruddha holding mace, conch, lotus, and discus.
To the form of Puruṣottama with lotus, conch, mace, and discus; / homage to the form of Adhokṣaja holding mace, conch, discus, and lotus.
To the Nṛsiṃha form holding lotus, mace, conch, and discus; / to the Acyuta form holding lotus, discus, conch, and mace, homage be to you.
Homage to the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa with mace, lotus, discus, and conch. / The śālagrāma stone having two contiguous discuses situated at the aperture,
with a white-hued line and full of splendor, is the deity Śrī Gadādhara. / When having two contiguous discuses, of reddish hue, with a prominent front part,
it is Saṃkarṣaṇa; next, Pradyumna has a minute discus and is yellowish; / with a very long hollow cavity is Aniruddha, who is circular;
blue and with three lines at the aperture. Next, Nārāyaṇa is black, / with a mace-shaped line in the middle and a very prominent navel lotus.
The one with a broad discus is Nṛsiṃha; the tawny one has three dots; / or rather, the one with five dots is for the worship of a student of sacred lore (brahmacārin).
Varāha is the one with three marks, having two uneven discuses, / blue, with three lines, and thick. Next, the Kūrma form has dots,
black, with a circular whorl, pale, and carrying a back. / Śrīdhara has five lines, wears a forest garland, and is marked with a mace.
The one named Vāmana is circular, with a central discus, and bluish; / the one of diverse colors, many forms, and with serpent coils is Ananta.
Dāmodara is thick, blue, with a discus in the middle, and bluish. / May the one having the opening of Saṃkarṣaṇa protect; next, Brahmā is bright red,
with a very long cavity of lines, one discus, a lotus, and broad; / with a broad discus, a thick opening, black, with a dot, and spotted.
Hayagrīva is hook-shaped, has five lines, and bears the Kaustubha gem; / Vaikuṇṭha appears like a wrestler, consists of a single discus, and is black.
Matsya is shaped like an elongated lotus, has a long line, and is pale; / the one with the Rāma-discus and a line on the right, dark in color, is Trivikrama.
Homage to the mace-bearer residing at Śālagrāma and Dvārakā. / May Sudarśana, bearer of the mace, characterized by one [discus], protect.
Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa is by two, and Trivikrama indeed by three; / Caturvyūha is by four, and Vāsudeva by five.
May Pradyumna protect by six, and Saṃkarṣaṇa by seven; / Puruṣottama is by eight, and Navavyūha is favorable by nine.
Daśāvatāra is by ten; may Aniruddha then protect; / Dvādaśātman is by twelve, and above this it is Ananta.
Brahmā is four-faced, with staff, water-pot, and rosary, prominent; / Maheśvara is five-faced, ten-armed, with the bull on his banner;
according to their weapons, so are Gaurī, Caṇḍikā, Sarasvatī, / Mahālakṣmī, the Mothers, and the sun god holding a lotus.
And the elephant-faced, the elephant-shouldered, the six-faced, and the many kinds of hosts — / if these are present, installed, or worshipped in a temple,
then dharma, profit, pleasure, and liberation are indeed attained by a man.

title: navasaptatitamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: The Lord said: / In a śālagrāma, in a gem, in a yantra, in a maṇḍala, and in images / the worship of glorious Hari must be performed daily, but never in a bare building.
In a region of the Gaṇḍakī river lies the great place Śālagrāma; / may the stone produced there, established under the name Śālagrāma, protect.
From touching a śālagrāma stone, the sins of ten million births are destroyed; / how much more so worshiping there, which is the cause of Hari’s presence!
From a single sacrifice to a śālagrāma, one obtains the fruit of a hundred liṅgas. / If through merits gained across many births one should obtain a black stone,
bearing the mark of a cow's hoof, through that his rebirth is brought to an end. / First, one should examine the stone: smooth, supreme, and glossy dark-blue;
a blackish one is said to be middling, while a variegated one yields mixed fruits. / Fire, ever residing in wood, is brought to light by churning;
just so all-pervading Hari is perceived in a śālagrāma. / He who daily worships twelve stones of śālagrāma,
joined with a stone from Dvāravatī, is exalted in Vaikuṇṭha. / But if a man spots a cavity in a śālagrāma stone,
his ancestors dwell satisfied in heaven until the end of the kalpa. / Where the Dvāravatī stone is, that place is the abode of Vaikuṇṭha;
he who dies there goes to the city of Viṣṇu, and that sacred place extends for three yojanas. / Recitation, worship, and oblation all become ten-millionfold [in merit].
Whatever desire of the mind one cherishes is fulfilled within the radius of a krośa, without doubt; / because even an insect, when it dies there, goes to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
The man who sets a price upon a śālagrāma stone, / its seller, its buyer, and he who approves of the examination,
all of them go to hell for as long as the sun and the deluge exist. / Therefore, O goddess, one should avoid buying and selling the disc-marked stone.
The god originating from Śālagrāma and the god originating from Dvārakā — / where the union of the two occurs, liberation is there, without doubt.
Rich in discs originating from Dvārakā, marked with many discs, / having the form of a stone with disc-shaped seats, of the nature of pure consciousness, unstained:
“Homage be to you whose form is the syllable Oṃ, whose nature is eternal bliss! / O greatly fortunate Śālagrāma, show grace to your devotee,
to me who desire your favor and am burdened by debt, O Lord!” / Henceforth I shall joyfully proclaim the rule for the sectarian mark,
hearing which all men may attain similarity of form with Viṣṇu. / One should place Keśava on the forehead, the glorious Puruṣottama on the neck,
the god Nārāyaṇa on the navel, and Vaikuṇṭha on the heart, / Dāmodara on the left side, and Trivikrama on the right,
Hṛṣīkeśa on the crown of the head, and Padmanābha on the back, / the Yamunā and the Gaṅgā on the two ears, and Kṛṣṇa and Hari on the arms.
The deities are declared to be twelve, rejoicing each in its respective place; / one should recite these twelve names while applying the sectarian mark.
With soul purified of all sins, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu. / On whose forehead is seen the vertical mark with upward-going lines,
even an outcaste is pure of soul and worthy of worship indeed, without doubt. / But on the forehead of whatever man the vertical mark is not seen,
one should not look upon him; having seen him, one should gaze upon the sun. / The brāhmaṇa on whom a horizontal mark is seen, and no vertical mark,
after seeing or even touching him, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on. / The mark should be made with an interval in the middle, having the shape of Hari's foot.
Whatever lowest of the twice-born should make the vertical mark without a space, / on his forehead there is constantly a dog’s foot, without doubt.
From the nose up to the hair, the vertical mark is very beautiful; / endowed with a gap in the middle, one should know it to be a temple of Hari.
Brahmā resides on the left side, while on the right is Sadāśiva; / one should know Viṣṇu to be in the center, therefore one must not smear the center.
Looking in a mirror or into water, he who carefully applies / the vertical mark, being greatly fortunate, goes to the supreme state.
Fire, the waters, the Vedas, the moon and the sun, and the wind — / all these constantly reside in the right ear of brāhmaṇas.
And the Gaṅgā is in the right ear, and the sacrificial fire in the nose; / simply by touching both, one becomes pure that very moment.
Having poured water into a conch, one should give it, mixed with tulasī, / to high-souled Vaiṣṇavas; one should drink it and revere it with the head bowed,
consume it, and sprinkle his body, sons, friends, and family. / The water from Viṣṇu's feet, when drunk, destroys the sins of ten million births;
that same sin becomes eightfold from letting a drop fall upon the ground. / Holding the water-conch in one's hand, having praised, bowed, and circumambulated,
if that water is kept continuously, by him the fruit of birth has been attained. / In whose house there is no conch or a bell marked with Garuḍa
in front of Vāsudeva, he is no devotee in the Kali age. / Going to the house of the Lord by vehicles or sandals,
and failure to serve during festivals of the god, not bowing before him, / and greeting the Lord when contaminated by food remnants or during ritual impurity;
bowing with only one hand, circumambulating directly in front of him, / stretching out the legs in front, and sitting on a couch,
sleeping, eating, and also speaking falsehood, / loud talking, muttering among themselves, weeping, and quarreling,
punishing and rewarding, and speaking harshly to women, / covering oneself entirely with a garment, blaming others and praising others,
speaking obscenities, releasing downward gas, / offering inferior services despite having the capacity, and eating food not offered to him,
not offering fruits and the like produced in their respective seasons, / offering the remainder of a cooked dish that has already been used,
eating openly, censuring others and praising others, / silence before the teacher, praising oneself, and insulting deities —
these are declared to be the thirty-two offenses against Viṣṇu.
“Thousands of offenses are committed day and night by me; / regarding me as ‘I am yours’, forgive them, O Madhusūdana!”
Uttering this mantra, one should bow like a staff upon the ground; / Hari always forgives thousands of transgressions.
Eating at evening and morning as prescribed by the Veda for the twice-born / from what remains after Viṣṇu’s devotee has eaten, one is freed from the sin of the day.
Food is Brahmā, its savor is Viṣṇu: one should eat uttering ‘meat’; / he who eats knowing this is not tainted by the faults of food.
A round bottle-gourd, lentils along with the skin, / a white palmyra fruit, and eggplant: a Vaiṣṇava man should not eat these.
On the leaves of the banyan, holy fig, and swallow-wort, on the leaves of the careya and ebony, / on the mountain-ebony and the kadamba: a Vaiṣṇava man should not eat.
In Śrāvaṇa one should avoid leafy vegetables; in Bhādrapada one should abandon curd; / in the month of Āśvina one should give up milk, and in Kārttika one should abandon meat.
Burnt food, the lime fruit, whatever has not been offered to Viṣṇu, / the citron fruit, leafy greens, and visible salt —
if by chance one should consume them, then one should meditate upon his name. / Winter rice, white, steamed grain, mung beans, sesamum, and barley:
Kalāya peas, kaṅgu millet, wild nīvāra rice, the herb hilamocikā, / kālaśāka, and goosefoot (vāstūka), radish, and red [salt] or other varieties;
among salts, rock salt and sea salt; cow's curd and clarified butter; / milk from which cream has not been extracted; jackfruit, mango, and myrobalan (harītakī);
long pepper, cumin, ginger, orange, tamarind, / plantain, star gooseberry (lavalī), emblic myrobalan (dhātrī) fruits, and sugar-cane products without molasses;
cooked without oil—this the sages declare to be haviṣya food. / Whatever man wears a garland made with tulasī leaves, flowers, and the like,
one should know him to be Viṣṇu himself; this is true, true, there is no doubt. / By planting an emblic myrobalan tree, a man becomes equal to Viṣṇu.
One should know [the sacred area around it] to be Kurukṣetra for three hundred and fifty cubits. / With [beads] carved from tulasī wood made in the shape of rudrākṣa seeds,
having placed the prepared garland around the neck, one should begin the worship; / likewise an āmalaka garland, and properly a puṣkara garland.
A worshipper of Viṣṇu should diligently wear a garland on the neck; / he should also wear the remnant garland of tulasī upon his head.
With sandal paste from the offerings he should mark his body with his names; / and on the forehead the mace should be borne, and on the head the bow and arrow,
and the Nandaka sword in the middle of the heart, the conch and discus on both arms. / If a twice-born marked with the conch and discus dies in a cremation ground,
the destiny that is proclaimed at Prayāga, that destiny is certainly his. / He who, devoted to Viṣṇu, bearing a tulasī leaf upon his head,
performs all ritual actions, obtains imperishable fruit. / Performing an action adorned with garlands of tulasī wood,
what is done for the ancestors and the gods becomes multiplied ten-millionfold. / Having offered to Keśava a garland made of tulasī wood,
when planted, brings about nearness to the blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa; / when laid at his feet, bestows the fruit of liberation—to that Tulasī, homage!

title: aśītitamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Pārvatī said: / When the terrible Kali yuga has arrived, crowded with the crocodiles of sensory objects, / how can that be maintained by those afflicted with children, wife, wealth, and the like, O Lord?
Tell the means for that, O Mahādeva, treasure of mercy! / The Lord said: / The name of Hari, the name of Hari, the name of Hari alone!
‘Hare Rāma, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa’—which is auspicious— / Kali does not afflict those who constantly speak thus.
Doing work from time to time, one should also remember the names, / saying repeatedly, ‘Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa.’
Combining my name and your name interchangeably, / even he would be freed from sin, as fire [burns] a heap of cotton.
Beginning with 'Jaya', or else preceded by the word 'Śrī', / repeating that auspicious name of mine, one is freed from sin.
By day, by night, and at twilight—at all times one should remember it. / Remembering Rāma day and night, one sees Kṛṣṇa with one's own eyes.
Whether impure or pure, at all times and ever, / from the mere recollection of the name, one is freed from worldly existence in an instant.
Even of one laden with various offenses, the name destroys the sin. / Sacrifice, vow, austerity, and gifting are not complete in the Kali yuga;
bathing in the Gaṅgā and the name of Hari—these two are unfailing.
A myriad murders, a thousand fierce sins, and intercourse with a crore of wives of one's teacher, / and other thefts do not remain, O auspicious one, through the name of Govinda, dear to Hari.
Whether impure or pure, or in whatever condition one may be, / whoever remembers the lotus-eyed one is clean both externally and internally.
From the mere recollection of the name and likewise from contemplating its meaning, / having made [an image] of gold, silver, or of flour in the shape of a garland,
marked upon the feet, one should indeed begin the worship. / He who bears the discus at the base of the big toe of the right foot,
for cutting off the transmigration of the person bowed down there— / and at the base of the middle toe Acyuta bears a lotus,
most beautiful, to entice the black-bee minds of meditators; / below the lotus he bears a flag, a flag of victory over all misfortunes.
From the base of the little toe [he bears] the thunderbolt, cleaving the mass of sins of devotees; / in the middle of the side [he bears] the goad, causing delight to the hearts of devotees.
On the joint of the big toe he bears the barley corn, full of the abundance of enjoyment; / and at the heel the mace, shattering the mountain of sins of all embodied beings.
That unborn Lord bears [them] for the manifestation of all knowledge. / The marks such as the lotus that are again on the right,
and those which dwell on the left foot, that ocean of compassion bears. / Therefore, the glorification of Govinda, delightful with the rasa of bliss,
one should hear and ever recite; he is liberated, there is no doubt. / I shall declare the duty of each month, supremely pleasing to Viṣṇu.
In Jyeṣṭha, being pure, one should carefully perform the bathing of Śrī Viṣṇu. / Sins committed daily, in a fortnight, in a month, in a season, or in a year,
thousands of murders of Brahmins, committed knowingly or unknowingly, / and myriads of thefts of gold, drinking of liquor, and violating the teacher's bed,
and whatever thousands of crores of minor sins there are— / all of them are destroyed on the day of the full moon.
Then one should sprinkle that pitcher-water upon the head of Acyuta / with the mantra of the Puruṣasūkta and with the Pāvamānī verses,
with coconut water, and likewise with palm-fruit water, / with jewel-infused water, with perfumed water, and with flower water.
Having worshipped with the fivefold offerings according to one's wealth and means, / one should offer the sound of the bell, saying: 'Ghaṃ, obeisance to the bell!'
'For me who am fallen into the great darkness, burdened with an accumulation of sins, / protect me, a sinner, falling into the dreadful ocean of saṃsāra!'
A learned, pure Brahmin learned in the Veda who acts thus / is freed from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, one should celebrate the great festival of sleep; / in Āṣāḍha one should hold the chariot [festival], and in Śrāvaṇa the Śravaṇā rite.
In Bhādra, on his birthday, one should be intent upon fasting; / in the month of Āśvina, one should arrange the turning over of him who is asleep.
One should perform the awakening of Śrī Hari, otherwise one harms Viṣṇu; / and in the auspicious month of Āśvina, one should worship Mahāmāyā,
made of gold or silver, having the form of Viṣṇu, without animal sacrifice. / Injury and malice must not be done; the worshipper of Viṣṇu is righteous.
In the months of Kārtika and Pauṣa, one should perform meritorious acts at will; / and one should offer a lamp to Dāmodara in an elevated place.
The lamp should measure four aṅgulas, with seven wicks; / and at the end of the fortnight an auspicious row of lights should be made.
In Mārgaśīrṣa, on the sixth day of the bright fortnight, with white garments, / one should worship the Lord of the world, and especially Brahmā.
In Pauṣa [one should perform] the shower of flowers, and avoid loose sandalwood paste; / at the Saṃkrānti in the month of Māgha, from perfumed grains of rice,
one should offer food to Viṣṇu and recite this mantra. / With devotion one should feed Brahmins standing before the God of gods.
Having honoured the devotees of the Lord and the twice-born with the thought that they are the Lord, / when one devotee is fed, a crore are fed.
By the mere feeding of Brahmins, that which is defective certainly becomes complete. / On the fifth day of the bright fortnight, having bathed Keśava,
and worshipped him according to the rules, with mango sprouts, / and with various fruit-powders, perfumed and refined through cloth,
in an enchanting grove illuminated by blazing lamps, / with grapes, sugarcane, plantains, limes, oranges, and betel nuts,
with coconuts, myrobalans, jackfruits, and yellow myrobalans, / and with various fragments of trees endowed with flowers of all seasons,
and with other various fruits and flowers, / with canopies covered with flowers, and with pitchers filled with water,
adorned with branches and twigs of mango, with umbrellas and chowries, / remembering, 'Victory to Kṛṣṇa!', preceded by circumambulation.
Especially in the Kali yuga, the swing festival is prescribed / in Phālguna, on the fourteenth day, during the period called the eighth yāma,
or on the full moon day at the junction called Pratipad, / one should worship according to rule with devotion, using four kinds of red powder,
white, red, light-yellow, and deep-yellow, blended with camphor and the like, / and enchanting with colored powders through the combination with turmeric dye,
or with other color forms one should please the Supreme Lord. / Beginning on the eleventh day, one should conclude it on the fifth;
the swing festival is prescribed for five days or for three days. / Men who even once see Kṛṣṇa swinging facing the south,
having seen him, are freed from heaps of offenses; of this there is no doubt. / Having placed in a vessel of water in the month named Mādhava,
in a vessel of gold, silver, copper, or earthen, / whoever worships the god dwelling in the water, originated from the Śālagrāma,
or an image, O highly fortunate one, his merit cannot be counted. / Having performed the offering of damana, one should present it to Śrī Viṣṇu.
In Vaiśākha, Śrāvaṇa, and Bhādra, the wind-cleansing should be performed; / when the wind is in the earlier directions during rites such as damana,
it should be performed according to rule; otherwise it becomes fruitless. / In Vaiśākha, especially on the third day, in the midst of water,
or in a maṇḍala, or in a pavilion in a great forest, / one should diligently nourish his body day after day with fragrant sandalwood,
just as one would nourish a person with an emaciated body. / Sandalwood, agallochum, hrībera, black saffron, and rocanā,
spikenard, and murā—they know these as the eight perfumes of Viṣṇu. / With those various perfumes one should smear the limbs of Viṣṇu.
Ground tulasī wood combined with camphor and agallochum, / or mixed with saffron, is called haricandana.
Those mortals who with devotion see Kṛṣṇa at the time of the festival / have no return [to rebirth] even in hundreds of crores of kalpas.
Those who bathe the god of gods with waters mixed with fragrances, / or indeed should place the Lord of the universe within flowers,
having gone there to Vṛndāvana and prepared fruits, / should feed that in its entirety to a worthy devotee of Viṣṇu.
One should offer coconut fruit having extracted the seed-capsule, / and one should offer jackfruit having extracted the pulp from its casing.
One should offer rice mixed with curds, bathed in ghee; / and cakes cooked with flour, eighteen kinds [of pastries] with ghee,
and ripe fruits [cooked] with sesame oils, one should present. / Whatever is pleasing to oneself, that one should offer to the Lord.
Having offered food, garments, and the like, one must never take it back; / and whatever was given up for Viṣṇu, [let it be given] especially to his devotees.

Thus has this been spoken to you briefly, O great goddess;
it should be concealed with great effort, like one's own vulva, O Pārvatī.

If there is qualification for understanding the class of scriptures describing the form and qualities of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, what need is there for other recitations? / If the mind is truly fixed upon the neck-garlands of devotion's play in the rasa of love for him, what use indeed are desirable women?

Therefore, let people worship with their minds the Lord of the cowherd boys of Vraja, the soil of Vṛndāvana, and the waters of the Yamunā. / When the body is anointed with the dust of the lotus feet of the protector of that realm, aloes, sandalwood, and the like are utterly in vain.

title: ekāśītitamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: The sages said: / Live long, O righteous Sūta! The nectar of Śrī Kṛṣṇa's deeds, / which carries devotees across existence, has all been revealed by you.
Declare, O lord, the entire daily sport of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, / by hearing which, O righteous one, devotion to Kṛṣṇa flourishes.
Tell us separately the rules and characteristics of the guru, the disciple, and the mantra, / O fortunate one, for you are our supreme friend.
Sūta said: / Once, bowing down to Sadāśiva, the teacher of the world, / seated on the bank of the Yamunā, Nārada addressed the god of gods:
Nārada said: / O god of gods, O Mahādeva, omniscient Lord of the universe, / knower of the truth of divine dharma, foremost among knowers of Kṛṣṇa's mantras!
Kṛṣṇa's mantras were obtained by me from you, and others from my father; / all of them—the king of mantras and the rest—have been mastered by me in accordance with the truth,
through many thousands of years by subsisting on vegetables, roots, and fruits, / consuming dried leaves, water, air, and the like, and fasting,
avoiding the sight and conversation of women, sleeping on the bare ground, / having conquered the sixfold qualities of desire and the rest, restraining the external senses.
Even when this was done, my soul was not satisfied, O Śaṅkara. / Therefore speak of that which is accomplished without purificatory rites and the like, O Lord,
which yields the highest fruit simply from being pronounced once. / If I am qualified, O Lord of gods, then tell me out of compassion.
Śiva said: / Well asked, O fortunate one, desiring the welfare of the world! / Even though it is closely guarded, I shall tell you the wish-fulfilling jewel of mantras,
the secret of secrets, the best mystery of mysteries, / which was not told by me to the goddess, nor earlier to your elder brothers.
I shall tell you the matchless couplet, the Kṛṣṇa mantra, / indeed the pair called the wish-fulfilling jewel of mantras.
The synonyms of this mantra are likewise 'the five-worded one': / the word 'gopījana', ending with 'vallabha', and then 'caraṇau' [feet],
and 'śaraṇam' [shelter] and 'prapadye' [I approach]. This consists of five words. / The wish-fulfilling jewel of mantras is declared to be a great mantra of sixteen syllables.
Having said 'namo gopījana', one should then say 'vallabhābhyām'. / This mantra consisting of two words is said to have ten syllables.
Having repeated this five-worded [mantra] even once with faith upon faith, / one certainly attains the presence of Kṛṣṇa's beloveds; there is no doubt.
There is no requirement of preliminary rites, nor of the order of rules for nyāsa; / there is no restriction of place or time, nor examination of enemy, friend, and the like.
And everyone here is eligible, right down to the Cāṇḍāla, O lord of sages: / women, Śūdras and the rest, and also the dull, the mute, and the lame,
and other Hūṇas, Kirātas, Pulindas, and Pukkasas, / Ābhīras, Yavanas, Kaṅkas, Khasas, and other low-born castes,
those intent on deceit and egotism, sinners, those devoted to slander, / slayers of cows, brāhmaṇas, and the like, those guilty of the greatest secondary sins,
those devoid of knowledge and dispassion, those excluded from hearing [the scriptures] and the like— / these and all others are eligible for this mantra,
if they possess devotion to Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of all lords; / then all are eligible, not otherwise, O best of sages.
Though one be a sacrificer, devoted to charity, a practitioner of all tantras, / truth-speaking, or an ascetic, one who has crossed over the Veda and the Vedāṅgas,
devoted to Brahman, high-born, or an ascetic intent on vows, / he is not eligible here if he is devoid of devotion to Kṛṣṇa.
Therefore, it should not be spoken to one who is not a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, to the ungrateful, to the arrogant, / nor to one lacking faith, nor to an atheist,
nor should it be told to one who does not wish to serve, nor to one who has not served for a full year. / To one with undivided devotion to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, free from deceit and greed,
and liberated from lust and anger, this should be given with effort. / And I myself am its seer, and the Gāyatrī is said to be the metre;
the deity of the mantra is proclaimed to be the beloved of the cowherd maidens. / Its application is declared to be in the servitude of Hari along with his beloved.
One should arrange the five bodily parts with the mantras beginning with the discus and the like; / or rather, one should perform the nyāsa on the hands and limbs with its own seed-syllable.
The first syllable of the mantra, adorned on its top with an anusvāra, / 'Gam', becomes the seed-syllable; 'namaḥ' is declared here as the śakti.
The ten limbs are formed by the final syllables, and with them also worship [is performed] / with perfumes, flowers, and the like, or with water alone if these are unavailable.
It should be performed according to the previous rule of nyāsa for the satisfaction of Hari. / Hence, others declare nyāsa and the like for this mantra,
which grants the state of having accomplished one's aim simply from being pronounced once. / Even so, one should constantly apply it ten times for the sake of repetition and the like.
Now I shall declare the meditation of this mantra, O best of the twice-born: / dressed in yellow garments, dark as a raincloud, two-armed, wearing a forest garland,
wearing a crest made of peacock feathers, his face resembling ten million moons, / his eyes rolling gently, adorned with an ear-ornament of karṇikāra flowers,
bearing on his forehead a circular tilaka fashioned / on both sides with sandalwood and in the middle with a dot of saffron,
radiant with two earrings resembling the newly risen sun, / with mirror-like cheeks shining with droplets of perspiration,
his eyes resting upon the face of his beloved, his eyebrows raised in playful side-glances, / his prominent nose glistening with a pearl placed at its tip,
his lower lip like a ripe bimba fruit shining with the moonlight of his teeth, / his hands splendid with armlets, bracelets, and rings set with excellent gems,
holding a flute and the like, and likewise a lotus in his left hand, / his waist gleaming with a girdle, his feet splendid with anklets,
restless with the surge of the rasa of amorous play, his eyes darting, / laughing with his beloved, and making her laugh repeatedly.
Thus, at the foot of the wish-fulfilling tree, upon a jeweled throne / in the forest of Vṛndā, one should meditate on Kṛṣṇa seated together with his beloved.
Then one should meditate on Rādhikā standing at his left side, / clad in a blue bodice, having a brilliance equal to molten gold,
with her gently smiling lotus face half veiled by the border of her silk garment, / her eyes fixed on the face of her beloved, her restless gaze like that of a cakorī bird,
and offering with her thumb and forefinger into the lotus mouth of her beloved / areca nut accompanied by betel leaf and [lime] powder;
her firm, elevated breasts gleaming with pearl necklaces, / slender-waisted, broad-hipped, adorned with an array of tinkling bells,
wearing jeweled earrings, armlets, signet rings, and bracelets, / with ringing bangles and anklets, and jeweled toe-rings,
her captivating limbs embodying the essence of beauty, lovely in every part, / immersed in the nectar of bliss, serene, endowed with fresh youth.
And her female companions, O best of brahmins, of equal age and virtues to her, / should be imagined as devoted to her service with chowries, fans, and other things.
Now I shall tell you the meaning of the mantra; listen, O Nārada: / by the external forms of the phenomenal world, through her partial aspects such as the powers of māyā and others,

and likewise by the internal forms, the eternal manifestations such as consciousness and the rest, / because she conceals [all these], the beloved of Kṛṣṇa is called Gopī, Rādhikā; / the goddess Rādhikā is declared to be identical with Kṛṣṇa, the supreme deity.

She is the essential form of all Lakṣmīs, the embodiment of Kṛṣṇa's joy;
therefore she is proclaimed by the wise as "the delight-giving potency" (hlādinī), O brāhmaṇa.
Durgā and others consisting of the three guṇas are a fraction of tens of millions of parts of her; / she, however, is directly Mahālakṣmī, and Kṛṣṇa is the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
There is not the slightest difference between these two, O best of sages: / she is Durgā and Hari is Rudra; Kṛṣṇa is Indra and she is Śacī;
she is Sāvitrī and Hari is Brahmā; she is Dhūmorṇā and Hari is Yama. / What is the use of saying much, O best of sages? Without the two of them, nothing exists.
The entire world, characterized by the sentient and the insentient, consists of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa. / Thus know everything to be the manifestation of just those two, O Nārada.
It cannot be told by me even in hundreds of millions of years. / In the three worlds, the earth is honored; superior to that is Jambūdvīpa;
even there, Bhārata-varṣa; even there, the city of Mathurā; / there, the place named Vṛndāvana; there, the multitude of gopīs;
there, the group of Rādhā's female companions; even there, Rādhikā is superior. / Owing to the greater degree of her proximity, each successive one is superior.
