with delightful flower gardens, worship, processions, festivals, and the like, / in order to maintain the continuous flow of worship and other rites on great festival days and daily.
By granting fields, shops, towns, and villages, he attains union [with Hari]. / By consecration [he gains the status of] a sovereign emperor; by [building] a temple, the three worlds;
by worship and other services, the world of Brahmā; by all three, he attains equality with him. / Through devotion that is free from desire, he attains him alone.
that intellect is white as a spotless moon and conch, which pervades Mādhava; / that tongue is sweet-speaking, O king, which repeatedly praises Nārāyaṇa.
Worship should also be performed by women and Śūdras using the basic mantra, / and by others with faith according to the path taught by their own guru, O Vaiṣṇava.
All this purifying worship of Mādhava has been told to you. / Do this especially in the month of Mādhava, O lord of the earth.
Sūta said: / Having heard these wonderful, meritorious, and purifying words of the son of Brahmā, / the king, foremost among the devotees of the Lord, bowed with joined palms and spoke eagerly:

Ambarīṣa said: / I am the lord of the entire circle of the earth, my commands unimpeded, a server of the wise, / my mind surrendered to the lotus feet of Govinda, having pleased the brāhmaṇas with my heart;
a renowned jewel of a royal lineage, constant in delight for dharma, famous, / endowed with beauty, valor, and the virtue of generosity, blessed with virtuous sons, my foes conquered;

by what merit was I born with a pure intellect, endowed with such virtues and glory? / Moreover, from where did I obtain this lovely wife, glowing with beauty, like Lakṣmī herself, the embodiment of merit?
Explain to me fully all this good deed practiced by me in a previous birth, / O sage; you are omniscient, an ocean of compassion.
Nārada said: / She who is now your very beautiful wife of truthful conduct / was in another birth a courtesan named Rūpavatī.
The noble woman lived by the duty prescribed for a courtesan, / performing indeed auspicious deeds at the instruction of a brāhmaṇa.
You were a goldsmith celebrated by the name Devadāsa; / in that previous birth, you were her lover, her paramour.
She served you eagerly, beautiful Rūpavatī; / and she adhered to the highest knowledge, the path of dharma for the sake of expending wealth.
Once, hearing the duty arising from the bath in the month of Vaiśākha, / that pious woman took a bath in the water when the sun had entered Aries.
The capable courtesan Rūpavatī constantly gave gifts, / offering salutations to a brāhmaṇa with devotion and respect.
Enjoined by her affection, you, as that Devadāsa, were awakened by her, / and reverently took the bath in the month of Mādhava with proper understanding.
There, on the pure third lunar day at the beginning of the Tretā age, / she respectfully said to that goldsmith Devadāsa:
The courtesan said: / Make an excellent golden image of Madhusūdana, Acyuta. / Having worshipped the god with barley grains and satisfied the fire with them,
I shall give it to a brāhmaṇa with the permission of brāhmaṇas. / In the Purāṇas, this gift given at that time is said to be inexhaustible.
I have heard from brāhmaṇas that that bright third lunar day / of the month of Vaiśākha is called Akṣayā, which grants inexhaustible fruit.
On this day, I will give that golden, imperishable Madhusūdana. / Nārada said: / Hearing her sweet words, the goldsmith,
free from deceit, for the sake of dharma, with a truthful disposition, / made a beautiful golden image of Acyuta,
and an image endowed with auspicious characteristics, as prescribed, of the moon; / having bathed according to rule, she gave that beautiful [image] to a brāhmaṇa,
having worshipped it, O king, on that Akṣayā tithi.
After some time, that courtesan, steadfast in dharma, died; / and Devadāsa also died constantly at the exhaustion of his lifespan.
By that merit, O king, the goldsmith in another birth / became you, O king, who obtained the earth, endowed with all virtues.
And that courtesan Rūpavatī, by that dharma, became yours— / your lovely wife named Kāntimatī, overflowing with affection.
Diverse are the latent impressions of past actions, O hero; / strange are their courses, dear one, not known even by the wise.
There is no doubt regarding the practice concerning this month of Mādhava; / it was kept hidden by that Lord, by Brahmā, and by Mādhava.

By those with bad company, who have not attained knowledge, who are undisciplined and devoid of the duty of the āśramas, / who have not visited holy fords and have performed no vows—by them the observance of the month of Mādhava is not attained.

Those on whose lips the excellent speech, 'Govinda, Keśava, Mukunda, Hari, Murāri, / Abode of Lakṣmī, Madhusūdana, Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu!' does not reside—to them the observance of the month of Vaiśākha does not belong.

Those who do not listen to virtuous words that are exceedingly beneficial, and to the nectarean deeds of Hari, / and who do not look upon the temples of the husband of Kamalā—they do not attain the observance of the month of Vaiśākha.

By whom gurus were not served, nor a maiden given in marriage, adorned, to a suitable groom at the proper time, / nor sons instructed in modesty and other virtues—they do not attain the observance of the month of Vaiśākha.

Sūta said: / Having thus instructed the king and bid him farewell, the sage, foremost of those who know mantras, / went to bathe in the Gaṅgā in the month of Mādhava, having then been worshipped by him, O brāhmaṇas.

Then that king too, of holy mind, celebrated throughout the world for his purifying fame, / performed the rite of the month of Vaiśākha taught by the sage, together with his wife, meditating on him alone.

title: ṣaṇṇavatitamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: The sages said: / Sūta, Sūta of great wisdom, live, live for a hundred years, / since we have been made to hear the auspicious season, beneficial to the world!
Speak even more abundantly! We drink your words; / drinking again and again that supreme [speech], we are not sated, O Sūta!
Sūta said: / Here too they cite this ancient legendary history, / the conversation of the primordial world, of the Lord of the worlds.
Six thousand [yojanas] in height, and three [thousand] in width; / thus, having made nine thousand yojanas,
Held by his left tusk, the earth was first lifted up; / indeed, the earth was supported on his tusk for a thousand divine years.
In the course of discussing dharma, she said with humility to the lord: / The Earth said: / “These twelve months indeed consist of three hundred and sixty days.
Among them, which is the most meritorious and dear to you, O Keśava? / The month of Kārtika is sacred when the sun is in Tulā.
The month when the sun is in Makara is traditionally regarded as purifying in the Purāṇa; / the month of Mādhava, when the sun is in Meṣa, is recited by the wise.
Mārgaśīrṣa also is proclaimed to be purifying among the months. / Thus are the sacred months; which days are proclaimed [likewise]?
The beginnings and ends of yugas, and likewise the beginnings of kalpas: / tell me of the purifying month that is superior even to all of these.
O glorious one, composed of all sacrifices, determine and tell me that one [month].” / The Boar said: / “Even according to the prescribed rules, those vile men who sacrifice,
if they worship me with devotion in the month of Mādhava, I am always to be worshipped by them. / O fair-hipped one, Hiraṇyākṣa was slain in [the month of] Mādhava, and Madhu too was slain.
Having slain both of these primordial daityas, you were rescued. / In the Tretā age, the threefold Vedic duty, knowledge, and the arrangement of castes
came into being in the month of Mādhava; therefore Mādhava is dear to me. / The Tretā age [began] on the third lunar day of the bright fortnight in the month of Mādhava;
it commenced, and the threefold Vedic duties commenced and flourished. / That third day is called inexhaustible (Akṣayā) in the world, beloved of Hari.
In bathing, giving gifts, worship, śrāddha, recitation of mantras, and libations to ancestors, / those who worship Viṣṇu with barley grains and perform the śrāddha with diligence—
to them I grant everything, whatever highest desire is in their hearts. / Those men who also give gifts are fortunate and righteous.
Those who constantly sacrifice to Hari with diverse rituals— / whoever sacrifices to me in Mādhava obtains a fruit greater than theirs.
Bathing, gift-giving, silent recitation, fire offerings, asceticism, sacrifices, vows, and the like: / hear the meritorious fruit of what is done in Vaiśākha, O goddess.
For seventeen crores of manvantaras, / they remain in my presence, free from fear.
Even if all planets should be cruel, in the house of birth, expense, or the eighth, / by bathing at dawn in Vaiśākha, they all become benign.
Whoever feeds brāhmaṇas in the month of Vaiśākha, intent on devotion, / for every morsel of food, there is satisfaction for the ancestors for the duration of a yuga.
Those who provide sweet foods in abundance, or meals of barley, and water with sesame seeds, / umbrellas, garments, and appropriate footwear—they alone are blessed, causing delight to Viṣṇu.
Especially here, sesame seeds mixed with honey should be given, / for the sake of great dharma and to cause the destruction of long-accumulated sins.
When this is done, the merit that is attained by those men— / by whom could it be calculated even in hundreds of millions of years?
Wealth of sons, grandsons, and the like, and a long life as desired, / he attains in this world, and in the next world he attains me alone.
The series of sins accumulated in many births dissolves through bathing in Mādhava, / or when a person takes shelter at dawn at a sacred pilgrimage place according to the injunction.
He who, abandoning Vaiśākha, undertakes some other observance, / leaves a great jewel resting in his hand and begs for a clod of earth.”
Sūta said: / Thus the lord, the ancient foremost god, the bearer of the earth, / spoke formerly concerning the month of Mādhava upon the earth.
What is the use of saying much here? There is nothing, O earthly gods, / that cannot be obtained by worshipping Mādhava in the month of Mādhava.
Hear also an ancient event on this subject, supreme and wondrous: / the conversation between a brāhmaṇa and the great-souled Yama.
In the Madhyadeśa there was a great village of brāhmaṇas, / between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, below the Yamunā mountain.
Very many learned brāhmaṇas dwelt there at that time. / Then Yama spoke to a certain dark and reddish-brown man,
with red eyes, hair standing on end, and legs, eyes, and nose like a crow's: / “Go, sir, to that great village, and having gone, bring a brāhmaṇa
born in the Vasiṣṭha lineage, Yajñadatta by name, / established in tranquility, learned, and skilled in the sacrificial rites.
And do not bring another from his clan beside him, / who possesses the same qualities, equal to him in learning and birth,
and equal to him, the best of men, in form and bodily marks; / bring the one designated, for I must pay him worship.”
Going there, however, he acted contrary to Yama's command; / he brought that very one whom Yama had forbidden.
Rising to meet him and having worshipped him, Yama, knower of dharma, / said: “Let him be led away, and let that other one be brought.”
Sūta said: / When these words were spoken by Dharmarāja, that twice-born man, / unwilling to depart, spoke to Dharmarāja:
The brāhmaṇa said: / “Why was I brought here, and why do you send me back again? / I do not wish to go back to that mortal world, O lord.”
Yama said: / “Here is the abode of meritorious men whose lifespans are exhausted; / this indeed is the realm of Dharmarāja, proclaimed as righteousness itself.
All this is a place of happiness, and I, Dharmarāja, am the ruler, / granting pleasure and pain to creatures according to their merits and demerits.
For sinners I have the form of Yama, bestowing hell upon men; / likewise, for the virtuous, I am the embodiment of dharma, bestowing bliss and heaven.
Go, O brāhmaṇa, this very day to your own home, just as you came; / ten years of your lifespan still remain today.
When your lifespan is exhausted, you will attain this world; / and if anything else is to be asked by you, ask: I shall tell you.”
The brāhmaṇa said: / “Tell me that by doing which very great merit is gained, leading to heaven; / for you are the authority for all in determining dharma and adharma.
If, O god, I must properly return to my own house, / then tell me: by what action do men fall into hell?
And by what do they go to heaven? Tell all that out of compassion.” / Yama said: / “Those men who are averse to dharma in action, mind, and speech,
and those devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu, are indeed bound for hell. / Those who see Brahmā, Śaṃkara, and Hari with a mind of division,
and men who are detached from the sacred knowledge of Viṣṇu, are bound for hell. / One who abandons the duty suited to his family and country and performs another,
whether from desire or from delusion, that man goes to hell. / One who officiates for those unfit to sacrifice, and one who abandons those fit to sacrifice,
and one averse to the sacred knowledge of Viṣṇu—he suffers many hells. / Without giving to the ancestors, gods, and brāhmaṇas, or among mortal kin,
a wealthy man dies a sinner; he goes to many hells. / One who, when all the food is prepared, makes distinctions in the cooking,
and eats without having performed the vaiśvadeva rite, goes to hell for a long time. / Those who acquire wealth by great injury to living beings, O twice-born,
wealthy, hypocritical men bound for hell, partake of suffering. / Those who, out of disbelief, greed, or delusion, at the prescribed time,
do not offer śrāddha with devotion—they are boiled in hells. / But the evildoer [who obstructs] wealth being given to brāhmaṇas,”
The man who causes an obstacle to the wealth given to Brahmins goes to hell. / When a common sacrificial fee has been received, one who out of delusion takes it alone,
and the man intent on atheistic views will abide in hell. / By his intolerance toward the virtues [of others], a reason will arise
for a great sin to be born, which is a cause of hell. / He who in time abandons the faultless wife of his friends,
and does not maintain their fame—that man will fall into hell. / He who, under the sway of delusion, calls adharma dharma,
and the rationalizing skeptic who is an atheist—that man has his dwelling in hell. / He who thinks one way in his mind and speaks otherwise with his speech,
and makes his heart foul—that man will dwell in hell. / And those men who treat the singing of the Lord's praises with contempt,
they go to a terrible hell because of that sinful deed. / Those who, seeing the Lord's doorway, his names, scriptures, and sacred attire,
do not offer obeisance and the like, go to dwell in hell. / Men who, without any fault, marry another wife over their first wife,
and those who abandon a virtuous wife—those men go to hell. / A man who does not listen to the word of his guru or to the dharmaśāstra,
and causes distress to the minds of others, will go to hell. / One who greedily eats sweet food while his relatives and children are watching,
merely filling his own belly, goes to a terrible hell. / He who does not perform the morning bath when the sun is in Libra, Capricorn, and Aries,
and is skeptical regarding rivers and the like, will have his abode in hell. / He who, having seen a Vaiṣṇava, does not rise to greet him,
out of love and respect, O Brahmin, that man is a guest of hell. / Those who block roads with pieces of wood, stakes,
spears, or even stones, certainly go to hell. / Those who do not think upon Viṣṇu, the primeval person, the Lord,
the great master of all the worlds, certainly go to hell. / Those men who cut off a field, a livelihood, or a home, or sever affection,
and cut off hope—those men are dwellers in hell. / When Brahmins worn down by their livelihood have arrived for a meal,
the foolish-minded person who interrogates them should be known as a guest of hell. / When a Vaiṣṇava is destitute, miserable, afflicted by disease, or old,
the fools who have no compassion for him certainly go to hell. / Those who, having undertaken religious vows, afterward fail to control their senses
and repeatedly violate them, certainly go to hell. / Listen, O Brahmin, how compassionate men go to heaven.
I shall tell you in brief, out of some respect for you. / Those who worship the god Hari, the victorious, eternal Viṣṇu,
Nārāyaṇa, the unborn, Kṛṣṇa, Viṣvaksena, four-armed, / who meditate on the divine person and remember Acyuta,
attain the abode of Acyuta; such is the ancient revelation. / For this alone is auspiciousness; this alone is the acquisition of wealth;
and this is the fruit of life: singing the praise of Dāmodara. / From praising the God of gods, Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor,
sins dissolve away just as darkness does at sunrise. / Those who daily sing a Vaiṣṇava hymn endowed with faith,
constantly intent on sacred study—those men go to heaven. / Those who, casting aside all afflictions, praise Viṣṇu alone,
constant in their own duty and steadfast—those men go to heaven. / Even towards people who have committed sin, if they are devoted to the recitation of Vāsudeva's name,
the terrible messengers of Yama do not approach them, O Brahmin. / For living beings, they see no other atonement that calms all sins
than singing the praise of Hari, O best of the twice-born. / Those who rejoice when asked, give and speak kindly,
and renounce the fruit of their gift—those men go to heaven. / Men who avoid sleeping by day, and who endure everything,
and who offer shelter on sacred days—those mortals go to heaven. / Those who never speak of the faults even of their enemies,
and proclaim their virtues instead—those men go to heaven. / Those who, seeing the prosperity of others, are not tormented by envy,
but are delighted and applaud—those men go to heaven. / In the path of active engagement and of renunciation, what is stated in the Veda and the scriptures,
those who faithfully respect it—those men go to heaven. / In whatever family they may be born, compassionate and renowned,
Those men who are compassionate and of good conduct go to heaven; / those who are pure, and do not delight in the wives of others
in action, thought, or speech, being established in goodness, go to heaven; / those who always perform rites as prescribed and execute what is ordained,
having understood their own capacity, those men go to heaven. / Whoever constantly has faith in dharma of mind, speech, and body,
and is approved by the virtuous, becomes a guest of the gods. / He who endures the urge of speech, the urge of the mind, the urge arising from the belly,
and the urge of the genitals—that man is born in heaven. / Those whose contentment lies in virtues, whose speech is directed toward sacred learning,
and whose intellect is fixed on the supreme truth—those cultured men go to heaven. / Those who guard their vow from anger, who guard prosperity from envy,
learning from honor and dishonor, and the self from carelessness, / who guard the intellect from greed, and the mind from lust,
and guard dharma from bad company—those men go to heaven. / Those devoted to fasting in the proper manner on the eleventh lunar day,
in both the bright and dark fortnights, O brahmin, those men go to heaven. / Like a mother to all children, like medicine to the sick,
the eleventh lunar day was created for the protection of all the worlds. / There is no protection equal to the eleventh lunar day;
having fasted on it according to the rule, men go to heaven. / Whatever sin has been committed by the eleven senses, O twice-born,
having shaken that off swiftly, a man goes to heaven with delight. / Thousands of horse sacrifices and hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices
are not worth a sixteenth part of a fast on the eleventh lunar day. / On one side are all the sacrifices and austerities at all sacred places,
gifts such as the great gifts—and on the other side is the Vaiṣṇava vow. / The dharma born of the Vaiṣṇava vow and the dharma produced by sacrifices and the like:
when weighed together by the Creator, the former is heavier. / For devotees of the day of Hari, who speak the names of Acyuta and Ananta,
I am not the punisher; in fact, O brahmin, I am afraid of them. / He whose son and grandson have fasted on the eleventh lunar day
forcibly delivers a hundred men along with himself. / Therefore, one should observe fasting on both fortnights;
on the eleventh lunar day, that man becomes the sole vessel of enjoyment and liberation. / Jayā, Vijayā, and Jayantī, destroying sins,
Trispṛśā, Vañjulī, the excellent Pakṣasaṃvardhinī, / the supreme Tiladugdhā, and likewise Akhaṇḍadvādaśī,
the one called Manorathā, and also the Bhīmadvādaśī— / such are the many varieties of the twelfth lunar day.
Those who are capable in these vows should be known as established in Brahman. / Those who listen to the treatises on dharma, joined with faith in dharma,
and who do good to children—they go to the world of heaven. / Men observing the vow of ancestral rites on the new moon, one day each month,
whose ancestors are gratified—they are blessed and go to heaven. / When meals are prepared, those who respectfully offer food
with an unchanged countenance—those cultured men go to heaven.
Those who have devotion to Madhusūdana, to Nārāyaṇa the lord of all, / even if devoid of truth and joined with passion, go to heaven with endless merit.
Those of auspicious conduct, devoted to bathing and giving gifts, / who resort to the Vitastā, the Yamunā, the Sītā, and the holy Godāvarī river,
never see the path of hell. / Those who bathe here in the Narmadā, the giver of happiness, or are pleased even by seeing it,
having shaken off their sins, go to the world of the Great Lord and delight there for a long time.
Restrained men who have bathed on the bank of the Carmanvatī river for three nights, / especially at Vyāsa's hermitage, are remembered as dwellers in heaven.
Those who have died in the water of the Gaṅgā, at Prayāga, at Kedāra, Puṣkara, / at Vyāsa's hermitage, and at Prabhāsa, go to Viṣṇu.
Those who have died at Dvāravatī, at Kurukṣetra, or through the practice of yoga, / and those who have the syllable 'Hari' on their mouth, do not have rebirth.
Those who have stayed even for three nights in the city of Dvāravatī, O brahmin, / and bathe on the bank of the Gomatī, are blessed and dear to Keśava.
Those who take refuge for three nights at the abode of Nara and Nārāyaṇa / in the mortal world, and at the Nandā, are blessed and dear to Keśava.
Having dwelt for six months near Puruṣottama, O brahmin, / they become united with Acyuta and, having seen him, surely have their sins removed.
Those who, by holy waters earned through many births, bathe in the waters of Maṇikarṇikā, / and having reached Kāśī bow to the Lord of the Universe, are indeed to be revered even by me here.
Having worshipped Hari with kuśa grass and sesame seeds on the ground, / having scattered sesame seeds, and having given iron and a milch cow,
those men who have died according to the proper manner, O brahmin, go to heaven. / Having fathered sons and established them in the paternal and ancestral position,
those who die devoid of selfishness and egoism also become dwellers in heaven. / Those continually turned away from theft, contented with their own wealth,
who live off their own fortune—those men go to heaven. / Those who speak gentle words that cause no affliction and are free from deceitful sweet means,
addressing others with a welcome—those men go to heaven. / Those who understand the maturation of the accumulation of fruits
of both good and bad deeds, O brahmin—those men go to heaven. / Those who foster the enthusiasm of those engaged in wealth and dharma,
and following the path of dharma—those men rejoice in heaven. / He who gives fire in winter, and likewise gives water in summer,
and gives shelter during the rains, rejoices for a long time in heaven. / At all auspicious times, during regular, occasional, and other occasions,
he who performs ancestral rites with devotion surely partakes of the world of the gods.

Gifts from a poor man, forgiveness from a powerful one, austerity of the young, silence of the wise, / restraint of desires in those accustomed to pleasure, and compassion toward living beings lead to heaven.
The connection of karma is twofold, arising from sin and merit; / relying upon truth alone, the decision is indeed made here.
Austerity combined with meditation is for crossing the ocean of worldly existence; / but sin is declared to cause a fall; this is the truth, without doubt.
Even for a man endowed with strength, retinue, and valor, / if he is devoid of merit, that strength and the rest will dissolve.
There are lofty, well-nourished trees in mountain strongholds; / yet, even though dense, they fall by the force of the wind along with their roots.
Likewise, those devoid of truth and dharma go to the abode of Yama. / Dharma is the common and sole strength for all living beings,
by which a creature crosses over in this world and the next. / All this that bestows the path to heaven has been duly
declared by me in brief. What more do you wish to hear?

title: saptanavatitamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: The brahmin said: / Even a fool knows this: a man who performs auspicious deeds / does not go to hell, nor does one devoted to sinful acts go to heaven.
Heavenly happiness is attained through various sacrifices properly offered, vows, gifts, recitations, and the like, / and by those skilled in truthful conduct.
Heaven is sometimes attained through the conjunction of merit, by sages possessing learning, conduct, and wealth, / who have crossed to the further shore of the Vedas, through sacrifices;
and without wealth, one cannot give much in gifts, / even with wealth present, for one whose mind is attached to his family.
[they go to heaven]. The duties such as the agnihotra, especially in the Kali age, / are difficult to perform; the duty of giving gifts is also considered difficult to perform, O Lord.
An accumulation of dharma is attained by a duty involving little exertion. / Tell me that in detail, O revealer of dharma and adharma.
Let that one dharma, the most supreme among all dharmas, be declared, / by performing which alone all sin here is destroyed;
by which wealth, grain, renown, dharma, and lifespan increase, / there is friendship even in the mortal world, and heaven becomes imperishable;
by which Nārāyaṇa himself, who bestows fearlessness on his devotees, / is pleased, and by whose grace desire is placed in the palm of one's hand;
and by which a fruit greater than all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, and attendance on sacred fords / is attained—if there is such a thing, O son of Vivasvat, instruct me in it.
If I am indeed worthy of grace, O god, by instruction in dharma, / kindly tell me that one essential practice of all dharma.
Appropriate atonements for sins have been declared in various ways / by the wise, who called them to mind in accordance with each [offense].
Men are not able to perform them individually, O god. / If there is a single meritorious act that removes all sins, speak of it."
Sūta said: / Having spoken thus, that best of Brahmins, desiring subtle dharma, / became attentive and praised Yama, the embodiment of dharma:
The Brahmin said: / "Salutations to you, all-destroyer; salutations to the lord of the worlds! / Salutations to the one whose form is divine, who bestows the path to heaven!
Salutations to you, O Dharmarāja, whose nature is the dharmaśāstra! / By you, O god, the earth is protected, and the mid-region, heaven, and Maharloka;
Janarloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka—everything is protected by you. / There is nothing whatever in the world, unmoving or moving,
that is devoid of you. When seized by you, the world indeed instantly perishes. / You are the self of all beings, possessing the nature of sattva for the virtuous;
you are the rajas of those of passionate nature, and likewise the tamas of the ignorant. / You, O god, have four feet, four horns, three eyes,
seven hands, and are bound three ways: salutations to you in the form of the bull! / Dharma consisting of all sacrifices has its physical embodiment in you.
You have been seen directly, O ruler of the world, O god! Salutations, salutations to you! / Situated in the heart of all beings, you are the watcher of merits and sins;
therefore, O god, you are the punisher of beings, the giver [of fruit], the governor. / For you are the promoter of dharma, the wielder of the staff on earth.
State the one firmly ascertained essence that comprises all dharmas." / Yama said: / "I am well pleased with you, O Brahmin, especially by your praise.
Furthermore, by the traditional law, you are to be honored by me, O best of men. / That which has not been declared to anyone, that supreme secret of mine,
that single [truth] ascertained by me having extracted the essence of all things, / which supremely banishes one from the masses of great hells—
even though it should not be told, O Brahmin, pleased by your humility, I shall speak."

Those Purāṇas and scriptures may indeed bewilder the moving and unmoving world; / let them proclaim this or that deity as supreme in various ritual rules and eons, / but in the final conclusion the blessed Viṣṇu alone is determined [to be the supreme], / once the discriminatory intellect resolves the contradiction among all scriptural practices.
Bhava, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu: these three alone are considered the triad. / Just as a lamp is composed of fire, wick, and oil, O brāhmaṇa, so is Hari.
Having worshipped Hari with devotion, one attains the auspicious Goloka realms; / when Hari is worshipped, all desires rest in the palm of one's hand.
Giving alone is the highest and best among all merits, O twice-born; / through giving, sin is destroyed; through giving, everything is attained.
Regular, occasional, motivated, another for prosperity, / and another supreme: thus giving is traditionally known to be of five kinds.
Whatever little is given with effort in the three times of day— / morning, midday, and afternoon—is declared to be regular giving.
A day should not be made empty by those who desire their own benefit; / whatever is given in a family stands by them here and there.
He who, devoid of intellect, eats by himself through delusion without giving, / for him I produce disease, which puts an end to his enjoyment.
Afflicted with these ailments, causing much torment, / accompanied by sluggish digestive fire, an entrance causing great suffering.
Those by whom nothing was given to brāhmaṇas and gods at the three times of day, / and who eat sweet food for themselves, have indeed committed a great sin.
I purify them by means of terrible expiation, / with fasts, O earthly god, that dry up the body, and the like.
Just as a leather-worker ruthlessly purifies skin over a pit, / and treats it with a whip and other tools, bursting bad matter,
so do I purify the sinner, there is no doubt, / surely through the proper administration of medicines, and through bitter decoctions,
and through hot waters and torments, in the form of a physician, not otherwise. / Others enjoy other desired pleasures before his very eyes.
Though capable, [he laments,] 'What shall I do? I did not give excellent gifts.' / One should encompass this man in the form of severe disease.
Because the regular gift for oneself was not given by sinners, / O earthly god, with faith and according to their capacity,
so indeed will I burn those who arrive, by cruel means. / Now I will declare before you the occasion for occasional giving.
When a major festival arrives, and likewise when a sacred ford is reached, / on the anniversary of a father's death, and with effort in months such as Vaiśākha—
giving in these months and sacred times is known as occasional. / I will declare the occasion for motivated giving, which yields desired results.
Targeting a vow and the like, intended for the fruit of a desire— / that is properly called motivated giving, joined with all its parts.
Imbued with that intention, by the power of that giving, / a human being partakes of corresponding fruit through its grace.
I will declare giving for prosperity, which is commemorated in sacrifices and the like: / in birth ceremonies and such rites, in investitures of the sacred cord, and wedding rituals,
and diligently in the consecrations of temples, flagstaffs, and deities— / such gifts, O earthly god, are called prosperity-yielding.
It brings increase of offspring, enjoyment, fame, heaven, and happiness. / And now I will declare the final gift; listen, O best of the twice-born.
Knowing that desire has vanished, afflicted by old age, / one should diligently give gifts and have no expectation from anyone.
[Thinking,] 'When I am dead, my sons, wife, kinsmen, uterine brothers, / and my friends—how will these go on without me?'
Or [thinking,] 'Bereft of wealth, how shall I go on living once again?'— / thinking thus, he gives nothing at all.
Bound by hundreds of bonds of expectation through evil delusion resulting from fate, / the foolish-minded soul goes to death, and then his sons weep.
Afflicted somewhat by grief, their minds troubled by delusion, / they somehow prepare a very meager gift.
When that time is gone, when that great sorrow is passed, / they then forget about giving, or out of greed they do not give at all.
Knowing, 'This father is dead,' the bond of affection departs. / He who dies, O earthly god, bound by my nooses,
overcome by thirst and hunger, afflicted by many sorrows, / cooks in a terrible hell for a long time, there is no doubt.
Therefore, gifts should be given by oneself alone, without a doubt. / Whose sons, whose grandsons, whose wife, or whose wealth are they?
In saṃsāra, no one belongs to anyone; therefore, let one give for oneself / drink, food, betel, water, and gold,
garments, a cow, land, umbrellas, and various vessels, / fruits, and various gifts of land, according to one's capacity.
These should be given, O earthly god; no hesitation should be made here. / O brāhmaṇa, I will declare before you the characteristics of sacred fords.
These are auspicious fords: this Gaṅgā shines, the sacred Sarasvatī, / the Revā, Yamunā, Tāpī, and the Carmaṇvatī river,
the Sarayū, the excellent Veṇī, the Pūrṇā that destroys sin, / the Kāverī, the Kapilā, and another, the Viśalyā which saves all,
the celebrated Godāvarī, the Tuṅgabhadrā, and the Gaṇḍakī; / the river Bhīmarathī is known as always dispelling fear of sins,
the Devikā, and the Kṛṣṇagaṅgā, and others that are the best of rivers. / In auspicious times, these are sacred fords in many ways.
Whether in a village or in a forest, rivers are everywhere purifying; / in those very places rites such as bathing and giving should be performed.
When the name of that sacred ford is not known, O twice-born, / then one should utter: 'This is a great sacred ford of Viṣṇu.'
Viṣṇu is the deity of the sacred ford everywhere, without a doubt. / When a practitioner remembers the name 'Nārāyaṇa' at sacred fords,
the full fruit of that sacred ford arises through Viṣṇu's name alone; / for unknown sacred fords and deities, there is no doubt,
a human being should recite the names through the name of Viṣṇu alone. / All sacred accomplishments are holy; the ocean is indeed a sacred ford;
lakes such as Mānasa, cascades, small pools, and the like, / and even minor streams—all of them are sacred fords through the name of Hari.
Mountains are forms of sacred fords, as are a sacrifice and the ground of sacrifice, / and wherever learned brāhmaṇas reside, even for sport—
that very place is considered a very great sacred ford that removes all sin; / also a ancestral rite, ancestral ground, a temple, and an oblation area,
where the sound of the Vedas resounds properly, where auspicious stories of Viṣṇu are told, / one's own house endowed with merit, and a cow-pen is purifying as well.
Where there is an aśvattha tree in a forest, where a house is purifying, / such are sacred fords; and likewise a father and a mother.
Where food is cooked for the sake of dharma, where the teacher himself resides, / where a virtuous wife is present, there is a sacred ford, there is no doubt.
Where a learned son is engaged, constantly devoted to dharma, / there that sacred ford is established for his deliverance.

Sacred places such as these, as well as the royal dwelling,
and especially at these sacred places on the conjunction of festive days.
Without worshipping Hṛṣīkeśa, who grants all things to all embodied beings, / no one anywhere attains anything here—this is certain.

Offspring, wealth, wives, high mansions, horses, and elephants,
pleasures, heaven, and liberation are not far away through devotion to Hari.

Nārāyaṇa is the supreme deity, Janārdana whose nature is truth.
The Blessed Lord, the supreme master, produced himself in threefold form.

Joined with rajas and tamas, the pervasive Lord became predominantly rajas and sattva;
he produced Brahmā, seated upon a lotus, in the navel-lotus.

Associated with rajas and tamas, the pervasive Lord created Rudra.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are thus declared to be this triad.

Through sattva a living being is liberated; sattva is of the nature of Nārāyaṇa.
Through rajas conjoined with sattva, one becomes prosperous and richly endowed with renown.

The Vedic declaration of dharma which one approaches and serves,
that is renowned as Rudra; it is declared to be distinguished for human beings.

Through it one becomes a king in the world, yet through rajas and tamas.
Whatever dharma is devoid of rajas and is purely an accumulation of tamas,

that brings misfortune to men in this world and the next.
He who is Viṣṇu is himself Brahmā; he who is Brahmā is himself Hara.

All three gods are worshipped constantly in this sacrifice among the gods.
O best of brahmins, whatever brahmin makes a distinction among these three,

that evil-doer, sinful at soul, will attain an undesirable fate.
Viṣṇu alone is the supreme Brahman; Viṣṇu alone is the world, O brahmin.

This month of Mādhava is dear to him above all ritual actions.
It is proclaimed as bestowing the fruits of great sacrifices such as the horse sacrifice,
exceeding the fruit of bathing at sacred places, asceticism, giving, recitation of mantras, and sacrifice.

Those who regularly bathe at dawn in a river when the sun is in Aries,
and who also perform the worship of brahmins in this [month], do not suffer my punishment.

Striking and striking the host of my servants before me, wiping and wiping away the writing of Citragupta,
bathing and bathing at a sacred place in the month of Mādhava, they rescue their ancestors here from sin.

This eliminates fear; therefore, this supreme secret should not be revealed.
It causes an expulsion from the realm of hell and brings about the destruction of my authority.

The Bhāgīrathī, the Narmadā, the Yamunā, the Sarasvatī,
the Viśokā, and the Vitastā are situated north of the Vindhya [mountains].

The Godāvarī, the Bhīmarathī, the Tuṅgabhadrā, the Devikā,
the Tāpī, and the Payoṣṇī are proclaimed to be south of the Vindhyas.

These twelve great rivers are continually entered by him
who according to rule bathes at dawn in a river during Vaiśākha.

All [rivers] flowing to the ocean are sacred, all best of mountains are sacred,
all sanctuaries are sacred, and all forest retreats are sacred.

They are plunged into, seen, bowed to, and extensively visited by him
who unfailingly performs bathing at half-sunrise during Vaiśākha.

O earthly deity, no one is able to recount his merit.
Even if there were thousands of thousands of mouths,

and the lifespan [allotted] by Brahmā were not brief, O best of brahmins,
even then [only] would the fruit of the month of Mādhava be capable of being told.

The month of Mādhava is like an all-consuming fire to the great hell; just as Mādhava [is],
[so it burns] the sin of killing a brahmin and the like, approaching forbidden women and the like,

sin committed intentionally or unintentionally, mortal sin,
minor sins, secret sins, and the supreme crime of causing mixture of castes,

dreadful offenses causing loss of caste, disqualification from ritual,
and the diverse impurities born of speech, mind, and body—

the month of Mādhava burns them away when observed according to rule.
For thousands of crores of eons and hundreds of crores of eons,
the prosperous man who worships Hari in the month of Mādhava shall dwell in the city of Viṣṇu.

title: aṣṭanavatitamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
Sūta said:
Having heard this speech of Dharmarāja, the brahmin
again asked concerning the auspicious rule for the month of Mādhava.

The brahmin said:
O Dharmarāja of great fortune, the secret has been properly revealed:
the supreme merit arising from the Mādhava bath, which bestows liberation on mortals.

Having bathed at dawn, composed in mind, in the month of Mādhava,
how should one worship the god Mādhava, and with which flowers? State that rule!

Dharmarāja said:
Among all kinds of leaves, tulasī is dear to Keśava.
Sacred places like Puṣkara, and rivers like the Gaṅgā,

and the gods headed by Vāsudeva abide in the tulasī leaf.
Always and at all times, tulasī is beloved of Viṣṇu.

Leaving aside the mālatī flower, and leaving the lotus,
one should take a tulasī leaf and worship Mādhava with devotion.

Even Śeṣa would not be able to declare the fruit of his merit.
If one gathers tulasī without having bathed, for a rite to the gods or an ancestral ceremony,

all of that becomes fruitless, and one is purified only by pañcagavya.
Poverty, the experience of sorrow, and very many sins—

tulasī removes them quickly, just as the harītakī removes diseases.
Tulasī is known as dark and light; having worshipped the enemy of Madhu with it,

a man, as a devotee of Hari in particular, becomes Nārāyaṇa.
Because he who worships the slayer of Madhu with tulasī throughout the entire month of Mādhava

at the three junctures of the day, has no rebirth.
In the absence of flowers and leaves, one may even worship with food and the like,

always [worshipping] Hari with grains of rice, wheat, or barley,
having bathed at dawn according to rule in Mādhava, the month dear to Mādhava.

One should offer libations to the ancestors, gods, men, and the moving and unmoving creation.
He who constantly sprinkles the base of an aśvattha tree with abundant water,

should then circumambulate it, which consists of all the gods.
He who worships the divine aśvattha tree on all sides with water—
by him ten thousand families are saved; of this there is no doubt.

Misfortune, ill omen, bad dreams, and ill thoughts—
all sorrow dissolves through the libation to the aśvattha, dear friend.

By him the ancestors are gratified, by him Viṣṇu is worshipped;
by that hero who worships the aśvattha, the planetary deities are worshipped as well.

One should touch white horses, flowers, the śamī tree, fire, sandalwood, the solar orb,
and the aśvattha tree, and then perform the duties of one's own caste.

Scratching a cow, offering food to a cow, bathing, offering libations to the pippala tree,
and performing worship of Govinda: doing this, one never reaches a bad state.

On the thirteenth, fourteenth, and full moon day of Vaiśākha, for three days,
even one entirely incapacitated, whether woman or man,

observing the previously mentioned rules, bathing at dawn according to one's capacity,
is freed from all mortal sins and enjoys imperishable heaven.

On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should feed ten brahmins according to one's capacity.
Having risen after a fast of three nights, bathing just once, restrained and pure,

having given light-colored or black sesame seeds mixed with honey
to twelve brahmins, one should have them pronounce blessings on that very day:

'May Dharmarāja be pleased with me!' and one should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods.
The sin committed throughout one's entire life is destroyed at that very instant.

He shall dwell comfortably in the heavenly realm for many myriads of years.
Worshipped by all deities, he will never see me [as judge of the dead].

Cooked food, water pitchers, and the like, for the gratification of the ancestors and the gods,
on the thirteenth, fourteenth, and the full moon day, for three days—

whoever gives these with devotion, O brahmin, is freed from great sins.
Moreover, [offering] vessels of gold and sesame to brahmins according to capacity every day,
If he satiates [them] with vessels of water, he dispels the murder of a Brahmin. / On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, they were created by the Lotus-born [Brahmā];
and sesamum seeds should be given with devotion for the sake of fortune and lineage. / Hear now, O observer of vows, the ancient event in this matter,
the exceedingly wondrous fruit of the full moon of the month of Mādhava. / Beginning with the entrance [of the sun] into Aries, the thirty lunar days are supreme;
they are proclaimed in the Purāṇas as meritorious and greater than all sacrifices. / Especially those three are pure and difficult for a sinner to attain.
Even more meritorious than those is the full moon of Mādhava, dear to Mādhava; / this initial lunar day, the beginning of the Vārāha Kalpa, yields great fruit.
Formerly on this [day], Nārāyaṇa deluded the two primal Daityas, / Hiraṇyākṣa and Madhu, O Brahmin, and the earth was raised up.
On the thirteenth, fourteenth, and the full moon day, this all-pervading Lord / performed these three in succession, in this bright fortnight of the month of Mādhava.
From then on, O chief of Brahmins, the full moon day especially / is declared purifying, the beginning of a kalpa, witnessing rites for a kalpa.
If one has not bathed in the morning with discipline in Vaiśākha, / what is the use of his birth, O Brahmin? Surely he harms his own self.
Particularly on the thirteenth, fourteenth, and the full moon day, / even a woman or a man, following the proper method,
who bathes in the morning with self-restraint, is freed from all sins. / One whose full moon day of Vaiśākha passes devoid of bath, gift, worship,
śrāddha rites, merit, and the like, certainly has his abode in hell. / There is no scripture equal to the Veda; there is no sacred bath equal to the Gaṅgā;
there is no gift equal to water and a cow; there is no lunar day equal to the full moon of Vaiśākha. / And whoever, intent on Viṣṇu, gives a water-cow on the full moon of Vaiśākha,
becomes a fourth in distinction even among the three gods. / Even a slayer of a mother, a slayer of a father, a slayer of an embryo, or a violator of the guru's bed,
is freed from all sins upon merely beholding the water-cow. / They deliver ten ancestors and ten descendants from hell.
Those who offer a water-cow according to the rite during these three [days] of Vaiśākha, / sugar, fruit, betel, shoes, hand-fans,
and give them to the foremost of the twice-born, are proclaimed fortunate here; / and jars of water, cooked food, and a sacrificial fee of gold,
whoever gives on the full moon of Vaiśākha obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice. / In this connection also they cite this ancient legendary history,
the dialogue of a Brahmin with spirits in a great forest. / Formerly in the Middle Country, O sinless one, there was a Brahmin named Dhanaśarman.
Having gone to the forest for kuśa grass and the like, he then saw this wonder: / terrified, he beheld three wicked and exceedingly dreadful spirits,
with hair standing erect, red eyes, black teeth, and emaciated bellies, / making various cries and running about hither and thither.
Seeing them, the Brahmin, trembling with fear, ran away swiftly; / wailing, they then pursued him.
Overwhelmed by those spirits, he spoke sweet words. / Dhanaśarman said: "Who are you? Whence has this state of yours, fit for hell, arisen?
You ought to protect me, afflicted with fear, pitiable, and distressed— / a Vaiṣṇava, a destitute Brahmin with many servants, who has come to the forest.
Keśava will surely grant fortune even to you; / the venerable Viṣṇu, benefactor of Brahmins, has been pleased with me out of compassion.
Viṣṇu, resembling the flax flower, is Hari clad in yellow garments, / by the mere hearing of whose name great darkness departs.
He is the beginningless and endless God, bearer of the conch, discus, and mace, / imperishable, lotus-eyed, the granter of liberation to departed spirits."
Yama said: / By the mere hearing of the name of Viṣṇu, those goblins were pleased; / resting in a virtuous state, restrained by compassion and courtesy,
gladdened by his speech and urged by his instruction, / the spirits, tormented by the flood of hunger and thirst, spoke this to the twice-born.
The spirits said: / "By your very sight, O Brahmin, and from hearing the name of Hari, / we have attained another state of mind and have become compassionate.
Association with a Vaiṣṇava indeed removes misfortune, / joins one with fortune, and swiftly spreads fame.
Made of elixir, cooling, bestowing supreme bliss, / whom indeed does the moonlight of Vaiṣṇava nectar not delight?
This one is named 'Ungrateful'; this second one is 'Without God'; / and this third is 'Without Vaiśākha', the sinner among all three.
Always did he practice extreme ungratefulness through sin; / therefore, his name derived from his deeds has been fixed as 'Kṛtaghna' [Ungrateful].
In a previous birth he was a Śūdra named Sudāsa. / By that sin of ungratefulness, O twice-born, he reached this state.
For an extreme sinner, a rogue, and one harmful to guru or master, / an expiation exists, O brāhmaṇa, but for the ungrateful there is no expiation.
Having experienced a multitude of various hells with bodies capable of torment, / he has now reached this final state, O twice-born.
He always ate food without performing worship of the gods / and without giving to gurus and brāhmaṇas; therefore he is 'Vidaivata' [Godless].
He was a king, the lord of ten thousand villages, / known by the name Harivīra in a previous birth.
Driven by anger, arrogance, and atheism, intent on transgressing the guru's command, / he ate without performing the great sacrifices, reviling brāhmaṇas.
By that sinful deed, having experienced the agony of great hells, / he became a ghost named Vidaivata.
I, Avaiśākha [Non-Vaiśākha-observer], am the third, a sinner among the three; / therefore my name was established by my deed, though I was a brāhmaṇa.
Born in Madhyadeśa, Gautamī by clan, / I was a sacrificer brāhmaṇa residing in Vāsapura in a previous birth.
Solely following the Vedic path alone, / I never bathed in the month of Mādhava with the god Mādhava in mind.
Nothing was given or offered in fire by me, especially on the full-moon day of Vaiśākha; / the slayer of Madhu was not worshipped then, nor were wise men gratified.
Neither were the ancestral spirits and gods gratified with water pots, water jars, and gifts, / nor were sesame seeds mixed with honey given to learned brāhmaṇas.
Learned men were not honored then with flowers, fruits, betel, sandalwood, fans, and garments / for the pleasure of ancestors and deities.
Not even one full-moon day of Vaiśākha, granting full fruits, was observed by me / through the meritorious deeds of bathing, charity, rites, and worship.
Therefore, all my Vedic ritual action was indeed completely fruitless; / hence I have become a ghost named Avaiśākha in all respects.
All this cause concerning all three of us has been told to you; / do you become our deliverer from sin, since you are indeed a brāhmaṇa.
Because the holy water of Brahman is released, and good men are supreme, / they deliver from great sin, and even from hells, those who take refuge in them.
Between a man who always bathes in sacred waters such as the Gaṅgā / and one who keeps company with the virtuous, association with the virtuous is superior.
Or rather, I have a son renowned as Dhanaśarman; / going to him, awaken him, O master, to make an effort for our sake.
Making an effort when the need of others presents itself, / one obtains abundant fruit, greater than sacrificial rites and gift-giving.
Yama said: / Having heard the ghost's words, Dhanaśarman was deeply grieved, / realizing that his own father had fallen into hell.
Censuring himself completely, he spoke this word: / Dhanaśarman said: / "O master, I am your son, yet useless to Gautama.
A son who does not unweariedly effect the deliverance of his father / cannot purify himself; he is called a non-giver though possessing wealth.
Dharma is indeed deep and difficult to know even with effort by a wise man, / since you, my father, have reached such an evil state.
And since you have obtained no succession of happiness from me / in either of the two worlds, how can I be considered a good son?
Two are the gurus of a person here according to dharma: father and mother; / even between them, the father is superior, in view of the primacy of the seed.
What shall I do? Where shall I go? How can you find a good state, father? / I do not know the truth of dharma; I rely on your word."
The ghost said: / "Listen, O son, to my true word, through the force of what is to come: / now, by some merit, my good state shall come to be.
While performing Vedic rites, indeed out of pride / the word of the guru was disregarded by me, and the guru was insulted there.
By disrespecting gurus, through arrogance, anger, and conceit, / meritorious deeds go to ruin, just as reputations do through bad conduct.
Whatever rite is according to Purāṇic prescription, not in conflict with Vedic scripture, [was ignored], / and only Vedic rites alone were performed by me out of ignorance.
Not a single full-moon day of Vaiśākha—a forest fire to the firewood of sin, / an axe to the tree of sin—was performed by me according to rule, O son.
A man whose Vaiśākha passes without vows becomes an 'Avaiśākha'; / he is then born for ten lifetimes in animal wombs.
After suffering grief for a long time, in the end he becomes a ghost in turn, / and only with difficulty does he somehow attain human birth.
I shall tell you a supreme remedy that effects release from the state of a ghost, / which I heard in a previous birth from the mouth of my own guru.

Go home, my son, and having bathed in the Yamunā according to rule— / for today, granting every goal, that commencement of the kalpa has also arrived; / on the western day, the full moon of Vaiśākha is beneficial for worshipping ancestors and gods.
Even water mixed with sesame seeds, together with water pots, food, and fruits, with devotion / one should give to the ancestors; by that, a śrāddha given for a thousand years is effected here.
Whoever feeds the gods of the earth on the full-moon day of Vaiśākha, / at every mouthful there will be satisfaction for the ancestors for the number of a yuga.
Having bathed according to rule on the full-moon day of Vaiśākha, if one feeds ten brāhmaṇas / with milk-rice pudding, he is freed from all sins; there is no doubt about this.
Giving either white or black sesame seeds mixed with honey / to ten brāhmaṇas, he should have them pronounce blessings.
Saying 'May Dharmarāja be pleased,' he should gratify the ancestors and gods; / the sin committed throughout a lifetime is destroyed that very moment.
Sesame seeds were created by the Lotus-born on the full-moon day of Vaiśākha; / they should be given with devotion, and touched over the entire body, O twice-born.
Whoever bathes with sesame seeds mixed with barley over the whole body then, / to him Brahmā and Dharma grant their desired boon here.
Whoever gives water pots for the pleasure of Dharmarāja, / by him seven and seven generations are delivered; of this there is no doubt.
On the thirteenth, fourteenth, and the full-moon day, intent on devotion, / having bathed, chanted mantras, offered oblation, given gifts, and worshipped Mādhava—
whatever fruit arises, O son, bestow that upon us! / I will not take refuge in going to heaven abandoning these two familiar ghosts.
Indeed, the end of the sin of these two as well has arrived." / Yama said: / Having said "So be it," that brāhmaṇa departed and then did all of that.
Pleased, with supreme devotion he performed bathing and gift-giving on the full moon of Vaiśākha; / having bathed, gladdened with devotion, having attained the Mādhava full moon,
giving many gifts, he bestowed the merit separately upon them. / That very instant, they all mounted celestial chariots and went to heaven.
Rejoicing by the application of that transfer of merit, O best of twice-born, / Dhanaśarman, too, a lord of brāhmaṇas, knower of Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇa,
having enjoyed pleasures for a long time, attained the world of Brahmā. / Therefore this full moon of Vaiśākha, the most holy, is the purifier of the universe.
It is told by me in brief, O brāhmaṇa, on account of its great weight.

Blessed are they, and successful are they born in the world; they alone are the men who attain the goals of life, / who, plunging into water in the morning with purified minds and restrained observance, worship the slayer of Madhu in the month of Mādhava.
The mortal who, having bathed at dawn in the month of Mādhava, worships the Lord of Ramā, / endowed with moral restraints and engaged in all religious vows, surely destroys sin.
By them alone has Time been conquered; they alone are blessed among men, free from sins; / they alone do not enter the womb again who, devoted, bathe in the month of Mādhava.
That Mādhava resounds through conjunction with sacrifice, through the performance of austerity and gifts; / in which month, howsoever small the merit performed here, it becomes equal to a kalpa.
For of the man plunging [into water] at sunrise in Mādhava to worship Mādhava, / even a dark body, from contact with drops of water, brings about purification.
Ascending the body of an embodied being, those sins wander about only so long / as this cosmic form, named Mādhava and beloved of the lover of Ramā, does not arrive.
Fierce and numerous sins equal to Mounts Meru and Mandara, / the month of Mādhava, dear to Mādhava, burns when one has bathed.
This has been spoken by me in brief out of grace to you, O twice-born, / the glorification of bathing in Vaiśākha, which destroys the sin of the hearer.
Whoever will hear with devotion this legendary history uttered by me, / he too, delivered from sin, will not see me [in judgment].
Even sins like killing a Brahmin, although committed many times, / are certainly destroyed by the ritual of Vaiśākha.
One who has bathed according to rule in Vaiśākha delivers ancestors from hell: / thirty prior, thirty subsequent, and thirty after that.
On one side are all sacred places and all sacrifices with their fees; / on the other is the month of Mādhava observed with vows.
Because to that Lord Hari of exalted deeds / this month of Mādhava is dear, superior and greater than all.
Do not harbour any doubt in any way, O earthly god [Brahmin], / concerning the month of Vaiśākha, which has been spoken by me in summary.
In this matter, hear that wondrous ancient event; / although not to be told, I shall narrate this short tale to you."

title: navanavatitamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Yama said: / Formerly there was a king known by the name of Mahīratha, / who obtained abundant treasures of sovereignty as the fruit of prior merit.
He stayed solely caressed by women, occupied with erotic art, / addicted solely to that vice, not established in dharma and wealth.
Having placed the royal fortune in his minister, the king enjoyed the objects of sense; / accompanied by beautiful women, he was averse to the affairs of the kingdom.
He saw neither subjects nor wealth, neither dharma nor purpose nor duty, / having impressions solely suited to sports and dalliance with lovely women.
Then after a long time, his family priest, Kaśyapa, / spoke righteous words to him, thinking thus in his mind:
"The guru who out of delusion does not restrain a king from adharma, / he too shares in that sin; therefore, he must be instructed by the family priest."
If, even when warned, he disregards the word of the royal priest, / the royal priest is blameless in that matter, and the king incurs all the guilt.
Listen, O King, to the word of my teacher, which is endowed with righteousness and purpose, / consistent in meaning, full of purpose, and free from desire, passion, and the like.
Standing by the word of the teacher is indeed the supreme dharma; / even a fraction of the teacher’s command increases the lifespan, glory, and happiness of kings.
You have not satisfied the Brāhmaṇas with gifts, nor have you worshipped Viṣṇu; / you have performed no vow, no penance whatever, and certainly no pilgrimage.
Under the sway of desire, you have not contemplated the name of Hari. / Alas, consorting with timid women, you have not sought the company of the learned.
To whom are beloved women, bearing the chowries of the god of love, not dear? / Yet they are as unstable as the leaf of a banana plant agitated by the wind.
High-minded men are not satisfied with riches as flickering as waves, / with pleasures as fleeting as the knit of a brow, or with youth to be enjoyed for but an instant.
What is the use of learning and penance, what of renunciation or prudent policy, / what of a solitary mind to one whose mind has been stolen by women?
Dharma is the only friend who follows one in death; / everything else goes to destruction along with the body.
One should accumulate dharma gradually, as ants build an anthill; / for with dharma as one’s companion, one crosses the darkness that is hard to cross.
As fickle as the surge of towering waves driven by the wind, / do you not know, O sovereign of kings, the deceptive illusion of men's lives?
For those whose jeweled crown is humility, whose earrings are truth and dharma, / and whose bracelet is generosity—what need have they for inert ornaments?
Leaving the dead body on the ground like a log or a clod of earth, / kinsmen turn their faces away and depart; dharma follows him.
When all things are passing away, when life is thus waning, / and when existence is slipping away, why do you not rise and run?
Family, sons, wives, and the rest, the body, and the accumulation of wealth / belong to others and are transient; only good deeds and bad deeds are truly one's own.
Since you must depart helplessly, leaving everything behind, / why are you attached to what is worthless and do not practice your own dharma?
Without resting place, without support, without provisions for the journey, without a guide, / how will you, once dead, walk the wilderness path alone?
For when you have departed, no one will follow behind you; / only your good deeds and your bad deeds will follow you as you go.
Perform without sloth the beneficial action declared by Śruti and Smṛti, / suitable for your family and country, the root of dharma, and righteous conduct.
One should abandon material wealth and sensual pleasure if they are devoid of dharma; / through dharma everything is attained: wealth, pleasure, and happiness.
One should practice the conquest of the senses and yoga day and night; / for one who has conquered his senses is able to establish his subjects on the right path.
Fortunes, as fickle as the side-glances of wanton women, / remain long with kings through humility and disciplined application.
Of the foolish whose nature is desire, pride, and the like, who act without reflection, / their fortunes perish together with their lifespan.
High-minded men do not dance with joy over fortunes seen and lost; / the ocean is neither filled by incoming rivers nor drained by outgoing ones.
Between vice and death, vice is said to be the more painful; / the vicious king sinks lower and lower, while the king free from vice goes to heaven.
Vices lead to ruin, especially those born of lust; / therefore, O great king, abandon lust, which is opposed to dharma.
Kingdoms enjoyed by destiny belong even to the dull-witted, the indiscriminate, / demons, evil-minded men, and also the unrighteous.
They are never stable here when attended by sins; / they dissolve just as fuel does in contact with fire.
Whether walking, standing, awake, or sleeping, / he whose mind is not devoted to discernment is truly dead.
Because he is an instructor of those learned in sacred lore, he is called a teacher; / yet teachings are like hair on the head to those whose misfortunes are imminent.
Leaving aside the fever of sensual objects with an even and healthy mind, / and with practical discernment, a wise man accomplishes his own welfare.
Wandering from the impure, it goes to the pure, and from that to the other again; / the mind of a living creature is like a child, so one should turn it away by force.
Reflecting upon the thought of the elders who see dharma, O King, / one should restrain with supreme intellect the mind that wanders onto evil paths.
Neither riches help, nor friends, nor relatives, / nor moving hand and foot, nor traveling to foreign lands.
Neither the misery of bodily affliction nor resorting to sacred shrines [helps]; / the supreme state is attained solely through the recitation of one whose mind is fixed on that.
Therefore, when the mind wanders among sensual objects, a wise man should strive / to control it, O King, just as a firm driver controls horses.
You should do whatever is necessary, O King, so that you are not deceived / by the sages and by those various fruits; listen now to that.
Even when bewildered, a man should consult wise friends; / and as they advise when consulted, that should be done properly.
By every means, the restraint of desire and anger must be undertaken / by one who desires the highest good; for both are bent on destroying one's welfare.
For desire is powerful, O King, a great enemy residing in the body; / a person who desires the highest good must not fall under its sway.
That desire which was formerly burned by the trident-bearing god of gods / with the fire of his forehead, and made bodiless—such is the established truth.
When that mind-born god desires to destroy a woman, / he enters the body of men and shows his true nature.
As a man continually contemplates the form of a woman, / [desire], resting upon that unseen form, drives the man mad.
In the same way, this [desire] drives the limb of a woman mad, without doubt; / therefore, O King, he came to be called Smara from remembrance.
Whatever color clothes a hero wears, / through the radiance of his own splendor, it would become fit to drink with streams of tears.
Mounting the form of a woman, it bewilders even a steadfast man; / and resorting to a man, it melts a woman.
He alone is innate, O King, bodiless yet dwelling in the body; / how is sin assigned even to the tiny body, O Lord?
Upon contacting which even the purest things, the five products of the cow and sacrificial offerings, / instantly become impure—what else could be more impure than that?
Even while smelling his own foul odor and seeing his own filth, / this person does not become detached, even while pinching his nose.
Upon contacting which delicious food and drinks, though fragrant, / quickly become impure—what else could be more impure than that?
Food that has entered the stomach abandons its own form; / mixed with worms, its impurity is quickly recognized indeed.
Even so in the body, O King, it abandons its own nature; / thereafter it truly attains the state of dog-filth, swarming with worms and foul stench.
There indeed lice and worms are born, without doubt; / that worm causes eruptions and an intense itching.
It produces severe pain and causes the whole body to twitch; / when scratched with the tips of fingernails, that itching is soothed.
In the same way, the pleasure of sexual intercourse arises, without doubt; / thus a mortal consumes savors, eats good food, and drinks again.
The internal fire cooks what is there and expels waste through the apāna; / and the essence, the fluid, becomes stimulated there.
Pure and spotless, the semen goes to the seat of Brahman; / drawn by the samāna breath, it is led by that very wind.
The semen finds no resting place, but remains in motion. / Indeed, within the skulls of living beings there are five worms,
two of them at the base of the ears, and then at the location of the eyes, / measured the size of a little finger, with red tails, O king,
having the colour of fresh butter, and with black tails, without doubt. / Listen from me as I tell their names, may it be well with you:
two worms named Piṅgalī and Śṛṅgalī are at the base of the ears; / Śṛṅgalī and Jaṅgalī, the other two, reside within the eyes.
There are one hundred and fifty similar worms, without doubt; / all of them reside within the forehead, the size of a mustard seed.
All suffering from skull-diseases become disordered, without doubt. / I shall speak of another thus: the great Prājāpatya worm,
the size of a grain of rice, and of that same colour, without doubt. / Two hairs exist at its mouth; listen, O king:
that intelligence of living beings decays from that very moment, without doubt; / even residing in its proper place, directly in the mouth of the Prājāpatya [worm],
that semen falls in the form of fluid, without doubt in this matter. / It drinks the semen with delight, and intoxicated by it, becomes wild.
Piercing the region of the palate, it continues in agitation. / The nāḍīs Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā reside there;
by its own force, the channel is shaken for a moment. / The itch of lust arises, O king, among all living beings indeed.
A man's phallus becomes erect, and a woman's vulva opens, O king; / both the woman and the man become intoxicated and then enter into union.
Rubbing body against body, it arises through sexual union; / there is pleasure for merely an instant, and then the same itch returns.
Everywhere this condition is seen, O hero, indeed of such a kind. / Tasteless is this culmination of sensual enjoyment, without doubt.
Dharma alone is the higher good when performed according to injunction. / Having taken recourse to steadfastness, therefore, practice dharma alone.
This breath is fickle, making hundreds of comings and goings in the midst of a moment; / the life of embodied beings is dependent on it: who would delay in dharma?
Though you have reached your tenth decade, O king, your mind even today / does not turn away from forbidden sense-objects—alas, alas!—fickle as it is.
Desire is never quenched by the enjoyment of desires; / like a fire with clarified butter, it only grows all the more.
Who else is capable of liberating a mind snatched away by an unchaste woman, / except the Lord who delights in the Self, the Blessed Mādhava?
Therefore, everything has come to futility through the impurity of lust; / yet your life remains now, O king: practice your own welfare.
I tell you, O king, what is the best of all the best for your welfare; / for I am your priest, sharing also in your good and bad deeds.
On the one side are all the merits for destroying the sins of sinners; / on the other side is the month of Mādhava, ever dear to Mādhava.
Killing a brāhmaṇa, drinking liquor, theft, and union with the teacher's wife— / these great sins alone have been proclaimed by the lords among sages.
Whatever [sin] has been committed by men with mind or body or even by a vow, / the month of Mādhava destroys all that, even the greatest darkness of sin.
Just as the sun destroys darkness on every side, O king, / so does the auspicious month of Mādhava; observe it according to rule.

Leaving behind those great, terrible sins committed since birth, O king, / mortals, through the merit born of observing the practices prescribed for the month of Vaiśākha, reach the abode of Hari in joy.
If they observe according to rule even one Vaiśākha / with faith, even sinners go to the abode of Hari in the end.
Therefore, you too, O best of kings, during this month of Mādhava now, / having bathed in the morning according to rule, worship the slayer of Madhu.
Just as the husk of a grain of rice, and just as the tarnish on copper, / are removed by ritual action, O hero, so is the impurity of a man.
Even the great innate impurity of the individual soul, like that of a grain of rice, / is indeed destroyed, there is no doubt; therefore perform the prescribed rite.

title: śatatamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: The glorious king said: / By your cool and spotless glances, like the water of the ocean of milk, / and by your true and wondrous words, I have been awakened.
Nectar not arisen from an ocean, an immaterial remedy for vice, / dispelling the affliction of mundane existence, has been given to me to drink by you, gentle one.
Bringing joy to men, causing the destruction of sin, a medicine for life, / removing old age and death, O brāhmaṇa, is association with the virtuous indeed.
Whatever desires are hard to attain on the surface of the earth, / all of them are obtained simply from the company of the virtuous.
For one who has bathed in the Ganges of association with the virtuous which takes away sin, / what need is there of gifts, what of holy bathing places, what of austerities, what of sacrifices?
For men sinking and rising in the ocean of mundane existence, the supreme refuge / is the virtuous who know dharma and are tranquil, like a sturdy boat for those drowning in the waters.
That disposition which was mine formerly, longing only for the pleasure of lust, / has today become reversed, O lord, from seeing you and from your word.
For the sake of the pleasure of one birth, one may ruin thousands [of births]; / a wise man, by means of one birth, gathers together thousands of births.
Alas, alas! With a mind longing for the pleasure of tasting the flavor of lust, / nothing for my own spiritual benefit was done by me, foolish as I was, O twice-born.
Ah, the delusion of my mind, by which the self, for the sake of women, / was cast into a terrible vice resulting in sorrow, difficult to overcome!
O venerable one, I am gratified, awakened by your word; / you should rescue me here by bestowing your instruction.
I must have performed merit in the past, since I have been awakened by you, / and have been purified especially even by the dust of your feet.
Tell me the rule for the month of Mādhava, O best among speakers, / which was proclaimed by you as bringing about the destruction of all sins.
What is the gift there, what is the bath, who is the deity, and what are the observances? / Declare this to me, O brāhmaṇa-seer, for my crossing over sins.
Yama said: / Thus addressed, the venerable Kaśyapa, a treasure-house of compassion, / spoke a righteous, universally beneficial, and auspicious word, O brāhmaṇa.
Kaśyapa said: / With an intellect capable of reconciling what precedes and what follows, O king, / you have asked; instruction should be given to a wise man, not to a base one with a sinful mind.
Likewise, having given auspicious understanding to one engaged in sin, O king, / the fruit of the gift of knowledge is properly attained, there is no doubt in this.
One should not speak to anyone unasked, nor to one who asks improperly; / even knowing, an intelligent person should act in the world like an ignorant fool.
Yet even unasked, the highest good and benefit should be spoken / to wise disciples, to sons, and to those engaged in rites who possess faith.
Now your heart has become pure through my word, / and through some merit performed in the past, O lord of the earth.
That body of yours which was in a state of sin has departed through taking refuge in me; / through hearing the dharmaśāstra, it has entered a state of righteousness.
The state of sin is called unrighteousness, devoid of the knowledge of dharma; / the other, which possesses good vows, should be known as righteous.
The third is beyond the senses, for experiencing dharma and adharma; / indeed, this threefold body is spoken of here by knowers of dharma.
to the extent that there is enjoyment of dharma and liberation; and this is threefold. / The body that is in a state of sin is called sinful.
Now, since you show devotion to the guru and listen to my words, / your body is established in the form of dharma.
By that alone, a spotless purity has arisen, suited for the rites of dharma. / Indeed, through destiny, the minds, deeds,
and bodies of embodied beings undergo change from time to time. / Presently, your mind certainly turns toward dharma;
therefore, I shall have you perform the supreme bath of Mādhava. / Yama said: Then, made to do so by that priest Kaśyapa,
that king [performed] bathing, giving, and worship in the month of Mādhava, / according to the injunction for bathing in Vaiśākha as seen in the ancient scriptures.
That sage spoke in return to the king, as prescribed, / and recited the essence of hymns, causing him to study that of Harimedhas,
upon hearing and studying which, one obtains the full fruit.
Having been guided by him, the king, pure in disposition, then duly performed / the praiseworthy rite in the glorious month of Mādhava, just as he had heard it with devotion:
the morning bath, water for washing the feet, water for offering, the worship of Hari, / and the food offering—the best of kings performed these with a devotional disposition.

Giving according to the rules, observing vows with devotion, he performs such an injunction in the month of Vaiśākha; / he who does so daily with devotion every year departs to Hari's abode, O best of earthly gods.
Then, in the other months, sporting with the breasts of lovely women, / he again became entirely eager for sensual enjoyment according to his desire.
He observed neither religious vows nor delved into royal affairs; / under the sway of passion, he neglected the month of Mādhava.
Even for the great, O best of Brahmins, passion is hard to restrain; / the sequence of latent impressions is indeed innate to the body and beginningless.
Shining with hair black as collyrium, difficult to touch, pleasing to the eyes, / women, like tongues of fire, burn a man as if he were grass.
Desire, residing in the body, is an awful enemy of men, as is well known; / made of the smoke of delusion and evil, whom does it not envelop in darkness?

title: ekottaraśatatamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Yama said: Then, regarded by the side-glance of Time, the king / died, his body emaciated by consumption arising from excessive sexual indulgence.
Led by the attendants of Yama, struck again and again, / weeping with great cries, he remembered his own sins.
The messengers of Viṣṇu, having arrived and struck my followers, / said, “This man is righteous,” and placed him upon a celestial chariot.
Praised by hosts of apsarases, the king was led to Hari's city, / his sins diminished by the morning bath of the month of Vaiśākha.
Then, thinking, “This man is devoid of dharma,” / by the command of Viṣṇu, those divine messengers / brought the king nearby the path of hell.
As he was going, he heard the varied cries / of weeping souls being boiled in hell.
Hearing the most dreadful wailing of sinners being cooked, / the king, filled with wonder, became exceedingly distressed, O Brahmin.
He said: “Messengers, what is this dreadful wailing that was heard / and is now heard no more? You ought to tell me the reason for this.”
The messengers said: Creatures who have abandoned proper conduct, sinful and devoid of good practice, / have been cast into the terrible hells, such as Tāmisra and others.
Those who have committed sins, after relinquishing their life-breaths, / take to the path of Yama and suffer terrible distress here.
Dragged here and there by the terrible servants of Yama, / fallen into darkness, they are eaten by extremely fearsome
