Thirty-fourth chapter. / Nārada said: / Tell me particularly, O Lord of all, about the vow called Trispṛśā, / by hearing which people are freed in an instant from the bondage of karma.
Mahādeva said: / Hear about the great vow called Trispṛśā, which quells the flood of all sins, / destroys great sorrow, and is an incarnation of Kṛṣṇa.
It grants desires to those who have longing, but grants liberation to the desireless. / Hear, O brāhmaṇa, as I explain the vow called Trispṛśā.
Keśava has been worshipped visibly by him in the Kali age, / who constantly proclaims the Trispṛśā, O great sage.
When a preliminary rite is performed, there is destruction of all sins; / by the mere name of Trispṛśā [sin] is destroyed, there is no doubt about this.
Not by the Āgamas, not by the Purāṇas and others, not by sacrifices, nor by tens of millions of sacred fords, / nor by numerous collections of vows, even if gods are worshipped,
does liberation come about, O best of brāhmaṇas, if Trispṛśā is not observed. / For the sake of liberation, this Vaiṣṇava lunar day was perceived by the God of gods.
For twice-born people, Sāṃkhya is hard to know, especially in the Kali age; / there is no restraint of the senses, nor is there stability of mind.
For those separated from sense objects [only in theory], devoid of meditation and concentration, / and attached to desires and pleasures, Trispṛśā bestows liberation.
It was told in ancient times to me and to the four-faced [Brahmā] in the ocean, / in the Milk Ocean, by the Discus-bearer in the form of a Fish, to us who were bowed down [before him]:
“Those who will observe Trispṛśā, even if attached to sense objects, / liberation is granted by me even to them who are devoid of Sāṃkhya.”
Trispṛśā bestows liberation to those attached to desires and pleasures; / and it has been observed by numerous hosts of sages, O great sage.
If Trispṛśā occurs in the bright fortnight of Kārttika, / on a Monday or even a Wednesday, it destroys tens of millions of sins.
By fasting on which, the skull of Brahmā, which had stuck to the hand / of the great Lord tainted with murder, fell to the earth that very moment.
Freed from millions of torrents of Kali's impurities was the goddess who goes along three paths, / by the instruction of Mādhava, through fasting completely on Trispṛśā.
Eight murders had been committed previously by the valiant-armed [king], O great sage; / they vanished through the instruction of Bhṛgu, by fasting completely on Trispṛśā.
A brāhmaṇa was killed in the forest by Śatāyudha, O best of brāhmaṇas; / he was completely freed from the killing of a brāhmaṇa by fasting completely on Trispṛśā.
By the instruction of Bṛhaspati, Indra's sin arising from the murder of Namuci / was destroyed, O supreme among prominent sages, through fasting completely on Trispṛśā.
Sins such as the killing of a brāhmaṇa, through fasting completely on Trispṛśā, / go to dissolution, O best of brāhmaṇas; what to speak of other sins?
Neither at Prayāga, nor at Kāśī, nor at the Gomatī in the presence of Kṛṣṇa, / does liberation occur, O best of brāhmaṇas, if Trispṛśā is not observed.
And from dying at Prayāga, or at the Gomatī in the presence of Kṛṣṇa, / [or] by the mere bath in the Gomatī, eternal liberation occurs.
Even at home liberation comes about through fasting completely on Trispṛśā, / for one living among sense objects and endowed with desires and pleasures.
Even for one detached from sense objects, liberation is hard to attain through Sāṃkhya; / therefore, O best of brāhmaṇas, observe Trispṛśā, which bestows liberation.
Nārada said: / What is that great vow called Trispṛśā like, O best of gods, / which bestows liberation upon twice-born people, about which you have just spoken to me?
Mahādeva said: / That Trispṛśā was spoken in ancient times, O brāhmaṇa, to Jāhnavī by Mādhava / on the bank of the Prācī Sarasvatī out of compassion.
Jāhnavī said: / Burdened with millions of torrents of Kali's impurities, such as the killing of a brāhmaṇa, / people bathe in my water in the Kali age, O Hṛṣīkeśa.
By their hundreds of sins and defects, my body is made impure. / How will my sin depart, O Lord whose banner is Garuḍa?
Prācī-Mādhava said: / I shall tell you, there is no doubt; daughter, do not weep. / The dark banyan tree is my abode, and the goddess Prācī is before me.
The daughter of Brahmā flows [here]; having seen the queen of gods in front, / bathe [here] constantly; you will become purified here.
Where the Prācī, Brahmā's daughter, flows, there I am, without a doubt; / accompanied by hundreds of tens of millions of sacred fords, I dwell with the gods.
This holy abode, dear to me, destroys tens of millions of murders; / it was given by me, well-pleased, because you are dearer to me than my own life.
Tens of millions and thousands of sacred fords remain constantly, O Jāhnavī, / in the waters of the Prācī Sarasvatī at all times by my command.

From the killing of a brāhmaṇa, from the drinking of liquor, from the slaying of a cow, from the murder of a Śūdra woman, / from stealing the property of a brāhmaṇa, and likewise from failing to worship mother and father,
from riding in a vehicle, from treachery towards a guru, and from eating what should not be eaten, / from committing every sin, O daughter, the Prācī, Brahmā's daughter,
removes sins through a single bath in front of me. / Bathe, O best of rivers; you will become free from sin.
Jāhnavī said: / I am not able to come constantly, O Lord of gods; / tell me how sins are destroyed [otherwise], O Mādhava.
Prācī-Mādhava said: / Since you cannot come constantly, O Jāhnavī, / then I shall tell you something else, because you originated from my foot:
That which is superior to the Sarasvatī, superior to hundreds of tens of millions of sacred fords, / superior even to tens of millions of sacrifices, and superior to vows and gifts,
superior to recitation and fire-offerings, which bestows the fruit of the four aims of life, / and is superior to Sāṃkhya and Yoga—let auspicious Trispṛśā be observed!
In whichever month it arrives, whether in the bright or the dark [fortnight], / it should be observed, O best of rivers; when it is observed, one is freed from sin.
Jāhnavī said: / What is Trispṛśā like, O Lord? Tell me, O good Mādhava, / whose majesty of such a kind has just now been spoken by you to me.
When the tenth, eleventh, and Bhadrā [twelfth] lunar days occur on a single day, / is that Trispṛśā, O Lord, or otherwise? Tell me, O master!

Kṛṣṇa said:
O goddess, the Trispṛśā that was described by you is demonic; / it must be zealously avoided, just like a husband destitute of means.
Indeed, it is declared to belong to the asuras, destroying lifespan and strength; / it must be zealously avoided, just like a menstruating woman.
Just as a woman who abandons her own caste has gone to the lowest castes, / that very day of mine conjoined with the tenth lunar day is particularly to be discarded.
Just as ignorant men are defiled by contact with a menstruating woman, / even so my day conjoined with the tenth lunar day is defiled for men.
A Trispṛśā properly fasted upon destroys hundreds of myriads of slayings: / [when there is] the eleventh, the twelfth, and, at the close of the night, the thirteenth lunar day.
That alone is to be known as Trispṛśā, not one accompanied by the tenth lunar day. / Having committed a transgression, a man may be freed when an expiation is performed;
but I do not forgive the fault arising from overlap with the tenth lunar day, O river of the gods! / By him deadly poison has been consumed; he has eaten poison,
by whom the vow of the eleventh lunar day has been observed mixed with the tenth lunar day. / Considering this, my day should not be observed when conjoined with the tenth lunar day.
Merit acquired over ten million births and one's lineage go to destruction; / he causes his family to fall from heaven and leads them to Raurava and other hells.
Having purified one's own body, my day is certainly to be observed. / In case of extension [of the tithi], it is to be abandoned without overlap when conjoined with Śravaṇa and other [nakṣatras].
The merit of lifetimes goes to ruin for those who fast on the eleventh lunar day / when there is an extension [overlapping the tenth], especially when a doubt has arisen.
And by my command the twelfth lunar day, dear to me, is to be observed.

Jāhnavī said:
O Lord of the Universe, I shall observe the Trispṛśā according to your word; / freed from all sins, I shall become [pure] by your command.

The venerable Kṛṣṇa said:
Go to your own abode, auspicious one; you should never fear. / O goddess, best of rivers, sin will not attach to you.
Having bathed in the water of the Sarasvatī, those who worship Mādhava / and bow down to the Lord of the Universe go to the supreme destination.

Jāhnavī said:
Tell me the procedure, O Brahman! I shall perform it with all my possessions; / I shall propitiate the Lord of gods, the flawless Dāmodara.

Prācī-Mādhava said:
Listen, O goddess! I shall declare the ritual procedure of the Trispṛśā, / hearing which even a human being is freed from sins, O best of rivers!
A golden image of mine should be made with a pala, half a pala, / or even half of that, O river, according to the extent of one's wealth.
A copper vessel filled with sesame seeds should be prepared, / and a bright pot filled with water, endowed with the five gems,
encircled with garlands of flowers, perfumed with camphor and aloe; / then one should place Dāmodara [there], having bathed and anointed him.
Then clothing equipped with a pair of garments should be provided; / and worship should be performed with mantras proclaimed in the Purāṇas, / with seasonal, pure flowers and tender tulasī leaves.
One should offer a parasol along with a good pair of sandals to Viṣṇu, / and charming offerings of food, and very abundant fruits.
A sacred thread with an upper garment, new and firm, is to be given; / one should present a bamboo staff, well-shaped, reaching to the shoulder, and strong;
[Saying:] 'To Dāmodara', [he should worship] the two feet; 'To Mādhava', the two knees; / 'To the Granter of desires', the private parts; 'To the Vāmana form', the waist;
'To Padmanābha', the navel; 'To the Womb of the Universe', the belly; / 'To Him who is attained through knowledge', the heart; 'To the One who goes to Vaikuṇṭha', the throat;
'To the Thousand-armed', the two arms; 'To the Embodiment of Yoga', the two eyes. / Having worshipped properly with devotion, he should offer the argha according to the rules:
With a bright coconut placed upon a conch, / wrapped around with threads, held indeed in both hands:
'O Janārdana, since when remembered You always take away sins, / bad dreams, bad omens, and evils devised in the mind;
the fear of hell, O Lord, and the fear arising from misfortune / which might be mine, O Mahādeva, whether belonging to this world or the next;
by that [remembrance], O Lord of gods, protect me! Accept the argha, homage to You! / May Your glance of grace ever rest upon me, O Dāmodara!'
Then he should offer incense, a lamp, and food offerings, and perform the waving of lamps. / O best of rivers, he should circle the lotus over the head of Hari.
Having performed this rite, he should then worship his own guru. / He should give gold, garments, a turban, and a tunic,
shoes too, an umbrella, a ring, and a water-pot, / a meal, betel leaf, the seven grains, and a priestly gift.
Having worshipped the guru [and] the Lord of gods, he should keep a night-vigil for Hari / accompanied by song and dance, and likewise accompanied by sacred scriptures.
And at the end of the night, having offered argha to the god according to rule / and performed rites such as bathing, he should eat together with the brāhmaṇas.
Śiva said: / O twice-born one, this wonderful, hair-raising narrative of Trispṛśā, / upon merely hearing it, one obtains the merit arising from bathing in the Gaṅgā.
The fruit of a thousand horse sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices, / that fruit one completely attains by fasting on Trispṛśā.
The father's side, the mother's side, and likewise his own side: / liberated together with all of them, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Whatever merit is in crores of sacred bathing-places, whatever fruit is in crores of sacred fields, / that fruit one completely attains by fasting on Trispṛśā.
Whatever brāhmaṇas observe it, kṣatriyas whose minds are on Kṛṣṇa, / vaiśyas, or those born of śūdra wombs, and likewise those of other castes,
they all attain liberation, having left this earth, O best of the twice-born. / Just as the twelve-syllable mantra is the king of mantras among mantras,
so too is this [vow] among vows, which Trispṛśā was performed / formerly by Brahmā, and afterwards performed by royal sages.
What need to speak of others, my child? Trispṛśā is the giver of liberation. / The vow arising from Trispṛśā according to this rule, O brāhmaṇa,
the man who performs it with devotion—listen, I shall declare its fruit: / The fruit, O brāhmaṇa, that comes from plunging into the Gaṅgā at Vārāṇasī
through thousands of manvantaras, that belongs to the performer of Trispṛśā. / The fruit that comes from bathing in the eastern Yamunā over crores of years,
that fruit a man performing the Trispṛśā vow fully attains. / That fruit [gained] at Kurukṣetra over crores of solar eclipses
through gifts of hundreds of loads of gold, is [attained] by performing Trispṛśā. / Thousands of crores of sins and hundreds of crores of killings
are reduced to ashes swiftly by a single fast. / This vow of Trispṛśā provides a refuge for the refugeless;
even those with hundreds of great sins desire refuge [through it], O brāhmaṇa-sage. / It was spoken by Kṛṣṇa Himself before the son of Parāśara.
And if someone, having written down this Vaiṣṇava [narrative], reveals it to a twice-born, / even if strung with hordes of sins, he will attain liberation.
Even through merit over hundreds of manvantaras, O wise one, / Trispṛśā is hard to obtain in this world; it is rarely attained by mortals.
Those vile men who, having found Trispṛśā in the Kali age, do not observe it, / the fruit of their birth and their very life will be in vain.

text_mt:
The state of a ghost has been crossed over by those, without śrāddhas and without sons, / by whom Trispṛśā was performed even once, O wise one, having obtained it in the Kali yuga.

Thirty-fifth Chapter. / Mahādeva said: / Next, I shall tell you about the unsurpassed Unmīlanī, / by the mere hearing of which, from the bondage of the cycle of birth,

a sinful soul is freed from sins and is glorified in the heavenly world; / deities and ancestors alike attain its course.

One seeking learning obtains learning; one obtains all desires; / through the vow of it, without doubt, he is glorified in the heavenly world.

Indeed, having attained his own abode there, he is glorified in the world of Śiva. / Therefore, O king, do you perform the worship of the Vaiṣṇavas?

Those who constantly serve Vaiṣṇavas, O king— / do you impose punishment on them, or does the ruler of men not [punish] them?

O king, one who eats after they have eaten— / by them alone is Viṣṇu worshipped, by whom He is worshipped with devotion.

Having placed on your head every day the Śālagrāma stone, / do you, O king, constantly wear it on your neck with great devotion?

Do you, O king, faithfully enjoy the remains of the incense of Viṣṇu? / Having always performed the waving of lights, O king, do you offer it to the devotees?

text_mt:
Having waved the conch-water with devotion over the head of Hari, / do you constantly carry it on your head and bestow the remainder upon the Vaiṣṇavas?

Having daily prepared food offering endowed with all ingredients, / and having given it to Viṣvaksena, do you yourself eat it, O brāhmaṇa?

And is the food offered to Viṣṇu eaten together with the Vaiṣṇavas? / Do you daily praise Janārdana with devotion using the thousand names?

Do you offer lamps and argha to Viṣṇu, and perform singing and dancing? / Do you worship the One worthy of worship with shoots of śyāmā grass, O best of kings?

Worship with shoots of śyāmā grass, my child, is always very hard to obtain. / Merit equal to the gift of the earth [is gained] when worship is performed with dūrvā grass.

Therefore, indeed, there is nothing like dūrvā grass in this world, on earth. / Worship should certainly be done with it by one desiring intimate union with Viṣṇu.

Therefore, do you constantly perform worship with dūrvā grass? / Or do you especially perform worship with barley grains and unbroken rice?

Fortnight after fortnight, O best of kings, the Dvādaśī vow according to rule, / which, when performed, O great king, destroys great sins,

bestows liberation, grants happiness, and always bestows long life— / this is declared as the vow of Viṣṇu, bestowing liberation upon the Vaiṣṇavas,

giving happiness to householders, bestowing liberation upon ascetics, / pacifying all diseases and afflictions, pure, purifying the body.

Do you perform this vow or not, O ruler of men? / Devoid of overlap with the tenth lunar day, do you observe it accompanied by a vigil?

Do you daily worship Hari with heaps of tulasī leaves? / Or a leaf-mark made of gopīcandana on your forehead, O best of kings,

worn, it brings purification to all people, O king. / Therefore, do you wear what is produced from gopīcandana?

A killer of a brāhmaṇa, a stealer of gold, a drinker of intoxicating liquor, / one who goes with forbidden women, a great sinner, and likewise one who speaks falsehood—

all of them attain liberation if intent on wearing the forehead mark. / Do you constantly wear on your neck [a garland] made of dhātrī fruit?

a garland equal to ten thousand chief leaves produced from tulasī foliage, / endowed with a Śālagrāma stone, originating from Dvārakā.

[Gautama said:]
You constantly worship [him], O king, who grants the fruits of enjoyment and liberation; / indeed, you recite the Purāṇa named Padma before Hari.

[…] the life of Prahlāda and of the daitya kingdom, O king;
men who observe the day of Vāsudeva overlapping [with the tenth lunar day] […]

you restrain, O king, diligently examining the scripture. / In whichever kingdom an overlapped day of Viṣṇu is practiced,

the king is tainted by that sin and becomes an inhabitant of hell. / Having abandoned the fourfold overlap and fasted on the day of Hari, / raising up ten million ancestors, he is honored in the world of Viṣṇu.

Gautama said:
Listen, O king! I shall declare the great vow named Vaiṣṇava, / hearing which all sinners attain liberation that very instant.

The merit arising from the twelfth lunar day has not been declared by me to anyone.

You are a Vaiṣṇava, O great king, a devotee devoted to the Lord among men; / listen to that vow, a great mystery of the Vaiṣṇavas.

Formerly, by devotion, [the vow] named Unmīlanī was told to me / by Mādhava when he was well pleased; I declare it to you, O king.

[When] the eleventh lunar day lasts day and night and extends a ghaṭikā into the dawn, / that is to be known as Unmīlanī, especially dear to Hari.

Whatever holy places and sacred shrines there are in the three worlds, / along with sacrifices, Vedas, and austerities, are equal to only a ten-millionth part of it.

There was nothing equal to Unmīlanī, nor will there ever be: / not Prayāga, nor Kurukṣetra, nor Kāśī, nor Puṣkara;

at the crown of the head to the Lord of Gods, on all limbs to the Universal Form; / and weapons and other implements should be worshipped with devotion by their own names.

An offering of arghya should be made together with coconuts and other fruits, / having placed [them] in water upon a conch, endowed with scents, flowers, and unbroken grains.

having wrapped [the fruit] with thread, one should offer the arghya according to the rules: / 'O God of gods, O Mahādeva, O Śrīkeśava, O Janārdana,

O Subrahmaṇya, homage to you, O augmenter of heaps of merit! / Rescue me from the ocean of worldly existence, from sorrow, delusion, and great sin!

No good deed was done [by me] even through hundreds of millions of births; / nevertheless, O Great Master, rescue me from the ocean of worldly existence!

Through this vow, O Lord of gods, whatever ancestors of mine / and others have fallen into degraded wombs or have come under the power of an evil death,

those who will be and those who are past, deliver them from the realm of the spirits! / I am weary; for one who is subservient, devotion is unswerving.'

'The arghya has been offered by me to you with devotion; accept it, O Gadādhara!' / Having offered the arghya with incense, lamps, and so forth, and with food-offerings dedicated to Viṣṇu,

one should satisfy Hari with hymns of praise, wave-offerings, songs, and attendants. / One should satisfy the guru with garments, gifts, gifts of cows, and meals.

It should be performed in such a manner that the guru indeed attains pleasure; / for the guru was created by the Creator for the deliverance of living beings.

Therefore, worship of the guru must indeed be performed with great care. / He who destroys what is unfavorable and always shows what is beneficial to oneself,

he is the guru, and he should be known as one skilled in the meaning of all dharma. / Without practicing deceit regarding wealth, one should present that to the guru.

When presented to the guru, O king, the vow becomes complete. / Having performed the midday rite, eating in the company of brāhmaṇas

should be done, O tiger among kings, and the day should be passed with sacred stories. / Whoever undertakes the Unmīlanī vow in according with this rule,

title: ṣaṭtriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
dwells in the presence of Viṣṇu for thousands of millions of kalpas.

Nārada said: / What is that called Pakṣavarddhanī like, O Mahādeva, / through the observance of which a living being is freed from great sin?

The glorious Mahādeva said: / If the new moon day becomes completely filled during the day, / and becoming sixty nāḍikās, extends into the day of Pratipad, / that becomes Pakṣavarddhinī, equal to ten thousand horse sacrifices.
Nārada said: / I ask now about the ritual of worship, O best of gods, / by performing which, O Mahādeva, one attains great fruit.
Mahādeva said: / I shall now declare the ritual of worship, O delight of the twice-born. / When Viṣṇu is worshipped and venerated, [the devotee] attains the fruit without doubt,
by which ritual of worship Mādhava attains satisfaction. / An unblemished pot filled with water and smeared with sandalwood,
furnished with the five gems and encircled with a garland of flowers, / [and] a vessel made of copper containing wheat should be placed upon the pot.
One should have a golden deity made bearing the name of the month. / A most charming bathing according to the prescribed rules with the five nectars
one should perform for the Lord of the gods of gods, the Lord of the world, the Protector of the world. / Anointing should indeed be done with saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood.
A pair of garments should be given, along with a parasol and sandals. / One should worship the supreme Lord of deities situated upon the vessel on the pot:
'To Padmanābha, indeed, the two feet; the two knees to Viśvamūrti; / the two thighs indeed to Jñānagamya; the waist to Dānaprada;
the belly to Viśvanātha; the heart to Śrīdhara; / the neck to Kaustubhakaṇṭha; the two arms to Kṣatrāntakārin;
the forehead to Vyomamūrdhan; the head indeed to Sarvarūpin.' / And [one should worship] Kamalā of divine form in all her limbs with her own name.
Having thus worshipped according to rule, the wise person should then offer an arghya / with a bright coconut to the discus-bearer, the God of gods:
'By this very offering of arghya the vow becomes complete. / Deliver me, sunk in the ocean of worldly existence, O Lord of the world!
You are the lord of all worlds, and you are visibly the master of the world. / Accept the arghya offered by me; homage to you, O Padmanābha!'
Heart-pleasing food-offerings, especially of the six flavors, / should be particularly given to Keśava with true devotion.
One should offer betel leaf with camphor to the god with devotion. / One should offer a lamp with ghee or with sesame oil.
Having performed [this] according to proper procedure, one should arrange for the worship of the guru. / One should give garments, a turban, and a jacket,
and one should present a priestly gift according to one's means to the guru. / Having offered food, betel, and an arghya, one should present it.
According to the measure of one's wealth, or according to their capacity by the poor, / the Pakṣavarddhinī Dvādaśī should be observed with proper effort.

Then one should keep a night-vigil accompanied by songs and dances,
along with recitation of the Purāṇa, accompanied by laughter and joy.
Those who praise and celebrate the vigil of the discus-bearer / will have an unbroken festival in their house for ten lives.
Therefore, this most blessed Pakṣavarddhanī must be observed; / by performing it, one attains all the meritorious fruit without doubt.
Those wise people who listen to the glorification of Pakṣavarddhanī— / everything done by them is well-done until the dissolution of elements.
Whatever merit there is in the practice of the five fires and in the practice of sacred bathing-places, / one attains that merit because of the vigil of Viṣṇu.
Pakṣavarddhanikā is meritorious, purifying, and destroys sin; / fasting [on it] destroys ten million slaughters of a brāhmaṇa.
Formerly performed by Vasiṣṭha and by Bhāradvāja, O sage, / and performed by Dhruva and Ambarīṣa, this [observance] is beloved by Viṣṇu.
This is equal to Kāśī in merit, this is indeed equal to Dvārakā; / and when fasted upon by a devotee, it grants desired wishes.
This is blessed, most blessed, destroying tens of thousands of killings; / it must be observed especially by Vaiṣṇavas intent upon knowledge.
Ah, the Lord of all, the God, is to be served by those intent upon vows! / What else is to be gained by saying much? This excellent vow should be performed.
Just as the moon increases, especially in the bright fortnight, / even so the devotee increases because of the Pakṣavarddhinī.
Just as darkness is destroyed immediately upon sunrise, / so sin meets destruction because of performing the Pakṣavarddhinī.

title: saptatriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Mahādeva said: / Listen, O Nārada, I will speak of the glorification of the vigil, / hearing which even a great sinner attains liberation, without doubt.
Nārada said: / Ah, Viṣṇu is the Lord of the universe, the eternal purifier! / The glorification of fasting for him has indeed been heard from your mouth, O Śiva.
Nevertheless, I wish to hear the glorification of the vigil: / What is the glorification of the vigil like, and what is the devotion in the night like?

Tell me of the worship during the watches of the night, O Lord of the universe! / You are always to be worshipped among the worlds; you indeed are the god Janārdana; / you indeed are the god who is Lord of the universe, because of devotion to Janārdana.
And you, Umā's husband, are the best among all devotees. / In this world, your renown always endures through devotion.
Therefore, O Lord of the universe, tell by what means liberation truly comes to people; / speak of the glorification of the night vigil.
Mahādeva said: / Having worshipped Viṣṇu with devotion at night on the eleventh day, a person / should keep a vigil before Viṣṇu in the company of Vaiṣṇavas,
With song, musical instruments, dance, and recitation of the Purāṇas, / with incense, lamps, food offerings, flowers, and fragrant unguent,
With fruit, water offering, faithful giving, restraint of the senses, / accompanied by truth, O chief of brahmins, endowed with proper speech and ritual action.
The man who, sleepless and filled with joy, always performs this, / is freed from all sins and becomes dear to Viṣṇu.
When the night vigil arrives, [if] Vaiṣṇavas sleep, / they forfeit the fast and the vow named after Viṣṇu.
Those men, O wise one, who keep the vigil called Viṣṇu's / with a devotional mindset toward Kṛṣṇa, and never sleep,
And who repeatedly utter the name of Kṛṣṇa with their minds, / should be known as the most blessed, especially on this night.
At every moment, it equals the gift of a cow; in each ghaṭī, it is fourfold; / in each three-hour watch, it is multiplied by ten million; in the four watches, it is beyond count.
Even for half an instant of vigil before Keśava especially, / the fruit is multiplied ten million times; there is no counting it.
The best of men who dances before Keśava / does not lose that fruit from his birth until his death.
Accompanied by wonder and enthusiasm, free from sinful talk and the like, / joined with circumambulation, preceded by prostration,
Accompanied by the waving of lights with an untroubled mind, / watch by watch, O fortunate one, one should perform the waving of lamps for Hari.
Endowed with twenty-six qualities, a vigil on the eleventh day / which a man performs with devotion—he is not born again on earth.
He who thus performs the vigil on the day of Viṣṇu with devotion, / free from financial deceit, merges into the Supreme Self.
A wealthy man who performs the vigil with financial deceit / has surely ruined his soul like a wicked gambler.
When the vigil of Viṣṇu arrives, he who mocks it / is born as a worm in feces for sixty thousand years.
A brahmin learned in the Vedas who, especially during dancing, / engages in mockery—he is indeed called an outcaste.
He who keeps the vigil for an instant or even half an instant / attains the imperishable state of dharma, wealth, desire, and liberation.
Though always devoted to the Vedas and scriptures, always an offerer of sacrifices, / when the night vigil arrives, if he engages in reviling, he goes down to ruin.
One who performs my worship while intent on reviling Viṣṇu / falls into hell along with twenty-one generations of his family.

Viṣṇu is Śiva, Śiva is Viṣṇu; one form existing in two ways.
Therefore one should never disparage in any way.
Bitten by the serpent of Kali, they sleep on the day of the slayer of Madhu.
Deluded by māyā, they do not keep the vigil at all. / Those for whom the eleventh day arrives without a vigil in the Kali age,
Are ruined, there is no doubt, because life is uncertain. / The pair of eyes is indeed elevated and gives the Vaiṣṇava state,
By which sinners behold the vigil of Hari. / In the absence of a reciter, one should then arrange for singing and dancing;
When a reciter is present, O divine seer, one should first recite the Purāṇa. / [Equal to] a thousand horse sacrifices and ten thousand Vājapeya sacrifices,
The merit is ten million times greater, dear child, when the vigil of Viṣṇu is performed. / On the paternal side, the maternal side, and the wife's side, O brahmin,
One delivers these families by performing the vigil of Hari. / If on an overlapping day of fasting one keeps a vigil and performs the worship of Hari,
Gifts and all else are in vain, just as what is done for ungrateful men. / If the vigil is undertaken on an overlapping day of fasting,
Viṣṇu leaves that place, casting a curse, and departs. / Those who perform the vigil on an un-overlapped day of Viṣṇu,
In their midst Hari indeed dances, being pleased. / For as many days as one keeps a vigil before Keśava,
For that many cosmic ages he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. / For as many days as one lives without the vigil of Hari,
For that many thousands of years he does not turn back from the Raurava hell. / Sleeping on the eleventh day without the vigil of Hari,
Or staying like a mute without singing or reciting— / muteness for seven births arises from not keeping the vigil of Hari.
The foolish-minded one who does not dance before Hari during the vigil— / know that lameness will be his for seven births, O brahmin.
He who, on the other hand, performs singing and dancing during the vigil of Hari— / the state of Brahmā and my own, and truly that of Viṣṇu, belong to him.
The Vaiṣṇava who, devoted to Viṣṇu's vigil, awakens people, / shall dwell for a long time in Vaikuṇṭha together with his ancestors.
The man who applies his mind toward the vigil of Hari / shall dwell in Śvetadvīpa for sixty thousand years.
Whatever sin is committed by humans in ten million births, / it all perishes during the night vigil of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, O brahmin.
For those who keep vigil before a Śālagrāma stone, / watch by watch, the fruit is declared to arise from ten million lunar fasts.
When the day of Viṣṇu arrives, for those who do not keep the vigil / and revile Vaiṣṇavas, their deeds become futile.
Desire, wealth, prosperity, sons, fame, and eternal worlds / cannot be obtained by ten thousand sacrifices without the vigil of the twelfth day.
He whose mind does not turn toward the vigil on the twelfth day / has no right at all to the worship of Keśava.
As many steps as one takes toward the abode of Keśava / to keep vigil, they equal horse sacrifices for the one who goes.
As much dust as falls upon the feet on the ground of those going, / for that many thousands of years the keeper of vigil dwells in heaven.
Therefore, one should go from one's house to Keśava's abode for the vigil / on every twelfth day to destroy impurities in the Kali age.
Accompanied by speaking ill of others, devoid of serenity of mind, / devoid of scripture, lacking celestial music, and likewise devoid of lamps,
Lacking worship according to one's means, indifferent, accompanied by reviling, / and especially joined with quarrel—the vigil is considered of nine [flawed] kinds.
The vigil that is accompanied by scripture, joined with dance and celestial music, / accompanied by musical instruments, endowed with rhythm, having lamps and sweet drinks,
Joined with recitations as prescribed, imbued with devotion, / clear, bringing satisfaction, captivating, and delighting people,
Endowed with twelve qualities, dear to Mādhava— / that vigil should be performed with effort in both the bright and dark fortnights.
What use are many vows performed? What use to him is living at a sacred ford / if, when the day of the twelfth arrives, he does not keep the vigil of Hari?
He who, though fatigued on the road during a journey, O brahmin, / does not abandon the vigil of Vāsudeva on the twelfth day, is dear to me.
My devotee who, deluded by sin, does not keep the vigil of Hari— / his worship of me is useless; he does not worship what is worshipped by me.
He is neither a Śaiva nor a Saura; he is neither a Śākta nor a worshipper of Gaṇeśa. / He who eats on the day of Viṣṇu should be known as worse than a beast.
What is displeasing has indeed been done by that wicked sinner / who, relying on the strength of devotion to me, eats on Hari's day.
Though his body inside and out is enveloped by ten million sins, / those who keep vigil on Viṣṇu's day are liberated.
An elbow [thrust] was given by him to the messengers of Yama and to Yama, / having kept the vigil of Viṣṇu, an unoverlapping dvādaśī vow.
All desire for heaven has been abandoned by him, O best of sages, without doubt; / the happiness of hell was chosen by making Hari's day overlapping.
The ancestors were struck down by him, and the gods were slain; / the kingdom was given to the daityas by observing Hari's day while overlapping.
He who dances delighted in heart, clapping his hands, / singing with his mouth, and showing many spectacles,
Standing in vigil at night before Vāsudeva, / reciting the deeds of Kṛṣṇa, delighting the assemblies of Vaiṣṇavas,
Playing instruments with his mouth, his bodily hair bristling with joy, / portraying various attendants, carrying on spontaneous conversations,
Whatever man maintains these states of feeling during the vigil of Hari, / at every moment his merit is remembered to be equal to the fruit of ten million pilgrimage places.
He who, with an undisturbed mind, offers incense and the wave-offering of lamps to Hari / during the night of vigil, becomes the sovereign of the seven continents.
Whatever sins there are, even equal to the murder of a brahmin, / from keeping the vigil on Kṛṣṇa's day, they dissolve away piece by piece.
On one side are all the sacrifices complete with the best sacrificial fees; / on the other side is the vigil of the God of gods, dear to Kṛṣṇa.
There are Kāśī, Puṣkara, Prayāga, Naimiṣa, and Gayā; / the great sacred region of Śālagrāma, and the forest of Arbuda;
Puṣkara, Mathurā, and indeed all sacred pilgrimage sites there, / the sacrifices, and the four Vedas—they all go to Hari's vigil.
The Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Tāpī, Yamunā, and Śatadrū, / the Candrabhāgā and Vitastā—all the rivers are indeed there.
The lakes, pools, and all the oceans indeed / go to Kṛṣṇa's vigil on the eleventh day, O best of the twice-born.
Desirable even to the gods are those men who, at Kṛṣṇa's vigil, / dance, sing, and rejoice with the sound of the vīṇā.
Having thus kept vigil and worshipped the great Hari, / having broken the fast on the twelfth day according to one's ability together with the Vaiṣṇavas—
Mahādeva said: / Listen, O Brahmā, I shall declare the supreme glorification of dvādaśī; / dvādaśī should always be known as granting sons and granting liberation.
Having bathed in the morning and worshipped Hari, one should dedicate the fast: / 'For one blinded by the darkness of ignorance, through this vow, O Keśava,
be gracious, turn a pleased face toward me, and grant the vision of knowledge.' / Then one should break the fast as appropriately as possible thereafter.
After this, one should act as one pleases and according to rule. / But when dvādaśī is short and breaking the fast cannot happen by day, O twice-born,
then breaking the fast should be done at night by one desiring liberation; / then there would be no fault of the night, nor is it forbidden in any case.
As for what is said: 'One should not bathe at night, nor eat in the dead of night,' / one should perform the rite like daytime during the first or last watch [of the night].
When dvādaśī is very short on the day of breaking the fast, / at dawn one should perform both the morning and noon rituals.
The merit of that man by whom dvādaśī is always observed on earth— / I am not capable of declaring it in full.
Having attained all their desires, great men reach [the goal]— / all those such as Ambarīṣa who are celebrated devotees on earth.
Having observed dvādaśī, they went to Viṣṇu's abode. / True, true, again true is what has been spoken by me to you!
There is no god equal to Viṣṇu, no lunar day equal to dvādaśī. / What is given here, what is eaten, and whatever worship or the like is done—
all of that attains completeness when Mādhava is worshipped. / What more is there to say? Hari is dear to his devotees;
he grants all desires until the dissolution of the elements. / And whatever is given on dvādaśī becomes fruitful.
What is given at Kurukṣetra never becomes fruitless; / likewise what is given on dvādaśī, O best of divine sages.

title: aṣṭatriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Mahādeva said: / Once upon a time, my son, I went into the presence of Viṣṇu; / there the glorification arising from dvādaśī was previously asked by me.
Nārada said: / What kind is the supreme Mahādvādaśī, O Mahādeva? / What is the fruit of its vow? Tell me, O Lord of all, O master!
Śiva said: / This ekādaśī, O sage, bestows the fruit of great merit; / conjoined with asterisms, it should be observed by the best of sages.
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, and Pāpanāśinī— / these take away all sins and should be observed by those who desire the fruits.
When the asterism on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight is Punarvasu, / it is called by the name Jayā, the best lunar day among lunar days.
Fasting on it, a man is freed from sin; of this there is no doubt. / And when on the bright twelfth day the asterism is Śravaṇa,
it is celebrated as Vijayā, the best lunar day among lunar days, / on which a gift is multiplied a thousandfold, as is the feeding of brahmins.
Likewise, a fire oblation and fasting grant more than a thousandfold fruit. / And when on the bright twelfth day the asterism is Prājāpatya,
it is called by the name Jayantī, a lunar day that takes away all sins. / Sins committed in seven lifetimes, whether small or great,
Govinda washes away when worshipped on it, surely. / And when on the bright twelfth day the asterism is Puṣya,
then it becomes greatly meritorious, the destroyer of sins. / He who gives a prastha of sesame seeds every single year,
and he who fasts on that [day]—these are remembered as equal. / On that day the Lord of the world, God Hari, the master of all, being pleased,
becomes visibly present indeed; infinite fruit is remembered therein. / It was accomplished by Sagara, Kakutstha, and Nahuṣa;
worshipped on that day, Kṛṣṇa gave them everything on earth. / From vocal, mental, or especially bodily sins,
committed across seven lifetimes, one is freed—of this there is no doubt. / Having fasted on that single [day] conjoined with an auspicious asterism,
a human being obtains the fruit of a thousand ekādaśīs. / Bathing, giving, silent recitation, fire oblation, Vedic study, and worship of the deity—
whatever little is done on it is remembered to have imperishable fruit. / Therefore, this should be performed diligently by those desiring fruits.
When bathed after the fifth horse sacrifice, the righteous Yudhiṣṭhira / inquired of Kṛṣṇa, the crest-jewel of the Yadu lineage.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: / Of the complete fast, of eating only at night, and of eating only once a day, O Lord, / tell me all the merit and the fruit thereof, O Janārdana.

The Blessed Lord said: / When the cold season has arrived in the beautiful month of Mārgaśīrṣa, / on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, O son of Pṛthā, one should fast on it, / having eaten only once on the tenth day, with a pure mind and firm in vows.
And likewise, understanding the nakta [meal] on the tenth [lunar day], ever self-restrained / in the eighth part of the day, when the sun has grown weak,
one should know that to be the nakta; the nakta is not eating at night. / For a householder, the nakta is prescribed upon seeing the stars;
for an ascetic, it is in the eighth part of the day; at night it is forbidden to him. / Then, having undertaken the observance in the morning, the practitioner of the vow,
and pure, O Pārtha, should perform bathing at midday. / Bathing in a small well is lowest, and bathing in a stepped well is mediocre;
bathing in a pond is best, and bathing in a river is superior to that. / Where living creatures are troubled when one is standing in the water,
upon bathing there, O Pārtha, sin and merit become equal. / Bathing at home is also excellent, and one should purify the water.
Therefore, O best of the Pāṇḍavas, one should perform bathing at home: / 'O earth traversed by horses, traversed by chariots, traversed by Viṣṇu,
O clay, take away my sin that was accumulated by me previously!' / Casting aside anger and greed, single-minded and firm in vows,
one should not speak with an outcaste, nor with heretical men, / nor with those devoted to lying, nor with revilers of Brahmins,
nor with other evildoers, those devoted to incestuous unions, / those who steal the property of others, and those who approach the wives of others.
Having worshipped Keśava, one should present the food-offering there; / with a mind endowed with devotion, one should offer a lamp in the house there.
On that day, O Pārtha, one should avoid sleep and sexual intercourse; / one should spend the entire day in the diversion of the Dharmaśāstras.
Having kept vigil at night, endowed with devotion, O best of kings, / one should give a sacrificial gift to the Brahmins and, bowing down, ask for forgiveness.
Just as the dark [fortnight], so also the bright [fortnight]: a twice-born should observe it in this manner by the rule; / O Pārtha, he should not make any distinction concerning Ekādaśī.
Listen indeed to the fruit of him who performs it thus: / If a man bathes at Śaṅkhoddhāra and sees the club-bearing God,
it does not equal a sixteenth part of the fast of Ekādaśī. / He who gives four hundred thousand [cows] at the solstices and equinoxes, O best of kings,
does not equal a sixteenth part of the fast of Ekādaśī. / The merit that exists at the sacred field of Prabhāsa during an eclipse of the moon or the sun,
that fruit surely accrues to one who fasts on Ekādaśī. / Having drunk water at Kedāra, there is no rebirth;
and likewise, O Pārtha, Ekādaśī brings about the destruction of dwelling in the womb. / The fruit that one may obtain on earth from a horse sacrifice,
the merit of one who fasts on Ekādaśī is a hundred times greater than that. / In whose house ascetics and best of Brahmins eat,
that fruit surely accrues to one who fasts on Ekādaśī. / The merit that is obtained by giving a thousand cows to one who has reached the end of the Vedānta,
the merit of one who fasts on Ekādaśī is a hundred times greater than that. / Those who fast on Ekādaśī are equal to those in whose bodies
the three gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—dwell. / Those men are performers of meritorious deeds who are devotees, worshippers of Hari.
There is no reckoning the merit even of the Ekādaśī vow; / to him belongs that merit which is difficult to attain even for the gods.
Half of this merit is obtained from eating the nakta [meal]; / half the merit of the nakta accrues to embodied beings from eating a single meal.
Sacred fords, gifts, and observances roar only as long / as a creature does not fast on the day beloved of Viṣṇu.
Therefore, O best of the Pāṇḍavas, perform this vow! / I do not know the number of the merit concerning which you ask, O Pāṇḍava.
For this has been told, O Pārtha, which is a secret, supreme vow; / there is nothing equal to Ekādaśī, even having performed a thousand sacrifices."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: / "How did that meritorious lunar day of Ekādaśī arise, O God? / How is it sacred in this universe, and how is it dear to the deity?"
The Blessed Lord said: / "Formerly in the Kṛta age, O Pārtha, there was a Dānava named Mura, / very wondrous, exceedingly terrible, terrifying to all the gods.
Even Indra was vanquished by him, as were all the gods, O king, / by that great Asura, like Death itself, evil-minded.
Expelled from heaven by him, they wandered upon the surface of the earth; / filled with apprehension and terrified with fear, they all went to Maheśvara.
Everything was told by Indra before the Lord: / 'Cast out from the world of heaven, they wander upon the surface of the earth.
Remaining among mortals, the gods do not shine, O Maheśvara; / tell me a means, O God, as to what destination the immortals shall reach.'
Mahādeva said: / 'O king of gods, best of deities, where the Garuḍa-bannered Lord resides, / the refuge, the Lord of the Universe, the protector, the supreme refuge,
go there, O best of deities! He will provide protection for you.' / Having heard the word of the Lord, the wise king of gods,
accompanied by the thirty [gods], went there where [the Lord was], O Yudhiṣṭhira. / Seeing that club-bearing God asleep in the midst of the waters,
having folded his hands in supplication, Indra uttered a hymn of praise.
Indra said: / 'Salutations, O Lord of the gods of gods, praised by gods and Dānavas! / O enemy of the Daityas, lotus-eyed one, save us, O Madhusūdana!
All the gods have come, terrified with fear of the Dānava; / you are our refuge, O Lord of the Universe; protect me, O lover of your devotees!
Save us, O Lord of the gods of gods! Save, save us, Janārdana! / Save us indeed, O lotus-eyed one, destroyer of the Dānavas!
All have come into your presence; you alone are our refuge, O Lord! / Render assistance, O Lord, to the gods who have come for refuge!
You are the master, you are the intellect, O God; you are the agent, and you are the cause; / you are the mother of all worlds, you alone are the father of the universe.
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, affectionate to those who come for refuge, / terrified with fear, the deities have come to your refuge.
All the deities have been conquered and cast out of heaven, O Lord, / by the exceedingly fierce Daitya named Mura, of great splendor.' / Hearing Indra's speech, Viṣṇu spoke these words:

The Blessed Lord said: / 'What kind of Dānava is he, O Śakra? What is his form, what kind of strength does he have? / Where is the abode of that wicked one? What is his prowess, what is his valor? / What is the boon of that wicked one? Tell me, O wise one.'
Indra said: / 'Formerly, O Lord of gods, there was born in the lineage of Brahmā / an exceedingly fierce, great Asura named Tālajaṅgha.
His son indeed, renowned as the Dānava named Mura, / is exceedingly violent, of great valor, terrifying to the deities.
There is a city named Candrāvatī; he dwells in that place. / All the deities were conquered and expelled from heaven by him.
Another Indra was installed by him, and another Wind and Fire; / and two others were made the Sun and the Moon, and another Vāyu and Varuṇa.
Everything has been appropriated to himself by him; truly, truly, O Janārdana! / The realm of the gods was made by him completely devoid of its places.'
Hearing that speech of his, Janārdana became enraged: / 'I shall slay the wicked Dānava, who causes terror to the deities.'
Together with the thirty [gods], the God went to the city of Candrāvatī. / The lord of Daityas was seen by the gods roaring again and again.
All the gods were conquered by him and fled in the ten directions. / Seeing Hari, the Dānava spoke: 'Stand, stand!'"

And the Lord, his eyes blood-red with wrath, spoke to him.
The Blessed Lord said:
“O evil-doing Dānava, behold my arm!”

Then all those wicked Dānavas faced Viṣṇu;
struck by his divine arrows, they were overcome with terror.

And the discus was released by Kṛṣṇa into the Daitya armies, O Pāṇḍava;
severed by it by the hundreds, many went to their doom.

Yet one Dānava there fought again and again;
by him all the gods were routed, and Madhusūdana was subdued.

Subdued by that Daitya, a hand-to-hand combat ensued;
he waged hand-to-hand combat for a thousand divine years.

Viṣṇu fell into anxiety, and all the gods fled;
and Viṣṇu, overpowered by him, went to Badarikāśrama.

There was a cave named Siṃhāvatī, and there Janārdana slept;
it was twelve leagues in extent, O Pāṇḍava, and had a single entrance.

Having entered it, he fell fast asleep, and the Dānava was intent on killing [him];
from that very great battle he was weary through Yogamāyā.

Following closely behind, the Dānava then entered the cave;
seeing me asleep there, the Dānava was filled with joy:

“Thinking that Hari has entered here in fear, vanquished by me in this manner,
I will surely slay him who brings fear to the Dānavas.”

A maiden came forth there from Viṣṇu’s body, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
beautiful, exceedingly fortunate, equipped with divine weapons and arms.

Born from a portion of his splendor, possessing great strength and valor,
she was seen by the lord of Dānavas, Mura by name, O Dhanaṃjaya.

A battle was joined by him, challenged by that woman;
the maiden fought there, skilled in all forms of combat.

With roaring shouts, the great Asura named Mura was reduced to ashes;
when that Dānava was slain, the God awakened there.

Seeing the Dānava fallen, he was then filled with wonder:
“By whom has this fierce, terribly formidable enemy of mine been slain?”

“And an exceedingly fierce deed has been done out of compassion for me.”
The maiden said:
“By him the gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, serpents, and Rākṣasas,

all headed by Indra, were conquered and expelled from heaven;
I saw Hari asleep, and Mura arrived at his back.

He was about to destroy the three worlds while Janārdana slept.”
Hearing her word, Viṣṇu spoke these words:

“When even I was subdued by him, how was he conquered by you?”
Ekādaśī said:
“O Lord, it is by your favor that the great Daitya was slain by me.”

The Blessed Lord said:
“Joy has come to the sages and the gods in the three worlds.
Tell me, auspicious one, what pleases your heart;
I shall grant it without a doubt, even that which is difficult for the gods to attain.”

Ekādaśī said:
“If you are pleased with me, O God, as truly spoken, O Janārdana,
I desire one boon in my heart, O Lord of the world.

I pray, O Lord of gods, for what is wished by me, O Lord;
if truly, O Lord of the universe, you grant me three promises.”

The Blessed Lord said:
“Truly, truly it has been spoken by me; it shall certainly be yours, O woman of good vows.
Three promises have been given by me, and my word shall not fail here.”

Ekādaśī said:
“In the three worlds, O Lord of gods, and in the four cosmic ages now,
make me like that everywhere in the three worlds, O Lord:

foremost among all sacred places, destroying all obstacles,
granting all spiritual accomplishments—may I become that goddess by your favor!

Those who fast for me with devotion, with devotion to you, O Janārdana,
may all spiritual accomplishments be theirs, if you are pleased with me, O Lord.

Whosoever observes a complete fast, an evening meal, or a single meal [for me],
grant him wealth, dharma, and liberation, O Mādhava.”

Those who are my devotees in the world, and those who are devotees in Kārttika,
are renowned in the four cosmic ages throughout the three worlds, O Lord.

And I consider you my power; established in the Ekādaśī observance,
they will worship me and attain liberation; of this there is no doubt.

Having granted this boon to her, three promises without a doubt,
Ekādaśī, of great vows, became joyful and thriving.

[Viṣṇu said:] “You slay the enemy, and you grant the supreme state;
you destroy all obstacles, bestowing boons of all spiritual accomplishments.

In both fortnights, O son of Pṛthā, the auspicious Ekādaśī is equal;
one should make no distinction between the bright and dark fortnights.

No distinction should be made by all who perform the observance.
Whether by day or by night, one who is intent on devotion listens [to this],

it becomes a single lunar day in both fortnights.
If both parts of Ekādaśī are small, and Trayodaśī appears at the end,

while in the middle Dvādaśī is complete, touching all three, that [day] is dear to Hari;
one should fast on that single [day], [reaping] the fruit of a thousand Ekādaśīs.

Indeed, it is multiplied a thousandfold when the fast is broken on Dvādaśī.
The eighth, the eleventh, the sixth, the third, and the fourteenth:

one should not observe them overlapping the preceding day; one should fast when they overlap the following.
If Ekādaśī lasts for a day and night, and a fraction of an hour remains at dawn,

that lunar day must be avoided; the fast must be observed combined with Dvādaśī.
Such has been declared by me for both fortnights.

One should certainly observe the fast on Ekādaśī, without a doubt;
they go to the Vaiṣṇava realm where the Garuḍa-bannered Lord resides.

Blessed are those mortals in the world devoted to Viṣṇu's devotion,
and whoever recites the glorification of Ekādaśī at all times,

that mortal obtains the meritorious fruit of a thousand cows.
Those who listen with devotion, whether by day or by night,

title: ekonacatvāriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
“I bow to Viṣṇu, the omnipresent Lord manifest, who brings joy to the three worlds,
the Lord of the universe, the creator of the universe, the ancient Supreme Person.

I ask, O God of gods, for a great doubt has arisen in me,
for the benefit of all people and for the purpose of destroying sins:

The Ekādaśī that occurs in the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa—
what is its name, what is its ritual, and what deity is worshipped there?
Explain this to me in detail and faithfully, O Lord.”

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
“You have asked well, O King; good and spotless is your renown!
I shall describe to you, O king of kings, that supreme day of Hari.

She was born in the dark fortnight, on Dvādaśī, dear to me;
[called] Utpatti in Mārgaśīrṣa, born from my body,

born for the destruction of the enemies of the gods, O bull of the Bharatas.
Indeed, she has already been described by me before you, O best of kings.

She is the first Ekādaśī, O King, in the three worlds of moving and unmoving beings,
in the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, named Utpatti.”
Beyond this, I will speak of the [ekādaśī] that falls in the bright half of Mārgaśīrṣa, / by merely hearing of which one obtains the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice.
She is named Mokṣā, the supreme destroyer of all sins. / O king, one should diligently worship the god Dāmodara
with tulasī blossoms, with incense and lamps, with utmost effort, / according to the previously stated rule, on the tenth and eleventh [lunar days] likewise.
The ekādaśī named Mokṣā destroys great sins. / A night vigil should be kept for me with dances, songs, and praises.
Listen, O king! I will narrate a divine legendary tale of the Purāṇa, / merely by hearing which destruction of all sins occurs.
If someone's ancestors have gone to a lower birth because of sin, / by dedicating the merit of this [day] to them, they attain liberation, without a doubt.
In the delightful city of Campaka, adorned with Vaiṣṇavas, / a king named Vaikhānasa protected his subjects like his own children.
Many brāhmaṇas who had mastered the Vedas and Vedāṅgas lived [there]; / indeed, the subjects of that King Vaikhānasa were prosperous.
As he was thus ruling his realm, in the middle of the night in a dream, / he saw his own ancestors fallen into a lower state of existence, O king.
Having thus seen them all, his mind overwhelmed with astonishment, / he related the event born of the dream to the twice-born.
The king said: / “O twice-born ones, in a dream I saw my own ancestors fallen into hell, / [crying:] ‘Deliver us, O son, from this ocean of hell!’
Speaking thus, they were indeed weeping again and again; / they were seen by me, O best of the twice-born, and because of this I have no happiness.
This great kingdom of mine brings me no joy; / neither horses nor elephants please me at all, O twice-born.
Neither wife nor sons please me, O best of the twice-born! / What shall I do? Where shall I go? My heart is choked.
Speak, O best of the twice-born, of that vow, that discipline of austerity, / by which my ancestors may immediately attain liberation.
For while the son is living, powerful, and noble-minded, / if the father remains in terrible hell, what is the fruit of that son?”
The brāhmaṇas said: / “O king, nearby is the great hermitage of the sage Parvata. / Let him be approached, O tiger among kings, since he knows past and future.”
Hearing their words, the great King Vaikhānasa / then went immediately right there to the hermitage of Parvata.
Surrounded by brāhmaṇas and accompanied by tributary kings, / the best of kings reached the sage's vast hermitage.
There [he saw the sage] surrounded by ascetics skilled in the study of the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda, / looking like a second Brahmā.
Beholding that tiger among sages, King Vaikhānasa / bowed down prostrate like a staff and touched the sage's feet.
That sage inquired after his welfare regarding the seven constituents [of the state], / the absence of obstacles in the kingdom, and the king's happiness.
The king said: / “By your favor, O master, there is welfare in my seven constituents. / For those who are devoted to Viṣṇu and the brāhmaṇas, how could there be obstacles?
In a dream, my own ancestors were seen by me residing in hell. / By the power of what merit do they attain liberation, O best of the twice-born?
This is my doubt, O master; I have approached you to ask about it. / Some remedy must surely be performed here, O best of sages.”
Hearing these words, Parvata, the best of sages, / an ascetic equal to Brahmā, became motionless of eye in meditation.
Remaining in meditation for a single muhūrta, he spoke to the king: / “The past deeds of your ancestors have been ascertained, O best of kings.
In a previous life, your father was a kṣatriya proud of his kingdom. / Bound to the duties of kingship, during his wife's fertile period,
having abandoned his own wife, he went to a village on state business. / But your father did not give her the due season.
By the power of that sin, O tiger among kings, your father / has fallen into a dreadful hell along with his ancestors.
Then King Vaikhānasa spoke this again to the sage: / “By the efficacy of what vow, O sage, could liberation be theirs?”
The sage said: / “In the bright half of Mārgaśīrṣa, there is the [ekādaśī] known by the name of Mokṣā. / This vow should be performed by all, and let its merit be dedicated to your father.
By the power of that merit, liberation will be theirs. / This is true, O fortunate one, just like the word of Brahmā.”
Having heard the word of the sage, he returned to his own home; / and indeed, with difficulty the month of Mārgaśīrṣa was reached by him.
King Vaikhānasa, performing that vow according to the word of the sage, / dedicated the merit, along with all [his household], to his father, that protector of the earth.
The moment the merit was given, a rain of flowers fell in heaven; / indeed, the father of Vaikhānasa entered liberation together with his ancestors.
And from the sky he spoke a sacred word to the king: / ‘May it be well, may it be well with you, O son!’ and having spoken thus, he went to heaven.
Whoever thus observes the auspicious Mokṣā ekādaśī, O king, / their sins are destroyed, and upon death they attain liberation.
There is no ekādaśī higher than this one that grants liberation. / I do not know the count of its merit, O king; this vow is pleasing to me.
Equal to a wish-fulfilling jewel, this indeed bestows liberation upon men. / From reciting it or hearing it, one obtains the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice.”

title: catvāriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / “In the dark half of Pauṣa, what is the name of the ekādaśī? / What is its procedure? Tell this in detail! / Declare this, O master: which deity is worshipped there?”
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: / “I will tell you, O king of kings, out of the bond of affection for you. / My satisfaction, O king, is not obtained through sacrifices accompanied by abundant gifts
in such a way as my satisfaction comes indeed through the ekādaśī vow. / Therefore, Hari's day should be observed with every effort.
This is true, not false, O expert among the most righteous! / The one in the dark half of Pauṣa is known by name as Saphalā.
On it, one should worship Lord Nārāyaṇa according to rule. / The auspicious ekādaśī should be observed according to the previously stated method.
Just as Śeṣa is among serpents, the eater of serpents among birds, / Viṣṇu among the gods, and the twice-born among two-footed beings,
and just as the lunar day of Ekādaśī is best among vows, O king, / so those people, O king, are ever worshipful to me
who, absorbed in Hari's day, observe the ekādaśī vow. / Endowed with wealth right in this world, at death they attain liberation.
On the Saphalā, O king, one should worship Hari with fruits according to their names: / with coconuts, betel nuts, and citrons,
with limes and pomegranates, and with auspicious myrobalan fruits, / with cloves, jujubes, and especially with mangoes.
One should worship the lord of the gods of gods with incense and lamps as well; / on the Saphalā, one should specifically make a donation of lamps.
And a night vigil should be performed together with Vaiṣṇavas: / as long as an eye winks, so long one should keep vigil in the night.
Hear, O king, the merit of one whose mind is one-pointed: / there is no sacrifice equal to it, nor indeed is there any pilgrimage place equal to it.
All vows, O lord of kings, are not worth a sixteenth part [of it]. / The fruit that is not obtained even by thousands of years of austerities—
that fruit he surely obtains who keeps the vigil. / Listen, O tiger among kings, to the auspicious story of Saphalā.
There was a city named Campāvatī belonging to Māhiṣmata; / and five young sons were born to that royal sage.
Among them, the eldest was ever devoted to great sin: / an adulterer, attached to harlots, and a drinker of liquor.
The wealth of his father was squandered by that evil-doer. / Ever devoted to wicked conduct, he was a slanderer of brahmins;
he constantly reviled Vaiṣṇavas and the gods. / Seeing his son to be such, King Māhiṣmata,
naming him Luṃpaka, excluded him from the royal sons. / He was banished from the kingdom by his father and relatives.
Cast out by his retinue like an enemy, / Luṃpaka, thus abandoned, then thought:
"I have been cast out by my kinsmen, expelled from the kingdom by my father!" / Thinking thus, he then turned his mind to evil:
"I must go into the terrible, dense forest; / and from there I will plunder my father's entire city!"

Having thus made up his mind, Lumpaka, through the working of fate,
departed from that city and went into a dense forest.
Constantly devoted to killing living beings, a treasury of the arts of theft and gambling, / the whole town was robbed by that evil-doer.
Committing theft in the city, he was caught by the night-watchmen; / he said to them: "I am the son of King Māhiṣmata!"
Released by them, that evil-doer went back to the forest, / always delighting in meat and eating the fruit of trees.
The dwelling of that wicked man was near [an image of] Vāsudeva; / an ancient peepal tree, many years old, stood there.
Great divinity resided in that tree in the forest. / Dwelling right there, Luṃpaka remained evil-minded.
After much time had passed, through some accumulation of merit, / on the tenth day of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa,
having eaten the fruits of the trees, afflicted by the cold at night, / the wretched man named Luṃpaka, devoid of clothing, his sight failing,
tormented by excessive cold near Hari's tree, / had neither sleep nor comfort; he became as if his life-breath were gone.
Covering his mouth with his teeth [chattering], he spent the whole night thus; / even at sunrise that wicked man did not regain consciousness.
Luṃpaka remained unconscious on the day of Saphalā; / only when the sun reached the zenith did Luṃpaka regain his senses.

Looking here and there, and afflicted by the cold at that time,
he walked with stumbling feet, limping again and again.
Having gone into the middle of the forest, he was emaciated with hunger and afflicted; / that wicked Luṃpaka had no strength to kill living beings.
Then, O king, Luṃpaka gathered fruits; / by the time he returned there, the sun had set.
Lamenting, "What will become [of me], O father?" / he placed the abundant fruits at the foot of the tree,

He said: "May Lord Hari, the husband of Śrī, be pleased with these fruits!"
Having spoken thus, Lumpaka did not get any sleep at night.
Viṣṇu considered that night of the wicked man as a vigil; / and he considered [the fruits] as worship for Saphalā, O sinless one.
Luṃpaka had accidentally performed this vow; / by the power of that merit, he obtained a kingdom free of thorns.
By the time the sun rose, Viṣṇu departed. / At that moment a bodiless voice arose in the sky and said:
"O son, you will obtain the kingdom through the grace of Saphalā!" / When this word was spoken, he assumed a divine form.
Then his mind became supremely devoted to Viṣṇu, O king; / adorned with the splendor of divine ornaments, he obtained an unmolested kingdom.
He ruled the kingdom in this manner for fifteen years; / he had sons who satisfied his heart and a wife, by the grace of Kṛṣṇa.
Quickly renouncing the kingdom and entrusting it to his son, / he went to the presence of Kṛṣṇa, having gone to which one does not grieve.
A person who thus performs the supreme vow of Saphalā, O king, / attains happiness in this world and, when dead, attains liberation.
Blessed are those mortals in the world who are devoted to Saphalā; / their birth is fruitful, there is no doubt about this.

By reciting, hearing, and observing [it], O ruler of the people, / a mortal obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.

Thus [ends] in the venerable Padma Purāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand verses, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa, in the dialogue between the husband of Umā and Nārada, [the chapter] named The Saphalā Ekādaśī of the Dark Fortnight of Pauṣa,

title: ekacatvāriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / The auspicious Saphalā Ekādaśī has indeed been related by you, O Kṛṣṇa; / speak out of your grace about that which falls in the bright fortnight:
What is its name? What is its ritual? Which deity is worshipped there? / With whom was Hṛṣīkeśa pleased—you yourself, O Puruṣottama?
The blessed Kṛṣṇa said: / Listen, O king, I will explain the bright [Ekādaśī] of Pauṣa; / I speak, O great king, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
It should be observed with effort, O king, according to the previous ritual; / it is named Putradā, supreme, removing all sins.
Nārāyaṇa is its presiding deity, the granter of desires, the giver of perfection; / there is none superior to this in the three worlds, with their moving and unmoving beings.
Hari makes a person learned and renowned. / Listen, O king, I shall relate the supreme story that removes sins.
Formerly in the city of Bhadrāvatī there was a king named Suketumān; / the queen of that king was named Campakā.
By that childless king time was spent in [unfulfilled] hopes; / the king did not obtain a son who would perpetuate his lineage.
For a long time that righteous king pondered: / "What shall I do? Where shall I go? How can I obtain a son?"
King Suketumān found no pleasure in his realm or in his city; / together with his virtuous wife, he was sorrowful every day.
Both of them, husband and wife, were constantly devoted to anxiety and grief. / His ancestors consume the water offered [by him] as lukewarm:
"After the king, we see no one who will gratify us!" / Remembering thus, his ancestors became sorrowful.
Neither kinsmen nor friends, neither ministers nor well-wishers, / nor elephants, horses, and foot-soldiers pleased this king.
Despair was ever present in the mind of that king: / "There is no fruit to the birth of a man who is sonless!
The house of a childless man is empty, his heart is ever grieving; / without a son there is no freedom from debt to the ancestors, gods, and men.
Therefore, with every effort, a man should beget a son; / theirs is fame in this world, and an auspicious state in the other world.
For those performers of meritorious deeds in whose house the birth of a son occurs, / life, health, and prosperity abide in their home."

"The birth of a son takes place in the house of people who perform meritorious deeds.
Without merit, and without devotion to Viṣṇu, O king,

there are no sons or prosperity; such is my firm conviction."
Thinking thus, that king found no peace.

At dawn the king pondered, and then at midnight he pondered.
Ketumān even considered destroying himself.

Then, reflecting on the wretched fate that follows suicide,
and seeing his own body fallen and likewise his sonlessness,

deliberating again with his intellect upon what would be beneficial for himself,
the king mounted a horse and went to a dense forest.

The royal chaplain and all others did not know that the king had departed.
In the deep forest frequented by beasts and birds,

the king then wandered, looking at the forest trees:
banyans, sacred figs, bilva trees, date palms, jackfruit trees,

bakulas, saptaparṇas, tiṃdukas, and tilakas;
the king saw śāla, tāla, tamāla, and pine trees,

iṅgudī and kakubha trees, and likewise śleṣmātaka trees,
śallakīs, karamardas, pāṭalas, and jujube trees,

aśokas, and palāśas; and also jackals, rabbits,
wild cats, buffaloes, porcupines, and yaks.

The king saw serpents half-emerged from ant-hills,
as well as rutting wild elephants accompanied by their calves,

and herd-leaders with four tusks amidst herds of female elephants.
Seeing those elephants, the king thought of his own [elephants].

Moving among them, the king attained beauty;
the king beheld a forest filled with great wonder.

Hearing the cries of jackals along the path, and likewise the hooting of owls,
watching various bears and deer, he wandered in the middle of the forest.

Thus the king surveyed the dense forest as the sun reached mid-sky.
Afflicted with hunger and thirst, the king ran here and there.

His throat parched, the king reflected:
"What action did I commit, that such suffering has befallen me?

Indeed, I gratified the gods with sacrifices and worship,
and likewise pleased the brāhmaṇas with gifts and delicious feasts,

and ever protected the subjects greatly like my own children.
Why has such terrible and severe sorrow befallen me?"

Thus absorbed in thought, the king went forward into the forest;
by the power of his good deeds, he saw an unsurpassed lake.

touched by fish, further adorned with lotuses,
and graced by kāraṇḍava ducks, cakravāka birds, and royal swans,

filled with many crocodiles, fish, and other aquatic creatures.
Near that lake, he saw many hermitages of sages;

the illustrious king saw them, with omens predicting auspiciousness.
Then his right eye twitched, and his right hand

twitched, foretelling an auspicious outcome for the king.
Seeing the sages on its bank chanting Vedic recitations,

the king's son was overcome with great joy.
Descending from that horse, he stood before the sages.

He bowed individually to those sages of celebrated vows,
folding his hands reverently and bowing like a fallen rod again and again.

Those sages also replied: "We are pleased, O king."
The king said: "Who are you here? Please tell me your names.
For what purpose have you gathered? Tell me the truth."

The sages said: "We are the Viśvedevas, O king, and we have come here to bathe.
Māgha has drawn near, on the fifth day from this.

And today, O king, is the eleventh lunar day known as Putradā.
Viṣṇu gives a son to people who observe Putradā."

The king said: "This is indeed my great distress regarding the begetting of a son.
If you are pleased, then please grant me a son."

A sage said: "Today itself is the day called Putradā, O king;
it is renowned as an ekādaśī. Perform this excellent observance.

Then, through our consecration and by the grace of Keśava,
you will certainly obtain a son, O best of kings."

Following this advice of theirs, the king observed the excellent vow
according to the rite of Putradā, by the instruction of the sages.

Having broken his fast on the twelfth lunar day and bowed repeatedly to the sages,
the king returned home, and then the queen conceived a child.

At the time of delivery, an illustrious son was born through his meritorious deed;
he brought joy to his father and became a protector of the people.

Therefore, O king, the excellent vow of Putradā should be observed.
For the welfare of mankind, this has been related by me to you.

Those mortals who single-mindedly observe the Putradā vow
obtain sons in this world and, upon death, go to heaven.
From reading or hearing this, O king, one attains the fruit of an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice."

title: dvicatvāriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Well said, O Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the Universe, primordial deity, Lord of the World!
Speak out of your grace; show mercy upon me.

Which ekādaśī occurs in the dark fortnight of Māgha?
What is its name and what is its rule? Tell this in detail."

The Blessed Lord said: "Listen, O tiger among kings, to the one that occurs in the dark fortnight of Māgha;
it is renowned as Ṣaṭtilā, destroying all sins.

Listen to the auspicious story of Ṣaṭtilā that removes sin,
which Pulastya, the best of sages, recounted to Dālabhya."

Dālabhya said: "Creatures who have arrived in the mortal world commit sin,
and are burdened with sins such as the killing of a brāhmaṇa and diverse others.

They steal others' wealth and are infatuated by other vices.
How do they not go to hell, O holy one? Tell me that in truth.

O lord, you should tell me this:
how can sin reach pacification easily, through some small gift?"

Pulastya said: "Well said, well said, O highly fortunate one! This is a profound secret, very difficult to obtain,
which has not been revealed to anyone by the deities Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Indra.

That I shall declare, questioned as I am by you, O best of the twice-born.
When the month of Māgha has arrived, pure, bathed, and with senses restrained,

free from desire, anger, arrogance, envy, greed, and slander,
remembering the God of gods, and having washed his feet with water,

a man should take cow-dung that has not fallen on the ground,
and, casting sesame seeds and cotton into it, he should make balls.

One hundred and eight of them indeed—no doubt should be entertained here.
Then, when Māgha has arrived, if there should be the constellation Āṣāḍhā,

or Mūla, of the dark fortnight, he should then undertake
the rules of the ekādaśī at an auspicious time. Hear its procedure from me.

Having thoroughly worshipped the God of gods, well bathed, disciplined, and pure,
and having praised the names of Kṛṣṇa whenever he stumbles or the like,

he should keep a vigil at night and first cause a fire oblation to be performed.
On the second day, he should worship Hari again, the Lord of the God of gods,

with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and an offering of kṛsara;
and then, remembering him again and again by the name of Kṛṣṇa,"

With ash gourds, coconuts, or indeed with citrons,
or, if all these are lacking, O lord of Brahmins, surrounded by auspicious betel nuts,
one should offer arghya according to rule after worshipping Janārdana:

“O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa! You are compassionate; be the refuge of those without refuge!
Have mercy, O Puruṣottama, on those sunk in the ocean of worldly existence!

Homage to you, O lotus-eyed one! Homage to you, source of the universe!
O friend of Brahmins, homage be to you, O Supreme Person, firstborn!
Accept the arghya offered by me, together with Lakṣmī, O Lord of the universe!”

Thus ends the argha mantra.
Then one should worship a brahmin and present a water-pot,
parasol, sandals, and clothes, saying: "May Kṛṣṇa be pleased with me!"

A black cow should be given to an excellent Brahmin according to one’s ability;
a vessel of sesame seeds should be given, O best of Brahmins, by one discerning of recipients.

for so many thousands of years he is glorified in the heavenly world.
Bathing with sesame, anointing with sesame, offering sesame into fire, giving water with sesame,

giving sesame, and eating [sesame]—these six sesames destroy sin.
Nārada said:
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, mighty-armed one! Homage to you, source of the universe!

title: śṛṇurājanyathāvṛttaṃdṛṣṭaṃtatkathayāmite
text_mt:
Formerly, in the mortal world, there was a certain Brahmin woman, O Nārada,
constantly devoted to the practice of vows, always devoted to the worship of the gods.

Devoted to month-long fasts, and always my devotee,
engaged in fasting for Kṛṣṇa, dedicated to my worship,

her body was indeed emaciated by fasts, O best of Brahmins.
Out of devotion to gods, Brahmins, and unmarried maidens,

that greatly chaste woman continually gave away houses and the like,
yet she was constantly devoted to extreme austerities, O Brahmin.
Alms were not given to mendicants, nor were Brahmins gratified [with food].

Then, after a great deal of time, it was thought by me, O Brahmin:
“Her body is indeed purified by severe vows, without a doubt;

the Vaiṣṇava realm has indeed been honoured by her through physical mortification,
yet the gift of food has not been given, by which supreme satisfaction might arise.”

Knowing this, O Brahmin, I arrived in the mortal world;
assuming the form of an ascetic with a skull-bowl, she was asked for alms:

“From where have you come, O Brahmin? Where are you going? Speak before me!”
Again it was said by me, “Give alms, O beautiful one!”

With great anger, a lump of clay was thrown by her into the copper vessel,
