whereupon, O Brahmin, I went back to heaven.

Then, after a great deal of time, that female ascetic of very great vows
came to heaven in her very body by the power of her practice of vows.

By giving the lump of clay, a charming house was obtained,
and yet, O Brahmin-sage, it was completely devoid of heaps of grain.

As she inspected the house, she saw nothing there;
then she went out of the house and came before me, O Brahmin.

Overcome with great anger, she spoke this word:
“By me, through vows, severe penances, and manifold fasts,

the god, the protector of the whole world, was propitiated with worship;
yet nothing is seen there in my house, O Janārdana!”

Then it was said by me to her: “Go home, O woman of great vows!
Filled with curiosity, they will surely come—

the wives of the gods, filled with wonder, indeed to see you.
Do not open the door except in return for their reciting the merits of Ṣaṭtilā.”

Having been spoken to thus by me, that mortal woman went then;
meanwhile, the wives of the gods arrived, O Brahmin.

And it was said by them there: “We have indeed come to see you.
Open the door for yourself today, O fair one, so that we may see you!”

The mortal woman said:
“If I am to be seen, the truth must be spoken in particular:
the sacred vow of Ṣaṭtilā, for the purpose of opening the door.”

Then, opening the door, the mortal woman was seen by them;
she was not a goddess, nor a Gandharva woman, nor an Asura woman, nor a serpent woman.

Never before had such a woman been seen as this one was, O bull among Brahmins.
By the instruction of the goddess, the vow of Ṣaṭtilā was performed

by that mortal woman of true vows, which bestows the fruit of enjoyment and liberation.
Endowed with beauty and radiance, in an instant she attained [abundance]:

wealth, grain, garments and the like, gold and silver as well,
a mansion supplied with everything, by the power of Ṣaṭtilā.
Endowed with beauty and radiance, she was transformed in an instant.

Excessive greed should not be harboured; one should abandon miserliness with wealth.
According to one's own wealth, one should cause sesame seeds and garments to be given.

And thus a man obtains freedom from disease in birth after birth;
neither poverty, nor hardship, nor misfortune

shall occur, O best of Brahmins, by fasting on Ṣaṭtilā.
By this rite, O king, a giver of sesame, without a doubt,

title: tricatvāriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
Yudhiṣṭhirā said:
Well spoken by you, O Kṛṣṇa! You are the primal god, O Lord!
Beings born of sweat, born of eggs, born of sprouts, and born of wombs—

you are their creator, transformer, protector, and destroyer.
In the dark fortnight of Māgha, Ṣaṭtilā was told by you;

and which one occurs in the bright fortnight, O God? Tell by your grace!
What is its name, what is its procedure, and which deity is worshipped there?

purifying and sin-destroying, granting desires and granting liberation to mortals,
destroying [the sin of] killing a Brahmin, and destroying the state of being a piśāca.

When its vow is observed, the state of a ghost does not occur to mortals at all;
there is none higher than this, sin-destroying and conferring liberation.

For this reason, O king, it should be observed with diligence.
Let the auspicious Purāṇic story be heard, O tiger among kings!

In the Lotus Purāṇa, its greatness has been related by me.
Once in the heavenly world, Indra indeed exercised his rule.

There the gods were living in comfort in a delightful [place],
devoted to drinking nectar, attended by hosts of apsarases.

There was the Nandana grove, attended by Pārijāta trees;
there the gods delight and sport with apsarases.

Once, sporting at his will, O king, that lord of the gods,
the ruler of fifty crores, caused dancing out of joy.

There the Gandharvas sing: the Gandharva Puṣpadanta,
and Citrasena was right there, and likewise the daughter of Citrasena;

and there was the woman named Mālinī, the wife of Citrasena,
and born of Mālinī was [a daughter] named Puṣpadantī.
Puṣpadanta had a son named Mālyavān. / Mālyavān was utterly infatuated with the beauty of Puṣpadantī.
Indeed, Mālyavān was captivated by her side-glances. / Behold her beauty, endowed with grace and loveliness!
Her arms seemed made by the god of love as nooses for the neck; / her eyes stretched to her ears, revolving with red corners.
Her ears were radiant with earrings, O best of kings; / she had a conch-like neck and was adorned with divine ornaments.
Her breasts were full and raised, like two golden pitchers; / the waist of that slender-limbed girl was thin, graspable with a fist, unsurpassable.
Her buttocks were broad, and the region of her hips expansive; / her feet were splendid, shining like red water-lilies.
Mālyavān was deeply infatuated with Puṣpavatī, who was of such [beauty]. / The two came together to dance for the pleasure of Śakra.
While the two were singing there, attended by the host of Apsarases, / the limbs of Puṣpadantī and Mālyavān were overcome by passion.
Through mutual passion they fell under the sway of bewilderment. / With their minds confused, they could not sing the song accurately.
With their gazes thus fixed on each other, fallen under the power of the arrows of love, / the chief of gods realized that their minds were united there.
Considering his own disrespect / due to the lapse in rhythm and musical tempo, and the abandoning of the song,
Maghavan, enraged on their account, pronounced this curse: / 'Fie, fie on you two, fallen fools, transgressors of my command!
May you two become piśācas, maintaining the status of husband and wife, / and reach the mortal world, experiencing the fruit of your action!'
Thus cursed by Maghavan, both sorrowful in mind, / bewildered by Indra's curse, they reached Mount Himavat.
Both fell into the state of piśācas, suffering terrible misery. / Agonized in mind there, both entered extreme hardship in the snow.
Bewildered, they did not remember their status as Gandharva and Apsaras; / they were tormented by heat arising from their physical lapse.
Afflicted by their deeds, they found no comfort or peace at night; / disputing with one another, they roamed in the mountain cave.
Tormented by the cold produced by the snow, / their bodies had hair standing on end, and their teeth chattered.
Then that male piśāca spoke to his wife, the female piśāca: / 'What great, terrible, hair-raising sin was committed [by us],
by which this state of piśāca was obtained through our own wicked deed? / Considering this piśāca state to be a terrible hell, causing misery,
one should therefore by every effort avoid committing sin.' / Absorbed in such reflections, the two remained there, emaciated with grief.
By the power of fate, there arrived for them the eleventh lunar day of Māgha, / renowned as Jayā, the best among lunar days.
When that day arrived, O king, / the two remained there destitute of food and without drinking water.
No killing of living beings was done, nor was there eating of leaves and fruits. / They were near a sacred fig tree, continually filled with sorrow.
As they remained in that very manner, O king, the sun set, / and the dreadful, terrible, life-stealing night arrived.
Trembling, the two then slept on the ground, / clinging to each other with their limbs and arms.
They found neither sleep nor pleasure there, nor any happiness. / Thus, O tiger among kings, were they tormented by Indra's curse.
As they were thus miserable, the night passed away. / The sun rose at the arrival of the twelfth day.
O tiger among kings, their liberation was conceived in my heart: / the excellent observance of Jayā had been performed, and an all-night vigil was kept.
Therefore, hear how it happened through the power of the observance: / when the twelfth day arrived and the observance of Jayā had thus been performed,
by Viṣṇu's power, O king, their state of piśāca departed. / Puṣpadantī and Mālyavān regained their former forms.
Endowed with their former love and wearing their former ornaments, / they mounted a celestial vehicle and went to charming heaven.
Approaching the lord of gods, they joyfully bowed before him. / Seeing them in such a state, Maghavan spoke in astonishment:
Indra said: / 'Tell me, by what merit has your piśāca state disappeared? / Having received my curse, by which god were you released?'
Mālyavān said: / 'By the grace of Vāsudeva and by the observance of Jayā, / our piśāca state has gone, O lord, through the power of devotion to Him.'

Hearing this, Maghavan then replied in turn:
"You two have become pure and purifying, worthy of homage even by me."
since you have observed the day of Hari and are devoted to Viṣṇu. / Those mortals who are absorbed in the day of Hari and devoted to Kṛṣṇa
are certainly worshipful even to us; there is no doubt. / Sport happily as you please with Puṣpadantī in the abode of the gods.'
Kṛṣṇa said: / 'For this reason, O king, the day of Hari should be observed. / Jayā, O tiger among kings, removes the sin of killing a brahmin.
By him all gifts are given, and all sacrifices are completely / performed, who has observed the vow of Jayā.
He surely rejoices in Vaikuṇṭha for ten million kalpas. / From reciting or hearing it, O king, one attains the fruit of an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.'

title: catuścatvāriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / 'In the dark fortnight of Phālguna, what is the name of the Ekādaśī? / Please tell me, O Vāsudeva, out of your grace.'

The venerable Kṛṣṇa said: / 'Nārada questioned Brahmā, who is seated on the lotus: / "In the dark fortnight of Phālguna, [the Ekādaśī] named Vijayā occurs; / O best of the twice-born, graciously relate its merit."'
Brahmā said: / 'Listen, Nārada, I will narrate the supreme tale that removes sins, / this observance of Vijayā, which I have not revealed to anyone.
For this ancient observance is pure and destroys sins; / it bestows victory upon kings, without a doubt.
Formerly, Rāma went to the forest for fourteen years. / Accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, he dwelt in Pañcavaṭī.
While Rāma of victorious nature was living right there, / his illustrious wife Sītā was abducted by Rāvaṇa out of lust.
Through that grief, Rāma too fell into despair at that time. / Wandering about, he then saw Jaṭāyus, whose life had ended.
Then Kabandha was slain by him as he wandered in the midst of the forest. / His friendship was established together with Sugrīva.
Armies of monkeys assembled for Rāma's sake, / and then Jānakī was seen in the garden of Laṅkā by Hanumat.
Rāma's token of recognition was given to her, and a great feat was performed. / Returning, he reported everything there to Rāma.
Then, hearing the words of Hanumat, / Rāmacandra resolved upon departure with the approval of Sugrīva.'

“O Saumitri, by what religious merit can the ocean, the abode of Varuṇa, be crossed? / It is fathomless, thoroughly agitated, and teeming with aquatic monsters. / I see no means at all by which it can be easily crossed.”
Lakṣmaṇa said: / “You alone are the primeval God, the ancient Puruṣottama. / Yet the sage Baka Dālbhya resides here in the midst of an island.
His hermitage is half a yojana from this place, O Rāghava; / and there are many other brāhmaṇas there, O delight of the Raghu lineage.
Go and ask that ancient, eminent sage, O king of kings.” / Having heard these most excellent words of Lakṣmaṇa,
Rāghava went to see the great sage Baka Dālbhya. / Rāma bowed his head to the sage, like an immortal to Viṣṇu.
The sage, knowing Rāma to be the ancient Puruṣottama / who had entered a human body for a particular purpose,
the pleased sage said, “From where have you come, Rāma?”
Rāma said: / “By your favor, O brāhmaṇa, I have come with my army / to the shore of the lord of rivers to conquer Laṅkā with its rākṣasas.
Through your benevolence, by what means can the ocean be crossed by me? / Tell me that means, O sage; grant your grace right now.
For this very reason have I come here to see you.” / Hearing the words of Rāma, the great sage Baka Dālbhya,
with a delighted mind, said to lotus-eyed Rāma: / “You must perform today, O Rāma, the most excellent of all vows,
by the performance of which victory will swiftly be yours. / Having conquered Laṅkā and the rākṣasas, you will attain pure renown.
With an attentive mind, undertake this vow. / In the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna occurs the Vijayā Ekādaśī.
By the vow of that [day], O Rāma, your victory will be assured; / without doubt you will cross the sea together with the monkeys.
Hear the rule, O king, that yields the fruit of this vow: / When the tenth day has arrived, one should have a water jar prepared,
made of gold, silver, copper, or clay; / adorned, filled with water, and adorned with sprouts, one should install it.
One should place the seven grains beneath it, and barley on top of it. / Upon that, one should install the divine Lord, the golden Nārāyaṇa.
When the eleventh day arrives, one should take a morning bath; / one should place the jar steadily, with garlands on its neck and with unguents.
One should especially worship it with betel nuts and coconuts, / with perfumes, incenses, lamps, and various food-offerings.
In front of the jar, O Rāma, that day is spent with virtuous discourses and the like; / and at night, a wise person should keep vigil before it.
One should light a lamp of clarified butter for the sake of the unbroken vow. / When the twelfth day arrives and the sun has risen,
having taken the jar to a watery place—a river, a mountain stream, / or a pond—and having set it down and worshipped it according to rule,
one should give that jar along with the deity to a brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas; / along with the jar, O king of kings, one should bestow great gifts.
According to this rite, O Rāma, joined together with your troop commanders, / perform the vow diligently, and victory will be yours.”

Hearing this, Rāma then did as had been told;
when the vow was performed, that joy of the Raghus became victorious.
Sītā was regained, Laṅkā conquered, and Rāvaṇa slain in battle. / Those men who perform this vow according to this rite, O son,
attain victory in this world and imperishable status in the next world. / For this reason, O son, the Vijayā vow should be performed.
The glorification of the Vijayā destroys all sins; / by reciting it and hearing it, one obtains the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice.

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, named "The Glorification of Vijayā of the Dark Fortnight of Phālguna," in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the compilation of fifty-five thousand [verses].

title: pañcacatvāriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: [Yudhiṣṭhira] said: / “The great-fruited glorification of the dark fortnight's Vijayā has been heard; / now tell of the one that is called by name in the bright fortnight of Phālguna.”
The holy Kṛṣṇa said: / “O highly fortunate son of Dharma, listen, I shall now tell you / what was spoken by the magnanimous Vasiṣṭha when questioned by Māndhātṛ.
A particular [vow] for Phālguna has been declared with special merit, O king: / the holy Āmalakī vow, which bestows the fruit of the world of Viṣṇu.
Going beneath an āmalakī tree, one should keep vigil there. / Having kept vigil at night, one obtains the fruit of [gifting] a thousand cows.”
Māndhātṛ said: / “When indeed did this āmalakī tree originate, O best of the twice-born? / Explain all this to me; indeed, my curiosity is very great.
Why is it pure, and why does it destroy sin? / Why, having kept vigil, does one obtain the fruit of a thousand cows?”
Vasiṣṭha said: / “I shall tell, O highly fortunate one, how this great āmalakī tree, / the destroyer of all sins, came to be on earth.
Formerly, when the single cosmic ocean had arisen and all moving and unmoving things had perished, / when the hosts of gods and demons had perished, and the serpents and rākṣasas had been destroyed,
the Lord of the foremost gods, the eternal Supreme Self, / entered the supreme Brahman, His own imperishable state.
Then, as He was awake, from His mouth a drop resembling the moon in luster / was produced from a spit, and it fell to the earth.
From that drop arose of itself the great dhātrī tree, / rich with boughs and branches, bent down by the weight of its fruit.
It is proclaimed as the first-grown of all trees. / Then, after that, these creatures were created by Brahmā.
The divine Lord created gods, dānavas, gandharvas, / yakṣas, rākṣasas, serpents, and spotless great sages.
Those gods came there where the dhātrī tree, dear to Hari, stood; / seeing it, O highly fortunate one, they fell into supreme wonder.
Standing together and pondering, they thought, ‘We do not recognize this tree.’ / As they were pondering thus, a bodiless voice spoke:
‘This āmalakī tree is the foremost, considered sacred to Viṣṇu. / By the mere remembrance of it, one obtains the fruit born of gifting cows.
By touching it the merit is doubled, and by wearing it, tripled. / Therefore, with all effort, the āmalakī is always to be resorted to.
It is declared to remove all sins, sacred to Viṣṇu, destroying wickedness. / At its base resides Viṣṇu, and above him the Grandfather [Brahmā].
On the trunk rests the divine Rudra, the Supreme Lord; / on the boughs are all the sages, and on the branches are the deities.
The gods sit on the leaves, and the Maruts on the flowers; / the lords of creatures are situated in the fruits.
Thus the dhātrī is declared by me to consist of all the gods; / therefore it is most worthy of worship by those devoted to Viṣṇu.’
The sages said: / ‘Who are you? We do not know. How have you become the cause? / Whether you are a god or someone else, tell us truthfully.’
The voice said: / ‘He who is the creator of all beings and of all the worlds everywhere, / seeing the wise astonished—I am that eternal Viṣṇu.’
Hearing that speech of the God of gods, the sons of Brahmā / set about praising that beginningless and endless God there:
‘Homage to the Self who is the self of all beings, to the Supreme Self; / homage always to Acyuta, homage, homage to Ananta!’”
"Salutations, salutations to Dāmodara, the wise seer, the lord of sacrifice!" / Thus praised by the sages, the blessed Hari was pleased.
He replied to those great sages: "What desired boon shall I give you?" / The sages said: / "If you are pleased, O Blessed One, out of a wish for our welfare,
explain a vow that yields heaven and liberation as its fruit, / that grants wealth and grain, is meritorious, and brings satisfaction to oneself,
involving little exertion, bearing great fruit, the best among vows, / by the performance of which, O Lord of gods, one is honored in the world of Viṣṇu."
Viṣṇu said: / "If in the bright fortnight of Phālguna the twelfth [lunar day] falls with the Puṣya nakṣatra, / that [day] is exceedingly meritorious, destroying the greatest sins.
Listen, O best among the twice-born, to the special practice to be performed then: / approaching an āmalakī tree, one should observe a vigil there.

Freed from all sins, one obtains the fruit of [gifting] a thousand cows. / This, O brahmins, is described to you as the best among vows: / having worshipped Acyuta on that day, one never falls from the world of Viṣṇu."
The sages said: / "Tell [us] the rule of this vow, how it may be completely fulfilled: / what are the mantras, what are the salutations, and which deity is proclaimed?
How is the gift to be made, how the bath, and what is recorded as the ritual of worship? / Tell [us] truly the mantra for offering the arghya and the worship."
Viṣṇu said: / "Listen, O foremost among the twice-born, to the complete rule of this vow: / having remained without food on the eleventh [day], on the following day,
[saying,] 'I shall eat, O Lotus-eyed One; be my refuge, O Acyuta!' / Having thus undertaken the observance, preceded by cleaning the teeth,
one should not converse with fallen men, thieves, or heretics, / nor with men of wicked conduct, breakers of proper bounds, or violators of the guru's wife.
Then in the afternoon, the wise person, with self-restraint, / should perform the bath according to rule in a river, a pond, a well, or at home.
First applying clay, one should then bathe, [reciting:] / 'O earth, traversed by horses, traversed by chariots, traversed by Viṣṇu,
O clay, take away my sin, whatever misdeed has been done by me!'

Thus ends the clay mantra.
"You, O water, are the life of all creatures, the protector of the body
of those born of sweat and of sprouting seeds; homage to the lord of tastes!"
I am bathed in all sacred waterplaces, in pools and waterfalls, / in rivers and gods' excavated ponds; may this be my bath!'"

Thus ends the bath mantra.
And having an image of the sage, the son of Jamadagni, fashioned of gold,
of a māṣaka of gold, or else of half of that half,
coming home, one should perform the worship and fire oblation of the worship. / Then one should go to the āmalakī tree, equipped with all paraphernalia.
Having gone to the āmalakī tree and cleaned all around it, / one should place an unblemished jar with mantras, standing firm,
supplied with the five gems, perfumed with divine scents, / accompanied by a parasol and a pair of sandals, and anointed with white sandalwood,
its neck draped with garlands of flowers, fumigated with every kind of incense; / one should arrange rows of lamps all around, highly enchanting.
Upon it one should set a vessel completely filled with divine parched grain; / on the vessel one should place the god, the son of Jamadagni, of great splendor:
'Salutations to Viśoka' for the two feet, to the Universal-formed for the two knees, / to Ugra for the two thighs, and to Dāmodara for the waist;
the belly to Padmanābha, the chest to the bearer of the Śrīvatsa; / to the Discus-bearer for the left arm, and salutations to the Mace-bearer for the right;
salutations to Vaikuṇṭha for the neck, and the mouth to Yajñamukha; / the nose to Viśokanidhi, and the two eyes to Vāsudeva;
the forehead with 'to Vāmana', salutations to the two eyebrows with 'to Rāma', / and one should worship that head with 'Salutations to the Universal Soul.'

Thus ends the worship mantra.
Then one should offer an argha to the god of the gods
with an unblemished fruit and with a mind filled with devotion.
Then one should keep a vigil with a devout mind, / with dances, songs, musical instruments, stories of dharma, and hymns,
and with Vaiṣṇava narratives one should spend the whole night. / Then one should circumambulate the myrobalan tree reciting the names of Viṣṇu,
one hundred and eight times, or twenty-eight times. / Then at dawn, having performed the waving of lights for Hari,
and having honored a brahmin, one should offer everything to him: / the jar for the son of Jamadagni, the pair of garments, and the two sandals,
[saying,] 'May Keśava be pleased with me in the form of the son of Jamadagni!' / Then, touching the āmalakī tree and circumambulating it,
and bathing according to rule, one should feed brahmins. / Then one may eat oneself, surrounded by one's family.
Whatever merit arises from this being done, all that I tell you: / whatever merit is in all sacred waterplaces, whatever fruit is in all gifts,
and exceeding all sacrifices, one obtains it—there is no doubt here. / All this has been declared to you, the best among vows."
Having spoken this much, the Lord of gods vanished right there. / And those sages too performed everything without omission.

text_mt:
Likewise you also, O king of kings, best of men, ought to perform / this irresistible vow that frees from all sins.

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, named "Āmalakī Ekādaśī of the Bright Fortnight of Phālguna," in the conversation between the husband of Umā and Nārada, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the compilation of fifty-five thousand [verses].

Chapter Forty-Six. Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Āmalakī has been heard about in the bright fortnight of Phālguna;
what is the name of the Ekādaśī in the dark fortnight of Caitra?"

The blessed Kṛṣṇa said: / "Listen, O king of kings, I shall tell the sin-destroying tale / that Lomaśa spoke when questioned by Māndhātṛ, the universal emperor."

in the first fortnight of Caitra, what is the name of the eleventh [lunar day]? / What is the rule, what is its fruit? Speak out of your grace!"

Lomaśa said: / "In the month of Caitra, in the dark fortnight, the eleventh [lunar day] / is indeed proclaimed by the name Pāpamocanī, destroying condition as a piśāca.

Listen, O king, I shall tell its wondrous, auspicious story / that grants wishes, yields success, destroys sins, and bestows dharma.

Formerly, in the Caitraratha region, frequented by groups of apsarases, / when the springtime arrived, in a forest teeming with six-legged bees,

daughters of Gandharvas sported with kinnaras to musical instruments, / and the dwellers of the third heaven, led by Pākaśāsana, were playing.

There was no other forest bringing pleasure like Caitraratha; / in that forest sages were performing intense austerities.

text_mt:
Toward a sage named Medhāvin, an ascetic residing there, / an apsaras set out to delude that best of sages.

Known as Mañjughoṣā, revealing her affection toward him, / she remained out of fear about a krośa away, near his hermitage,

singing sweetly and melodiously, plucking her lute. / Beholding her singing thus, adorned with flowers and sandalwood,

even Kāma, eager for victory over the lords of sages devoted to Śiva, / that son of the mind took up residence in her body.

Making her two eyebrows the curved ends of his bow, her sidelong glance the bowstring, / and making her two eyes with their eyelashes the arrows in due order,

Making her breasts his tent, he set forth for victory; / Mañjughoṣā became the very army of that Kāma.

Seeing the sage Medhāvin, she too was afflicted with desire; / Medhāvin, whose body was bursting with youth, shone brightly.

Endowed with a white sacred thread, he looked like a second god of love. / Medhāvin was living in the auspicious hermitage of Cyavana.

Seeing that best of sages dwelling there, Mañjughoṣā / fell under the sway of love and began to sing very softly.

text_mt:
Seeing her singing in such a manner, adorned with jingling bangles / and a tinkling girdle with anklets, that bull among sages,

led forcibly into the power of infatuation by Kāma along with his army, [succumbed]. / Mañjughoṣā approached, and seeing the sage in such a state,

the woman fascinated him with gestures, expressions, and sidelong glances; / setting down her lute, she embraced that lord of sages.

Like a creeper entwining a tree shaken by the force of the wind, / he, Medhāvin, the best of sages, sported with her.

Seeing her excellent body right there, / his knowledge of the truth of Śiva vanished, and he fell under the sway of the principle of desire.

Sporting with her, the lustful sage knew neither night nor day; / much time passed while the sage’s conduct fell into neglect.

Mañjughoṣā prepared to go to the heavenly world. / As she was leaving, she said to the best of sages while he was dallying: / 'Give permission, O brāhmaṇa, for my departure to my own land.'

Medhāvin said: / 'You have arrived only today at twilight, O fair-faced one; / stay near me until the morning twilight.' / Hearing these words of the sage, she became filled with fear.

text_mt:
Afraid of the sage's curse, O best of kings, / she made love again with that ṛṣi for many years.

For fifty-five years, nine months, and three days / she dallied with the sage, and to him it seemed like only half a night.

When that time had passed, she spoke again to the sage: / 'Give permission, O brāhmaṇa; I must go to my own home.'

Medhāvin said: / 'It is morning now, so listen to my word; / remain steadfast, indeed, as long as I perform the twilight devotion.'

Hearing this statement of the sage, overwhelmed with joy,
smiling slightly, she of pure smiles replied.

The apsaras said: / 'O lord of brāhmaṇas, O sinless one, how long has your twilight devotion lasted? / Show favor to me and consider the time that has passed!'

Hearing her words, his eyes wide with astonishment,
the best of brahmins then took the measure of the time that had passed.

Fifty-seven years had passed with her. / Then he became angry with her, becoming like a wreath of flames.

Emitting sparks from his eyes, exceedingly furious, / seeing her as the embodiment of death who had destroyed his ascetic heat,

Seeing that the ascetic heat earned with hardship was destroyed with her, / the sage, trembling-lipped and his senses agitated, replied there.

Medhāvin then cursed her: 'Become a female goblin! / Fie on you, wicked, ill-behaved, unchaste woman, fond of sin!'

Burned by his curse, bowed low with humility, / that fair-browed one spoke words to the sage, seeking his grace: / 'Show favor, O lord among brāhmaṇas; grant mitigation of the curse!

Friendship with the virtuous is formed by seven words and steps; / O brāhmaṇa, I have spent many years with you! / For this reason, O master, O observer of good vows, show favor!'

The sage said: / 'Listen to my word, O blessed woman, which grants mitigation of the curse: / What can I do, O sinful one, since my great ascetic heat was brought to ruin by you?

In the dark fortnight of Caitra, there is the auspicious Ekādaśī / named Pāpamocanikā, which destroys all sins.

When its observance is kept, O radiant one, your state as a goblin will depart.' / Having said this, Medhāvin went to his father’s hermitage.

Seeing him arrive, Cyavana said to him: / 'What is this that you have done, son? You have destroyed your merit!'

text_mt:
Medhāvin said: / 'Father, a great sin has indeed been committed by me, and an apsaras was enjoyed; / tell me an expiation, father, by which my sin may be destroyed.'

Cyavana said: / 'In the dark fortnight of Caitra, there is indeed the one named Pāpamocanī; / when its observance is performed, O son, the mass of sin will be destroyed.'

Hearing the words of his father, he performed that excellent vow;
his sin went to destruction, and he became endowed with ascetic power.

Mañjughoṣā too, having performed this best of vows, / was completely freed from goblin-hood by the Pāpamocanikā vow; / assuming a divine form, that excellent apsaras went to heaven.

Lomaśa said: / 'O king, the best among men who observe Pāpamocanikā— / whatever sin is theirs, all of that comes to an end.

By reading or hearing [of it], O king, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows: / the killer of a brāhmaṇa, the stealer of gold, the drinker of liquor, and the violator of the guru's bed—

By performing this vow, they are freed from sin; / for this best of vows yields great merit when performed.'

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, named "Pāpamocanī Ekādaśī of the Dark Fortnight of Caitra," in the conversation between the husband of Umā and Nārada, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the compilation of fifty-five thousand [verses].

title: saptacatvāriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / 'O Vāsudeva, obeisance to you! Tell me before me: / In the bright fortnight of Caitra, what is the name of the Ekādaśī?'
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: / 'Listen with one mind, O king, to an ancient, holy story / which Vasiṣṭha formerly told to Dilīpa when he questioned him.'
Dilīpa said: / 'O lord, I wish to hear; please tell me out of favor: / In the month of Caitra, in the bright fortnight, what is the name of the Ekādaśī?'
Vasiṣṭha said: / 'You have asked well, O king! I shall tell it before you: / In the bright fortnight of Caitra, it is known by name as Kāmadā.
It is the most sacred Ekādaśī, a forest fire to the fuel of sins; / hear, O king, this story that destroys sins and bestows merit.
Formerly, in the delightful city of Nāgapura adorned with gold and jewels, / very fierce nāgas, headed by Puṇḍarīka, dwelt.
In that city, Puṇḍarīka ruled as king; / he was served by gandharvas, kinnaras, and apsarases.
The excellent apsaras Lalitā and the gandharva Lalita, / both impassioned with love, were a married couple smitten with desire.
They dallied then in their delightful home filled with wealth and grain; / in Lalitā's heart her husband dwelt at all times,
and in his heart the passionate woman Lalitā dwelt constantly. / Then, once upon a time, Puṇḍarīka was sporting while seated in the assembly;
Lalita was singing songs without his beloved; / his tongue stumbled over the metrical meter as he remembered Lalitā.
Understanding the feeling of his mind, Karkaṭa, the best of nāgas, / reported to Puṇḍarīka that lapse in his metrical cadence.
Hearing Karkoṭaka's words, Puṇḍarīka, the king of serpents, / his eyes red with anger, became exceedingly terrifying.
He cursed Lalita who was singing there, smitten with love: / 'Become a rākṣasa, O wicked-minded one, a carnivore and an eater of men!
Since you sang before me while under the influence of your wife!' / By his word, O lord of kings, he assumed the form of a rakṣas.
With a dreadful face, deformed eyes, terrifying merely at sight, / his arms extended a yojana wide, his mouth like a mountain cavern,
his two eyes like the moon and the sun, his neck like a mountain, / his nostrils two chasms, his lips stretching a yojana,
and his body, O king of kings, standing eight yojanas high. / Having become such a rākṣasa, he experienced the fruit of his deed.
Lalitā, however, seeing her husband thus deformed in shape, / pondered in her mind, tormented by great sorrow:
“What shall I do? Where shall I go? My husband is afflicted by a curse.” / Reflecting on this again and again, she found no peace in her mind.
Lalitā wandered with her husband in the dense forest; / that rākṣasa, changing his form at will, roamed in the impassable woods.
Pitiless, devoted to sin, deformed, a devourer of men, / afflicted by sin, he found no happiness by night or by day.
Lalitā, exceedingly sorrowful seeing her husband in such a state, / roamed with him, weeping, in the dense forest.
Seeing a charming hermitage and a sage of tranquil form, / Lalitā went swiftly, bowed down, and stood before him.
Seeing her distressed, that sage, full of compassion, said: / “Who are you? Why have you come here? Speak the truth before me.”
Lalitā said: / “There is a Gandharva named Vīradhanvan; know me to be the daughter of that great soul, / named Lalitā, who have come here on account of my husband.
By fault of sin my husband has become a rākṣasa, O great sage, / dreadful in form, of vile conduct; seeing him, I have no happiness.
Now instruct me, O brahmin; tell me what must be done, O lord.” / [The sage said:] “Perform that vow according to rule, O auspicious one, which is spoken by me.”
The sage said: / “It is now the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, O woman with thighs like plantain stems; / there is the supreme Ekādaśī named Kāmadā, which destroys sin, O Lalitā.
Perform that vow, O auspicious one, according to rule as spoken by me; / whatever merit comes from this vow, let it be given to your husband.
When the merit is given, the fault of his curse will vanish in an instant.” / Having heard the sage’s words, Lalitā was filled with joy.
Having fasted on the Ekādaśī, O king, on the day of Dvādaśī, / right near the brahmin and before Vāsudeva,
Lalitā spoke these words for the deliverance of her husband: / “By me that vow of fasting on Kāmadā was indeed observed;
by the power of its merit, let his state of being a piśāca depart!” / Merely upon Lalitā’s words, even as he was there in that instant,
Lalita, freed from sin, came to possess a divine body; / his state of being a rākṣasa departed, and he attained his Gandharva nature again.
Adorned with gold and gems, he sported with Lalitā; / mounted upon an excellent aerial chariot, they were even more beautiful than their former forms.
The couple shone exceedingly through the power of Kāmadā. / Knowing this, O best of kings, this [vow] must be performed with exertion.
It has been related by me before you for the welfare of the worlds; / it destroys sins such as brahmin-killing and abolishes the state of being a piśāca.
There is nothing superior to this in the three worlds of the moving and unmoving; / from reciting or hearing it, O king, one obtains the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice.

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, named "Kāmadā of the Bright Fortnight of Caitra," in the conversation between the husband of Umā and Nārada, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the compilation of fifty-five thousand [verses].

title: ekonapañcāśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
Yudhiṣṭhira said: / “In the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, what is the name of the Ekādaśī? / Tell me its greatness, O Vāsudeva; homage to you!”

Yudhiṣṭhira said: / “In the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, what is the name of the Ekādaśī? / What is the fruit, what is the rule there? Tell me, O Janārdana!”

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Long ago, O king of kings, the wise Rāmacandra asked this very same question / to Vasiṣṭha, which you are now asking me.

Rāma said:
Lord, I wish to hear about the best vow among vows, / which destroys all sins and removes all sorrow.
I have experienced sorrows born of separation from Sītā; / therefore, filled with fear, I ask you, O great sage.

Vasiṣṭha said:
Well asked by you, O Rāma! Such is your resolute intellect; / merely by uttering your name a mortal becomes purified.
Nevertheless, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, I shall describe / the pure among purifying things, the highest vow among vows.
In the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, O Rāma, there is an Ekādaśī; / it is celebrated by the name Mohinī, supreme, removing all sins.
People are released from the net of delusion and from heaps of sins / by the power of its vow; truly, truly do I say this.
For this reason, O Rāma, it ought to be observed by those like you; / it destroys sins and eradicates great sorrow.
Listen with focused mind, O Rāma, to the supreme tale that takes away sins, / by the mere hearing of which great sin is destroyed.
On the delightful bank of the Sarasvatī was the auspicious city of Bhadrāvatī; / there a king named Dyutimān indeed ruled the kingdom.
Born in the lunar lineage, steadfast, true to his word; / in that city lived a vaiśya, wealthy and prosperous in grain,
known as Dhanapāla, a promoter of meritorious deeds, / a builder of water booths, wells, monasteries, gardens, ponds, and rest-houses.
Devoted to Viṣṇu, peaceful, he had five sons: / Sumanas, Dyutimān, Medhāvin, Sukṛta,
and the fifth was Dhṛṣṭabuddhi, ever engaged in great sin, / constantly attached to the company of others' wives, an expert in gatherings of rogues.
Addicted to vices like gambling, craving intercourse with others' wives, / he had no thought for worshiping the gods, nor towards the ancestors, nor towards the twice-born.
Unjust in conduct, wicked-minded, squandering his father's wealth, / an eater of forbidden food, sinful, constantly engaged in drinking liquor;
with his arm around a harlot's neck, wandering vilely at crossroads, / he was cast out of the house by his father and abandoned by his relatives.
The ornaments of his own body were utterly brought to ruin by him; / he was abandoned by courtesans and reviled due to the loss of his wealth.
Then he became overcome with worry, stripped of clothes, tormented by hunger: / “What shall I do? Where shall I go? By what means can I survive?”
He took up thievery right in that city of his father; / he was seized by the king's men and released out of respect for his father.
Bound again, released again, bound again in haste; / the ill-behaved Dhṛṣṭabuddhi was bound fast with tight fetters,
struck with whip-lashes, and tormented repeatedly. / [The king said:] “O dull-witted one, you must not stay within the domain of my realm!”
Having spoken thus, he was released by the king from the firm bond; / out of fear of him, he departed and went to the dense forest.
Tormented by hunger and thirst, he ran hither and thither; / like a lion, he slew deer, boars, and spotted antelopes.
Constantly staying in the forest, intent on eating meat, / holding a bow in hand with a quiver attached to his back,
moving on foot, he killed the creatures that roam the forest and birds: / cakoras, peacocks, herons, partridges, and mice.
Blinded, the pitiless Dhṛṣṭabuddhi destroyed these and others; / sunk in the mire of sin due to sins committed in previous lives,
filled with sorrow and grief, tormented day and night, / he once reached the hermitage of Kauṇḍinya through the advent of merit.
In the month of Mādhava, afflicted by a burden of grief, / Dhṛṣṭabuddhi approached the ascetic who had bathed in the Gaṅgā.
By contact with drops of water from his garment, his sins departed and bad fortune was destroyed; / standing before Kauṇḍinya, he spoke with folded hands.

Dhṛṣṭabuddhi said:
O holy one, O best of the twice-born, have compassion on me; / tell me that through whose meritorious power liberation comes about.

Kauṇḍinya said:
Listen with an attentive mind to that by which your sin will be destroyed; / in the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha is the celebrated one named Mohinī.
Observe the vow of that Ekādaśī, urged by my word; / sins equal to Mount Meru meet destruction for embodied beings,
accumulated over many lifetimes, by those who fast on Mohinī. / Having heard this word of the sage, Dhṛṣṭabuddhi, with a gladdened heart,
performed the vow according to the rules, following Kauṇḍinya's instruction; / when the vow was performed, O best of kings, he became freed from sin.
Attaining a divine body, mounted upon Garuḍa, / he then went to the realm of Viṣṇu, free of all afflictions.
Such, O Rāmacandra, is the supreme vow of Mohinī; / there is nothing higher than this in the three worlds, movable and immovable.
Sacrifices, pilgrimages, and gifts do not equal a sixteenth part of it; / from reciting or hearing it, O king, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.

title: pañcāśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What Ekādaśī is there in the dark fortnight of Jyeṣṭha? / I wish to hear its glorification; tell that, O Janārdana.

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Well asked by you, O king, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds! / It indeed bestows much merit and destroys great sins.
It is named Aparā, O king of kings, boundless and granting sons; / whoever observes Aparā attains renown in the world.
Even one tainted by the murder of a brahmin, a slayer of his kinsman, a slayer of an embryo, / a slanderer of others, or one who takes pleasure in others' wives—
by observing Aparā, O king, he surely becomes free from sin. / One who gives false testimony, uses false measures, or cheats with the scale,
one who recites a fraudulent Veda, and likewise a fraudulent treatise, / a fraudulent astrologer, a fraudulent reckoner, or a fraudulent physician reciting the Veda,
joined with false testimony, should be recognized as an inhabitant of hell; / by observing Aparā, O king, they become liberated from sins.
A kṣatriya who abandons the duty of a kṣatriya and flees from battle / goes to a terrible hell, cast out from his own dharma;
by observing Aparā, he too, abandoning sin, goes to heaven. / Even an educated disciple who reviles his guru,
bound by great sins, goes to a frightful hell; / by observing Aparā, even that man attains a good state.
Hear the majesty of Aparā, O king, as I describe it: / the fruit men obtain at Prayāga when the sun is in Capricorn during Māgha,
the merit that is gained in Kāśī by bathing during an eclipse, / or the satisfaction given to the ancestors by offering the funerary ball at Gayā,
a man bathed in the Gautamī when the guru of the gods is in Leo, / or by plunging into the Kṛṣṇaveṇī when Jupiter is in Virgo, O king,
the fruit one obtains by beholding Kedāra during Kumbha, / or by journeying to the hermitage of Badarī and resorting to that sacred ford,
the fruit one obtains at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse / by giving gifts of elephants, horses, and gold, and performing a sacrifice with sacrificial fees—
Such fruit one obtains from observing the vow of Aparā. / Giving a cow half in birth, gold, and also land,
that fruit which a man obtains, he obtains through the vow of Aparā. / It is an axe to the tree of sin, a forest fire to the firewood of sin,
a sun to the darkness of sin, a lion to the deer of sin. / Like bubbles in water, like ants among living creatures,
they are born only to die, without the vow of Ekādaśī. / Having fasted on Aparā and worshipped Trivikrama,

freed from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. / For the welfare of the worlds, this was told by me before you; / from reading and hearing it, O king, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.

title: ekapañcāśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / All the glorification of Aparā has been heard, O Janārdana. / Tell me of that which falls in the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, O giver of honor.

The Blessed Kṛṣṇa said: / The righteous Vyāsa, son of Satyavatī, will speak of this— / he who knows the truth of the meaning of all treatises, who has crossed to the further shore of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: / The duties taught by Manu have been heard by me, and the duties taught by Vasiṣṭha have been heard by me. / O Dvaipāyana, you ought to speak properly of the Vaiṣṇava [duties].
The Blessed Vedavyāsa said: / The duties taught by Manu have been heard, and the Vedic duties have been heard by you; / but in the Kali age, they cannot be performed, O lord of men.
An easy means, of little expense, of little hardship, yielding great fruit, / and the very essence of all the Purāṇas, O great-minded one:
one should not eat on Ekādaśī in both fortnights. / Having become pure on Dvādaśī, having worshipped Keśava with flowers,
having shown hospitality, one should then eat food preceded by [feeding] brāhmaṇas. / One should not eat even in childbirth-impurity, nor in death-impurity, O lord of people.
Throughout life, this vow must be performed, O bull among men, / by those desiring to attain the heavenly path; of this there is no doubt.
Great sinners, evil-doers, the most wicked, devoid of dharma, / not eating on Ekādaśī, do not go into the presence of Yama.
Hearing those words of his, trembling like a leaf of the sacred fig tree, / the mighty-armed Bhīmasena bowed and spoke to the guru:
Bhīmasena said: / O grandfather of great intellect, hear my supreme word. / Yudhiṣṭhira, Kuntī, and also the daughter of Drupada,
Arjuna, Nakula, and also Sahadeva— / they never eat on Ekādaśī, being observers of good vows.
They always say to me indeed: 'Do not eat, O Vṛkodara!' / I tell them, O father: 'My hunger is unbearable.
I will give gifts according to rule, I will worship Keśava.' / Hearing Bhīmasena's words, Vyāsa spoke [this] word:
Vyāsa said: / If heaven is desired by you, and [to avoid] hell which is indeed terrible, / one must not eat on Ekādaśī in both fortnights.
Bhīmasena said: / O grandfather of great intellect, I speak before you: / I am able [only] with a single meal; how could there be fasting, O lord?
The fire named Vṛka is always in my belly; / only when I eat excessively does it subside.

I am not able to observe even a single fast, O great sage. / By whatever means heaven is attained, that I will do properly; / tell that one [vow] with certainty, by which I may attain the highest good.
Vyāsa said: / When Ekādaśī occurs while [the sun] is in Taurus or in Gemini / in the month of Jyeṣṭha, it should be fasted with effort, free from water.
Except for water for rinsing the mouth and sipping, a wise person / should not consume water at all here; otherwise, there would be a breach of the vow.
A man abstaining from water from sunrise to sunrise— / listen!—obtains the fruit of twelve Dvādaśīs.
Then, in the clear morning on Dvādaśī, he should take a bath, / and having given water and gold to the twice-born according to rule,
self-controlled, having accomplished his duty, he should eat together with brāhmaṇas. / And when this is done, hear the merit of that, O Bhīmasena:
Whatever Ekādaśīs occur indeed in the year, / he obtains the fruit of all of them; here there is no doubt in my mind.
“Thus Keśava, bearer of the conch, discus, and mace, spoke to me: / ‘Abandoning everything, a man should take refuge in me alone.’”
Without food on Ekādaśī, he is then freed from sin. / There is no purity of substances in the Kali age, nor traditional purificatory rites;
how could there even be Vedic [rites] when the corrupt Kali age has arrived? / What need to say much to you again and again, O son of Vāyu?
One should not eat on Ekādaśī in both fortnights. / On the Ekādaśī in the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha, without water,
the meritorious fruit one obtains, hear that, O Vṛkodara: / whatever [Ekādaśīs] in a year are spoken of, bright and dark, O Vṛkodara,
all those Ekādaśīs indeed become fasted; of this there is no doubt. / Bestowing wealth and grain, holy, granting sons, health, and auspiciousness,
it is fasted, O tiger among men; thus I speak truth to you. / The messengers of Yama, huge-bodied, terrifying, dark in form,
bearing staff and noose, dread, do not approach that man. / Wearing yellow garments, gentle, with discuses in hand, swift as thought,
these lead Vaiṣṇavas to the city of Viṣṇu at the time of death. / Therefore, with all effort, [it is] to be fasted without water.
Giving a water-cow at that time, he is freed from all sins. / Therefore you, on this [day], O son of Kuntī, fasting, worshipping Hari,
act with all effort for the pacification of all sins. / 'Whether in sleep, may there be no offense by me, or through [food] entering my teeth;
I will eat food on the next day, O lord of gods, on the day of Hari.' / Uttering this mantra, one should then be intent on fasting,
for the destruction of all sins, endowed with faith and self-control. / Whatever sin as huge as Mount Meru or Mandara has been committed by a woman or man,
all that goes to ashes through the power of Ekādaśī. / Those who are unable to give a water-cow, O lord of men,
a water-pot with gold and cloth should be given. / Whoever undertakes the restriction of water on this [day] shares in merit.
The fruit of ten million [measures] of gold in every watch is heard as the fruit. / Bathing, giving, recitation of mantras, and offering oblations which a man performs on this [day]—
all that becomes imperishable; this was declared by Kṛṣṇa. / What need of any other dharma, without Nirjalā Ekādaśī?
Fasting properly according to rule, one attains the state of Viṣṇu. / Gold, food, or garment, whatever is given on this [day],
all that of his, O tiger of the Kurus, becomes imperishable. / He who eats food on the day of Ekādaśī eats sin;
in this world he is an outcaste, and dead, he meets an evil destiny. / And those who give gifts on Dvādaśī, having fasted,
in the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, will attain the supreme state. / The killer of a brāhmaṇa, a drinker of liquor, a thief, one who hates the guru, one who is always untruthful—
they are freed from all sins, having fasted on Nirjalā. / Hear the special duty, O son of Kuntī, on the day of Nirjalā Ekādaśī,
which is to be performed by men and women endowed with faith as a gift: / the One who reclines on the waters is to be worshipped, and a cow made of water is to be given.
Or an actual cow, O best of kings, or a cow made of ghee, / with well-nourished priestly fees and various kinds of sweet foods,
the twice-born should be zealously pleased, O best of upholders of dharma. / When the brahmins are pleased, Hari, the bestower of liberation, is indeed pleased through them.
Indeed, treason against oneself was committed by those by whom this [vow] was not observed; / they are sinful, ill-behaved, and robbed—there is no doubt of this.
A hundred future generations and likewise a hundred past generations / are brought along with themselves to the abode of Vāsudeva
by those who are peaceful, self-controlled, devoted to charity, and worshipping Hari, / keeping a vigil through the night, by whom this [vow] is observed.
Food, clothing, cows, water, a bed, an auspicious seat, / a water pot, and an umbrella should be given on the day without water.
Whoever gives a pair of shoes to an eminent, worthy twice-born / is honored in the heavenly realm upon a golden chariot.
Whoever hears this with devotion and whoever proclaims it— / both of them attain heaven; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Whatever fruit a mortal obtains by performing an ancestral rite at Saṃnihitā / when the sun is seized by Rāhu, he obtains that even from hearing this.
And the vow should be undertaken after first cleansing one’s teeth: / 'On the eleventh day, fasting, I shall certainly abstain from water,
for the sake of pleasing Keśava, with no other [water] except for sipping.' / On the twelfth day, Trivikrama, the lord of the gods, should be worshipped
with perfumes, incense, flowers, and lovely garments; / having worshipped according to the rules, one should utter this mantra:
'O god of gods, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O savior from the ocean of worldly existence, / lead me to the supreme goal by this gift of a water-jar.'
Indeed, in the month of Jyeṣṭha, O Bhīma, the bright eleventh day is auspicious; / having fasted without water on it, [and] water-jars with sugar
having given to the foremost brahmins, one rejoices in the presence of Viṣṇu. / Then water-jars should be given to brahmins with devotion;
having fed the brahmins, one should then eat oneself, fully devoted. / Whoever thus fulfills the sin-destroying twelfth day

is freed from all sins and goes to the sorrowless abode. / From that time onward, this auspicious eleventh day was observed by Bhīma; / it indeed became known in the world by the name Pāṇḍava-dvādaśī.

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, named the Nirjalā Ekādaśī of the bright half of Jyeṣṭha, in the dialogue between the Lord of Umā and Nārada, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand [verses].

title: dvipañcāśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / In the dark fortnight of Āṣāḍha, which eleventh day indeed occurs? / Please tell me by your grace, O Vāsudeva, in my presence.
The blessed Kṛṣṇa said: / O king, I shall tell you the foremost of vows, / which destroys all sins and bestows all liberation.
In the dark fortnight of Āṣāḍha is the eleventh day named Yoginī, / O best of kings, which destroys great sins,
serving as an eternal boat for those drowned in the ocean of worldly existence, / the essential substance in the three worlds for those who perform the Yoginī vow.
I shall tell you an auspicious puranic tale: / In Alakā was the king of kings [Kubera], devoted to the worship of Śiva.
He had a flower-gathering page named Hemamālin. / His wife was beautiful and named Viśālākṣī.
His mind was attached to her, falling under the sway of love's snare. / Having brought a collection of lotuses from Lake Mānasa, he stayed in his own house.
Clinging to the sweet nectar of love for his wife, he did not go to Kubera’s dwelling. / Kubera was performing the worship of Śiva in the temple of the god.
At noon, O king, while [Kubera was] waiting for the arrival of the flowers, / Hemamālin was sporting with his beloved in his own house.
Then the king of the yakṣas, angered by the passing of the appointed time, said: / 'Why does the wicked Hemamālin not come, O yakṣas? / Ascertain this!' he said again and again.
The yakṣas said: / 'Desiring his woman, he sports in his home as he pleases, O king.' / Hearing their words, Kubera was filled with rage.
He quickly summoned the servant Hemamālin. / Realizing the delay of time, his eyes agitated with fear,
he came without even bathing and stood before Kubera. / Seeing him, the giver of wealth [Kubera] was enraged, his eyes reddened with fury.
Overcome with anger, his lip trembling with rage, he replied. / Dhanada said: / 'Ah, sinful, wicked, ill-behaved one, you have shown contempt for the god!
Stricken with the eighteen kinds of leprosy, separated from that beloved woman, / fallen from this place, go now to a wretched state, vile one!'
When those words were spoken, he fell down from that spot, / overcome by immense misery, his body afflicted with leprosy.
He had no comfort by day and found no sleep at night; / his body was tormented in the shade and exceedingly tormented in the heat of summer.
By the power of his worship of Śiva, his memory was not lost; / though overwhelmed by his sin, he remembered his past deeds.
Wandering about, he then went to Himādri, the best of mountains; / there he saw the eminent sage Mārkaṇḍeya, a treasure of asceticism,
whose lifespan, O king, was equal to the age of Brahmā. / The doer of evil deeds saluted his feet from afar.
Seeing him trembling thus, Mārkaṇḍeya, the best of sages, / summoned him for the sake of helping others, and spoke this:
'Why are you stricken with leprosy? Why are you utterly blameworthy?' / Thus addressed, he replied to the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya.
Hemamālin said: / 'I am an attendant of the king of kings, named Hemamālin. / Having fetched a collection of lotuses daily from Lake Mānasa, O sage,
I offer them to Kubera at the time of Śiva’s worship. / On one day, the time went unnoticed by me,
as I was attached to the pleasure of my wife, my mind agitated by grief. / Then, O sage, I was cursed by the angered king of kings.
I became stricken with leprosy and separated from that beloved woman. / Now, through some meritorious deed, I have come into your presence.
By nature, the mind of the virtuous is capable of helping others. / Knowing this, O best of sages, instruct me, who have committed an offense.'
Mārkaṇḍeya said: / 'Since you have spoken truth here and have not uttered untruth, / therefore I shall tell you the instruction on a vow that brings auspiciousness.
Observe the Yoginī vow in the dark fortnight of Āṣāḍha; / by the religious merit of this vow, your leprosy will surely disappear.'
Hearing the words of the sage, he fell like a staff upon the ground; / raised up by the sage, he became exceedingly joyful.
When the vow was performed by him as instructed by Mārkaṇḍeya, / his eighteen leprosies vanished completely.
By the word of the sage, when the vow was properly observed, he became happy. / In this manner, O best of kings, the Yoginī vow has been narrated.
The man who performs the Yoginī vow / obtains a fruit equal to that of one who feeds eighty-eight thousand twice-born.
It pacifies great sins and bestows the fruit of great religious merit; / from reading it and hearing it, a mortal is freed from all sins.

Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, named the Glorification of the Yoginī Ekādaśī of the dark half of Āṣāḍha, in the dialogue between the Lord of Umā and Nārada, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand [verses].

title: tripañcāśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Which ekādaśī occurs in the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha? / What is its name, and what is its rite? Tell this in detail.

Lord Kṛṣṇa said:
I will tell [you] of the supremely meritorious [ekādaśī], bestower of heaven and liberation, / named Śayanī, supreme, remover of all sins,
merely by hearing of which one obtains the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice. / Truly, truly have I declared: there is nothing higher than this for human beings.
It was created by the Creator for the destruction of sinners' sins, most exalted; / beyond this, O king of kings, there is none other that grants liberation.
For this reason, O king, let it be heard; the highest destination / shall be attained by men who listen even to the hearing of this tale.
They are ever Vaiṣṇavas, O king, wholly devoted to my bhakti. / In Āṣāḍha, indeed, the Supreme Lord Vāmana is worshipped.
By whoever Vāmana, the lotus-eyed, is worshipped with lotuses / in the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha on the day of Kāmikā,
by him the entire universe and the three eternal gods are worshipped, / and by him the ekādaśī, the highest day of Hari, has been observed.

Yudhiṣṭhira said:
I have a great doubt in this matter; listen, O Puruṣottama: / How did you fall asleep, O Lord of gods, and how did you take refuge with Bali?
And how did you lie down upon the earth? What do other people do? / Tell me this, O greatly wise one; I have a great doubt.

Lord Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O tiger among kings, to the supreme tale that removes sin, / merely by hearing of which the destruction of all sins occurs.
Formerly in the Tretā age, O king, there was a daitya named Bali, / who constantly worshipped me, devoted to me, intent upon me.
With sacrifices according to rule, the daitya worshipped me, the eternal one, / and with supreme devotion, O king, he was an agent of sacrifices and performer of vows.
Having deliberated at length with Indra and with hymns of praise, / and together with the preceptor and the gods, I was worshipped in many ways.
Then, in the form of Vāmana, in my fifth incarnation, / assuming a most formidable form, embodying the entire universe,
the daityas were overcome through a trick of speech, while he stood firm relying on truth. / Śukra warned him, saying, 'This is Nārāyaṇa.'
Land measuring three and a half strides was begged by me, O king; / and as soon as the water of solemn resolve was placed in [my] hand by him,
hear, O king, the kind of form I assumed then: / placing the feet on the earth-world, and the knees on the atmospheric world;
placing the waist on the heavenly world, and the belly likewise on Maharloka; / the heart on Janaloka, and the neck on Tapoloka;
establishing the face on Satyaloka, and the head above it. / The moon, the sun, the planets, and likewise the lunar mansions,
the gods with Indra, the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras / praised [me] with various hymns born from the Vedas.
Taking Bali by the hand, the earth was encompassed in three strides, / and then half a stride was placed by me upon his back.
The dānava, my worshipper, went to the underworld, O king. / The dānava was cast below; what did they do after that?
Bent with humility, he [pleased] Janārdana, who became exceedingly gracious. / In the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha is the Kāmikā day of Hari.
One form of mine stands relying on Bali; / a second [reclines] upon the back of Śeṣa in the midst of the ocean of milk.
He sleeps in this way, O great king, until the coming Kārtikī. / Until then, one should become truly righteous, foremost among all performers of dharma.
And a mortal who performs this vow goes to the supreme state. / For this reason, O king, it should be observed with diligent effort.
There is nothing higher than this, purifying and destroying sins, / on which the Lord of the gods, bearer of the conch, discus, and mace, sleeps.
And on that day one should worship the god bearing the conch, discus, and mace, / keeping an all-night vigil, and doing so especially with devotion.
Even the four-faced [Brahmā] is unable to calculate its merit. / The person who thus observes the supreme vow of the eleventh day, O king,
which removes all sins and bestows enjoyment and liberation, / is ever dear to me in this world, even if he be a dog-cooker.
Those who spend the four months here by offering lamps, / eating from leaves of the palāśa tree, and observing vows, are dear to me.
During the four months, while Hari is asleep, a person should sleep on the bare ground. / In Śrāvaṇa one should avoid greens, and likewise curd in Bhādrapada.
Milk is to be abandoned in Āśvayuja, and pulses must be abandoned in Kārtika; / or, remaining steadfast in celibacy, he goes to the supreme state.
Only by the vow of the eleventh day is a man freed from sins. / It must always be performed, O king, and never forgotten.
Whatever dark eleventh day falls between the sleeping one and the waking one, / that alone should be fasted on by a householder, no other dark [eleventh day] ever.
And whatever man listens, O king, to this supreme tale that takes away sins, / he obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice.

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, named the Devaśayanī Ekādaśī, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, a compendium of fifty-five thousand [verses].

title: catuṣpañcāśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / What is the name of the eleventh day in the bright half of Śrāvaṇa? / Tell that to us, O Govinda, O Vāsudeva! Praise be to you!
The venerable Kṛṣṇa said: / Listen, O king; I will tell you the sin-destroying account / which was formerly spoken by Brahmā to Nārada when he inquired.
Nārada said: / O Blessed One, born on the lotus, I desire to hear from you: / What is the name of the eleventh day in the dark half of Śrāvaṇa?
Who is its deity, what is its procedure, and what is its merit? Tell me, O Lord! / Hearing his words, Brahmā spoke these words.
Brahmā said: / Listen, O Nārada; wishing for the welfare of the worlds, I tell you: / The dark eleventh day of Śrāvaṇa is celebrated by the name of Kāmikā.
Merely by hearing of it, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice. / On it, whoever worships the Lord of gods, bearer of the conch, discus, and mace,
Hari, Viṣṇu, Mādhava, Madhusūdana, named Śrīdhara— / whoever indeed worships and meditates on him, hear his meritorious fruit:
Neither at the Gaṅgā, nor in Kāśī, nor in Naimiṣa, nor in Puṣkara / does one obtain that fruit which is obtained from the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
Whatever fruit one obtains at the Godāvarī when Jupiter is in Leo, at Vyatīpāta, and in Daṇḍaka, / that fruit one obtains from the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
One who gives the earth together with its oceans and forests, / and one who performs the vow of Kāmikā—both are remembered as having equal fruit.
A man who gives a cow that is calving along with all its accessories / obtains that [same] fruit by performing the vow of Kāmikā.
Whatever best of men worships the god Śrīdhara in Śrāvaṇa, / by him alone are the gods, Gandharvas, Urugas, and Pannagas worshipped.
Therefore, on the day of Kāmikā, Hari must be worshipped with every effort / by mortals fearing sin, according to their ability.
For those who are sunk in the ocean of worldly existence filled with the mire of sin, / the excellent vow of Kāmikā exists for the sake of their deliverance.
There is nothing higher than this, purifying and removing sin; / know it thus, O Nārada: supreme Hari has said so himself.
Know that the fruit of those who practice the vow of Kāmikā / is far greater than what is obtained by men dedicated to the knowledge of the Supreme Self.
The man who performs the vow of Kāmikā, having kept an all-night vigil, / does not behold the terrible Yama, nor does he go to a miserable state.
Nor does he see an evil birth, because of observing the vow of Kāmikā. / When the vow of Kāmikā was observed, yogins attained isolation.
Therefore, it should be performed with every effort by those whose minds are restrained. / The man who worships Hari with leaves grown from the tulasī plant,
is not smeared with sin, just as a lotus leaf [is not smeared] with water. / A bhāra of gold and four times as much silver—
he attains that fruit from worship with a tulasī leaf. / Viṣṇu, worshipped with gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, corals, and the like,

is not so pleased as he is with a sprig of tulasī. / And one by whom Keśava has been worshipped with tulasī blossoms—

Who, when seen, pacifies the multitude of all sins; when touched, purifies the body; / when praised, drives away diseases; and when sprinkled [with water], terrifies Death:
when planted, brings about nearness to the blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa; / when laid at his feet, bestows the fruit of liberation—to that Tulasī, homage!
The mortal who gives a lamp day and night on the day of Hari— / Citragupta is not at all able to calculate his merit.
One whose lamp burns before Kṛṣṇa on the day of the eleventh, / his ancestors resting in heaven are satisfied with nectar.
Having lit a lamp with ghee or again with sesame oil, / he travels to the world of the sun, honored with hundreds of millions of lamps.
This glory of Kāmikā has been described by me before you; / therefore, it must be performed by men, taking away all fallen deeds,
removing the murder of a brahmin, destroying the killing of an embryo, / giving a place with Viṣṇu, and bestowing the fruit of great merit.
Having heard this glorification endowed with faith, a man / attains the world of Viṣṇu and is completely freed from all sins.

title: pañcapañcāśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / What is the name of the eleventh day in the bright half of Śrāvaṇa? / By your grace, speak before me, O Madhusūdana!
The venerable Kṛṣṇa said: / Listen attentively, O king, to the supreme tale that takes away sin, / merely by the hearing of which there is the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
In ancient times, at the beginning of the Dvāpara age, in the city of Māhiṣmatī, / a king named Mahījit was ruling his kingdom.
Because he was childless, that kingdom brought him no happiness. / For a sonless man there is no happiness, in this world or in the next.
Much time passed for him thus in anxiety over a son, / and a son, who gives all joy to men, was not obtained by the king.
Seeing himself advanced in years, the king became filled with worry. / Then, having gone into the midst of his subjects, he spoke these words:
'In this birth, O people, no wickedness has been done by me; / wealth acquired unjustly was not deposited in the treasury by me.

The property of brahmins or the wealth of gods was never taken by me anywhere; / no appropriation of another's trust, which produces great sin, was committed; / the subjects were protected like sons, and the earth was conquered through righteousness.'
'Punishment has been inflicted upon the wicked, even when equal to kinsmen or sons; / but the virtuous have ever been honoured, and no people are hated by me.'
“O best of the twice-born, while I profess such a righteous path, / why has no son been born in my house? Let that be considered!”
Hearing this speech, the twice-born, along with the subjects and the family priests, / took counsel for the king's welfare and went into the dense forest.
Looking here and there at the hermitages frequented by ṛṣis, / seeking the king's welfare, they saw an excellent sage,
performing severe penance, without support, free from ailment, / taking no food, self-controlled, having conquered anger, eternal,
Lomaśa, knower of the truth of dharma, skilled in all scriptures, / long-lived, great-souled, endowed with hair, equal to Brahmā.
With the passing of each kalpa, one hair of his falls out; / therefore this great sage, knower of the three divisions of time, is named Lomaśa.
Seeing him, all rejoiced and approached his presence; / according to rule and merit, they made their salutation as prescribed.

Bowed down with humility, they all said to one another: / 'Only through the power of our good fortune has this best of sages been found!' / Beholding them accompanied by the subjects, the best of ṛṣis spoke.

Lomaśa said:
For what purpose have you arrived here? Tell me the reason. / With glad minds from the sight [of me], why are you praising me?
Without doubt I shall do whatever brings you welfare. / The birth of people like me is for doing good to others, without doubt.

The people said:
Listen, we shall tell the reason for our coming; / we have come to your presence to cut off our doubt.
Other than the lotus-born [Brahmā], there is none superior to you or more exalted. / Therefore, driven by our task, we have approached your presence.
This king named Mahījit is at present without a son. / We are his subjects, O brāhmaṇa, protected by him like sons.
Seeing him bereft of a son, afflicted with sorrow through his sorrow, / we have come here to perform penance, having formed a firm resolve.
By his good fortune you have indeed been seen by us, O best of the twice-born; / solely by the sight of the great does success in undertakings occur for men.
Declare instruction, O sage, so that a son may be born to the king. / Hearing their words, the sage remained in meditation for a moment; / having known his former birth, the sage replied.

Lomaśa said:
In a former birth he was a vaiśya, devoid of wealth, a doer of cruel deeds, / intent on commercial activities, wandering from village to village.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, in the bright fortnight, on the tenth day, / when the sun had reached the middle of the sky, he arrived at a reservoir on the village boundary.
Seeing a small well containing water, he set his mind on drinking water. / Just then, a cow with her calf arrived there.
Afflicted by thirst, distressed by the summer heat, she drank water there; / driving away the drinking cow, he drank the water himself.
Through that sinful act, the king has become sonless; / through the merit of some birth, a kingdom free from thorns was obtained.

title: puṇyātpāpaṃkṣayaṃyātipurāṇeśrūyatemune
text_mt: Tell of meritorious instruction by which the destruction of sin may occur, / so that by your favour a son may be born to the lord of the earth.

Lomaśa said:
In the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, there is the famous ekādaśī / named Putradā, granting desires; perform that vow, O people!
Having heard this and bowed down to the sage, they went to the city and observed the vow / according to rule and according to right, accompanied by a vigil.
Its completely spotless merit was given to the king by the people; / the merit being given, that queen conceived a handsome child.
When the time of delivery arrived, she gave birth to a vigorous son. / In the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, when the sun stands in Cancer,
on the twelfth lunar day, the investiture with the sacred thread for Vāsudeva is prescribed: / with threads of gold, silver, copper, linen, silk, or lotus fibres,
with kuśa grass, kāśa grass, and auspicious cotton spun by a brāhmaṇa woman. / Having bathed, one should purify the triple-twisted thread by tripling it.
The preliminary consecration [takes place] on the previous day at the time interval of cow-milking. / Having bowed to the Brahmins and having saluted the feet of the guru,
one should then keep vigil amidst the auspicious sound of songs. / Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Bhillas, and likewise Śūdras,
all established in their own duty, should make the sacred thread with devotion. / Then one should offer the sacred thread to the guru according to the rules.
One should worship Brahmins and Vaiṣṇavas with perfumes, flowers, and the like. / A twice-born should offer it to Viṣṇu with the mantra beginning with ‘Ato devā’.
A Śūdra, however, [should offer it] with the root mantra; as unto Viṣṇu, so unto Śiva. / The investiture of the sacred thread must be performed year after year by men
who desire enjoyment and liberation in the ocean of sorrow of worldly existence. / But whoever does not perform the investiture of the sacred thread according to rule,

that Vaiṣṇava's annual worship is entirely fruitless. / Hearing the glorification of this, a man is freed from sin; / having obtained the happiness of sons in this world, he goes to heaven in the next.

Thus, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa, in the compendium of fifty-five thousand verses,

in the Uttarakhaṇḍa, in the dialogue between the husband of Umā and Nārada, the fifty-fifth chapter, named ‘The investiture of the sacred thread of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa and the Putradā Ekādaśī’.

title: saptapañcāśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / What, indeed, is the name of the Ekādaśī in the dark fortnight of Bhādra? / I wish to hear this; tell me, O Janārdana.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: / In the bright fortnight of Nabhasya, what would be the name of the Ekādaśī? / Which is the deity, what is its procedure? Tell this to me, O Keśava.

title: aṣṭa pañcāśattamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Nārada said: / Speak out of your grace, O Four-faced One, homage to you! / In the bright fortnight of Nabhasya, what would be the name of the Ekādaśī? / I wish to hear this for the sake of worshipping Viṣṇu.
I shall tell before you an auspicious, ancient tale, / by the mere hearing of which a great sin is destroyed.
It bestows enjoyment and liberation, and grants happiness to people; / from reading it and hearing it, O king, one is freed from all sins.

title: ekoniṣaṣṭitamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / "Tell me graciously, O Madhusūdana: / what is the name of the Ekādaśī in the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina?"

title: ṣaṣṭitamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
The king said: / "Explain to me graciously, O venerable one, the Indirā observance: / by what rite is it to be performed, and in which fortnight and lunar day?"

Yudhiṣṭhira said: / Speak out of grace, in front of me, O Madhusūdana: / In the bright fortnight of Iṣa, what is the name of the Ekādaśī?
The Blessed Kṛṣṇa said: / Let it be heard, O tiger among kings; I shall speak in your presence: / In the dark fortnight of Kārttika, there is the very beautiful Ramā,
declared to be an Ekādaśī that removes great sins, supreme. / In connection with this, O king, I shall tell you its glorification.
In ancient times there was a king known as Mucukunda; / he had friendship with the king of gods, O king,
and had friendship in every way with Yama, Varuṇa, / Kubera, and also Bibhīṣaṇa, O king.
A devotee of Viṣṇu, true to his word, he was an exalted king. / While he was thus ruling the kingdom with all thorns eradicated, O king,
there was born in his house a daughter, Candrabhāgā, the best of rivers [by name]; / and she was given in marriage to Śobhana, the son of Candrasena.
Once he came to his father-in-law's house, O king; / and the day of the Ekādaśī observance arrived, granting great merit.
When the day of the vow arrived, Candrabhāgā thought: / 'What will happen, O lord of gods? My husband is extremely weak;
he cannot endure hunger, and my father's command is severe: / when the tenth day arrives, his drum is beaten [announcing]:
"One must not eat, one must not eat, one must not eat on the day of Hari!"' / Hearing the sound of the drum, Śobhana said to his beloved:
'What should I do, my darling? Give me counsel, O fair-faced one!' / Candrabhāgā said: / 'In my father's house, O lord, no one may eat today;
even by elephants, horses, young elephants, and other animals / grass, grain, and water must not be consumed on the day of Hari.
How, then, could human beings eat on the day of Hari, my dear? / If you eat, my beloved, you will incur censure.
Reflecting thus in your mind, make your resolve very firm.' / Śobhana said: 'True is this word, my love; I will observe the fast.
Whatever is ordained by destiny will indeed happen.' / Having thus made a firm resolve, he undertook the observance for the vow.
With his body tormented by hunger, he became extremely distressed. / While he was pondering thus, the sun sank down the mountain.
That night brought increasing joy to Vaiṣṇava men / devoted to the worship of Hari, whose minds were attached to the vigil.
It brought great suffering to Śobhana, O tiger among kings; / at the hour of sunrise, Śobhana met his death.
The king had him cremated with woods fit for royalty; / Candrabhāgā did not burn her own body along with her husband.
Having performed his funeral rites, she remained in her father's home; / and Śobhana, O best of kings, by the power of the Ramā vow,
reached a delightful celestial city upon a peak of Mount Mandara, / unsurpassed, unassailable, endowed with countless virtues,
with mansions made of golden pillars, adorned with jewels and lapis lazuli, / crystal, of diverse shapes, and splendidly beautified.
Seated upon a throne, with an auspicious white parasol and fly-whisks, / crowned and wearing earrings, adorned with necklaces and armlets, / praised by gandharvas and attended by hosts of apsarases,
there Śobhana shines forth like a second king of kings. / A man renowned as Somaśarman lived in the city of Mucukunda;
wandering in the course of a pilgrimage, the brāhmaṇa saw him. / Recognising him as the king's son-in-law, he approached him.
