text_mt:
Having obtained devotion alone as nectar, sorrow does not arise again; / having attained the abode named Vaikuṇṭha, one rejoices in the presence of Viṣṇu.

Just as the swan leaves the water and constantly drinks milk, / so, abandoning other duties, one should take refuge in devotion to Viṣṇu.

Abandoning devotion to others, one should take refuge in devotion to Viṣṇu; / having tied up water with a cloth, how could an end be accomplished?

Having obtained a body, [action] without devotion is done as wasted toil. / Those people who teach duties without devotion to Viṣṇu / fall perpetually into a dreadful hell; there is no doubt in this.
Just as a fool wishes to cross the ocean with his two arms, / so does a man [wish to cross] the ocean of worldly existence without devotion to Viṣṇu.
And if they protect devotion to Viṣṇu, [yet] one is brought low by action, / [he is like] a destitute man full of longing who directs his desire toward Mount Meru.
Even so, O goddess, a longing is made by me for your devotion; / for in another birth that devotion of mine brings about [liberation].
Just as here a fire, though very small, burns up a vast forest, / even so is that devotion, [even if] performed by me merely to the size of an atom.
Devotion is heard by hundreds, and understood even by thousands; / yet among them, O queen of gods, only a single devotee is born.
Many kinds of people in the world will give advice to others; / but the man who personally practices it is seen [only] among millions.
Devotion is attained through worship; it is brought about through victory. / When such a disposition exists, O queen of gods, devotion is grasped by that alone.
Just as a descent into the ocean [or] sitting down for safety in a well [is accomplished], / so he whose inner disposition is [firm] grasps that devotion.
When a tree is watered at the root, the foliage is seen upon the branches; / from adoration alone, O goddess, the fruit is established in front.
Just as a water-bearer fixes her mind upon the water-pot, / so, having fixed the mind upon the god Hari, one would attain liberation.
And just as in childhood a mother gives a little molasses, / and the boy begs again for molasses because of longing;
as water cast into water, milk into milk, or clarified butter into clarified butter [is merged], / even so, by the grace of devotion to Viṣṇu, they see no difference.
Just as the sun is omnipresent, and as fire is omnipresent, / so the devotee established in devotion is not bound at all by rituals.
Ajāmila, having abandoned his own duty and practicing sin, / remembered his son Nārāyaṇa and truly attained liberation with certainty.
And those devotees who day and night live by the name alone / are truly dwellers in Vaikuṇṭha; the Vedas are indeed witnesses to that.
The fruit of sacrifices like the horse sacrifice is seen even in heaven; / but having completely experienced that fruit, they surely fall down.
So, O goddess, having experienced pleasures in many ways through devotion to Viṣṇu / or having attained Vaikuṇṭha, when is there any return for them?
He by whom devotion to Viṣṇu is performed dwells in the world of Viṣṇu; / behold the example, O queen of gods, through the grace of devotion to Viṣṇu:
Hundreds of stones standing in the water were brought across by him; / [like] a moonstone without water is the mind of a devotee of Viṣṇu.
The frog dwells in the water, but the bee in the distant forest / perceives the fragrance of the night-lotus; even so is the devotee in devotion to Hari.
Some dwell on the bank of the Gaṅgā, while others are a hundred leagues away; / someone knows the fruit of the Gaṅgā, and another [knows] devotion to Viṣṇu in the same way.
A camel constantly carries a load of camphor and aloe wood, / [yet] does not know the fragrance within; so are those turned away from Viṣṇu.
Deer sniff the śāla tree, desiring the scent of musk, / [yet] do not know it resides in their own navel; so are those turned away from Viṣṇu.
Instruction given to fools is utterly in vain, O daughter of the mountain; / just so is instruction in devotion to Viṣṇu given to one turned outward.
When milk is drunk by a snake, that milk turns into poison; / just so does devotion to Viṣṇu turn into poison for devotees of others.
Just as those without eyes, having looked toward a lamp and a mirror, / do not see what stands near them, so those turned outward do not see Viṣṇu.
Just as fire is covered by smoke, and a mirror by dust, / and as an embryo is enveloped by the amnion, so Kṛṣṇa is veiled in the body.
Just as clarified butter is present in milk, and oil is always in sesame seeds, / so Viṣṇu is in the moving and unmoving, [yet] is not seen, O daughter of the mountain.
Just as many gems are held upon a single thread, / so this universe, beginning with Brahmā, is strung upon the spiritual Brahman.
Just as fire dwelling in wood is seen only through churning, / so Viṣṇu, who is omnipresent, is seen only through meditation.
There may be a single original lamp, and from it thousands are produced; / in the same way, Viṣṇu stands alone, pervading all.
Just as at sunrise the light is always present in the sky, / and is seen manifoldly in water, so is Viṣṇu in the world.
Though staying in nature, the wind continually carries various fragrances; / the Lord, dwelling in all living beings, experiences the qualities born of nature.
Just as water becomes whatever it is through combination with sugar or poison, / so the self, having become involved, experiences the fruit of action.
And the earth, through union with water, produces various trees; / through contact with the qualities of nature, it is born in various wombs.
In an elephant or in a mosquito, in a god or in a human being, / it is neither greater nor lesser; it remains firm and motionless in the body.
From Brahmā down to a clump of grass, whatever humans are here on earth, / the gods, sacrifices, and serpents, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and others—
in all of them [reflections] are seen like that of the moon in water; / he is seen as Śiva, being, consciousness, and bliss, the Great Lord.
He indeed is declared to be Viṣṇu; he is that omnipresent Hari, / known through the Vedānta, the Lord of all, beyond time, free from affliction.
Whoever knows Revanta, O goddess, he is a devotee—of this there is no doubt. / For the One is to be known as manifold, and the manifold is indeed only One.
He is spoken of in various ways on earth by distinctions of name and form; / the eye sees through the light of the sun, and by the sun the eye flourishes.
So are the Supreme Self and the individual self always in every body; / just as space is in pot after pot, remaining as it was when that is broken,
so are you in form after form, utterly motionless when that is broken; / just as a wooden form collapses without a master,
the body made of various worms collapses without the self; / the colors of gold [change], but through fire they return to their former state;
similarly, individual souls attain their original form through devotion; / covered by their own cloud, fools see the sun as devoid of light;
so those whose minds are clouded by ignorance do not know that Lord; / he is recited by the Vedāntas as without conceptual construct, formless.
And from the formless he appears as possessing form by his own will; / from him space was born, soundless and devoid of qualities.
From space the wind was born, and it then became possessed of sound; / from the wind light was born, and from light water came to be.
In that water was the golden womb, the cosmic person bearing the universal form, / and in his navel-lotus are tens of millions of cosmic eggs.
From him came primordial nature and the person; the threefold world was made; / from the union of those two, the combination of principles was born.
Viṣṇu's manifestation is pure goodness; Brahmā is traditionally known as passion; / Śiva is declared to be darkness; by these everything is set in motion.
There is a single state of Brahmā in the world, according to the seed of actions; / by that, Viṣṇu dissolves all worlds without remainder.
The imperishable Lord Viṣṇu remains there at that time; / thus Viṣṇu is omnipresent, the beginning, the middle, and the end.
Through ignorance people do not know, being fixed on ritual action; / whoever performs actions appropriate to their caste at proper times,
that action whose deity is Viṣṇu is certainly not a cause of entering the womb; / in the Vedānta scripture, this is always deliberated by the sages.
This is knowledge of Brahman in the body; that I now proclaim. / The mind alone is the effect and the cause of both good and evil.
When all is purified by the mind, then eternal Brahman [is attained]. / The mind alone is always a friend, the mind alone is always an enemy.
Some are saved by the mind, and some are tormented by the mind. / Renunciation of everything within, while performing action outwardly,
one acting thus is not tainted even while performing action, / just as a lotus leaf is not tainted even by drops of water.
As fire thrown into fire, so what need is there with devotion? / When the nectar of devotion is known, liberation is not relished then.
Viṣṇu cannot be attained by the eightfold yoga in this birth; / or rather, Viṣṇu is attained through devotion, [by which] he is always easily attained.
Knowledge is attained through the Vedāntas, and through knowledge the object to be known is attained. / When that object to be known is attained, then this world is empty.
Viṣṇu is not attained by force, and what use are the eightfold yogas? / Purity of inner disposition is praised above all states.
Just as a beloved woman is embraced, so the fruit corresponds to one's disposition. / Indeed, a foot shod with a shoe perceives the earth as made of leather.
In whatever manner one's intellect is, in that manner one considers the world. / Even if watered with milk, a neem tree does not abandon its bitter nature.
Creatures follow their innate nature; instruction is useless. / Having cut down a mango tree, how can one obtain fruit or leaf?
Why should one waste a birth for the sake of the pleasure of the senses? / Just as medicine is cooked in a pot made of lapis lazuli,
and the remedy is burnt up, so why should a birth be in vain? / And having placed a treasure in the house, how could a fortunate person perform servitude?
Having abandoned the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, how could one delight in another path? / What is the use of the four Vedas studied devoid of devotion?
Even a dog-cooker endowed with devotion is worshipped even by the thirty [gods]. / Having bound a bracelet on one's own wrist, what is the use of mirrors?
And the servants whose sovereignty was granted by gods such as Brahmā and Rudra, / do not take anything offered by the Lord.
He did not go to give a boon to a devotee who possessed nothing. / How could there be meditation on bodyless Kṛṣṇa?
Many, having beheld the embodied form, have gone to that realm through devotion. / How can worship and devotion be directed toward the void? The wise speak of the embodied form.
How does a man walk upon the empty path without a support? / He who has form is himself the master; the formless is indeed the Lord.
He who has form is easily seen; the formless is not seen. / The sweetness of service is with the embodied; with the formless there is no flavor.
By means of the embodied, the formless is known spontaneously. / When one's body thrills with hair standing on end by grace of the remembrance of Hari,
and joyful tears fill the eyes, then liberation becomes a handmaid. / How does the sin committed in childhood not perish
through worship, gifts, vows, sacred fords, recitations, and burnt offerings dedicated to you? / Abandoning one's own dharma, how could one perform severe austerity?
Death in one's own dharma is better; another's dharma brings fear. / Forsaking the scriptural ordinance, how could one perform severe austerity?
Without an stage of life, the foolish man cannot attain perfection. / The castes were created by Brahmā, appointed each to its own dharma.
Wealth acquired through one's own dharma is called white wealth. / A gift given with faith using white wealth,
even if small, yields great religious merit; there is no count to it. / Wealth brought for household deeds through association with the base,
the gift given with that wealth by human beings and others / does not bear fruit for them; they do not partake of that fruit at all.
Whatever sort of action a person performs desiring the pleasure of the senses, / into that sort of womb the foolish man, weak in knowledge, enters.
Whatever action one performs here is experienced in the other world. / If suffering arises for a man who practices virtue,
then sorrow should not be felt; that is an action born of a former body. / And when suffering arises for a man who practices sin,
joy should not be felt in that pleasure, O ruler of the gods! / And just as beasts bound with ropes by a master at his will,
so men on the earth are led by the bondage of action. / A monkey living in the forest dances from house to house,
and in this way living beings are led by action into all wombs. / Just as a ball is driven at will by a playing master,
so a creature is led by action into pleasure and pain. / A living being bound by its own actions is unable to restrain the bondage.
Even gods are bound by actions, and likewise other sages. / The poison-eating serpents on Rudra's body on Kailāsa
are unable to drink nectar; the womb of action is very powerful. / He who grants a healthy body is indeed called the Sun by the wise,
yet the charioteer of his chariot is lame; the womb of action is very powerful. / Indradyumna, the royal sage, attained elephant-hood through action.
By the capable master, the womb of action in him was made void. / The gods headed by Rudra and Brahmā, and the humans and asuras who exist,
all of them, bound by action, wander upon the surface of the earth. / The entire world, subject to action, was created long ago by Viṣṇu.
That action is subject to Keśava; it is destroyed by the name of Rāma. / Water is found everywhere, yet it gives liberation at the confluence of the white and black [rivers].
Thus for those who act, the worship of Keśava grants liberation. / He who performs action with the mind for the sake of the pleasure of the senses,
might consider the body alone through egotism. / A creature, remembering with the mind, should perform atonement;
he is the experiencer of past action, and action does not increase in the future. / Some praise the planets, some ghosts and goblins,
some praise the gods, and some speak of herbs; / some speak of mantras and perfection, and some of intelligence and valor;
some speak of effort, daring, fortitude, and likewise policy and strength. / All follow desires through praises of ego-driven action.
This is my settled conviction, as taught by the ancient wise: / when a creature is full of merit and no sin exists [in him],
Knowledge is twofold, and then merit becomes auspicious. / One whose sin and merit are equal, for him action exists.
when yoga and the pairs of opposites are equal, then he attains the state of bliss. / Renouncing all externally, he should be full of longing in his mind.
his conduct is useless, and because of that, such people experience sin. / If one performs actions externally, yet is desireless in mind,
that renunciation should be known as intermediate; he does not attain the full fruit. / Having renounced both externally and internally, relying upon the void through intellect,
that renunciation should be known as the highest, rare even for yogins. / Some abandon everything out of anger; some, under the influence of dispute;
some abandon everything out of hardship; all such renunciations are merely intermediate. / Endowed with right intellect and faith, not fallen under the sway of anger and the like,
a person, even though untouched by actions, goes to a good state. / In the house of the pure and prosperous, of the wise and of yogins,
one fallen from yoga is born in a family preceded by the twice-born; / and in a very short time he attains complete yoga.
One may go to the realm of consciousness and bliss through the grace of yoga and devotion. / Just as mud [cannot be washed away] by mud, or blood indeed by blood,
how can one wash away action by violent action? / How can a sacrifice, which consists of violent action, destroy action?
Sacrifices performed out of desire for heaven bestow little happiness in heaven; / and pleasures, though many, are impermanent.
There is no eternal happiness in them anywhere without devotion to Hari. / The happiness of universal rule, kingship, and likewise happiness in heaven—
I desire nothing else; I fear dwelling in the womb. / A stone indeed is broken by iron, but a ruby is not broken;
devotion to Viṣṇu, full of various desires, is not broken by the intellect. / A crane eats creatures living in water, but avoids frogs and the like;
likewise Yama, the killer of all, avoids the servants of Kṛṣṇa. / He who protects and destroys is indeed called the protector.
Where they dwell in their own place, burdened with hundreds of offenses, / Kṛṣṇa is merciful to one who has committed offenses;
and if he attains the fruit, what can the protector do? / Thus the Self in this body, dependent on another, is merciful.
The other shore was reached slowly; accompanied by wrestlers, it was not reached. / The giver of liberation to the hunter, he himself ferried Kubjā across.
Hard to reach even in a dream by Brahmā and others, he was easy to reach in the cowherd's house. / When he ate the leftovers of the cowherds, then they were ferried across by him.
The supreme Self, Janārdana, is constantly sung by yogins. / Seeing the imperishable, glorious Puruṣa, they [stood] in wonder, O goddess.
Those who recite this divine remembrance day by day, / freed from all sins, go to the eternal [realm] of Viṣṇu.

text_mt:
Viṣṇu, Janārdana, the lord of all, residing among the wise. / This one hundred and eight sacred bathing-places have been declared.

Whoever recites or hears [this] is completely freed from all sins. / Having bathed in these sacred bathing-places, whoever sees Nārāyaṇa Hari,

freed from all sins, goes to the eternal [realm] of Viṣṇu. / The great sacred place Jagannātha is remembered as the purifier of the worlds.

Those best of men who go [there] also attain the supreme state.
One should cause the highly meritorious one hundred and eight [names] to be heard during rites for the ancestors.

Having enjoyed happiness in this world, he goes to the eternal [abode] of Viṣṇu.
During the gift of a cow, or in offering a śrāddha, or day after day,

in the rite of worshiping the deity, the wise person attains the supreme Brahman.

I shall proclaim the glorification of the Vetravatī; listen, O beautiful lady,
bathing in which they are liberated until the dissolution of beings.

A well named Mahāgambhīra was constructed by Vṛtra;
from that well emerged that goddess who destroys multitudes of great sins.

As is the Gaṅgā, so is this excellent river, O best among the gods;
by the mere sight of her, the floods of sins are subdued.

Listen, O goddess, I shall relate an ancient legendary history,
hearing which sinners are freed from faults and the bondage of karma.

title: mahādevauvāca
text_mt:
In the city of Campaka, a king was ruling the kingdom;
he was ever wicked, wicked in appearance, and an oppressor of the people.

He was unrighteousness in the form of righteousness, intent on reviling Viṣṇu,
a killer of gods and twice-born, and a defiler of hermitages,

intent on reviling the Vedas, wealthy yet foolish, merciless, dishonest,
devoted to false scriptures, and an abuser of others' wives.

He was named Vidāruṇa, and he was indeed a fool.
Once, by the power of destiny, he came to that river.

Engaged in hunting, he himself had become a leper, O queen of gods;
this had arisen from a great sin—from reviling the brāhmaṇas.

He was an idle disputant, an evil-souled rogue, merciless, like a beast,
ever engaged in reviling the Vedas, and a defiler of cows and scriptures.

Wandering thus in the forest, afflicted with thirst and surrounded by his companions,
that king dismounted from his horse, drank the water, and went home.

By that very drinking of water, his leprosy vanished without doubt;
and the intellect of that king especially became spotless.

Devotion to Viṣṇu then arose in him, O queen of gods.
From that time on, he regularly performed his bath.

text_mt:
He became spotless and endowed with great beauty there, O queen of gods;
having enjoyed happiness in this world and performed many sacrifices,

and having given priestly gifts to the brāhmaṇas, he went to the realm of Viṣṇu.
Knowing this, O goddess, especially regarding the Vetravatī,

those brāhmaṇas who bathe [there] are liberated, O daughter of the mountain;
whether a kṣatriya, a vaiśya, or a śūdra, O best among the gods,

wherever they bathe, they are liberated from the bondage of sin.
Whether in Kārttika or in Māgha, an outcaste or a reviler of the Vedas,

having bathed at the confluence of the rivers, O goddess, he is freed from sin.
Where her confluence with the Sābhramatī is seen,

having bathed especially there, a slayer of a brāhmaṇa is ever freed.
There is the heavenly city of Kheṭaka, having the nature of heaven, O sinless one.

Many yogas were performed there by Brahmā, O goddess;
having bathed and eaten there, there is no rebirth.

She is remembered as a second Gaṅgā, especially in the Kali age, O goddess.
Men who desire happiness, and men who desire wealth,

And those people who desire heaven, having bathed again and again, / and having enjoyed happiness in this world, go to the eternal [realm] of Viṣṇu.

and those born in the solar dynasty as well as in the lunar dynasty,
having come to the Vetravatī and bathed, attained supreme bliss.

text_mt:
By the sight [of her], she takes away sorrow; by touch, she takes away mental sin;
having bathed and eaten, O goddess, one partakes of liberation, no doubt.

From bathing, recitation, and likewise from offering oblations, one attains endless fruit.
If, having gone to the sacred place of Vārāṇasī, one should practice the cāndrāyana vow with devotion,

great merit is attained by going there; but that same merit [is obtained], O best among the gods,
especially if one meets death in the Vetravatī.

Becoming four-armed, he goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Whatever sacred places there are on earth, whatever gods and ancestors,

all of them dwell here in the Vetravatī, O queen of gods.
What is the use of saying much more, again and again, O fair-faced one?

There is no sacred place on earth equal to the Vetravatī, O eternal one.
I, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, the gods, and the supreme sages,

all the deities reside in the Vetravatī, O great goddess.
Those who perform bathing there once, twice,

or especially three times a day, are indeed liberated; there is no doubt.

I shall tell you, O goddess, the glorification of the Sābharmatī exactly as it is. / Kaśyapa, the best of sages, indeed performed great austerity.

title: śrīmahādevauvāca
text_mt:
For many years great austerity was practiced by him
on the delightful Mount Arbuda, crowded with various trees.

Having gone there, austerity was performed by the sage Kaśyapa,
where the charming Sarasvatī is pure and destroys sins.

One day, O goddess, he went to Naimiṣa;
then all those sages held many conversations.

Then that sage Kaśyapa was properly asked by those twice-born:
"Ah, Kaśyapa! For our pleasure, let the Gaṅgā be brought here, O lord!

Bearing your name, she will become the best of rivers."
Having heard their words and bowed to those twice-born,

he came to the forest of Arbuda, near the bank of the Sarasvatī.
There he then performed extremely difficult austerity.

Indeed, I was propitiated by him, by the twice-born Kaśyapa;
and then I appeared visibly to that best of the twice-born:

"Choose a boon; may it be well with you; whatever is in your mind."

Kaśyapa said:
"You are capable of granting a boon, O god of gods, O lord of the universe!
This Gaṅgā, pure and removing sin, who resides upon your head,

should especially be given to me, O Mahādeva; reverence to you!"
Then, O goddess, it was said by me: "Take it, O best of the twice-born!"

Releasing one matted lock of hair, the Gaṅgā was then given by me.
Receiving her, the best of the twice-born went with joy to his own dwelling.

text_mt:
The residence of Kaśyapa was a sacred place named Keśarandhra;
he went there, O queen of gods, surrounded by sages.

The Kāśyapī, that best of rivers, was brought along by Kaśyapa,
by the mere sight of whom even a slayer of a brāhmaṇa is indeed liberated.

Pārvatī said:
Tell me what merit comes merely from bathing in that sacred place,
O lord of the universe! You are compassionate; show mercy to me.

What merit is there from the sight, what from bathing? Tell me, O king of gods!
What is her greatness, O holy one? You should tell me everything.

Mahādeva said:
Many sacred places and sanctuaries have been heard of by me,
as well as rivers that flow to the ocean by the grace of the lord, glorious Viṣṇu:

The Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Revā, and the great river Tāpī,
the Godāvarī, Tuṅgabhadrā, Kauśikī, and also the Gallikā,

the Kāverī, Vedikā, Bhadrā, and the sin-removing Sarayū,
and various other rivers on earth that take away all sins;

Prayāga, the king of sacred places, and Kāśī, and Puṣkara,
as well as the sacred place named the forest of Naimiṣa, and Amarakaṇṭaka.

The excellent sacred place of Dvārakā, and the excellent Arbuda forest, / and various divine sacred places of such kinds,

were heard of there, O queen of gods, by the grace of Māyāviṣṇu. / Formerly, indeed, I was beseeched by Bhagīratha, O Pārvatī;

then this Gaṅgā was given [to him] desiring the world of Viṣṇu. / By me, she was given again to Kaśyapa at the word of the sages.

This indeed is the Kāśyapī Gaṅgā, forever removing diseases and defects. / She who is spoken of in the world in each age by distinct names—

that I shall relate; listen in truth, O fair one: / In the Kṛta age her name is Kṛtavatī; in the Tretā age, Girikarṇikā;

in the Dvāpara age her name is Candanā; in the Kali age she is remembered as the Sābhramatī. / Those men who especially [go there] day after day for the sake of bathing,

freed from all sins, go to the eternal [abode] of Viṣṇu. / At the sacred bathing place Plakṣāvataraṇa, and at the Sarasvatī, O sovereign goddess,

and at Kedāra and Kurukṣetra, whatever fruit is obtained from bathing— / that very fruit surely belongs to men day after day from the Sābhramatī.

There is no doubt that it is so, as is the word of Vyāsa. / In the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, or daily, O queen of gods,

whatever fruit there is in properly giving śrāddha on the new-moon day, / a man attains that fruit from immersing in the Sābhramatī.

On the full-moon day of Kārttika under the conjunction with Kṛttikā, at Śrīsthala before Mādhava, / a mortal obtains that fruit from immersing in the Sābhramatī.

Viśvāmitra, Bharadvāja, and the powerful Jamadagni, / the son of Ṛcīka, Garga, and the sage Uddālaka,

Devaśarman, Dhaumya, Āstīka, Kaśyapa, / Lomaśa, Nābhiketu, and Lomaharṣaṇa,

the sage Ugraśravas, and Cyavana the descendant of Bhṛgu, / and those headed by the Vālakhilyas—all indeed go there.

Having bathed, abstaining from food, always devoted to Viṣṇu, / bearing the conch, discus, and mace, they continually dwell on the bank.

The sacred place of the ancestors named Gayā, auspicious and the best among all sacred places, / where the lord of the gods, the Grandfather [Brahmā] himself, resides—

this verse was sung by the ancestors who desired a share of the śrāddha: / 'Many sons are to be desired, in case even one goes to Gayā!'

en:

And that which, through my presence, grants the fruit of enjoyment and liberation— / by my command, the lord of gods named Bindumādhava

dwells constantly, O queen of gods, especially in Vārāṇasī; / therefore, this city of mine is always the most blessed and supreme.

The holy place beloved by the ancestors, holy Vimaleśvara indeed, / and the ancestral sacred place Prayāga, united with all sacred places,

come into the water of the Sābhramatī by my command, O goddess. / And the blessed lord Vaṭeśvara along with Mādhava,

holy Daśāśvamedhaka, and likewise Gaṅgādvāra— / by my appointment, O queen of gods, they dwell indeed in the Sābhramatī.

The river, then the goddess Lalitā, the sacred place called Saptadhāraka, / likewise Mitrapada by name, and Kedāra the abode of Śaṅkara,

and Gaṅgāsāgara, they say, which is auspicious and consists of all sacred places; / the sacred place Brahmasaras likewise, and in the pool of the Śatadru river,

and the sacred place named Naimiṣa—always by my command, / they dwell in the water of the Sābhramatī, O goddess, without a doubt.

The holy Śvetāvalkalinī, and then Śvetā, Hiraṇmayī, / Hastimatī, and Vārtaghnī, a river flowing to the ocean—

these are beloved by the ancestors, granting the fruit of ten million śrāddhas. / There śrāddhas should be offered by sons for the welfare of the ancestors.

The cities named Pāṭala and Vāḍava are there, O beautiful one; / these rivers have especially reached into the Sābhramatī forever.

Those men on earth who perform bathing and gifting there, / having enjoyed happiness in this world, go to the eternal [abode] of Viṣṇu.

Jambūdvīpa is highly sacred, where merit increases; / therein is the highly sacred [tract] called Ārya, fulfilling all desires.

The sacred place known as Nīlakaṇṭha, and Nandahrada, / likewise Rudrahrada, and the holy Rudramahālaya,

the most holy Mandākinī, and the great river Acchodā— / these flow into the Sābhramatī, having made themselves visible.

Likewise Dhūmrā, Mitrapada, Baijnāth, the excellent stone, / the Kṣiprā river, Mahākāla, and the mountain Kāliñjara,

Gaṅgodbheda, Harodbheda, and Narmadākāra— / the wise declare them equal [to all shrines] through the offering of rice-balls in the Gaṅgā.

These holy places of Brahmā on the northern bank of the Sābhramatī / were kept hidden, O queen of gods, by the gods headed by Brahmā.

Silver, darbha grass, cows, a daughter's son, kutapa blankets, and sesame seeds; / sin is called 'bad' (kutsita), and they cause torment to it.

Since there are these eight, they are renowned as 'kutapa's. / After the kutapa muhūrta, the four muhūrtas,

and this period of five muhūrtas is desired for the time of a śrāddha. / Kuśa grass and black sesame are remembered as having arisen from the body of Viṣṇu,

for the protection of the śrāddha—so the gods have said. / A handful of water with sesame should be offered by those staying at a tīrtha, standing in the water,

with darbha in their hands; in this one way the śrāddha is not violated. / Entering the tīrthas on the Sābharmatī under their specific names,

having caused [it] to be made, O goddess, it was given by me to Kaśyapa. / That Kaśyapa is my devotee, ever dear to me.

Therefore, this pure Gaṅgā, destroyer of sins, was given [to him]. / On the Sābharmatī, O blessed lady, at the tīrtha called Brahmacārika,

having established myself by that name, I, Śaṅkara, / remained for the welfare of the world under the name Brahmacārīśa.

having enjoyed happiness in this world, he goes to the great abode of Śiva. / If one afflicted by severe diseases goes there,

his disease is quickly destroyed merely by the sight of it, O great goddess. / Having gone to that abode, fasting and with senses conquered,

if he performs worship with devotion, staying perfectly still at night, / then I indeed go to appear before him in the form of an ascetic.

I grant his desired wishes; truly, truly, O fair-faced lady! / And those people who especially come to my place,

I alleviate their disease, even of very long standing. / Eighty-four diseases have been enumerated by me;

each and every disease is destroyed merely by the sight of it, O beautiful woman! / No liṅga of mine is situated there, O daughter of the mountain;

there is only bathing there [in relation] to me; of this there is no doubt. / At one time on this earth, there was a man of great austerities,

a king of the solar dynasty, powerful, named Brahmadatta. / By that king, great austerity was performed for a long time, O ruler of the gods.

The practice of the five fires was performed by him repeatedly, / and austerities such as fasts lasting a month were undertaken many times.

text_mt:
[and] having established Gaṅgādhara, and having resided there for five days, / that king then went back to his own kingdom.

Brahmadatta, renowned in the world as exceedingly great, / knowing dharma, ruled the kingdom for ten thousand years.

Then, after some time, having enjoyed the kingdom, that king / went to the world of Śiva, the supreme abode known as Brahman.

Two gods abide there indicating my names: / one is known as Brahmacārīśa, the other as Gaṅgādhara.

Those people who perform worship especially in my place, / to them I give everything desired here; of this there is no doubt.

The place itself is the liṅga; it should always be visited by men. / There flowers, incense, and various offerings of food,

whichever wise man offers, he surely attains everything. / With bilva leaves, flowers, or with sandalwood and the like,

they worship in my place; to them I grant everything. / Whoever constantly listens to this Brahmacārin narrative,

having obtained happiness in this world, goes to the presence of Śiva, / where the god Gaṅgādhara, the bestower of prosperity, constantly remains.

text_mt:
The second, named Brahmacārīśa, is always present. / Through the union of meditation on the two, one surely attains Śivahood.

From seeing [them], disease is destroyed; from worship, one attains long life; / and from bathing there, O ruler of the gods, one shares in liberation; of this there is no doubt.

Listen, O beautiful woman, I shall declare a most wonderful tīrtha / renowned as Rājakhaṅga, situated particularly on the Sābharmatī.

Born in the solar dynasty was a king named Kartana, / of evil conduct, sinful, and a reviler of Brahmins,

treacherous to his guru, ever angry, a scorner of all rites, / constantly devoted to others' wives, and constantly reviling Viṣṇu,

he constantly oppressed the subjects in many ways. / Such a wicked soul always lived on the earth.

When some time had passed in this manner, listen truthfully, O beautiful woman: / through sin and through the turn of fate, leprosy arose [in him].

Gazing upon his own body and reflecting again and again, / wondering 'What should be done?', he became filled with anxiety.

Once, by the turn of fate, he went into the forest to amuse himself; / reaching the bank of the Sābharmatī there, he remained.

text_mt:
Bathing was performed by him there, and the excellent water was drunk. / Instantly through bathing there, his body became celestial,

seen as a beautiful golden form, O daughter of the mountain! / At that very moment, that king was transformed; of this there is no doubt.

Having obtained a divine form, the king then, for some time, / having enjoyed the kingdom, O ruler of the gods, went to the supreme abode.

Then this tīrtha became known by the name Rājakhaṅga. / Those who perform ablutions here, or whoever makes a gift,

having enjoyed happiness in this world, goes to Viṣṇu's eternal [abode]. / There is no disease for them, nor sorrow at any time.

A man who daily bathes in this pool known as the royal pool / attains heaven and is honored by Brahmā and others.

In the Kṛta age, it was named Satyeśvara; in the Tretā age, Bhuvaneśvara; / it was renowned as Rājeśvara in the Dvāpara age, O daughter of the mountain.

In this terrible Kali yuga, it became hidden, and the sovereign of the universe [is concealed]; / hence the sacred tīrtha came to be named Rājakhaṅga.

Those who offer libations with faith to the ancestors here, / those men are praised as performers of meritorious deeds on earth.

text_mt:
Even slayers of Brahmins and slayers of children who bathe here / are freed from those sins and go to the presence of Śiva.

And those men who perform the release of a dark bull into the Sābhramatī, / their ancestors indeed remain satisfied until the universal dissolution.

This divine narrative named Rājakhaṅga, / those men who hear it, O Goddess, have no fear.

Diseases and blemishes are destroyed by hearing and reciting it.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, entitled "The Glorification of the Sābharmatī," in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand verses.

The one hundred and thirty-sixth chapter. Pārvatī said: / The Sābharmatī, emerging from the Nandikuṇḍa, through which lands [did it flow]?

purify as she flowed? Tell me which regions [they were], / and which sacred places she made after crossing Mount Arbuda.

Sūta said: / When this was spoken there by the goddess, Mahādeva, the sovereign of the universe, / spoke words to Pārvatī, who enchants the universe.

Mahādeva said: / First from Nandikuṇḍa, the supremely purifying sacred place, / the sacred place Kapālamocana was proclaimed by the sages.

It is a sacred place surpassing all in splendor, supreme purifier among purifiers; / here the skull known as Brahmā's was cast off by me.

Therefore, O Pārvatī, the sacred place became known as Kapālamocana, / purifying all beings, manifest, renowned in the world.

magnanimous beings dwell in that spotless, auspicious sacred place, / celebrated in the three worlds, granting gifts and bestowing liberation.

Having bathed there and become pure, one should worship the Lord of the Skull; / having fasted for one night, and having fed Brahmins,

even by the gift of cloth there one obtains the fruit of an Agnihotra sacrifice. / But whatever person who, undertaking the vow of seeing [the shrine] at that sacred place,

title: mahādevauvāca
text_mt:
the fifth is declared as Hastimatī, which removes all sins; / the sixth is the Vetravatī, fashioned of old by Vṛtra.

This supreme goddess issued forth from the well of Vṛtra; / thus arose the Vetravatī, destroying great sins.

The seventh is Bhadrāmukhī, mostly auspicious and purifying the worlds. / Having purified those various territories with these seven streams, O Goddess,

she was established as the seven-streamed [river] through that single [source]. / He who will offer a ancestral rite dedicated to the ancestors at the sacred place of Vikīrṇa,

the fruit that comes from offering a rice-ball at Gayā will be his. / Those who are scattered, fallen, and deprived of the rites of rice-balls and water,

they are liberated at Vikīrṇa, [as though] the rites of rice-balls and water were given. / But he who performs an ancestral rite there will surely attain the status of a gaṇa.

Therefore, one should faithfully perform the ancestral rite according to the ordinances of the three Vedas. / In this sacred place especially, at the rising of the seven rivers, O twice-born ones,

bathe, O best of Brahmins, desiring the realm of the sages! / Thus it was spoken especially to the twice-born by Kaśyapa.

If a bath is taken [here], it always removes all suffering; / it is the best sacred place among sacred places, the most excellent of sacred fields.

This sacred place Vikīrṇa grants good fortune and removes disease and blemishes. / Those who especially bathe here at all times in the Kali age,

text_mt:

Thus ends the Vikīrṇa Ford. / Beyond this ford is an unequaled ford born of Śvetā, / where the Śvetā River was born from the ashes of my back and belly.

renowned in the three worlds, destroying all sins, / born from contact with the ash of Hara's limbs and honored by the gods.

A man who bathes in it, pure and restrained, having dwelt [there] for three nights / and beholding Mahākāleśvara, is glorified in the world of Rudra.

He who offers a rice-ball to the ancestors with kuśa grass and sesame seeds upon its bank, / his ancestors become fully satisfied; of this there is no doubt.

Śvetagaṅgā is exceedingly meritorious, releasing from suffering and poverty; / by bathing there, O Goddess, supreme happiness is attained.

At its holy confluence, O Pārvatī, I always dwell; / those who make gifts here and bathe there, O beautiful one,

infinite fruit shall be theirs; of this there is indeed no doubt. / There the god Bhūteśvara surely dwells at the confluence.

Those best of men who offer incense, lamps, flowers, and the light-waving ceremony there, / those men are embodiments of merit.

He who takes a bilva leaf and offers it atop Śiva, / always obtains his desire in the Śvetā in the presence of Śiva.

title: aṣṭatriṃśādhika śatatamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Mahādeva said: / Then, intent on the pilgrimage to sacred places, one should go to Gaṇatīrtha, / proclaimed as Triviṣṭapa by the gaṇas on the bank of the Candanā.
A man having bathed with composure at Triviṣṭapa on the full-moon day— / no doubt should be entertained here—is liberated from the killing of a Brahmin.
He whose stay at Triviṣṭapa lasts for the four rainy months, / he too is meritorious, O noble goddess, and is honored in the realm of Rudra.
A man having bathed at Gaṇatīrtha while fasting on the dark eighth day, / having bathed at the confluence with the Bakulā, goes to heaven.
A man having bathed at that tīrtha and having beheld Bakuleśa, / by the grace of Gaṇeśvara shall attain the status of a gaṇa.
This supreme, purifying [narrative] increases merit and longevity; / hearing it, a man indeed obtains merit equal to bathing in the Gaṅgā.
Staying here without food, self-controlled and focused, / he who thus chants to the supreme god, the charming Lord of Gaṇas,
attains all enjoyments—truly, truly, O fair-faced goddess. / Here the heroic king Viśvadatta, born of the lunar dynasty,
performed great austerities for a long time, O ruler of gods; / he then attained the status of a gaṇa through the grace of the glorious Gaṇeśa.
Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Hoḍa, Kauśītaka the sage, / Bharadvāja, Aṅgiras, Viśvāmitra, and Vāmana—
all these sages indeed, of meritorious form, O supreme goddess, / constantly render service through the grace of the glorious Gaṇeśa.
The childless obtains sons; the penniless obtains wealth; / the unlearned obtains learning; one seeking liberation attains liberation.
What need is there to say more, again and again, O fair-faced goddess? / Whoever performs a bath here, or performs worship,
is freed from all sins and goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. / Between Śiva in the form of Viṣṇu and Viṣṇu in the form of Śiva,
I see no difference, O goddess, and through the grace of the glorious Viṣṇu [this is so].

title: ekona catvāriṃśadadhikaśatatamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
Mahādeva said:
On the northern bank of the Sābhramatī there is the renowned Agnitīrtha; / to the northeast of it, not very far away, is situated
the tīrtha named Pāleśvara, where Caṇḍī is installed; / that is a seat of the Mothers of Yoga, which bestows all accomplishments,
where those Mothers reside for the sake of all the gods, / having undertaken supreme effort for the sake of favoring the worlds.
Having stayed three nights at that tīrtha, firm in his vow, / one should approach that lord, Caṇḍikeśvara, the ruler of gods.
Having bathed in the Sābhramatī in the vicinity of Mātṛtīrtha, / engaged in the proper rule of absorption, one should indeed go to the circle of the Mothers.
A person attains the fruit of giving a thousand cows. / A man having bathed at Agnitīrtha, when sight of Cāmuṇḍā has been made,
no fear arises for him born of rākṣasas, bhūtas, or piśācas. / Where the river Gokhurā joins with the Sābhramatī,
thousands of tīrthas abide there, O ruler of gods. / A śrāddha should be performed there with sesame powder, O Pārvatī;
having offered rice-balls and fed the twice-born, one reaches the imperishable realm. / Where King Kukardama, most sinful, uncontrollable, and wicked,
foolish, filled with arrogance, a reviler of the twice-born, / a slayer of cows, a killer of the strong, most sinful and ever intractable,
was ruling in the city called Piṇḍāra— / then death arrived in the course of righteousness, O ruler of gods.
Having died, he was born there in the form of a preta, O great goddess, / yellow-faced, with a shriveled mouth, yellow hair, and rough,
very tall, hairy, tormented by hunger and thirst, / subsisting on air, wandering here and there,
accompanied by many pretas, weeping piteously, crying "Alas! Alas!" / "What should be done?" said those pretas who were near him;
they too were then weeping, afflicted by hunger, thirst, and the like. / Other pretas of wicked soul joined the king's company.
Along with the king they wander through many deserted lands; / neither water nor food is ever seen along the road.
Those pretas of terrible appearance roam upon the surface of the earth; / they eat corpse flesh and continually drink blood.
Thus King Kukardama, ever surrounded by them, / once by the workings of fate came upon the hermitage of his guru.

There was merit done in a former birth; by that connection he came [there]. / Pārvatī said:
What merit indeed was done by him? Tell me, O Lord, Master of the Universe!
This sinful and wicked soul who brought distress to brāhmaṇas— / how did the company of the virtuous happen for him? Tell me that, which is difficult to comprehend.

Mahādeva said:
What was done in a former birth by this lord of men, / I shall relate all that to you; listen, O daughter of the mountain.
In a former birth, O goddess, he was a brāhmaṇa, a reciter of the Vedas; / having worshipped Mahādeva and performed the worship of guests,
that best of brāhmaṇas would eat his daily meal. / By the power of that merit, in the city called Piḍāra,
he was born as a king known as Kukardama. / In deed and in thought, no merit whatsoever was done by him [as king];
by that divine ordinance, having died, he became a king of pretas, / dry-faced, of shriveled form, yellow in color, terrifying.
Merit acquired in a previous birth does not perish, O ruler of gods; / through the connection of that merit, he came to his guru's hermitage.
Kahoḍa resided there; by him the king of pretas was then seen, / dry-faced, of shriveled form, yellow in color, terrifying,
deep-eyed, a great sinner, accompanied by evil pretas, / with erect hair, matted locks, appearing like Death, dreadful.

Having seen him thus, O goddess, the brāhmaṇa became agitated. / Kahoḍa said:
In this charming, truly exceedingly wonderful place,
at the tīrtha of Agnipāleśvara, I continually dwell, O king. / You were our patron of sacrifice; how have you become a king of pretas,
evil-minded, of wicked form, resembling Death, and terrifying? / By the fruition of what deed were you born [thus] on the auspicious surface of the earth?

The preta said:
Listen, O brāhmaṇa, to my sin that was committed in my previous birth: / I was King Kukardama in the city named Piṇḍāra.
While residing there, O lord, hear what was indeed done by me: / the harming of brāhmaṇas, and formerly the speaking of untruths and the like;
the oppression of subjects, and constant injury to living beings; / I was an inflictor of suffering upon cows, a breaker of the vows of brāhmaṇas,
always unbathed, O vipra, a reviler of virtuous people, / constantly intent on slandering Viṣṇu, and a reviler of Vaiṣṇavas,
ill-behaved and wicked-souled, ever consorting with a Śūdra woman; / eating here and there without care, never devoted to purification.
By the conjunction of that karma, having died, O king among the twice-born, / I fell into the womb of a preta and became miserable in many ways.
For him who has neither mother nor father, nor kinfolk and relatives, / the guru is his relative, the guru is his mother, and the guru is indeed his father.
Knowing this, O brāhmaṇa, you ought to grant liberation.

Kahoḍa said:
Listen, O best of kings, I shall carry out your request: / you shall indeed attain liberation immediately here, there is no doubt.
And the pretas led by eleven who are associated with you, / they too shall attain liberation, especially at this excellent tīrtha.
Then, having gone to the sacred bathing place with that brāhmaṇa, O goddess of gods, / he had the rites of sesame, funeral cakes, and water performed by all.

There is no restriction of month nor lunar day, O goddess, having gone to the sacred bathing place again and again; / the ancestral offering and other rites should be performed: this was declared to me by Brahmā in ancient times.
When the rite was performed, O sovereign of the gods, they were freed at that king of sacred bathing places; / mounted on excellent celestial chariots, they went to my own city.
Where the Gokhurā joins with the Sābhramatī, O goddess of gods, / bathing and giving there yields the fruit of ten million sacrifices.
Where Agnitīrtha is situated, known as Kapāleśvara, / liberation is proclaimed there; truly, truly, it shall surely be so.

title: catvāriṃśadadhikaśatatamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: The venerable Mahādeva said: / O goddess, I shall speak of another, the great confluence of the Hiraṇyā, / when the Sābhramatī Gaṅgā became seven streams in ancient times.
Then that daughter of Brahmā was celebrated as "having seven streams"; / the seventh is called the stream named Hiraṇyā.
A person, even a sinner, having bathed in that sacred place, attains the highest destiny. / Between the Ṛkṣu and the Mañju lies the mountain named Satyavat.
To the east of it is the auspicious, very great sacred place, the confluence of the Hiraṇyā; / having bathed and sipped water there, one attains an auspicious destiny.
Then one should go to the forest site, having seen Nārāyaṇa Hari, / the holy sacred place of the celestial nymphs, Hiraṇyāsaṃgameśvara,
where Urvaśī, the auspicious one among all celestial nymphs, was born in ancient times; / Nara and Nārāyaṇa performed supreme asceticism there,
at the delightful, auspicious confluence of the Hiraṇyā which removes great sins, / where all the sages, freed from impurities, indeed bathe.
The brāhmaṇas beginning with Vasiṣṭha, and those beginning with the Vālakhilyas, / bathe, O sovereign of the gods, at the confluence with the Hiraṇyā.
Where a golden form is surely obtained from bathing; / whatever fruit comes from the gift of a thousand brown cows,
that fruit one always obtains at the confluence of the Hiraṇyā. / Whatever religious merit [is gained] at ten horse sacrifices, or during an eclipse of the moon and sun,
that is proclaimed to be multiplied infinitely at the confluence of the Hiraṇyā. / And whatever fruit one may obtain from the gift of one's weight in gold,
that fruit one always obtains at the confluence of the Hiraṇyā. / The great Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa performed great asceticism there;
his body became gold-like there in ancient times. / Likewise, when King Janamejaya bathed there,
the sin of killing a brāhmaṇa departed, O goddess, at the confluence of the Hiraṇyā. / Then the royal sage Viśvāmitra arrived for the purpose of bathing;
having taken a bath particularly [well], he went to my own city.
Brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and also śūdras, O goddess of gods, / who take a bath here go to Śiva's abode.

title: ekacatvāriṃśadadhika śatatamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Mahādeva said: / Then, O goddess, I shall speak after the confluence of the Hiraṇyā, / where the river Dharmāvatī joins with the Gaṅgā.
A blessed man, having bathed there, goes to heaven without doubt; / whoever sees the sacred place made by Dharma shares in religious merit.
Those who perform an ancestral offering right there are released from debt to the ancestors. / And next is Madhurātīrtha, destroying all sins;
one should bathe in Madhurātīrtha, and Hari, the slayer of Madhu, should be seen, / where Kṛṣṇa, distressed by fear of Jarāsandha, rested,
after the slaying of the demon Kaṃsa had occurred, desiring to go to Kuśasthalī. / Having stayed for seven nights on the bank of the Candanā,
surrounded by the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas, the heroic bulls of the Yādavas, / having reached Madhurātīrtha and bathed according to the proper rite,
where Hari established the one named Madhurāditya; / having settled eighteen thousand brāhmaṇas rich in sacrifices,
and having given various conveyances, he departed. / And thousands of sacred places reside there, O goddess of gods;
an ancestral offering should be performed there with the desire for the ancestors' benefit: / "No fear should be felt of Jarāsandha by those always dwelling in my sacred place."
Having spoken thus to those twice-born, Kṛṣṇa departed toward Dvārakā. / Having bathed at that ford, a man should worship Madhurārka.
by donating a brown cow on the bright seventh of Māgha, / he enjoys pleasures for a long time here, and goes to the realm of the sun.
Listen, O beautiful woman, I shall tell an ancient history, / hearing which a person is released from sins such as the killing of a brāhmaṇa.
At one time, O goddess, the excellent sage Māṇḍavya / performed great, highly meritorious asceticism at Gaṅgādvāra,
eating leaves, eating fruit, and always consuming air; / day and night, O goddess, always devoted to the meditation on Viṣṇu,
ever delighting in the practice of yoga, ever devoted to righteousness. / In that country, O goddess, there was a king, Viśvamohana;
he possessed abundant wealth of elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers on the earth. / His son, famous as Somacandra, possessed auspicious marks.
Once upon a time, O goddess, he went into the forest on a hunt; / having gone there at that time, having performed the acts of the hunt,
he amused himself, surrounded by his own people. / While the king was engaged in sporting, O goddess of gods, night fell.
During that night, the king stayed in the hunting forest. / When that night had passed, at the moment called the hour of Brahmā,
a horse was specially stolen there by an evil-minded thief. / Then an outcry arose: "Where did the horse go? Where did it go?"
Then, out of fear of the king, all were anxious and eager to go, / saying indeed: "The horse was carried away by a thief!"
Searching all around, they all came to Haridvāra; / there, indeed, the sage Māṇḍavya was constantly performing asceticism,
and absorbed in meditation, he was seen by those soldiers then: / "This thief, always a sinner, remains absorbed in meditation!
He came here after tying up the horse!"—so it was considered by the royal soldiers then. / Thinking thus, all of them seized that great sage,
and presented that excellent sage as a thief to the king: / "The horse-stealer has been brought; this thief always [acts thus], O king!"
Then an order was given by him for impaling on a stake; / then, having gathered together, all those soldiers bound him.
Afterwards, he was impaled on a stake from that very moment; / that act of piercing by the stake was not known by him,
because he was absorbed in yoga, devoted to the meditation on Viṣṇu. / After some time had passed, the impalement on the stake was perceived [by him]:
"I am Māṇḍavya, the best of sages; by whom was this act done?" / The lord, omniscient and knowing the three divisions of time, reflected on it:
"This is the deed of Dharma, and never of anyone else." / That righteous one, absorbed in yoga, went to the presence of Dharma.
Having gone there, he said this: "Listen now, O Dharma! / You are indeed celebrated as Dharma in the world and in the Veda at all times;"
"Why was the deed of impalement upon a stake done by you? / I wish to hear all that from you, O god; there is no doubt."
Dharma said: / "Listen, O best of twice-born, to the sin in your previous birth. / I shall tell you that; have mercy upon me.
This deed was a sin committed in your previous birth during your childhood. / Listen to that, O very wise one, because of which this falling was brought about in this life.
At one time, O vipra, you went into a solitary forest. / Having gone there, O vipra, a living creature called a grasshopper
was indeed impaled upon a thorn by you, afflicted by that deed. / You were indeed placed upon a stake by the king because of this deed, O you of good vows.
The deed done, good or bad, must by all means be experienced. / This was merely a small deed experienced by you; there is no doubt.
May you be happy, O lord of vipras; go as you wish." / Hearing this speech, then, Māṇḍavya, best of the twice-born,
spoke words there, his eyes fierce with anger: / Māṇḍavya said: / "Hey, most sinful, wicked-minded one, why was so great a sin caused,
on account of which this deed of impalement on a stake was done? / By the fury of my curse, you shall by all means become a śūdra!"
In the course of some time, in the lunar lineage, / he was born by the name of Vidura, devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu.
Under the pretext of a pilgrimage, he went to the Sābhramatī River, / where the confluence with the Dharmāvatī exists, O goddess of the gods.
There indeed Vidura, the embodiment of dharma, took a bath; / there his śūdra status was abandoned in the Dharmāvatī; there is no doubt.
For this reason, O goddess, wherever men take a bath [there], / those men of meritorious deeds go to the supreme abode.

Those men on earth who perform a śrāddha and give gifts here, / having obtained supreme prosperity in this world, rejoice in heaven.

Thus in the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand verses, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara, in the glorification of the Sābharmatī, the glorification of Madhurāditya,

title: dvicatvāriṃśadadhika śatatamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: The glorious Mahādeva said: / A man, having bathed in Kaṃbutīrtha or having offered libations to the ancestors, / should worship the lord of the gods, the disease-free Nārāyaṇa.
Having given gifts duly to the brāhmaṇas according to the precept, / he attains the world of Viṣṇu by the power of this tīrtha.
Here, in the past, by the wise royal sage Viśvāmitra / austere asceticism was performed especially, desiring offspring, O beautiful woman.
Where he lived subsisting on wind, taking no food, eating only air, / constantly devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, intent on meditating upon Viṣṇu.
Through this asceticism, he became one who obtained his desire for offspring. / And whatever man desiring offspring goes to Kaṃbutīrtha,
he constantly obtains offspring; it is true, it is true, O fair-faced woman!
Thus ends the glorification of the Kaṃbu Ford. / Then one should go, O best of gods, to the ford named Kapīśvara, / in the presence of the red lion, which destroys great sins.
Formerly, when the bridge was being built during the war between Rāma and Rāvaṇa, / taking the best of mountains, it was constructed particularly by the monkeys.
They established the unsurpassed tīrtha named Kapīśvarāditya. / Where, after bathing in the tīrtha or offering libations to the ancestors,
having seen Kapīśvarāditya, one is freed from the murder of a brāhmaṇa. / A bath should be taken there especially on the eighth day of Caitra,
where a bath was taken for three days by those headed by Hanumat. / This power of Kapitīrtha has been related to you.
Having bathed in this tīrtha and having worshipped Kapīśvara, a man / becomes handsome and endowed with many enjoyments; there is no doubt here.
Whatever person desires strength, or dharma, or a son, / he always obtains all that by the power of Kapitīrtha.

title: tricatvāriṃśadadhika śatatamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Then one should go to Ekadhāra, the supremely purifying tīrtha. / Having bathed at Ekadhāra, fasting for one night,
worshipping the lord of the gods, the Master, he can save a hundred families. / The immersion in this tīrtha is to be known as equal to Svāmitīrtha.
A man would go to the world of Rudra by the power of this tīrtha; / and having bathed and drunk there, he also goes to the world of Brahmā.
Those of meritorious deeds in the three worlds reside indeed upon this bank.
They have no fear, and whatever [fear of] sword's edges and the like exists, / all that is quickly destroyed at this chief Ekadhāra tīrtha.
Thus ends the description of the Ekadhāra Ford. / Then one should go to Saptadhāra, the supreme of sacred fords, / named Saptasārasvata, which was formed by the sages for its sake.
In the Tretā age, Maṅkitīrtha was made by the great sage Maṅki; / but in the Dvāpara age, Saptadhāra was established by the sons of Pāṇḍu.
The tīrtha fallen from Hara's matted locks attained the state of having seven streams. / The seven forms of the Gaṅgā that flow in the seven worlds,
those sacred waters flow in this Saptadhāra tīrtha. / A śrāddha performed at Saptadhāra grants satisfaction to the ancestors.
Listen, O goddess, I shall proclaim an ancient legendary history, / hearing which, O goddess of the lords of gods, one will surely go to the world of Brahmā.
There was a son of Kauṣītaka, known indeed by the name of Maṅki, / constantly delighting in meditating on Viṣṇu, worshipping the world of Viṣṇu,
a reciter of the Vedas, and devoted to the agnihotra. / In his house were two wives: Surūpā and Viśvarūpā.
Seeing them devoid of sons, O goddess, he became apprehensive. / Pondering 'What is to be done?', he became filled with immense anxiety:
"A lineage becomes firm only through a son; otherwise one goes to hell." / Thus brooding with anxiety, he found no happiness anywhere.
Then, having left his home, he went into the presence of his guru: / "Salutation indeed to you, O guru, benefactor of the gods!
You are the protector of all worlds and the preserver of the brāhmaṇas. / You are the performer of sacrifices, O king of the twice-born; obeisance to you.
I am sonless, O sage among vipras; what is to be done, O lord? / Speak in such a manner that a son will certainly be born.
For a sonless man there is no destination in heaven, none at all; / by whatever means possible, one should bring about the birth of a son."
"Remembering this statement, I have come into your presence."
The guru said: / "Go, O tiger among sages, where the Sābhramatī River is; / having gone there, O best of sages, you will surely obtain sons."
Having heard that statement of his and bowed like a stick, / that king among vipras went toward the Sābhramatī River.
The sage among vipras named Maṅki, having gone there, / then performed great asceticism, O goddess, for a period of four years.
Where a tīrtha was established by that Maṅki who spoke the Veda, / in the Tretā age then, O goddess, that tīrtha of great wonder
arose there, without doubt, bestowing sons and granting all desires. / Even today, there has never been nor will there be anything equal to Maṅkitīrtha.
Having obtained sons as he wished and enjoyed diverse pleasures, / that best of twice-borns, Maṅki, went to my abode.

This divine narrative is supreme, purifying, and great; / merely by hearing it, one attains happiness through sons and everything else.

Then one should go, O goddess of the gods, to Brahmavallī, a great ford. / Listen directly to the nature of that ford, O best of the gods.

Where the water of the Sābhramatī unites with the water of the Brahmavallī, / that Brahmatīrtha is considered equal to Prayāga.

By offering a rice-ball there, the ancestors certainly attain satisfaction / for twelve years, in accordance with the word of Brahmā.

The merit at Brahmavallī is especially equal to a śrāddha at Gayā; / performing it there consciously, the ancestors find satisfaction.

The gift of a cow, the gift of land, and likewise the gift of food— / the merit [obtained] especially at Brahmavallī is equal to these gifts.

Right here, Sanaka and the others, having bathed according to the rules, / reached the world of Viṣṇu through meditation on the supreme state of Brahman.

Whatever fruit a man obtains by going to Puṣkara, / to the Gaṅgā, and to the sacred field of Amarakaṇṭaka, O ruler of the gods,

they go to heaven, having bathed [there], O ruler of the gods. / Wearing a garland of tulasī and remembering Nārāyaṇa, / one indeed goes to the imperishable realm, divine and blissful Vaikuṇṭha.

Thus ends the glorification of the Brahmavallī Ford. / Then one should go to the Vṛṣa Ford, renowned in Khaṇḍatīrtha, / where, having bathed in ancient times, cows attained heaven and Goloka.

Because cows, the mothers of the world, fallen through a curse, were rescued / by Dharma in the form of a bull, it is therefore called Khaṇḍatīrtha.

Pārvatī said: / Whose curse, indeed, fell upon the cows, the mothers of the worlds, in the past? / How did they fall from their world, and how were they protected by Dharma?

Mahādeva said: / Formerly in Goloka, as a bull was sporting with the cows, / dung and urine were dropped and fell upon the head of Hara.

Then Hara gave them a curse on account of that fault: / 'Deprived of consciousness, cows, you shall depart from your own world to the earth!'

Cursed by the Lord, the cows propitiated Hara again, / and begged the god: 'May we regain our world!'
