He, the best among upholders of dharma, protecting the earth with dharma, / delighted the people with his abundant virtues as a lord of the earth.
The queen of that king was the daughter of the ruler of Magadha, / known by the name Sudakṣiṇā, like Śacī to the lord of heaven.
When a great amount of time had passed and no son was born to the queen, / that emperor, the lord of Kośala, reflected in his own mind:
'The earth-circle, held up and adorned with ocean, Mount Meru, and other precious mountains, / serves only as an ornament, not bringing offspring to me who am childless.'
'The three aims of life have been pursued in due season without contradiction, / yet in my heart, being childless, there is no happiness.'
[The king thought:] / “Viṣṇu and the foremost gods headed by Indra have been worshipped with sacrifices, / and oblong ponds, pleasure-gardens, and wells have been constructed everywhere on earth.
With cows, lands, gold, clothes, and meals endowed with the six flavors, / brāhmaṇas and guests have indeed been pleased by me with devotion.
Having uprooted rulers of the earth in battle according to dharma for sustenance, / the treasury has indeed been augmented by me with immense wealth.
Those who walk on wrong paths, the intoxicated, those who transgress their own duty, / and those who turn away from the ancestors and gods—those who deserve punishment have been punished by me.
On the five festival days, on the Vaiṣṇava day, on the day of the Sun, during rites for the ancestors, / and on the tenth and eleventh lunar days, intercourse with women was not practiced by me.
I did not neglect my own wife when she had bathed at the end of the fertile period, / and even during an infertile period, if I was requested by her at an appropriate time,
then sport was enjoyed with her, full of passion, since she was passionate. / In this way, duty, wealth, and pleasure were pursued by me according to the appropriate time.
By what fault does no offspring arise in my queen? / Vasiṣṭha is our teacher, who knows the past and the future.

He will declare that fault because of which a son is not born to me.” / Devala said: / Having reflected thus, that king, intending to go to his guru's hermitage, / entrusted the Kosala country, rich in prosperity, to his ministers.
Then, having worshipped the god who creates offspring, on an auspicious day / the couple, desiring a son, set out for their guru's hermitage.
Traversing the path in a few days, seated in a single chariot, / the couple reached their guru’s auspicious hermitage in the evening—
[to the hermitage of] the sage who had completed the Vaiśvadeva rite and was receiving newly arrived guests, / who was purifying the resident sages as well as arriving visitors
with the wreaths of smoke rising from the substances offered in the fire; / which was sluggish due to deer whose bellies were completely filled with masses of dūrvā grass,
who were approaching all around the pavilion along with herds of does; / bustling with the clamor of flocks of birds gathering in roosting trees;
where tigers, deer, and others had mutually abandoned their natural enmity; / where the sound of the Vedas had momentarily grown quiet due to the ṛṣis engaged in silent recitation and meditation;
where young boys were engaged in play that had arisen at the time of non-study. / In that [hermitage], the couple saw Vasiṣṭha, who had finished his rituals,
seated untroubled on a seat of sacred grass, attended by Arundhatī. / He bowed to the feet of his guru, and the queen bowed to his wife.
The guru also blessed him with a benediction, and Arundhatī blessed her. / Then, having honored that guest with madhuparka and other offerings,
Vasiṣṭha, the foremost among the venerable, asked him with honors: / Vasiṣṭha said: / “Hail, O best among kings! Is there prosperity in your realm,
in your family, and among your people, who follow their own duty? / Is the earth righteously protected by you, O hero?
Does your intellect, being sattvic, augment your treasury? / Do your countrymen and citizens, O king, being full of essence,
not abandon their own station, just as the oceans [do not abandon their bounds], / through affection, companionship, and cohabitation, O lord?
Are the couples in your city like Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa to you? / Do the desired vows of the subjects in your city, O best of kings, / bear their desired fruit, like the Haricandana tree in heaven?”
Devala said: / Having asked thus, that best of sages, Vasiṣṭha, the eminent ascetic, / fed the king with foods brought forth by the power of his yoga.
And Arundhatī of noble mind, endowed with great respect, / fed that queen with various condiments and cooked dishes.
The sage, having composed himself, took by the hand the king who had finished his meal, / was sitting peacefully, and was bowing down, and asked him again:

Vasiṣṭha said: / “A kingdom endowed with the seven limbs, whose subjects are devoted to their own duties, / whose kinsmen and ministers are pleased, whose warriors know the rules of weapons and missiles,
whose friends are subdued, whose enemies are removed, and whose mind is intent on the worship of Kṛṣṇa— / of what use is the kingdom of heaven to that king who possesses such a realm?
The righteous kings of the Ikṣvāku dynasty, having begotten sons / and having placed the kingdom upon them, repaired to austerities, O lord.
You are young and have not yet seen a son's face; you are not eligible for the performance of penance. / For what purpose have you come here, having abandoned such a kingdom?”
The king said: / “O brāhmaṇa, I have not come to your hermitage to perform penance / having abandoned such a kingdom out of a desire for heaven.
"O brāhmaṇa, what you have said is true: having placed the kingdom upon their sons, / the scions of the Ikṣvāku lineage went to the penance grove.
Even after going to heaven, this earthly kingdom was not abandoned by them; / for their lineage stands here dejected in this my form.
Just as childhood has passed, O father, and youth has arrived, / so too will it pass away today, and old age will certainly come.
After old age comes death for a man, without a doubt. / When I have met death, O brāhmaṇa, without the birth of a son,
to whom will this kingdom of the earth belong? Tell me, O guru! / Therefore, even as I dwell in the kingdom without offspring,
there is no sense of possessiveness for me here, because of its future absence. / Indeed, you thoroughly know the three aims of life, O my guru!
By what fault is no son born to me, O treasury of penance? / Seeing that fault through meditation, tell it to me quickly, O guru;

having heard it, I shall apply a remedy to obtain offspring."
Devala said:
Having thus heard the words of that lord of the earth,

Vasiṣṭha perceived the cause of the obstruction to his lineage through deep concentration and spoke.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Formerly, O tiger among kings, having served the leader of the gods,
you set out for your own palace, remembering this wife of yours who had bathed [after her period]. / As you were going in haste, O dear one, longing for offspring,
the Wish-Fulfilling Cow was standing at the root of a celestial tree on your path. / You aroused intense anger in her, whose foot-dust is worthy of worship,
as you failed to perform the customary circumambulation and obeisance. / Out of excessive fury, she cursed you: 'A son will not be born to you,
as long as you do not perform service to my offspring!' / Going in haste to provide during the fertile period, desirous of a son,
you did not hear that curse even slightly, on account of the roar of the sky's chariots. / Worship Nandinī, the daughter's daughter of that cow, [who is here] with her calf at my [hermitage],

together with this your wife; she will bestow a son upon you."
Devala said:
While the sage Vasiṣṭha was speaking thus,

Nandinī returned from the penance grove, her udders dripping milk out of affection for her calf. / Seeing her, Vasiṣṭha, best of sages, became glad of heart; / pointing out Nandinī, he spoke once more to the king.

Vasiṣṭha said:
"O king, she whose name is auspicious at the mere recollection has indeed arrived; / therefore know that the success of your objective stands close at hand.
Worshipped by you and your wife by following her in the forest and in the hermitage, / she will bestow a son upon you through her grace; of this there is no doubt.
See to it that no wild creature attacks her; / pasture her thus in the forest, O best of kings, bearing a bow against predatory beasts."

Devala said:
Saying 'So be it' to the king who spoke briefly, and to his daughter-in-law, the ascetic gave a hut for the night's sleep; / having laid down upon the earth strewn with darbha grass together with his wife, the ruler of men spent the night there with a controlled mind.

title: tryadhikadviśatatamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
Devala said:
Then, at dawn, the lord of men took the cow Nandinī, / worshipped with flowers and other offerings by the queen, and went to the forest.
Following behind the divine cow as she walked, the king went like a shadow; / following her as she ate young grass and the like, he too ate roots and wild produce;
he sat down following her when she sat in the shade of a tree; / the king also drank water following her when she drank water.
Thus the king served the Wish-Fulfilling Cow of his guru / with tender mouthfuls of grass, by warding off gadflies, and by scratching her.
Then, in the evening, she returned toward the hermitage, / purifying the body of the lord of the earth with particles of dust raised by her hooves.
Walking slowly beneath her heavy weight [of udders], Nandinī shone / as if oppressed by the great burden of the king's enterprise.
Near the sage's hermitage, the queen went out to meet her, / bringing sandalwood paste, unbroken rice, food offerings, incense, and the like;
having worshipped her according to the rule, bowing repeatedly, / and performing circumambulation, the queen stood before her with folded palms.
Having accepted that worship performed with faith by her, / resting steadily with the king, she went with the two of them to the hermitage.
While Dilīpa was thus worshipping her, firm in his vow, / twenty-one days passed.
Then, wishing to ascertain the king's disposition, / she entered a grassy cave of the Himālaya, her heart free from fear.
Then, while the king was looking at the beauty of the slopes of the Himālaya, / a lion whose approach went unnoticed seized Nandinī by force.
The cow cried out intensely with a pitiful sound like one distressed, / awakening an upsurge of compassion in the heart of that archer.
Hearing her cry of distress, that ruler of the world / turned his gaze which was fixed on the slope of the Himālaya.
Seeing that cow with tears streaming down her face, / and the lion with sharp fangs and claws upon her, the king was stricken with grief.
Perceiving that she was seized by that lion, the archer / sent forth his right arm to draw an arrow from his quiver.
Having drawn the arrow from the quiver to slay that king of beasts, / the ruler of the earth fitted it and drew it back fully with the bowstring.
His entire body rendered stiff by the lion's glance, / the king was unable to release the arrow; thereupon he was astonished.
Perceiving the king in such a state, that king of beasts / spoke in human speech, causing him to experience still greater amazement:

The lion said:
"O king, I know you to be Dilīpa, born in the solar lineage; / and know me to be Kumbhodara, an attendant of Śambhu.
This cedar tree which stands in your field of view / was nourished like a son by Pārvatī with an affectionate heart.
Once, O great king, as a wild elephant was rubbing its temples [against it], / its exceedingly soft bark was torn away.
Perceiving it in such a state, Mṛḍānī, filled with compassion, / stationed me here as a lion to protect it.
The goddess said to me: 'Listen, Kumbhodara! / Residing here, you may eat whatever creature comes here.'
From that time forth, O best of kings, obeying her command, / I reside in this cave which is guarded by all the gods.
You should not be amazed at the numbness of your own body; / great is the power of Śiva's illusion here on the Himālaya.
You cannot strike at me as if at an ordinary lion, / for the Lord steps upon my back when mounting his bull.
Turn back and protect your own body, the instrument for accomplishing all ends; / by destiny this cow has been brought here, O hero, for my food."

Devala said:
Having heard his speech addressing him as 'hero', / Dilīpa, whose body had been frozen stiff, replied to him.

The king said:
"O king of beasts, I bow to Śiva, the cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction of the universe, / and to Ambikā, the mother of the world.
And you are worthy of my respect, O king of beasts, as their servant; / hear the words that I speak, and instruct me: what should I do?"
Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā, is our preceptor known to you. / His cow named Nandinī is this one, fulfiller of all desires.
She was given by him to me to worship, for the generation of offspring. / This very [cow] has been properly worshipped by me for several days.
This mother of a young calf has been seized by you in the mountain cave. / She cannot be rescued from you by force by Śambhu's servant [like me].
How can I go before that sage without her? / She is the granddaughter of Kāmadhenu, glorious, worthy to be served by the world.
There is no other cow equal to her with which I might appease him. / Therefore, having released this cow, make me your prime food.

I offer my own body, soiled with dishonour. / Thus there would be no loss of dharma for the sage, and there will be food for you; / and for me, giving up my life for the sake of the cow, the highest state [will be attained].’
Devala said: / Having heard this, when silence was kept by the lion, O lord of men, / the king, skilled in dharma, fell down before him with downcast face.
As he was awaiting the extremely unbearable leap of the lion, / a shower of flowers dropped from above, released by the lords of the gods.
Hearing the words, ‘Arise, son!’, that king arose. / He beheld that cow like a mother, and not the lord of beasts.
Nandinī spoke this to that astonished best of kings. / Nandinī said: / ‘You were tested by me through an illusion in the form of a lion.
By the power of the sage, O king, even Antaka is unable to seize me / even in thought; whence would there be the power in other embodied beings to seize [me]?
By the offering of your own body, you were intent on protecting me. / Therefore I am pleased with you; choose a desired boon.’
The king said: / ‘The conduct that exists within embodied beings is not hidden from one like you. / Therefore, O mother, you know my desired [wish]; give that to me.
Grant me a son by the daughter of the king of Magadha, the founder of the lineage. / Nothing is impossible for pure ones like you.’
Having spoken thus, the king folded his hands and stood before him, / silent, awaiting his answer, with eyes fixed upon him.
Devala said: / Having heard these words of that king, Nandinī, / who accomplishes the purposes of the ancestors, gods, sages, and humans, said:
Nandinī said: / ‘Son, having milked my milk in a leaf-cup, drink as you desire. / When instructed by the preceptor at the hermitage, you will drink what remains again.

A son, the founder of your lineage, knower of the true nature of weapons and missiles, will be [born] to you.’ / Devala said: / Addressed thus by the daughter of Surabhi, he spoke to her with humility:
Dilīpa said: / ‘O mother, I shall drink the remainder only after every rite has been performed. / Having obtained the sweet nectar of your words, I am satisfied, O mother.
I desire nothing else, just as the cātaka bird desires water from a row of clouds. / By serving you, O mother, I have become the source of everything.
Like a fool towards knowledge that is worthy of worship by all people, / even the curse given by your grandmother became a boon to me.

Without that, whence would be the attainment of a son for me, and whence the sight of you? / Nevertheless, O mother, one like you is to be worshipped only for a boon; / for surely no one desires poison from Mahādeva, the giver of the three aims of life.’
Devala said: / Having heard those words of his, that cow, pleased, saying ‘Well done, well done!’, / addressed [him] and, of great pride, went to the hermitage together with him.
There also, worshipped by the king's wife just as on the previous day, / that cow appeared pleased, like the success of a task embodied.
Perceiving the serene face of the lord of the earth, the deer-eyed woman / knew that her desired purpose, for the sake of which the effort was made, was accomplished.
Then the couple, with the cow whose worship was duly performed, / went with her before the preceptor, having accomplished their purpose.
Looking at the two of them whose lotus-faces were cheerful, that best of sages, / a treasury of suprasensory knowledge, spoke this, gladdening [them]:
Vasiṣṭha said: / ‘O king, I know that this cow has indeed become pleased with you both; / indeed, an extraordinary radiance of face is observed in you two today.
Surabhi and the wishing tree are renowned as fulfillers of desires. / Having worshipped her offspring, if one's purpose is accomplished, what wonder is there?
She gives every wish when praised even from afar, O sinless one; / what then when served with faith nearby, like the celestial river?
Through knowledge, the wonderful test made by her of you was known to me; / O lord of the earth, you also protected your own dharma, and just as that [happened].
In you, she recognized the favour of my mind as the disposition in herself, / and was pleased just as Kamalā is with Hari, or as Pārvatī attaches herself to Giriśa.
Let this night be spent here together with your wife, intent upon the worship of the cow. / O noble king, you will go to your own city tomorrow, the rite being completed.’

Devala said: / ‘O vaiśya, having thus worshipped the cow, having obtained his desire along with his wife, / in the morning, having yoked his chariot and having received the instruction of the preceptor, he went home.
Within a few days, Raghu was born to that Dilīpa, / by whose name the lineage of Raghu became renowned on earth.
The man who recites this story of King Dilīpa / shall obtain wealth, grain, and a son in this world, O vaiśya.

O Śarabha, for the sake of obtaining an excellent son, quickly please Gaurī together with her according to your intellect; / she will indeed give you an irreproachable son, possessed of virtues, the bearer of the family’s burden.’

Śivaśarma said: / Having related this holy and most charming conduct of King Dilīpa to Śarabha, / and having instructed him in the rite for the worship of Ambikā, the sage went to his desired destination.

title: caturadhikadviśatatamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Śivaśarma said: / ‘O Viṣṇuśarma, then the vaiśya Śarabha together with his wife, / having taken the worship materials, went to the temple of glorious Caṇḍikā.
There, having bathed according to rule, filled with devotion, / they worshipped Caṇḍikā with flowers, incense, and lamps, wishing for a son.
Worshipped by the two of them with faith for seven days, Ambikā, / having become visible with a serene mind, spoke with [her] voice.
Pārvatī said: / ‘O vaiśya, I am pleased with your very firm devotion; / I grant you a son, O virtuous one, for whose sake you strive.
Go, do not delay, to the Indra-forest and Khāṇḍava; / there is an excellent, greatly holy sacred site named Indraprastha.
There is a sacred site there, awakening the Vedas, granting all desires, / created by Bṛhaspati; having bathed there, desiring a son,
by your bathing there, O dear one, a son will surely be born to you. / Having bathed there, O dear, even I obtained Skanda, the slayer of the enemies of the gods.’
Śivaśarma said: / Having heard these words of the goddess, my father along with his wife / came here to this good sacred site and bathed, desiring a son.
He gave a hundred cows with accessories to the brāhmaṇas, / and the wise man duly gratified the gods and the ancestors here.
Having dwelt there for seven nights with restrained minds, / the couple went to their own home, their lotus-faces blooming with the attainment of their desired object.
In that very month the embryo developed day by day in my mother; / after the ninth month had passed, I was born in the auspicious tenth.
O Viṣṇuśarman, what has been told to you by me is an ancient event; / all this was heard from my father's mouth when I was just twenty years old.
Once, seeing me capable of managing household affairs, my father, / attaining detachment from the world, handed over the household to me.
And that righteous soul, his mind attached to Govinda, spoke to me, / censuring attachment to sense-objects and praising devotion to Viṣṇu again and again.
The father said: / "O wise one, old age has arrived, and my hair has turned gray. / I shall serve the lotus feet of Govinda, served by the virtuous.
By serving Him, the mind becomes pure and very steady; / that man, content in the self, desires nothing at all.
Free of desire, experiencing natural good and bad deeds through pleasure and pain, / when they are exhausted, casting off the body, he becomes unborn.
Material wealth and the pleasure of the guṇas last only so long as the bliss of consciousness is not attained; / upon attaining that, they become worthless, like buttermilk compared to nectar.
Hari's māyā is powerful, which deludes the embodied soul; / he does not know what is beneficial for him, just like intoxication from liquor.
Through knowledge and ignorance, He brings about active life and cessation at will in due time, / for that Lord engages in child's play.
When action prescribed by the Veda is performed by one desiring its fruit, / that is worldly action, dear one; superior is the offering of those actions to the Lord.
Just as burnt seeds do not sprout despite effort, / so actions offered to the Lord of the Universe without desire [bear no binding fruit].
The dissolution of actions that bestow pleasure and pain is liberation, / whereas their generation is bondage—this is the conclusion of the scriptures.
Therefore, performing the action taught by the Veda without desiring any fruit, / I shall wander among holy bathing places, holding devotion to Hari in my heart.
Thus experiencing commenced actions without dreading others, / I shall destroy the disease of worldly existence by drinking the medicine of company with the virtuous."
Śivaśarman said: / "Having heard such words of that father of mine, / I said—O Viṣṇuśarman, listen to it in truth:
The vaiśya's son said: / 'These people are hard to please; they will tell of no glory of yours, [saying]: / "He has gone away, fleeing in distress from a wicked family."
This is the Viṣṇupadī, father, the purifier of the three worlds; / remembered even from afar, she takes away sin. Why do you abandon her?
A sinful person, father, who dies even in Magadha, / his sins cast off in the Gaṅgā, goes to heaven. Cast aside what is inauspicious.
The sixty thousand sons of the great-souled Sagara, / burned by Kapila's wrath, went to heaven by her touch.
Leaving her, this staircase to heaven that even grants liberation, / attended by seekers of liberation, father, do not go elsewhere.
Do not despise the nearby Gaṅgā, honored by the gods; / served, she will grant whatever you desire, fortunate one.'"

“Even animals, when their life ends in its water without knowledge,
reach Brahman. How then can you abandon it?”

Śivaśarman said:
Hearing this speech, my father, lover of truth,
lived in his house, turned away from all sensual pleasures.

Taking a bath every day in the Gaṅgā at the three divisions of the day,
he regularly went wherever a Purāṇa was [recited] in a house.

Once, the wise man, listening to the greatness of the Yamunā’s holy sites,
heard there, O son, the glorification of this holy site:

“Compared to Avimukta, Haridvāra, Prayāga, and Puṣkara,
Ayodhyā, Dvārikā, Kāñcī, Mathurā, and other places,

the merit of this [place], containing all holy sites, is a hundred times greater.”
Having heard this spoken by that learned Sūta, my father,

abandoning his home, went to that holy site unnoticed by everyone,
just like us two, noble one, serving the feet of Govinda.

Having come here, noble one, desiring liberation, my father,
bathing at the three divisions of the day at the holy site Nigamodbodhaka,
lived for several months indeed at this best of holy sites.

Performing his daily rites, the wise man, free from desires even in the house of Brahmā,
was suddenly struck once by an extremely severe fever.

Through his great torment, he lost consciousness and swooned;
for a muhūrta my father remained in that condition, fainting.

Afterwards, his life-breath returning, reflecting on this at that time:
“Alas, what distress has befallen me! My righteous son is far away,

the wise one who would comfort me whose limbs are tormented by fever!
The terrible sin of approaching an illicit woman that was committed by me,

for that not even an expiation was performed; what will be my fate?
My son will come; to him I shall give my wealth.”

“What was hidden by me in the house was not seen by me either.”
Śivaśarman said: As he was thinking thus, a traveler oppressed by rain,

suffering from the cold, his body trembling, entered the hut then.
Seeing him lying down, going once again near him,

recognizing, “This is an ascetic,” the wayfarer bowed with his head,
and said: “Why are you asleep, O sage? The twilight has arrived.

The sun is setting; this is not the time for your sleep.”
Upon these words being merely spoken by the traveler, my father,

Śarabha, his limbs burning with fever, said to him somehow: “Ah!
Śarabha said: Let the word that I speak before you be heard, O traveler!

Hearing it, O good man, who have arrived by my good fortune, please do this:
I am a vaiśya named Śarabha; my home is in Kānyakubja.

Though forbidden by wife, friends, and sons, I came here,
having heard the glorification of this holy site proclaimed from the mouth of my son.

A few months have passed, O good man, since I arrived;
three days have now elapsed while I have been suffering from fever.

My vital breaths had departed, and today have returned again;
surely some remainder of life still remains for me, O good man,

since, having seen the abode of Yama, I have returned once more!
By some rise of fortune you have arrived here near me.

Lead me to my home, friend; I shall give you much wealth!
I will give even more upon reaching home; show mercy, O ocean of compassion!

Digging in the ground here, take my wealth.”
Śivaśarman said: Hearing this, that evil-minded rustic, addicted to sensual pleasures,

greedy for wealth, said to him: “I will carry out what you said.”
Having said this, digging up the wealth from that spot of ground then,

he placed it before Śarabha, and the traveler said:
The traveler said: “This wealth has been extracted by me from your ground, O lord of vaiśyas.

Give it quickly to me to bring a litter,
mounting you on which, suffering from fever, I may take you to your dwelling.”

Śivaśarman said: Addressed thus by him, he then gave three palas of gold.
He too, taking the father's wealth, went to Lavaṇapattana.

Having stayed for one night, he brought a litter with its accoutrements,
along with bearers, O son, having given two palas of gold.

The two palas [remaining] were taken by that very one of unrighteous mind.
Having mounted Śarabha, the best of vaiśyas, onto the litter,

that traveler set out, urging the bearers toward Kānyakubja.
Taking the water in a water-pot from this excellent holy site,

giving it little by little to drink to him who was tormented by thirst, the traveler went on.
Then they alighted on the bank of a lake along the way to eat.

Having bathed and eaten, they set out again from that place with haste.
Traversing some distance, suffering from thirst, from the water-pot

having drunk water, he also gave [it] to drink to that Śarabha who was tormented by thirst.
Then a certain terrifying rākṣasa, named Vikaṭa,

wandering in the lonely forest, caught sight of them as they went.
Seeing them, seized by hunger, swift, with mouth wide open,

he rushed toward them, making the earth tremble with the striking of his feet.
Arriving swiftly at their side, those bearers and that traveler

he seized along with the palanquin, and, moving in the air, whirled them around;
by that very whirling, when their lives were gone, he dashed them to the earth.

He ate their flesh, and drank their blood from the palanquin.
“Where will this man stricken with disease go before me?

Him I will eat, but first I shall drink water.”
Resolving thus, the water from the water-pot of this holy site

that foremost of night-roamers threw into his mouth at that time.
As soon as the water was thrown in, memory of his previous birth

arose, and he turned back from the slaughter of that Śarabha.
The sin committed in his previous birth also came to his memory,

by which he had become a rākṣasa despite being born a brāhmaṇa.
Remembering his sin, quickly approaching near Śarabha,
the rākṣasa, having attained knowledge, spoke to my father:

The rākṣasa said:
“O tiger among men! Who are you, and who are these people
who were eaten by me, a vile rākṣasa of terrible form?

Of which excellent holy site is this water, by whose power
even for me, a sinner, memory of my previous birth has arisen?”

The vaiśya said:
“I am a vaiśya, O best of rākṣasas; my home is in Kānyakubja.
Wandering among holy sites, I arrived at Indraprastha.

He was requested by me: ‘Bringing a litter, take me home.’
And that traveler, bringing a litter quickly,

and mounting me on it, the firm man set out toward my home.
That traveler and those bearers of the litter have now been eaten

by you. And of which holy site this water is, hear that:
In the Khāṇḍava forest of Indra there is the Yamunā, best of rivers.

On its bank is Hariprastha, a holy site best among the best holy sites.
There is the holy site of the teacher of the gods, accomplishing all aims,

Nigamodbodhaka, by drinking whose water your memory was born.
All this has been recounted to you, since I was questioned here by you.

I ask you something, O night-roamer; tell it quickly!
Do you remember here now the action done in your previous birth?
Say, what sin was committed by you, because of which you became a rākṣasa?”
The rākṣasa said: / "Formerly I was a brāhmaṇa in an auspicious family of Vedic scholars, / but of evil conduct and unrighteous mind. Listen, I tell you all.
Indeed, continually gambling with dice alongside experts in it, / I lost vast wealth, my own and my father's.
My father reported my deeds to the king, and by his men / I was expelled penniless from the city. I went to a nearby village.
There was a friend of mine, an excellent brāhmaṇa named Devaka; / by him I was sheltered in his house, showing me hospitality for a long time.
Living there comfortably, overcome by lust, I forcibly enjoyed / his beautiful wife once when my friend had gone away.
Having consumed deadly poison, that virtuous woman died instantly; / seeing her, I fled in the dead of night, enveloped in darkness.
Fleeing swiftly, I was seized by the king's servants; / [shouting], 'This is a thief!' they severed my head with a sword.
Entering me, who was dead, into a body of torment, Yama's servants / threw me into the dreadful Raurava hell at Yama's command.
Having suffered intense torment there for sixty thousand years, / by that very sin I became a rākṣasa.
A hundred years have passed in the state of a rākṣasa, O lord of the people; / tell me the means by which I may attain release from this.
I tell you of the merit that was performed, good sir, listen respectfully, / by which this water of the excellent holy place entered my mouth.
In that very birth, having observed the fast on Hari's day, / out of association rather than desire, O vaiśya, I kept awake at night.
Then, on the twelfth day, having bathed and preparing to eat, / a certain Vaiṣṇava, bearing the form of Viṣṇu, arrived at my house.
Angered upon seeing him, I spoke harsh words before him: / 'Where are you going, you hypocritical wrongdoer, among the women?'
When he was spoken to thus by me, the steadfast [sage], equal in honour and dishonour, / silently walked out of my house and departed,
Then my devoted wife, coming toward him, / fell at his feet and brought that holy man back to the house.
Though insulted by me, the great-souled man felt no anger, / nor did he feel joy when honored by her, for he looked upon enemy and friend alike.
Having worshiped him properly and seated him on a seat, she said, / 'Feed him food, lord of my life; may the three worlds conquer!'
thus addressed by that virtuous woman, I, dejected of face, said to that noble-minded [guest] with a bright countenance: / “Rise, appease your hunger.”
Having said this, that slender-waisted woman, urged [by me], / washed his feet and seated him again upon an excellent seat.
I gave a vessel filled with food to that discerning man / and water in his hand, repeatedly impelled by that virtuous woman.
Having eaten at his leisure, undisturbed, that righteous soul / went away, chanting: 'Hare Rāma, Hare Kṛṣṇa!'
This merit was performed in my former birth, O vaiśya, when urged by my wife, / by which this water of the holy place was brought to me."
Śivaśarman said: / "O Viṣṇuśarman, while the rākṣasa stood there after speaking these words, / that traveler and those who had carried him, possessing divine bodies, spoke from the sky.
The palanquin-bearers of the traveler said: / 'O virtuous lord of the people, though we met an untimely death, / by your grace, having drunk this water, we have attained godhood.
Since we set out in your company, O lord of the vaiśyas, out of greed for wealth, / our desire for wealth was entirely gone at the time of death.
Indeed, as the water of this king of holy places remained in our bellies / at the moment of death, by its power friendship with the Lord of Wealth was attained.
We bow to you; we are going to the city of the Lord of Wealth, O master, / by celestial chariots brought by his attendants and adorned with various gems.
Depart, do not delay, to the holy place that teaches the Veda; / along with this one, O good man, quickly liberate him as well!'"
Śivaśarman said: / "Having spoken thus, dear one, they departed in the northern direction completely, / making heaven and earth resound with the chiming of bells from their celestial chariots.
Then the vaiśya, my father, spoke to that night-wanderer. / Śarabha said: / 'Rise, take me quickly to the holy place that teaches the Veda.
Afflicted with fever, I cannot go there on foot; / there is no one other than you who can take me to that holy site.
Śivaśarman said: / "Saying, 'So be it,' and comforting the vaiśya, that night-wanderer / placed him on his shoulder and went swiftly to that purifying holy place."
Both of them, the merchant and the rākṣasa, dwelt there, / performing merely ablutions in that highest of all holy places.
Then, having heard of the great and severe pain of my father, / I was urged on by my mother and set out from my home.
Arriving here, I saw him afflicted with a severe fever. / I bowed my head to him, and he blessed me and spoke:
Śarabha said: / For what purpose have you come here on this long road, my son? / Stay for a few days, performing your duties here.
A friend of mine, a rākṣasa named Vikaṭa, is approaching. / Rise up and prostrate with your body like a staff at his feet.
You must not fear him, for he has abandoned violent acts and the like; / having now reached the sacred ford, he stays near me.
Śivaśarman said: / Thus addressed at that time by my noble father Śarabha, / I rose and fell prostrate like a staff at his feet upon the earth.
Lifting me up with both arms, the rākṣasa embraced me tightly, / and said, 'Welcome, son of my friend,' bestowing a blessing.
The rākṣasa said: / Fortunate are you, my son, that you have come here / upon hearing of the terrible fever-affliction of your righteous father.
You pay your debt to your father by offering water with sesamum in the sacred ford. / Having bathed, perform your rites; you will remember your past birth.
Śivaśarman said: / Thus addressed then by him, I entered into the sacred ford's excellent waters to bathe, / remembering, my son, the good and evil of my previous birth.
Having bathed according to rule, I returned right here to my father's side, / and asked about the story of the rākṣasa: 'From where has this righteous mind of his arisen?'
The account of the rākṣasa, the beasts of burden, and the traveler was recounted by my father. / Having heard it, I indeed praised this king of holy fords.
'When my father becomes free from disease, then / I will go home'—so resolving, I stayed here for ten days.
Within ten days, my son, the death of my father / occurred, half-submerged in the water, as the king of holy fords looked on.
Then, mounted upon Garuḍa and bearing Śrī upon his chest, / Viṣṇu himself arrived, his body like a fresh cloud,
clad in yellow garments, four-armed, with eyes reddish like lotuses, / accompanied by Brahmā, Indra, and the celestial beings, along with the foe of Andhaka,
being attended by Kinnaras singing the multitude of his virtues, / and being praised on all sides by Hāhā, Hūhū, and others.
Having granted his own form and placing him on Garuḍa, / he ascended to Vaikuṇṭha with my father, surrounded by Brahmā and the others.
Beholding my father attain the form of Viṣṇu, I thought, / observing this in my heart, then the dawn of ultimate reality arose:
'The majesty of this crest-jewel of holy fords cannot truly be described, / in half of whose water a dying creature becomes four-armed!
I must by no means abandon this king of holy fords / of manifestly firm greatness, out of thirst for wealth, relief from illness, and the like.
I must remain here in my father's hut / as long as the fruits of commenced actions are experienced on the face of the earth.'
Reflecting thus and having performed the funeral rites for my father, / I stayed, longing for liberation, in the company of that rākṣasa.

title: paṃcādhikadviśatatamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Śivaśarman said: / Once, seeing a milk-giving cow sunk in the mire at this great holy ford, / that foremost of rākṣasas entered it to rescue her.
'In protecting a cow lies great dharma; heavenly destination comes to the protector'— / while reflecting thus in the midst, he was seized by an alligator.
Dragged down beneath the waters, his belly filled with water, / his body crushed by it, he instantly gave up his life.
Assuming a divine form, an aerial chariot brought for him / by an attendant sent by the gods headed by Indra,
as he was departing, that foremost of night-wanderers was questioned by me: / 'Having met death here at this great, rarely attained holy ford that bestows liberation,
how has the attainment of the realm of the gods come to you, O noble-minded one?' / Thus addressed, he said to me: 'Such was my wish here, O sinless one.'
When that virtuous soul had gone to heaven, the realm of the meritorious, / alone then, I took Viṣṇu as my true refuge.
Walking, standing, sleeping, waking, and bathing constantly, / I meditated with single-minded focus on that very Lotus-Eyed One:
'O Hari, I have taken refuge in your lotus feet; / my mind has no desire for the status of Brahmā, Maheśa, or Indra!'
Praying thus, my son, to that very Supreme Being, / I dwelt at this great holy ford, making my mind detached from sense objects.
Viṣṇuśarman said: / If your death occurred while dwelling at this great holy ford, / how is it that you have attained rebirth again? This is my doubt.
Even those who, abandoning the sacred boundary of this holy ford out of greed for wealth, / were killed by the rākṣasa—the traveler and the beasts of burden—
went to heaven simply by drinking the water of this best of holy fords. / Likewise, even that rākṣasa, meeting an untimely death in this place,
went to heaven by his own desire before your very eyes, killed by a crocodile. / Surely your death did not take place there, since rebirth is seen.
Nārada said: / Hearing the auspicious words of his son through Śiva, Śivaśarman / told the former account, the reason for his own birth.
Śivaśarman said: / Viṣṇuśarman, listen to this reason for my birth; / I shall relate it before you; having heard it, be free from doubt.
Once, while I was established in meditation during the worship of Viṣṇu, / Durvāsas, angry by nature, arrived at my hermitage.
Not knowing that he had arrived, devoted to the meditation on Viṣṇu, / I remained in that state for a long time, recollecting his name.
Having stood before me for an hour, fainting with rage, / that sage, his eyes deeply reddened, said this loudly to himself:
Durvāsas said: / 'Ah, I am the son of Atri, born of the womb of Anasūyā, / a portion of Śiva, yet I am utterly disregarded by this mortal!
By me Śakra was cast down from kingship over the three worlds; / even me this evil-minded mortal disregards!
Who is there that does not fear me as if from the fire of cosmic dissolution? / Leaving aside the triad of gods, the worlds are under my control!
Which deity is this fool meditating on, absorbed in contemplation? / Why does it not awaken him, seeing that Yama stands before him in bodily form?
Surely he meditates upon the god Nārāyaṇa, the teacher of the world, / satisfied by the nectar of whose meditation he has no external awareness.
Whether he meditates on Hari, or Brahmā, or Śaṃbhu, or another, / he must by all means be punished by me, for he has insulted me.'
Śivaśarman said: / Having reflected thus, he awakened me, despite my good intention, / and as I awoke, he cursed me, his eyes red with anger:
'Since in your heart, having disregarded me, a desire was formed during your meditation, / it shall not be fulfilled for you in this birth, but in every way it will happen [in the next]!'
When, having spoken thus, O dear one, that sage born of Atri departed, / then he was seized by the feet by me, who was terrified with fear.
And he was addressed: “O best of sages, let it be forgiven, let anger be cast away! / Those like me do not truly comprehend the actions of those like you.”
"You have pronounced a dreadful curse, which is now considered [unavoidable] by me. / Be gracious to me, bowing low, and grant me a favor at the curse's end!"
Addressed thus, Durvāsas abandoned his rage and became calm. / How could this not be proper, O dear one, since he is Śiva himself?
Becoming still, that wise best of brahmins said to me: / "Attaining death right here, you will not obtain birth again."
Thus having shown grace to me, the sky-clad sage departed, / having stayed for that day, O dear one, honoured with hospitality by me.
"The sage's word is not false," thinking thus also,
he went to his own home, carrying regret in his heart, [thinking] thus: / "Alas! For me, who constantly meditate and dwell in holy pilgrimage sites and hermitages,
the vision of the lord of Śrī has become hard to obtain in this birth, / as for a cātaka bird [the sight] of a cloud during the burning heat of summer.
From where did this obstructor of my journey to Vaikuṇṭha come to me, / like an unseasonal raincloud releasing water for a person about to set out?
There is surely no fault in the sage; it is truly the will of Hari himself. / For having granted a good vision, another birth has been ordained for me.
By me, terrified of saṃsāra, Hari's lotus feet must be clasped, / like a tree by a traveler scorched by the summer sun.
What is the use of wealth, children, wives, and other impermanent relatives / to me who repeatedly utter, 'Govinda, Supreme Bliss, Rāma'?
Sitting like an indifferent person among family members, worshipping Hari, / I will experience only what is begun by past deeds (prārabdha), holding off other actions."
Thinking thus, dear one, after a few days / I reached my own home, having bathed in the water of Hari's feet [the Gaṅgā].
The death of my father was told to my mother and to my kinsmen; / having heard it, they also grieved, but did not shake my steady [resolve].
Without desire for the worlds such as the world of Satya, living at home, / I met death on the bank of the Gaṅgā frequented by sages.
By the curse of the sage Durvāsas, I was born in a Vaiṣṇava family, / and obtaining death here at this true holy place, I will attain the abode of Hari.

Nārada said: / Thus, O fortunate one, those two best of twice-born ones, staying at that holy place established by the teacher of the gods [Bṛhaspati], / having narrated their past deeds to each other, remained contemplating the sprout-like feet of Hari.

Contemplating Hari, the lotus-eyed, four-armed one whose form is dark as a raincloud, / shining with the ornaments of his own weapons, they attained resemblance of form (sārūpya) with Hari right there by remembering [him].
This holy sacred field is named Indraprastha; / its legend has been told; hear its fruit, O Śiva:
Whatever merit arises from bathing in the Gaṅgā and whatever arises from the gift of a maiden, / a man attains that merit with faith from listening to this.
Whatever fruit arises on earth from the gift of a cow when a son is born, / and from bathing in the water of the Godāvarī when Jupiter is in Leo,

that fruit arises from listening to this; there is no doubt here. / Therefore, there is no other holy place yielding all desires than this best of holy places, / where upon dying, even animals surely become four-armed.

title: ṣaḍadhikadviśatatamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Saubhari said: / Hearing that speech of the sage Nārada, the glorious king Śibi, Dharmarāja, / with a pleased mind, said to him, that highest one:
Śibi said: / "O sage, the glorification of this best of holy places, which awakens knowledge of the Vedas, / has been properly described by you and heard by me as destroying sin.
In this Indraprastha there are indeed hundreds of holy places, O sage. / Explain the glorification of another one also, if there is any."
Nārada said: / "O king, this Dvārakā which lies within Indraprastha— / what happened here formerly, that I tell you; listen to me:
In Kāmpilya, there was a certain twice-born man, like the flower-arrowed [Kāma] embodied; / he would captivate the hearts of all women with his foremost charms.
Skilled in the science of music, possessing the sweet voice of a cuckoo, / once, holding a lute in his hand, playing it repeatedly,
and singing with a throat sweet like the call of a cuckoo, O king of men, / that intelligent man wandered in the city from street to street.
Hearing the sound of his singing, accompanied by melodic sweeps (mūrcchanā) and tonal patterns (tāna), / the city women abandoned their household tasks and went to him.
Bewitched by his beauty, they could not endure the surge of desire; / their vital essence flowed from them upon hearing the song before them.
By whom the mind of Brahmā was enticed toward Sarasvatī, / and by whom half of Śiva's body was caused to be given to Pārvatī,
what other person in the world, even if self-controlled or possessing knowledge, / is able to conquer that Love-god (Smara)? Women are fickle by nature.
They were unable to bear the onset of love, nor could they be restrained; / what is there to say, O king? For desire is hard to conquer in the world.
Then they went there, wherever he went, / as he sang forth with voice and lute, singing enchanted by his own tones.
Then, O ruler of men, their husbands, sons, brothers, and fathers, / arriving and scolding them, led them each to their own homes.
When, searching for him, all of them went to his presence again and again, / then the citizens reported that occurrence to the ruler.
The king also, having summoned that twice-born man, asked him in private: / 'By what mantra, O vipra, have those city women been infatuated?
Tell that to me, O best of vipras, and I will give you much wealth; / otherwise, I will banish you from my kingdom, without a doubt.'
Nārada said: / Hearing this speech of the king, that best of twice-born men, / an ocean of beauty and virtue, spoke the true word before him.
The twice-born man said: / 'In me, a beggar, there is neither mantra nor herb, O king; / but all the women in your city have uncontrolled senses.
Looking at my beauty and hearing the sound of my singing, / the women in your city cannot endure the urge of love, O king.
What can I do, O great king? What fault of mine is there, O lord? / A decree [of fate] is not to be transgressed, like past karma, O protector of the earth.'
Nārada said: / While the twice-born man was speaking thus, O king Śibi of the Uśīnaras, / then all the citizens gathered together and spoke thus to the ruler of the earth.
The citizens said: / 'O king, the city women have been bewitched by this vipra; / unrestrained by us, they do not stay in the houses.

If this bewitcher of women dwells in the city, O lord, / then today itself we will surely go to other countries. / Our bull of dharma, whose essence is the rites of offering to gods and ancestors, has departed;
like the cow of sinners, this [city] has departed after him from the field; / without him, O lord of men, it has gone to ruin, abandoned by fortune.
Now they will follow him, like cows in heat following a bull. / In an empty house, how can prosperity (Lakṣmī) remain, even with effort?
Dharma, wealth, and this home—these three depend on the woman, because / the wife is dependent on dharma and wealth, and does not remain when the two are lost.'
Nārada said: / While the citizens were speaking thus, their women arrived; / seated near the king, they spoke thus to one another.
The city women said: / 'Attaining this twice-born man whose form is fair as Kāma, our minds / blossom with joy, like lotuses in water at the sight of the sun.'
[and] without him they contract, like white water-lilies without the moon. / Joining together, let us seize him as he comes before the king.
He may not be killed, and we are his; what can the ruler of the earth do?" / Nārada said: Having spoken thus, they in haste seized that best of the twice-born,
in full view of their own husbands and in front of the king as well at that time. / And they said to him: "O lord of our hearts, come to [our] homes; appease
our passion at once! Without you today we simply cannot live!" / Having heard their words, that brahmin replied:
The brahmin said: / "I am your son; you are my mothers. / Why do you abandon your homes and wander about?
Worship your own husbands, through whom both worlds are assured. / When husbands are worshipped, Viṣṇu, the lord of all the gods,
becomes pleased; and when he is pleased, what indeed is hard to obtain in this world? / The woman who, abandoning her own husband, serves another out of desire for pleasure,
incurs blame and goes to a terrifying bad rebirth. / Having dwelt there until the end of a kalpa, as long as that deceit of her husband [merits],
emerging again from that [state], she falls into the condition of an immobile being; / from that, too, she obtains the status of an animal for many births.
Released from that, in a human existence she becomes deformed in that life. / Knowing thus the destiny of sin, turn back from this person!
Otherwise, at the end of the body, you will go to a most terrible hell. / If you desire my pleasure, you will not obtain it here; / for it is sin alone for you, by which men fall down."
Nārada said: / Hearing his words and seeing the faces of their husbands, / with faces bent low in shame, they [drooped] like creepers struck down by the wind.
The most terrible fire of passion of those women of the city / subsided through the cooling water of the words of that brahmacārin.
Rising, all of them went along, reproaching Love / who brings delusion even upon the gods headed by Brahmā and Indra, O king.
The women said: / "Fie upon this evil-doing [Kāma], the axe to the timber of good conduct! / kāma [was born] for the pleasure of lovely-eyed women; blessed is he by whom Love was destroyed!
What shall we say of Rukmiṇī, adored by the world, by whose womb / was borne this one named Pradyumna, a Rāhu devouring the moon of women's virtue?
If that worst of gods should come within our range of vision, / we would cast him once more into the fire of the eye of the Lord engaged in meditation!
By Viṣṇu, who rejoices in himself, this sinner was fathered / and made the darling of sixteen thousand women—what then is our story?"
Having thus reproached Kāma, they praised that best of the twice-born, / by whom both his own conduct and theirs was preserved, O ruler of the earth.
"Blessed is the mother of that man, by whom this best of brahmins, / conqueror of Love, protector of the dharma of others, was brought forth in the world!"
"Fie on us who were conquered by desire and mocked by the king's men, / by whom grievous sin was generated through speech and mind!"
Nārada said: / Thus reflecting, those women, joined in a single mind, / all went each to her own house, enlightened by the brāhmaṇa's words.
Then the king of Kāmpilya, too, having honored that brāhmaṇa / who controlled his senses with garments and ornaments, sent him to his virtuous home.
Then, as time passed, the powerful lord of Kārūṣa / besieged the city of the lord of Kāmpilya with his armies.
A terrible battle occurred between the two; in that battle he was killed; / the entire city was looted, and the warriors were slain everywhere.
Those women, having consumed deadly poison, met their death, / but no expiation was performed by them for that sin.
By that sin, they were all born in the city / of the rākṣasa named Bhīṣaṇa as rākṣasīs of immense bodies, terrifying.
There, all those women of the city were killed by Hanumān / standing on the chariot banner of Arjuna who was protecting the sacrifice.
Again they became those very rākṣasīs in the desert wasteland, / tormented by hunger and thirst, terrifying to behold.
Thus, by that sin committed through speech and mind, / two births were obtained by them mixed with a rākṣasī womb.
By their sin, two cities along with their kings were destroyed; / therefore, one must never pursue another woman's husband.
By women fearing sin, even through speech and mind, O lord— / whether diseased, dull, poor, or deprived of both eyes— / one's own husband should not be abandoned by women desiring a good destination.

This sin generated through mind and speech by devotion to another's beloved has been related by me, / and whatever fruit was obtained by them, that also [has been related] in great detail to you, O Śibi.

From the falling of drops of water of that [Yamunā] upon their bodies, which is seen reaching Indraprastha, sinless, leading to Dvārakā, those women of the city

title: rebhire
text_mt: […] abandoning that fierce nature of a flesh-eater born of longing for another lover in thought and speech, and attaining heaven and the state of a divine woman who brings joy to the gods.
Thus ends the two hundred and sixth chapter, named ‘Description of Dvārakā’, in the Kālindīmāhātmya in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand verses.

title: saptādhikadviśatatamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Saubhari said: / O son of Dharma, hearing these words of the great-souled / Nārada, King Śibi spoke this politely:
Śibi said: / O best of sages, from where did those rākṣasīs / dwelling on the desert road obtain water from that Dvārikā?
Nārada said: / Listen, O king, to the divine, purifying story that destroys sins, / of a brāhmaṇa named Vimala who lived in a valley of the Himavat.
In a valley of the Himavat was a brāhmaṇa named Vimala, / a worshipper of gods, sages, ancestors, and fires, a worshipper of guests,
devoted to worshipping the feet of Hari, knowing the Vedas, Vedāṅgas, and dharma, / whose mind was on the Purāṇas and revelations recounting the virtues of Vāsudeva.
In his old age, by the grace of the disc-wielder, he had a son; / the father then named him Haridatta.
He performed his tonsure and other rites according to rule; / Haridatta took the Vedic metres from the presence of his guru.
Having studied the Vedas according to rule and given the guru's fee, / he renounced, detached, [forsaking] the two stages of life together with their root.
Learning of that deed, his mother, devoted to her son, wept, / bathing her pair of breasts with tears born of separation from her son.
The mother said: / Leaving me, a helpless woman, O father, where have you gone, / and your father who is seized by old age, like a bee [abandoning] reed grass?
In old age you were obtained by me through worship of the feet of the Lord of Śrī; / leaving me, you worshipped his feet for liberation!
Truly I was foolish, child, in that, having worshipped the eternal Hari, / I wished for you, who are transient, for the sake of obtaining happiness!
You are wise, my child, since you yourself worship Viṣṇu for every goal; / having known this world to be impermanent, you too have attained permanence.
What shall I do? Where shall I go? Delusion cuts down my knowledge, / like an axe that violently cuts down the root of a plantain tree yielding good fruit.
Blessed is King Daśaratha, who died from grief over Rāma; / fie on me, who hold onto my life despite separation from my son!
Come, grant me a sight [of you], child, save me! / Speak words filled with the Veda before your father, O ocean of virtues!
Nārada said: / Thus lamenting, O king, his mother fell to the ground, / like the crescent of the moon [falling] from being crushed by Rāhu.
Then the brāhmaṇa sage Vimala came, O best of kings; / seeing her fallen on the ground, he said: 'What is this? What is this?'
'Why has she fallen on the ground with disheveled hair, / garments, and ornaments thrown into disarray? Is Haridatta well?'
All her female companions said to that Vimala, O king: / The companions said: / 'Having studied the Vedas and given the guru's fee,'
'Haridatta, devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa, has renounced the world; / in the grief of separation from him, she has fallen onto the surface of the earth.'
Nārada said: / Hearing their words, the very wise Vimala / comforted his wife with this nectar of speech:

Vimala said: / 'Arise, wife! Listen to the word spoken by me. For what reason do you grieve, fallen down? / Blessed is your son who, having realized this [world] to be perishable, worshipped the sprout-like feet of Hari!'
'You too are blessed, the giver of his birth, whose son has become a partaker of Hari's feet; / he will undoubtedly deliver me, the family, and the men born of our line, O auspicious one!'

'Where is this transient and perishable universe on the one hand, and where is the service of Hari, bestowing the eternal world, on the other? / Reflecting thus, kings such as Bharata worshipped Hari, O virtuous woman, and so indeed did your son!'
'Wife, wealth, house, body, and kinsmen—these bring sorrow in birth after birth / until a wise person, free from all desires, worships the sprout-like feet of Hari.'
Nārada said: / Thus awakened by that wise man, having risen / from the surface of the earth, she spoke to her husband in a plaintive voice.
The wife said: / 'I know all that you have spoken so well, my dear; / [yet] I do not see a bearer of the family's burden, on account of which I suffer greatly.'
'When a son is present, what need is there of a great holy place or the service of Keśava? / If our death should occur right at home, both worlds would be [secured].'
'Effort must surely be made by men to produce a good son, / because sons rescue their ancestors from the ocean of worldly existence.'
'Worship the creator and sustainer of all creatures with the desire for a son, / if you desire a son who will bear the family's burden, O highly wise one.'
Nārada said: / Hearing her words, the brāhmaṇa Vimala replied: / 'Indeed, I am going to Prayāga, the domain of Brahmā, with the desire for a son.'
Having spoken thus, the twice-born departed and went to Haridvāra; / bathing there also according to rule, he then went to Indraprastha.
After some days, O hero, in the evening, [at that place] bestowing all desires, / having bathed and eaten, he slept at night on the bank of the Yamunā.
At midnight, while he slept, Brahmā, the lord of gods, mounted upon a swan, / accompanied by all the holy sites, [came] into the presence of that pure man.
arrived and raised up Vimala, who was longing for a son; / and the best of the gods spoke words of sweet syllables.
Brahmā said: / "I know the desire that resides in your heart; / I am not able to fulfill that, so hear the reason for it.
Once on the peak of Meru all the gods assembled / and, headed by myself and Śiva, praised Mādhava for the accomplishment of their purpose.
Praised with compassion by the gods headed by us, the blessed Hari / was pleased at that time, and Viṣṇu said: 'Choose [a boon]!'
Addressed thus by him, those gods obtained from the husband of Śrī / the boon they desired, and all went to their respective abodes.
It was said by me: 'O lord of the gods, grant me an excellent boon: / May my holy place named Prayāga grant all desires!
May my second holy place situated in Indraprastha / have a hundredfold greater [merit] than that!' The whole event, O sinless one, was [told] to you by me.
Having heard those words of mine, the Blessed Lord then said to me: / “So be it,” and spoke these words again; let my words be heard.
The Blessed One said: / 'In Indra's Khāṇḍava forest is an auspicious holy place named Indraprastha, / on the bank of the Yamunā; those who die there are equal to me.
O Viriñci, my own city of Dvārakā was established there / with a hundred times more qualities than the one that stood on the shore of the ocean in ancient times.
Whatever man transgresses it and resorts to another holy place, / that man does not obtain the fruit of a holy place—what has been said is not false.
A man obtains at Śakratīrtha the religious merit spoken of all holy places; / and the city Dvārakā protects the Māyātīrtha and other holy places.
Whoever, having bathed in other holy places and performed various rites, / comes here, he will certainly obtain the fruit [of those rites] from them.'
Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu vanished; and I too, O chief of the twice-born, / went to my own world situated below Vaikuṇṭha.
Kāśī is remembered as a hundred times [more meritorious] than my holy place Prayāga; / the holy place Nigambodhaka is likewise a hundred times [more meritorious] than Kāśī.
This group of seven holy places is remembered as equal in fruit to that triad. / Whoever goes to the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā without transgressing these three,
to him, O brahmin, I indeed grant what is desired, not otherwise. / Some great sages say that the merit is equal to the seven cities;
they declare Indraprastha to be a hundred times greater than those, such as Ayodhyā. / Having come here, O best of brahmins, to this holy place that yields the fruits of all desires,
indeed named Dvārakā, perform a bath out of desire for a son. / As many holy places as exist within the jar of the egg of Brahmā,
the merit is far greater than those when its hundred names are recited. / This holy place will grant you a son who will bear the burden of the family;
and through your bath Govinda will become pleased in his heart." / Nārada said: Having spoken thus, Brahmā, the god of gods, vanished there.
Vimala too bathed then and offered libations to the gods and others; / that righteous-minded one spoke thus at Dvārakā, dear to Kṛṣṇa:
"Grant me, your devotee, a son who will continue the lineage! Salutation to you!" / When spoken to thus by that brahmin, a divine voice arose at that time.
The divine voice said: / "Your son will be a knower of the truth of dharma and a perpetuator of the lineage, / through the grace of this holy place, the crest-jewel of all holy places.
Go home; do not delay; your bathing has been well performed!" / Nārada said: Hearing that voice, confident in the birth of a son,
he set out, taking water of Dvārakā in his water-pot. / On the road, a brahmin friend of his whose residence was Mount Malaya,
met [him] as he was traveling to his home after visiting holy places on all sides. / To him he recounted his own story consisting of the conversation with Brahmā,
which occurred at the Dvārakā holy place; and having heard it, he too was astonished. / And that righteous-minded one said: "O friend, hear my words!
As many holy places as are established for me in the realm of Bhārata, / that many I wish to perform at the supreme holy place spoken of by you.
Having taken me, show me, O friend, that holy place that grants all desires! / Those are excellent friends on earth who assist their friends;
neither a father, nor a mother, nor even a son is equal to them. / In this world all relatives abandon a destitute man;
but friends do not abandon him, sorrowing through his sorrow. / A friend rescues his friends immersed in the ocean of cyclic existence,
by teaching the path of devotion to Hari, which is a fire to the fuel of rebirth. / Therefore, you are my best friend; render me assistance!"
Show [me] Dvārakā, that best of sacred places, O twice-born one!"

title: aṣṭottaradviśatatamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt:
Nārada said:
Taking that twice-born one with him, Vimala arrived here at Dvārakā.
Then those two wise men bathed, desiring devotion to the Lord of Śrī.
Once again in the sky, O king, there arose a voice deep as thunder.

The voice from the sky said:
"Listen, O tigers among twice-borns! This auspicious sacred place belongs to Hari.
By the grace of this sacred place, you two will attain devotion to Viṣṇu,
by which this world abandons dreadful ignorance and delusion."

Nārada said:
Hearing that incorporeal voice, the two best of twice-borns
said to one another: "This was the grace of Hari!"

Bathing there according to the rule, having obtained supreme devotion to Hari,
they bowed down and departed, speaking thus to each other at that time.

title: yathāvayorhisaṃyogaḥ pathijāto vicārataḥ
text_mt:
just as the union with home, wife, and the like occurs on earth,
so now separation is inevitable, even as we journey on the road.

Likewise is it for wife, sons, and others, who stand in the mouth of Time.
Blessed is that man in the world who, understanding that association

with wife and sons is fleeting, ever takes refuge in and worships the Lord of Śrī."
Nārada said:
[Each said:] "You must remember me; I am a servant taking shelter at your feet.

A message must be sent to me." Having spoken thus, they went each to his own home.
Listen, O king, how by that friend of Vimala
liberation was effected for the demonesses as he walked along the path.
As he journeyed, that brāhmaṇa arrived at a region devoid of water,

where those demonesses, scorched by sins, were afflicted with hunger and thirst.
Then, seeing from afar that best of twice-borns walking along the path

with a water-vessel in his hand, they spoke thus to one another.
The demonesses said:
"A certain traveler is coming, holding a water-pot in his hand.

Our hunger and thirst will be somewhat appeased.
We will devour him, and we will drink the water located in the vessel

in his hand, for we have been afflicted by thirst and hunger for a hundred years!"
Nārada said:
One of them said, "First, after eating his warm liver

and then drinking his blood, I shall regain my life!"
Another said: "O elephant-faced one, how much substance is there in him?

It does not seem enough to drink even for me, who am tiger-faced!"
Another, named Rathacakrā, said: "Hear my words:

I will make an earring, and a girdle out of his entrails!"
Another said: "I, with sixteen of his teeth

blackened on one side, will play in the gambling hall, being skilled in that!"
Having spoken thus to one another, they all rushed toward that twice-born one,

with open mouths, lolling tongues, and huge arms flashing like lightning.
Seeing them approaching, the brāhmaṇa, overwhelmed with fear,

cast around himself the protection prescribed in the Vedas, O king.
Having arrived, those demonesses of terrible prowess stood at a distance,

repelled by his splendor and his mantras, O ruler of men.
And they said: "Who are you here? From where have you arrived? Tell us that!

From the sight of you our minds attain tranquility.
Will not the fruit [of liberation] arise for us from touching your feet, O vipra?
Therefore, place your own lotus-feet upon our heads!"

Nārada said:
Hearing their speech, the son of Haridatta spoke.
The twice-born said:
"Having visited holy places, I, a brāhmaṇa, have arrived.

Now I am going to Puṣkara. What is desired by you?
Ask for that, and if I am capable of giving it, I will give it then."

title: yeṣutīrtheṣuvipreṃdratvayāsnātaṃvadasvanaḥ
text_mt:
Deliver us by all those merits from this wretched birth,
and completely from thirst and hunger, which cause terrible suffering!"

Then I reached the holy place named Prabhāsa, situated on the seashore;
from there, I bathed at the supremely purifying Setubandha.

From there I came to most holy Kiṣkindhā,
where Vālin, the lord of the monkey troops, was slain by Rāma.

From there I came to the hermitage on the Sarasvatī situated on the bank of the Narmadā,
where Sarasvatī resides, served by all.

Then, having bowed to that confluence in the south, I entered;
there I saw the two cities, Śivakāñcī and Viṣṇukāñcī,

through death in which a creature becomes Śiva or Viṣṇu.
Then I reached Utkala, where Hari the Supreme Lord resides,

bestowing the four aims of life, the very wish of his devotees.
Having worshipped him according to rule and eaten what was offered,

which was his own prasāda, [I went to] the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
Having gratified the gods, sages, and ancestors there according to the rule,

I came to where the Gaṅgā becomes hundred-mouthed.
Then, having arrived at Gayā and offered funeral cakes according to the rule

to the ancestors, worshipped with tulasī, flowers, sandalwood, and water,
I came to the Sarayū in Kośala, whose waters, carried by the breeze like a helmsman,

purify all people by their touch.
There is the sacred place named Gopratāra, difficult even for the gods to attain;

there, O roamers of the night, bathing and other rites were performed by me.
Then I reached Kāśī, the capital of Umā's husband.

Bowing to Lord Viśveśvara and to Bindumādhava,
I bathed with devotion at Maṇikarṇikā and Jñānavāpī.

Dwelling there for three nights, I came again to Prayāga,
where Prajāpati himself [abides], on the fourteenth day of the bright half of Pauṣa.

Having bathed at daybreak in the single month of Māgha,
I arrived again from there at Naimiṣa on the bank of the Gomatī,

where all the sacred places dwell by their own supernatural power.
Then I reached Mathurā, where there is the sacred place named Viśrānti,

and near it the supreme holy place named Asikuṇḍa,
and the sacred places Kṛṣṇagaṅgā, Dhruvatīrtha, Akrūratīrtha, Keśitīrtha, and Kālīyatīrtha.

There is the Yamunā, highly auspicious, granting all desired objects.
On both of her banks are twelve forests, shining with beauty,

O roamers of the sky, fulfilling all purposes.
Having bathed and drunk in them, a man is not born again.

Then I came to holy and supreme Hastināpura,
where the Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, born from the lotus-foot of the Lord of Śrī, [flows].

Then, having arrived at the abode of Nārāyaṇa situated in the land of the Himavat
and having seen Mādhava, I came to Kedāra.

Having worshipped the Lord of the Universe there and drunk the water of the Haṃsodaka,
I came again to highly sacred Haridvāra on the bank of the Jāhnavī.

Bathing there and gratifying the ancestors, gods, and sages,
I came to Kurukṣetra, where the eastward-flowing Sarasvatī lies.

There too, with my senses restrained, I performed all rites.
And having worshipped the lotus-foot of the Lord of Śrī, toward Puṣkara

I departed. On the way, however, my friend named Vimala,
going home from the holy place Indraprastha, met me.
I was taken back by that twice-born man, O demonesses, / to that holy ford, Śakraprastha, which grants all aims,
where holy Dvārakā is situated, fashioned by Viṣṇu himself. / There Viṣṇu was directly perceived by his voice, not by form.
There he and I bathed together to attain devotion to Viṣṇu; / that devotion was granted to me and to him by Viṣṇu appearing in the form of Kṛṣṇa.
Having heard the voice of Hari there, though no form was seen, / devotion was obtained from that place; hence I am going toward Puṣkara.
This holy water held in my water-pot belongs to that lord of holy places / called Dvārakā, O night-roaming women, I tell you.
Since you asked me, this is what I have related to you. / Seeing this wretched condition of yours, compassion arises in my heart.
Speak: what shall I do today? For I am at your disposal. / May knowledge come to you! Saying this, he sprinkled them with the water.
Touched by that water, having remembered all their actions / from past births, they discarded their dreadful demon body.
Having attained a divine body and mounted the seven celestial chariots that arrived, / becoming apsarases, they bowed to the twice-born man.
And they said: 'O best of the twice-born, through contact with the water of Dvārakā, / we have been released from the state of demons and are going to the abode of the gods.
O twice-born, this Dvārakā situated within Indraprastha— / there is no other holy place in the world superior to it that grants all aims.'
Nārada said: / Having spoken thus, O king, mounted on celestial chariots, / they went toward the eastern quarter, permitted by that twice-born man.
Hearing this glorification of Dvārakā situated on the bank of the Yamunā, / a man is freed from sins, O king.
Whatever fruit arises from feeding a hundred brāhmaṇas versed in the Veda / according to their desires, that arises from hearing this glorification.
Just as there is sensual happiness in proper worship of Govinda, / so it is from hearing the glorification of this Dvārakā, O king.
Whatever fruit is attained from giving twenty palas of gold during an eclipse of the sun or moon, / that is obtained by one hearing her glorification.
Hearing of the obtaining of a son by Vimala, a son is attained in this world; / hearing of the attainment of devotion by his friend, supreme devotion is attained.
Whoever full of faith hears of the liberation of the demonesses, / he goes, just like them, to the supreme abode of the gods in a celestial chariot.

O best of kings, the glory of Dvārakā, served by the people of the three worlds / and situated at Śakratīrtha, has been described to you; / what other exceedingly holy matter should I relate before you? / Speak, for no delay should be made regarding one's own welfare.

title: navadhikadviśatatamo'dhyāyaḥ
text_mt: Yudhiṣṭhira said: / O Saubhari, the glorification of which holy place situated at Śakratīrtha / did the sage Nārada describe to Śibi?
A desire to hear arises in me regarding this, O best of sages; / recount to me, who am bowed, the holy dialogue between Śibi and Nārada.
Saubhari said: / O Dharmarāja, King Śibi, having heard the glorification of Dvārakā / described by Nārada, asked him with reverence.
Śibi said: / O son of Brahmā, best of gods, the excellent and wondrous glorification / of Dvārakā situated on the bank of Indraprastha has been heard by me.
If there is any purifying account regarding Ayodhyā, O sage, / recount that to me, who am thirsty for the nectar of your speech.
Nārada said: / In this regard there is a holy story that destroys great sins, / concerning an anciently engaged barber and a twice-born man named Mukunda.
The barber was a slayer of a brāhmaṇa, O king, and the twice-born man met an untimely death; / yet through the grace of Kośalā, both went to the heavenly realm.
That city was settled on the bank of the Candrabhāgā river; / there lived a sinful and despicable barber named Caṇḍaka.
A committer of sin, he was a stealer of others' wealth by theft; / a murderer with weapons, nooses, and the like, and a plunderer of wayfarers.
Always addicted to gambling and liquor, his senses lecherous after other men's wives, / breaking down the wall of a temple, he was a seller of bricks and stones.
Near his residence lived a brāhmaṇa endowed with fortune, / knower of Vedic rituals, named Mukunda, O king.
Once, having embraced his young wife, / he fell asleep fearlessly at night, his limbs slack from the exhaustion of lovemaking.
Then, in the dead of night, Caṇḍaka entered that dwelling / of Mukunda in order to steal whatever items such as ornaments were in the mansion.
Taking whatever was outside the royal tent, he went to his house, / and then entered that brāhmaṇa's house again.
Desiring to rip open the door, he made a great effort, / but, blocked by an iron mechanism, he was unable to open it.
Then he climbed up and entered the house of that brāhmaṇa; / having entered that house, cruel, holding a dagger in his hand,
that most wicked barber, engaged in thievery, reached the upper story; / there he saw the married couple deeply asleep, overcome with lovemaking.
And he went to their side with a desire to take the golden ornaments; / having taken many ornaments lying on one side of the bed,
that barber stretched out his hand to seize [the rest] from his body. / At the thief's touch, the brāhmaṇa awoke, stricken with fear.
He said nothing; closing his eyes, he remained right there. / When that sinful thief, having taken the ornaments from the body,
moved away, he was seized with both arms by that twice-born man, / who, coming from behind, could not bear the loss of his wealth.
Then by that thief, O king, the twice-born man was struck with a dagger; / with the middle of his belly torn open, he cried out: 'Father! Mother!'
Saying 'What is this? What is this?', people came to his side; / they saw him with his intestines fallen out and his body smeared with blood.
And they asked: 'Mukunda, by whom has such a deed been done?' / He too, with great difficulty, spoke this to his kinsmen:
Mukunda said: / 'This is the ripening of deeds previously accumulated by myself alone; / no one is the giver of happiness or sorrow to any embodied being.
Righteousness and unrighteousness performed in the past are the sole roots of them.' / Nārada said: / Having spoken thus, deeply tormented by immense pain,
he abandoned his life-breaths, O king, while his friends were looking on. / Then, O king, his mother, a virtuous twice-born woman, lamented,
placing on her lap his head adorned with earrings. / The mother said: / 'Alas, I am ruined by you reaching your final state, my child,
as the beauty of day [is lost] by the sun sinking down the western mountain! / That body of yours, O wise one, which was worthy of being anointed with sandalwood paste,
is now covered with dust, plunging me into an ocean of anguish and grief!

That practice of chewing betel which was observed by you, / is certainly being imitated now mixed with an outpouring of blood! / Those eyes of yours that previously conquered the splendor of the lotus,
have now become as if enveloped by a mass of darkness! / Arise, arise, child! Teach your pupils!
Properly honor the guest who has arrived at the end of the Vaiśvadeva rite! / Your companions standing at the door are calling you; go to them!'

"Give to them what is to be given, and take what is to be taken.
Alas, alas! Give me an answer; I fall at your feet!

Otherwise, I shall give up my life right by your side!"
Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, the mother of that Mukunda then fainted.

His wife, placing his head upon her lap, lamented.
The wife said:
